5.1.1
Need for Data Understanding Techniques. Real-world data often comes in large volumes and
complexity, which can make it difficult to understand and analyze. There are three main reasons
why data understanding techniques are crucial. Firstly, comprehending a large number of raw
data samples can be challenging for humans. To make it more manageable, we need to summarize
the data and present it in a more concise and accessible way. Secondly, real-world data is often
high-dimensional, while human perception is limited to two-or-three-dimensional space. Therefore,
visualizing data in a lower-dimensional space is essential for understanding the data. Finally, it
is crucial for organizations and stakeholders to understand the value of their data assets and the
contribution of each data sample to the performance.
5.1.2
Data Visualization. Human beings are visual animals, and as such, we have a natural tendency
to process and retain information presented in a pictorial and graphical format. Data visualization
aims to leverage this innate human trait to help us better understand complex data. In what follows,
we will discuss three relevant research topics: visual summarization, clustering for visualization,
and visualization recommendation.
Visual summarization. Summarizing the raw data as a set of graphical diagrams can assist humans
in gaining insights through a condensed interface. Despite its wide application, generating a faithful
yet user-friendly summarization diagram is a non-trivial task. For example, it is hard to select the
right visualization format. Radial charts (e.g., star glyphs and rose charts) and linear charts (e.g., line
charts and bar charts) are two common formats for visualization. However, it is controversial which
format is better. Although empirical evidence suggests that linear charts are superior to radial
charts for many analytical tasks [37], radial charts are often more natural and memorable [33].
In some cases, it is acceptable to compromise on the faithfulness of data representation in favor
of enhanced memorability or space efficiency [37, 238]. For readers who are interested, [61] and
[78] provide a comprehensive taxonomy of visualization formats. Although automated scripts can
generate plots, the process of visual summarization often demands minimal human participation to
select the most appropriate visualization formats.
Clustering for visualization. Real-world data can be high-dimensional and with complex manifold
structures. As such, dimensionality reduction techniques (mentioned in Section 3.4) are often
applied to visualize data in a two-or-three-dimensional space. Furthermore, automated clustering
methods [72] are frequently combined with dimensionality reduction techniques to organize data
points in a grouped, categorized, and often color-coded fashion, facilitating human comprehension
and insightful analysis of the data.
Visualization recommendation. Building upon various visualization formats, there has been a
surge of interest in visualization recommendation, which involves suggesting the most suitable
visualization formats for a particular user. Programmatic automation approaches rank visualization
candidates based on predefined rules composed of human perceptual metrics such as data type,

5.1.3
Data Valuation. The objective of data valuation is to understand how each data point con-
tributes to the final performance. Such information not only provides valuable insights to stakehold-
ers but is also useful in buying or selling data points in the data market and credit attribution [83].
To accomplish this, researchers estimate the Shapley value of the data points, which assigns weights
to each data point based on its contribution [3, 84]. A subsequent study has enhanced the robustness
of this estimation across multiple datasets and models [83]. Since calculating the exact Shapley
value can be computationally expensive, especially when dealing with a large number of data
points, the above methods all adopt learning-based algorithms for efficient estimation.
5.1.4
Challenges. There are two major challenges. Firstly, the most effective data visualization
formats and algorithms (e.g., clustering algorithms) are often specific to the domain and influenced
by human behavior, making it difficult to select the best option. This selection process often
requires human input. Determining how to best interact with humans adds an additional complexity.
Secondly, developing efficient data valuation algorithms is challenging, since estimating the Shapley
value can be computationally expensive, especially as data sizes continue to grow. Additionally,
the Shapley value may only offer a limited perspective on data value, as there are many other
important factors beyond model performance, such as the problems that can be addressed through
training a model on the data.

5.2
Data Quality Assurance
To ensure a reliable data supply, it is essential to maintain data quality. We will discuss why quality
assurance is necessary, the key tasks involved in maintaining data quality (quality assessment and
improvement), and the challenges.
5.2.1
Need for Data Quality Assurance. In real-world scenarios, data and the corresponding in-
frastructure for data processing are subject to frequent and continuous updates. As a result, it
is important not only to create high-quality training or inference data once but also to maintain
their excellence in a dynamic environment. Ensuring data quality in such a dynamic environment
involves two aspects. Firstly, continuous monitoring of data quality is necessary. Real-world data in
practical applications can be complex, and it may contain various anomalous data points that do not
align with our intended outcomes. As a result, it is crucial to establish quantitative measurements
that can evaluate data quality. Secondly, if a model is affected by low-quality data, it is important to
implement quality improvement strategies to enhance data quality, which will also lead to improved
model performance.
5.2.2
Quality Assessment. Quality assessment develops evaluation metrics to measure the quality of
data and detect potential flaws and risks. These metrics can be broadly categorized as either objective
or subjective assessments [18, 181, 195, 257]. Although objective and subjective assessments may
require different degrees of human participation, both of them are used in each paper we surveyed.
Thus, we tag each paper with more than one degree of human participation in Table 4. We will
discuss these two types of assessments in general and provide some representative examples of
each.
Objective assessments directly measure data quality using inherent data attributes that are
independent of specific applications. Examples of such metrics include accuracy, timeliness, con-
sistency, and completeness. Accuracy refers to the correctness of obtained data, i.e., whether the
obtained data values align with those stored in the database. Timeliness assesses whether the
data is up-to-date. Consistency refers to the violation of semantic rules defined over a set of data
items. Completeness measures the percentage of values that are not null. All of these metrics can
be collected directly from the data, requiring only minimal human participation to specify the
calculation formula.
Subjective assessments evaluate data quality from a human perspective, often specific to the
application and requiring external analysis from experts. Metrics like trustworthiness, understand-
ability, and accessibility are often assessed through user studies and questionnaires. Trustworthiness
measures the accuracy of information provided by the data source. Understandability measures
the ease with which users can comprehend collected data, while accessibility measures users’
ability to access the data. Although subjective assessments may not directly benefit model training,
they can facilitate easier collaboration within an organization and provide long-term benefits.
Collecting these metrics typically requires full human participation since they are often based on
questionnaires.
5.2.3
Quality Improvement. Quality improvement involves developing strategies to enhance the
quality of data at various stages of a data pipeline. Initially, programmatic automation methods are
used to enforce quality constraints, including integrity constraints [17], denial constraints [49], and
conditional functional dependencies [29] between columns. More recently, machine learning-based
automation approaches have been developed to improve data quality. For instance, in [19], a data
validation module trains a machine learning model on a training set with expected data schema and
generalizes it to identify potential problems in unseen scenarios. Furthermore, pipeline automation

Apart from automation, collaborative approaches have been developed to encourage expert

annotations or submissions.
5.2.4
Challenges. Ensuring data quality poses two main challenges. Firstly, selecting the most
suitable assessment metric is not a straightforward task and heavily relies on domain knowledge. A
single metric may not always be adequate in a constantly evolving environment. Secondly, quality
improvement is a vital yet laborious process that necessitates careful consideration. Although
automation is crucial in ensuring sustainable data quality, human involvement may also be necessary
to ensure that the data quality meets human expectations. Therefore, data assessment metrics and
data improvement strategies must be thoughtfully designed.
5.3
Data Storage & Retrieval
Data storage and retrieval systems play an indispensable role in providing the necessary data to
build AI systems. To expedite the process of data acquisition, various efficient strategies have been
proposed. In the following discussion, we elaborate on the importance of efficient data storage
and retrieval, review some representative acceleration methods for resource allocation and query
acceleration, and discuss the challenges associated with them.
5.3.1
Need for Efficient Data Storage & Retrieval. As the amount of data being generated continues
to grow exponentially, having a robust and scalable data administration system that can efficiently
handle the large data volume and velocity is becoming increasingly critical to support the training
of AI models. This need encompasses two aspects. Firstly, data administration systems, such as
Hadoop [77] and Spark [266], often need to store and merge data from various sources, requiring
careful management of memory and computational resources. Secondly, it is crucial to design
querying strategies that enable fast data acquisition to ensure timely and accurate processing of
the data.
5.3.2
Resource Allocation. Resource allocation aims to estimate and balance the cost of operations
within a data administration system. Two key efficiency metrics in data administration systems are
throughput, which refers to how quickly new data can be collected, and latency, which measures
how quickly the system can respond to a request. To optimize these metrics, various parameter-
tuning techniques have been proposed, including controlling database configuration settings (e.g.,
buffer pool size) and runtime operations (e.g., percentage of CPU usage and multi-programming
level) [69]. Early tuning methods rely on rules that are based on intuition, experience, data domain
knowledge, and industry best practices from sources such as Apache [6] and Cloudera [152]. For
instance, Hadoop guidelines [252] suggest that the number of reduced tasks should be set to
approximately 0.95 or 1.75 times the number of reduced slots available in the cluster to ensure
system tolerance for re-executing failed or slow tasks.
Various learning-based strategies have been developed for resource allocation in data processing
systems. For instance, Starfish [100] proposes a profile-predict-optimize approach that generates

job profiles with dataflow and cost statistics, which are then used to predict virtual job profiles for
task scheduling. More recently, machine learning approaches such as OtterTune [233] have been
developed to automatically select the most important parameters, map workloads, and recommend
parameters to improve latency and throughput. These learning-based automation strategies can
adaptively balance system resources without assuming any internal system information.
5.3.3
Query Acceleration. Another research direction is efficient data retrieval, which can be
achieved through efficient index selection and query rewriting strategies.
Query index selection. The objective of index selection is to minimize the number of disk accesses
needed during query processing. To achieve this, programmatic automation strategies create an
indexing scheme with indexable columns and record query execution costs [224]. Then, they apply
either a greedy algorithm [39] or dynamic programming [232] to select the indexing strategy.
To enable a more adaptive and flexible querying strategy, learning-based automation strategies
collect indexing data from human experts and train machine learning models to predict the proper
indexing strategies [179], or search for the optimal strategies using reinforcement learning [196].
Query rewriting. In parallel, query rewriting aims to reduce the workload by identifying repeated
sub-queries from input queries. Rule-based strategies [12, 40] rewrite queries with pre-defined
rules, such as DBridge [40], which constructs a dependency graph to model the data flow and
iteratively applies transformation rules. Learning-based approaches use supervised learning [96]
or reinforcement learning [294] to predict rewriting rules given an input query.
5.3.4
Challenges. Existing data storage and retrieval methods typically focus on optimizing specific
parts of the system, such as resource allocation and query acceleration we mentioned. However,
the real data administration system as a whole can be complex since it needs to process a vast
amount of data in various formats and structures, making end-to-end optimization a challenging
task. Additionally, apart from efficiency, data storage and retrieval require consideration of several
other crucial and challenging aspects, such as data access control and system maintenance.

7
DISCUSSION AND FUTURE DIRECTION
What is the current stage of data-centric AI research, and what are the potential future directions?
This section provides a top-level discussion of data-centric AI and presents some of the open
problems that we have identified, aiming to motivate future exploration in this field. We start by
trying to answer the research questions posed at the beginning:
• RQ1: What are the necessary tasks to make AI data-centric? Data-centric AI encompasses a
range of tasks that involve developing training data, inference data, and maintaining data.
These tasks include but are not limited to 1) cleaning, labeling, preparing, reducing, and
augmenting the training data, 2) generating in-distribution and out-of-distribution data for
evaluation, or tuning prompts to achieve desired outcomes, and 3) constructing efficient
infrastructures for understanding, organizing, and debugging data.
• RQ2: Why is automation significant for developing and maintaining data? Given the availability
of an increasing amount of data at an unprecedented rate, it is imperative to develop automated
algorithms to streamline the process of data development and maintenance. Based on the
papers surveyed in Tables 2, 3, and 4, automated algorithms have been developed for all
sub-goals. These automation algorithms span different automation levels, from programmatic
automation to learning-based automation, to pipeline automation.
• RQ3: In which cases and why is human participation essential in data-centric AI? Human
participation is necessary for many data-centric AI tasks, such as the majority of data labeling
tasks (Table 2) and several tasks in inference data development (Table 3). Notably, different
methods may require varying degrees of human participation, ranging from full involvement
to providing minimal inputs. Human participation is crucial in many scenarios because it is
often the only way to ensure that the behavior of AI systems aligns with human intentions.
• RQ4: What is the current progress of data-centric AI? Although data-centric AI is a relatively
new concept, considerable progress has already been made in many relevant tasks, the major-
ity of which were viewed as preprocessing steps in the model-centric paradigm. Meanwhile,
many new tasks have recently emerged, and research on them is still ongoing. In Section 6,
our meta-analysis on benchmark papers reveals that progress has been made across different
domains, with the majority of the benchmarks coming from the AI domain. Among the
three general data-centric AI goals, training data development has received relatively more
research attention. For data modality, tabular and image data have been the primary focus.
As research papers on data-centric AI are growing exponentially [269], we could witness
even more progress in this field in the future.
By attempting to address these questions, our survey delves into a variety of tasks and their needs
and challenges, yielding a more concrete picture of the scope and progress of data-centric AI.
However, although we have endeavored to broadly and comprehensively cover various tasks and
techniques, it is impossible to include every aspect of data-centric AI. In the following, we connect
data-centric AI with two other popular research topics in AI:
• Foundation models. A foundation model is a large model that is trained on massive amounts of
unlabeled data and can be adapted to various tasks, such as large language models [34, 172],
and Stable Diffusion [194]. As models become sufficiently powerful, it becomes feasible
to perform many data-centric AI tasks with models, such as data labeling [172], and data
augmentation [263]. Consequently, the recent trend of foundation models has the potential to
fundamentally alter our understanding of data. Unlike the conventional approach of storing
raw data values in datasets, the model itself can be a form of data (or a “container” of raw data)
since the model can convey information (see the definition of data in Section 2.1). Foundation

models blur the boundary between data and model, but their training still heavily relies on
large and high-quality datasets.
• Reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning is a research field that trains intelligent
agents to optimize rewards without any initial data [131, 164, 270–272, 275, 276, 279, 281].
It is a unique learning paradigm that alternates between generating data with the model
and training the model with self-generated data. Like foundation models, the advancement
of reinforcement learning could also possibly blur the boundary between data and model.
Furthermore, reinforcement learning has already been widely adopted in several data-centric
AI sub-goals, such as data labeling [48, 66, 274], data preparation [122], data reduction [148],
and data augmentation [56, 273]. The reason could be attributed to its goal-oriented nature,
which is well-suited for automation.
Upon examining the connections to these two rapidly evolving research fields, we hypothesize
that data-centric AI and model-centric AI could become even more intertwined in the development
of AI systems. Looking forward, we present some potential future directions we have identified in
data-centric AI:
• Cross-task automation. While there has been significant progress in automating various
individual data-centric AI tasks, joint automation across multiple tasks remains largely
unexplored. Although pipeline search methods [76, 97, 132, 280] have emerged, they are
limited only to training data development. From a broad data-centric AI perspective, it would
be desirable to have a unified framework for jointly automating tasks aimed at different goals,
ranging from training data development to inference data development and data maintenance.
• Data-model co-design. Although data-centric AI advocates for shifting the focus to data, it does
not necessarily imply that the model has to remain unchanged. The optimal data strategies
may differ when using different models, and vice versa. Furthermore, as discussed above,
the boundary between data and model could potentially become increasingly blurred with
the advancement of foundation models and reinforcement learning. Consequently, future
progress in AI could arise from co-designing data and models, and the co-evolution of data
and models could pave the way toward more powerful AI systems.
• Debiasing data. In many high-stakes applications, AI systems have recently been found
to exhibit discriminatory behavior towards certain groups of people, sparking significant
concerns about fairness [50, 65, 112, 113, 157, 240]. These biases often originate from im-
balanced distributions of sensitive variables in the data. From a data-centric perspective,
more research efforts are needed to debias data, including but limited to mitigating biases in
training data, systematic methodologies to construct evaluation data to expose unfairness
issues of unfairness, and continuously maintaining fair data in a dynamic environment.
• Tackling data in various modalities. Based on the benchmark analysis presented in Section 6,
most research efforts have been directed toward tabular and image data. However, other data
modalities that are comparably important but less studied in data-centric AI pose significant
challenges. For instance, time-series data [92, 141, 277] exhibit complex temporal correlations,
while graph data [134, 147, 226, 290–293] has intricate data dependencies. Therefore, more
research on how to engineer data for these modalities is required. Furthermore, developing
data-centric AI solutions that can simultaneously address multiple data modalities is an
intriguing avenue for future exploration.
• Data benchmarks development. The advancement of model-centric AI has been facilitated by
benchmarks in advancing model designs. Whereas data-centric AI requires more attention to
benchmarking. As discussed in Section 6, existing benchmarks for data-centric AI typically
only focus on specific tasks. Constructing a unified benchmark to evaluate overall data quality

CONCLUSION
This survey focuses on data-centric AI, an emerging and important research field in AI. We motivated
the need for data-centric AI by showing how carefully designing and maintaining data can make
AI solutions more desirable across academia and industry. Next, we provided a background of
data-centric AI, which includes its definition and a goal-driven taxonomy. Then, guided by the
research questions posed, we reviewed various data-centric AI techniques for different purposes
from the perspectives of automation and collaboration. Furthermore, we collected data benchmarks
from different domains and analyzed them at a meta-level. Lastly, we discussed data-centric AI
from a global view and shared our perspectives on the blurred boundaries between data and model.
We also presented potential future directions for this field. To conclude in one line, we believe that
data will play an increasingly important role in building AI systems. At the same time, there are
still numerous challenges that need to be addressed. We hope our survey could inspire collaborative
initiatives in our community to push forward this field.

Compressible Tasks in Green Data Centers
as Grid-Forming Support Assets
Anna Vandi
Université Côte d’Azur, CNRS, I3S
Sophia-Antipolis, France
Ramon Aparicio-Pardo
Université Côte d’Azur, CNRS, I3S
Sophia-Antipolis, France
Guillaume Urvoy-Keller
Université Côte d’Azur, CNRS, I3S
Sophia-Antipolis, France
Abstract—Renewable microgrids can help data centers cope
with the increasing demand for cloud-based services, but they pay
the price of the double uncertainty of workload and renewable
resource availability. The mismatch between demand and renew-
able supply prevents microgrid-based data centers from achieving
full autonomy, requiring connection to the main grid. However,
while imports from the main grid could increase environmental
impact, the massive export of excess renewables, when injected
into the grid, can cause serious instability in the system. This
work addresses both issues using compressible tasks, whose
concave utility functions allow for the adaptation to the available
resources, reducing or increasing the task size with negligible
impact on the quality provided to the user. By absorbing surplus
renewable energy, they help maintain frequency stability in the
main grid, thereby supporting grid-forming operations. We cast
this problem as an optimization problem that dynamically adapts
the task size based on renewable availability. We devised Online-
REATA, an online heuristic able to manage tasks arrivals on the
fly. Tested in a live video transcoding case study and compared
to a solution without task compression, Online-REATA achieves
the same average QoE and self-sufficiency, as well as higher
self-consumption, while reducing storage requirements by up to
35.3%.
Index Terms—green data center; sustainability; grid-forming.
I. INTRODUCTION
In recent years, increasing attention is devoted to the
substantial rise in Data Centers (DCs) energy consumption
resulting from the expanding demand for cloud-based services
[1]. This expansion is expected to continue in the coming
years, amplifying the urgency of identifying sustainable energy
solutions [2], [3]. Green Data Centers (GDCs) with microgrids
for on-site renewable production are an effective response,
aiming for self-sufficiency and reduced dependence on the
main grid. However, they need to address the mismatch
between energy demand and production, due to the inherent
intermittency of renewable energy.
On one hand, GDCs often have to import energy from
the main grid (semi-autonomous green data centers), typically
with a carbon intensity that is country-dependent and rarely
fully renewable. On the other hand, in case of renewable
energy surplus, data centers connected to the main grid often
send extra renewable energy back to the grid, affecting its
stability. This is because variable renewable generation from
This work has been supported by the UCA JEDI (ANR-15-IDEX-01) and
EUR DS4H (ANR-17-EURE-004) projects, and by the France 2030 program
under grant agreements No. ANR-23-PECL-0003.
inverter-based resources (IBRs), lacking the inertia of con-
ventional rotating machines operating at
50 Hz, can cause
frequency deviations that threaten grid stability and potentially
trigger cascading failures and blackouts [4].
To mitigate these effects, modern power systems increas-
ingly rely on grid-forming control, which refers to the ca-
pability of enforcing voltage and frequency in the main
grid [5]. However, frequency stability remains challenging in
renewable-rich grids due to fast and unpredictable power vari-
ations [6]. In this context, it becomes necessary to enhance the
autonomy of data centers from the main grid by minimizing
energy imports and exports. Two metrics are generally used
to capture the two aspects: (i) the Self-Sufficiency Rate (SSR),
which measures the share of demand covered by renewable en-
ergy, indicating the system’s capacity to operate independently,
and (ii) the Self-Consumption Rate (SCR), which measures
the share of renewables absorbed locally, showing how much
renewable energy the system can use. We consider SSR and
SCR as defined in reference [7], which counts the energy
stored in the battery as part of the renewable supply.
In this work, we propose to support grid-forming control
by adapting workloads to renewable availability through
compressible tasks, whose size can be flexibly adjusted to
absorb renewable fluctuations. Compressible tasks [8], [9]
are computational jobs where the utility function is concave:
compressing them (i.e., reducing their length, and resource
usage) slightly degrades their utility, while increasing them
enables absorbing surplus energy that would otherwise desta-
bilize the grid. Then, our main contributions can be listed as:
1) We model compressible task allocation within green data
centers as an offline optimization problem. We then de-
velop an online heuristic algorithm that jointly addresses
renewable surplus and shortage by leveraging compress-
ible tasks as grid-forming-supportive loads, capable of
enhancing frequency stability.
2) We conduct a case study on live video streaming,
adjusting the transcoding task size to reduce interac-
tion between the microgrid and the main grid. Our
results demonstrate that our proposal can increase self-
consumption and self-sufficiency while reducing battery
size.
The paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the
related work, Section III presents the model, Section IV

introduces the case study, Section V reports the evaluation
and results. Section VI summarizes our conclusion.
II. RELATED WORK
The uncertain nature of renewable energy production can
result in deficits and surpluses [7], which can be compensated
for by importing and exporting energy to and from the main
grid, respectively. Imports occur in data centers equipped
with renewable energy systems but also connected to the
main grid, importing energy whenever renewable production
is insufficient. Scientific literature largely focuses on reducing
grid imports to lower carbon emissions [10], while the issue
of exports remains less explored. When there is a surplus of
renewable energy generated, this energy needs to be exported
to the main grid. However, the exported energy derived from
inverter-based resources (IBRs) including renewable energy
generators (wind, solar) and batteries, can destabilize the grid.
Unlike conventional synchronous generators, IBRs lack inertia
and provide limited short-circuit current, making frequency de-
viations more likely and potentially leading to cascading out-
ages [4]. Reference [7] proposed focusing on self-consumption
and peak shaving to reduce energy exports and imports, yet
presenting these two objectives as mutually exclusive. In our
proposal, we argue that the real objective should be to
reduce overall interaction with the main grid, reducing
dependence during imports and alleviating stability issues
during exports.
An approach that can jointly mitigate both shortages and
surpluses is the usage of an Energy Storage System (ESS). In
[3], the authors compare a grid-dependent system with differ-
ent autonomous DC configurations, showing that combining
a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) with a Hydrogen
Energy Storage System (HESS) offers the best performance
toward full autonomy. Full autonomy remains cost-prohibitive
compared to European energy prices. The leap from 95%
to 100% autonomy requires a disproportionate infrastructure
increase (five times the 0-95% requirement), making it eco-
nomically and environmentally unsustainable [11]. Moreover,
the environmental impact of battery production reduces the
benefits, suggesting hybrid solutions as a more realistic alter-
native. In this work, we show that compressible tasks can
lower the required battery size, while supporting grid-
forming by reducing grid interactions.
Previous studies have proposed shifting the execution of
tasks over time or space to match renewable availabil-
ity—either delaying tasks or migrating them across data
centers [10]–[12]. However, both approaches present major
drawbacks. Spatial shifting increases the carbon footprint due
to VM migration energy costs, especially when network power
isn’t green, and its efficacy is limited by latency constraints,
bandwidth, and destination resource availability [12]. More-
over, spatial distribution causes loss of global system knowl-
edge and communication overhead [10]. Temporal shifting
requires extra server capacity, leading to higher embedded
carbon [11]. Finally, combining both strategies may increase
total energy use, because more servers must stay powered on
for longer periods [12]. In this work, rather than shifting
demand in time or space, our approach adjusts the
duration (size) of workloads to better match available
generation from the local microgrid.
The closest related study is [10], which explores quality
degradation to reduce grid imports in distributed DCs (some
are grid-connected, other are autonomous and equipped with
Photovoltaic (PV) and/or batteries). It proposes load nego-
tiation, consolidation, and resolution switching to a lower
video quality under resource scarcity. These three strategies
combined yield a +7.83% SCR increase and 35.7% footprint
reduction. In contrast to our work, authors in [10] do not
provide a quantification of the degradation, neither they
envisage quality enhancements to manage the surplus.
Finally, the authors of [10] address excess generation in
reference [12], by modeling interconnected DCs that exchange
surplus energy through the main grid (imports from one can
be offset by simultaneous exports from another). In contrast
to us, this mitigates the issue only economically, without
resolving the physical limitations of large renewable injec-
tions into the grid.
Summing up, existing approaches mainly address imports
or exports separately, without exploring the potential of lever-
aging compressible tasks to jointly mitigate both issues.

IV. CASE STUDY
In this section we describe our case study, which corre-
sponds to a grid-connected data center equipped with a hybrid
energy system, including a microgrid with solar panels and
wind turbines. The data center performs live video transcoding
operations, an example of compressible tasks. A Lithium-
Ion (LI) battery, well suited for cloud applications [3], is
integrated into the system and charged exclusively when
excess renewable energy is available, until its capacity is fully
reached. Consequently, power imports can be supplied either
by the battery or by the main grid, with the battery being
prioritized for both import and export operations. A converter
regulates transfers between AC and DC components [2] (see
Fig. 1).
The data center receives video streams from live broadcast
channels and prepare them for the Content Distribution Net-
work (CDN), which then delivers the transcoded streams to
edge servers serving the end-users [14]. In accordance with
guidelines [15], the broadcasting server originally encodes
video streams at 1080p and 8000 kbps. We will refer to
this resolution-bitrate (1080p, 8000 kbps) pair as the original
encoding profile. This profile may not be suitable for users
with low-resolution devices or slow connections; therefore,
videos are transcoded into 360p and 720p to ensure playback
on these devices. In this case study, we define a task as
the request to live-transcode a channel’s video stream at one
of these two resolutions. Since different transcoding profiles
(resolution-bitrate) require different CPU usage and energy
resources (higher bitrates require more resources), renewable
availability must be considered when choosing a profile.
CPU usage model. The computational effort for transcoding
operations varies with the video content type (Table II) and the
selected target profile. We obtained these values by transcod-

V. EVALUATION
A. Experimental Settings
We evaluate Online-REATA over a three-day scenario
(2021-06-15, 2021-06-16, and 2021-06-19), where both traffic
intensity and renewable energy availability vary over time.
All simulations were run on a 13th generation Intel Core i7-
13850HX (2.2–5.3 GHz, 20 cores with 8 performance and 12
efficiency cores), with 32 GB RAM, under Ubuntu 22.04 LTS.

Assuming a maximum per-core frequency of 5.1 GHz, additional
cores are allocated when a single core is insufficient.
Traffic Intensity. We rely on the Twitch traffic dataset
published in [17], [18]. From this worldwide dataset, we
extract French-language live streams to align user demand
with renewable energy sources from the French grid in terms
of timezone. Timestamps are adapted to UTC+2. To capture
content diversity, we identify the most popular Twitch cat-
egories [19] (e.g., Just Chatting, Minecraft) and map them
to three representative video classes: documentary (25.4%),
movie (45.8%), and sports (28.8%), based on visual and
dynamic similarity. Traffic intensity is defined as an estimate
of maximum number of concurrent tasks per slot ( ˆNl). In this
work, we assume that this estimate is highly accurate (we use
actual values), since many reliable techniques are available
to forecast seasonal streaming patterns, such as SARIMA,
Fourier analysis and recurrent neural networks (RNNs).
Renewable Availability. For the same three days, we ob-
tained hourly wind and solar production data from the French
grid [20]. These values were interpolated to capture finer fluc-
tuations (15-minute time slots). To align renewable supply with
the Twitch workload, we compute the daily renewable budget
E24h, i.e., the energy required to serve all tasks at a target QoE
of 0.99. This budget is distributed across slots proportionally to
the grid’s renewable profile: even if the daily renewable budget
is theoretically sufficient, mismatches between demand and
supply occur since the temporal distribution does not follow
the workload’s trend (see Fig. 3).
Benchmarks. We compare Online-REATA against three ref-
erence strategies: (1) Benchmark-0.99, which assigns each
task the number of cores needed to reach a target QoE of
0.99 (maximum QoE), importing energy when renewables are
insufficient. It provides the upper bound for QoE and import
and a lower bound for export; (2) Benchmark-0.75, which
assigns each task the allocation to achieve a target QoE of
0.75 (minimum QoE), providing a lower bound for export and
an upper bound for import; and (3) Benchmark-0.89, which
satisfies every task with a QoE of 0.89, the average QoE that
Online-REATA achieves.
Data center and energy system. Battery charging and dis-
charging efficiencies are set to ηch = ηdisch = 0.9, assuming
a Depth of Discharge (DoD) = 0.8 [3]. DoD defines the
usable portion of battery capacity [11] and it is set to avoid
premature degradation. The battery prioritizes renewable en-
ergy exchange over any interaction with the grid. For the tests
involving a battery, the system is initialized with the battery
initially discharged, and charging and discharging processes
of the battery are simulated. Converter efficiency is 1, battery
degradation and idle power are neglected (the latter would
add constant offset to dynamic consumption and it has been
reduced by recent hardware efficiency improvements [1]). All
cores are assumed homogeneous, with frequency F and power
consumption P.
B. Results
We evaluate Online-REATA against different benchmarks
by varying battery size and analyzing its impact on grid
interactions, QoE, and the effective use of storage. First, we
ran the tests without batteries. Fig. 4 reports, for each time
slot of June 17, 2021, the reduction in total imports plus
exports (i.e., interactions with the main grid) together with the
average QoE achieved. Over the three-day simulation, Online-
REATA reduces average daily imports by 52.76% relative to
Benchmark-0.99 and cuts exports by 21.62% compared to
Benchmark-0.75, while ensuring an average QoE of 0.89.
Secondly, experiments are conducted by introducing batter-
ies and varying their capacity in 500 Wh increments, ranging
from 0 Wh to 5500 Wh. Fig. 5 illustrates the results, where

Fig. 5: SSR and SCR metrics for each algorithm and battery capacity.
SSR indicates the share of total load supplied by renewables, while
SCR measures the share of renewable energy used over that available.
the performance of each algorithm is evaluated using the
SSR and SCR metrics, as defined in [7]. SCR and SSR
computation for the considered case study is discussed in
the supplementary material (Section III).1 We observed that
increasing battery size past a certain point yields diminishing
returns for SCR and SSR. This occurs because larger batteries
take longer to reach the minimum DoD, delaying the discharge
phase. This reduced utilization of stored renewable energy
leads to lower effective SCR and SSR values, since all the
discharged energy from the battery counts as renewable supply.
Fig. 5 confirms that, among all benchmarks, Online-REATA
achieves the best trade-off between SCR and SSR, without
requiring large battery storage, while maintaining an average
QoE that is only about 10% below the maximum value. We
also observe that Online-REATA, for an equivalent average
QoE (0.89), is able to match the best SSR performance of
Benchmark-0.89 (≈0.97), while improving SCR by about
3.4% and doing so with a 35.3% smaller battery capacity
(from 5035 Wh to 3257 Wh). Additionally, for an equal
battery size (500 Wh), Online-REATA is able to deliver an
SCR improvement of +11.24% while maintaining an SSR
improvement of +7.57%. We underline that the high self-
consumption observed in Benchmark-0.99 is mainly due to the
fact that the renewable availability was dimensioned according
to the energy required to achieve the maximum QoE of
0.99. Despite this, in the absence of a battery, Online-REATA
is able to almost match Benchmark-0.99 in terms of SCR
(only –0.62% difference), while significantly outperforming
it in SSR, with an improvement of +23.18%. Moreover, for
almost all battery sizes, Online-REATA maintains a higher
SSR level compared to Benchmark-0.75 (up to a battery size
of ≈4000 Wh), and substantially increases SCR, achieving
up to a +17.78% improvement with a 500 Wh battery while
maintaining a higher average QoE.
VI. CONCLUSION
This work proposes an approach based on compressible
tasks to reduce green data centers’ reliance on the main
grid while preserving QoE. The approach jointly addresses
imports reduction, final QoE, grid stability, and suitability
for delay-sensitive workloads. We also aimed to reduce the
reliance on storage systems. These aspects, to the best of our
knowledge, have not been addressed together in prior work.
We developed the Online-REATA heuristic, and we evaluated
it in the case study of live video transcoding: Online-REATA
achieved up to ≈11% higher SCR and ≈8% higher SSR
than constant allocation (Benchmark-0.89), while maintaining
the same average QoE without additional dependence on
energy storage. The gains came from adjusting the bitrate,
reducing the import from the main grid but also absorbing
the energy surplus. Future work will extend the proposed
approach to other compressible tasks (e.g., ML inference) and
to distributed environments, including space-shifting of delay-
tolerant compressible tasks across data centers.

A Smart Green Data Center of Energy Conservation in Cloud and Mobile 
Cloud Computing 
 
M. R. Sudha1* , C. P. Sumathi2 
 
1Department of Computer Applications, Faculty of Science and Humanities, SRM Institute of Science and Technology, 
Kattankulathur, Chennai 603203, Tamil Nadu, India  
2Department of Computer Science,  Shrimathi  Devkunvar Nanalal Bhatt Vaishnav College for Women, Vaishnava College 
Road,  Chromepet, Chennai 600044, Tamil Nadu, India 
 
*Corresponding Author: sudha.mr@ktr.srmuniv.ac.in 
 
Available online at: www.ijcseonline.org 
 
Accepted: 16/Jan/2019, Published: 31/Jan/2019 
Abstract – This paper focused to green system of the small data centers with sustainable energy power generation. The 
estimation must start with a baseline view of power consumption in every part of the data center. The primary vital issues of 
data centers are increasingly under intervention of their energy consumption and operations. This paper takes first step toward 
exploring green data centers powered by renewable energy system that include base load  power supply, intermittent power 
supply and backup energy storage systems. The required energy assists in an embryonic attitude of data centers being saved 
energy with a "greener" consequence. Data centers are the factories of the digital world and the cloud is coming back to earth 
that ethereal place where data is being stored. The convention of renewable energy resources has been the vital role in our 
future development of modern technology and cloud computing is the fastest evolving paradigm of the modern age of 
computers. This requires more and more remote host machines such as servers. Naturally, data centers are required large 
amounts of energy to power the growing demand. Now, data centers are turning to energy-efficient data facilities to cut costs 
and green power for their operations. This paper presents small-scale routing algorithm used energy consumption by instead of 
using conventional energy, thus increasing the effective performance up gradation of the virtual data center. We bring new 
thought in energy saving of the data centers. This presents the technological way of power consumption in the records of data 
center. 
 
 
Keywords – Cloud data center, Small scale algorithm, Energy consumption, Renewable energy 
 
I. INTRODUCTION 
A small-scale, cloud computing data center, still, could 
advantage of modern technological inventions to alternately 
dependent on solar energy. Cloud computing has developed 
as new energy utilized technology and virtualization model 
for the computing world. It provides an appropriate service 
based on the request of demand in resource pooling and 
measured service in a highly customizable practice with 
least effort [1]. However, there is a growing concern to 
optimize the output of the cloud infrastructure and to make it 
more mobile to ease the burden on aging computer 
infrastructure. The Computer infrastructure is becoming 
outdated and is causing significant problems in the overall 
energy grid, and non-renewable energy is the energy which 
is currently used to power most of the world's electricity, 
only recently due to global warming and other problems 
such as economics, the need for renewable energy is 
necessary more than ever. The below Fig. 1 Cisco provides 
77% of the traffic exist in the data center by 2020. Center to

1. Introduction 
Digital infrastructure has become the main pillar supporting modern-day economic, social, and technological 
systems. Data centers offer computational resources and storage for AI, cloud computing, digital banking, 
and health systems. The global population's reliance on digital technologies is steadily increasing, and 
consequently, the demand for physical infrastructure continues to grow. This demand has resulted in more 
and larger data center projects across diverse regions (Al Kez et al., 2022). 
However, the expansion is accompanied by a substantial environmental price. Data centers rank among 
Abstract: The rapid expansion of digital infrastructure intensifies the 
environmental burden of data centers through high energy consumption, 
freshwater depletion, land-use change, and waste heat emission. Conventional 
sustainability strategies focusing on efficiency and carbon offsets prove insufficient 
to address these escalating ecological challenges. This study proposes a 
transformative net-positive model where data centers actively restore and enhance 
surrounding ecosystems rather than merely reducing harm. A mixed-methods 
approach integrating literature synthesis, conceptual modeling, and case study 
analysis develops a Four-Pillar Framework comprising Energy Synergy, Water 
Stewardship, Ecological Integration, and Thermal Circularity. To measure 
performance rigorously across disparate environmental dimensions, we introduce a 
distance-to-target normalized, non-compensatory Composite Net-Positive Index 
(CNPI) aggregated via a weighted geometric mean. The model incorporates 
dynamic Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) contextual weighting based on site-
specific ecological stressors (θi) and a bounded degradation penalty function for 
biodiversity impacts. Application to two illustrative cases, a Nordic urban facility 
and an arid-zone data center, demonstrates CNPI scores of 1.30 and 1.28, 
respectively, confirming measurable ecological regeneration. This research offers a 
scalable, interdisciplinary blueprint for transitioning data centers from 
environmental liabilities to regenerative assets that support climate resilience and 
biodiversity recovery. 
Keywords Green data center, Net-positive, Waste heat reuse, Water balance, 
Biodiversity gain, Regenerative infrastructure 

Electrical Engineering and Energy | (2027) 6(1):79 
 
Tariq (2026),  Electr. Eng. Energy 
2 
the largest electricity consumers and represent one of the fastest-growing contributors to global power 
demand. Beyond power consumption, data centers significantly deplete freshwater resources through 
cooling requirements, raising particular concern in water-scarce regions. They also disrupt local 
environments, generate electronic waste through hardware replacement, and fragment habitats through land-
use changes. Large physical footprints alter local ecosystems, increase surface temperatures, and reduce 
species diversity in affected areas (Kumar et al., 2023). 
The industry typically responds with sustainability-based mitigation strategies, including enhanced energy 
efficiency and carbon offset purchases. While these measures provide some benefits, their primary objective 
is harm reduction rather than ecological restoration. The limitations of harm reduction become apparent as 
environmental crises intensify (Jozaghi, 2024). 
A net-positive data center represents a new paradigm that extends beyond harm prevention to active 
ecosystem restoration. This model gives more to the local ecosystem than it takes away. For example, the 
facility may supply renewable energy to the grid, plant native vegetation, and eliminate potable water 
consumption. It may also create wildlife habitat and utilize waste heat for greenhouses or district heating. 
This paper advances existing knowledge in several distinct ways. First, it proposes the Four-Pillar 
Framework as the first comprehensive model integrating energy synergy, water stewardship, ecological 
integration, and thermal circularity specifically for data centers. Second, it introduces the Composite Net-
Positive Index (CNPI) as a distance-to-target normalized metric for assessing net-positive performance 
across multiple environmental domains. Third, it develops a contextual weighting system based on Analytic 
Hierarchy Process (AHP) and regional ecological stressor coefficients (𝜃𝑖). Fourth, it employs a non-
compensatory Weighted Geometric Mean aggregation to eliminate scale disparities and prevent multi-
dimensional trade-offs. Fifth, it provides step-by-step verified case study calculations using empirical 
operational datasets. By making this measure available, the study aims to transform the narrative around data 
centers from unavoidable ecological burdens to regenerative assets that support environmental resilience 
and local community well-being (Wiegand, 2025). 
The implementation of net-positive data centers aligns with broader international sustainability 
frameworks, such as the CEO Water Mandate (United Nations Global Compact, 2021) seeking to codify 
environmental accountability and regenerative design. The LEED Zero program by the U.S. Green Building 
Council sets rigorous certification pathways for net-zero carbon, energy, water, and waste (U.S. Green 
Building Council, 2023). The EU Taxonomy for Sustainable Activities provides a legal framework to classify 
environmentally sustainable economic activities across Europe. Integrating these standards into the CNPI 
framework reinforces its alignment with international best practices and ensures policy compatibility for 
global deployments of net-positive infrastructure. 
2. Literature Review 
Recent studies have highlighted the significant impact data centers have on the environment, especially in 
energy use, freshwater consumption, land-use change, and related areas. The infrastructure that supports the 
digital economy continues to expand, and data centers are now running at levels comparable to small 
industrial complexes, where the majority of the electricity is used to power the servers and also to keep them 
cool. In areas where the air is very hot, or there is little water, the environmental pressure is even higher 
because conventional cooling takes up a lot of water, most of which is potable. Besides, the land taken up 
by data centers, usually covered by concrete and asphalt, causes the local ecosystem to lose its habitat, and 
also leads to stormwater runoff and the disruption of the local ecosystem (McCall, 2024). 
Technical progress has improved operational efficiency, but the focus is still mostly on the negative 
impacts rather than the positive ones. Innovations like immersion cooling and AI-based energy management 
systems have not only improved but also made the energy intensity per unit of computation lower in the 
data centers. Still, these advancements are within the traditional sustainability framework of harm reduction, 

Electrical Engineering and Energy | (2027) 6(1):79 
 
Tariq (2026),  Electr. Eng. Energy 
3 
spending resources and effort enabling "less bad" instead of creating long-term environmental value through 
prospective eco-design solutions (Spreafico et al., 2023). 
To some extent, other sectors have adopted alternative sustainability paradigms, giving rise to new 
concepts for data center design. One such paradigm is Regenerative Design, which virtually causes the 
infrastructure to take cues from natural systems whereby the ecosystems are rejuvenated. Then, the Circular 
Economy favors material and energy reuse while closing the loop on linear resource flows. Similar to the 
Circular Economy, Industrial Symbiosis advocates the exchange of waste products, like heat or water, among 
nearby facilities. These circular and symbiotic approaches have been increasingly applied across digital 
infrastructure operations (Samberger, 2022), complemented by material traceability and lifecycle 
accountability in ICT hardware supply chains (Calvão & Archer, 2021). Biodiversity Net Gain expects new 
constructions to positively improve local ecology after construction (Nassar, 2025). 
2.1. Literature review protocol 
This study conducts a systematic literature review following established guidelines for replicable synthesis. 
The review protocol defines clear inclusion and exclusion criteria to ensure comprehensive coverage of 
relevant scholarship. The search strategy targets peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings, industry 
white papers, and doctoral dissertations published between 2020 and 2026. Selected databases include 
Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. Search terms comprise "green data center," 
"net-positive infrastructure," "waste heat reuse," "water stewardship data center," "biodiversity net gain," 
and "regenerative design." Initial search yields 347 records. Duplicate removal eliminates 89 records. Title 
and abstract screening exclude 238 records based on irrelevance. Full-text assessment of the remaining 20 
records confirms direct relevance to the four domains. 
3. The Four-Pillar Framework for Net-Positive Design 
For a data center to yield a net-positive outcome, it needs to move from minor sustainability efforts to a 
comprehensive, systems-oriented approach that integrates regenerative strategies across all major 
environmental domains affected by facility operations. The areas of energy consumption and water use, but 
also biodiversity impact, land use, and waste heat emission are included. A net-positive data center must 
operate according to the design principles of giving, storing, and enhancing the ecosystems it is sited in, 
rather than being footprint-conscious only. It means that the data center operators have to look beyond the 
traditional models that are strictly concerned with operational efficiency and adopt a new one that is based 
on ecological contribution. This paper responds to this need by proposing a comprehensive and adaptable 
framework built upon four foundational pillars. Each pillar addresses a unique aspect of the environmental 
interface of data center infrastructure, thus forming a synergistic regenerative performance model. These 
include the pillars of Energy Synergy (𝑆ESI, Energy Synergy Index), Water Stewardship (𝑆WBR, Water Balance 
Ration), Ecological Integration (𝑆BNG, Biodiversity Net Gain), and Thermal Circularity (𝑆TUF, Thermal 
Utilization Factor), anchored in circular resources nexus principles (Samberger, 2022). Figure 1 illustrates the 
Four-Pillar Net-Positive Framework, showing how these domains connect to the data center core and jointly 
generate regenerative, ecosystem-level environmental outcomes. 
3.1. Energy synergy 
Data centers possess the operational capacity to play a transformative role in regional energy networks by 
drastically optimizing internal consumption while actively generating and sharing clean power. Facilities 
transition from passive bulk consumers into decentralized energy prosumers by deploying on-site renewable 
generation, including solar photovoltaic (PV) arrays, micro-wind turbines, and biogas systems. When they 
are connected to utility-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS), the data centers can hold onto their 
excess power and release it to the grid during times of high demand or low supply (Ramirez-Meyers et al., 
2021). Besides, data centers can participate in power grid services including voltage stabilization, load 

Electrical Engineering and Energy | (2027) 6(1):79 
 
Tariq (2026),  Electr. Eng. Energy 
4 
balancing, and frequency regulation; hence, their advantages would accrue not only to their operating area 
but also to the entire system. Such support indicates a significant step in the transition of data centers from 
passive consumers to active contributors in the clean energy ecosystem (Ramirez-Meyers et al., 2021).  
 
Figure 1. Schematic diagram of the Four-Pillar Net-Positive Data Center Framework. The architecture illustrates the integration 
of Energy Synergy (𝑆ESI), Water Stewardship (𝑆WBR), Ecological Integration (𝑆BNG), and Thermal Circularity (𝑆TUF), incorporating 
distance-to-target normalization (𝑆𝑖= 𝑀𝑖/𝑇𝑖), dynamic ecological stressor weighting (𝜃𝑖), and non-compensatory Weighted 
Geometric Mean aggregation (CNPI = ∏𝑆𝑖

3.2. Water stewardship 
Water-positive data centers aim to eliminate net freshwater depletion while actively replenishing surrounding 
watersheds and subterranean aquifer systems. Evaporative cooling losses are virtually eliminated by 
deploying air-assisted dry cooling, closed-loop liquid cooling, and air-side economizers. In water-stressed 
arid regions, facilities prioritize non-potable water sources, including treated municipal effluent and industrial 
greywater, for auxiliary processes. Beyond internal facility boundaries, net-positive stewardship encompasses 
external watershed intervention. Facilities support natural hydrological filtration and groundwater recharge 
by investing in local wetland restoration, constructing bioswales, and implementing deep-well drywell 
injection systems for stormwater harvesting (Boroomandnia et al., 2021). Collaborative partnerships with 
regional agricultural stakeholders further reduce watershed strain by funding conversions from flood 
irrigation to high-efficiency drip systems, transforming the data center into a regenerative hydrological asset. 
3.3. Ecological integration 
Through the application of ecologically sensitive site planning and landscaping practices, data centers can 
significantly contribute to the local biodiversity. Brownfield or previously developed land is one of the 
strategies that can be used very effectively, as it will not harm any untouched natural environments. Using 
plants that are native to the area for landscaping is a plus for the regional ecosystems as it provides the local 
fauna with the right food sources, shelter, and breeding places. Adding features such as green roofs, 
bioswales, and living walls not only provides co-benefits such as insulation and stormwater management, 

Electrical Engineering and Energy | (2027) 6(1):79 
 
Tariq (2026),  Electr. Eng. Energy 
5 
but also allows facilities to act as corridors for the movement of pollinators, birds, and other migratory 
species, thus connecting small ecosystems in urban and industrial areas. The planning and execution of these 
ecological enhancements are quantitatively guided by Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) principles, ensuring that 
post-construction ecological value demonstrably exceeds pre-development baselines (Di Sacco et al., 2021).  
3.4. Thermal circularity 
The low-grade waste heat (60∘C–80∘C) generated by server processing operations represents a valuable 
energy resource for regional industrial symbiosis rather than an operational thermal liability. Net-positive 
facilities capture liquid loop waste heat and redirect it into adjacent thermal networks instead of dissipating 
it into the atmosphere via cooling towers. In cold-climate urban settings, recovered heat is pumped into 
municipal district heating grids to warm commercial and residential buildings during winter months (Wang 
et al., 2024). In rural or suburban contexts, thermal energy is supplied to commercial greenhouses for year-
round agricultural production or to maintain regulated water temperatures in aquaculture operations. 
Capturing and reusing waste thermal energy reduces regional reliance on fossil-fuel heating systems, 
establishing mutually beneficial circular relationships between data center infrastructure and local 
communities. 
3.5. Framework validation 
The Four-Pillar Framework undergoes validation through three complementary approaches. The first 
approach involves expert review, where five sustainability professionals with experience in data center design 
evaluate the framework for comprehensiveness and practical applicability. The evaluation uses a five-point 
Likert scale for each pillar, with average scores ranging from 4.2 to 4.8, indicating strong agreement on the 
framework's relevance and completeness. The second approach involves cross-validation against established 
frameworks, including the LEED Zero certification criteria, the EU Taxonomy for Sustainable Activities, 
and the Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact. The analysis demonstrates that the Four-Pillar Framework 
encompasses all environmental domains addressed by these existing frameworks while adding the novel 
dimension of thermal circularity and explicit biodiversity metrics. The third approach involves sensitivity 
analysis of the CNPI. Varying each sub-index by ±20 percent shows that the CNPI remains robust, with 
overall scores changing by less than ±8 percent. This sensitivity analysis confirms that the framework 
produces stable and reliable assessments across a range of input variations. Together, these validation 
approaches provide evidence that the conceptual framework is both theoretically sound and practically 
applicable (Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact, 2021; European Parliament & Council of the European Union 
2020). 
4. Methodology and Mathematical Formulation 
To evaluate multi-domain net-positive performance without mathematical distortion, variable scale 
suppression, or unfair pillar compensation across multi-stage index systems (Peng et al., 2024), the 
Composite Net-Positive Index (CNPI) employs distance-to-target normalization, dynamic contextual 
weighting, and non-compensatory geometric aggregation. 
4.1. Distance-to-target sub-index normalization

To demonstrate the practical application, mathematical consistency, and context-sensitive behavior of the 
Composite Net-Positive Index (CNPI), the framework is evaluated across two contrasting, empirically

data center operating in a water-scarce environment. Input parameters (𝑴𝒊) for both facilities are calibrated 
against published operational benchmarks from live digital infrastructure deployments (Samberger, 2022; 
Wang et al., 2024). 
5.1. Case study 1: Nordic urban data center (Stockholm, Sweden) 
The first case study evaluates a 50 MW enterprise data center located in the metropolitan Stockholm region,

replenishment and solar power) can maintain net-positive status without violating non-compensatory rules. 
6. Discussion and Comparative Sensitivity Analysis 
6.1. Non-compensatory sensitivity analysis and model proof 
Conventional composite indicators frequently utilize linear additive aggregation models. However, in 
environmental sustainability assessment, linear models introduce a severe flaw known as perfect 
compensability, where extreme degradation in one domain can be masked by high performance in another. 
To mathematically prove the superiority of the proposed non-compensatory Weighted Geometric Mean 
model, consider an extreme failure scenario: a data center generates massive surplus solar energy (𝑀ESI =
2.00 ⟹𝑆ESI = 2.00) but causes severe local groundwater depletion (𝑀WBR = 0.05 ⟹𝑆WBR = 0.05), 
while meeting baseline targets in ecology and thermal reuse (𝑆BNG = 1.20, 𝑆TUF = 0.80). 
• (1) Linear Additive Sum Model: 
CNPIlinear = (0.25 × 2.00) + (0.35 × 0.05) + (0.25 × 1.20) + (0.15 × 0.80) = 0.9375 
Under a linear model, the facility achieves a score of 0.9375—deceptively signaling "near-passing" 
performance despite near-total hydrological collapse in the local community. 
• (2) Weighted Geometric Mean Model (Proposed): 
CNPIgeometric = (2.00)0.25 × (0.05)0.35 × (1.20)0.25 × (0.80)0.15 = 0.4218 
Under the geometric aggregation model, the composite index collapses to 0.4218, triggering an unequivocal 
"FAIL" score that accurately reflects the ecological crisis caused by water depletion. This non-compensatory 
behavior ensures that data center operators cannot engage in "environmental trade-off greenwashing."  
Furthermore, traditional data center efficiency metrics—such as Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), 
Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE), and Carbon Usage Effectiveness (CUE)—focus strictly on internal 
operational efficiency (harm reduction). While a low PUE (e.g., 1.10) indicates an efficient facility, it provides 
zero information regarding whether the facility restores local natural capital. The CNPI framework 
complements these legacy metrics by providing an external, regenerative ecosystem assessment tool.

6.2. Limitations 
This study has several methodological and operational limitations that should inform interpretation of the 
findings. First, while the case study operational parameters are calibrated against published empirical facility 
benchmarks, they represent retrospective evaluations rather than continuous, real-time telemetry datasets 
from multi-year live operations. Second, although the framework introduced dynamic AHP-ecological 
stressor weighting (𝜃𝑖) to resolve static weighting subjectivity, determining these stressor coefficients in 
developing nations requires further empirical calibration where regional environmental data may be sparse.

Third, the CNPI target thresholds (𝑇𝑖) derive from established international standards (e.g., LEED Zero, 
CEO Water Mandate [United Nations Global Compact, 2021; UK Environment Act 2021; UK Parliament, 
2021)), which may require contextual adjustment in emerging markets where regulatory frameworks and 
ecological baselines differ significantly from those in Europe and North America. Fourth, the current 
framework focuses strictly on operational environmental impacts; it does not explicitly encompass embodied 
carbon in building construction, server supply chain circularity, or electronic waste management—all of 
which represent vital dimensions for complete life-cycle assessments. Finally, framework validation relies on 
expert review, cross-standard comparison, and mathematical sensitivity modeling rather than longitudinal 
empirical field testing. These limitations suggest that while the CNPI provides a rigorous mathematical 
foundation, future research should focus on live IoT telemetry integration, scope 3 life-cycle expansion, and 
multi-region field testing across live data center deployments. 
7. Conclusion 
The rapid expansion of digital infrastructure demands a fundamental paradigm shift in environmental 
responsibility, rendering conventional harm mitigation and isolated efficiency metrics insufficient. Data 
centers increasingly influence regional power grids, municipal freshwater allocation, local habitat 
connectivity, and thermal microclimates. In response, this study establishes a transformative model that 
redefines data centers from passive, extractive energy consumers into active environmental stewards. The 
proposed Four-Pillar Framework, encompassing Energy Synergy, Water Stewardship, Ecological 
Integration, and Thermal Circularity, shifts the operational narrative from merely "reducing harm" to actively 
generating "net-positive good." To operationalize this framework, the Composite Net-Positive Index 
(CNPI) provides a distance-to-target normalized, context-sensitive instrument that evaluates regenerative 
performance across disparate ecological domains. By employing a Weighted Geometric Mean aggregation 
coupled with dynamic AHP-ecological stressor coefficients (𝜃𝑖), the CNPI eliminates compensatory trade-
offs, ensuring that severe underperformance in one pillar cannot be masked by overperformance in another. 
This provides data center operators, structural engineers, architects, and policymakers with a transparent, 
mathematically sound blueprint to establish, monitor, and enforce verifiable restorative goals beyond carbon 
neutrality. As digital infrastructure continues to evolve, emerging technologies offer compelling pathways to 
amplify this regenerative model. Real-time AI-driven cooling architectures can dynamically optimize thermal 
loads based on ambient predictive analytics and adaptive facility control models (Wang et al., 2024) , 
minimizing water and power consumption. Concurrently, digital twins—virtual replicas of local hydrological, 
biological, and thermal flows—allow operators to align facility operations seamlessly with surrounding 
ecosystem dynamics. By coupling rigorous mathematical accountability with adaptive intelligence, data 
centers can be fully embedded into regional natural capital, aligning the imperative of digital expansion with 
the ultimate goal of planetary resilience and ecological regeneration.

ABSTRACT
A HIERARCHICAL FRAMEWORK FOR ENERGY-EFFICIENT RESOURCE MANAGEMENT IN
GREEN DATA CENTERS
Data centers and high performance computing systems are increasing in both size and number.
The massive electricity consumption of these systems results in huge electricity costs, a trend that
will become commercially unsustainable as systems grow even larger. Optimizations to improve
energy-efﬁciency and reduce electricity costs can be implemented at multiple system levels, and
are explored in this thesis at the server node, data center, and geo-distributed data center levels.
Frameworks are proposed for each level to improve energy-efﬁciency and reduce electricity costs.
As the core count in processors continues to rise, applications are increasingly experiencing per-
formance degradation due to co-location interference arising from contention for shared resources.
The ﬁrst part of this thesis proposes a methodology for modeling these co-location interference ef-
fects to enable accurate predictions of execution time for co-located applications, reducing or even
eliminating the need to over-provision server resources to meet quality of service requirements,
and improving overall system efﬁciency. In the second part of this thesis a thermal-, power-, and
machine-heterogeneity-aware resource allocation framework is proposed for a single data center
to reduce both total server power and the power required to cool the data center, while maximizing
the reward of the executed workload in over-subscribed scenarios. The ﬁnal part of this thesis
explores the optimization of geo-distributed data centers, which are growing in number with the
rise of cloud computing. A geographical load balancing framework with time-of-use pricing and
integrated renewable power is designed, and it is demonstrated how increasing the detail of system
knowledge and considering all system levels simultaneously can signiﬁcantly improve electricity
cost savings for geo-distributed systems.
