Eco-centric leadership as a 
catalyst for environmental 
performance in hospitality SMEs: 
a serial mediation of green 
culture and green innovation
Ahmed Mohamed Hasanein  *
Management Department, College of Business Administration, King Faisal University, Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia
Introduction: Environmental sustainability has become a strategic priority for hos­
pitality small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), particularly in emerging econ­
omies where environmental challenges and resource constraints are increasingly 
pronounced. Drawing on the Natural Resource-Based View (NRBV), this study inves­
tigates the role of eco-centric leadership in enhancing environmental performance 
through the sequential mediating effects of green culture and green innovation.
Methods: Data were collected from 329 employees working in environmen­
tally oriented hotels in Greater Cairo, Egypt. The proposed conceptual model 
was tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) 
to examine both direct and indirect relationships among eco-centric leadership, 
green culture, green innovation, and environmental performance.
Results: The findings reveal that eco-centric leadership has a significant posi­
tive effect on environmental performance, green culture, and green innovation. 
Green culture positively influences both green innovation and environmental 
performance, while green innovation significantly enhances environmental per­
formance. Furthermore, green culture and green innovation individually and 
sequentially mediate the relationship between eco-centric leadership and envi­
ronmental performance, indicating that leadershipdriven environmental values 
become embedded within organizational culture and are subsequently translated 
into tangible environmental outcomes through innovation.
Discussion: The results highlight the strategic importance of eco-centric leadership 
in fostering sustainability-oriented organizational capabilities. By cultivating a strong 
green culture and promoting green innovation, hospitality SMEs can achieve superior 
environmental performance and strengthen their long-term ecological competitive­
ness. This study contributes to the sustainability literature by empirically integrating 
leadership, culture, and innovation within the NRBV framework and providing evi­
dence from the underexplored context of hospitality SMEs in an emerging economy.
KEYWORDS
eco-centric leadership, environmental performance, green culture, green innovation, 
hospitality SMEs, Natural Resource-Based View
1 Introduction
The global tourism and hospitality sector has faced increasing societal and regulatory pres­
sure to reduce its environmental impact and adopt more sustainable operational practices 
(Bramwell et al., 2017; Gössling and Higham, 2021; Hasanein, 2025). As one of the most 
resource-intensive industries, hospitality businesses contribute substantially to carbon 

Hasanein 
10.3389/frsus.2026.1801535
Frontiers in Sustainability
02
frontiersin.org
emissions, energy consumption, and waste generation (Scott et al., 
2024). In this changing environment, leadership plays an important 
role in guiding small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) toward 
environmental responsibility and sustainable competitiveness 
(Murtaza et al., 2024). Among emerging leadership approaches, eco-
centric leadership has gained attention for incorporating environmen­
tal awareness into organizational vision, managerial decisions, and 
workplace behavior, thereby supporting improved environmental 
performance in hospitality SMEs (Zada et al., 2025).
Eco-centric leadership moves beyond the conventional focus on 
profit and productivity by emphasizing the responsible use of natural 
resources and long-term environmental sustainability (Abdou, 2025). 
Leaders with eco-centric values encourage organizational change 
through promoting environmental awareness, supporting sustainable 
innovation, and integrating green principles into business strategies. 
An important aspect of this process is the development of a green 
culture, which reflects a shared organizational commitment to sus­
tainability and environmental ethics in routine activities (Wolor et al., 
2025). Such a culture encourages environmentally responsible behav­
ior among employees and supports creative efforts aimed at minimiz­
ing ecological impact (Abdelwahed et al., 2025).
Within this context, green innovation represents the practical pro­
cess through which eco-centric leadership contributes to environmen­
tal outcomes. Green innovation refers to the development and 
implementation of processes, products, and technologies that reduce 
resource consumption, minimize waste, and improve sustainability 
performance (Shahbaz et al., 2025). In hospitality SMEs, where limited 
resources and operational pressures may restrict large-scale environ­
mental initiatives, leadership that supports innovation is particularly 
important for encouraging gradual and adaptable sustainability 
improvements. Previous studies have shown that eco-centric leader­
ship can promote employee-driven innovation and strengthen the 
relationship between environmental knowledge and organizational 
performance (Sarifudeen et al., 2025).
The relationship between green culture and green innovation 
explains how eco-centric leadership may improve environmental per­
formance through a sequential process. Green culture provides a 
foundation by aligning employees’ values and attitudes with environ­
mental objectives, while green innovation converts these values into 
practical sustainability initiatives and measurable outcomes 
(Manigandan and Raghuram, 2024). This process enables SMEs to 
integrate sustainability more effectively into their operations and 
improve both environmental efficiency and competitive performance. 
In addition, eco-centric leadership can strengthen trust, motivation, 
and shared environmental responsibility among employees, which 
supports the successful adoption of green innovation practices (Brohi 
et al., 2024).
Although interest in sustainable leadership and environmental 
management has increased, several gaps remain in the existing litera­
ture. First, many studies have concentrated on green transformational 
or servant leadership, while limited attention has been given to the 
specific role of eco-centric leadership in promoting sustainability out­
comes. Second, relatively few studies have examined the combined 
mediating effects of green culture and green innovation in the rela­
tionship between leadership and environmental performance, espe­
cially in hospitality SMEs. Third, sustainability research has focused 
primarily on large organizations, whereas SMEs have received less 
attention despite their collective environmental impact and resource 
limitations. Therefore, this study aims to: (1) examine the effect of 
eco-centric leadership on environmental performance in hospitality 
SMEs; (2) investigate the mediating roles of green culture and green 
innovation; and (3) evaluate the serial mediating effect of these vari­
ables in explaining how eco-centric leadership contributes to 
improved environmental outcomes. By integrating leadership, culture, 
and innovation perspectives, the study offers theoretical and practical 
insights into how hospitality SMEs can strengthen sustainability 
through leadership-driven organizational change.
2 Literature review and hypotheses 
development
2.1 Theoretical foundation – Natural 
Resource-Based View (NRBV)
The Natural Resource-Based View (NRBV), introduced by Hart 
(1995), extended the traditional Resource-Based View (RBV) by 
incorporating environmental sustainability into the analysis of orga­
nizational capabilities and competitive advantage (Kruesi and 
Bazelmans, 2022). The theory proposed that firms could achieve long-
term success by developing valuable and difficult-to-imitate environ­
mental capabilities that improved both ecological and financial 
performance. In the context of hospitality SMEs, where sustainability 
and operational efficiency are increasingly interconnected, the NRBV 
offers an appropriate framework for explaining how leadership, cul­
ture, and innovation contribute to environmental outcomes (Efrina et 
al., 2024; Dey et al., 2025; Hasanein and Rashwan, 2025).
Within this framework, eco-centric leadership can be viewed as a 
strategic capability that directs organizational resources and behaviors 
toward sustainability objectives. Leaders with eco-centric orientations 
promote environmental awareness, encourage collaboration, and inte­
grate ecological values into managerial decision-making processes 
(Utami et al., 2024). In hospitality SMEs, where financial and opera­
tional constraints often limit large-scale sustainability investments, 
eco-centric leadership supports adaptive capabilities such as employee 
involvement, operational improvements, and gradual green innova­
tion, which are consistent with the NRBV perspective on dynamic and 
path-dependent capabilities (Janjua et al., 2025).
According to the NRBV, green culture represents an intangible 
organizational resource that strengthens alignment with environmen­
tal objectives. When leaders consistently demonstrate environmen­
tally responsible behavior, employees are more likely to adopt shared 
sustainability values and norms, transforming environmental aware­
ness into an organizational capability (Wang et al., 2024). This cultural 
orientation encourages learning, commitment, and cooperation, 
which are important conditions for supporting green innovation. In 
this sense, green culture acts as an internal mechanism that translates 
leadership values into daily organizational practices.
Green innovation represents the practical application of sustain­
ability-oriented capabilities. From the NRBV perspective, innovation 
functions as a dynamic capability that enables firms to reconfigure 
resources in ways that reduce environmental impact and improve sus­
tainability performance (Aslam et al., 2024). In hospitality organiza­
tions, green innovation may include eco-friendly services, 

Hasanein 
10.3389/frsus.2026.1801535
Frontiers in Sustainability
03
frontiersin.org
energy-saving systems, and waste reduction practices. Prior studies 
have indicated that eco-centric leadership encourages such innovation 
by supporting employee creativity, experimentation, and investments 
in environmentally responsible practices and technologies (Maleki 
Minbashrazgah and Shabani, 2019).
In this study, the NRBV provides the theoretical foundation link­
ing eco-centric leadership, green culture, green innovation, and envi­
ronmental performance. Eco-centric leadership is conceptualized as 
the initiating capability that promotes sustainability-oriented values 
and practices. Green culture reflects the organizational capability that 
embeds these values across employees and organizational routines, 
while green innovation represents the operational capability that con­
verts these values into measurable environmental outcomes. This 
sequence is consistent with the NRBV argument that firms achieve 
superior environmental performance when intangible resources, such 
as leadership values and organizational culture, are transformed into 
innovation-based capabilities (Dey et al., 2025; Janjua et al., 2025). 
Therefore, the NRBV offers a suitable theoretical explanation for 
examining how eco-centric leadership contributes to environmental 
performance in hospitality SMEs through the development of internal 
sustainability capabilities.
2.2 Eco-centric leadership and 
environmental performance
Eco-centric leadership (ECL) had emerged as a critical determi­
nant of environmental performance (ENVP) by embedding ecological 
values and sustainability-oriented practices into organizational strat­
egy. Across sectors, ECL strengthened pro-environmental behaviors 
through mechanisms such as green consciousness and voluntary envi­
ronmental behavior (Hasan et al., 2024; Biswas et al., 2025). Abdou 
(2025) further emphasized that employees’ green commitment medi­
ated the link between ECL and organizational citizenship behavior for 
the environment, thereby advancing sustainable practices in eco-
friendly hotels. Beyond behavior, ECL enhanced environmental out­
comes by driving green knowledge sharing and innovation through 
ambidexterity (Zada et al., 2025), while Aftab et al. (2025) confirmed 
its role in improving performance outcomes in the manufacturing 
sector. Similarly, Owusu-Nyantakyiwaa et al. (2025) highlighted ECL’s 
dual impact on ecological and economic results through stakeholder 
collaboration and resource management. Finally, Hasan et al. (2024) 
confirmed that ECL positively influenced green knowledge sharing 
and performance in healthcare, offering cross-sectoral validation of its 
relevance.
Within the hospitality sector, ECL assumed particular importance 
due to the industry’s intensive use of resources and high environmen­
tal footprint. Research indicated that eco-centric leaders cultivated 
psychological green climates that encouraged employees’ innovation 
behavior and strengthened their pro-environmental commitment 
(Sarifudeen et al., 2025). Yoo (2024) showed that when ECL was inte­
grated with green HRM practices, it enhanced environmental citizen­
ship and organizational commitment, embedding sustainability 
within the service culture. Abdou (2025) likewise demonstrated that 
green commitment mediated the leadership–behavior relationship in 
eco-friendly hotels, while Hasan et al. (2024) illustrated that green 
consciousness enabled pro-environmental practices that improved 
organizational performance in service settings. Complementary 
insights from Murtaza et al. (2024) revealed that green improvisation 
and environmental orientation also strengthened both environmental 
and social performance in the hotel industry, further underscoring 
leadership’s role in shaping adaptive sustainability practices. Together, 
these findings reinforced that eco-centric leadership not only elevated 
environmental performance in hospitality but also aligned organiza­
tional culture with guests’ sustainability expectations, enhancing com­
petitiveness in an increasingly eco-conscious market. Therefore, we 
hypothesize:
H1: Eco-centric leadership positively affects environmental 
performance.
2.3 Eco-centric leadership and green 
culture
Green culture (GC) developed within organizations when ecologi­
cal values, sustainability-oriented norms, and pro-environmental 
behaviors were consistently modeled and reinforced by leadership 
(Uddin et al., 2021; Pichlak, 2024; Sun et al., 2024). Across sectors, 
eco-centric leaders shaped employees’ psychological attachment to 
ecological goals and fostered voluntary sustainability practices, creat­
ing an organizational climate that prioritized environmental respon­
sibility (Biswas et al., 2025). Zada et al. (2025) demonstrated that ECL 
promoted green knowledge sharing and ambidexterity, which facili­
tated green innovation and strengthened the cultural embedding of 
sustainability. Younas et al. (2025) further illustrated that integrating 
ECL with green digital transformation initiatives amplified employee 
engagement in sustainability, fostering a culture in which green behav­
iors were normalized and reinforced at multiple organizational levels.
In the hospitality context, where resource use was intensive and 
service experiences highly visible, ECL played a central role in culti­
vating green culture. Sarifudeen et al. (2025) showed that eco-centric 
leaders fostered a psychological green climate that encouraged innova­
tive behavior and strengthened employees’ commitment to sustain­
ability in hotels. Saputro and Nawangsari (2025) highlighted that 
green culture and leadership together enhanced employee green 
behavior, supported by organizational training and engagement prac­
tices. Abdou (2025) confirmed that green commitment mediated the 
relationship between ECL and organizational citizenship behavior for 
the environment, fostering trust and shared responsibility for sustain­
ability goals. Yoo (2024) proved that aligning ECL with green HRM 
practices strengthened environmental citizenship and embedded sus­
tainability within the service culture. Abdelwahed et al. (2025) empha­
sized that green culture mediated the effect of green knowledge 
management on innovation, bridging leadership intent and organiza­
tional outcomes. Reinforcing these insights, Younas et al. (2025) and 
Biswas et al. (2025) demonstrated that green culture amplified ECL’s 
impact on employee behaviors and overall organizational sustainabil­
ity. Accordingly, we hypothesize:
H2: Eco-centric leadership positively affects green culture.
2.4 Eco-centric leadership and green 
innovation
Green innovation (GI) emerged in organizations when ECL fos­
tered a climate that encouraged creativity, experimentation, and sus­
tainability-driven problem-solving (Sarifudeen et al., 2025; Pichlak, 

Hasanein 
10.3389/frsus.2026.1801535
Frontiers in Sustainability
04
frontiersin.org
2024). Across sectors, ECL motivated employees to engage in environ­
mentally responsible initiatives, facilitated knowledge sharing, and 
supported ambidextrous practices that enhanced both incremental 
and radical innovation (Zada et al., 2025; Younas et al., 2025). 
Integrating ECL with green HRM practices strengthened employees’ 
green identity, commitment, and creative capacity, embedding sus­
tainability into innovation processes (Akbar and Ahmad, 2024; Yoo, 
2024). Uddin et al. (2021) and Al-Amin et al. (2021) underscored that 
eco-centric leadership promoted biospheric values and voluntary 
environmental behaviors, acting as catalysts for continuous green 
innovation. Wolor et al. (2025) and Owusu-Nyantakyiwaa et al. (2025) 
showed that ECL drove eco-friendly workplace innovations and sus­
tainable business outcomes by aligning operational routines and stra­
tegic initiatives with environmental priorities.
Within the hospitality context, where resource use was intensive 
and service experiences highly visible, ECL played a pivotal role in 
promoting green innovation. Sarifudeen et al. (2025) demonstrated 
that eco-centric leaders cultivated a psychological green climate that 
encouraged employees to innovate in environmentally responsible 
ways. Murtaza et al. (2024) showed that green improvisation and envi­
ronmental orientation, guided by ECL, enhanced both environmental 
and social performance in hotels. Yoo (2024) highlighted that integrat­
ing ECL with green HRM practices fostered environmental citizenship 
and embedded sustainability into operational culture. Studies (e.g., 
Akbar and Ahmad, 2024; Sarifudeen et al., 2025) highlighted that 
green knowledge management, employee engagement, and ECL col­
lectively bridged leadership intent and tangible innovation outcomes. 
Therefore, we hypothesize:
H3: Eco-centric leadership positively affects green innovation.
2.5 Green culture and environmental 
performance
Green culture plays an important role in improving environmen­
tal performance by integrating shared ecological values, sustainability-
oriented norms, and environmentally responsible behaviors into 
organizational practices (Al-Alawneh et al., 2024; Manigandan and 
Raghuram, 2024; Sun et al., 2024; Abdelwahed et al., 2025). 
Organizations with strong green cultures often demonstrate better 
resource utilization, stronger employee environmental responsibility, 
and greater commitment to pollution prevention, which contribute to 
improved sustainability outcomes (Shahbaz et al., 2025; Aggarwal and 
Agarwala, 2023; Abbas and Khan, 2023). Green culture also helps 
translate strategic goals, leadership initiatives, and HRM practices into 
measurable environmental results by connecting employee behavior 
with organizational performance (Shahzad et al., 2023; Lin J. et al., 
2024). In addition, green knowledge management, employee training, 
and ethical work practices strengthen this culture and encourage 
greater participation in environmentally friendly activities aligned 
with organizational sustainability goals (Fok et al., 2023; Ak et 
al., 2025).
In the hospitality sector, the impact of green culture on envi­
ronmental performance is particularly significant because of the 
industry’s intensive resource use and visible environmental foot­
print. Research has shown that organizations with established 
green cultures are more likely to adopt practices such as energy 
conservation, sustainable procurement, waste reduction, and 
green talent management, leading to improvements in both 
environmental and operational performance (Murtaza et al., 2024; 
Brohi et al., 2024; Alkhozaim et al., 2024; Loedphacharakamon 
and Worakittikul, 2025). Studies also indicate that green culture 
mediates the influence of leadership styles, such as green trans­
formational and servant leadership, on employee environmental 
behavior and sustainability performance (Sarifudeen et al., 2025; 
Hasanein and Metwally, 2025; Al-Romeedy et al., 2025; Ayad and 
Hasanein, 2025). Furthermore, promoting employee engagement 
and creativity through a strong green culture enhances the effec­
tiveness of environmental initiatives and helps organizations align 
their practices with customer expectations and sustainability stan­
dards (Alkhozaim et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024). Consequently, we 
hypothesize:
H4: Green culture positively affects environmental performance.
2.6 Green innovation and environmental 
performance
Green innovation (GI) emerged as a central mechanism link­
ing sustainability and organizational competitiveness, particularly 
in hospitality SMEs (Zada et al., 2025; Manigandan and Raghuram, 
2024; Singh et al., 2020). It encompassed the development and 
implementation of eco-efficient technologies, sustainable opera­
tional processes, and environmentally conscious designs that 
reduced waste, energy use, and carbon footprint (Murtaza et al., 
2024; Ha et al., 2024; Chiou et al., 2011). Empirical studies dem­
onstrated that green innovation enhanced environmental perfor­
mance (ENVP) by improving resource efficiency, mitigating 
ecological degradation, and fostering stakeholder trust (Rehman 
et al., 2021; Shahbaz et al., 2025). Moreover, integrating eco-cen­
tric leadership and green HRM practices amplified the effect of 
innovation on ENVP by cultivating employee engagement and 
voluntary sustainability behaviors (Akbar and Ahmad, 2024; 
Akhtar et al., 2024; Niazi et al., 2023). Research also indicated that 
green innovation contributed to financial and economic perfor­
mance, highlighting its strategic role beyond ecological outcomes 
(Gu, 2023; Ha et al., 2024; Aftab et al., 2023).
Within the hospitality sector, green innovation was particularly 
impactful because service delivery relied on intensive resource use 
and highly visible operational processes. Studies revealed that lead­
ership-driven green initiatives, including transformational and ethi­
cal leadership, enhanced employees’ pro-environmental behavior, 
strengthened green organizational culture, and fostered organiza­
tional pride (Ayad et al., 2023; Ayad and Hasanein, 2025; Hasanein 
and Metwally, 2025; Yasir and Alam, 2025). Research in hotels and 
restaurants showed that innovation mediated the relationship 
between green leadership, corporate social responsibility, and envi­
ronmental performance, ensuring that sustainability practices were 
embedded in both employee behavior and organizational systems 
(Moustafa et al., 2024). Additionally, green HRM practices enhanced 
the adoption and institutionalization of green innovation by influenc­
ing retention, creativity, and climate for sustainable practices 
(Hassanein et al., 2024; Al-Romeedy et al., 2025; Marfo et al., 2024). 
Collectively, these findings demonstrated that green innovation 
served as both a practical tool and strategic driver for environmental 
performance, translating eco-centric leadership and employee 

Hasanein 
10.3389/frsus.2026.1801535
Frontiers in Sustainability
05
frontiersin.org
engagement into tangible sustainability outcomes. Therefore, we 
hypothesize:
H5: Green innovation positively affects environmental 
performance.
2.7 Green culture and green innovation
A strong green culture plays an important role in promoting sus­
tainable innovation within organizations by encouraging environmen­
tal awareness, knowledge sharing, and collective responsibility toward 
ecological goals (Shahbaz et al., 2025; Sarifudeen et al., 2025; Abbas 
and Khan, 2023). When environmental values are integrated into 
organizational practices, employees are more likely to adopt green 
technologies, improve service processes, and develop operational 
practices that reduce environmental impact (Manigandan and 
Raghuram, 2024; Hafeez et al., 2025; Lin Z. et al., 2024). Previous stud­
ies have shown that green culture supports both the exploration and 
implementation of eco-friendly solutions and also strengthens the 
relationship between leadership and innovation outcomes (Zada et al., 
2025; Şengüllendi et al., 2024; Shahbaz et al., 2025).
In the hospitality sector, organizations with strong green cultures 
encourage employees to participate in sustainable problem-solving 
and continuous improvement activities, which enhance operational 
efficiency and environmental performance (Brohi et al., 2024; Murtaza 
et al., 2024; Lin J. et al., 2024; Mukhtar et al., 2024). Research has also 
shown that combining green HRM practices, employee motivation, 
and talent management with a supportive green culture improves 
employees’ ability to generate eco-innovative ideas and ensures that 
sustainability initiatives are translated into practical organizational 
outcomes (Aggarwal and Agarwala, 2023; Shahzad et al., 2023; Qalati 
et al., 2023; Hasanein and Metwally, 2025; Seraj et al., 2025). In addi­
tion, employee engagement, training, and green knowledge sharing 
strengthen creativity and support the development of innovative solu­
tions that align with environmental objectives and customer expecta­
tions (Khassawneh et al., 2024; Seraj et al., 2025; Husnain et al., 2025; 
Gürlek and Kılıç, 2025). Accordingly, we hypothesize:
H6: Green culture positively affects green innovation.
2.8 Mediating role of green culture between 
eco-centric leadership and environmental 
performance
ECL exerted a pivotal influence on organizational environmental 
performance, frequently operating indirectly through the cultivation 
of a robust green culture (Abdou, 2025; Sarifudeen et al., 2025). 
Leaders who embedded ecological ethics, sustainability-driven values, 
and pro-environmental norms into organizational routines enhanced 
employees’ environmental self-efficacy and commitment, thereby 
establishing a psychologically supportive milieu that encouraged eco-
conscious behaviors (Zada et al., 2025; Manigandan and Raghuram, 
2024). Empirical evidence indicated that organizations with 
entrenched green cultures demonstrated heightened environmental 
citizenship, improved resource optimization, and diminished ecologi­
cal risks, collectively fostering superior environmental performance 
(Hasanein and Metwally, 2025; Lin Z. et al., 2024).
Cross-sectoral studies underscored this mediating function. 
Al-Alawneh et al. (2024) highlighted that green culture served as a 
conduit through which leadership-driven green HRM initiatives 
translated into measurable environmental outcomes in higher educa­
tion institutions. Similarly, Aggarwal and Agarwala (2023) reported 
that managerial support enhanced environmental performance pri­
marily via the development of green organizational culture within 
service firms. By institutionalizing shared ecological norms, green 
culture operationalized leadership’s sustainability vision into consis­
tent, organization-wide pro-environmental practices, thereby generat­
ing long-term value for both the enterprise and its stakeholders 
(Shahzad et al., 2023). So, we hypothesize:
H7: Green culture mediates the link between eco-centric leader­
ship and environmental performance.
2.9 Mediating role of green culture between 
eco-centric leadership and green 
innovation
Empirical research confirmed the mediating role of green cul­
ture. Abbas and Khan (2023) demonstrated that organizations with 
a deeply embedded green culture facilitated enhanced knowledge 
sharing, which in turn drove green innovation. Mukhtar et al. 
(2024) further observed that the synergistic integration of corporate 
social responsibility initiatives with green culture significantly 
amplified innovation outcomes in service-oriented organizations. 
Within hospitality, the effect was particularly pronounced: a well-
institutionalized green culture encouraged experimentation with 
sustainable service designs and operational processes, effectively 
translating leadership intent into tangible innovation outcomes 
(Aljoghaiman et al., 2024; Khassawneh et al., 2024). Accordingly, we 
hypothesize:
H8: Green culture mediates the link between eco-centric leader­
ship and green innovation.
2.10 Mediating role of green innovation 
between eco-centric leadership and 
environmental performance
ECL exerted a profound impact on environmental performance 
through its ability to stimulate green innovation, thereby translating 
ecological vision into concrete organizational outcomes (Zada et al., 
2025; Shahbaz et al., 2025). Leaders who championed environmental 
ethics fostered knowledge dissemination, employee engagement, and 
creativity in developing green products and processes, ensuring that 
sustainability objectives were effectively operationalized (Akhtar et al., 
2024). A growing body of evidence demonstrated that green innova­
tion mediated the effect of ECL on environmental outcomes. Murtaza 
et al. (2024) found that hospitality organizations implementing ECL-
driven innovation strategies enhanced resource efficiency while miti­
gating environmental risks. Similarly, Ha et al. (2024) reported that 
green innovation served as a critical intermediary between leadership 
practices and environmental performance in manufacturing contexts, 
illustrating the generalizability of this mechanism. Integrating green 
HRM practices further amplified this effect, fostering employee 
engagement, voluntary sustainability behaviors, and a more robust 
translation of leadership vision into measurable environmental gains

2.11 Mediating role of green innovation 
between green culture and environmental 
performance
Green culture established the social and cognitive scaffolding nec­
essary for fostering green innovation, which subsequently enhanced 
environmental performance (Manigandan and Raghuram, 2024; 
Abbas and Khan, 2023). Organizations that embedded green values 
into their cultural DNA promoted knowledge sharing, collaborative 
problem-solving, and experimentation with sustainable practices, pro­
ducing measurable improvements in environmental and operational 
outcomes (Brohi et al., 2024; Shahbaz et al., 2025).
Empirical studies demonstrated that green innovation functioned 
as a critical mechanism through which culture affected performance. 
For instance, Murtaza et al. (2024) and Sarifudeen et al., (2025) 
observed that innovation operationalized the values ingrained in 
green culture, yielding enhancements in energy efficiency, waste 
reduction, and sustainable service delivery. Hafeez et al. (2025) further 
confirmed that culture-driven innovation mediated the relationship 
between sustainability-oriented leadership and environmental perfor­
mance within hospitality settings, highlighting the functional role of 
innovation in translating cultural norms into tangible ecological out­
comes. Consequently, we hypothesize:
H10: Green innovation mediates the link between green culture 
and environmental performance.
2.12 Sequential mediation of green culture 
and green innovation
The impact of eco-centric leadership on environmental perfor­
mance often unfolded through a sequential chain of influence, begin­
ning with green culture and culminating in green innovation (Zada 
et al., 2025; Manigandan and Raghuram, 2024). Initially, leaders 
instilled sustainability-oriented norms and values, nurturing a green 
culture that prioritized ecological responsibility and knowledge dis­
semination (Abbas and Khan, 2023; Sarifudeen et al., 2025). This cul­
tural foundation subsequently facilitated green innovation by 
providing employees with psychological safety, motivation, and cogni­
tive resources necessary for engaging in environmentally conscious 
experimentation and creativity (Shahbaz et al., 2025; Hafeez et al., 
2025; Lin Z. et al., 2024).
Empirical research supported this sequential mediation. Brohi et 
al. (2024) found that organizations with ECL-driven green cultures 
enhanced environmental performance via innovative operational and 
service practices. Likewise, Murtaza et al. (2024) and Şengüllendi et 
al. (2024) demonstrated that culture-driven innovation ensured that 
leadership vision was effectively operationalized, leading to measur­
able sustainability outcomes. Collectively, these findings indicated that 
green culture and green innovation acted as complementary mecha­
nisms, enabling eco-centric leadership to generate systemic and 
enduring improvements in environmental performance. Accordingly, 
we hypothesize:
H11: Green culture and green innovation sequentially mediate 
the relationship between eco-centric leadership and environ­
mental performance.

3 Method
3.1 Sampling and data collection
This study examines the effect of Eco-Centric Leadership (ECL) on 
Environmental Performance (ENVP) in hospitality SMEs, with par­
ticular attention to the mediating roles of Green Culture (GC) and 
Green Innovation (GI). The conceptual framework was developed 
through a review of relevant theoretical and empirical studies based on 
the Natural Resource-Based View (NRBV). This review supported the 
formulation of the study hypotheses and guided the development of 
the research instrument. A structured self-administered questionnaire 
was designed to test the proposed model and distributed to employees 
working in environmentally oriented small and medium-sized hotels 
in Greater Cairo, Egypt. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares 
Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to assess both the measure­
ment and structural models, including the proposed mediation rela­
tionships. In addition, several procedural and statistical methods were 
applied to identify and reduce potential common method bias (CMB).
A pilot study was conducted with twenty hospitality professionals, 
including hotel managers, supervisors, and sustainability coordinators 
from hotels with green certifications or active environmental sustain­
ability initiatives. The participants had practical experience in envi­
ronmental management and familiarity with leadership and 
innovation practices, enabling them to evaluate the clarity, relevance, 
and suitability of the questionnaire items. Following the recommenda­
tions of Presser et al. (2004) and Dillman et al. (2014), the pilot study 
assessed item wording, structure, and comprehensibility through 
short interviews and written feedback. Based on the participants’ com­
ments, several revisions were made to improve conceptual clarity, 
language simplicity, and contextual suitability for hospitality SMEs.
The main study used a convenience sampling approach targeting 
employees in deluxe and midscale hotels in the Greater Cairo region. 
A cross-sectional research design was adopted, and data were col­
lected between August and October 2025 through an online question­
naire. The survey link was distributed via professional and 
industry-related online platforms, including LinkedIn, Facebook, and 
hospitality-focused WhatsApp groups, to reach employees from dif­
ferent hotel departments such as front office, food and beverage, 
housekeeping, and administration. The questionnaire introduction 
explained the academic purpose of the study, assured respondents of 
anonymity and confidentiality, and stated that participation was vol­
untary. Participants provided informed consent electronically before 
completing the survey, and the researchers’ contact information was 
included to address any inquiries. All collected data were used only 
for academic research purposes.

To reduce the risk of common method bias (CMB), the study fol­
lowed the recommendations of Podsakoff et al. (2003) and Kock 
(2015). Several procedural measures were applied during data collec­
tion. Respondents were assured that their responses would remain 
anonymous and confidential in order to minimize social desirability 
bias and evaluation concerns. Questionnaire items were carefully writ­
ten to avoid ambiguity, leading questions, and complex wording. In 
addition, predictor and outcome variables were organized into sepa­
rate sections of the questionnaire to reduce consistency bias.
The study also applied statistical tests to assess the presence of 
common method bias. First, Harman’s single-factor test showed that 
no single factor explained most of the total variance, indicating that 
common method bias was unlikely to be a major concern. Second, the 
full collinearity assessment approach suggested by Kock (2015) was 
used. The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) values for all constructs 
were below the recommended threshold of 3.3, confirming that mul­
ticollinearity and common method bias were not problematic in the 
dataset. Together, these procedural and statistical measures support 
the reliability and validity of the study findings.
3.2 Measures
The survey instrument was organized into five distinct sections. 
The first section captured respondents’ demographic information. The 
second section measured Eco-centric Leadership using a six-item 
scale originally developed by Zafar et al. (2023). The third section 
assessed Green Culture (GC) through a seven-item scale adapted from 
Umrani et al. (2022), while the fourth section evaluated Green 
Innovation (GI) using a seven-item scale based on Ning et al. (2023). 
The fifth and final section examined Environmental Performance 
(ENVP) employing a five-item scale established by Melnyk et al. 
(2003). To ensure content validity, the questionnaire was scrutinized 
by a panel of academic experts specializing in hospitality manage­
ment, sustainability, and organizational studies, who evaluated each 
item for clarity, contextual relevance, and alignment with the 
conceptual framework of the study. Recommendations from this panel 
were integrated to refine item phrasing and enhance measurement 
precision. Additionally, internal consistency and reliability were veri­
fied through the computation of Cronbach’s alpha (α) coefficients for 
each construct. All items were measured on a seven-point Likert scale, 
ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
3.3 Data analysis
A total of 400 questionnaires were distributed among full-time 
employees working in hospitality SMEs, of which 329 were returned 
as valid, yielding a response rate of 82.3%, with no missing data 
observed. The sample size met the recommended minimum ratio 
of 10 respondents per survey item, as suggested by Nunnally and 
Bernstein (1978). Among the valid responses, 269 participants 
(81.8%) were male, and 60 (18.2%) were female. Most of respon­
dents (87.3%) were aged between 26 and 40 years, representing the 
demographic composition of middle-level professionals in the hos­
pitality sector. Furthermore, 84.3% of participants reported possess­
ing advanced awareness and knowledge of sustainable practices and 
environmental management, indicating that the workforce is well-
positioned to engage with eco-centric initiatives and contribute to 
the development of green culture and green innovation within their 
organizations.
Preliminary data screening and descriptive analyses were con­
ducted using SPSS version 24. Subsequent statistical analyses 
employed a two-step Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) approach, 
as recommended by Leguina (2015), with measurement and structural 
models estimated to use SmartPLS version 4. Partial Least Squares-
SEM (PLS-SEM) was selected due to its suitability for exploratory and 
predictive research, its tolerance for smaller sample sizes, and its lack 
of assumptions regarding data normality (Henseler et al., 2009; Hair 
et al., 2017; do Valle and Assaker, 2016). To assess potential common 
method variance (CMV), Harman’s single-factor test was performed 
following the procedure outlined by Podsakoff et al. (2003).

4 Results
4.1 Measurement model
To examine the potential for common method variance (CMV), 
an Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) was conducted on the 24 mea­
surement items. The first unrotated factor explained 28% of the total 
variance, which is well below the recommended threshold of 50%, 
suggesting that CMV is unlikely to bias the study results (Podsakoff et 
al., 2003). The convergent validity and internal consistency reliability 
of the constructs were evaluated using Average Variance Extracted 
(AVE), Composite Reliability (CR), and Cronbach’s alpha. Following 
Hair et al. (2017) and Fornell and Larcker (1981), AVE values ≥ 0.50 
indicate that a construct explains at least half of the variance in its 
indicators, CR values ≥ 0.70 demonstrate sufficient internal consis­
tency, and Cronbach’s alpha ≥ 0.70 reflects acceptable reliability 
(Nunnally and Bernstein, 1978). Standardized outer loadings of ≥ 0.70 
further confirm that each indicator contributes meaningfully to its 
construct (Hair et al., 2017).
All constructs in this study met these criteria, confirming that 
they captured more than 50% of the variance of their indicators and 
exhibited strong internal consistency. As shown in Table 1, all item 
loadings exceeded 0.70, reflecting high reliability. Variance Inflation 
Factor (VIF) values were all below 5, indicating the absence of multi­
collinearity (Hair et al., 2017; Kock, 2015). Overall, the measurement 
model demonstrated robust psychometric properties, providing evi­
dence of both reliability and validity consistent with PLS-SEM guide­
lines (Hair et al., 2017; Henseler et al., 2009; Fornell and Larcker, 
1981). These results support the suitability of the constructs for sub­
sequent structural analysis.
The results presented in Table 2 indicate that each construct 
within the proposed model exhibits stronger associations with its own 
indicators than with those of other constructs, providing robust evi­
dence of discriminant validity. Specifically, the square roots of the 
Average Variance Extracted (AVE) values, highlighted in bold along 
the diagonal, exceed the inter-construct correlations, in accordance 
with the criteria established by Fornell and Larcker (1981). Moreover, 
all Heterotrait–Monotrait (HTMT) ratios, reported in brackets, fall 
below the recommended threshold of 0.90, further substantiating the 
empirical distinctiveness of the constructs. Collectively, these findings 
affirm the discriminant validity of the measurement model, thereby 
enhancing the credibility and methodological rigor of the subsequent 
structural model analyses (Hair et al., 2017; Chin, 1998).
4.2 Testing research hypotheses
As shown in Table 3 and Figure 2, all hypothesized relationships 
in the proposed model were statistically significant and positive, dem­
onstrating the central role of Eco-Centric Leadership (ECL) in pro­
moting Green Culture (GC), Green Innovation (GI), and 
Environmental Performance (ENVP) within hospitality SMEs. The 
first hypothesis examined the direct effect of ECL on ENVP and was 
supported [β = 0.722, T = 2.748, p = 0.006]. This indicates that leaders 
who actively prioritize environmental stewardship and sustainability 
initiatives directly enhance the organization’s environmental out­
comes. Practically, this suggests that eco-centric leaders influence 
operational practices, resource utilization, and decision-making pro­
cesses in ways that reduce ecological footprints, improve compliance 
with environmental regulations, and strengthen overall environmental 
performance. The second hypothesis tested the effect of ECL on GC 
and was confirmed [β = 0.878, T = 8.797, p < 0.001], illustrating that 
eco-centric leadership is a powerful driver in shaping an organiza­
tional culture that values sustainability, ethical environmental prac­
tices, and collective commitment to green objectives. Operationally, 
this means that when leaders consistently model and reward eco-
conscious behaviors, employees internalize these values, creating a 
culture that supports pro-environmental decision-making and col­
laborative green initiatives.
The third hypothesis assessed the influence of ECL on GI and was 
supported [β = 0.544, T = 6.432, p < 0.001], highlighting that leader­
ship fosters the development and implementation of innovative green 
solutions. This indicates that eco-centric leaders do not merely pro­
mote awareness but also actively stimulate novel practices, such as 
energy-efficient operations, waste-reduction initiatives, or sustainable 
service innovations, which collectively enhance organizational sus­
tainability outcomes. The fourth hypothesis examined the effect of GC

In terms of the fifth hypothesis tested the impact of GI on ENVP 
and was supported [β = 0.757, T = 2.179, p = 0.029], indicating that

Regarding indirect effects, the seventh hypothesis tested the medi­

supported [β = 0.476, T = 2.428, p = 0.015]. This implies that leader­

by cultivating a culture that embeds eco-conscious values, thereby 
facilitating employee engagement in sustainable practices. The eighth

culture is present, highlighting that leadership alone may be insuffi­

encourages experimentation, knowledge sharing, and proactive envi­

The ninth hypothesis (H9) evaluated the indirect effect of ECL on 
ENVP via GI [β = 0.536, T = 5.335, p < 0.001], indicating that innova­
tive green practices act as tangible pathways through which eco-cen­
tric leadership translates into measurable environmental outcomes. 
This underscores the notion that environmental performance emerges 
not solely from strategic guidance but also from operational innova­
tions that reduce resource consumption, emissions, and ecological 
impact. The tenth hypothesis tested the indirect effect of DC on ENVP 
through GI [β = 0.413, T = 2.197, p = 0.028], demonstrating that green 
culture strengthens environmental performance by fostering innova­
tion. In essence, when an organization’s culture emphasizes sustain­
ability, employees are more likely to develop novel eco-solutions that 
enhance environmental outcomes, reinforcing the mediating role of 
innovation. Finally, the eleventh hypothesis assessed the sequential 
mediation pathway from ECL through GC and GI to ENVP [β = 0.663, 
T = 2.097, p = 0.036]. This finding confirms that the impact of eco-
centric leadership on environmental performance is maximized when 
leaders cultivate a supportive green culture that, in turn, stimulates 
innovative practices. The sequential mechanism illustrates a systemic 
process in which leadership vision, cultural alignment, and opera­
tional innovation collectively reinforce environmental outcomes, 
ensuring sustainable competitiveness in hospitality SMEs.
Collectively, the empirical evidence confirms a coherent system 
of structural dependencies through which eco-centric leadership 
(ECL) shapes environmental and innovation-oriented outcomes in 
hospitality SMEs via both direct and multi-layered indirect pathways. 
The direct effects reveal that ECL exerts a strong and statistically sig­
nificant influence on environmental performance (ENVP), green 
culture (GC), and green innovation (GI), while GC and GI them­
selves further contribute meaningfully to ENVP, indicating a rein­
forcing architecture of sustainability-driven capabilities. The 
mediation results further demonstrate that GC and GI function as 
critical transmission mechanisms, both independently and sequen­
tially, amplifying the influence of ECL on environmental outcomes, 
with particularly notable effects observed in the chained mediation 
pathway (ECL → GC → GI → ENVP).
From a predictive standpoint, the structural model exhibits 
acceptable to moderate explanatory power across endogenous con­
structs. Specifically, GC demonstrates an R2 of 0.364 (Adjusted 
R2 = 0.352, Q2 = 0.352), indicating moderate variance explanation 
driven primarily by ECL. GI records an R2 of 0.273 (Adjusted 
R2 = 0.265, Q2 = 0.274), reflecting a modest yet meaningful predictive 
capacity, while ENVP yields an R2 of 0.167 (Adjusted R2 = 0.114, 
Q2 = 0.217), suggesting that environmental performance is influenced 
by a more complex constellation of antecedents beyond the immediate 
predictors specified in the model. In addition, the magnitude of F2 
effect sizes confirms that several structural relationships possess sub­
stantive explanatory relevance, particularly those involving ECL as an 
exogenous driver, thereby underscoring its central role in shaping 
both cultural and innovation-based green transformations. Finally, the 
global model fit indices—SRMR = 0.056, NFI = 0.959, RMS_
theta = 0.071, and RMSEA = 0.051—consistently fall within estab­
lished methodological thresholds, collectively affirming the statistical 
adequacy, structural robustness, and overall empirical credibility of 
the proposed model.
5 Conclusion and discussion
The present study set out to examine how Eco-Centric 
Leadership (ECL) drives Environmental Performance (ENVP) 
within hospitality SMEs through the serial mediating effects of 
Green Culture (GC) and Green Innovation (GI). The results col­
lectively provide strong empirical support for the proposed model, 
underscoring the pivotal role of leadership in shaping cultural and 
innovative mechanisms that strengthen sustainability performance 
in an era of growing ecological responsibility. The results indicated 
that ECL positively affects ENVP. This finding highlights that envi­
ronmentally conscious and ethically driven leaders are central to

Abdou, 2025). Leaders who integrate sustainability into strategic 
planning, decision-making, and daily operations foster behaviors 
that reduce waste, conserve resources, and enhance compliance 
with environmental standards. In hospitality SMEs—where opera­
tions are highly resource-dependent—eco-centric leadership 
ensures that sustainability initiatives are embedded within service 
delivery and performance systems. This outcome supports the logic 
of the Natural Resource-Based View (NRBV), which posits that 
leadership can serve as a strategic capability enabling firms to 
achieve lasting ecological and competitive advantages (Hart, 1995; 
Dey et al., 2025).
As well, the results highlighted the positive effect of ECL on 
GC. This confirms that leadership behaviors substantially influence 
how environmental values and beliefs become institutionalized across 
the organization (Wolor et al., 2025). Eco-centric leaders who demon­
strate ecological commitment, communicate sustainability visions, 
and reward pro-environmental actions cultivate a culture of shared 
responsibility and stewardship (Younas et al., 2025). In hospitality set­
tings, where service quality and environmental awareness are inter­
linked, such a culture enables employees to internalize green values, 
enhancing collective participation in sustainability initiatives. This 
reinforces the NRBV’s assertion that organizational culture constitutes 
an intangible resource critical for long-term environmental perfor­
mance (Utami et al., 2024).
Besides, the results reported that ECL positively affects GI. This 
finding suggests that leadership acts as a catalyst for creativity and 
experimentation directed toward eco-efficient solutions (Zada et al., 
2025). By fostering collaboration, empowering employees, and allocat­
ing resources for sustainable projects, eco-centric leaders promote 
innovative practices such as energy-saving technologies, waste reduc­
tion systems, and eco-friendly service designs (Sarifudeen et al., 2025). 
This aligns with the NRBV perspective that innovation represents a 
dynamic capability through which firms reconfigure resources to 
achieve superior environmental outcomes (Aslam et al., 2024).
In addition, the results clarified that GC positively affects 
ENVP. This relationship emphasizes the importance of cultural foun­
dations in achieving ecological efficiency and performance 
(Manigandan and Raghuram, 2024). A strong GC enables employees 
to engage in responsible behaviors, integrate sustainability into opera­
tional decisions, and continuously improve environmental practices. 
In hospitality SMEs, this cultural embedding ensures that sustainabil­
ity is not a compliance obligation but a shared organizational ethic 
that strengthens competitiveness and stakeholder trust.
Furthermore, the results showed that green innovation (GI) posi­
tively affects environmental performance (ENVP). This finding indi­
cates that innovation acts as a practical mechanism through which 
sustainability objectives are achieved (Ha et al., 2024). Green innova­
tions, including environmentally friendly technologies and sustainable 
process improvements, help organizations improve resource efficiency, 
reduce environmental risks, and strengthen service reputation. The 
result is consistent with the NRBV perspective, which considers envi­
ronmental innovation a tangible expression of a firm’s dynamic capa­
bilities and an important driver of sustainable performance (Rehman 
et al., 2021; Shahbaz et al., 2025).
Moreover, the results confirmed the positive effect of GC on 
GI. This demonstrates that an organization’s cultural orientation 
toward sustainability, learning, and collaboration directly influences 
its capacity to generate and adopt green innovations (Brohi et al., 
2024; Lin Z. et al., 2024). When employees internalize environmental 
values, they are more inclined to design creative solutions that mini­
mize ecological footprints. This interplay between culture and innova­
tion reflects the NRBV’s emphasis on the coevolution of intangible 
(culture) and tangible (innovation) resources as foundations of sus­
tainable advantage (Hafeez et al., 2025).
Likewise, the results concluded that GC and GI partially mediate 
the link between ECL and ENVP. This suggests that while leadership 
directly enhances environmental performance, much of its effect is 
transmitted through cultural and innovative mechanisms. The results 
also revealed that GC mediates the relationship between ECL and GI, 
implying that leadership fosters innovation indirectly by first estab­
lishing a supportive environmental culture. Additionally, GI mediates 
the link between ECL and ENVP, confirming that innovative practices 
operationalize leadership’s ecological vision into measurable out­
comes. The study further established that GC and GI sequentially 
mediate the ECL–ENVP relationship, illustrating a cascading process 
where leadership instills ecological values, which then nurture innova­
tion, ultimately enhancing environmental performance.
This sequential mediation supports the NRBV framework, which 
suggests that leadership, as a strategic capability, contributes to the 
development of intangible cultural resources that subsequently pro­
mote innovative capabilities and improve environmental outcomes 
(Dey et al., 2025; Brohi et al., 2024). In hospitality SMEs, this process 
explains how sustainability transformation becomes integrated within 
the organization, as leadership values shape organizational culture and 
are translated into innovation practices that support long-term envi­
ronmental performance.
6 Research implication
6.1 Theoretical implications
This study advances the theoretical understanding of sustainabil­
ity and environmental management by extending the Natural 
Resource-Based View (NRBV) into the domain of leadership-driven 
environmental performance within hospitality SMEs. The findings 
collectively affirm that eco-centric leadership (ECL), green culture 
(GC), and green innovation (GI) are interdependent mechanisms that 
explain how organizations cultivate and sustain environmental per­
formance (ENVP) in increasingly sustainability-focused markets. 
Theoretically, this integration contributes a multi-layered model that 
redefines how leadership-driven capabilities evolve from intangible 
environmental values into tangible innovation outcomes, thus moving 
beyond static conceptualizations of green management and corporate 
responsibility.
First, the finding that eco-centric leadership (ECL) positively 
affects green culture (GC), green innovation (GI), and environmental 
performance (ENVP) provides important theoretical support for 
viewing eco-centric leadership as a higher-level environmental capa­
bility rather than only an ethical or behavioral leadership style. The 
study shows that eco-centric leadership acts as a key mechanism 
within the NRBV framework by encouraging both cultural alignment 
and innovation. By confirming the influence of ECL on organizational 
culture and innovation, the study extends the NRBV perspective and 
demonstrates that leadership can function as a strategic capability that 
mobilizes human, cognitive, and relational resources toward sustain­
ability goals. This finding suggests that leadership is not only a

supporting factor for sustainability but also an important mechanism 
that shapes and strengthens organizational environmental

Second, the finding that green culture (GC) and green innovation 
(GI) are important pathways to environmental performance expands 
the conceptual scope of the NRBV by identifying them as core ele­
ments of sustainability capabilities. While the NRBV traditionally 
emphasizes valuable and difficult-to-imitate resources, this study 
demonstrates that green culture functions as an intangible organiza­
tional resource that integrates environmental awareness into employee 
behavior and organizational practices. At the same time, green inno­
vation represents a dynamic capability that converts these shared envi­
ronmental values into measurable environmental outcomes. Together, 
GC and GI explain how ecological values are translated into innova­
tion activities that support sustainable competitiveness.
Third, the finding that green culture positively influences green 
innovation provides an important theoretical link between cultural 
and operational dimensions within the NRBV framework. The results 
indicate that environmental innovation is not driven only by techno­
logical investments but also by the collective mindset and shared 
values within the organization. This relationship highlights the role of 
green culture as a supporting context that encourages innovation and 
strengthens sustainability-oriented behavior. As a result, the study 
broadens the NRBV perspective by emphasizing that environmental 
capability development depends not only on physical resources but 
also on social and cultural factors.
Fourth, the mediating and sequential mediation effects identified 
in this study contribute to the understanding of how sustainability 
capabilities are interconnected and developed over time. The findings 
show that green culture and green innovation mediate the relationship 
between eco-centric leadership (ECL) and environmental performance 
(ENVP), suggesting that environmental performance is achieved 
through multiple connected processes. These results support the view 
that sustainability capabilities develop progressively, beginning with 
leadership influence, followed by cultural commitment, and ultimately 
leading to innovation and environmental outcomes. This explanation 
strengthens the NRBV framework by demonstrating that sustainabil­
ity-oriented resources evolve across different organizational levels 
rather than through a simple direct relationship.
Furthermore, the finding that green culture and green innovation 
sequentially mediate the relationship between ECL and ENVP pro­
vides additional theoretical support for the multi-stage development 
of sustainability capabilities. The results indicate that environmental 
performance is not achieved directly through leadership alone but 
through a process in which leadership first shapes organizational cul­
ture and then encourages innovation practices that improve environ­
mental outcomes. This perspective extends the NRBV from a relatively 
static framework to a more process-oriented model of sustainability 
capability development that includes collective learning, shared envi­
ronmental values, and green creativity as interconnected stages. 
Collectively, this study contributes to both leadership and sustainabil­
ity literature by integrating eco-centric leadership, green culture, and 
green innovation as interrelated dimensions of environmental capabil­
ity. The findings confirm the relevance of the NRBV within hospitality 
SMEs while also extending the theory by emphasizing the importance 
of leadership, culture, and innovation in achieving sustainability. In 
this context, environmental performance can be understood as a mul­
tidimensional outcome that emerges through the interaction of lead­
ership vision, organizational culture, and innovation-driven 
sustainability practices.
6.2 Practical implications
The findings of this research provide actionable insights for man­
agers, policymakers, and industry practitioners aiming to strengthen 
environmental performance through leadership-driven transforma­
tion. The results emphasize that sustainability is not merely a compli­
ance objective or operational task but a leadership-activated, culturally 
embedded, and innovation-oriented process. Translating these 
insights into practice requires deliberate strategies that align leader­
ship behaviors with organizational systems, employee engagement, 
and innovation management.
First, the positive influence of eco-centric leadership on green 
culture and green innovation highlights the need for hospitality orga­
nizations to invest in environmental leadership development pro­
grams. Hotels and hospitality SMEs should support leaders who 
possess environmental awareness, strategic thinking, and a strong 
commitment to sustainability. This can be achieved through sustain­
ability training programs, environmental leadership workshops, cer­
tification courses, and mentoring initiatives that encourage 
environmentally responsible decision-making. Senior managers 
should also demonstrate eco-centric practices in daily operations, 
such as sustainable resource management, green purchasing, and 
transparent environmental reporting, to strengthen sustainability 
values throughout the organization.
Second, the mediating role of green culture emphasizes the 
importance of building an organizational commitment to environ­
mental responsibility. Managers should integrate sustainability into 
routine organizational activities by including environmental values in 
recruitment, employee training, and performance evaluation systems. 
Practical initiatives may include incorporating sustainability respon­
sibilities into job roles, recognizing employees for environmentally 
responsible behavior, and organizing activities that encourage employ­
ees to contribute ideas for reducing waste and conserving energy. 
Developing a strong green culture helps ensure that sustainability 
becomes a shared organizational value rather than only a managerial 
objective.
Third, the significant effect of green innovation demonstrates that 
innovation provides a practical mechanism for implementing sustain­
ability initiatives. Hospitality managers should encourage employees 
to participate in environmentally oriented innovation by establishing 
green idea programs, cross-functional innovation teams, and sustain­
ability committees. SMEs can also adopt affordable digital technolo­
gies for monitoring resource consumption, implement circular 
economy practices, and collaborate with local suppliers to introduce 
environmentally friendly products and materials. Treating innovation 
as an ongoing organizational process can help firms achieve continu­
ous and measurable environmental improvements.
Fourth, the sequential mediation effect suggests that environmen­
tal performance is achieved through an integrated system involving 
leadership, culture, and innovation rather than through isolated sus­
tainability initiatives. Managers should create organizational struc­
tures that connect sustainability values with innovation activities and 
performance goals. Aligning departmental objectives with broader 
sustainability targets can strengthen consistency between leadership 
vision, employee involvement, and innovation practices. In addition, 
organizations can use environmental performance indicators, such as 
waste reduction, energy efficiency, and adoption of green practices, to 
evaluate progress and support continuous improvement.
Finally, policymakers and industry regulators can support sustain­
ability efforts in the hospitality sector by encouraging eco-centric

When leadership commitment is supported by a strong green culture

7 Limitations and future directions
While this study provides important theoretical and empirical 
insights into eco-centric leadership (ECL), green culture (GC), green 
innovation (GI), and environmental performance (ENVP) in hospital­
ity SMEs, several limitations should be acknowledged. These limita­
tions do not undermine the validity of the findings but help clarify 
boundaries and suggest directions for future research.
First, the study is limited by its empirical focus on small and 
medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the hospitality sector. Although 
SMEs represent a major component of the tourism industry, larger 
hotel chains and other tourism-related organizations such as travel 
agencies, destination management organizations, and eco-tourism 
enterprises may exhibit different dynamics in how leadership influ­
ences sustainability outcomes. Future research should expand the 
scope to include these organizational types. In addition, cross-sector 
and cross-country comparisons could help identify how institutional 
environments, regulatory frameworks, and cultural differences shape 
the relationships among ECL, GC, GI, and ENVP. Such comparative 
studies would improve the generalizability of the model.
Second, the generalizability of the findings requires careful con­
sideration. This study focused specifically on hospitality SMEs in 
Egypt, which may limit the applicability of the results to other indus­
tries and cultural environments. Future research should extend the 
investigation to different sectors such as healthcare, banking, manu­
facturing, retail, and education to validate the robustness of the pro­
posed relationships across diverse organizational contexts. Moreover, 
comparative cross-cultural studies could provide deeper insights into 
how eco-centric leadership practices influence green culture, green 
innovation, and environmental performance in different regional and 
institutional settings.
Third, the mediating mechanisms examined in this study are lim­
ited to green culture and green innovation. While these variables 
explain a significant portion of the relationship between eco-centric 
leadership and environmental performance, they do not capture the 
full range of possible mechanisms. Future studies could incorporate 
additional mediators such as organizational learning, green knowl­
edge management, employee environmental motivation, and stake­
holder engagement. Similarly, moderating variables such as 
technological readiness, resource availability, and environmental 
uncertainty could be examined to better understand the conditions 
under which eco-centric leadership is most effective.
Fourth, environmental performance in this study was measured 
mainly in terms of ecological outcomes such as energy efficiency, 
waste reduction, and pollution control. However, environmental 
performance is a broader and multidimensional construct that may 
also include social and economic aspects of sustainability. Future 
research should adopt a more comprehensive approach by incorporat­
ing triple bottom line indicators that capture environmental, social, 
and financial performance simultaneously. Longitudinal designs could 
also provide deeper insights into how sustainability capabilities evolve 
over time and how eco-centric leadership influences long-term per­
formance outcomes.
Fifth, the cross-sectional design of the study limits the ability to 
draw strong causal conclusions. Since data were collected at a single 
point in time, the dynamic and evolving nature of leadership, culture, 
and innovation could not be fully captured. Future research should 
use longitudinal, panel, or mixed-method approaches to better under­
stand causal relationships and temporal changes. Qualitative methods 
such as interviews or case studies could also provide deeper insights 
into how eco-centric leadership is practiced and how it shapes orga­
nizational behavior in real contexts.
Finally, the findings are context-specific to hospitality SMEs in an 
emerging economy setting, which may limit their applicability to other 
industries or regions. Future studies should test the proposed model 
in other service sectors such as healthcare, education, aviation, and 
retail, where sustainability challenges differ. Comparative research 
between developed and developing countries would also help explain 
how institutional pressures, cultural values, and governance systems 
influence the effectiveness of eco-centric leadership. Taken together, 
these limitations outline fertile directions for future inquiry. 
Addressing them will not only refine the conceptual robustness of the 
eco-centric leadership framework but also deepen theoretical under­
standing of how leadership, culture, and innovation interact as mutu­
ally reinforcing capabilities that drive sustainable competitiveness. By 
advancing this line of inquiry, future research can strengthen the intel­
lectual foundations of leadership-based environmental management 
and inform transformative sustainability practices across the global 
hospitality and service industries.

IJE TRANSACTIONS A: Basics  Vol. 40, No. 04, (April 2027)  1145-1164 
 
  
Please cite this article as: Geng YH. Optimizing Cooling Mode Switchovers in Green Data Centers via a SC Metric and TRNSYS-PSO Simulation. 
International Journal of Engineering, Transactions A: Basics. 2027;40(04):1145-64. 
 
International Journal of Engineering 
 
J o u r n a l H o m e p a g e : w w w . i j e . i r 
 
 
Optimizing Cooling Mode Switchovers in Green Data Centers via a SC Metric and 
TRNSYS-PSO Simulation 
 
Y. H. Geng*a,b 
 
a Department of Civil Engineering, Hebei University of Water Resources and Electric Engineering, Cangzhou, China 
b Hebei Technology Innovation Center of Phase Change Thermal Management of Data Center, Cangzhou, China 
 
 
P A P E R I N F O  
 
 
Paper history: 
Received 12 March 2026 
Received in revised form 09 July 2026 
Accepted 23 July 2026 
 
 
Keywords:  
TRNSYS 
Cooling System 
Optimization 
Comprehensive Metric 
Rear Door Heat Pipe 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A B S T R A C T 
 
 
Driven by the demand for green and efficient data center cooling, this study develops a rack-level rear-
door heat pipe (RDHP) cooling system and proposes a comprehensive metric SC by integrating Power 
Usage Effectiveness (PUE), Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE), Carbon Usage Effectiveness (CUE), 
and scoring components from the Chinese green data center standard GB/T 44989-2024. Optimizing 
the switchover between free, hybrid, and mechanical cooling modes is critical for improving the energy 
efficiency and reducing the carbon footprint of data centers. A delimiting temperature (Tdelimit) of 17°C 
was established to optimally balance enhanced free cooling utilization with operational safety, ensuring 
server inlet temperatures remained within the limits. The switchover temperatures were optimized for 
four climatically diverse Chinese cities using TRNSYS simulations coupled with the GenOpt tool and 
a Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm. Results show that SC-oriented optimization effectively 
prolongs free cooling duration, reduces PUE, WUE, and CUE simultaneously, and outperforms 
empirical temperature settings. Also, the SC metric presents higher sensitivity than single indicators, 
while its optimization remains stable under varying grid carbon emission factors. This work provides a 
valuable methodology and a practical tool for advancing the green and low-carbon transformation of 
data centers, offering significant implications for policy-making and sustainable infrastructure planning.
