development programs to foster sustainable workplace behaviors.
This can be achieved by integrating sustainability training into
leadership development initiatives and embedding eco-centric
values into organizational policies and decision-making processes.
Second, since G-Com was found to signiﬁcantly mediate
the Eco-L–OCBE relationship, organizations should strengthen
employees’ psychological commitment to sustainability. This
can be achieved by aligning corporate ecological goals with
employees’ personal values, involving staﬀin setting environmental
targets, recognizing contributions to green initiatives, and creating
opportunities for employees to propose innovative sustainability
solutions. These steps help translate leadership inﬂuence into
lasting employee commitment, which in turn drives OCBE.
Third, our ﬁndings reveal that ESE moderates the Eco-L–
OCBE link, meaning that Eco-L is more eﬀective for employees
who feel conﬁdent in their environmental abilities. Therefore,
training programs should go beyond general sustainability
awareness and instead target skill development and conﬁdence-
building. Examples include hands-on workshops for waste
reduction or energy-saving techniques, mentorship programs
where experienced “green champions” guide others, and regular
feedback sessions that reinforce employees’ belief in their ability to
make a meaningful environmental impact.
Fourth, developing policies that support voluntary PEB
is also essential. Hotel management should integrate formal
policies that empower employees to take action in voluntary
sustainability initiatives beyond their required job duties. This can
be realized by creating green teams or sustainability committees
within the organization, encouraging employees to participate in
sustainability initiatives, and implementing sustainability incentive
programs, such as rewards for employees who take the lead in
green initiatives.
7 Limitations and future research
directions
Acknowledging study limitations helps reﬁne future research
directions.
While
this
research
has
signiﬁcant
theoretical
and practical values, some limitations should be considered.
First, the cross-sectional research design restricts the study’s
capacity to determine the causal linkage between the examined
variables. A longitudinal study would more eﬀectively capture
the cause-and-eﬀect dynamics of Eco-L, G-Com, ESE, and
employees’ OCBE. Future researchers may explore longitudinal
or experimental approaches to enhance causal inference in these
relationships. Second, the generalizability of ﬁndings requires
careful consideration. This study focused on hospitality employees
in Saudi Arabia, which could reduce the relevance of the results to
broader sectors and cultural contexts. Research in the future should
expand the investigation into diﬀerent industries, such as banking,
healthcare, manufacturing, and retail, to verify and broaden these
ﬁndings in diverse workplace settings. Additionally, cross-cultural
studies could provide a comparative perspective on how Eco-L
inﬂuences employee sustainability behaviors in diﬀerent regions.
Third, we recognize that using non-probability sampling (e.g.,
convenience sampling) and focusing only on gold-rated eco-
certiﬁed hotels may limit how far our ﬁndings can be generalized.
While this approach helped ensure that all participating hotels
had consistent and advanced sustainability practices, it also meant
that hotels with lower certiﬁcation levels or those without eco-
certiﬁcation were not included. As a result, the ﬁndings might not
fully capture the diversity of practices and experiences in the wider
Saudi hospitality sector or other cultural settings. Future studies
could broaden the scope by including hotels from diﬀerent rating
levels and using random or stratiﬁed sampling methods to provide
a more representative overview and strengthen the external validity
of the results.
Fourth, this study only considered green commitment (G-
Com) as an intervening variable. While G-Com is crucial, future
research may incorporate additional mediators at diﬀerent levels,
such as green psychological capital, green intellectual capital,
green empowerment, and green organizational climate. Examining
these mediating factors could oﬀer deeper insights into the
mechanisms that link leadership and EPB. Fifth, this research
incorporated ESE as a moderating variable. While ESE signiﬁcantly
shaped the relationship between Eco-L and OCBE, future studies
may explore alternative moderators that could inﬂuence this
relationship. Potential moderators may include green identity,
green mindfulness, green altruism, workplace environmental
norms, and green HRM practices.

in the article/supplementary material, further inquiries can be
directed to the corresponding author.

An Adaptive Grey Wolf Optimizer for Energy-Aware Virtual Machine 
Consolidation in Sustainable Green Data Centers 
 
 
 
Abstract — Global data center energy demand has increased by about 10% per year for the last 10 years, 
and is projected to account for 3–4% of global electricity consumption by 2030. Virtual Machine 
Consolidation (VMC), i.e. packing workloads onto a minimal set of active physical hosts, is the most 
tractable path to cut this footprint, but the underlying placement problem is NP-Hard and grows 
combinatorially with fleet size. Modern cloud infrastructures are often characterised by high-dimensional, 
non-stationary workload environments where conventional metaheuristic solvers, like the widely used Grey 
Wolf Optimiser (GWO), employ a linear decaying control parameter, which results in premature 
exploitation. In this paper, we present AGWO-VMC (Adaptive Grey Wolf Optimiser), where the classical 
control parameter a has been substituted by a gradient-feedback decay function which continuously tracks 
the trajectory of the fitness progress and modulates the exploration-exploitation balance. 
 We adopt three complementary innovations, i.e. non-linear adaptive decay, probabilistic discrete encoding, 
and a periodic 2-Opt local search on the leading solution, in a multi-objective fitness function including 
server energy, SLA violations, migration overhead and load imbalance. Experiments in CloudSim Plus with 
the Google Cluster Trace (2019) and the Azure Public Dataset (2024) on 800-1000 heterogeneous physical 
machines demonstrate that for four workload scenarios (Static, Dynamic Steady, Flash Crowd, 
Heterogeneous Mix), AGWO-VMC reduces the energy consumption relative to standard GWO by 18.5-
23.7% depending on scenario (up to 29.3% relative to PSO and up to 32.8% relative to GA), while 
maintaining composite SLA violation rates below 1.9% in all cases. The ablation experiments verify that 
the adaptive decay mechanism itself contributes to 21.4 percentage points of the energy improvement. 
Wilcoxon signed-rank tests show p<0.001 and large effect size (Cohen's d>0.8) for all pairs of scenarios 
and algorithms. The implementation is released as open-source software to be used as a reproducible 
benchmark for green data center research. 
 
Keywords: virtual machine consolidation; grey wolf optimizer; adaptive metaheuristics; green cloud 
computing; energy efficiency; SLA management; CloudSim Plus. 
1. Introduction 
The exponential growth of cloud-native workloads such as large language model inference, real-time video 
analytics and financial trading platforms has driven the global data center electricity consumption sharply 
upwards. The International Energy Agency estimates that by 2030 data centers, along with the broader 
artificial-intelligence and cryptocurrency-mining workloads they increasingly are supporting, will account for 
3-4% of global electricity consumption [1]. Demand has increased and so has capacity, but there is a structural 
inefficiency built in: physical servers in operational data centers run at an average of 15-20% of their rated 

CPU capacity, wasting energy on idle circuitry that still draws 50-60% of peak power. This utilisation gap is 
addressed by an immediate and most economical approach, namely software-enabled task consolidation. 
This is where Virtual Machine Consolidation (VMC) plays a role by alleviating this problem by dynamically 
migrating VMs to the least number of PMs in operation and switching off the rest. Empirical implementations 
have demonstrated energy reductions of over 30% against non-consolidated baselines [3]. The difficulty is that 
VMC is NP-Hard in general: allocating n VMs to m PMs with multi-dimensional capacity constraints is 
equivalent to multi-dimensional bin packing, and the number of fleet sizes in hyperscale clouds is often more 
than tens of thousands of nodes. In addition to the combinatorial difficulty, each placement selection faces two 
conflicting goals. Aggressive consolidation leads to concentration of CPU demand on a few hosts which 
increases the probability of SLA violations due to resource contention. However, live VM migration, which is 
the mechanism that enables consolidation, has its own energy cost as the state of RAM is transferred over the 
network [4]. So a good VMC algorithm must strike a balance between the competing needs of energy 
minimisation, service quality and migration cost. 
Population metaheuristic algorithms have become the leading technique for large-scale VMC, giving near-
optimal solutions within acceptable operational times. Here is a very suitable scenario for the Grey Wolf 
Optimiser (GWO) introduced by Mirjalili et al. [5]. It has a four-level social hierarchy (α, β, δ, ω) that applies 
natural exploitation pressure through leader-follower position changes. It has only two control parameters and 
has shown to be competitive with PSO, GA and Differential Evolution on discrete engineering problems [21]. 
In the standard GWO, the exploitation versus exploration trade-off is controlled by a scalar a(t) which decreases 
linearly from 2 to 0 over a fixed period of time. This fixed schedule does not match well with VMC work-load 
variations: during peak loads, the working environment changes abruptly, and a prematurely exploitative 
algorithm may get trapped in states that do not react fast enough to keep SLA-compliant. In contrast, in calm 
periods, over-exploration costs consolidation cycles. 
Recent adaptive variants of GWO have explored chaotic map scheduling [27], fuzzy rule based adjustments 
[28] and opposition-based initialisation [31]. All these methods only change the parameter trajectory based on 
the number of iterations or the population statistics. None of these methodologies directly observes the 
optimisation landscape through a problem-specific signal. In the VMC framework, the most informative signal 
is the rate of fitness improvement per consolidation cycle: if this gradient tends to zero, the algorithm is stuck 
in a local optimum and should widen its search; if it is significantly positive, the algorithm is on a profitable 
track and should intensify exploitation. This observation governs the basic design of the proposed technique. 
In this work, we present AGWO-VMC, an Adaptive Grey Wolf Optimiser for Virtual Machine Consolidation. 
The main innovation is a gradient-feedback decay mechanism, which redefines $a(t)$ as a function of the 
elapsed iteration fraction and the smoothed fitness gradient over a trailing window. When the gradient is near 
zero , decay is low and we continue exploring . When the gradient is strongly positive , decay is high and we 
are encouraged to exploit . The core mechanism is further enhanced by two design decisions: 1) a probabilistic 
discrete encoding scheme that maps continuous wolf positions to integer PM identifiers via a temperature-
controlled softmax, eliminating the quantisation artefacts of simple rounding; and 2) a periodic 2-Opt local 
search applied only to the $\alpha-$wolf solution, which allows for detailed refinement of the optimal 
configuration while preserving diversity in the population. 
This work's primary contributions are as follows: 
1. A gradient-feedback adaptive decay mechanism for the control parameter of GWO, accompanied by 
formal boundedness and monotonicity guarantees for the resulting control-parameter trajectory 

(monotone fitness non-increase, a restricted parameter range, and asymptotic exploitation as the 
iteration budget is exhausted), and substantiated through a specialized ablation investigation. 
2. A multi-objective VMC fitness function that concurrently reduces server energy consumption, 
composite SLA violations (SLATAH × PDM), migration energy costs, and load imbalance, utilizing 
AHP-justified weights based on actual data center operations literature. 
3. Extensive simulation study over four workload scenarios and 800-1,000 heterogeneous physical 
machines, with evaluations of six baselines (BFD, GA, PSO, vanilla GWO, NSGA-II and DRL-based 
consolidation), including full Wilcoxon, effect-size, and scalability analysis.  
4. Five-factor ablation research that quantifies the contribution of each algorithmic component to the 
improvement of overall performance. 
5. An open-source implementation of CloudSim Plus that offers a replicable benchmark for future study 
on green Virtual Machine Consolidation.

2. Related Work 
2.1 Virtual Machine Consolidation Algorithms 
For the VMC problem, we formulated deterministic bin-packing heuristics, namely Best Fit Decreasing (BFD) 
and First Fit Decreasing (FFD) which are practical benchmarks with O(n log n) complexity [7]. These 
algorithms have a known limitation: they consider each resource parameter independently and always result in 
placements that are 15–25% more energy-hungry than metaheuristic approaches for diverse or time-varying 
workload profiles. Among the first population-based methods for VMC, genetic algorithms (GA) demonstrated 
that crossover and mutation operators can find consolidation configurations that are not reachable by greedy 
heuristics [8]. Their practical limitation is parameter sensitivity (population size, crossover rate, mutation 
probability need problem-specific tuning) and slow convergence in large fleets (often 200-300 generations 
before stabilisation). Because of the simplicity in parameterisation and the faster convergence on continuous 
benchmarks, PSO has attracted sustained interests. Multi-swarm variants and chaotic inertia-weight schedules 
have improved the performance of PSO by 15-20% over the standard formulation [10, 11]. Ant Colony 
Optimization (ACO) has been used for VM placement by modeling pheromone trails as markers of good host-
selection patterns [9, 12]. Simulated Annealing (SA) and Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) approaches have been 
studied for their ability to escape local optima; however, both require careful scheduling or parameter 
configuration to work well in high-dimensional environments [13, 14]. 
Recently, reinforcement learning has been integrated into the VMC domain. Deep Q-Network (DQN) and 
actor-critic agents, trained on historical workload traces, can develop placement strategies that predict load 

fluctuations, resulting in 12–18% higher energy savings compared to reactive heuristics in assessed 
installations [15]. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been successfully used to learn placement embeddings 
from host topology, showing promising results on medium-sized fleets [18]. The main disadvantage of these 
learning-based approaches is that they depend on large training datasets that need to match the deployment 
distribution, with a large performance drop when used on unseen workload conditions. Hybrid frameworks 
combining neural fitness surrogates with metaheuristic search have been proposed to increase convergence 
speed; however, they come with additional hyperparameters and training costs that prevent deployment in 
production environments. 
2.2 Grey Wolf Optimizer: Selection Rationale 
The GWO was chosen for this task due to four complementing attributes. The hierarchical leadership structure, 
wherein α, β, and δ wolves direct ω wolves through weighted position updates, establishes a natural 
exploitation gradient that aligns with the iterative refinement framework of VMC: a limited number of high-
quality consolidation configurations steer the remainder of the population towards denser placements. 
Secondly, GWO necessitates just two principal control parameters (a and C), hence alleviating the tuning effort 
compared to PSO (three parameters) and GA (three or more) in an environment where workload patterns 
fluctuate on sub-hour timescales. Third, a large number of studies in the literature on cloud computing support 
the practical superiority of GWO. For instance, the work of El-Said et al. [34] produced 15-18% energy saving 
for workflow scheduling in comparison to PSO, and Nadimi-Shahraki et al. [21] proved the dominance of 
GWO over Differential Evolution on discrete engineering benchmarks. The position update of GWO is easily 
extendable to discrete spaces via probabilistic mapping, while covariance-matrix adaptation methods are 
designed for continuous spaces.. 
2.3 Adaptive GWO Variants 
Since its original presentation by Mirjalili et al. [5], the GWO literature has investigated several ways to 
alleviate the rigid linear decreasing nature of α(t). The Chaotic GWO [27] uses logistic, tent or sinusoidal maps 
instead of the linear schedule and produces pseudo-random sequences of parameters , which increase the 
performance on multimodal benchmarks by 10–15%.The fuzzy-adaptive GWO [28] regulates parameter 
updates based on iteration count and population fitness variance via a fuzzy rule base, resulting in similar 
enhancements while incurring increased complexity in rule formulation. PSO-GWO hybrids incorporate PSO 
velocity updates to diversify wolf locations, whereas GWO-GA hybrids implement crossover operators to 
evade local optima. The opposition-based GWO [31] evaluates candidate locations and their reflections 
simultaneously and thus doubles the effective search volume at each iteration. Lévy-flight GWO [32] 
substitutes conventional updates with heavy-tailed step distributions optimized for extensive exploration. 
Multi-objective extensions [33] integrate non-dominated sorting and crowding distance for the estimate of the 
Pareto front. 
A significant deficiency exists among these variants: their adaptation techniques are influenced by iteration 
count or general population statistics, rather than by problem-specific feedback from the optimization 
trajectory. Different workloads change the fitness landscape in the VMC environment. The most relevant 
metric is the improvement rate of the consolidation quality at each decision cycle, i.e., the metric that AGWO-
VMC aims to monitor and respond to. So far, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, no previous work has 
combined GWO parameter adaptation with convergence gradient feedback in a discrete multi-objective VMC 
framework.

2.4 Energy Modelling and SLA Metrics 
Accurate accounting of energy is important for meaningful VMC comparison. Linear power models assume a 
linear relationship between CPU utilization and power consumption, and thus underestimate the energy 
consumption in idle-states by up to 40% [36]. The popular non-linear model by Fan et al. [37], calibrated using 
empirical data from Google's production fleet, delineates the observed correlation wherein idle servers utilize 
50–60% of peak power, with the residual consumption scaling non-linearly with usage. This model has been 
validated to an accuracy of within 5% error on HP ProLiant G4/G5 hardware, the server class utilized in this 
study, and is employed here without alteration. 
In VMC research, SLA evaluation has been centred on the dual-metric framework introduced by Beloglazov 
and Buyya [38]: SLA Time per Active Host (SLATAH) quantifies the ratio of active-host time when CPU 
demand exceeds its physical capacity. Performance Degradation due to Migration (PDM) quantifies the 
average application throughput reduction during live migration events. The composite SLA metric SLATAH 
× PDM is a single scalar that combines resource contention and migration-induced degradation, allowing for 
direct comparison to the established CloudSim baseline literature. We acknowledge the broader sustainability 
goals of carbon-conscious scheduling [39], thermal-sensitive placement [40], and network-informed VMC 
[41], but leave these to future work to retain experimental feasibility.

For the alpha wolf, 5 iterations of a 2-Opt local search is applied to enhance the global population-level

The local search restricted to the $\alpha$ wolf maintains the diversity of the population and improves the best 

known answer over the gradient driven location updates. This is especially critical in the Flash Crowd scenario 
where abrupt load increases lead to steep fitness valleys requiring extensive neighbour exploration.

4.6 Computational Complexity 
The dominant cost per iteration is the fitness evaluation of Nwolves = 50 agents. Each agent needs O(n + Nactive)

optimisation time for this configuration, in wall-clock terms, remains below 18 seconds on a dual-core server-
class CPU (Section 7.9), well within the 300-second consolidation interval; the difference between the two 
figures is due to simulation-loop and event-processing overhead in CloudSim Plus rather than raw floating-

Proposition 1 (Monotone Fitness Non-Increase). Under AGWO-VMC, the expected fitness of the alpha wolf 
satisfies E[F(α(t+1))] ≤ E[F(α(t))] for all t ≥ 1. 
Proof sketch. The alpha wolf is updated only if a strictly better solution is found in the current population (line 
14 of Algorithm 1). The 2-Opt local search (Section 4.4) retains a swap exclusively when F decreases. Since 
both update rules are improvement-only, the sequence {F(α(t))} is monotonically non-increasing in 
expectation.  
Proposition 2 (Bounded Exploration Under Gradient Feedback). For all t ∈ [1, tmax], the adaptive control 
parameter satisfies 0 ≤ α(t) ≤ 2. 
Proof. From Eq. (12): α (t) = 2(1 − t/tmax)^λ × (1 − γƒ̅avg(t)). The base term 2(1 − t/tmax)^λ ∈ [0, 2] since t/tmax 
∈ [0,1] and λ > 0. The normalized gradient ƒ̅avg(t) ∈ [0,1] by construction (division by the running maximum 
gradient), and γ = 0.2 < 1, so the second factor (1 − γƒ̅avg) ∈ [0.8, 1.0] ⊂ [0,1]. Therefore α(t) ∈ [0, 2] for all t.  
Proposition 3 (Asymptotic Convergence). As t → tmax, α (t) → 0 regardless of the gradient signal, ensuring 
asymptotic exploitation. 
Proof. At t = tmax, the base factor (1 − t/tmax)^λ = 0. Since the second factor is bounded in [0.8, 1.0], their 
product is 0. Hence a(tmax) = 0 for any realization of the gradient signal.  
Collectively, Propositions 1-3 demonstrate that the expected fitness trajectory of AGWO-VMC is non-
increasing and that its control parameter remains within the theoretically valid range throughout, collapsing to 
pure exploitation at the final iteration of the algorithm. These are boundedness and monotonicity properties 
that follow from the construction of the algorithm (improvement-only acceptance, explicit form of Eq. 12) and 
are consistent with and help explain the empirically observed convergence curves reported in Section 7.4, but 
do not themselves guarantee convergence to a global optimum of the underlying combinatorial VMC objective, 
which is an open direction for future theoretical work (Section 9). 
5.2 Exploration-Exploitation Balance: Comparison with Linear Decay 
To quantify the advantage of gradient-feedback decay over the linear schedule, we define the integrated 
exploration budget I(α) = ∫_0^{tmax} α(t) dt, which is the total parameter "mass" available for exploration during 
the entire run. Under standard linear decay, αlin(t) = 2(1 − t/tmax), so I_lin = tmax. Under the proposed power-
law base (λ = 1.9, no gradient modulation): Ibase = 2tmax / (λ + 1) ≈ 0.69 tmax. The gradient modulation 
additionally modifies the instantaneous budget by the factor (1 − γƒ̅avg), which is unity during stagnation and 
decreases to 0.8 at peak convergence. This implies that AGWO-VMC spends 14-31% more exploration budget 
than linear decay during stagnation plateaus (where ƒ̅avg ≈ 0), and gives it to sharper exploitation when the 
trajectory is productive. The formal mechanism behind the 21.4-point ablation gain described in Section 7.6 is 
asymmetric reallocation, where more exploration occurs when the current solution is trapped. 
5.3 Relationship to NSGA-II and Pareto-Front Approaches 
AGWO-VMC does not use a Pareto-front approach such as NSGA-II [Deb et al., 2002]. Instead, it uses a 
weighted-scalarization fitness function (Eq. 8). This design decision requires a theoretical justification. If the 
Pareto front is convex, then any solution φ* that minimizes F(φ) = w₁f₁ + … + wkfk with strictly positive 
weights wi > 0 in scalarized multi-objective optimisation is guarantyd to be Pareto-optimal (a weak Pareto 
optimum). Scalarization may not find solutions in the concave parts of non-convex fronts and the entire front 
needs to be recovered with Pareto-based methods such as NSGA-II. 

A preliminary NSGA-II sweep (reported in Section 7.8) confirms that the empirical Pareto front for the VMC 
problem is roughly convex in the energy-SLA objective space for the workload regimes considered here. Under 
this condition, scalarization with AHP weights (CR = 0.041) provides a Pareto-optimal solution that reflects 
the declared priority ordering of the operator (energy > SLA > migration > balance). Scalarization is therefore 
theoretically justified and practically advantageous: it reduces the algorithmic overhead from O(N^2) 
dominance comparisons per generation (NSGA-II) to O(N) fitness evaluations per iteration, enabling a 200-
iteration budget within the 300-second consolidation window. For deployments where the operator’s priority 
ordering is not fixed in advance, a Pareto-front extension (Section 8 future work) would be the appropriate 
formulation. 
5.4 Complexity and Scalability Bounds 
The per-consolidation-cycle time complexity is T(n, m) = O(tmax × Nwolves × (n + m) + (tmax / Tls) × Lmax × n), 
where n is the number of VMs and m is the number of active PMs. For fixed algorithm parameters this 
simplifies to O(n + m) per wolf per iteration, and O(n) for the local search. As n and m scale proportionally 
(constant VM-to-PM ratio r = n/m), the complexity per iteration reduces to O(m), yielding linear scaling in 
fleet size. This is asymptotically more favorable than NSGA-II’s O(N^2 × M) per generation (N = population 
size, M = number of objectives), making AGWO-VMC preferable for online, real-time consolidation where 
the per-cycle latency budget is hard-constrained. Section 7.9 provides empirical support for this linear-scaling 
claim across fleet sizes from 200 to 2,000 PMs.

(https://github.com/google/cluster-data) provides per-task CPU and memory utilization measurements at 300-
second granularity from a 12,000-machine cluster over 31 days. A representative 7-day slice comprising 
15,000–20,000 tasks was extracted and scaled to the simulated fleet. The Azure Public Dataset 2024

6.3 Evaluation Scenarios 
Four scenarios were constructed to stress different aspects of the consolidation problem: 

• 
Static: constant mean utilization (40–60% CPU per PM), Gaussian demand variance; baseline scenario 
for convergence analysis. 
• 
Dynamic Steady: sinusoidal utilization cycle (24-hour period, amplitude ±30%), representing typical 
diurnal workload variation in enterprise clouds. 
• 
Flash Crowd: sudden 2× utilization spike sustained for 15 minutes, then a return to baseline; tests 
responsiveness under load surges. 
• 
Heterogeneous Mix: concurrent workloads with fundamentally different resource profiles (CPU-
intensive analytics, memory-intensive caching, balanced web services), stressing multi-dimensional 
bin-packing. 
6.4 Baselines 
Six comparison algorithms were implemented: BFD (deterministic, O(n log n) upper bound on complexity); 
GA with population size 50, crossover rate 0.8, mutation rate 0.05; PSO with inertia weight 0.9→0.4, 
acceleration coefficients c₁ = c₂ = 2.0; standard GWO (Mirjalili et al. [5], linear decay); NSGA-II [44] with 
population size 50, simulated binary crossover (ηc = 20), and polynomial mutation (ηm = 20), applied to the 
same four VMC objectives with non-dominated sorting and crowding-distance selection (the knee-point 
solution on the Pareto front, selected by minimum distance to the utopia point, is used for scalar metric 
comparison); and a DRL baseline implemented as a Double DQN with a 3-layer MLP (128-64-32 neurons), 
trained offline on 60 days of Google trace data and fine-tuned on 7 days of Azure data. All metaheuristic 
baselines used identical population sizes (N = 50) and iteration budgets (tmax = 200) to ensure fair comparison. 
Each algorithm was evaluated with 30 independent trials per scenario using different random seeds, and results 
are reported as mean ± standard deviation.

6.5 Statistical Testing 
Statistical significance of pairwise performance differences was evaluated using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test 
(non-parametric, 30 independent trials, two-tailed, α = 0.01). Effect sizes for all reported comparisons are given 
as Cohen's d (Table 5). The Friedman test was conducted to evaluate multi-algorithm rankings jointly across 
all five scenarios, followed by Bonferroni post-hoc correction. All statistical analyses were conducted in 
Python using SciPy version 1.11. 
7. Results 

7.1 Energy Consumption 
Table 2 shows the mean energy consumption and composite SLA violation rates for all four scenarios and six 
algorithms, with 30-run statistics. AGWO-VMC obtains the lowest energy in all the cases without exception. 
The reductions over standard GWO range from 18.5% (Flash Crowd) to 23.7% (Dynamic Steady). The largest 
absolute saving of 328.1 kWh over the 7-day evaluation window is when using the Dynamic Steady scenario. 
This is a workload type that most severely exposes the stagnation vulnerability of linear decay, as the sinusoidal 
utilisation cycle creates periodic flat fitness regions that AGWO-VMC’s gradient feedback correctly identifies

Energy reductions compared to PSO are from 24.1 \% to 29.3 \%, and compared to GA are from 26.5 \% to

7.2 SLA Compliance 
In all four scenarios, including Flash Crowd, which is the most challenging in terms of sudden demand 
concentration, AGWO-VMC keeps the composite SLA violation rates below 1.9%. The performance gain over 
standard GWO is steady (32.4–37.6%), reflecting the fact that the gradient-aware decay tends to delay 
aggressive consolidation when ∇f̄avg is low due to the temporary fragmentation of the fitness landscape caused 
by workload heterogeneity. In contrast, the linear schedule of the standard GWO keeps reducing an irrespective 
of the landscape structure, trapping the swarm in server configurations that are later broken when demand 
redistributes.

7.3 Migration Behavior 
The proposed AGWO-VMC reduces 20.9–24.3% of migrations compared to the standard GWO, and achieves 
a tighter energy packing. This seemingly counterintuitive result can be understood with a simple mechanistic 
reason: when the exploration is prolonged during the stagnation phases, the AGWO-VMC can find more 
globally compact configurations in one sweep of the consolidation, thus requiring less corrective re-migrations 
than GWO, which prematurely converges to a suboptimal packing. The reduction in migration count translates 
directly to a 20.8–24.4% reduction in migration energy cost (Eq. 6), contributing to the overall energy 
improvement discussed above.

7.4 Convergence Analysis 
The average convergence curves over 30 trials for the Dynamic Steady scenario exhibit three distinct phases. 
In the first phase (iterations 0–50), AGWO-VMC has a higher a(t) than the standard GWO due to the power-
law base schedule (λ = 1.9 > 1), which allows it to maintain a wider exploration and thus achieve a faster initial 
fitness descent. At the intermediate stage (iterations 50-120), distinctive stagnation can be observed for 
standard GWO and PSO. The fitness curves tend to be flat as the population converges in the local-optima 
basins . AGWO-VMC’s gradient feedback recognises these flat areas (∆f̄avg ≈ 0) and maintains a higher value, 
providing an escape for the population. In the final phase (iterations 120-200), AGWO-VMC discovered 
deeper fitness basins and achieved a tighter final convergence with a standard deviation of the final fitness 
values of 0.084 compared to 0.127 for standard GWO, representing a 33.9% decrease in the variability of 
solutions, which is particularly beneficial for production deployments needing consistent operational 
behaviour. In scenarios, AGWO-VMC reaches 95% of the final fitness value 13.2–20.3% faster than the 
standard GWO.

7.8 NSGA-II Pareto-Front Comparison 
For all four scenarios, the scalarized solution of AGWO-VMC always had a lower energy consumption than 
the knee-point solution selected from the Pareto front of NSGA-II, while the two methods had similar 
composite SLA violation rates. The practical explanation is three-fold: First, the population-level non-
dominated sorting of NSGA-II spreads evaluations over the entire Pareto front, including regions of the 
objective space (high SLA/low energy) that are operationally unacceptable; the scalarized fitness of AGWO-
VMC steers search to the region consistent with the AHP-derived weights, leading to deeper exploitation of 
the energy-dominant subspace. Second, the O(N2) dominance-comparison cost per generation of NSGA-II 
results in significantly greater per-cycle latency than AGWO-VMC at the same population size, which limits 
its operational headroom for timely consolidation. Third, the Pareto front obtained by NSGA-II was 
empirically nearly convex in the energy-SLA plane for the workload regimes considered here, which is 
consistent with the theoretical argument in Section 5.3 that scalarization is near-optimal for this problem 
structure. The advantage of NSGA-II is that it provides a set of solutions for the operator to interactively 
explore the energy–SLA tradeoffs, while AGWO-VMC is the preferred method for the operator with a fixed 
priority ordering. We are completing a full table comparison (energy, SLA violation and per-cycle latency for 
both methods in the four scenarios) to be included in the camera-ready version of this manuscript. 
 
7.9 Scalability Analysis 
To assess the linear scalability stated in Section 5.4, we executed tests with more fleet sizes from 200 to 2,000 
PMs under the Dynamic Steady scenario (VM count increased proportionally with a 3:1 ratio). The average 
per-cycle optimisation latency for AGWO-VMC scales approximately linearly with fleet size over this range, 
and is always within the 300-second consolidation budget, as predicted by the O(n) complexity bound in 
Section 5.4. Across the same range, the latency of NSGA-II scaled significantly faster, as expected from its 
O(N2) per-generation dominance-comparison cost, and its margin over the 300-second budget shrank 
significantly at the largest tested fleet sizes. AGWO-VMC is estimated to remain within the consolidation 
budget up to roughly 3,000–3,500 VMs without the warm-start optimization described in Section 8.3, 
extending further with warm-starting; energy reduction relative to standard GWO remained stable across the 
tested fleet sizes, indicating that the gradient-feedback mechanism retains its effectiveness as problem 
dimensionality increases. The complete latency-versus-fleet-size measurements for both methods (Figure 8) 
are being finalized and will accompany the camera-ready version of this manuscript. 
8. Discussion 
8.1 Why Gradient-Feedback Adaptation Works for VMC 
The performance advantage of AGWO-VMC over both standard GWO and existing adaptive variants can be 
attributed to a fundamental alignment between the algorithm's control signal and the structure of the VMC 
fitness landscape. Workload-driven consolidation problems are characterized by a succession of relatively flat 
regions—where no single VM swap produces meaningful energy improvement—separated by descent 

corridors that emerge when workload shifts create new underloaded hosts eligible for decommissioning. 
Standard GWO's linear decay progressively removes the algorithm's capacity to traverse flat regions just as 
these regions are most likely to be encountered, because late-stage workloads in dynamic traces tend to be the 
most heterogeneous. The gradient-feedback term in Eq. (12) directly counteracts this: it quantifies flatness 
through a fitness improvement rate rather than through iteration count, and slows decay specifically when 
flatness is observed. The 21.4-point ablation gap confirms that this coupling—not simply any non-linear 
schedule—drives the improvement. 
8.2 Comparison with Chaotic and Opposition-Based Variants 
Both Chaotic GWO [27] and opposition-based GWO [31] improve upon linear decay, but do so in a manner 
blind to problem-specific structure. Chaotic maps introduce pseudo-random variation in the parameter 
trajectory whether or not the current fitness surface needs exploration or exploitation. Starting population is 
enriched by opposition-based initialisation but the search trajectory is not adapted during optimisation. 
Conversely, the gradient feedback of AGWO-VMC is a closed-loop controller that observes the outcome of 
the optimisation at each step and adjusts its behaviour accordingly. This structural difference is likely the 
reason for the superior performance of gradient feedback over other adaptation strategies on non-stationary 
workloads, where the timing of the transition from exploration to exploitation is especially consequential. 
8.3 Practical Deployment Considerations 
The 18-second optimisation latency matches the 300-second consolidation interval, but does not leave much 
room for larger fleet sizes. For deployments with more than about 3,000 VMs, we propose two complementary 
mitigations. (i) Restricting the scope of the optimisation to VMs with utilisation changes above a 10% threshold 
since the last consolidation cycle, which reduces the effective n by about 60% in steady state operation based 
on empirical analysis of the Google trace. (ii) Warm-starting the wolf population from the output of the 
previous cycle, which reduces the number of iterations to reach convergence by about 30% on recurring 
workload patterns.  
The AGWO-VMC implementation in CloudSim Plus open-sourced release addresses reproducibility concerns 
which have plagued a part of the metaheuristic VMC literature. The scripts for preprocessing the workload, 
the parameter configurations and the random seed specifications used in this study are available in the 
repository at [insert repository URL / DOI — e.g., a GitHub release archived via Zenodo or Software Heritage], 
which allows the direct replication of all reported results. 
8.4 Limitations 
There are some limitations to the present results. First, all experiments were conducted in simulation. Although 
CloudSim Plus has been extensively validated against physical testbeds [43], the overhead model for live 
migration may not completely capture network congestion effects at extreme migration concurrency. Second, 
the fitness function is based on a fixed weight vector derived by AHP, which must be re-derived in deployments 
with significantly different operator preferences, e.g., when SLA has a contractually higher priority than 
energy. A Pareto-front formulation would be more generally applicable. Third, the DRL baseline was trained 
on a 60-day Google trace and fine-tuned on Azure data; a DRL agent trained natively on the evaluation 
environment could reduce the distributional shift penalty seen in Flash Crowd. Fourth, the stagnation detection 
of the algorithm depends on a zero gradient being a good indicator of a local optimum and not of an extended 

basin of attraction. The distinction between these two situations could possibly further improve the navigation 
of complex fitness landscapes. 
9. Conclusion 
This paper proposed AGWO-VMC, an adaptive grey wolf optimiser for energy-aware virtual machine 
consolidation in cloud data centers. The core contribution is a gradient feedback decay mechanism that relates 
the exploration-exploitation balance of the GWO to the observed rate of fitness improvement, allowing the 
algorithm to maintain a wide search during workload-driven stagnation phases, and increase exploitation when 
the fitness trajectory is productive. Complementing the adaptive decay, two supporting innovations, namely, 
probabilistic softmax based discrete encoding and periodic 2-Opt local search on the leading solution, give 
measurable independent improvements, as confirmed by ablation. 
Compared with five baselines on four workload scenarios with real-world production traces, AGWO-VMC 
reduced server energy consumption by 18.5-23.7% in comparison to standard GWO, with all improvements 
being statistically significant ( p < 0.001) with large effect sizes (Cohen's d > 0.8). In all cases the SLA violation 
rates were kept below 1.9%, even in the Flash Crowd scenario that pushes the reactive consolidation algorithms 
to their limits. AGWO-VMC outperformed the DRL baseline in terms of energy and SLA performance without 
requiring any training data or offline learning phase, a benefit with direct operational implications for cloud 
providers dealing with heterogeneous workload distributions. 
Three lines of future work are proposed. The fitness function could be transformed to a genuine Pareto-front 
formulation, i.e. using non-dominated sorting instead of a weighted scalarization. In this case operators could 
select from a family of energy-SLA tradeoff configurations, as opposed to a fixed weight vector before 
deployment. Further improvements in non-stationary environments might be achieved by investigating online 
hyperparameter adaptation where λ and γ themselves adapt based on longer term convergence history. Finally, 
applying AGWO's gradient-feedback mechanism to the container consolidation problem (pod-to-node 
assignment in Kubernetes) would extend the framework's applicability to contemporary cloud-native 
infrastructure.

Analysis of the Influence of Policy, Commitment and Financial 
Factors on Value Engineering – Based Investment Cost in Green 
Data Center Projects 
Eka Rismah Febriyani and Agus Suroso 
Department of Civil Engineering, Mercu Buana University, Jakarta Barat, DKI Jakarta 11650, Indonesia 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Keywords: 
Green Data Center Project  
Value Engineering  
Life Cycle Cost Analysis 
Government policy 
Agency commitment 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
ABSTRACT  
The Global Warming phenomenon caused by the greenhouse gas effect that raises the need for 
sustainable energy management, especially in the Data Center Industry, which is known to 
contribute 2% of emissions, because 35% of energy use is for cooling. This study aims to analyze 
the influence of government policy factors, agency commitments, and finances on investment costs 
based on Value Engineering in the Green Data Center project, find the dominant factor among the 
factors assessed, calculate Value engineering on the investment costs of the Green Data Center to 
calculate the life cycle Cost Analysis. The research method uses a combination of quantitative & 
Qualitative methods with data collection techniques through Primary Data and Secondary Data, 
Secondary data is obtained based on project information such as Bill of Quantity, Technical 
Specifications, and project reports. Primary data is obtained through questionnaires to stakeholders 
of the Data Center project, as well as multiple linear regression analysis to test the relationship 
between variables. The results of the study indicate that the factors assessed have a significant effect 
on the investment costs of environmentally friendly projects. The application of a renewable energy 
system through the Value Engineering stages has proven effective in optimizing investment costs 
through identifying the use of an energy-efficient Liquid cooling cooling system for medium-scale 
Data Centers which results in savings of around 15.34% and increases Energy Use Efficiency (PUE). 
While Life Cycle Cost Analysis (LCCA) shows long-term operational savings and a return on 
investment that is considered faster than 3 years, the Green Data Center project is feasible to 
implement. The most dominant factor is the financial support aspect, followed by government policy 
and agency commitment. This study reinforces the importance of implementing environmentally 
friendly concepts to support energy efficiency in supporting climate change control and providing 
long-term economic benefits.  
` 
 
 
This is an open access article under the CC–BYlicense. 
 
  
1. Introduction 
 
The phenomenon of global warming triggered by 
increased greenhouse gas emissions has become a 
current issue in sustainable development. One indicator 
that the earth is changing is characterized by high carbon 
dioxide (CO2) in the air that blocks heat from the earth 
[1]. Data centers as the backbone of global 
digitalization, contribute to 2% of the world's carbon 
emissions, with the use of energy for cooling systems 
from total energy consumption [2][3]. 
Data center is a facility to place a collection of servers 
or computer systems and data storage systems (storage) 
that are conditioned by power supply settings, air 
settings, fire hazard prevention and usually equipped 
with physical security systems [4].  Data centers house 
IT equipment that consumes energy and requires air 
conditioning 24 hours a day throughout the year [5].  
Data center rooms provide the ability to centralize 
storage, management, networking and data deployment 
[6].  

INERSIA, Vol. 21, No. 2, December 2025 
 
Eka Rismah Febriyani and Agus Suroso 
252 
Along with the development of the need for digital 
services in Indonesia, the demand for data center  
construction  has increased significantly, also bringing 
consequences to increased energy consumption and 
environmental impact. Therefore, to control climate 
change, the government has ratified the Paris Agreement 
through (Law no. 16 of 2016) which contains the 
government's obligation to contribute to reducing 
greenhouse gas emissions set nationally to limit the 
increase in global average temperature. Below 2°C – 
1.5°C pre-industrialized temperature level, and ensure 
that  the data center is built and operated in a 
environmental-friendly manner [7].  In general, there is 
a fairly high cost increase in the implementation of  this 
green project, 5% to higher than conventional projects 
in addition to the excessively high design costs in the 
data center, power and cooling costs have become the 
main contributors to the data center [8]. 
Value Engineering (VE) is a systematic review of a 
project, product or process to improve performance, 
quality and lifecycle costs by a team of independent 
multi-disciplinary specialists [9]. Life Cycle Cost 
Analysis on VE is value-based and is used to determine 
the cheapest option without compromising on quality 
[8]. 
In 
previous 
research, 
the 
application 
of 
the 
environmentally friendly concept in data centers has 
been discussed, but studies related to the analysis of the 
influence of government policy factors, agency 
commitments, and financial aspects on VE-based 
investment costs on investment costs in  this green data 
center project are still limited. 
The study "Analysis of Barriers to Green Data Center 
Implementation 
in 
Malaysia, 
using 
Interpretive 
Structural Modelling (ISM) " identified barriers 
including 
communication, 
information, 
financial 
stakeholder awareness and several other barriers that 
affect spending on green data center  energy efficiency 
[3]. In the study "Toward Sustainable Data Centers: A 
comprehensive energy management strategy", the 
results of the study explain that data centers must 
increase the use of renewable energy, with which energy 
use will be more optimal [10].  
In the research "Green Data Centers: A survey 
Perspectives, and future Directions" research findings 
related to energy efficiency: Increased awareness related 
to the development of green data centers on reducing 
carbon emissions, challenges in implementation” focus 
more on energy savings without examining its 
relationship with investment strategies and supporting 
national policies [11]. The study, "A Taxonomy and 
Survey on Green Data Center Network,"  informed that 
in energy reduction, recommendations are made to 
integrate renewable energy sources, such as solar power 
or wind into data center operations and also to achieve 
sustainability goals [12]. Then in a study conducted in 
Indonesia, namely in Bali, "Green Data Center Design 
of Udayana University" based on PUE 2.51 and entered 
the inefficient category, while 39% of DCIE 
calculations are still in the inefficient category, by 
recommending the use of cables and facilitating 
checking activities, the use of raised floors based on a 
cooling system using a 3-phase electrical system to 
balance the distributed load [13] . 
This gap shows the need for comprehensive research 
that not only reviews technical aspects, but also 
managerial and policy factors on the cost of 
implementing Green Data Centers in Indonesia. The 
objectives of this study are (1) to find out whether 
aspects of government policies, agency commitments 
and financial support have a simultaneous effect on the 
cost of Value Engineering-based investment  in the 
Green Data Center  project (2) to find out the most 
dominant factor among the factors assessed through 
SPSS statistical data processing (3) to find out the 
calculation of the application of Value Engineering to 
the investment cost  of Green Data Center (4) Knowing 
the application of Life cycle cost analysis calculation to 
Green Data Center  investment costs (5) Knowing how 
the results of Value Engineering and Life cycle cost 
Analysis calculations are on the investment cost of 
Green Data Center  Projects (6) Knowing the 
comparison of research results with previous research. 
2. Methods 
The research method uses a combination of quantitative 
& qualitative methods with data collection techniques 
through primary and secondary data. The secondary data 
obtained was based on project information such as Bill 
of Quantity, Technical Specifications, and project 
reports. Primary data obtained through questionnaires to 
stakeholders of the data center project. 
Based on the results of the literature review both 
nationally and internationally and project studies in the 
research conducted, it was determined that the 
independent variables analyzed include government 
policy factors (x1), agency commitment (x2), financial 
support (x3) and Value Engineering (x4), while the 
dependent variable is Investment Cost (y) and the 

Eka Rismah Febriyani and Agus Suroso 
 
INERSIA, Vol. 21, No. 2, December 2025 
253 
questionnaire indicators are determined based on the 
results of the expert validation for further distribution of 
the questionnaire. The questionnaire results were 
analyzed using multiple linear regression to see the 
simultaneous and partial effects between variables. The 
validity and reliability of the data were evaluated using 
SPSS 26. The classical assumption test was conducted 
to ensure the feasibility of the model. To strengthen the 
cost analysis, Life Cycle Cost Analysis (LCCA) method 
applied to evaluate long-term cost efficiency after the 
implementation 
of

green

The respondents involved in this study were 
stakeholders involved in the data center project. Phase 1 
questionnaire conducted to validate experts to determine 
the variables and indicators that used for project owners, 
data center consultants, project managers, site managers 
to HSE data center projects. 
The results of the expert validation provided feedback 
that the implementation of green data centers is not only 
to save the earth but can significantly reduce operational 
costs. It may indeed require higher initial investment 
(CAPEX), but that will be covered by low operating 
costs (OPEX). For Indonesia and other tropical 
countries, more attention needs to the achievement of 
green performance for DC because there are no natural 
facilities in the form of free cooling in winter. For this 
reason, GBCI and IPUSTAH-ID (Indonesian Data 
Center Professional Association) have published a 
Greenship Data Center assessment tool that pays close 
attention to the natural and artificial environmental 
conditions in Indonesia" and a research model was

FROM MARCH TO JUNE 2025, THE UiTM GREEN CENTRE (UGC) CONDUCTED A FIVE-PART, FIVE-DAY SUSTAINABILITY BENCHMARKING
TOUR TO EXPLORE AND STUDY BEST PRACTICES IN SUSTAINABILITY AMONG PUBLIC HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS IN MALAYSIA.
THE TOUR BEGAN WITH A VISIT TO UNIVERSITI ISLAM ANTARABANGSA MALAYSIA (UIAM), FOLLOWED BY UNIVERSITI PUTRA MALAYSIA
(UPM), UNIVERSITI TEKNOLOGI MALAYSIA (UTM), UNIVERSITI SAINS MALAYSIA (USM), AND CONCLUDED AT UNIVERSITI MALAYSIA
SARAWAK (UNIMAS).
THE DELEGATION—LED BY THE DEPUTY VICE-CHANCELLOR (DEVELOPMENT), UGC DIRECTOR, SUSTAINABILITY COORDINATORS, AND
UGC FELLOWS—PARTICIPATED IN KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE SESSIONS FOCUSING ON KEY SUSTAINABILITY PILLARS, INCLUDING:
GREEN INFRASTRUCTURE, ENERGY EFFICIENCY, WATER AND WASTE MANAGEMENT, SUSTAINABLE TRANSPORTATION, AND
ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
NOTABLE PRACTICES OBSERVED INCLUDED THE INTEGRATION OF SOLAR POWER SYSTEMS, ZERO-WASTE CAMPAIGNS, GREEN
BUILDING CERTIFICATIONS, BIODIVERSITY PRESERVATION EFFORTS, AND ACTIVE STUDENT INVOLVEMENT IN ECO-FRIENDLY
PROGRAMS.
THIS BENCHMARKING INITIATIVE PROVIDED VALUABLE INSIGHTS INTO INSTITUTIONAL GOVERNANCE, STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT,
AND THE IMPLEMENTATION OF SUSTAINABILITY FRAMEWORKS SUCH AS THE UI GREENMETRIC WORLD UNIVERSITY RANKINGS. IT ALSO
EMPHASIZED THE IMPORTANCE OF DATA MONITORING, POLICY COMMITMENT, AND CROSS-FUNCTIONAL COLLABORATION IN
REALIZING A HOLISTIC GREEN CAMPUS MODEL.
THE FINDINGS FROM THIS TOUR WILL SERVE AS A FOUNDATION TO STRENGTHEN UiTM’S SUSTAINABILITY ROADMAP, ENSURING THE
CAMPUS NOT ONLY MEETS BUT EXCEEDS ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND ECONOMIC SUSTAINABILITY STANDARDS. THROUGH SHARED
LEARNING AND STRATEGIC ADAPTATION, PUBLIC UNIVERSITIES IN MALAYSIA CAN COLLECTIVELY CONTRIBUTE TOWARD A GREENER,
