Assessment of the spatial inequality 
and configuration of recreational green spaces 
in the urban centre of Nowshera, Pakistan
Muhammad Ibrahim1*, Niaz Ahmad1, Waqas Ahmed Mahar2 and Muhammad Jamal Nasir3
1  Introduction
Globally, the population ratio between urban and rural is rapidly changing, which causes 
rapid urbanisation and its associated consequences [1]. Similarly, urbanisation in Paki­
stan is 36.4% and it is expected to reach up to 40% by 2030 [2]. Urbanisation challenges 
in Pakistan include urban environment degradation, i.e. the land, watersheds, infrastruc­
ture, air and water quality, and damage to urban ecology [3]. Urbanisation has changed 
Discover Cities
Abstract
Green spaces are vital for fostering sustainable and healthy urban living. This study 
examines the spatial inequality in the provision and distribution of recreational 
facilities in the rapidly growing urban centre of Nowshera District, Pakistan. Field 
surveys, spatial statistics, and geospatial analysis were used to evaluate both the 
accessibility and spatial arrangement of recreational spaces. The Two-Step Floating 
Catchment Area (2SFCA) analysis revealed that 67% of residential areas exceed the 
recommended 1-km service radius, indicating significant gaps in spatial coverage. 
Notably, an inverse relationship was observed, with higher-density neighbourhoods 
experiencing lower accessibility to recreational facilities, highlighting inequity in 
provision. Overall, only 2.7% of the city’s land is allocated to recreational green 
spaces, offering just 4.1 m² per capita, well below the WHO (9 m²), EU (26 m²), and 
UN (30 m²) standards, as well as national planning guidelines of 5–10%. Landscape 
metrics further indicated a fragmented network, with a patch density of 26.77 
patches/km², a low patch cohesion index of 9.73, and an average shape ratio of 0.56, 
reflecting irregular and ecologically weak green spaces. These results underscore a 
significant shortfall in both the quantity and spatial equity of recreational facilities. 
This study provides data-driven insights for urban planners and policymakers, 
emphasising the importance of prioritising green space development in densely 
populated areas and improving spatial planning to enhance urban livability, climate 
resilience, and alignment with Sustainable Development Goal 11 (Sustainable Cities 
and Communities).
Keywords  Recreational spaces, Sustainable land use, Spatial distribution, Spatial 
analysis, Per capita provision, Catchment area

Page 2 of 23
Ibrahim et al. Discover Cities           (2025) 2:113 
the pattern of urban development, as the natural areas, such as cultivation fields, forests, 
and other open spaces, are taken up and converted into built-up areas due to agglom­
eration and a consistent increase in population [4, 5]. This process has exacerbated the 
transformation in land uses within the urban enclaves, leading to environmental deg­
radation through deforestation and alterations of natural topography to accommo­
date taller buildings, water supply, sewage, and transportation works, which negatively 
impact land and soil, ecosystem diversity, flora, noise levels, and water and air quality 
both inside the city and in surrounding areas [6].
Researchers around the world define urban green spaces as public, semi-public or pri­
vate areas within cities, mainly covered with vegetation. These spaces provide oppor­
tunities for active and passive recreation, directly enhance the urban environment, and 
indirectly exist to serve the public [7, 8]. According to this study, the word ‘Recreational 
facility’ means an area referred to as all spaces covered primarily by vegetation, includ­
ing parks, gardens, playing fields, golf courses and woodland that fall within the urban 
enclave. These facilities are generally classified into active and passive types, depending 
on the nature of recreational use [9]. Recreation facilities are essential to maintaining 
the socio-environmental balance within cities [10]. However, recreational facilities in 
developing countries are under threat and in decline over time. The decrease is not only 
occurring in quantity and quality, but it is also difficult to maintain and sustain the exist­
ing facilities [11]. Livability and sustainability largely depend on the quantity and spatial 
distribution of green spaces within the city. A sustainable urban ecosystem and quality of 
life are greatly influenced by green spaces that exist in the city [12]. Similarly, the spatial 
distribution of green spaces aims to achieve equitable access and benefits for residents 
across urban areas, considering factors like population density, existing infrastructure, 
and local needs. This approach ensures that green spaces are strategically located to 
maximise their positive impacts on health, well-being, and community cohesion [13].
The availability of recreational facilities or green space per person serves as an impor­
tant metric for determining the necessary quantity to sustain an urban ecosystem by 
utilising per capita as a tool for provision [14]. Vienna, the world’s most liveable city, 
has reserved 51% of its land for green spaces. The per capita green space is 120 square 
meters [15]. This per capita provision is far higher than the World Health Organisation 
(WHO) suggested of a minimum of 9 square metres of green space per person [16]. 
Istanbul, the third-densest city in the world, serve as a role model for spatial planning as 
it successfully combines extensive green spaces within high population density. However, 
it falls short in providing only 6.4 square metres of green space per person. Other cities 
like Tokyo and Buenos Aires provide even less green space per person [17]. In contrast, 
Pakistani cities, including Nowshera, face even greater challenges, with per capita green 
space provision far below the International benchmarks. This underscores the urgency of 
assessing and addressing spatial inequality in green space distribution at the local level.
The comparative analysis of cities with the highest per capita green space is depicted 
in Fig. 1. below.
  
Green spaces should be developed from a micro to a macro level. However, the major 
problem is the unavailability of land within the densely populated neighbourhoods of 
cities [19]. The per capita green space in cities is reducing due to high population growth 
rates and less provision of green spaces [20].

Page 3 of 23
Ibrahim et al. Discover Cities           (2025) 2:113 
Therefore, this study seeks to evaluate the vulnerability of urban green spaces and 
to analyze the extent to which factors such as the decline of green space, expansion of 
built-up areas, population growth, and urban sprawl contribute to this vulnerability. The 
United Nations (UN), European Union (EU), and World Health Organisation (WHO) 
standards were used to determine the vulnerability of cities to green space reduction, 
namely UN’s recommendation of more than 30 m² per person [21], the EU’s minimum 
value of 26 m² per person [22], and WHO’s benchmark of 9 m² per person [23].
This study focuses on District Nowshera Urban Centre, strategically located between 
Peshawar and Islamabad, which serves as a vital urban and economic corridor in Khy­
ber Pakhtunkhwa. Its proximity to the Motorway (M-1), major trade routes, and the 
Kabul River has positioned it as a growing hub for industrial, residential, and transit-
oriented development. The city is currently experiencing rapid urbanisation and land 
use transformation, prompting the need for sustainable spatial planning and infrastruc­
ture improvement. Despite these issues, there has been limited scholarly attention to the 
spatial distribution and equity of recreational green spaces in Nowshera, as most stud­
ies in Pakistan focus on larger metropolitan centres. Examining Nowshera, therefore, 
addresses an important research gap and provides insights that can inform planning for 
other rapidly urbanising secondary and tertiary cities [24].
This study is significant because it addresses the critical issue of spatial inequality in 
recreational green spaces in a rapidly urbanising tertiary city, a topic that has received 
limited attention in Pakistan compared to larger metropolitan centres. The main objec­
tives are to (i) assess the quantity and per capita provision of recreational green spaces, 
(ii) evaluate their spatial distribution and accessibility using the Two-Step Floating Catch­
ment Area (2SFCA) method, and (iii) analyse their spatial configuration through land­
scape metrics. By achieving these objectives, the study provides evidence on the extent 
of inequality in access to recreational spaces and highlights how these disparities affect 
urban livability. The implications extend to urban planning and policy, underscoring the 
need for equitable provision and improved green infrastructure in line with international 
standards and Sustainable Development Goal 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities).
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Sect. 2 describes the study area, 
data sources, and methods used for spatial analysis. Section  3 presents key findings 
related to green space distribution, accessibility, and layout. Section 4 discusses the impli­
cations of these findings. Section 5 outlines limitations and recommends directions for 
future research. Section  6 provides recommendations for city green spaces. Section  7 
concludes with planning and policy suggestions for improving recreational green space 
provision in Nowshera City.
Fig. 1  Per capita green space provision in most livable cities of the world [18]
 

Page 4 of 23
Ibrahim et al. Discover Cities           (2025) 2:113 
2  Materials and methods
2.1  Study area
This study was conducted in Nowshera Urban Centre, a tertiary-level city located in the 
Peshawar Valley, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. The district is situated between 33° 04′ 
00′′to 34° 10 ′ 00′′ N latitude and 71° 44 ′ 50′′ to 72° 15 ′05′′ E longitude, and bordered 
by Peshawar to the west, Charsadda to the northwest, Mardan to the north, Swabi to 
the east, and Attock District to the south. The total area of District Nowshera is 1,712 
km², with the core urban area covering approximately 20.8 km² [24], which was selected 
for analysis as it constitutes the main administrative boundary of Nowshera City and 
contains the highest concentration of population and recreational facilities. Administra­
tively, the city is divided between the Tehsil Municipal Administration (TMA) and the 
Cantonment Board Nowshera (CBN). Due to rapid population growth and urban expan­
sion, the city is increasingly under pressure to accommodate essential public facilities, 
particularly recreational spaces [25]. Figure 2 shows the location of the study area.
2.2  Research methodology
This study used an integrated methodological framework that combines geospatial data 
and spatial analysis to evaluate urban landscape patterns, accessibility, and land use. 
Population, satellite, and infrastructure data inform three main analyses: landscape 
metrics (e.g., patch density, shape index), accessibility mapping using the 2SFCA, and 
equity analysis, as well as green space statistics. The findings are synthesised to support 
evidence-based policy recommendations for sustainable and inclusive green space plan­
ning. Figure 3 depicts the methodological framework adopted for the study.
Fig. 2  Location Map of Nowshera City. Source: Author (2025)
 

Page 5 of 23
Ibrahim et al. Discover Cities           (2025) 2:113 
2.3  Data
2.3.1  Secondary data
In this study, we utilized a variety of secondary data sources to ensure a robust and 
evidence-based analysis. Demographic and population data were acquired from the 
Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS), providing historical population figures essential for 
projecting future urban growth using a geometric growth model [2]. Official land use 
plan and GIS shapefiles were sourced from the Urban Policy and Planning Unit (UPPU) 
of the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, aiding in the mapping and categorisation 
of existing land use as per the Land Use and Building Control Act (The Khyber Pak­
htunkhwa Land Use and Building Control Act, 2021) [26]. Additionally, national and 
international planning and design standards were referenced to benchmark green space 
provision, including the Pakistan National Reference Manual [9], the World Health 
Fig. 3  Research Methodology Flowchart
 

Page 6 of 23
Ibrahim et al. Discover Cities           (2025) 2:113 
Organisation [27], the United Nations [28], and the European Union’s guidelines [29], 
ensuring that per capita recreational space calculations aligned with globally recognised 
norms.
2.3.2  Survey data
Primary data for this study were obtained through a structured and self-administered 
field survey, carried out by the principal researcher with the assistance of two trained 
survey enumerators hired specifically for this purpose. The fieldwork spanned over four 
weeks and was designed to validate satellite-based land use classifications, with a par­
ticular focus on identifying, assessing, and geolocating recreational and green spaces 
within the study area.
To ensure systematic data collection, a standardised field survey checklist was devel­
oped and used during site visits. This checklist captured key attributes, including the 
type of recreational facility (e.g., park, playground, green belt), its approximate area 
(measured on-site), physical condition, level of maintenance, accessibility, user activ­
ity levels, surrounding land use context, and any visible environmental issues such as 
encroachment or degradation. We measured the user activity levels qualitatively by 
noting visible patterns of use observed during site visits (e.g., children playing, fami­
lies sitting, or the facility remaining vacant). Notes and photographs were also taken for 
qualitative documentation.
Ground truthing activities were supported by the use of a Garmin eTrex 32x handheld 
GPS device, which provided reliable coordinates with an average horizontal accuracy of 
± 3 m. No formal accuracy assessment metrics were conducted, as the device’s ± 3 m pre­
cision was considered adequate for the urban-scale spatial analysis in this study. Like­
wise, no additional corrections for potential urban canyon effects were applied, since 
most recreational sites in Nowshera are situated in open or low-rise areas where such 
errors are minimal. The GPS points were recorded for each recreational site and later 
imported into ArcGIS Pro 3.4 for geospatial digitisation and spatial analysis. All GPS 
coordinates were initially recorded using the WGS 84 datum and later refined in ArcGIS 
Pro through high-resolution satellite imagery embedded within the software’s basemap 
gallery. This process ensured precise georeferencing and consistency across all spatial 
datasets. The field data not only facilitated the validation of remotely sensed land use 
classifications but also enabled the real-time identification of new or unregistered recre­
ational facilities and ongoing development activities not yet reflected in official datasets 
or satellite archives. This ground-based approach significantly enhanced the reliability 
and spatial accuracy of the urban green space inventory and provided critical insights 
into the state and distribution of recreational facilities in the study area.
2.4  Methods
2.4.1  Demographic analysis
Population dynamics were analysed to determine the spatial needs and distribution of 
public recreational facilities, which are often devised by national and international stan­
dards. Data for current and historical population levels were acquired from the Pakistan 
Bureau of Statistics. Using a geometric growth model based on past trends, the popu­
lation of Nowshera City was projected for two decades to estimate future recreational 
demand. We use the geometric growth model to forecast future population dynamics 

Page 7 of 23
Ibrahim et al. Discover Cities           (2025) 2:113 
and estimate the demand/need for recreational facilities. This model assumes a constant 
annual growth rate and is expressed by the following equation:
P t = P 0 × (1 + r)t
where:
 	•
Pₜ = projected population after t years.
 	•
P₀ = base year population.
 	•
r = annual growth rate (in decimal form).
 	•
t = number of years from the base year.
This approach assumes that the population grows at a constant rate annually, with each 
year’s growth building on the previous year’s total, resulting in exponential growth over 
time.
This projection is crucial to determine the future demand for parkland and open 
spaces, especially as the city’s population is expected to grow rapidly. The relation­
ship between population growth and per capita green space availability was assessed to 
determine how well the city meets minimum standards set by organisations such as the 
WHO, the UN, and the National Reference Manual of Pakistan.
2.4.2  Existing land use distribution
We determined the green spaces’ spatial distribution through field surveys. The exist­
ing land use classes were categorised following the Land Use and Building Control Act 
(2021) [26]. Secondary data, such as official land use plans and GIS shapefiles, were 
obtained from the Urban Policy and Planning Unit (UPPU) of the Government of Khy­
ber Pakhtunkhwa. This data was complemented by ground-truthing conducted through 
field surveys, which verified recent land use changes and helped to assess the size, condi­
tion, and extent of recreational facilities across the urban fabric.
2.4.3  Mapping and Spatial analysis of recreational facilities
Based on the definitions provided in the Pakistan National Reference Manual [9], Rec­
reational facilities encompass public parks, community playgrounds, open green spaces, 
botanical and zoological gardens, sports complexes, and similar land use categories. 
These features were digitised and mapped using ArcGIS Pro 3.4. Additionally, field-
verified geolocations were incorporated with spatial layers to facilitate a comprehensive 
GIS-based analysis.
2.4.4  Per capita provision and planning standards comparison
To determine the adequacy of recreational land provision, the per capita green space was 
calculated using the formula: total recreational area divided by the urban population. 
These values were compared against national and international benchmarks. Pakistan’s 
National Reference Manual standard of 5.2 m² per person, WHO’s minimum standard of 
9 m², the UN’s recommended 30 m², and the EU’s 26 m². Deficiencies were calculated for 
each benchmark to quantify the shortfall in recreational service provision. Additionally, 
population density and future growth projections were used to estimate the additional 
green space required to meet future standards.

Page 8 of 23
Ibrahim et al. Discover Cities           (2025) 2:113 
2.4.5  Two-Step floating catchment area (2SFCA) method for assessing park accessibility
To assess spatial accessibility to recreational spaces in the study area, the Two-Step 
Floating Catchment Area (2SFCA) method was applied using ArcGIS Pro. The method 
evaluates the balance between the supply of parks and the population demand within 
defined spatial catchments. This approach integrates both supply (availability of parks 
within catchments) and demand (population density within those catchments) to quan­
tify the degree of service provision. The accessibility index is computed as:
AIi =
∑
jϵdij≤D
Sj
Pj
where the accessibility index AIi​ represents the accessibility score for a population loca­
tion i, based on its proximity to available recreational facilities. It is calculated by sum­
ming the ratio of available supply Sj​ to demand Pj for all recreational facilities j that fall 
within a predefined catchment distance D from location i. Here, Sj​ refers to the supply of 
recreational facility j, typically measured by the park area in square meters or hectares. 
Pj​ represents the total population residing within the catchment area of facility j, which 
is considered to be the demand on that facility. The term dij​ denotes the Euclidean or 
network distance between population location i and facility j. Finally, D is a user-defined 
threshold that sets the maximum catchment distance, commonly set to 1-km, depending 
on policy standards or pedestrian mobility assumptions. The centroids of Neighbour­
hood Councils (NCs), each containing population data, were used as demand points. In 
the first step, 1-km Euclidean buffers were created around each park to define their ser­
vice areas. Using the Spatial Join tool, the population within each park’s catchment area 
was calculated by intersecting the park buffers with the NC centroids. A park-to-pop­
ulation ratio was computed for each park by dividing the park area (in square meters) 
by the population within its 1-km buffer. In the second step, a 1-km buffer was created 
around each NC centroid to identify accessible parks within walking distance. A spatial 
join between these population buffers and the park ratio layer identified all parks that 
each NC centroid could access. The Accessibility Index (AI) was calculated for each NC 
centroid by summing the park-to-population ratio of all accessible parks. The resulting 
AI values were then joined to the NC centroid layer and symbolised using graduated 
colours to visualise spatial disparities in park access. Areas with higher AI values indi­
cated better accessibility to green spaces, while lower values highlighted underserved 
neighbourhoods in need of recreational infrastructure improvements.
2.4.6  Landscape metrics analysis
To quantitatively evaluate the spatial arrangement and fragmentation of recreational 
green spaces within Nowshera City’s urban fabric, four key landscape metrics were cal­
culated: Patch Density (PD), Edge Density (ED), Aggregation Index (AI), and Landscape 
Shape Index (LSI). These metrics offer insights into the complexity, distribution, and 
connectivity of green spaces and are commonly used in urban landscape ecology. The 
analysis was carried out using the LecoS (Landscape Ecology Statistics) plugin in QGIS 
3.34, an open-source GIS platform designed for raster-based landscape analysis. The 
green space polygon shapefile was rasterised in ArcMap 10.8 using the Polygon to Ras­
ter tool, assigning a value of 1 to all green space patches. The raster was projected using 
EPSG:32,642 (WGS 84/UTM Zone 42 N), with a cell resolution of 10 m. This resolution 

Page 9 of 23
Ibrahim et al. Discover Cities           (2025) 2:113 
was chosen to provide sufficient detail to capture small urban recreational patches while 
maintaining computational efficiency for landscape metrics analysis.
After that, we imported the resulting GeoTIFF raster into QGIS for landscape metrics 
computation and analysis. Patch Density (PD) was utilised to determine the number of 
discrete green space patches per square kilometre within the urban landscape, serving 
as a key indicator of spatial fragmentation. A higher patch density value reflects a more 
fragmented pattern, characterised by numerous small, isolated green spaces rather than 
larger, contiguous ones. To further understand the configuration of these patches, Edge 
Density (ED) was computed, which quantifies the total length of green space edges per 
unit area. This metric highlights the extent to which green spaces are exposed to adja­
cent land uses, with higher edge density indicating increased edge effects and ecological 
vulnerability. The Aggregation Index (AI) was employed to measure the degree of spatial 
cohesion among green space patches. This index illustrates the degree to which patches 
are clustered or dispersed within the landscape, with higher values indicating stronger 
connectivity and more compact spatial configurations. Lastly, the Landscape Shape 
Index (LSI) was calculated to assess the geometric complexity of green space patches rel­
ative to standard shapes. An elevated LSI value denotes more irregular and fragmented 
patch forms, which can affect both ecological function and recreational accessibility. 
Together, these four metrics provide a comprehensive assessment of the spatial struc­
ture, connectivity, and quality of urban green spaces.
2.4.7  Results validation
Several validation techniques were taken into consideration in order to guarantee the 
accuracy of the findings. The study’s spatial data came from official sources and was con­
firmed by in-depth field surveys, which allowed for on-site verification of recreational 
facilities. To verify position accuracy (± 3 m), GPS coordinates were compared to Arc­
GIS Pro datasets. While no formal statistical accuracy assessment was conducted, con­
sistency between field observations, municipal records, and geospatial analysis provides 
confidence in the validity of the mapped facilities. Moreover, the results showing a 2.7% 
green space share and 4.1 m² per capita provision are broadly consistent with figures 
reported in studies of other Pakistani cities (e.g., Lahore, Karachi, and Peshawar), further 
supporting the credibility of the analysis. Nonetheless, the study recognises that omis­
sion of informal or incidental green spaces may slightly underrepresent actual availabil­
ity, a limitation that future research should address.
3  Results
3.1  Population analysis in Nowshera City
According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, the population of Nowshera City 
increased from 89,849 in 1998 to 136,008 in 2023, indicating a compound annual growth 
rate of approximately 2.07% [2]. Using the geometric growth model, the population of 
Nowshera City was projected from the base year 2023 (136,008 persons) up to the year 
2040. These projections assume that the annual growth rate of 2.07% remains constant, 
without accounting for potential migration flows, major policy changes, or unforeseen 
demographic shifts. Thus, the results are to be interpreted as baseline estimates under 
current growth conditions.

The projections indicate that the population will reach approximately 192,678 by 2040. 
Similarly, the number of housing units is expected to rise from 19,430 in 2023 to 27,525

3.2  Population-based provision of recreational facilities
In Pakistan, the provision of recreational facilities was legally instrumented through the 
National Reference Manual (NRM) [9]. This comprehensive document elaborates on the 
importance of recreational facilities and their benefits. The report outlined population- 
and area-based standards to serve as a tool for guiding provision and implementation by 
development authorities in the country. The active and passive recreational facility type, 
level, and size were presented in Tables 1 and 2.
Based on the existing and projected population, a plan was formulated to address both 
the present gap and future needs for recreational facilities. The calculations follow the 
guidelines drawn in the National Reference Manual. Nowshera City should have one 
community-level, five neighbourhood-level and twenty-two sub-neighbourhood parks, 
as per the 2023 population. Similarly, one community-level playground and five neigh­
bourhood-level playgrounds are to be provided by 2023. The analysis detail is given in 
Table 3.

3.4  Recreational facilities in Nowshera City

3.5  Spatial disparities: concentration and deficiency patterns
Recreational facilities are unevenly distributed across the study area. The inner city, 
despite its high population density, lacks designated recreational spaces, while newer 
residential areas such as the ASC Colony include several mini-parks within their local­
ity. Nowshera Kalla has limited recreational provision, with little room available for new 
development. The city is also rapidly expanding toward the north and northeast, under­
scoring the need for development authorities to allocate land for future parks and play­
grounds. Accessibility in terms of distance from residents’ homes to the nearest facility 
remains a key indicator of the sustainability of these spaces. Figure 7 illustrates the spa­
tial provision of recreational facilities, showing that approximately 78% of inner-city 
residents and 85% of peripheral residents live beyond the recommended 1-km service 
radius. These results confirm that most settlements lack adequate recreational facilities 
within their jurisdiction. Figure 7 shows the spatial provision of recreational facilities 
within the city. It has been observed that most of the settlements lack these facilities 
within their jurisdiction.

3.6.1  Accessibility index and coverage assessment (Simplified 2SFCA)
The resulting index values were mapped across the study area. Neighbourhoods with an 
accessibility index below 1 were classified as underserved. These included dense urban

versely, neighbourhoods with an index greater than or equal to 1 demonstrated adequate 
recreational coverage.
Overlaying the population density data with the accessibility index revealed signifi­
cant spatial disparities. High-density areas were often those with the lowest recreational 
access, creating an inverse relationship between need and provision. This reflects both 
the legacy of unplanned urban growth and the under-prioritisation of recreational infra­
structure in core urban planning policies. The analysis strongly suggests that without 
immediate intervention, these underserved zones will continue to face heightened risks 
of social exclusion, environmental stress, and diminished quality of life. Prioritisation 
of infill parks and conversion of community-owned vacant land (such as the Shamelath 
land near DHQ hospital) into green public space is a strategic imperative. Figure 8 shows

3.7  Per capita recreational space in Nowshera City
Cities’ livability mostly depends on their social, economic, and environmental condi­
tions. To make our cities liveable, the provision of green spaces according to the stan­

National and International standards set for the most livable and sustainable city.
3.8  Landscape metrics of green spaces
The spatial configuration of urban green spaces in Nowshera was analysed using four 
key landscape metrics derived through the LecoS plugin in QGIS. The analysis of urban 
green space structure in Nowshera reveals a landscape experiencing moderate ecological 
pressures from urbanisation while retaining some functional connectivity. With a patch 
density of 26.77 patches/km², the city’s green infrastructure shows considerable frag­
mentation, with natural areas subdivided into numerous smaller patches due to urban 
expansion. This fragmentation pattern is further characterised by a patch cohesion index 
of 9.73, indicating that while green spaces maintain some degree of ecological connectiv­
ity, there exists room for improvement through strategic urban planning. The edge den­
sity measurement of 20.46 m/ha suggests considerable interface between green spaces 
and built environments, creating transitional zones that may experience ecological edge 
effects while simultaneously increasing human accessibility. Notably, the shape ratio of 
0.56 reflects a landscape where green spaces exhibit moderately geometric forms, sug­
gesting a combination of intentionally designed recreational areas and remnant natural 
vegetation. These metrics collectively paint a picture of an urban ecosystem where green

4  Discussion
The analysis reveals that recreational facilities in Nowshera are in a poor state, with lim­
ited maintenance, inadequate basic amenities, and a lack of greenery. Land use analysis 
shows that only 2.47% of the city’s total area is dedicated to recreational spaces. This 
2.47% recreational land coverage in Nowshera is stark when compared with other urban 
centres in Pakistan. For instance, Karachi allocates about 5% of its area to green spaces 
[30], while Peshawar and Multan fall in a similar range of 4–6% [31, 32]. Islamabad per­
forms comparatively better, with approximately 7–9% green cover, reflecting its planned 
urban structure [33]. Nowshera’s figure not only falls below the national standard of 
5–7% but also lags behind other major cities, emphasising the critical shortage of rec­
reational green space provision. which falls significantly below the national planning 
standard of at least 5–7% for urban areas. This deficiency indicates that recreational pro­
vision has not been prioritised in local planning agendas.
These findings have strong implications under the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Land-Use and 
Building Control Act, 2021. For example, Sect. 15(3) classifies ‘recreational area’ as a dis­
tinct land-use category; Sect. 16 mandates that district master plans include description 
and measurement of open and green spaces; and Sect. 52 authorizes rules for ‘green area 
regulations in land use zones.’ Taken together, these clauses legally support more equi­
table provision of recreational green spaces in high-density areas.
Demographic projections further intensify this concern. The city’s population of 
136,008 in 2023 is expected to increase to approximately 192,678 within the next two 
decades. This rapid growth will create additional demand for recreational spaces that 
the current supply is far from capable of meeting. At present, Nowshera has only 1 city-
level, 10 neighbourhood-level, and 5 sub-neighbourhood-level recreational facilities. 
Their spatial distribution is uneven, with newer residential societies such as ASC Colony

Per capita availability is also critically low, standing at 4.1 m² per person. This is far 
below international benchmarks, including the WHO (9  m²), EU (26  m²), and UN 
(30  m²) standards, and does not even meet national planning thresholds. The WHO

mental stress, reduced opportunities for physical activity, and diminished community

expand and equitably distribute recreational facilities. Future planning should prioritise 
high-density neighbourhoods, safeguard existing green areas from encroachment, and 
incorporate health-oriented design principles to enhance urban livability. Importantly, 
these findings align with the provisions of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Land Use and Build­
ing Control Act 2021, which mandates the integration of recreational areas into formal 
planning frameworks.
Landscape metrics confirm that the existing recreational areas form a fragmented 
network, with low cohesion and irregular shapes that reduce their ecological and social 
value. Such fragmentation undermines not only recreational quality but also the broader 
functions of green infrastructure, including biodiversity support, heat mitigation, and 
improved urban resilience.
To situate Nowshera’s green space provision in a broader South Asian context, a com­
parative assessment was undertaken with other regional cities where similar studies have 
been conducted. As shown in Table 4, Nowshera records only 2.7% of its urban area as 
recreational green space, equivalent to 4.1 m² per capita. This figure is lower than Lahore 
(5% and 7.3 m²) [34], Karachi (6.3–11.3% and 4.17 m²) [35], and Dhaka (8.5% and 4.8 
m²) [36]. Delhi shows significant variation depending on the definition applied, with 
estimates ranging from 10.6% (5.5 m²) [37]. These comparisons highlight that Nowshera 
lags behind several regional counterparts in both the absolute share of green land and in 
per capita provision. Importantly, all of the reported figures remain below international 
benchmarks set by WHO, EU, and UN standards, underscoring a region-wide challenge 
of inadequate recreational space provision in rapidly urbanizing South Asian cities.
The challenges are compounded by rapid land-use changes and residential densifi­
cation in the inner city, where little to no land is available for new green space devel­
opment. Existing spaces are increasingly threatened by competing land uses and 
conversions, often driven by a lack of awareness among both authorities and residents 
about the long-term environmental, social, and health benefits of urban green spaces.

These findings emphasise the urgent need for strategic urban planning measures. 
Priority should be given to safeguarding existing recreational spaces, reclaiming unde­

This study resonates strongly with the objectives of Pakistan’s Vision 2040 and the 
United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communi­

table service provision, and climate resilience, which are directly connected to adequate 
green infrastructure. Similarly, SDG 11 emphasizes universal access to safe, inclusive, 
and accessible green and public spaces, particularly for vulnerable groups such as 
women, children, and the elderly. By identifying the stark shortfall in recreational green 
space in Nowshera (4.1 m² per capita versus the WHO benchmark of 9 m²), this study 
highlights a critical area where urban policy interventions can make tangible contri­
butions toward achieving both national and international development commitments. 
Enhancing green space provision in Nowshera would not only improve urban livabil­
ity and public health but also position the city as a model for applying the principles of 
Vision 2040 and Sustainable Development Goal 11 in medium-sized urban centers of 
Pakistan.
5  Study limitations
Although this study offers valuable insights into the spatial arrangement and accessibil­
ity of green spaces in Nowshera City, several limitations must also be recognised. Firstly, 
the analysis was limited to officially designated parks and playgrounds, and informal 
or incidental green spaces (e.g., vacant plots, riverbanks, roadside vegetation) were not 
systematically assessed. This focus may introduce sampling bias, as residents often use 
such spaces for recreation in the absence of formal facilities. In addition, the absence 
of disaggregated secondary datasets constrained opportunities for statistical valida­
tion. Future research should incorporate both formal and informal green spaces, com­
bined with household surveys or perception studies, to capture a more complete picture 
of recreational accessibility. Secondly, the analysis relies on Euclidean distance rather 
than network-based travel routes, which may not accurately reflect actual walkability or 
pedestrian access, particularly in areas with complex street layouts or obstacles. Thirdly, 
the field survey, though comprehensive, was constrained in duration and scope and may 
have overlooked informal or underutilised recreational spaces not officially acknowl­
edged by planning authorities. Fourthly, the study depends heavily on static population 
data from 2023, without accounting for dynamic population movements or seasonal 
fluctuations that could affect park usage and demand. Fifthly, due to the absence of dis­
aggregated socioeconomic data, the study was unable to evaluate the equity of access 
across income groups, genders, or age cohorts. While this study provides a comprehen­
sive spatial analysis of recreational green spaces, formal validation of results was con­
strained by the absence of detailed secondary datasets for Nowshera. Nevertheless,

6  Recommendations
Based on the above analysis and field surveys, specific recommendations have been 
made to address the challenges faced by residents and authorities regarding green space 
provision.
i.	 It is the most crucial fact that recreational facility provision in the city centre is a 
gigantic task for authorities due to several limitations. For example, in the study 
area, there are several private plots still vacant that can be utilised for the quantity 
improvement of recreational facilities. There are high land prices in the inner city, 
making it quite difficult for the authorities to purchase these plots by giving due 
compensation to the owners. The authorities can acquire these plots by providing 
annual under-development incentive fees to the owners. The under-development fees 
fund may also be recovered from the user of these spaces and facilities, or by raising 
the holding tax for that particular community person for whom these dedicated 
spaces have been provided.
ii.	 Nowshera City is suffering from an acute shortage of recreational facilities. The existing 
parks are also inaccessible to marginalised communities of the city. Accessibility 
must be given due consideration when building a recreational facility within the city. 
Women, children and elderly people shall be able to reach the nearby facility within 5 
to 10 min of walking distance.
iii.	Within the study area, some parcels of barren or vacant land remain underutilised. 
The case of Shamelat (community-owned), with ownership shared collectively rather 
than by a single individual. The land in front of the DHQ hospital provides a unique 
opportunity for local authorities to initiate a pilot project. Converting this 29-kanal 
parcel into a model community park by 2025 would demonstrate the feasibility of 
repurposing community-owned land for public benefit. Such a project could showcase

7  Conclusion
Developing countries like Pakistan have densely populated urban centres with multiple 
activities occurring in the centre of these cities. The recreational facilities have a posi­
tive impact on the lives of the residents. It is one of the most important indicators for 
the sustainable development of the city. However, it is in greater decline due to popula­
tion increase, which is replacing these spaces with other competing land uses. To assess 
this issue and the challenges for the provision of recreational facilities to the existing 
and future population of the city. Therefore, this research is articulated to evaluate the 
recreational facilities within the tertiary-level urban centre of Nowshera City. This city 
is facing an acute shortage of recreational facilities. The city’s land use shows that a 
major portion of land is occupied by residential and other land uses, while only 2.7% is 
dedicated to recreational uses. There are only 15 recreational facilities, which are not 
sufficient for the existing residents. Based on the results obtained with the help of GIS 
technology, it was determined that these recreational facilities are not equally distrib­
uted throughout the city. The accessibility/coverage is also extremely limited compared 
to the national and international benchmarks set around the world. This research identi­
fied several localities that had few or no green spaces provided. Some residential areas 
were far from the existing facilities. Subsequently, the study area shows a significant 
shortfall of adequate recreational facilities to improve the quality of life and sustain­
ability. The specific recommendations regarding the planning and development of these 
facilities were given to improve the quality, quantity, and accessibility in the study area.
This research provides a benchmark for the development authorities to prioritise 
accessible, gender-inclusive, and good-quality recreational facilities, which are environ­
mentally sound and socially acceptable. This research contributes to the overall livability 
of the built environment, which is the primary focus of the Sustainable Development 
Goals.

Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through 
Green Contents: Exploring Eco-centric 
Consciousness among English Language Learners in 
Pakistan 
 
Imran Hussain 
PhD Scholar Faculty of Social Sciences & Humanities 
MY University, Islamabad, Pakistan  
Email: imranhussain.uol@gmail.com 
Tahira Parveen 
PhD Scholar Faculty of Social Sciences & Humanities 
MY University, Islamabad, Pakistan  
Dr. Ziarab Mehmood 
Associate Professor Faculty of Social Sciences & Humanities 
MY University, Islamabad, Pakistan 
 
Abstract 
Current study is projected to explore eco-centric consciousness and 
ecological literacy among English Language Learners (ELLs) in Pakistan 
through the eminence of integrating green contents in English Language 
Textbooks (ELT) or in curricula. The study supplementary demonstrates the 
requisite and essentiality to instigate ELLs conscious about environmental 
concerns and their potential imprints on human health in particular and life 
in general. In order to analyse the eco-centric consciousness and eco-literacy 
among ELLs for nurturing a sustainable ecological environ, the research has 
inferred a qualitative method of analysis to investigate green contents. Data 
is collected from ELT contents and to delimit the data green contents are 
extracted from elementary level ELT curriculum being taught under SNC 
2023 in Pakistan. Purposive sampling technique is being exploited to extort 
two units i.e. “Smog” from grade 7 and “Trees Plantation” from grade 8. The 
findings of the study designate that ELT contents are manoeuvred to foster 
environmental sustainability and eco-centric consciousness among ELLs of 
elementary level in Pakistan. It is derived through contrastive approach that 
has been espoused by the researcher with regard to assimilation of green 
contents in ELT. At one hand, ecological issues and challenges are 
incorporated through green contents and on the other hands, steps that are 
taken or being engaged to augment ecological literacy among ELLs are 
encapsulated in ELT contents. It is put in a nutshell through the analysis that 
green contents in ELT contents at elementary level in Pakistan have 
manipulating imprints on ELLs in order to nurture eco-centric consciousness 
and environmental sustainability. It has been undertaken through the 
projection of contrastive approach, i.e. projection of ecological menaces at 

 
 
72
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
one hand and tree plantation as a source of protecting environment and 
nurturing ecological literacy and sustainability among ELLs.  
Keywords: Eco-centric Consciousness, Eco-Literacy, Environmental 
Sustainability, Green Contents, Going Green, ELT, ELLs 
 
Introduction 
Climatic or environmental concerns and menaces have underway to spot 
their emergence since long are, at this instant, upsetting human life 
significantly in terms of health, mental and social dynamics (Stibbe, 2020). 
It is also an actuality, due to the climatic menaces, that if these are endorsed 
to keep going in an identical rate of knots these will have even more negative 
and adverse imprints on life and society (Faramarzi & Janfeshan, 2021). 
Hence, there is a mounting materialization among human to integrate eco-
literacy, environmental responsiveness and eco-centric consciousness into 
curriculum so that learners can be made conscious of these menaces. 
Environmental issues and language exploit are interrelational as language 
learning and teaching have immense persuasion in shaping learners thoughts 
and perceptions (Zia et al., 2022). Likewise, language has also deep-rooted 
sway as far as the social and cultural dynamics related to ecological menaces 
are concerned for a sustainable ecological future (Dash, 2019). 
Keeping in view, the essential correlation between language i.e. ELT and 
eco-literacy it turns out to be indispensable to slot in ecological insides i.e. 
green contents in English Language Teaching or Textbooks (ELT) as it will 
urge ELLs to be cognisant regarding the global environmental phenomenon 
(Zahoor & Janjua, 2020) at one hand and nurture their eco-centric 
consciousness for sustainable ecological future on the other. Faramarzi & 
Janfeshan (2021) encapsulated that integration of environment allied insides 
in ELT contents are effectual to construct ELLs attentiveness concerning 
global concerns with regard to nature, environment and eco-literacy. 
Students are better capable to grasp ecological issues, menaces and 
challenges, likewise they can be trained efficiently how to evade such issues 
and protect the ecological system for a sustainable environmental future 
primarily through incorporating green contents in ELT contents (Majeed et 
al., 2022). 
Luardini and Sujiyani (2018) avowed the notion that ELT contents are not 
merely effectual outfits for nurturing ELLs language skills but are uniformly 
advantageous for fostering attentiveness with regard to global concerns i.e. 
climatic or environmental issues for a global citizenship. In addition, ELT is 
an influential connectivity agent as language is utilized both either to 
construct a world-view or to contrive a certain notion (Mliless & Larouz, 
2018). Language, its learning or teaching, functions as a dominant agent to 
maximize the constructive action plan for societal networks in all facets of 
human bustle. Likewise, it is an imperative channel that can be resourcefully 
operated to tackle global climatic, environmental and ecological concerns at 

 
 
73
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
one hand and to develop ELLs mindfulness and enthralment to nurture their 
eco-centric literacy for an enhanced, secure and sustainable ecological future 
on the other (Goulah, 2017). 
Statement of the Problem  
Green contents in ELT are influential mediums to cultivate eco-centric 
consciousness among ELLs of Pakistan to promote environmental 
sustainability and ecological literacy through pinpointing global ecological 
menaces at one hand and instigate them to protect and endorse eco-centric 
future on the other. Academic contents are not simply restricted to academic 
activities and language learning abilities, rather these have the influencing 
and manipulating sway on the psyche of the young mind, especially at 
elementary level. Green contents integrated in ELT contents are effectual as 
far as the Going Green campaign is concerned. Likewise environmental and 
climatic concerns i.e. global warming, ozone layer depletion, population, 
overpopulation, water pollution, climate change, smog and deforestation are 
the green contents which are obligatory to be incorporated in ELT contents 
to assimilate eco-literacy among ELLs. Keeping in view, it is indispensable 
to weigh up the persona of green contents in ELT to craft ELLs eco-centric 
consciousness at one hand and activate them to sponsor environmental 
sustainability on the other. Therefore, the under view study is anticipated to 
highlight climatic and environmental menaces engulfing the globe to prop 
up eco-literacy. It is, in addition, intended at to figure out the steps being 
taken to promote environmental sustainability. Likewise, how ELLs react 
and are manipulated by these insides are also brought to light through their 
enthralment towards Going Green, tree plantation and budding garden at 
homes and schools. 
Research Objectives  
At hand, study is designed to accomplish the following research aims or 
objectives. 
• To probe the effectiveness of fostering green contents into ELT 
curriculum as denote to nurture eco-centric consciousness among 
ELLs of Pakistan.  
• To explore the empirical imprints of eco-centric consciousness on 
ELLs of Pakistan towards their approach and conduct towards 
environment. 
• To underline the key ecological menaces and environment friendly 
insides being integrated in green contents to incorporate eco-literacy 
among ELLs of Pakistan. 
Research Questions  
Bearing in mind the research objectives, subsequent research questions are 
intended to seek their answers in the study. 

 
 
74
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
• How far the integration of green contents in ELT contents is effectual 
as a mean to nurture eco-centric consciousness among ELLs of 
Pakistan? 
• How has eco-centric consciousness through green contents among 
ELLs urbanized their psyche towards environmental sustainability?  
• What and how are the ecological menaces and environment affable 
contents being incorporated in ELT contents? 
Significance of the Study  
As globe is in front of relentless ecological menaces and concerns, so the 
imperativeness of the under view study lies in exploring eco-centric 
consciousness of ELLs of Pakistan to enable them ecological cultured to 
exert for environmental sustainability. By spotlighting on how ELLs counter 
and intimate with climatic sustainability through green contents, the current 
study donates influentially to intersect learning and eco-literacy at the same 
time. The shot is further illustrated how green insides incorporated in ELT 
contents sponsor environmental responsiveness and hence nurturing a global 
world-view of ELLs. In addition, this attempt may pave way for curricula 
more focused on eco-centric themes and thus fostering learners to be more 
ecological literate and are enthusiastic to contribute for environmental 
sustainability in their societal, cultural and linguistic paradigms.  
Limitations of the Study  
Keeping in view the objectives and rational of the under view study, it is 
delimited to merely green contents embedded in ELT at elementary level in 
Pakistan. Further, it is demarcated to two units i.e. Smog and Trees 
Plantation for focused analysis. It is also confined to the thematic, contents 
and textual analysis to devise thematic patterns pertinent to ecological 
menaces and eco-centric consciousness.  
Review of the Literature  
Ecological disarray is a global phenomenon which ranges from Africa to 
Asia and from America to Europe alike. Ecological degradation and the need 
for environmental sustainability have grown to be a matter of immense 
concerns among academician and researchers around the globe to construct 
people as well as learners eco-centric consciousness and to ensure the 
maximum protection of ecological prospect. In this regard, academic texts 
in the form of textbooks in general and ELT textbooks in particular have 
donated considerably to craft ELLs consciousness headed for eco-literacy 
and environmental attentiveness (Buzo, 2010). Hickman and Portfilio (2012) 
encapsulated the same notion, as “Textbooks can help or hinder our ability 
to face the environmental challenges of a changing world”. Keeping in view 
the noteworthy persona of textbooks and green contents for ensuring 
ecological sustainability and eco-centric consciousness among learners, 
assorted studies have been conducted. 

 
 
75
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
Cristovoa (2022) dissected Brazilian EFL textbooks with regard to their 
ecological contents; summed up that there is hardly any considerable 
involvement such contents have on the ELLs to assimilate eco-literacy 
among them. Majeed et al. (2022) explored ELT textbooks at secondary 
level in Pakistani context and encompassed with the scheme that activities 
in textbooks stimulate ELLs to seize steps to ensure conscientiousness 
towards our sphere and to confiscate immediate steps to guarantee 
environmental sustainability. Bistrom and Lundstrom (2021) appraised the 
persona of textbooks in Swedish schools, where it is originated that there is 
a very inadequate function that ELT insides in the form of green contents 
have on ecological expansion of ELLs. Hookoomsing and Ooze (2020) 
scrutinized the same in Mauritian context with regard to ELT texts of grade 
3 and summed up that ELT textbooks failed to put any impact on ELLs with 
regard to eco-centric consciousness, rather these sponsor destructive 
behaviour towards environment. 
Zahoor and Janjua (2020) investigated the imprints of ELT insides of 
primary level on ELLs with regard to environmental concerns and derived 
that ELT contents principally the utilization of language spotlights 
considerable persona to pack in ELLs cognisant towards the destruction of 
the nature and environment and thus accenting the essentiality to promise 
ecological well-being. Zhou and Haung (2017) evaluated green contents of 
ELT textbooks of secondary level in Chinese context and affirmed the role 
of language learning and teaching along with contents as substantial to 
endorse eco-literacy among ELLs. Dastenaee and Poshtvan (2018) put in a 
nutshell the reconsider of previous studies conducted in Iran with regard to 
role of ELT in sponsoring eco-literacy among ELLs and encompassed that 
Iranian context in this regard is still in an era of infancy if put in global 
context with regard to eco-centric consciousness.  
Hamed (2021) executed a study to weigh up the facade of Egyptian ELT 
textbooks or insides for ecological discourse rationale and summed up that 
there is a superficial variety of conservationism that existed in green contents 
of ELT textbooks with regard to environmentalism. Ekasiwi and Bram 
(2023) travelled around eco-linguistics essentials in Indonesian ELT and 
derived that not all the ELT contents surround eco-linguistics features in 
terms of words, sentences, themes and topics to take care of eco-centric 
perception among ELLs. Bearing in mind the connotation of the ecological 
menaces, eco-literacy and the scarcity of the study in Pakistani context 
principally at elementary level with regard to imprints of green contents 
among ELLs of Pakistan in nurturing their eco-centric consciousness for 
sustainable ecological prospect current study is significantly indispensable, 
vital and the need of the time. 
Theoretical Underpinning  
Ecological Discourse Analysis (EDA) has been manoeuvred as a theoretical 
framework to scrutinize the eco-centric consciousness of ELLs of Pakistan. 

 
 
76
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
EDA has the sway to evaluate ecological themes and contents in ELT 
through green contents. EDA abets the researcher to unearth how language 
and communicative patterns in ELT insides contribute in shaping and 
scheming ELLs environmental behaviour through inculcation of green 
contents (Fairclough, 2013). Mliless and Larouz (2018) encapsulated the 
constructive and destructive persona of discourse in contents.  Language 
operates as a framing in the course of vocabulary and linguistic strategies to 
boost ELLs consciousness towards environmental sustainability. Power 
dynamics in discourse function as a driving force to persuade the psyche of 
ELLs. In addition, analysis is conceded out through depiction of nature and 
environment to pervade eco-centric outlook among learners. Environmental 
narrative is yet an added key attribute of EDA theory which has instigated 
persona on learners. Cultural and social dimensions of EDA theory also have 
a say in analysing the facade of green contents in nurturing eco-centric 
alertness for ecological sustainability (Fairclough, 2013). Last but not the 
least, environmental education spots the theory of EDA as a moving facet to 
accomplish the objectives of the study.  
Methodology  
In order to investigate the role of green contents in nurturing eco-centric 
consciousness among ELLs of Pakistan for environmental sustainability, a 
qualitative method of analysis has been extracted by the researcher. For that 
intent, green contents incorporated in ELT of elementary grade under SNC 
2023 has been extorted for the study. ELLs at this level are typically ranges 
between 10 and 13 years of age. A sample consisted of two units from ELT 
of grade 7 and 8 are extracted for the purpose. Smog is derived from grade 7 
textbook and Tree Plantation is devised from grade 8 textbook. For the 
extraction of data, a purposive sampling technique has been inferred by the 
researcher. In addition, green contents criteria have been extorted by the 
researcher to formulate the data in lines with the objectives of the study. In 
order to analyse the data, a contrastive approach of analysis has been 
encompassed by the researcher. Smog manifests the ecological and 
environmental concerns of today world, while Tree Plantation highlights the 
steps being taken out to protect the environment and to foster eco-centric 
consciousness among ELLs. Contents, thematic and textual patterns 
evaluation has been kept in view to analyse the data.  
Findings and Discussion  
Eco-centric Consciousness through Smog 
Multifaceted layers of Ecological Issues 
Through a dialogic mode, ELLs of Pakistan are tended conscious about the 
environmental issues that the world in general and Pakistan in particular is 
facing these days. It is conceded by means of diverse thematic patterns that 
are pertinent to eco-literacy or consciousness. It is indicated that the world 
is facing numerous environmental and climatic concerns which are enticing 
as severe challenges with the passage of time. At the very start of discussion 

 
 
77
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
the teacher has conveyed and recapitulate the environmental issues that the 
world is undertaking as “These include deforestation, overpopulation, water 
pollution, climate change, global warming, ozone layer depletion and air 
pollution” (PTB, p. 42). So, it is the first influential feature in the unit to 
underline the issue allied with climatic concern to craft ELLs conscious 
about the severity of the issue. After summing up the crux of environmental 
hazards, the unit is shifted toward a foremost environmental concern which 
is surrounding by the world at present and that is “smog”. 
Issue of Smog  
The unit has distinctive the notion of smog as an outline of air pollution to 
devise ELLs conscious about this ecological menace. In addition, the history 
of smog is mentioned as old as five decades. After that, reasons of the smog 
are being transferred to ELLs as “It is mainly a product of burning a large 
amount of high Sulphur coal and vapours and smoke emitting from 
automobiles” (PTB, p. 42). It swells all around in winter season. Then the 
teacher involves the learners in an interactive session in the unit to 
contextualize the hazard of smog in local i.e. Pakistani context “Every winter 
cities in upper and central parts of Pakistan wear a blanket of fog” (PTB, p. 
42). Besides, the severity of the issue is also exposed to ELLs by indicating 
“During December and January smog slows down everything and on some 
occasions brings life to a standstill” (PTB, p. 42) to construct this ecological 
menace more intensified to make the learners conscious. 
Reasons and Impacts of Smog on Health  
Reasons following this ecological menace incorporate “rapid and sustained 
industrialisation and the addition of thousands of vehicles” (PTB, p. 42). So 
as to persuade ELLs more considerate about ecological menace, its far-
reaching multifaceted layers of impacts on human life, which are negative in 
terms of both physical and mental health point of view, are enlisted. When 
invisible particles of smog infiltrate in human bodies it results in “acute and 
chronic diseases including asthma, strokes, heart attacks and dementia. They 
can increase the risk of respiratory diseases as well as lung cancer." (PTB, 
p. 43) It is also specified that “poor air quality results in poor mental health” 
(PTB, p. 43) with regard to mental health impacts. Punjab province chiefly 
Lahore is severely affected by smog due to “vehicle and industrial emissions, 
smoke from brick kilns, the burning of crops residue, general waste and dust 
from construction sites...large scale cutting of trees to build new roads and 
buildings” (PTB, p. 43). 
Minimising 
Ecological 
Menace 
to 
Accentuate 
Eco-centric 
Consciousness  
Keeping in view the multifaceted layers of ecological and environment 
concern and its hazards on human life in terms of physical and mental health, 
the unit “Smog” also hint steps that are indispensable to put off smog as an 
ecological menace. It is recommended directly that by wearing mask and 
glasses can be handy measures to reduce the risk of air particles being 

 
 
78
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
penetrated into human bodies caused by air pollution in the form of smog. 
Drinking extra amount of water, blowing nose at regular intervals, cleaning 
contaminants, washing hand and face, remaining indoors, utilizing air 
purifiers and by means of fog lights during driving are the steps that can 
minimise the effects of smog considerably. While the unit is indicative of 
the indirect reminder of rooting out the causes, that escort to smog to 
construct a sustainable and eco-friendly environment all around. So, by 
means of green contents in ELT textbooks, ELLs are made conscious about 
the ecological menaces and instigate them to seize eco-friendly steps for 
sustainable eco-centric literacy. 
Strategies of Nurturing Eco-centric Consciousness  
In the unit Smog, there are several ways and means that have been espoused 
to expertise ELLs realization concerning climatic or eco-centric literacy. 
Firstly, instead of being instructive or didactic, the approach is collaborative 
and dialogic. Through a dialogue and interaction between teacher and the 
learners, an outline about global issues with relevant to eco-literacy or 
climatic change has been incorporated. Then it is specified through the 
hazard of smog widespread in Pakistan at a severe form. Secondly, a 
comprehensive approach is being integrated as smog is defined, its causes 
are enlisted, its consequences are elaborated and how to reduce its effects on 
human health have also been penned down. Thirdly, contextualization 
approach is espoused as Punjab, Lahore and its surrounding locale are 
indicated as most hit areas where this issue is at relentless form.  
Fourthly, vocabulary utilization relevant to eco-literacy have been implied 
to infer ELLs conscious about nature and environmental issues i.e. 
“deforestation, overpopulation, water pollution, climate change, global 
warming, ozone layer depletion and air pollution...smog, fog, coal, vapours, 
industrialisation, air quality, The Air Quality Index, smoke and burning of 
crops.” Another influential tool is the exploitation of graphic and textual 
illustrations that construe ELLs ecologically conscience. Critical thinking 
and enticement to inscribe about smog in the exercise is yet another striking 
strategy that has been made use of in the unit. In the concluding session of 
the unit ELLs are prompted to write “causes of air pollution and its 
solutions” so along with critical thing, fostering creativity has also been 
inspired in the unit to infuse ELLs attentiveness about nature, climate, 
ecological issue in general and smog as an eco-centric concern in particular 
to shield nature and ecological well-being. 
Eco-centric Consciousness through Trees Plantation  
Presentation of Natural Magnificence 
In this unit, through the utilization of talk time technique which is conceded 
via email the nature, its exquisiteness and purity has been propagated to 
devise ELLs conscious about natural world and ecological environ. Email is 
an invitation from a friend Asjad to his friend Fahad for a vacation trip to 
Kashmir which is replete with natural magnificence and that too in the purest 

 
 
79
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
form. Nature and its loveliness have been portrayed with the assistance of a 
rhetorical expression i.e. simile as “it is known as heaven on earth due to its 
evergreen forests, freshwater lakes and streams” (PTB, p. 115). Here, the 
approach of textbook discourse in Tree Plantation is dissimilar from the 
discourse of “Smog” as there is a contrastive view towards nature has been 
depicted. In Smog climatic issues are projected but here nature and its 
prettiness has been manipulated as a contrivance to manoeuvre the 
consciousness of ELLs towards nature, its purity and the ways to safeguard 
it from being effected or destroyed. 
Trees Plantation Day as a Fun Activity  
In the second portion of the unit, “Diary Writing” has been consumed as a 
gadget to exhibit the ecstasy and fun that a student experiences during tree 
plantation at school. During National Tree Plantation, teachers and school 
gardener planted rose’s plants in school garden. So, through plantation, roses 
and school garden natural appeal is being nurtured among learners. On the 
other hand, through the speech specified by the headmaster in the morning 
assembly, the other dimension of the picture is depicted as “cutting of trees 
has increased the risk of natural disasters. If we want to save our earth and 
creatures living on it, we should plant more and more trees to make the 
mother earth beautiful and green.” (PTB, p. 116) It is also publicized that 
government has situate a target to “Go Green” in order to avert the earth 
from natural and climatic challenges that are engulfing the land at large.  
Tree Plantation Competition  
In addition, there is a tree plantation competition that is also being 
anticipated to hold among groups of students to craft the learners’ 
mindfulness about the essentiality of going green to avert climatic menaces 
at one hand and to construct earth a better place to live in. It is also projected 
in the unit that mere plantation is not enough, rather intriguing care of the 
planted trees into healthy and growing trees is also indispensable and it is 
embedded through incentive of reward pronounced by the head teacher “the 
group whose sapling would grow into a healthy tree will be rewarded” (PTB, 
p. 117). For that, students are assigned duties to tend the planted trees. 
Furthermore, it transports attentiveness and eco-centric consciousness 
among ELLs that they map to fetch tree pots to their homes to plant and let 
them grow into a healthy tree at home as a token to exhibit their ecological 
literacy. The student who is scripting the diary is shown excited about his 
school plantation competition as “oh! I really wish that my group wins this 
competition.” (PTB, p. 117) 
Plastic Bottles Tree Pots  
In the culminating slice of the unit through an oral communication between 
Saima and Nasir, the factual reflection of consciousness towards nature, 
climate and eco-centric literacy that ELT textbooks inspire among ELLs in 
Pakistan are anticipated through an activity. Nasir is publicized making 
plastic bottle pots of diverse designs with the intention to seed and grow 

 
 
80
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
plants in them. He acquires the scheme of going green from the day they 
celebrated at school under the title “National Trees Plantation Day” as he 
contemplates that in order to turn aside the challenges posed to climatic and 
ecological well-being it is not merely sufficient to cultivate plants at school. 
Additionally, Saima draws attention towards the imperativeness of having a 
garden at home also signifies the eco-centric literacy and consciousness that 
textbook has fostered among ELLs. Saima and Nasir enthusiasm and 
collaboration in creating pots is a momentous indicator of ecological literacy 
among ELLs for a sustainable ecological environ at school, home and all 
where.  
Techniques of Nurturing Eco-centric Consciousness  
The unit under analysis “Trees Plantation” has exploited assorted strategies 
in order to foster eco-centric consciousness among ELLs. Firstly, the 
presentation of natural exquisiteness has been rendered as a means to 
manoeuvre the interest of the learners towards nature. Bringing into play 
simile and flowery language is yet an added technique that is pertinent to 
manipulate the inquisitiveness of ELLs. Thirdly, “National Trees Plantation 
Day” has been propagated as a considerable endeavour to craft ELLs 
conscious about the essentiality to cultivate and grow trees in order to turn 
aside the climatic challenges. The persona of headmaster and head teacher 
is also essential to industrialize ELLs conscientiousness towards ecological 
literacy and attentiveness about the essentiality of going green. The 
government target of “Going Green” is also promulgated as an emblem to 
foster eco-centric literacy among ELLs. 
Competition and incentive of reward is also a well-thought-out strategy that 
has been contrived to make ELLs enthral towards plantation as a measure to 
counter and avert climatic challenges. Ecological vocabulary utilization is 
yet an added noteworthy approach that has been inspired by the discourse of 
the text to persuade the psyche of ELLs towards eco-centric consciousness 
and for sustainable ecological environ. Talk time, diary writing and oral 
communication are the mode which are being operated as a manipulating 
agent to sway the minds of ELLs towards nature, climate and eco-centric 
literacy which are considerable as far as sustainable ecological environ in 
the world is concerned. The enthusiasm among ELLs through Saima and 
Nasir is sketched out as an emblem that the textbook discourse has been 
successful in nurturing eco-centric consciousness among ELLs in Pakistan.  
Conclusion 
The findings of the study signify that in ELT insides are adequately equipped 
to foster environmental sustainability and eco-centric consciousness among 
ELLs of elementary level in Pakistan. In addition, there is a contrastive 
approach that has been espoused with regard to incorporation of green 
contents. At one hand, ecological menaces and challenges are incorporated 
through green contents and on the other hand, measures that are engaged or 
being taken to augment ecological literacy among ELLs are also 

 
 
81
 
Nurturing Environmental Sustainability through Green Contents: …..  
Pakistan Research Journal of Social Sciences (Vol.3, Issue2, June 2024) 
encapsulated in ELT contents. Ecological menaces like over population, 
deforestation, smoke, water & air pollution, ozone layer depletion, climatic 
change and global warming are fostered to put together ELLs conscious 
about environmental issues. In addition, through smog, the challenge of this 
environmental haphazard is indicated as a matter of concern.  
On the contrary, steps that are essential to shield nature and nurture 
environmental sustainability are implied in the course of natural beauty and 
tree plantation campaign. The approach of illustrating both the dynamics 
exclusively as a comprehensive overview of the reasons, imprints and steps 
to minimise the menace of smog are anticipated in the unit Smog. On the 
other hand, environmental sustainability are nurtured through the delineation 
of natural magnificence of Kashmir, celebration of National Trees 
Plantation, Plantation competition and making plants pots activities. In 
Smog, ecological vocabulary, thematic and textual patterns, graphic 
depiction and contextual parameters are inspired to manipulate eco-centric 
consciousness among learners.  
While in the unit Tree Plantation, the spotlight is on the activities, 
enthusiasm and collaborative approach among learners to plant tree at school 
and home has been extracted to infuse the psyche of ELLs. Here, the concept 
of garden has been contrived as an emblem of nurturing environmental 
sustainability parameter among ELLs of Pakistan at elementary level. 
Likewise with the contrastive approach there is a similarity as interactive 
approach is espoused in both the dynamics of projecting eco-centric 
consciousness among ELLs. In addition, diary writing, oral skills, talk time, 
critical thinking and creative writing have been inferred in order to nurture 
eco-centric consciousness among ELLs for a protective ecological 
sustainability at large. 
Recommendations 
To construct the eco-centric consciousness among ELLs of Pakistan, it is 
recommended to incorporate additional green content as the substance in 
ELT textbooks. Dynamic instructional stratagems i.e., outdoor activities 
footed on eco-friendly ventures and hands-on practice can be an effectual 
medium to elevate eco-centric literacy among ELLs in Pakistan. Community 
rendezvous in eco-centric initiatives through ELT discourse can also 
capitalize on the enterprise between society and environmental 
organizations. The operation of technology to showcase green content 
interactively and compellingly can further cater to eco-centric attentiveness 
among ELLs. Last, but not least, it is suggested that policymakers should be 
heedful of the function of environmental sustainability through green content 
in academic discourse in general and language discourse in particular.

Abstract
Science is and always has been based on data, but the terms ‘data-centric’
and the ‘4th paradigm’ of materials research indicate a radical change in how
information is retrieved, handled and research is performed. It signifies a trans-
formative shift towards managing vast data collections, digital repositories, and
innovative data analytics methods. The integration of artificial intelligence and
its subset machine learning, has become pivotal in addressing all these chal-
lenges. This Roadmap on Data-Centric Materials Science explores fundamental
concepts and methodologies, illustrating diverse applications in electronic-
structure theory, soft matter theory, microstructure research, and experimental
techniques like photoemission, atom probe tomography, and electron micro-
scopy. While the roadmap delves into specific areas within the broad inter-
disciplinary field of materials science, the provided examples elucidate key
concepts applicable to a wider range of topics. The discussed instances offer
insights into addressing the multifaceted challenges encountered in contem-
porary materials research.
Keywords: data, centric, materials, science, molecular simulations, roadmap

1. Introduction
Peter Benner1, Dierk Raabe2, Jan-Michael Rost3, Matthias Scheffler4 and Gerhard Weikum5
1 Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems, Magdeburg, Germany

Germany
