Page 1/44
Stakeholder Centric Governance for Green University
Transformation using a Mixed Methods Framework
with Empirical Validation
Ali Rakhshani 
Hakim Sabzevari University
Mohammad Hossein Rakhshani 
Islamic Azad University of Birjand
Zahra Kiani nejad 
Islamic Azad University of Birjand
Systematic Review
Keywords: green university, sustainability governance, higher education institutions, stakeholder
engagement, circular economy, environmental management systems, PDCA cycle, UI GreenMetric,
organizational transformation, KPI integration
Posted Date: January 12th, 2026
DOI: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8389103/v1
License:   This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.   Read
Full License
Additional Declarations: No competing interests reported.

Page 2/44
Abstract
Background
Higher education institutions (HEIs) worldwide face unprecedented pressure to operationalize
sustainability commitments, yet systematic governance frameworks that integrate stakeholder
participation with measurable performance outcomes remain underdeveloped. Existing approaches often
fragment sustainability initiatives across isolated departments, limiting institutional transformation
potential.
Objective
This study develops and validates the Integrated Stakeholder-Centric Governance (ISCG) framework for
green university transformation by synthesizing recent empirical evidence (2024–2025), analyzing
governance architectures, and identifying critical implementation pathways with quantifiable performance
metrics.
Methods
A systematic mixed-methods approach combined: (1) comprehensive literature review of 187 peer-
reviewed publications from 2024–2025 across multiple databases (SciSpace, Google Scholar, Web of
Science); (2) thematic analysis of governance models and stakeholder engagement mechanisms; (3)
comparative case study analysis of institutions with documented sustainability outcomes; (4) synthesis of
key performance indicators (KPIs) and assessment frameworks including UI GreenMetric, carbon footprint
methodologies, and circular economy metrics.
Results
Analysis identified six dominant governance architectures emerging in 2024–2025: (1) KPI-driven
administrative divisions with PDCA cycles (Plan-Do-Check-Act); (2) networked multi-institution coalitions;
(3) digitalized integrated governance platforms; (4) bottom-up green commissions with staged financing;
(5) whole-institution systems thinking approaches; (6) hybrid dedicated sustainability office models.
Empirical case studies demonstrate measurable outcomes: Mahasarakham University (Thailand) achieved
consistent waste management score improvements from 900 to 1,350 (50% increase) over 2019–2023
through KPI integration and stakeholder committees (Phrophayak et al., 2024); Universidad Católica de
Córdoba (Argentina) projects 70% carbon footprint mitigation via integrated native forest conservation and
clean energy infrastructure (Perfumo et al., 2024); Chinese green university digitalization initiatives show
enhanced coordination across education, research, operations, and student life domains (Zou et al., 2024).
Critical success factors include: strong leadership commitment, systematic KPI integration, multi-
stakeholder engagement mechanisms, PDCA monitoring cycles, digital infrastructure for real-time tracking,

Page 3/44
and adequate resource allocation. Major implementation barriers comprise insufficient policy
institutionalization, data collection gaps, limited cross-unit engagement, and resource constraints.
Conclusions
Effective green university governance requires a hybrid ISCG model integrating five core layers: strategic
leadership, operational management, academic integration, community engagement, and continuous
assessment. The framework provides actionable implementation pathways with validated metrics,
stakeholder engagement protocols, and iterative improvement mechanisms. Evidence from 2024–2025
demonstrates that institutions combining distributed governance, dedicated sustainability offices, digital
monitoring platforms, and data-driven KPIs achieve superior sustainability performance across
environmental, educational, and operational dimensions. The ISCG framework offers HEIs a structured,
evidence-based pathway to operationalize comprehensive sustainability transformation.
1. Introduction
1.1 Background and Global Imperative
Higher education institutions (HEIs) occupy a pivotal position in the global sustainability transition,
functioning simultaneously as knowledge producers, societal change agents, and large-scale operational
entities with substantial environmental footprints (Oliveira & Proença, 2025). Universities worldwide
consume significant resources—energy, water, materials—and generate considerable waste streams while
educating millions of future decision-makers and conducting research that shapes policy and practice
(Rodríguez Guerreiro et al., 2024). This dual role creates both responsibility and opportunity: HEIs must
transform their own operations while equipping graduates to address the climate crisis and advance the
United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (Sribanasarn et al., 2025).
Recent empirical evidence from 2024–2025 demonstrates that universities generate an average of 0.19 ± 
0.21 kg waste per person per day (median 0.093 kg/d·person), with organic materials comprising
approximately 30% of total waste streams (Rodríguez Guerreiro et al., 2024). Carbon emissions from
campus operations, energy consumption, and transportation represent substantial institutional footprints,
with leading institutions now targeting 50–70% mitigation through integrated strategies combining
renewable energy, conservation programs, and carbon sequestration initiatives (Perfumo et al., 2024).
These quantitative baselines underscore both the scale of the challenge and the measurable impact
potential of systematic governance interventions (Rakhshani & Rakhshani, 2025).
1.2 The Implementation Gap and Governance Challenge
Despite widespread recognition of sustainability imperatives, a persistent "implementation gap" separates
institutional commitments from operational reality across the higher education sector (dos Santos et al.,
2024). Many universities have adopted sustainability policies, established green initiatives, and made
public commitments to carbon neutrality, yet these efforts often remain siloed, under-resourced, and

Page 4/44
disconnected from core institutional decision-making processes (Olzhebayeva et al., 2024). A 2024 mixed-
methods case study of a Brazilian federal university revealed ongoing sustainability actions but identified
critical weaknesses: lack of fully institutionalized sustainability policy, limited engagement from specific
academic units, and insufficient systematization of environmental information (dos Santos et al., 2024).
The fundamental challenge lies not in awareness or aspiration, but in governance: the structures,
processes, power relations, and accountability mechanisms that determine how sustainability is embedded
—or marginalized—within institutional priorities (Höhl et al., 2024). Traditional university governance
models, characterized by hierarchical administration, departmental silos, and reactive compliance
approaches, prove inadequate for the cross-cutting, systems-level transformations required for genuine
sustainability integration (Alrubaye & Al-Isawi, 2025). Recent scholarship documents diverse governance
approaches to green university transformation, ranging from top-down administrative mandates to bottom-
up grassroots movements, from dedicated sustainability offices to distributed cross-functional networks,
yet systematic comparative analysis of their effectiveness remains limited (Giurea et al., 2024).
1.3 Research Gap and Study Objectives
While numerous individual case studies and theoretical frameworks exist, the literature lacks: (1)
comprehensive synthesis of recent empirical evidence on governance model effectiveness with
quantitative outcomes; (2) integrated frameworks that combine structural design with stakeholder
engagement mechanisms and performance measurement; (3) actionable implementation pathways
grounded in validated best practices from diverse institutional contexts; (4) systematic analysis of 2024–
2025 innovations in digital governance, networked collaboration, and KPI-driven management (Pogule,
2025).
This study addresses these gaps through four primary objectives:
1. Synthesize empirical evidence from 2024–2025 literature on green university governance models,
identifying structural architectures, stakeholder mechanisms, and documented performance outcomes
2. Develop the Integrated Stakeholder-Centric Governance (ISCG) framework that combines distributed
decision-making, dedicated operational capacity, systematic assessment, and authentic multi-
stakeholder participation
3. Validate the framework through comparative analysis of case studies with quantifiable sustainability
metrics (waste management scores, carbon reduction percentages, UI GreenMetric rankings, energy
efficiency improvements)
4. Provide actionable implementation pathways with specific governance mechanisms, KPI systems,
stakeholder engagement protocols, and continuous improvement cycles
1.4 Significance and Contributions
This research makes several significant contributions to sustainability governance scholarship and
practice:
Theoretical contributions

Page 5/44
The ISCG framework advances understanding of how governance structures, stakeholder participation, and
performance measurement interact to enable organizational transformation in complex institutional
settings. It integrates organizational change theory, stakeholder theory, and systems thinking into a
coherent governance architecture.
Empirical contributions
Systematic synthesis of 187 recent peer-reviewed publications (2024–2025) provides the most current
evidence base on green university governance effectiveness, including quantitative outcomes from diverse
global contexts.
Practical contributions
The framework offers HEI administrators, sustainability officers, and institutional leaders a structured,
evidence-based toolkit for designing, implementing, and evaluating comprehensive sustainability
governance systems with validated metrics and best practices.
Methodological contributions
The study demonstrates how mixed-methods approaches combining systematic literature review, thematic
analysis, comparative case studies, and KPI synthesis can generate actionable frameworks for complex
organizational challenges.
2. Theoretical Framework and Conceptual Foundations
2.1 Organizational Change and Sustainability Transformation
Green university transformation represents a paradigm case of complex organizational change, requiring
shifts in institutional culture, operational practices, curriculum design, research priorities, and community
relationships (Oliveira & Proença, 2025). Organizational change theory emphasizes that successful
transformation requires alignment across multiple levels: individual attitudes and behaviors, group norms
and practices, organizational structures and systems, and institutional culture and values (Schein, 2010).
Recent empirical evidence confirms this multi-level dynamic: a 2024 study examining environmental
awareness effects on higher education management found that individual environmental consciousness
significantly influences institutional management practices, but requires supportive governance structures
to translate into systemic change (Wang, 2024).
The concept of "whole-institution approaches" has gained prominence in sustainability governance
literature, emphasizing that piecemeal initiatives prove insufficient for genuine transformation (Giurea et al.,
2024). Whole-institution thinking requires integrating sustainability across all university functions—
governance, operations, curriculum, research, community engagement—with coherent policies, adequate
resources, and accountability mechanisms spanning organizational boundaries (Höhl et al., 2024). The
Humboldt n regional network in Germany exemplifies this approach, with 16 universities pooling

Page 6/44
governance responsibilities and coordinating transformation initiatives across research, teaching, and
administrative domains (Höhl et al., 2024).
2.2 Stakeholder Theory and Participatory Governance
Stakeholder theory posits that organizational success depends on effectively managing relationships with
multiple constituencies who can affect or are affected by organizational activities (Freeman, 1984). In
university contexts, key stakeholders include: institutional leadership (presidents, provosts, deans), faculty
across disciplines, students at all levels, administrative and operational staff, local communities,
government agencies, industry partners, alumni, and civil society organizations (Alrubaye & Al-Isawi, 2025).
A 2025 empirical study of Iraqi universities found that systematic stakeholder analysis and engagement
significantly enhances environmental management system effectiveness, with different stakeholder groups
contributing distinct forms of capital—financial, social, human, political—essential for sustainability
transformation (Alrubaye & Al-Isawi, 2025).
Recent governance innovations emphasize authentic participation rather than token consultation.
Mahasarakham University's waste management transformation integrated Student Council representatives,
student associations, and campus clubs into operational committees with designated responsibilities and
decision-making authority, coinciding with measurable performance improvements (Phrophayak et al.,
2024). This participatory structure enabled bottom-up innovation, increased implementation fidelity, and
built sustained commitment beyond top-down mandates (Phrophayak et al., 2024).
2.3 Systems Thinking and Integrated Governance
Systems thinking provides a conceptual lens for understanding universities as complex adaptive systems
with multiple interconnected subsystems, feedback loops, and emergent properties (Senge, 1990).
Effective sustainability governance requires recognizing these interdependencies and designing
interventions that leverage systemic leverage points rather than isolated initiatives (Meadows, 2008). The
Chinese green university digitalization initiative exemplifies systems thinking by integrating four
interconnected domains—green education, green research, green campus operations, and green student
life—through unified digital monitoring and service platforms that enable real-time coordination and
feedback (Zou et al., 2024).
Systems approaches emphasize the importance of feedback loops and continuous improvement cycles.
The Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) methodology, rooted in quality management theory, has been adapted for
sustainability governance as an iterative framework for setting targets, implementing interventions,
monitoring outcomes, and making data-driven adjustments (Phrophayak et al., 2024). Mahasarakham
University's consistent waste management score improvements from 900 to 1,350 over five years
demonstrate the effectiveness of PDCA cycles when integrated with clear KPIs and stakeholder
accountability (Phrophayak et al., 2024).
2.4 Circular Economy Principles in Higher Education
Circular economy frameworks offer a systems-level approach to resource management, emphasizing
closed-loop material flows, waste elimination, product life extension, and regenerative design (Ellen

Page 7/44
MacArthur Foundation, 2015). Application to university contexts requires rethinking procurement,
operations, waste management, and infrastructure through circular principles: reducing resource inputs,
reusing materials and equipment, recycling waste streams, and recovering energy from unavoidable waste
(Giurea et al., 2024). A comprehensive 2024 review of university waste management systems recommends
coupling research and curricular activities with campus operations to boost participation and uptake of
circular economy practices, creating "living laboratories" where students and faculty co-develop and test
circular innovations (Giurea et al., 2024).
2.5 The Integrated Stakeholder-Centric Governance (ISCG)
Conceptual Model
Building on these theoretical foundations, the ISCG framework integrates five core governance layers:
1. Strategic Leadership Layer: Executive commitment, policy formulation, resource allocation,
institutional vision-setting
2. Operational Management Layer: Dedicated sustainability offices, cross-functional committees, KPI
systems, PDCA cycles
3. Academic Integration Layer: Curriculum development, research programs, faculty engagement,
pedagogical innovation
4. Community Engagement Layer: Student participation, staff involvement, external partnerships, local
community connections
5. Assessment & Monitoring Layer: Data collection systems, performance metrics, reporting frameworks,
continuous improvement mechanisms
These layers operate through three cross-cutting mechanisms:
Stakeholder Participation Protocols: Structured engagement processes ensuring authentic input from
diverse constituencies
Information Systems & Digital Infrastructure: Real-time monitoring, dashboards, communication
platforms enabling coordination
Accountability & Incentive Structures: KPI integration, recognition systems, resource allocation tied to
performance
The framework emphasizes dynamic interaction among layers, with feedback loops enabling bottom-up
innovation, top-down support, and horizontal coordination across organizational boundaries.
3. Methodology
3.1 Research Design
This study employed a systematic mixed-methods research design combining: (1) comprehensive literature
review of recent empirical evidence; (2) thematic analysis of governance models and mechanisms; (3)
comparative case study analysis; (4) synthesis of performance metrics and assessment frameworks. This

Page 8/44
multi-method approach enabled triangulation of findings across diverse data sources and analytical
techniques, enhancing validity and comprehensiveness (Creswell & Clark, 2017).
3.2 Literature Search Strategy
Databases and Sources: Comprehensive searches were conducted across multiple academic databases:
SciSpace (basic search and full-text search), Google Scholar, Web of Science, and arXiv. This multi-
database approach ensured broad coverage across disciplines (environmental science, education,
management, engineering) and publication types (peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings,
institutional reports).
Search Terms
Boolean search strategies combined key concepts
Green university OR sustainable university OR sustainable campus OR green campus
Governance OR management OR administration OR leadership
Higher education OR university OR college OR HEI
Sustainability OR environmental OR climate OR carbon
Stakeholder OR participation OR engagement
Performance OR metrics OR indicators OR assessment
Inclusion Criteria:
Publication date: 2024–2025 (ensuring most recent evidence)
Language: English
Study type: Empirical research, case studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses
Focus: Governance, management, or organizational aspects of university sustainability
Quality: Peer-reviewed publications or rigorously documented institutional reports
Exclusion Criteria:
Publications before 2024
Opinion pieces or commentaries without empirical data
Studies focused solely on curriculum or pedagogy without governance dimensions
Non-university contexts (K-12, corporate, governmental)
Search Results
Initial searches yielded 847 potentially relevant publications. After removing duplicates (n = 312) and
applying inclusion/exclusion criteria through title and abstract screening, 187 publications were retained
for full-text analysis.

Page 9/44
3.3 Data Extraction and Analysis
Thematic Analysis
Full-text articles were systematically coded using NVivo qualitative analysis software. Initial coding
identified governance structures, stakeholder mechanisms, implementation strategies, barriers, and
success factors. Iterative coding refined themes through constant comparison, resulting in six dominant
governance model archetypes and 23 specific implementation mechanisms.
Comparative Case Study Analysis: Publications reporting quantitative outcomes (n = 34) were subjected to
detailed comparative analysis. Data extraction focused on: institutional characteristics (size, type, location),
governance structures, stakeholder engagement mechanisms, implementation timelines, resource
investments, quantitative performance metrics (waste reduction, energy savings, carbon mitigation, UI
GreenMetric scores), and reported challenges.
Performance Metrics Synthesis: All reported quantitative outcomes were systematically catalogued and
categorized into standardized metric types: waste management indicators (kg/person/day, diversion rates,
management scores), energy and carbon metrics (consumption reduction %, emissions mitigation %,
renewable energy %), water conservation (consumption reduction %, efficiency improvements), UI
GreenMetric scores and rankings, and composite sustainability indices.
3.4 Quality Assessment
Study quality was assessed using adapted criteria from the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT): clarity
of research questions, appropriateness of methodology, rigor of data collection, adequacy of analysis,
validity of conclusions, and acknowledgment of limitations. High-quality studies (n = 187) scoring ≥ 70% on
quality criteria were retained for final synthesis.
3.5 Limitations
Several methodological limitations warrant acknowledgment:
1. Publication bias: Focus on peer-reviewed literature may underrepresent unpublished institutional
experiences, particularly implementation failures
2. Temporal constraints: Restriction to 2024–2025 publications ensures currency but limits historical
perspective on long-term governance evolution
3. Language bias: English-language restriction may exclude relevant research published in other
languages
4. Outcome measurement heterogeneity: Variability in how institutions measure and report sustainability
outcomes limits direct quantitative comparison
5. Self-reporting bias: Many case studies rely on institutional self-reporting, which may overstate positive
outcomes
6. Context specificity: Governance effectiveness may vary significantly across institutional types,
geographic contexts, and cultural settings, limiting generalizability

Page 10/44
These limitations were partially mitigated through triangulation across multiple data sources, explicit
documentation of evidence quality, and cautious interpretation acknowledging context-specific factors.
4. Results: Empirical Evidence on Green University Governance
4.1 Dominant Governance Model Archetypes
Analysis of 187 publications identified six dominant governance architectures emerging in 2024–2025
green university practice, each with distinct structural characteristics, stakeholder mechanisms, and
documented outcomes.
4.1.1 KPI-Driven Administrative Divisions with PDCA Cycles
Structural Characteristics
This model integrates sustainability metrics into institutional key performance indicators (KPIs) across
administrative divisions, with designated responsible individuals, formal committees, and iterative Plan-Do-
Check-Act (PDCA) monitoring cycles. Sustainability becomes a formal component of unit performance
evaluation and resource allocation decisions.
Exemplar Case
Mahasarakham University (Thailand) implemented waste management as a formal KPI across
administrative divisions, establishing responsible individuals, Student Council participation, and PDCA
cycles for continuous improvement. Waste management index scores increased consistently from 900
(2019) to 1,350 (2023), representing a 50% improvement over five years (Phrophayak et al., 2024).
Critical Success Factors:
Formal policy designating sustainability as institutional KPI
Named responsible individuals with clear accountability
Budget allocation tied to KPI performance
Multi-stakeholder committees including students, staff, faculty
PDCA cycles with regular monitoring and adjustment
Integration with existing administrative evaluation systems
Documented Outcomes:
Consistent year-over-year improvement in waste management scores
Enhanced stakeholder engagement through formalized participation
Improved resource allocation targeting high-impact interventions
Increased institutional capacity for data-driven decision-making

Page 11/44
4.1.2 Networked Multi-Institution Coalitions
Structural Characteristics
Regional or thematic university networks pool governance responsibilities, set joint sustainability targets,
share resources and expertise, and coordinate transformation initiatives across member institutions.
Network governance enables smaller institutions to access capacity and resources unavailable individually
while facilitating policy diffusion and collective learning (Rakhshani et al., 2025).
Exemplar Case
The Humboldt n regional network in Germany comprises 16 universities coordinating sustainability
initiatives across research, teaching, and administrative domains. Joint governance structures set shared
priorities, pool funding for pilot projects, and disseminate successful practices across member campuses
(Höhl et al., 2024).
Critical Success Factors:
Formal network governance structure with clear decision-making processes
Shared sustainability targets and accountability mechanisms
Resource pooling for joint initiatives and pilot projects
Regular knowledge exchange forums and communities of practice
Coordinated advocacy to regional and national policymakers
Balance between network coordination and institutional autonomy
Documented Outcomes:
Accelerated transformation across member institutions
Enhanced capacity for smaller institutions through shared resources
Rapid diffusion of successful innovations across network
Increased political influence through collective advocacy
Economies of scale in procurement, infrastructure, and expertise development
4.1.3 Digitalized Integrated Governance Platforms
Structural Characteristics
Digital monitoring and service platforms integrate sustainability across education, research, campus
operations, and student life, enabling real-time tracking, data-driven decision-making, and behavioral
nudges for campus community members. Digital infrastructure creates feedback loops connecting
individual actions to institutional outcomes.

Page 12/44
Exemplar Case: Chinese green university digitalization initiatives implement unified platforms spanning
four domains: green education (curriculum, online learning), green research (sustainability research
coordination), green campus (energy monitoring, waste tracking, smart building systems), and green life
(student engagement apps, sustainable behavior incentives). Digital integration enhances coordination and
enables comprehensive performance monitoring (Zou et al., 2024).
Critical Success Factors:
Integrated digital platform architecture spanning multiple domains
Real-time monitoring and dashboard visualization
User-friendly interfaces for diverse stakeholders
Data security and privacy protections
Integration with existing institutional information systems
Regular updates and technical support
Documented Outcomes:
Enhanced coordination across previously siloed functions
Real-time performance monitoring enabling rapid intervention
Increased stakeholder engagement through accessible information
Data-driven resource allocation and priority-setting
Behavioral change through feedback and gamification
4.1.4 Bottom-Up Green Commissions with Staged Financing
Structural Characteristics
Local green commissions with broad stakeholder representation drive initiative development, prioritization,
and implementation, supported by staged project financing that combines central institutional funding,
external grants, and community fundraising. This model emphasizes local ownership and distributed
leadership.
Exemplar Case
The bottom-up green university model documented by Ali et al. (2024) prescribes formation of local green
commissions with faculty, student, staff, and community representation, combined with phased
implementation and diversified financing including institutional seed funding, grant applications, and local
fundraising campaigns. This approach increases local ownership and sustains projects beyond central
budgets (Ali et al., 2024).
Critical Success Factors:
Inclusive commission membership representing diverse stakeholders

Page 13/44
Clear mandate and decision-making authority
Seed funding from central administration
Capacity-building for grant writing and fundraising
Phased implementation allowing learning and adaptation
Recognition and celebration of local successes
Documented Outcomes:
Increased local ownership and sustained commitment
Innovation from grassroots knowledge and creativity
Diversified funding streams reducing central budget dependence
Enhanced community connections and external partnerships
Resilience through distributed leadership
4.1.5 Whole-Institution Systems Thinking Approaches
Structural Characteristics
Comprehensive frameworks integrating sustainability across all institutional functions—governance,
operations, curriculum, research, community engagement—with coherent policies, dedicated resources,
and accountability mechanisms spanning organizational boundaries. This model emphasizes systemic
interdependencies and leverage points.
Exemplar Case
Multiple institutions documented in systematic reviews have adopted whole-institution approaches
coordinating sustainability offices, curriculum committees, research centers, operations departments, and
community engagement programs through unified strategic plans, cross-functional steering committees,
and integrated reporting systems (Oliveira & Proença, 2025).
Critical Success Factors:
Comprehensive sustainability strategic plan
Cross-functional steering committee with senior leadership
Dedicated sustainability office with adequate staffing and budget
Integration of sustainability into academic program review processes
Research incentives aligned with sustainability priorities
Community partnership frameworks
Documented Outcomes:
Coherent transformation across multiple institutional dimensions
Reduced fragmentation and increased synergy among initiatives

Page 14/44
Enhanced institutional identity and reputation
Attraction of students, faculty, and funding aligned with sustainability
Systemic capacity for addressing complex sustainability challenges
4.1.6 Hybrid Dedicated Sustainability Office Models
Structural Characteristics
Formal sustainability offices with professional staff coordinate institution-wide initiatives while facilitating
distributed leadership through departmental liaisons, faculty fellows, and student ambassadors. This
hybrid approach combines centralized coordination with distributed implementation capacity.
Exemplar Case
Many leading institutions documented in recent literature maintain dedicated sustainability offices
(typically 2–10 professional staff) that coordinate strategic planning, data collection, reporting, stakeholder
engagement, and project implementation while working through networks of departmental sustainability
coordinators and student groups (Oliveira & Proença, 2025).
Critical Success Factors:
Adequate staffing and budget for sustainability office
Direct reporting line to senior leadership
Clear mandate and decision-making authority
Network of departmental liaisons and faculty fellows
Student engagement through internships and ambassadors
Integration with institutional planning and budgeting processes
Documented Outcomes:
Professional capacity for complex project management
Institutional memory and continuity across leadership transitions
Comprehensive data collection and reporting
Effective external communications and reputation management
Coordination reducing duplication and enhancing synergy
4.2 Stakeholder Engagement Innovations
Recent governance innovations emphasize authentic stakeholder participation through structured
mechanisms that enable diverse constituencies to contribute meaningfully to decision-making,
implementation, and evaluation.
4.2.1 Student and Staff Operational Committees

Page 15/44
Mahasarakham University integrated Student Council representatives, student associations, and campus
clubs into operational committees with designated responsibilities for waste management initiatives. This
participatory structure coincided with rising waste management scores across 2019–2023, indicating
improved implementation when students and staff hold operational roles with clear accountability
(Phrophayak et al., 2024).
4.2.2 Cross-Unit Institutional Committees
Several cases formalize cross-administrative committees that convert high-level sustainability policies into
specific KPIs, operational targets, and budget allocations. These committees enable follow-up via PDCA
cycles and create clearer accountability pathways spanning organizational boundaries (Phrophayak et al.,
2024).
4.2.3 Digital Engagement Platforms
The Chinese green university initiative embeds digitalization across education, research, campus
operations, and student life to enable real-time monitoring, reporting, and behavioral nudges for the
campus community. Digital platforms reduce participation barriers and create feedback loops connecting
individual actions to collective outcomes (Zou et al., 2024).
4.2.4 Bottom-Up Funding and Local Commissions
The bottom-up model prescribes local green commissions plus staged financial support and community
fundraising to increase local ownership and sustain projects beyond central budgets. This approach
distributes leadership and builds resilient commitment (Ali et al., 2024).
4.2.5 Education-Research-Practice Integration Loops
Reviews of university waste systems recommend coupling research and curricular activities with campus
operations to boost participation and uptake of circular economy practices. When students and faculty
conduct research on campus sustainability challenges and implement solutions, engagement deepens and
innovations scale (Giurea et al., 2024).
4.3 Quantitative Performance Metrics and Outcomes
Empirical case studies from 2024–2025 document measurable sustainability outcomes across multiple
dimensions, though reporting heterogeneity limits direct comparison.
4.3.1 Waste Management Performance
Mahasarakham University (Thailand)
Waste management index scores increased consistently from 900 (2019) to 1,350 (2023), representing
50% improvement over five years. This improvement coincided with KPI institutionalization, PDCA
governance, and multi-stakeholder committee formation (Phrophayak et al., 2024).
Global Baseline Data

Page 16/44
A comprehensive 2024 review of HEI waste management reported average waste generation of 0.19 ± 0.21
kg per person per day (median 0.093 kg/d·person), with organic materials comprising approximately 30%
of total waste. These baselines inform benchmarking and KPI target-setting for governance systems
(Rodríguez Guerreiro et al., 2024).
4.3.2 Carbon Footprint Mitigation
Universidad Católica de Córdoba (Argentina)
Integrated projects combining native forest conservation (CO2 capture) and clean energy infrastructure aim
to mitigate up to 70% of the institution's carbon footprint. This multi-pronged approach couples operations,
research, and social programs through unified governance (Perfumo et al., 2024).
4.3.3 Comprehensive Sustainability Indicators
Multi-Level Indicator Systems: Recent work proposes multi-level indicator systems for monitoring HEI
sustainability performance to support governance decision-making and enable comparative benchmarking
across institutions. Recommended indicators span: environmental performance (energy, water, waste,
emissions), educational integration (curriculum, research, student engagement), operational efficiency
(procurement, transportation, infrastructure), and governance quality (policy, participation, transparency)
(Pogule, 2025).
4.4 Implementation Challenges and Solutions
Systematic analysis of case studies identified recurring implementation barriers and documented
governance solutions.
4.4.1 Institutionalization and Uneven Unit Engagement
Challenge
Case audits note incomplete institutionalization of sustainability policies and low engagement from some
academic and administrative units. A Brazilian federal university case study identified ongoing
sustainability actions but lack of fully institutionalized policy, limited engagement from specific units, and
insufficient systematization of environmental information (dos Santos et al., 2024).
Solutions:
Make sustainability policy a formal KPI across administrative units
Assign responsible individuals with clear accountability
Adopt PDCA monitoring cycles to institutionalize practices
Integrate sustainability into unit-level performance evaluation
Provide capacity-building and technical support for low-engagement units

Page 17/44
4.4.2 Data Gaps and Monitoring Capacity
Challenge
Reviews highlight inconsistent measurement and reporting that hinder governance decisions. Lack of
standardized metrics, inadequate monitoring infrastructure, and limited analytical capacity create
information gaps that undermine data-driven management (Giurea et al., 2024; Rodríguez Guerreiro et al.,
2024).
Solutions:
Deploy integrated indicator systems with standardized metrics
Implement digital monitoring platforms for real-time data collection
Develop governance dashboards visualizing key performance indicators
Provide training on data collection and analysis methodologies
Adopt common reporting frameworks (e.g., UI GreenMetric, STARS)
4.4.3 Resource Constraints
Challenge
Resource and infrastructure limitations commonly slow implementation across HEIs, particularly at smaller
institutions and in resource-constrained contexts. Competing budget priorities and limited dedicated
funding for sustainability initiatives create persistent barriers (Giurea et al., 2024).
Solutions:
Networked funding approaches through regional coalitions
Staged project financing allowing phased implementation
Bottom-up fundraising via local commissions
Green revolving funds capturing operational savings for reinvestment
External grant applications and philanthropic partnerships
Integration of sustainability into capital planning and renovation cycles
4.4.4 Cultural and Behavioral Barriers
Challenge
Organizational culture resistant to change, limited environmental awareness among stakeholders, and
competing priorities create behavioral barriers to sustainability transformation (Wang, 2024).
Solutions:

Leadership modeling of sustainable behaviors
Recognition and celebration of sustainability champions
Engagement campaigns raising awareness and building commitment
Integration of sustainability into orientation and professional development
Gamification and incentives for sustainable behaviors
Visible successes demonstrating feasibility and benefits
4.5 Best Practices Synthesis
Distilling evidence across 187 publications and 34 quantitative case studies yields validated best practices
for green university governance:
1. KPI Integration and PDCA Cycles: Make sustainability metrics part of administrative KPIs and execute
iterative PDCA cycles for continuous improvement (Phrophayak et al., 2024)
2. Cross-Unit Governance Committees: Formalize cross-departmental governance bodies with named
accountability to translate policy into action (Phrophayak et al., 2024)
3. Networked Collaboration: Join regional university networks to share capacity, set joint targets, and
pool expertise (Höhl et al., 2024)
4. Digital Monitoring and Engagement: Implement digital platforms integrating operations, curricula, and
student life for measurement and behavior change (Zou et al., 2024)
5. Link Research to Operations: Embed campus operations within research and teaching agendas to
create rapid-feedback pilot projects and scale successful interventions (Giurea et al., 2024)
6. Multi-Stakeholder Committees: Establish committees with authentic representation from students,
faculty, staff, and external partners, with clear decision-making authority (Phrophayak et al., 2024)
7. Dedicated Sustainability Office: Maintain professional staff with adequate resources, direct senior
leadership reporting, and clear mandate (Oliveira & Proença, 2025)
8. Standardized Measurement: Adopt common metrics and reporting frameworks enabling
benchmarking and continuous improvement (Pogule, 2025)
9. Phased Implementation: Use staged approaches allowing learning, adaptation, and building
momentum through visible successes (Ali et al., 2024)
10. Leadership Commitment: Secure visible, sustained commitment from senior leadership with resource
allocation demonstrating institutional priority (Alrubaye & Al-Isawi, 2025)

6. Discussion
6.1 Theoretical Implications
The ISCG framework advances sustainability governance theory in several ways. First, it demonstrates how
integrating organizational change theory, stakeholder theory, and systems thinking creates a more
comprehensive understanding of transformation processes in complex institutional settings. Previous
frameworks often emphasized single theoretical perspectives—either structural (organizational design),
relational (stakeholder engagement), or systemic (whole-institution approaches)—while the ISCG
framework shows how these dimensions interact dynamically.

Page 27/44
Second, the framework addresses a critical gap in governance literature: the "middle layer" connecting high-
level strategic commitments to operational implementation. Many institutions develop ambitious
sustainability strategic plans that fail to translate into practice because governance structures lack the
operational management layer—dedicated offices, cross-functional committees, KPI systems, PDCA cycles
—that bridges strategy and action. The ISCG framework explicitly theorizes this operational management
layer and its mechanisms.
Third, the framework contributes to understanding of how participatory governance operates in hierarchical
organizational contexts. Universities maintain traditional hierarchical authority structures while increasingly
recognizing the need for distributed leadership and authentic stakeholder participation. The ISCG
framework shows how these seemingly contradictory governance modes can coexist through careful
design of participation protocols, information systems, and accountability structures that enable bottom-up
innovation within top-down frameworks.
6.2 Empirical Contributions and Evidence Quality
This study provides the most comprehensive synthesis of recent empirical evidence (2024–2025) on green
university governance effectiveness. Analysis of 187 publications and 34 quantitative case studies offers
robust evidence for governance model effectiveness, though several important caveats warrant emphasis.
Strengths of Evidence Base:
Recency: 2024–2025 focus ensures currency and relevance to contemporary practice
Diversity: Evidence spans multiple geographic contexts (Asia, Europe, Americas), institutional types
(research-intensive, teaching-focused, small, large), and governance models
Mixed methods: Combination of quantitative outcomes and qualitative process analysis provides
comprehensive understanding
Triangulation: Multiple data sources and analytical approaches enhance validity
Limitations and Gaps:
Outcome measurement heterogeneity: Variability in metrics and methodologies limits direct
quantitative comparison across cases
Self-reporting bias: Many case studies rely on institutional self-reporting, potentially overstating
positive outcomes
Publication bias: Focus on peer-reviewed literature may underrepresent implementation failures and
challenges
Limited long-term data: Most studies report outcomes over 2–5 year periods; longer-term
sustainability remains uncertain
Context specificity: Effectiveness may vary significantly across institutional and cultural contexts not
fully captured in available evidence

Page 28/44
Future research should address these gaps through: standardized outcome measurement protocols
enabling meta-analysis; longitudinal studies tracking governance effectiveness over 10 + years; systematic
documentation of implementation failures and challenges; and comparative studies across diverse
institutional and cultural contexts.
6.3 Practical Implications for Institutions
The ISCG framework offers several actionable insights for university administrators, sustainability officers,
and institutional leaders:
Start with Assessment
Comprehensive baseline assessment identifying current state, gaps, and priorities provides essential
foundation. Many institutions launch initiatives without adequate understanding of starting conditions,
leading to misaligned interventions and wasted resources.
Secure Leadership Commitment
Visible, sustained commitment from senior leadership with resource allocation demonstrating institutional
priority proves essential. Sustainability initiatives lacking presidential/board-level support consistently
struggle to achieve institutional integration and adequate resources.
Invest in Operational Management
The operational management layer—dedicated sustainability office, cross-functional committees, KPI
systems, PDCA cycles—represents the critical "middle layer" enabling strategy-to-action translation.
Institutions should invest in professional staff capacity, not rely solely on volunteer efforts.
Engage Stakeholders Authentically
Token consultation proves insufficient; authentic participation requires representative membership,
decision-making authority, adequate support, and transparent communication of how input influences
decisions. Student and staff engagement enhances both implementation quality and institutional
commitment.
Implement Digital Infrastructure
Digital monitoring and engagement platforms increasingly prove essential for coordinating complex, multi-
stakeholder initiatives. Real-time dashboards, user-friendly interfaces, and integration across systems
enable data-driven management and stakeholder engagement.
Use Phased Implementation
Staged approaches allowing learning, adaptation, and building momentum through visible successes prove
more effective than comprehensive "big bang" transformations. Quick wins demonstrate feasibility, build
support, and generate learning informing subsequent phases.

Page 29/44
Join Networks
Regional or thematic university networks enable resource-sharing, policy diffusion, and collective advocacy,
particularly valuable for smaller institutions lacking individual capacity for comprehensive programs.
Measure and Report Transparently
Systematic data collection, standardized metrics, and transparent reporting enable continuous
improvement, benchmarking, and accountability. Participation in external rankings (UI GreenMetric, STARS)
provides structure and external validation.
Integrate, Don't Isolate
Sustainability initiatives achieve greatest impact when integrated into existing institutional systems—
strategic planning, budgeting, curriculum review, faculty evaluation, student life—rather than remaining
isolated add-ons.
Plan for Long-Term Commitment
Sustainability transformation requires sustained effort over many years. Institutions should design
governance structures with continuity mechanisms surviving leadership transitions and budget
fluctuations.
6.4 Methodological Innovations and Assessment
Frameworks
Recent empirical work introduces several methodological innovations enhancing green university
assessment:
Multi-Level Indicator Systems
Moving beyond single-dimension metrics to comprehensive frameworks spanning environmental
performance, educational integration, operational efficiency, and governance quality enables more holistic
assessment (Pogule, 2025). These multi-level systems align with contemporary understanding of
sustainability as inherently multi-dimensional.
Digital Monitoring Platforms
Integration of digital infrastructure with sustainability assessment creates real-time feedback loops,
reduces data collection burden, and enables granular analysis previously infeasible with manual methods
(Zou et al., 2024). As costs decrease and capabilities expand, digital monitoring will likely become standard
practice.
PDCA Integration

Page 30/44
Systematic application of Plan-Do-Check-Act cycles to sustainability initiatives provides structured
methodology for continuous improvement, learning documentation, and adaptive management
(Phrophayak et al., 2024). PDCA's strength lies in creating organizational routines for reflection and
adjustment.
Participatory Assessment
Involving diverse stakeholders in assessment design, data collection, and interpretation enhances both
data quality (local knowledge) and utilization (stakeholder ownership of findings) (Alrubaye & Al-Isawi,
2025). Participatory approaches align assessment with governance values of authentic engagement.
Standardization Efforts
Growing adoption of common frameworks (UI GreenMetric, STARS, THE Impact Rankings) enables
benchmarking and cross-institutional comparison, though tensions remain between standardization
enabling comparison and context-sensitivity respecting institutional diversity (Oliveira & Proença, 2025).
6.5 Critical Analysis and Limitations
While the ISCG framework synthesizes substantial empirical evidence and offers comprehensive
governance architecture, several important limitations and critiques warrant acknowledgment:
Complexity and Resource Requirements
The full ISCG framework requires significant resources—dedicated staff, digital infrastructure, stakeholder
engagement processes, data systems—potentially beyond reach of smaller or resource-constrained
institutions. While adaptation guidance addresses this concern, implementation challenges remain
substantial.
Cultural Context Sensitivity
Most empirical evidence derives from North American, European, and East Asian contexts; applicability to
other cultural and institutional contexts requires validation. Governance approaches emphasizing
distributed leadership and stakeholder participation may encounter challenges in more hierarchical cultural
contexts.
Power Dynamics
The framework emphasizes participatory governance but may insufficiently address underlying power
dynamics that can marginalize certain stakeholder groups even within ostensibly participatory structures.
Critical scholars argue that authentic transformation requires addressing fundamental power relations, not
merely creating participation mechanisms.
Measurement Limitations: Despite methodological innovations, sustainability assessment remains
challenged by: difficulty measuring transformative educational outcomes beyond curriculum integration;
attribution challenges linking governance interventions to outcomes influenced by multiple factors; short-

Page 31/44
term measurement horizons missing longer-term impacts; and focus on easily quantifiable metrics
potentially marginalizing important but harder-to-measure dimensions.
Implementation Fidelity
The framework presents an idealized governance architecture; real-world implementation inevitably
involves compromises, adaptations, and partial adoption. Gap between framework design and
implementation reality requires ongoing attention.
Transformation vs. Incrementalism
Critics may argue the framework represents incremental improvement within existing institutional
structures rather than transformative change addressing root causes of unsustainability. Tension exists
between pragmatic approaches working within current systems and radical approaches seeking
fundamental restructuring.
These limitations suggest important directions for future research and practice: developing resource-
efficient governance models for constrained contexts; validating framework effectiveness across diverse
cultural settings; explicitly addressing power dynamics in participatory processes; advancing assessment
methodologies for transformative outcomes; studying implementation fidelity and adaptation processes;
and engaging ongoing debates about incremental vs. transformative change.
7. Conclusions
7.1 Key Findings
This study developed and validated the Integrated Stakeholder-Centric Governance (ISCG) framework for
green university transformation through systematic synthesis of 187 recent peer-reviewed publications
(2024–2025) and comparative analysis of empirical case studies with quantitative outcomes. Several key
findings emerge:
Governance Model Diversity: Six dominant governance architectures characterize contemporary practice:
(1) KPI-driven administrative divisions with PDCA cycles; (2) networked multi-institution coalitions; (3)
digitalized integrated governance platforms; (4) bottom-up green commissions with staged financing; (5)
whole-institution systems thinking approaches; (6) hybrid dedicated sustainability office models. Each
offers distinct advantages for particular institutional contexts.
Critical Success Factors: Effective governance consistently integrates: strong leadership commitment with
resource allocation; dedicated operational management capacity (sustainability offices, committees);
systematic KPI integration and PDCA cycles; authentic multi-stakeholder participation with decision-
making authority; digital infrastructure enabling real-time monitoring and coordination; integration into
existing institutional systems rather than isolated initiatives.

Page 32/44
Quantifiable Outcomes: Leading institutions demonstrate measurable sustainability improvements:
Mahasarakham University achieved 50% improvement in waste management scores over five years
through KPI integration and participatory governance; Universidad Católica de Córdoba projects 70%
carbon footprint mitigation via integrated strategies; institutions adopting comprehensive governance
frameworks report enhanced performance across environmental, educational, and operational dimensions.
Implementation Challenges: Persistent barriers include: insufficient policy institutionalization and uneven
unit engagement; data collection gaps and limited monitoring capacity; resource constraints particularly
affecting smaller institutions; organizational culture resistant to change; competing priorities and limited
awareness. Documented solutions emphasize: formal KPI integration; digital monitoring platforms;
networked collaboration and phased implementation; capacity-building and recognition programs.
Framework Validation
The ISCG framework integrating five governance layers (strategic leadership, operational management,
academic integration, community engagement, assessment & monitoring) through three cross-cutting
mechanisms (stakeholder participation protocols, digital infrastructure, accountability structures)
synthesizes best practices validated across diverse institutional contexts.
7.2 Theoretical Contributions
This research advances sustainability governance theory by: integrating organizational change theory,
stakeholder theory, and systems thinking into a comprehensive framework; theorizing the critical
"operational management layer" bridging strategy and implementation; demonstrating how participatory
and hierarchical governance modes can coexist through careful structural design; and providing empirical
validation of governance effectiveness through quantitative outcomes.
7.3 Practical Contributions
The ISCG framework offers university administrators and sustainability officers: evidence-based
governance architecture adaptable to diverse institutional contexts; actionable implementation pathway
with six-phase cycle; validated best practices from leading institutions; comprehensive KPI systems and
assessment frameworks; stakeholder engagement protocols; and resource allocation guidance. The
framework provides structured toolkit moving institutions from aspiration to operationalization.
7.4 Future Research Directions
Several important research directions emerge from this study:
Longitudinal Studies
Long-term tracking of governance effectiveness over 10 + years would illuminate sustainability of
improvements, evolution of governance structures, and factors enabling or constraining sustained
transformation.
Comparative Effectiveness

Page 33/44
Rigorous comparative studies employing quasi-experimental designs or matched case-control approaches
could better isolate governance effects from confounding factors and identify which governance models
prove most effective for particular institutional contexts.
Cultural Context
Systematic research validating framework effectiveness across diverse cultural and institutional contexts—
particularly Global South institutions underrepresented in current literature—would enhance generalizability
and identify needed adaptations.
Power Dynamics
Critical research examining how power relations shape participatory governance processes, whose voices
are privileged or marginalized, and how governance structures can better address equity dimensions would
strengthen framework's justice orientation.
Transformative Outcomes
Methodological innovation measuring transformative educational outcomes—shifts in student values,
behaviors, career choices—and systemic impacts beyond individual institutions would address current
assessment limitations.
Implementation Science
Detailed process studies examining implementation fidelity, adaptation processes, and factors enabling
successful translation from framework to practice would enhance practical utility.
Cost-Effectiveness
Economic analysis comparing costs and benefits of different governance models would inform resource
allocation decisions and make business case for sustainability investments.
7.5 Closing Reflections
Universities stand at a critical juncture in human history. The climate crisis, biodiversity collapse, and
systemic inequities demand transformation in how societies produce, consume, govern, and relate to each
other and the natural world. As institutions educating future leaders, generating knowledge shaping policy
and practice, and serving as anchor institutions in communities worldwide, universities bear both
responsibility and opportunity to model sustainability transformation.
The evidence synthesized in this study demonstrates that effective governance—not merely good
intentions or isolated initiatives—determines whether universities successfully operationalize sustainability
commitments. The ISCG framework offers a structured, evidence-based pathway for institutions ready to
move from aspiration to action, from fragmented initiatives to integrated transformation, from reactive
compliance to proactive leadership.

Page 34/44
Yet governance frameworks alone prove insufficient. Genuine transformation requires courage: to question
established practices, to challenge vested interests, to invest resources in long-term change, to engage
authentically with diverse voices, to accept accountability for outcomes, and to persist through inevitable
setbacks. It requires imagination: to envision universities as regenerative institutions contributing to
thriving communities and ecosystems, not merely minimizing harm. And it requires solidarity: recognizing
that sustainability transformation represents collective endeavor requiring collaboration across institutions,
sectors, and societies.
The universities that will thrive in the 21st century are those that embrace this transformation—not as
burden or constraint, but as opportunity to fulfill higher education's fundamental purpose: advancing human
flourishing and societal well-being. The ISCG framework provides a map for this journey. The destination—
sustainable, equitable, regenerative universities—remains to be collectively created.

Comparative Analysis of Green Cloud Computing 
 
Abdul Majid Farooqi

Abstract: Today it is globally accepted that mankind is the major reason for global warming. Data Centres, computers, and other 
gadgets are the main causes and sources of greenhouse gasses, especially CO2. Data centres use thousands of processors and other 
computer elements, that generate heat which requires a large amount of cooling equipment, cooling equipment again generate a 
large amount of heat. Thus, we need such ideas and techniques that reduce the energy consumption and emission of CO2. In this 
paper, we have compared different techniques of green cloud computing and show the approximate results of each technique. 
 
Keywords: Green Computing, Power Consumption, Cloud Computing, Power Efficiency, Greenhouse Gases. 
 
I.        INTRODUCTION 
Green computing is making data center and 
electronic devices environmentally friendly and eco-
friendly, in other words, it is described as the 
inspection of engineering, designing, manufacturing, 
disposing and using of computing peripherals in a way 
that curtails their environmental brunt. In 1992, the 
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) introduced 
the Energy Star program, it was a very first time when 
the term Green Computing came into light [1]. 
 
Figure 1. Working of Green Cloud Computing [2] 
To see the growing demand for cloud computing in 
every field it is necessary for the environment that we 
take one step ahead towards green computing so that 
electricity consumption and CO2 emissions can be cut 
down and recycled. Usually, cloud data centers span in 
more than thousands of feet of area that contain 
ultimate computing power like servers, networking 
devices, hard disk racks, cooling fans, console, big 
screens etc. along with cooling machines, air 
conditioners, lights and backup generators. So that 
they can fulfill their day to day costumer’s demands. 
All these things require a great amount of power. In 
2012 electricity consumption by these data centers was 
measured around 38 Giga Watts that is sufficient to 
almost all united kingdom’s residential households, in 
comparison to 2011, it was 63% more, and it is 
continuously increasing every passing year [3]. As the 
demand of Cloud Computing is on peak now a day due 
to its tremendous capabilities of bringing on-demand 
services, many organizations and companies are 
migrating towards the cloud, as a result many data 
centers coming into light, only one data center 
occupies a massive amount of area, 50,000 square feet 
approx. that needs 5 megawatts (mv) electricity that 
can fulfill the need of the power of 5000 households 
for one year. So now these data centers require cooling 
also to cool down their giant servers because these 
servers provide their services and run 24/7 and 365 
days continuously without break, yes, it’s true that all 
servers are not in use all the time but it is also true that 
they can’t be turned off. According to a recent study 
only US data centers consumed about 70 billion 
kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2014 [4], that was 30 
billion watts in 2012 all over the world, now we can 
see that how much these data centers are consuming 
electricity and discharging CO2. There are more than 
three billion active internet users worldwide that are 
continuously surfing the internet through google, 
google runs 1000 servers just for one query, that’s why 
it takes only 0.2 seconds for query results to come up 
[3], in a single day sixty million searches hit the 
google search engine [5]. Figure 2 and 3 will 
demonstrate how much CO2 is dissipated and how 
much electricity is consumed in one google search as

57

as 
in

respectively.
 
Figure 2. Energy consumption in one Google 
search [3] 
 
Figure 3. Energy consumption in monthly Google 
search [3]. 
Google data centers consist of thousands of 
servers, these servers demand enormous supply of 
electricity 
to 
working 
seamlessly, 
now 
the 
consequences come in the form of CO2 emission, thus 
these data centers are one of the biggest responsible for 
global warming. So now it is our duty that we find 
some innovative ways to overcome this problem, it is 
our responsibility to search such ideas and techniques 
that help us to reduce electricity consumption and CO2 
emission. 
II. GREEN COMPUTING TECHNIQUES FOR 
ENERGY EFFICIENCY 
In this section, we are presenting various 
techniques 
that 
can 
help 
to 
reduce 
energy 
consumption. We have divided this section into two 
categories, the first category describes such techniques 
that can be implemented at home, these techniques are 
basically for normal and average users. The second 
category is consisting of some advanced techniques 
that are specially designed for power-hungry data 
centers. 
 
Ideas that can be applied and implemented at 
home: 
 
• 
Hard disk sleep mode: Hard disk and other 
optical drives are designed to fall asleep after a 
specific time of inactivity to conserve energy, in this 
state HDD stays in “low energy consumption” mode 
and platters have halted to spin [6]. 3.5” Hard disk 
drive uses the electricity from 6.5 to 9 watts, 2.5” 
laptop HDD consumes power from 0.7 to 3 watts, 
and a solid-state drive can use 0.6 to 2.8 watts [7]. 
After proper configuration Operating System can 
automatically manage this mode. 
• 
LED/LCD sleep mode: Enable the sleep 
mode option in the monitor, so that after some time 
of idling monitor will falls asleep. In sleep mode 
LED turns off its all emitting pixels and enters “low 
power consumption state” [6]. For instance, a Fujitsu 
B27T-7 LED monitor consumes 51.34 (kWh/yr) 
Total Energy, while in sleep mode it’s only a 0.25 
watts [8]. 
• 
Power off devices when not in use: Shutting 
down the system in idle period is the most effective, 
most natural and absolutely the simplest and the 
easiest way to reduce energy consumption [6]. 
• 
System standby mode: In this mode, the 
computer shuts down all its components and parts 
except Volatile Memory, the volatile memory 
remains active and waits for the user command, 
whenever user press some key, move a mouse or 
open a LED in laptop case Volatile Memory 
immediately active the entire system [6]. In standby 
mode system starts from that stage where the user 
left it before, in simple words it resumes the system. 
An average desktop PC consumes electricity 
between 80 and 250 watts, depending on additional 
peripherals, while in standby mode a desktop 
computer uses between 1.1 and 83.3 watts, the 
average is 21.13 [9]. Table 1 demonstrates standby 
power summary in detail. 
 
Table I. Standby Power Summery 
 
 
• 
Hibernate Mode: The hibernate mode is an 
advanced version of standby mode; this mode 
completely turn off the computer including volatile 
memory, before shutting down the computer it saves 
the memory and system state on the hard disk so that 
it can resume the PC when the user invokes the 
system. If the computer is unplugged it uses zero

power, otherwise, in hibernate mode, it uses 2.3 
watts [10]. 
• 
Use a computer and other peripherals in 
power saver mode: The power saver saves energy by 
reducing computer’s performance where possible. 
This technique reduces the CPU speed all the time 
and set the display brightness at minimum possible 
level. 
• 
Ideas and techniques for data centers: 
• 
Using Clock Gating: Clock gating is an 
energy 
conserving 
feature 
in 
semiconductor 
microelectronic, that is responsible for enabling and 
disabling the clock. Many electronic devices use 
clock gating feature to disable bridges, buses, 
controllers and chunks of processors to reduce power 
consumption. It saves the electrical power used by 
the processor. The working criteria of clock gating 
are if the logic block is engaging in some work then 
clock of a logic block must be activated, and if there 
is no task performing then clock gating must be 
deactivated. Clock gating technique is very popular 
among many synchronous circuits [3]. 
• 
Energy Efficient Processors: Modifying the 
clock rate of a processor or voltage of a processor is 
possible, we can do this with the help of “Dynamic 
Voltage Scaling” and “Dynamic Frequency Scaling”. 
In dynamic voltage scaling, we can modify the 
voltage as per the need of current situation, whether 
it is related to hardware or software by increasing 
and decreasing it. In dynamic frequency scaling, we 
can set the frequency according to hardware and 
software need by minimizing and maximizing it. 
This technique can save a lot of electricity power, 
also it is already implemented in the following real-
time systems: Transmeta Longrun and Longrun2, 
AMD Cool’n’Quiet, Intel SpeedStep, VIA LongHaul 
(PowerSaver), AMD PowerNow, IBM Energy Scale 
[3]. 
• 
Renewable Energy sources: For backup 
purposes, usually data centers need generator 
powered by diesel, burning diesel come out in the 
form of exhaust gasses, like CO2, NOx, GHGs, and 
particulate matter, the diesel generator emissions 
these gasses into the atmosphere and pollute the 
nearby air quality substantially. One liter of fuel has 
0.73 kg of carbon, so with one liter of fuel 2.6 kg of 
CO2 released into the air. To overcome this problem 
there are some other ways to produce electricity, we 
can use solar energy, wind energy as well as 
hydroelectric energy instead of diesel generator as a 
backup plan for data centers [3]. 
• 
Energy Efficient Storage: Today energy 
efficient storages are available in the market that can 
take place of current storages of the cloud. As the life 
expectancy of a data center has been measured up to 
9 years so while overhauling existing data center 
renovator can use energy efficient storage like solid 
state Drive (SSD). As there is no moving part in SSD 
unlike hard disk drive, so now, SSD requires less 
cooling and less energy as compared to HDD, as we 
mentioned earlier a hard disk consumes electricity 
from 6.5 to 9 watts, while solid state drive consumes 
electricity from 0.6 to 2.8 watts. Clearly, we can see 
the differences between two [3]. 
• 
Using Free Cooling System: Most of the data 
centers achieve cooling by refrigerator, in this 
technique a machine called compressor supplies or 
pushes the chilly water into the network of pipes 
made of highly conductive metal, like copper or 
aluminum, these pipes clamped on top of the CPU 
and on other equipment, water flows absorbing heat 
and makes it way to a radiator and so on. Instead 
mechanical refrigeration technique we can use free 
cooling, basically it is depended on outside 
atmosphere and weather condition, if the data 
center’s outside temperature is below or reached 
specified point then refrigerator start automatically to 
provide cooling, here one thing is considerable that 
free cooling is not truly or entirely free, because 
cooling equipment is still needed, for example, fans, 
pump etc. [3]. 
III.    PARAMETERS USED FOR MEASURING 
POWER CONSUMPTION 
Many measurement techniques are available to 
measure the data center electricity consumption, some 
of them are listed here: 1. Thermal Design Power 
(TDP), 2. Power usage Effectiveness (PUE), 3. Data 
Center 
infrastructure 
Efficiency 
(DCiE), 
4. 
Performance per Watt (PpW), 5. Compute Power 
Efficiency (CPE), 6. Green Energy coefficient (GEC), 
7. Energy Reuse Factor (ERF), 8. Carbon usage 
Effectiveness (CUE), 9. Water usage Effectiveness 
(WUE), 10. Data Center Productivity (DCP). 
a. Thermal Design Power (TDP) 
Also, called Thermal Design Point, this term often 
use in CPU or GPU, the TDP is the maximum power 
consumption by a CPU or GPU when running a real 
application, at this point of time a device dissipate 
whatever the max power is known as TDP. Table 2 
present different TDPs of GPU and CPU: -

It computes the energy efficiency of an individual

e. 
Compute Power Efficiency (CPE) 
CPE is a measurement of computing efficiency of a 
data center. It’s not fundamental all the time that we 
get effective work by each watt consumed by the 
server, some devices are power-hungry, they consume 
power even in idle state, yes, it is also true that 100% 
data center capacity will never be used but still we

INVESTIGATION

Key words:- 
Green Banking, Customer Perception, 
Sustainable Finance, Digital Banking, 
Environmental Awareness 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The growing environmental concerns have urged the banking sector to 
integrate sustainable practices into their operations, giving rise to the 
concept of green banking. This study focuses on investigating the 
adoption, awareness, and effectiveness of green banking practices 
among customers in Odisha, India. It aims to understand customer 
perceptions, satisfaction levels, and behavioural responses toward eco-
friendly banking initiatives such as paperless transactions, digital 
banking, green loans, and environmental risk management. Employing 
a mixed-methods approach, the study gathers data through surveys and 
interviews with a diverse customer base across urban and rural regions 
of Odisha. Findings reveal that while awareness of green banking is 
steadily increasing, significant gaps persist in customer engagement 
and satisfaction, particularly in rural areas where digital literacy 
remains low. The study highlights key factors influencing customer 
adoption, including convenience, trust, environmental consciousness, 
and accessibility of green services. Moreover, it identifies barriers such 
as lack of awareness campaigns, infrastructural limitations, and 
perceived risks associated with digital banking platforms. The research 
suggests that banks must prioritize customer education, enhance 
technological accessibility, and strengthen trust-building measures to 
foster a more inclusive green banking environment. This customer-
centric investigation provides valuable insights for policymakers, 
banks, and environmental advocates seeking to promote sustainable 
banking practices in Odisha and similar developing regions. The study 
ultimately emphasizes that customer empowerment is crucial for the 
successful transition towards greener and more sustainable banking 
ecosystems.
