occupant become blurred and virtualized
rather than traditional physical isolation. The
original static, natural physical boundaries
within the network, is replaced by dynamic
and virtual logical boundaries.
2.
The deployment of middle boxes need
repositioning
3.
Security requirements for different
occupant is different
4.
The migrations of virtual machines
result change in security domain
B.
Software defined network in data
centre network:
The cloud data centre needs to ensure the
occupants or the security domains with
complete and isolated network boundaries.
Due to different virtual machines of different
occupants shares the same physical resource,
system security provides prevention from
virtual machine escaping.
The core change of SDN is switches,
routers and some other forwarding devices
forwards according to flow table created by
controller, which results in more efficiency
and less cost. The controller collects network
status 
information, 
discovers 
network
topologies, checks the network forwarding
policies, generates and updates the flow table.
The traditional Packet Filtering Firewall or
Access Control List should be deployed to the
header so that, the first packet’s header of a
flow in the controller will not be forwarded to
the controller again
Network access control deployed on
physical gateway should still arrange to
"logical" gateway. Openflow protocols and
controllers, network security based on SDN in
cloud data centre by setting flow table and
guiding traffic that matches the policies,
address the problems of Middle boxes
deployment and “fragmentation” of security
rules.  It is possible to optimize the controller
by configuration and management, and make
rules 
for 
dynamic 
migration 
and
reconfiguration to solve security policy
inconsistencies caused by the Middle boxes
reposition and the virtual machine migration.
2. COLLABORATIVE SECURITY
IN DCN
A.
Collaborative security for Antivirus

Security
Centre
imports the virus
signature database: There is an option to
import the virus signature database in
Security Centre and disseminate them to peer-
UTMs.

Security
Centre
issues the virus
signature database: There is an option to issue
the virus signature database in Security
Centre.

Interface displays the virus database
has been updated in PEER-UTM: The time
stamp or version number changes.

Virus 
signature 
database
synchronization among peer-UTMs, which
use p2p mode.
B.
Collaborative security for Firewall

Importing Firewall rules to Security
Centre: The option of importing Firewall
rules to Security Centre.

Security Centre issues the Firewall
rules: The option of issuing the Firewall rules.

Interface displays the Firewall rules
have been updated: There is a web panel in
peer-UTM collaborative security module. The
web panel shows the new Firewall rules have
loaded in.

The peer-UTM chooses to apply the
rules which are updated by Security Centre:
In the display panel of the update rules, the
peer-UTM can also invalid some rules as
required.
3. VIRTUALIZATION BASED ON
SDN
Network topology and host’s IP
allocated as follows, each virtual machine is
bridged to eth0 192.168.0.0 segment for ssh
control. Controller is also through ssh to
communicate with openflow switch. In
openflow switch, there are three Ethernet
ports, which can be connected according to
the experimental needs. Each client has an
Ethernet port that can be connected to any

VCNSMS
A. Function settings
Security Centre, centrally managed
security 
rules, 
collect 
the 
feedback
information from the rule deployment, and
store them into the security log.
1. 
Security 
rules
are
incrementally
downloaded.

The current rule set and temporary
rule set is implemented. In the Security
Centre, remove the duplicate rules in new
rules. The new rule set will be added in a
package and issued to the peer-UTM.
2. Firewall module.

Firewall rules will be downloaded
from the Security Centre and activated in the
Firewall module, and the corresponding
function will be achieved. Security events are
collected and feedback to the Security Centre.
3. UDP content filtering module.

Block the specified types of data
packets matched with the specified patterns.
B. Enhanced security functions
The Protocol Control module in the
prototype system to achieve the instant
loading patterns and pattern matching for
UDP protocol is modified.
1.
UTM routinely update security rules.

UTM regularly obtain and utilize
configuration information of Firewall rule
from the specified server. The configuration
information includes the rules of content
inspection of UDP and the blacklist based on
“quintuple”.
2.
Filtering based on the content of UDP
packet.

According to the rules, the packets
which contain specified features will be
blocked
3. Blocking with blacklist

update rule.
C. Security Level based Protection Policy
The security level based protection
policy is described as:
1.
Security level settings are indicated by
Red, Yellow, Orange and Green.
2.
Intelligence network flow processing

According to the security level setting,
different security rule set and packet verdict
scheme are used with the consideration of
different performance and load requirements.
3.
Multi-function security gateway Peer-
UTM can configure different security plugins
on the demand of security level, and incurs
different processing costs. Working mode of
peer-UTM is also divided into Red, Yellow,
Orange and Green.
D.
Smart packet verdict scheme with
untangle Shield:
Shield is a module of untangle, which
function is to prevent DDoS. Shield reads a
packet from nfqueue, and starts four threads,
including a main thread, an event dispatch
thread, an admission packet processing thread
and a frontend microhttpd daemon. The main
task of shield is to collect packet
processing thread, and there is no parallel
structure in the origin Shield implementation.
CONCLUSIONS
The usage of vCNSMS to address
network security in data centre network with
multiple 
occupants and 
vCNSMS
with
centralized collaborative scheme is explained.

packet verdict algorithm for smart packet
inspection to defence possible network attack
inside data
centre
network. SDN based
virtualization network in data centre can
deploy vCNSMS for flexibility and scalability
to protect multiple tenant with different
scrutiny policy and security requirement. The
smart packet verdict scheme can be used for
deep defence in data centre network.
Future work
As the practical deployment and
operation experience of vCNSMS in data
centre network, vCNSMS Security Centre can
collects more and more security rules and its
events. It is possible to detect network policy
violation and intrusion attack with
AI
(artificial intelligence).

33 
Overview of Liquid Cooling Technology Development in 
Data Centers 
Junliang Liu 1, 2, Xiaoya Zhang 1, 2, *, Lique Shi 1, 2 
1 Hebei Air Conditioning Engineering Installation Co., Ltd., Hengshui Hebei, 053000, China 
2 Hebei Provincial Innovation Center for Central Air Conditioning System Installation and Operation Technology, Hengshui Hebei, 053000, 
China 
* Corresponding author: Xiaoya Zhang 
 
Abstract: This paper conducts a systematic study on the development of liquid cooling technology in data centers. It analyzes 
the energy consumption challenges faced by data centers amid the explosive growth of AI and computing power demands, as 
well as the limitations of air cooling technology in high-heat-density scenarios. The article highlights that liquid cooling 
technology, with its advantages of high thermal conductivity, low energy consumption, and high-density deployment, has become 
a key technological pathway for achieving green and low-carbon development in data centers. The paper elaborates on the 
principles, characteristics, and current applications of three liquid cooling technologies: cold plate, immersion, and spray cooling. 
Through practical case studies and comparative data, it demonstrates that liquid cooling can significantly reduce PUE to below 
1.2, achieving 1.1 or lower in certain scenarios, while offering outstanding energy efficiency and heat recovery potential. 
Although challenges remain in cost, operational maintenance, and material compatibility, liquid cooling technology plays an 
irreplaceable role in advancing the efficient, green, and sustainable development of data centers. 
Keywords: Data Center; Liquid Cooling Technology; Air Cooling Technology. 
 
1. Introduction 
Currently, the global AI industry is experiencing rapid 
expansion, while domestic computing power capacity is 
surging exponentially. In this era of accelerated deep 
computing development, data centers have become the core 
infrastructure underpinning the global digital transformation 
process. According to the International Energy Agency's 
World Energy Outlook 2024 report: From 2014 to 2023, 
global electricity consumption growth significantly outpaced 
overall energy demand. The rapid development of the digital 
economy has driven electricity demand for data centers, 
artificial intelligence, and related sectors from approximately 
460 TWh in 2022 to potentially exceeding 1,000 TWh by 
2026[1]. Research indicates that data center energy 
consumption will rise from 0.9% of global energy use in 2015 
to 8% by 2030[2]. However, the rapid growth of data centers 
today is accompanied by challenges. Issues such as energy 
consumption, carbon emissions, resource efficiency, and 
security are becoming increasingly prominent. Particularly 
since the introduction of the “dual carbon” goals, relevant 
policies have set higher requirements for data center PUE. To 
support China's “dual carbon” objectives, achieve intelligent 
and green development in data centers, and advance the 
industry, researching more efficient cooling systems has 
become a shared goal across the entire sector. 
Air cooling technology remains the most widely adopted 
thermal management solution in global data centers[3], yet its 
drawbacks are increasingly apparent. First, the cooling 
efficiency of air-cooled systems is significantly impacted by 
ambient temperature and airflow[4]. In high-temperature or 
high-density computing environments, relying solely on air 
convection struggles to rapidly dissipate heat generated by 
equipment. This often leads to localized cooling challenges, 
compromising server performance and potentially triggering 
hardware failures. Second, air-cooled systems rely on 
numerous fans for air circulation, resulting in high energy 
consumption and persistent noise that disrupts both the data 
center environment and operations personnel[5]. Furthermore, 
air as a heat transfer medium has low thermal mass and 
thermal conductivity, limiting further improvements in 
cooling capacity and making it difficult to meet future data 
center demands for high computing power and low PUE. 
Finally, air-cooled architectures typically require substantial 
data center floor space and complex supply/return ducting 
designs, consuming valuable building area. They also present 
challenges for future expansion or retrofitting, lacking 
flexibility. These drawbacks are driving the industry toward 
more efficient cooling technologies like liquid cooling. 
2. Analysis of Liquid Cooling 
Technology Advantages in Data 
Center Applications 
A data center is a centralized facility designed to house 
computer systems and related components. Virtually all 
digital services in our daily lives—such as sending emails, 
using mobile apps, and shopping online—are powered by 
servers within data centers that provide computing and 
support. Data centers underpin the advancement of all 
cutting-edge technologies, including cloud computing, big 
data, and artificial intelligence. With the proliferation of AI 
servers and GPU clusters, the power consumption per cabinet 
has surged dramatically, placing higher demands on 
electricity and cooling systems. Consequently, servers 
generate substantial heat during operation, necessitating its 
removal through refrigeration systems. This maintains the 
ambient temperature within a stable, optimal range, 
preventing equipment overheating and system crashes. 
PUE is an internationally recognized metric for measuring 
data center power usage effectiveness. A value closer to 1 
indicates a higher level of data center sustainability. The 

 
34 
majority of data center energy consumption stems from IT 
equipment and cooling systems[6]. 
The energy consumption breakdown for data centers at 
different PUE levels is shown in Table 1. As the table 
demonstrates, reducing the energy consumption share of the 
cooling system is a highly effective approach to lowering a 
data center's PUE value. 
 
Table 1. System Energy Consumption Distribution at Different PUE

In typical air-cooled data center cooling systems, the 
equipment with the highest energy consumption is primarily 
the chillers and terminal air distribution units. Data center 
rooms feature a plenum chamber beneath the raised floor, 
with room air conditioners installed on one side of the room. 
The pressure differential between the plenum chamber and 
the room drives the cooling capacity. However, traditional air-
cooled data centers suffer from localized overheating and cold 
air leakage. Attempting to cool overheated areas by reducing 
the temperature of the entire room leads to redundant cooling 
capacity, reduced cooling efficiency, and limitations imposed 
by air's thermophysics properties. The heat dissipation limit 
for air cooling is 34W/cm²[7], while the heat flux density of 
current mainstream chips can reach up to 100W/cm². The 
average PUE for air-cooled data centers currently hovers 
around 1.5. The Action Plan for Green and Low-Carbon 
Development in the Information and Communications 
Industry (2022-2025) requires that by 2025, the PUE of newly 
built large and extra-large data centers nationwide shall be 
reduced to below 1.3. 
Air cooling can no longer meet the PUE requirements of 
modern data centers. Compared to air-cooled data centers, 
liquid cooling technology offers significant advantages for 
data centre applications. For example, it can satisfy the 
thermal dissipation demands of high-power cabinets. The 
selected liquid medium has a thermal conductivity that far 
exceeds that of air, which substantially enhances thermal 
performance and improves data centre cooling efficiency. 
Liquid cooling systems also require less floor space than air-
cooled systems, making them easier to deploy in a variety of 
scenarios and greatly improving the utilization of building 
space. They also simplify heat exchange processes, as using 
high-specific-heat-capacity liquid working fluids reduces 
energy consumption during the cooling cycle. When using 
liquid cooling for heat dissipation, temperatures are higher 
than in conventional air-cooled systems, resulting in superior 
heat recovery performance. Table 2 presents information on 
selected data centers.

As shown in Table 2, in actual data center applications, the 
PUE of liquid-cooled data centers is significantly lower than 
that of air-cooled data centers. In summary, data center liquid 
cooling technology has become a key driver propelling data 
centers toward greener, more efficient, and sustainable 
evolution, thanks to its core advantages of highly efficient 
heat dissipation, low energy consumption, high-density 
deployment, green and low-carbon operation, and long-term 
economic viability. 
3. Liquid Cooling Technology 
Data center liquid cooling technology utilizes liquid as a 
cooling medium to dissipate heat from thermal components 
such as server chips. Compared to air, liquids possess higher 
specific heat capacity and superior thermal conductivity 
(water conducts heat 25 times more efficiently than air), 
enabling faster and more effective removal of heat from 
thermal 
components 
to 
achieve 
enhanced 
cooling 
performance. Liquid cooling technologies can be categorized 
into cold plate, immersion, and spray cooling. Cold plate 
liquid cooling further divides into single-phase and phase-
change cold plates. Cold plate systems operate non-contact, 
while immersion and spray cooling employ contact methods. 
3.1. Non-contact 
Non-contact liquid cooling involves placing server heat-
generating components close to a cold plate, with liquid 
flowing within the plate to dissipate heat from these 
components. The liquid does not directly contact the heat 

 
35 
source, primarily utilizing a cold plate solution. Cold plate 
liquid cooling addresses heat dissipation for high-heat-
generating components within servers, while other lower-heat 
components still rely on air cooling. The overall PUE 
advantage is limited. Furthermore, the close contact between 
the coolant and the load imposes strict requirements for leak 
prevention and flow control. Coolants typically use special 
fluids such as ethylene glycol and deionized water. Non-
contact cold plate liquid cooling exhibits higher thermal 
resistance. Compared to traditional air cooling designs, it 
achieves 60%–90% energy savings. Consequently, a small 
number of fans are typically still required for partial heat 
exchange. Cold plate data centers can achieve a PUE below 
1.2 while maintaining traditional cabinet deployment 
methods, enabling higher deployment density. Current data 
center infrastructure and server retrofitting present minimal 
difficulty and cost, but liquid leakage risks must be 
considered. 
Cold plate liquid cooling technology can be categorized 
into single-phase and phase-change cold plates. Compared to 
air cooling, the closed-loop system of cold plate liquid 
cooling enables more precise cold distribution and supply. 
The specific heat capacity of liquid coolants is significantly 
higher than that of air, allowing cooling water temperatures to 
be raised to 40-55°C. This contrasts with the 18-27°C supply 
temperatures of air cooling, resulting in substantial reductions 
in refrigeration energy consumption. 
Compared to conventional cold plate liquid cooling, phase-
change coupled liquid cooling reduces system pressure drop, 
lowers the risk of fluid leakage, and enhances system 
reliability. Research on cold plate liquid cooling technology 
primarily focuses on optimizing cold plate channel structures. 
This can be achieved through manifold micro-channels, 
corrugated micro-channels, fin-column array micro-channel, 
microbial channel, Z-shaped manifold micro-channel, conical 
manifold micro-channel, layered manifold micro-channel, 
and parallel manifold micro-channel. These approaches 
generally improve flow characteristics by optimizing channel 
structures, enhance heat transfer capacity by increasing heat 
exchange surface area, and reduce data center energy 
consumption by minimizing pressure drops. 
3.2. Contact 
Contact liquid cooling involves direct contact between the 
liquid and the heat source. 
(1) Immersion liquid cooling: Its core principle involves 
fully submerging computing equipment in a highly thermally 
conductive insulating coolant (such as fluoridated liquids, 
mineral oils, or synthetic fluids). The liquid directly contacts 
the equipment surfaces to absorb and rapidly dissipate heat. 
All electronic components are directly submerged in the 
cooling medium liquid. Heat transfers from the electronic 
components to the liquid. A circulation pump then transports 
the heated coolant to an external primary-side water system 
for liquid-to-liquid heat exchange. The cooled coolant returns 
to the reservoir, repeating the cycle continuously. 
The cooling system consists of a cooling tank, coolant, heat 
ex-changer, and circulation pump. The cooling tank features 
a sealed structure to prevent coolant evaporation and 
contamination; 
the 
coolant 
possesses 
high 
thermal 
conductivity and electrical insulation properties, ensuring 
safety and efficient heat dissipation; the heat ex-changer 
facilitates heat exchange between the liquid and external 
cooling systems (such as chillers or dry coolers), while the 
circulation pump maintains coolant flow within the system. 
Heat generated by the equipment is efficiently conducted 
through the liquid. The liquid circulation system transports 
this heat to the heat ex-changer, where it is dissipated via the 
external cooling system before returning to the equipment 
enclosure. Key advantages of immersion liquid cooling 
technology include high heat dissipation efficiency, low 
energy consumption (significantly reduced PUE values), high 
equipment density, low noise levels, and simplified 
maintenance.  
Immersion liquid cooling is categorized into single-phase 
immersion cooling and two-phase immersion cooling. The 
primary distinction between single-phase and two-phase 
immersion systems lies in whether the coolant undergoes a 
phase change during heat absorption. After absorbing heat, 
the coolant reaches its boiling point temperature and 
evaporates, utilizing latent heat of vaporization to carry away 
the heat. It then contacts the external circulation cooling 
system where the gas condenses back into liquid. Throughout 
this process, the coolant undergoes two distinct states—
commonly known as phase change. While phase change 
offers extremely high efficiency, it demands a more complex 
system with stringent requirements for cabinet sealing 
integrity 
and 
operational 
maintenance. 
Single-phase 
immersion liquid remains in a consistent state, resulting in a 
relatively simpler and more controllable structure. 
(2) Spray-type liquid cooling: In spray-type liquid cooling, 
the coolant drips down from spray modules at the top of the 
server chassis. It cools heat-generating components through 
convective heat exchange via direct contact between the 
coolant and these components. The heat is then dissipated 
through channels within the server that collect the coolant and 
direct it to heat ex-changers. The coolant typically consists of 
non-conductive, non-corrosive liquids such as mineral oil or 
fluoridated fluids. Spray-type liquid cooling can completely 
eliminate cooling fans, offers strong heat exchange 
capabilities, and saves coolant compared to immersion 
cooling, reducing data center PUE to around 1.1. However, it 
requires modifications to cabinets and server chassis, 
presenting greater operational and maintenance challenges. 
4. Summary 
This paper presents a systematic investigation into liquid 
cooling technology for data centers. Research indicates that 
despite practical challenges in large-scale deployment—
including high initial investment costs, coolant material 
compatibility issues, and the need for fundamental 
operational system reforms—this technology demonstrates 
irreplaceable advantages in overcoming the limitations of air 
cooling and significantly reducing data center PUE energy 
consumption metrics. Its widespread adoption holds profound 
significance for advancing the green and low-carbon 
transformation of the data center industry. Particularly 
noteworthy is that the medium-to-high temperature cooling 
medium generated by liquid cooling systems creates 
favorable conditions for waste heat recovery. This enables 
integrated energy utilization applications such as district 
heating and agricultural greenhouse heating, substantially 
enhancing the energy recycling efficiency and environmental 
benefits of data centers. This paves the way toward truly 
efficient, green, and sustainable next-generation data centers.

for cheering me on through the ups and supporting me through the

Words cannot describe my endless love and dedication for you

To my sister and brother, Anninka and Ben, and their significant

To Mom Havel and Nana, you both have been a source of

thanks to my uncle, Prof Brian Havel, whose own academic career

To those family members who were artists, curiosity seekers and

have taught me what it means to be an academic, but most 
importantly, a mentor. Your lessons shape this thesis, and it is 
better because of it. My appreciation is boundless. 
 
To each and every Alliance and GPNI activist, and non-party

how grateful I am and amazed at the generosity you all showed in

To those who proofed my thesis and offered insight, I truly

To Adam Ballance and Ciarán Hartley, thank you dearly for the

process. Also, thank you to all my girls who have gone on to be 
such amazing people, but remain my biggest source of fun and 
acceptance. To other pals in DCU and newer friends in Trinity, I 
look forward to our friendships flourishing further. 
 
To my former business teacher, Ms O’Brien who sadly passed in 
2021 and the wider community of St. Angela’s Secondary School

To all those who I have not mentioned here today, let it be known 
that I am where I am because of you and your support. I look

I acknowledge and appreciate the support of the Irish Research

Abstract 
 
Title: ‘Stuck in the Centre with you’: Navigating identity and 
constitutionality among Alliance and Green Party activists in 
Northern Ireland 
Candidate: Louisa Barry 
 
Since the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, Northern Ireland has 
experienced a striking growth in the level of support for centrist, 
non-aligned political parties with support for such parties more than 
doubling from the first NI Assembly elections in 1998 by the latest 
Assembly elections in 2022. There has simultaneously been a 
notable decline in strong unionist and nationalist identification and 
a growth in aligned voters voting for these centrist parties, both 
contributing to corresponding electoral gains for centre-ground 
parties. Brexit has intensified debate around these shifts, 
particularly in relation to a potential border poll and Irish unity. Yet 
the internal dynamics of centre-ground parties including how their 
activists navigate identity, ideology, and the constitutional question 
remain poorly understood. This thesis addresses that gap. The 
thesis examines the two parties constituting the contemporary NI 
centre-ground: the Alliance Party and the Green Party of Northern 
Ireland (GPNI). Drawing on forty-four semi-structured interviews 
with party activists, supplemented by archival research, media 
analysis, and polling data, it offers an intrinsic case study of what 
occupying the centre-ground means from the inside. The 
conceptual framework defines the centre-ground through two 
markers: civic orientation and constitutional neutrality on Northern 
Ireland's status while issue orientation is also critical for the GPNI. 
This framework identifies Alliance and the GPNI as the core 
instances of the centre-ground while preserving meaningful 
distinctions between them. Three central findings emerge. First, 
the centre-ground is populated by the less-aligned rather than non-
aligned: activists who negotiate with, rather than transcend, 
inherited ethno-national identities. From Alliance, this manifests as 
residual communal attachments and a decline in British 
identification driven less by Brexit than by discomfort with 
unionism's inflection of Britishness. Second, Alliance and the GPNI 
approach constitutional neutrality differently. Alliance activists are 
heterogeneous on Irish unity, but broadly support organisational 
neutrality; GPNI activists, shaped by an eco-socialist ethos and 
operating as an issue-based party, are increasingly open to 
constitutional deliberation as a party responsibility, assessing 
options through the lens of environmental governance and post-
growth economics. Third, both parties exhibit distinct conditionality 
cultures linked to commitments to inclusion and effective

Introduction 
 
Since the 1998 Good Friday Agreement (GFA) and the 
introduction of institutionalised power-sharing, Northern Ireland 
(NI) has seen strikingly significant growth in support for centrist, 
non-traditionally aligned parties. The Alliance Party and the Green 
Party of Northern Ireland (GPNI) have experienced a growth in 
their share of the first preference vote from a combined 6.6% in the 
first NI Assembly elections in 1998 to 15.4% in the last elections in 
May 2022 (British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) News, 2022). 
While there are a variety of factors at play in these changing 
dynamics including the impact of wider changes in United Kingdom 
(UK) politics and the impact of Brexit and the Covid-19 pandemic, 
this growth in support for the centre-ground of NI politics is linked 
to wider domestic social changes in NI since the GFA. Since 1998, 
Northern Ireland has seen more individuals who no longer choose 
to self-identify strongly, or at all, as Irish/Nationalist or 
British/Unionist. Specifically, in 2018 50% of Northern Ireland Life 
and Times Survey (NILT) respondents identified as neither 
nationalist nor unionist, compared to just 33% in 19981. Of course, 
the degree of detachment during this period is not equally drastic. 
For instance, there was a comparable percentage pattern in 2018 
to that in 1998 of respondents identifying as Irish, British and 
Northern Irish (Devine, 2021). However, by the 2000s, research 
had already found2 significant ‘distancing from conventional 
practices and understandings of ethno-religious and national 
divisions’ including from two-thirds of Northern Irish respondents3 
(see Todd, 2017, p. 68).

favoured of the three political identity categories (Hayward and Rosher, 2020). 
2 Follow-ups interviews on identity processes were also conducted in 2014 as part of 
Todd’s research, which revealed some repolarisation in NI, but still a lot of distancing.

Although this change did not generally translate into 
respondents’ political preferences, distancing from group divisions 
could (partly) explain the changing voting patterns and 
constitutional dynamics in contemporary Northern Ireland. As more 
voters no longer align to traditional unionism or nationalism, this 
opens space for the growth of centrist parties while at the same 
time, there are more aligned voters who are supporting non-aligned 
parties, particularly Alliance. Considering this, this thesis seeks to 
better understand the emerging space in NI politics that does not 
neatly fit into the ‘two communities’. Significantly, post-2016 
questions exist as to whether said ideological dealignment or 
Brexit, which Alliance opposed, holds more explanatory power in 
the centre’s rise (e.g. Tonge 2020). This is also at a time when there 
is increased focus on the potential for a border poll referendum on 
a United Ireland and with the nationalist and unionist blocs 
balanced at roughly 43% each, centrist parties’ voters will be the 
deciding voters in any referendum and therefore their views and 
the views of the parties they vote for are crucially important. Within 
this scholarly context, this research does not re-visit the ‘identity-
vis-a-vis-Brexit’ debate in explaining political centrism’s growth 
(see for example, Gormley-Heenan and Aughey, 2017). Rather, it 
profiles the centre’s identity (including internal dealignment) and 
recognises Brexit as one (of many) factors which could shape 
centrist party activists’ constitutional thinking.  
 
Despite increasing research on those who do not strictly sit 
within the two political traditions, this group was largely forgotten 
during Brexit even as exemplified by a lack of public imagery that 
targeted them in their visual narratives (Armstrong et al., 2024, p. 
1400)4. However, the non-aligned centre was ‘forgotten’ or (at 
least) marginalised in NI’s socio-political context long prior.

Individually, when trying to understand identity change, Todd 
recognised the essentialist assumptions around the fixed nature of 
ethnicity and that ethnic identities require accommodation over 
transformation (see McBride, 2020). However, these primordialist 
ideas partially underpin the consociationalist framework which 
informs Northern Ireland’s power-sharing governance. Despite 
suggestions that consociations can help foster new identity 
dimensions - and hence may partly explain the degree of group 
‘distancing’ in NI (e.g. Garry, 2009) - the accommodation of the 
main ethnicities (arguably) leads to the entrenchment of ethnic 
divisions in post-conflict societies (see McCulloch, 2014)5.  
 
Although the labels and indicators vary, ‘not’ ethnic parties 
benefit from operating in centripetalism institutional systems, albeit 
advocates of consociationalism may view centripetalism as leading 
to instability and deadlock, despite suggestions it incentivises 
moderation, non-ethnic or cross-ethnic voting. ‘Exclusion amid 
inclusion’ (‘EAI’) proponents explain that in an effort to 
institutionally include the main cleavages, other non-dominant 
interests and identities – which ‘civic parties’ mobilise around – can 
be excluded from power-sharing (see Agarin et al., 2018). Alliance 
and the Green Party in Northern Ireland (‘GPNI’) are often 
exemplars within EAI studies and this thesis seeks to explore these 
parties of the centre in depth. The focus, counter to much previous 
work however, is not specifically on examining their marginalisation 
in institutionalised power-sharing. Rather it conducts an ‘intrinsic’ 
case study ‘to understand particularities’ of the centre since Brexit, 
including the centre’s engagement with the constitutional issue of 
whether Northern Ireland should unify with the Republic of Ireland

consociationalist approaches would also argue that they do not view ethnic identities in

internal dynamics and ‘conceptual markers’ as they shape the 
vision, strategy, organisation and articulation of what being a party 
of the centre-ground involves internally and externally in a post-
conflict divided society such as Northern Ireland. The term 
‘conceptual markers’ is used to signify the defining criteria that 
structure what it means to be a party of the centre-ground. Of 
course, considering these features of the parties and their 
relationship to consociational institutions are not mutually exclusive 
areas of study – even the seminal book studying the party itself as 
the unit of analysis The Alliance Party of Northern Ireland: Beyond 
Unionism and Nationalism dedicates sections to discussing 
consociational institutions. While this provides part of the context, 
this thesis fits more comfortably with debates on what counts as a 
non-ethnic party, drawing on, for example, Horowitz (2000) who 
differentiates an ethnic party from a non-ethnic party based on if it 
receives at least 85% of its electoral support from one ethnic group. 
 
In examining non-ethnic parties of the centre-ground, this 
dissertation explores Alliance and the GPNI as the core case 
studies. These parties share certain similarities in their positioning 
and articulation of identities and interests distinct from traditional 
ethno-national affiliations in NI but with alternative profiles and 
positions internally and in terms of the wider political landscape in 
NI. Relatively-speaking, the GPNI closed the gap on Alliance in the 
2016 Assembly election with Alliance retaining the same number of 
seats as 2011, but the GPNI successfully taking home two seats, 
one more than previously (Ark, 2016). More broadly, Alliance 
outperforms the GPNI, acting as a cross-segmental party that can 
appeal across the NI divide, due to its specialised focus on issues6 
that cut across the entire electorate (Agarin and Jarrett, 2022, pp.

centre-ground and primarily responsible for the growth of the 
centre-ground in purely voting terms, in the lead-up to the fieldwork 
for this thesis conducted between July 2022 and March 2024, the 
GPNI grew the fastest in terms of voters and seats. 
 
Although the GPNI considers environmental social justice 
as a cross-community issue, and despite indications 73% of NI’s 
public held concerns about the environment (DAERA, 2025) – this 
does not translate to electoral gains for ‘the Greens’. This civic or 
non-ethnic (or even post-ethnic) party operates in a different 
context to Alliance. The ‘left-wing’ GPNI is likely more conscious 
and critical of the so-called ‘double transition’ that followed the GFA 
- from conflict to peace, from peace to the neoliberal model - which 
could explain NI’s prioritisation of the economy over eco-
sustainability (McCabe, 2012; Hwang, 2022). Also, it is part of the 
European Greens and an all-island framework, which may interact 
with its framing of unification, especially given the eco-impacts from 
NI now being outside the European Union (EU). For instance, EU 
infraction fines previously pressurised NI to (slowly and poorly) 
update its eco-systems and environmental approach (Brennan et 
al., 2017, p. 134), but said progress is now under greater risk with 
Brexit. Therefore, while Alliance and the GPNI are both the ‘political 
centre-ground’ their individualism should not be downplayed. 
Hence, individual fieldwork chapters on them are included in this 
dissertation. In this way, the thesis provides insights into the 
commonalities but also the distinctiveness of these parties and 
speaks to the diversity of parties that together fall within the non-
ethnic party rubric.

Nearly a decade since the Brexit vote, the identity and 
constitutional impacts are not fully realised. Shelly et al (2023) 
explain the ‘strategic political functions’ attached to identities and 
how political contextual changes can cause group members to 
attempt to take advantage of ‘new political opportunities’ (pp. 2-3). 
Quite clearly, many nationalists see Brexit as an opportunity for 
unity, but in less readily apparent and complex ways, Brexit also 
confused the centre’s own constitutional dynamics and political 
goals. Brexit’s fall-out and the new interconnections between Irish 
unity and EU membership has seen both more internal division and 
greater fluidity in how the centre view and engage with this debate. 
Amid this period of flux, this research examines in depth the 
evolving constitutional mind-set of the political centre and the 
dynamics shaping the thinking and strategies of these parties – 
albeit it reveals Brexit is only one (maybe minor) issue that currently 
informs their constitutional deliberations. 
 
Against this backdrop, Chapter 1 asks who or what is the 
political ‘centre-ground’ in contemporary Northern Ireland. The 
conceptual framework justifies this research’s conceptualisation, 
ruling out the individual-level and selecting a party-based 
definitional scope. Chapter 2 outlines the methodological 
approach, but also thoroughly re-examines the narrative that 
Alliance evolved from a small ‘u’ unionist party and explores the 
GPNI’s approach as an all-island, pro-Remain party. Chapter 3 
profiles the identity of Alliance activists showcasing how in reality a 
party that considers itself non-aligned is better understood as ‘less 
aligned’ but with a residual role for identity backgrounds. Chapter 
4 examines the factors that shape Alliance activists’ attitudes 
towards engagement with and positioning on the constitutional 
question and a potential border poll. In particular, it emerges that 
Brexit is not as significant a factor as one may expect in a pro-
Remain party while identity continues to exert an influence.  
Chapter 5 considers the manifestation of party-level conceptual 

 
7
markers within individual-level party activists in the GPNI and notes 
specifically the interplay between issue ownership and ethno-
national identity. Chapter 6 examines the issues themselves as 
they condition GPNI activist’ perspectives on the constitutional 
question and how these fit into the Greens’ vision of the future.  
Chapter 7 concludes the dissertation summarising the key findings 
from the empirical examination of the centre-ground, points 
towards potential future developments in line with the takeaways 
from the project’s analyses and identifies avenues for further 
scholarly investigation into the internal dimensions of non-ethnic 
parties and the political centre in post-conflict divided societies. 
 
A number of key findings follow. First, in terms of identity, 
although non-alignment is core to the self-presentation of the 
Alliance Party, activists illustrate it is more of an ongoing aspiration 
than an achieved condition. Less alignment appears to be more 
the reality. Second, despite historic associations with British 
identity, Alliance activists demonstrate a decline in Britishness and 
an increased propensity to identify as Irish (in a civic sense), but 
this does not appear to be solely or primarily driven by Brexit. Third, 
in terms of personal preference on the constitutional question, 
there are different types of undecided within the Alliance Party as 
well as a specific Alliance brand of ‘decided’. Fourth, there are 
different degrees of apprehension among activists about the party 
taking a position on the constitutional question and different 
envisioned roles the party could play in a border poll process. Fifth, 
due to the realities of lesser alignment as opposed to non-
alignment, there is a role for identity affiliations in constitutional 
deliberations within Alliance, but pragmatic material considerations 
will take precedence. Sixth, despite a historical belief within the 
party that the best economic and social interests of NI were served 
by remaining in the UK, Alliance activists are now less convinced 
by this, albeit they are not necessarily advocating for Irish 
unification as the alternative either. Seventh, despite prominent 

 
8
public discourse, Brexit is not necessarily a clear determining factor 
in shaping constitutional preferences of activists and has not 
awakened a new sense of ‘Europeanness’ within Alliance as such.  
 
For the Green Party of Northern Ireland, the findings 
indicate class tends to dominate over ethno-nationality for activists 
although the two intersect in how activists understand themselves 
and the constitutional issue. Second, the party’s leftism is not the 
only or a strictly static factor in encouraging activists to join and 
stay in the party, but this leftism is itself key in structuring how it 
competes with other parties such as Alliance and PBP. Third, the 
GPNI’s issue-based party status conditions how activists evaluate 
their party now engaging more with the constitutional question. 
Fourth, in terms of developing constitutional preferences, the 
activists present different logics as to why a United Ireland as 
opposed to just an all-island approach is required for better 
environmental outcomes. Fifth, due to the greater Euroscepticism 
but ultimate pro-Remain preference of GPNI activists, some are 
indifferent about a United Ireland within the EU while at the other 
extreme, some other activists’ constitutional deliberations are 
instead strongly shaped by returning to the EU via reunification. 
Finally, it is observed that key Green principles such as 
commitments to non-violence and deliberative democracy are 
weighed to different degrees and inform a variety of perspectives 
among activists on the constitutional issue.

Chapter 1: Conceptualisation Framework 
 
Who or what is the political centre-ground in contemporary 
Northern Ireland? 
 
Introduction 
 
This chapter reviews possible conceptions of the ‘political 
centre-ground’ in NI today. At the individual-level (e.g. people’s 
identity formations), there are ‘established’ descriptions of the 
middle (e.g. often used in literature or as a survey option) - but not 
all may be deemed political, or centrist and neutral8. Also, party 
type conceptions - moderate parties, issue-based parties and 
constitutionally neutral civic parties - hold associated ‘conceptual 
risks’ such as being too all-encompassing or limiting (e.g. if multiple 
aligned parties are bracketed as centrist, or only including issue-
based parties excludes Alliance, the largest non-aligned party). 
Given the limited literature on centrism in NI, the chapter 
reflectively presents a constructed (and non-exhaustive or mutually 
exclusive) ‘menu’ of ‘centre-ground’ conceptions, before outlining 
this thesis’ case focus – the Alliance Party and the Green Party in 
Northern Ireland.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
8 Centrism is deemed equivalent to being neutral on the constitutional question unless 
stated otherwise. 

 
10
Conceptual option 1 – Individual-level9 
 
A. The ‘Neithers’ 
 
Established conceptions of the ‘middle-ground’ exist, often 
associated with persons with unconventional distancing from group 
divisions, or alternative identities in NI (see Coakley, 2021). The 
‘neithers’ (not unionist nor nationalist) are a category of ‘Other’ as 
they embrace a non-ethnic or civic identity, maybe because they 
come from mixed families - albeit this is not a pre-condition10 - or 
they just reject ethnicity as a means to identify themselves 
(Stojanovic, 2018, p. 346). Those ‘neithers’ resemble those 
Sarajevo citizens in a comparable post-conflict society who 
resonate with civic, nonethnic, alternative identity forms for reasons 
including opposition to the ‘ethnic collectivism’ coupled with the 
well-established ‘cosmopolitan conception of citizenship’ found 
particularly in urban Sarajevo (Piacentini, 2020, p. 718). However, 
given the increase in neithers saying they don’t know which party 
they ‘feel closest to’ in the NILT survey (Hayward and McManus, 
2019, pp. 149-150), this grouping is potentially too apolitical to 
‘represent’ the political centre, especially as neithers are 
synonymous with non-voting (Hayward and McManus, 2019). For 
instance, Sinn Féin (SF)’s pre-Brexit rise would not be explained 
by those neithers (or Others) moving to back this explicitly 
nationalist party, especially as nationalists were much more likely 
to generally vote in the 2011 Assembly elections than the neithers 
were (Evans and Tonge, 2013, pp. 52-53).  
 
9 Other definitions at the ‘individual-level’ were also researched including ‘moderates’ 
on the traditional left-right spectrum. However, the most established conceptual options 
in the Northern Ireland context are included here, and relevant collected research was 
integrated back into these conceptions ‘A-D’. The conceptual difficulties also existed in 
these non-NI specific debates. For example, although ‘undecided’ means something 
specific in the NI context (unsure how would vote in BP), it also is a term that describes 
voters in USA, but being undecided, a moderate or independent are often and 
inaccurately grouped as the same categories do not have the same meaning, albeit they 
overlap (ABC News, 2019).  
10 As the empirical chapters on Alliance also reveal to some degree. 

 
11
 
Additionally, the neithers are not obviously ‘centrist’ between 
the aligned parties. Of course, centrism here is defined differently 
to how this dissertation defines centrism which is based on 
neutrality on the constitutional question. Although most would not 
vote for an aligned party, some would vote for a nationalist, not a 
unionist party or vice versa (see Tonge and Loughran, 2024, p. 
602). Also, if centrism is associated with constitutional neutrality 
(which will be the more common usage in this chapter), although 
neithers are more likely to support non-aligned over aligned 
parties, they are not personally neutral. As Pow (2023) notes ‘it is 
perfectly compatible to be a neither and to still hold a preference 
on Northern Ireland’s constitutional status - as most clearly do’ (p. 
5).  
 
Moreover, supporting non-aligned parties could indicate, not a 
support for a centrist vision, but just a rejection of other parties. 
This reflects a similar idea that significant numbers of non-
nationalist identifiers supporting nationalist parties could illustrate 
how party support in NI may be about rejection over acceptance – 
you support nationalist parties only as you reject unionist parties 
(Evans and Duffy, 1997, p. 63). According to Piacentini (2020) 
many civic Sarajevo citizens are supporting nonethnic and civic 
political parties (e.g. Naša Stranka) out of political disappointment 
and dissatisfaction. Similarly, those non-aligned in NI came out to 
vote in 2019 in force primarily for the centre, partly motivated by 
their frustrations with the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP)-SF 
stalemate and flawed devolution system (and their pro-remain 
position) (Hayward, 2020, p. 55). If so, some might consider 
whether those ‘neithers’ (or holding civic identities) are voting for 
Alliance or civic parties because they are pulled to their vision, or 
because they reject the other parties on offer. Hayward and 
McManus (2019) highlighted that being neither does not mean you 
will definitely support the centrist parties – and again, most have 

 
12
tended to not vote at all. Overall, the neithers are often labelled the 
‘middle’ in NI but are not sufficiently politicised in general or centrist 
‘enough’ in the first instance to effectively and neatly represent ‘the 
political centre-ground’. The Northern Irish identity - another 
established ‘middle’ identity – may be a potential alternative.   
 
B. Northern Irish 
 
Northern Irish appears more ‘neutral’ given it has fewer 
ideological connotations than Irish or British. However, studies 
reveal the Northern Irish identity is taken as neutral in terms of 
religious background, but not necessarily as constitutionally 
neutral, given some nationalists see it as an identity legitimising the 
Northern Irish state i.e. it is seen as more unionist-coded11 
(McNicholl et al., 2019, p. 494). Of course, whether Northern Irish 
is deemed unionist-coded is subjective, but this perception is 
commonly held given that being British-Protestant is also 
associated with being Northern Irish (e.g. McKeown, 2014). This 
link is tighter when an age element is added in, given the pre-Brexit 
time series analysis by Tonge and Gomez (2015) reveals that 
young Protestants are now more likely to identify as Northern Irish 
(p. 294). It should also be noted that even if ‘Northern Irish’ is more 
unionist-coded, it was not always the preferred ‘somewhat neutral’ 
identity (to just British or Irish) for this group12. Initially, it was the 
Ulster identity which performed this function before it dipped in its

Overall, if Northern Irish is to be considered as representing the 
‘centre-ground’, this presents challenges given it is not without non-
neutral connotations, and ultimately being Northern Irish does not 
equate to being non-aligned in terms of the traditional divide. 
Therefore, the next option for the political centre-ground is ‘non-
religious.’  
 
C. Non-religious 
 
Religion and constitutionality often overlap in NI. Emerging 
research from 2002-2022 reveals that unification attitudes are 
predictively linked to religious affiliation despite increased 
secularisation14 e.g. Catholics are more likely to be pro-United

albeit there are intra-religious differences on constitutionality that 
are not routinely engaged with, such as between Catholics around 
whether unification is a goal in the medium or long-term (Smith and 
Chambers, 1991). Theoretically, the non-religious appear ‘less 
constitutionally biased’ given Hayes and McAllister (1995)15

(p. 94). However, given the previous 2002-2022 research also 
found unionist Protestants’ anti-UI position appears to have 
softened over time (p. 54), potentially the ‘religion-constitutionality’ 
dynamic is open to temporal flux.  Therefore, using this conception 
means accepting that even if the non-religious are generally more 
neutral or agnostic, this could change (potentially by the time of a 
border poll). Illustratively, post-GFA, Hayes and McAllister (2004) 
assessed that religious independents’ support for unification 
appears to be trending up: ‘It is not inconceivable that at some 
future point, independents will represent a key group capable of 
determining the constitutional future of Northern Ireland’ (p. 10).   
 
Furthermore, the directional relationship between religious and

and ‘the political’ is not conceptually straightforward. For instance, 
does being in a bi-confessional party (e.g. Alliance) intensify a 
supporter’s movement away from a set of religious beliefs, or does

D. Don’t know 
 
When conceptualising the centre-ground at the individual-level, 
the most ‘neutral’ grouping is likely those who do not have a strict 
loyalty to unification or NI remaining in the UK. A respondent being 
a ‘don’t know’ / unsure (or undecided) on how they would vote in a 
referendum is a well-established survey marker, but the meaning 
of said answer may not simply be ‘uncertainty’. For instance, ‘DK’ 
responses can be motivated by respondents’ refusal to pick from 
the other unsatisfactory options or is a ‘cost-saving heuristic’ 
selected because they required more ‘thinking time’ on the 
question (Purdam et al, 2024, p. 220). Therefore, a respondent 
being undecided on their referendum vote choice could reflect how 
they would prefer a different (albeit non-legal) constitutional 
permeation to just a UI or remaining in the Union (e.g. an 
independent Ulster) or needed more time to reflect upon their 
preferred constitutional outcome. Similarly, being undecided may 
reflect a certain ‘conditionality’ such as the respondent would 
support a UI or Union specifically if ‘X, Y, Z’ options were offered 
in the question18. As an example, Pow et al (2018) found that 
Catholic support for a UI was strongly conditional upon the 
outcome of the negotiations between the UK and the EU-27 and 
on economic expectations (p. 10). In addition, it should be noted 
that being don’t know’ / unsure may not translate to respondents’ 
ignorance of the constitutional issues, but rather potentially an 
‘ambivalence’ (having both negative and positive affect), rather 
than ‘indifference’ (lack of positive or negative affect) (Yoo, 2010). 
Both indifference and ambivalence are forms of ‘neutrality’, but 
 
18 Noelle-Neumann (1984) recognised how question wording and format can impact 
decisions to select ‘DK’ answers. 

 
17
they should be treated differently.  Broadly, not offering a ‘don’t 
care’ option in the NILT survey may mean missing out on 
alternative meanings such as the respondent is uninterested in, or 
equivocal about, the question topic or does not hold a position on 
it (Devine, 2012, p. 27). Often, there is commonly an option for the 
respondent to select they will not vote in a referendum which, if 
selected, could imply the respondent does not care either way 
about the constitutional outcome. However, this is not a definite, as 
it may show a general lack of interest in partaking in the democratic 
process in general rather than anything specific about a lack of 
constitutional preference. Ultimately, it is subjective to determine 
whether being a DK or a don’t care on the CQ is perceived as 
‘more’ neutral. Nevertheless, choosing either of these options 
accepts conceptualising the centre by the individual. As detailed 
above, there are significant challenges with conceptualising the 
political centre-ground using any single, or any straightforward 
combination of, individual-level identifier(s) without risking 
reductive assumptions and/or failing to fulfil the criteria of being 
political and neutral. However, as the next conceptual options 
reveal, the centre can be defined by categories of parties, not 
people.  
 
Conceptual option 2: Moderate Parties - Beyond the Northern 
Ireland context 
 
The centre overlaps with ‘moderates’ in the ‘moderate-
radical’ dichotomy (e.g. referenced in Islamist group research), 
albeit this binary itself is contested. Scholars debate whether 
Islamists should be categorised as ‘moderate’ or ‘radical’ based on 
their objectives (e.g. whether they want to change existing power 
relations) or their tactics to achieve said objectives (Schwedler, 
2011, p. 350). Within pre-GFA NI, the ‘extremes/radicals’ were the 
DUP and SF, while the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) and Social 
Democratic Labour Party (SDLP) were the ‘moderates’ without 

 
18
obvious paramilitary associations (i.e. tactics) and were primarily 
against 
disruptive 
politics 
(i.e. 
objectives). 
Conceptually, 
confusingly, radicals can ‘moderate’ themselves (making them not 
a radical anymore) such as via political system integration in which 
they downplay their ideological positions to gain in other ways (e.g. 
electorally) (see Tezcür, 2010). Within post-GFA NI, the 
extremes/radicals gradually moderated their platforms with the 
DUP conditionally opening itself up to power-sharing with SF and 
SF softening its’ own anti-British positions (McGlynn et al., 2014, 
pp. 275-276).  However, when exploring ‘centrism’ in NI, the 
moderate-radical dichotomy only partly categorises the Alliance 
Party. Alliance candidates in an early survey evaluated their party 
as more of a moderate party as it too supported power-sharing in 
government. This was the ‘operational distinction’ they made from 
extreme parties (McAllister and Wilson, 1978, pp. 220-221). Yet, 
Tonge (2003) applied similar power-sharing (pro-GFA) criteria to 
label Alliance as a moderate pro-Agreement party alongside the 
SDLP and UUP, but also separated it as a non-aligned centrist 
party. Notably, the early candidates in 1978 did see their party 
living in the middle between the extremes of both party sides (p. 
220), but Tonge (2003) emphasised how Alliance did not see itself 
as just a combination of or compromise between, the two traditions. 
Alliance’s centre space occupation itself can be contested – is it 
centre because it is a party made up of two sides without being 
aligned to either, or because it has a vision beyond just a mix of 
the traditional blocs? Of course, Alliance should not be considered 
completely alien to both sides. For instance, Evans and Tonge’s 
(2003) Alliance membership survey study illustrated how Alliance 
can fit along the nationalist-unionist spectrum, being closer to one 
side or the other on different issues.  However, for this ‘radical third 
tradition’ the main conclusion is the party ‘cannot be comfortably 
accommodated within either’ of the ethnic pillars’ (p. 48) and as 
such is more than a moderate version of either, or blend of both, 
traditional bloc(s). Importantly, lexically this idea of Alliance being 

 
19
‘radical’ as a third tradition is very different to what it means to be 
‘radical’ in the initially mentioned ‘moderate-radical’ dichotomy.  
 
Recognisably, Alliance itself does not just evaluate what a 
‘moderate’ party is based on whether it supports power-sharing. 
Alliance doubted the SDLP’s and UUP’s ‘moderate’ credentials 
also because these parties prop up ethnic politics, appeal to just 
one traditional side, and do not strive for a shared future like 
Alliance does. For example, former Alliance leader David Ford 
stated ‘That is why Alliance stands in a fundamentally different 
position to the so-called moderates. We believe in the need to build 
a united community, to establish liberal values. We oppose any 
attempt to impose ethnic politics...’ (Party News Archives, 2003, a). 
By seemingly equating ‘moderate’ with ‘non-alignment’ Alliance 
combines Tonge’s (2003) two categories (moderate pro-
agreement party and non-aligned centrist party) into one mutually 
exclusive category (to be moderate is to be non-ethnic/non-
aligned, and vice versa). Now, of course, Alliance might not be the 
best determinant of what a ‘moderate’ really is given it may always 
struggle to evaluate initiatives by aligned parties to build a shared 
future without suspicion. For instance, back in 2011 Ford was not 
convinced that the then leader of the DUP’s proclamations of 
building a shared future in NI had real party backing (Belfast 
Telegraph, 2011, a)19.   
 
Both Alliance and GPNI have mentioned they represent 
‘anti-sectarian’ politics or called for the construction of more than a 
non-sectarian but instead an anti-sectarian society as, for example, 
in the GPNI 2015 Westminster election manifesto (see CAIN, 
2015). However, anti-sectarian implies an active opposing to

who transferred his vote to the SDLP - suggests people should vote based on government 
workings over tribalism. Therefore, maybe Alliance does recognise ‘sometimes’ when 
the aligned parties look to move beyond ethnic politics (Belfast Telegraph, 2017).  

 
20
unionism and nationalism, which would suggest that being ‘aligned’ 
is something that should not be strived for at all and is difficult to 
straightforwardly categorise as ‘moderate.’ 
 
Ultimately, as a framing device, the ‘moderate party’ 
concept is difficult to measure and justify. Defining the ‘centre-
ground’ broadly by ‘moderate parties’ risks downplaying the 
distinguishing characteristics of the SDLP and UUP (aligned) and 
Alliance (non-aligned). However, defining the ‘centre-ground’ as 
only ‘issue-orientated’ parties - which mobilise on issue agendas, 
trying to move beyond the ethnic cleavage – avoids conceptual 
stretching and contestation on what is a ‘moderate’ in and outside 
the NI context. 
 
Conceptual option 3: Issue-orientated parties 
 
Although consociations do not lend themselves to new 
policy dimensions (e.g. the economic left-right) a moral liberal-
conservative political dimension exists in NI that impacts voting - 
albeit people are not necessarily voting for parties different from 
their community (Garry et al., 2017, p. 507). Therefore, (limited) 
spaces exist for issue parties, some of which are ‘niche’ parties in 
wider theory that have a non-centrist ‘niche’, or extreme ideology 
(Adams et al., 2006, p. 513). Similar to ‘moderates’, how ‘niche 
parties’ are defined and measured is critically varied. For instance, 
defining them against ‘mainstream’ parties based on party ideology 
could downplay distinctions between and within party families 
(Meyer and Miller, 2015, p. 259). Importantly, the ‘niche’ category 
is not conceptually matched in NI’s context. While the DUP and SF 
are more ‘extreme’ nationalist (not just Irish nationalist) parties, 
which leans them towards a ‘niche’ definition, they are 
‘mainstream’ within NI’s ethnic-based political system. Now, if 
niche and mainstream parties are differentiated by relative issue 

 
21
salience (not party position per se), then a niche party could switch 
to being a mainstream party20 by changing the degree of attention 
paid to each issue (Meyer and Wagner, 2013, pp. 1248-9). 
Therefore, theoretically, the one exemplar of a ‘niche’ party in NI – 
the Green Party - is becoming ‘less niche’ in NI because many 
mainstream parties now include environmental and sustainability 
policies in their manifesto, i.e. mainstream parties are becoming 
‘more niche’ 21, albeit they are not suddenly ‘niche parties’.  
 
Of course, the Greens themselves may argue it is not a 
niche party which implies a single-issue focus on environmental 
justice and the climate. The Greens would rather see themselves 
as ‘eco-socialist’ (environmentalism mixed with social justice). But 
even Kovel (2002) would separate green politics and ecosocialism 
as, for instance, demands for labour emancipation and issues 
around the means of production are not build into the fundamental 
pillars and values of the Green Party (GP). The GPNI is 
conceptually grouped then as a niche party because it is ‘green’ 
not ‘socialist’ per se, but the eco-socialist dimensions are seen 
internally as more interlinked in the GPNI ideology according to 
interviewees as a decision that is good for the environment is seen 
as a good one socially. Ultimately, the ‘niche’ category overlooks 
another issue-based party in NI, the socialist People Before Profit 
(PBP). Murtagh (2020) groups the GPNI and PBP as non-ethnic, 
integrationist civic parties as they ‘tend to campaign on alternative 
issues and cleavages, such as class or the environment, and 
attempt to transcend the ethnic cleavage moving towards a more 
‘normal’, issue-based politics’ (p. 76). Arguably, PBP is ‘less non-
ethnic’ compared to the GPNI which makes greater attempts to

Labelling issue parties like the Greens or PBP as ‘centre’ 
requires downplaying their non-ethnic, issue aspect to fit a 
‘Northern Ireland specific context’ – being centre in NI might mean 
not being unionist or nationalist, but these parties are certainly not 
ideologically centrist. This reflects one thesis interviewee (7) who 
does not like the centre-ground term, ‘…but I understand why it's 
being used in terms of between, unionism and nationalism…if 
you're in the centre, you get run down in middle-of-the-road…so 
pick a side and we do pick a side, we're on the left, we're not on 
the centre in that respect…’. Ultimately, as a conceptual frame, 
issue-orientated parties face opposite issues to ‘moderates’ as the 
basis for the political centre, because it narrows the definition of 
‘centre-ground’ to exclude the most commonly perceived ‘centrist’ 
party in NI which is Alliance.  
 
Conceptual option 4: Civic parties 
 
A broader party-level conceptualisation which includes the 
previous issue-based parties, but also Alliance would be ‘civic 
parties’, ‘which attempt to draw support from and represent all 
significant groups in a divided society, to the exclusion of none’

placed ‘in contrast’ to ethnic parties and squeezed in as ‘non-

definition of an ethnic party, such as by recognising a party can be 
non-ethnic and ethnic at different times, both are criticised for 
downplaying how parties may not fit into just one or the other 
category (Hamza and Maeda, 2025, p. 3).  As with previous labels 
(e.g. moderates), debate persists on what counts as an ethnic 
versus a non-ethnic party. For instance, Ishiyama and Breuning 
(2011) differentiate these categories depending on how the party 
portrays itself to the electorate (i.e. ethnic group name in title) albeit 
this name-based indicator is criticised for downplaying a key ethnic 
party characteristic – ‘their culturally-defined electoral base’ 
(Debus and Schulte, 2024, p. 129). Although there may be a 
‘conceptual question’ around which ‘alternative’ to ethnic party is 
more representative of the ‘centre’ – i.e. is it ‘multi-ethnic’ parties 
that are ‘centre’ as they promote without exclusion all ethnic 
identities in a society or ‘non-ethnic’ parties that are ‘centre’ as they 
do not champion any specific ethnic interests (Chandra, 2011, p 
155). The best understanding potentially is non-ethnic, only 
because ethnicity is not at all part of the party campaign. Even in

Within Northern Ireland specifically, those ‘not ethnic’ or 
‘civic parties’ may benefit from how the consociational setup also 
combines centripetal elements through its use of STV (Bogaards, 
2019, p. 525). Civic parties have been given opportunities to 
effectively operate, for instance, in balance of power-roles, such as 
Alliance holding the Justice Ministry24 role, albeit civic parties might 
find it easier to navigate amongst liberal over corporate rules 
(Murtagh, in Agarin and McCulloch, 2019). These types of parties 
are also referred to as ‘non-nationalist’ with studies exploring why 
they attract support in ethically saturated societies. For example 
Pickering (2009) explores reasons for greater support of non-
nationalist parties – i.e. those which are open to cross-ethnic 
cooperation, although this willingness is situational and temporally 
varied (p. 572). There is greater support for such parties in 
Macedonia over Bosnia, with Pickering casting doubt on the 
assumption that support comes from voters’ engagement in civil 
society and social tolerance (p. 565). Within NI, Mitchell (2018) is 
less than convinced that Alliance’s non-nationalist politics has been 
constrained politically by the GFA consociational setup.

ground for civic parties, hence, the new-found focus on studying 
their relevance. Within the NI Assembly, cross-ethnic parties battle

institutional

informal over the formal barriers but ideological dealignment in the

may have broken down to a degree to allow cross-ethnic parties to 
rise and a generational change (e.g. post-GFA babies) has eroded 
some of the enduring ethnic-based political culture in NI. Also, 
there are still unanswered questions in terms of these barriers for 
cross-ethnic parties which speak to the complexities of how these 
parties navigate the NI system and how it may change. For 
example, if the formal institutions are dealt with (e.g. reforms 
removing designation are enacted) what happens to the smaller 
minorities like the issue-based parties? Do they become even more 
micro? There is the potential risk that without designation and with 
the emergence of classical left-right mass party politics, this could 
squeeze the space for these smaller or alternative types of parties. 
In turn, potentially the ‘barriers’ themselves are overstated in the 
first place, and there may be scope for greater cooperation and 
engagement between civic parties and ethnic parties themselves 
for mutual benefit. Ethnic parties in NI have made certain efforts to 
engage with Others (‘non-dominant groups’) in different arenas 
within the power-sharing arrangement motivated by both 
‘principled and strategic concerns’ (Murtagh and McCulloch, 2021, 
p. 547). Questions remain as to how cross-ethnic parties view their 
relationship to these traditional blocs. Also, Murtagh reveals how 
parties can ‘evolve out’ of civic party categorisations. Alliance 
moved from its cross-ethnic accommodationist position when it 
was a mediator between the two sides in peace negotiations and 
bridged the position between them, to a more post-ethnic 
integrationist party as it is issue-based with its own specific agenda 
(2020, p. 78). This is suggestive that these signifiers may 
themselves be more flexible than is sometimes understood. 
 
However, the categories of civic parties or, more broadly, 
party-level Others sometimes do not fit neatly onto the parties. For

oriented Other’ over being an ‘Ethnic-rejecting Other.’ While this 
potentially follows, it does not allow for much distinction between 
Alliance and issue-based parties like the GPNI or PBP, specifically 
given the definitions of these two types of ‘Other’ are similar. For 
instance, ‘Ethnic-rejecting Others’ includes those who seek political 
participation ‘on a socially relevant identity other than ethnicity’ and 
‘Issue-oriented Others’ ‘includes those rejecting all identity-driven 
labels and who instead pursue ideologically underpinned forms of 
political participation’ (p. 4). However, the authors’ justification was 
framed around comparison to other parties on the NI political 
spectrum and did not allow another clear categorisation for non-
orange/green parties25. Again, this reinforces the conceptual 
difficulties in placing civic parties in boxes, that ultimately this 
chapter does, which is that different parties can fit into many 
definitions depending on how the ‘box’ itself is defined. Even in 
practical terms, although initially differentiating them, Coakley 
(2008) recognises the political centre as ‘the terrain not just of 
underbidders, but also of counterbidders’ (p. 784). Ethnic 
underbidders define themselves ‘as centrist and abjure all ethnic 
loyalties’ (i.e. Alliance) and ‘nonethnic counterbidders who seek to 
impose an alternative, nonethnic cleavage’ (i.e. GPNI) (pp. 766-
767). Therefore, the broader centre space can be formulated by 
both Alliance and the GPNI, even if they often are deemed different 
types of Others.  
 
Ultimately, as a framing device, civic parties would direct a 
study on the ‘Other’ parties in NI, like Alliance, the GPNI and PBP, 
but it would remove an arguably essential component marker of 
‘being centre’ – not taking a ‘binary’ position on the constitutional 
question. Also, certain supporters of the SDLP and some previous

Conceptual option 5: Only the constitutionally neutral civic 
parties (i.e. ‘centrist parties’) 
 
The next conception, which puts constitutionality as the key 
marker, and is aligned with Murphy (2023) who says ‘instead the 
label ‘middle ground’ or ‘centre party’ implies—first and foremost—
neutrality on the constitutional question’ (p. 95)26. However, there 
is a built-in conceptual assumption that the ‘opposite’ to alignment 
is ‘neutral’ but potentially supporting ‘joint authority’ or federalism 
could be the ‘centre’ between pro-union and pro-unity. At one stage 
in 2000, even the non-aligned Alliance recognised in an internal 
document that joint authority was one optional alternative to 
collapsing the GFA (Belfast Telegraph, 2000). Given this, joint 
authority is not ‘logically centrist’ because it still puts NI in the 
Union, even if it could be considered a stepping stone towards a 
united Ireland. Secondly, there is a question of what counts as 
‘taking a constitutional position’, could advocating for Northern 
Ireland to move towards a more conventional democracy be seen 
as Alliance’s or the GPNI’s ‘constitutional’ agenda? Similarly, 
certain interviewees27 also motivated a re-evaluation of what it 
means to take a CP, given some considered that ‘technically’ the 
party currently has a valid ‘non-binary’ CP and this binary way of 
thinking about it (i.e. that a party has to pick one side or the other) 
is itself problematic (e.g. activist 10). Of course, it is suggested that

Conclusion – the ‘Intrinsic Case Study’ 
 
This chapter has reviewed a non-exhaustive menu of 
conceptions of the political centre-ground in contemporary 
Northern Ireland, moving from individual-level identifiers through to 
party-level frameworks. Each option was assessed against three 
criteria: whether it is sufficiently political, genuinely centrist in the 
NI-specific sense, and sufficiently neutral on the constitutional 
question to anchor this research. 
 
Individual-level identifiers (Conceptual Option 1) offer an 
intuitive starting point. Survey categories such as the ‘neithers’, 
those identifying as Northern Irish, the non-religious, and 
constitutional 'don't knows' all map onto a recognisable middle 
space. Yet none can reliably anchor a study of the political centre. 
The ‘neithers’ are disproportionately non-voting; Northern Irish 
identity carries Protestant-coded connotations that render it non-
neutral in nationalist eyes; the non-religious category is temporally 
fluid; and 'don't know' responses reflect a mix of ambivalence, 
conditionality, 
and 
strategic 
non-response 
that 
resists 
interpretation as centrism. Individually and collectively, individual-
level identifiers lack the political agency and organisational 
coherence this study requires. 
 
Party-level conceptualisations resolve the agency problem 
but introduce fresh difficulties. The 'moderate parties' frame 
(Option 2) offers useful historical perspective, illuminating how the 
pre-GFA moderate-radical dichotomy mapped onto the party 
system. However, it is too elastic to serve as a precise conceptual 

 
31
tool, applying simultaneously to Alliance, the SDLP, and the UUP 
and thereby flattening the meaningful distinction between 
ethnically-aligned parties that moderate their strategies and 
genuinely non-ethnic parties that reject the ethno-national 
framework altogether. 
 
The 'issue-oriented parties' frame (Option 3) has the 
opposite problem: it is too narrow. Focusing on parties mobilising 
around non-ethnic issue agendas captures an important dimension 
of NI's pluralism but excludes Alliance, the largest non-aligned 
party and the primary electoral beneficiary of post-Brexit 
dealignment. Defining the centre by issue salience alone obscures 
the constitutional neutrality that gives the centre its distinctive 
character. The 'civic parties' frame (Option 4) recovers Alliance and 
is analytically more productive, encompassing parties that prioritise 
and receive cross-community support. It connects the research to 
a rich comparative literature on non-ethnic parties in divided 
societies. However, it does not necessarily entail constitutional 
neutrality. Supporting the constitutional status quo can itself be 
read as implicit pro-union alignment, and parties conventionally 
described as civic, including elements of the SDLP or UUP at 
various 
points, 
have 
retained 
discernible 
constitutional 
orientations.  
 
Conceptual Option 5, constitutionally-neutral civic parties, 
here termed 'centrist parties', addresses this gap. It combines two 
component markers that are, taken together, most analytically 
precise for this study: these parties are civic in that they do not 
champion any single community's ethnic interests and seek cross-
community support, and they are constitutionally neutral in 
Murphy's (2023) sense, whereby the centre-ground label implies, 
first and foremost, non-alignment on the constitutional question. 
This combined criterion deliberately excludes even moderate 
aligned parties and individual-level groupings whose political 

 
32
engagement is too attenuated to sustain systematic analysis. It 
includes, with clear justification, the two parties at the core of this 
research: Alliance and the Green Party in Northern Ireland. The 
empirical chapters examine carefully the differences between 
Alliance and the GPNI rather than treating them as interchangeable 
and this framework does not homogenise individuals within these 
parties, whose personal constitutional views frequently diverge 
from official non-aligned positioning. Instead, this is key to what the 
empirical chapters seek to map. 
 
Conceptual Option 5 is therefore adopted as the working 
definition of the political centre-ground for the remainder of this 
dissertation. By holding together the civic and the constitutional, it 
provides the most analytically coherent foundation for examining 
what it means to occupy the centre-ground in Northern Ireland 
today. Chapter 2 sets out the thesis’ methodological approach and 
contextualises the two case study parties whose activists form the 
basis of the empirical investigation.

unionist) party and the GPNI’s position as not just a pro-Ireland 
party (despite being part of an all-island framework). Prior to the 
fieldwork chapters on the identity and position on the CQ of party 
activists, it contextualises these parties’ key markers which mark 
them as the ‘centre-ground’. In the case of Alliance, the central self-
