Alliance Party of Northern Ireland (‘Alliance’):  
 
Stage 1 of evolution: A pro-union (not unionist!) party 
 
Alliance’s pro-union (not unionist) origins 
 
Given Alliance’s pressure group predecessor, the New 
Ulster Movement (NUM) established in 1969 was explicitly pro-
union, Alliance’s origins, at least, are more unionist-leaning. 
However, this requires some contextualisation. The NUM was not 
‘disgusted’ by a united Ireland, but outlined minimum conditions on 
which it may be ‘workable’ even though it did not accept unity in 
‘principle’ (McQuaid, 2012, p. 82). More broadly, the NUM itself 
identified not as moderate ‘unionist’ but ‘on the most moderate-
wing of those who support’ Northern Ireland’s maintenance in the 
UK (NUM, 1972). Similarly, even to argue that Alliance was more 
union-leaning precisely because the NUM was, downplays that 
Alliance, founded in April 1970, was not a replica of the NUM and 
carved out distinct positions from early on. For instance, some in 
the NUM were ‘content with direct rule from Westminster’ (a very 
unionist position, albeit the NUM itself was opposed to direct rule), 
while Alliance continuously supported the region having its own 
devolved Assembly (Eggins, 2015, p. 38). Also, while both 
ultimately favoured devolved government, the NUM by 1971 came 
to, reluctantly, support Stormont’s suspension for three years with 
commission rule. However, the justification for said support was 
‘Alliance-flavoured’ (i.e. aligned to Alliance’s own ethos) given 
suspension was seen as a means to address the lack of progress 
in Northern Ireland’s politics and political sectarianism in the region 
(NUM, 1971). Overall, despite differences and overlaps, Alliance 
would take the NUM’s pro-union preference with it as it continued 
to establish itself as a party in the early 1970s but the nature of this 
preference, already complex, would continue to evolve and be 
subject to refinement. 

 
35
 
The big border poll ‘test’ in early establishment 
 
Early on, Alliance was challenged to differentiate itself from 
the United Ulster Unionist Council (UUUC), a unionist party 
coalition which shared Alliance’s pro-union stance. However, 
unlike the UUUC, Alliance was pragmatically, rather than 
ideologically, pro-union; not for reasons of nationhood and 
because of ‘British Unionist allegiance’, but because it was in the 
best social and economic interests of Northern Ireland’s people29. 
Illustratively, Alliance’s position against internment in 1971 was not 
‘very unionist’. Specifically, one of the party’s unionist founders, Sir 
Bob Cooper, was later commended by the leader David Ford for 
rejecting the Unionist government’s approach to internment, 
despite Bob’s own background (Party News Archives, 2005, a).  
However, in turn, this is not to suggest that Alliance’s interment 
approach was ‘green’ as unlike the SDLP who initially refused, 
Alliance wanted to participate in negotiations on forming power-
sharing, despite the continuation of internment. The example of the 
position on internment does though indicate the iterative process 
by which Alliance came to stand out from other ‘pro-union’ entities.  
 
Already not helped by prominent names in unionism 
defecting to Alliance30 (e.g. in 1952 Phelim O'Neill was elected as 
a UUP MP to Westminster, but switched to Alliance in 1972), 
Alliance’s early pro-union position is difficult to deny, given its 
‘active campaign’ for it in the 1973 border poll. Alliance’s Denis 
Loretto wrote ‘It was one thing to have a party principle which 
supported the British link as the majority view but quite another to

around the referendum and the absence of a real proposal for it 
was not something Alliance wanted. Moreover, Alliance’s pro-

the 1973 border poll questions to reflect a moderate perspective, 
so structured in a way which was appealing to ‘moderates’ who

Nevertheless, regardless of desired question modifications, 
Alliance’s 1973 pro-Union support is still used as evidence of its 
more unionist-leaning credentials. 
 
Prioritising the Ulster dimension first  
 
Dating back to 1974, Alliance entirely accepted the people’s 
right to aspire towards a united Ireland, but it also supported the 
dropping of the ROI’s territorial claim to NI, calling the continued 
existence of Article 2 and 3 in the Constitution as ‘nonsense’ (see 
NAI, 2005/7/622). However, Alliance did not prioritise the British 
dimension (it recognised it and the Irish dimension) but prioritised 
the Ulster dimension meaning it supported the internal power-
sharing governance within the 1973 Sunningdale Agreement. Its 
position on the proposed Council of Ireland however was not ‘so 
green’. It strongly rejected any notion of direct control of the police 
being given to the Council which the SDLP supported. Alliance

Ultimately, Alliance settled in as ‘not nationalist in the early

Alliance was against the 1981 hunger strike, although it framed this

option despite knowing it would hurt party support32. Former leader 
John Cushnahan stated, ‘We were opposed to the hunger strikes 
and this doubtless lost us some support…But we deal in reality and

Alliance’s next ‘not nationalist’ move was its decision to 
decline to partake in the ROI-organised New Ireland Forum (1983-

organised’ event33. Rather, Alliance disagreed with how the event

support and protect minorities, but Alliance saw that unity solved

even larger minority of non-nationalists in the new framework’ (NAI,

South’ perspective given even certain Republic of Ireland parties 
disliked the Forum’s premise while some (alongside Alliance) met 
as an ‘alternative Forum’ and some (not all) of these parties too 
were critical of the Forum’s ‘maximalist demand’ for a form of unity 
(Keatinge, 1985, p. 166). More broadly, the decision not to attend 
the Forum should not straightforwardly be read as an ‘anti-South’

party during this period is clearly reductionist and overlooks the 
variety and complexity of its positions and their rationale. This is 
even before the mid-1980s when Alliance would face a much more 
significant test of its unionism as it responded to the Anglo-Irish

Another Forum, Another Test  
 
Alliance’s next opportunity to refute that it would never 
partake in ‘Irish-organised events’ came when it engaged in the 
Forum for Peace and Reconciliation. Although some accounts 
suggest that the leader Alderdice defended the absence of  
unionist parties (see Associated Press, 1994) which again shows 
an understanding, although not agreement, with unionists’ 
ideological position; others reveal that the leader was critical of 
their decision to stay away (Tonge et al., 2024, p, 84). Even if 
Alliance was more ‘critical’ of unionist absence, it would treat an 
equivalent choice by nationalist parties in the same way. 
Previously, Alderdice called upon the SDLP leader not to support

Unionist party's attitude to the Dublin Forum for Peace and 
Reconciliation’ (Sunday Times, 1996). Overall, instead of 
considering joining any unionist (or later nationalist) boycott, 
Alliance took the Forum as an opportunity to consider how to 
pragmatically move Northern Ireland forward. For instance, 
Alderdice used Alliance’s attendance in 1994 to question the 
economics of a future unification model, foreshadowing the party’s 
practical, rather than ideological, concerns around constitutional 
change which is a major theme discussed more in later chapters 
(Irish Times, 1994, a).  
 
Alliance’s engagement with SF - not so ‘orange’ 
 
 
Alliance’s interactions with SF and paramilitary ceasefires in 
the 1990s also separates it further from unionism. Alliance was 
ever the optimist in terms of ceasefires. For instance, even though 
the British government and Unionist side were fairly sceptical about 
the Irish Republican Army (IRA)’s 1994 ceasefire, Alderdice 
welcomed it36, encouraging Britain’s’ PM to not get bogged down 
by the wording used in the ceasefire statement (see NAI, 
2021/48/205). Even more telling, in terms of SF’s inclusion in the 
peace negotiations, unionist parties continued to demand that the 
IRA start disarming first, but Alliance was prepared to meet with SF 
during the IRA's cease-fire. Alliance’s approach, contrary to that of 
unionism, helps to explain why the SF leader, Gerry Adams himself 
seemed to think of Alliance as more courageous in dealing with 
issues than the British government and other unionist parties, 
despite also seeing Alliance as approaching security and policing 
in the same way to unionists (see CNN, 1994). However, even if

Prior to the GFA, Alliance’s most ‘anti-orange’ move was that

no change in the constitutional position without their consent’ (see 
Agarin and Jarrett, 2022, p. 731). This ‘sudden’ change may be 
partially attributable to how in the 1997 local government elections, 
unionists lost control of Belfast City Council for the first time, and 
Alliance held the ‘balance of power’ between the main blocs. 
Therefore, Alliance wanted to more firmly position itself as the more 
neutral option between unionists and nationalists. This was a

focused less on ending violence and more on bringing about a 
‘shared future’43. Following from its one-community approach, 
Alliance (pessimistically) wondered without a ‘common’ regional 
identity could NI communities be united through loyalty to the GFA, 
similarly to how the USA is united through its loyalty to the 
constitution and rule of law (Party News Archives, 1999, f). 
Alliance’s pessimism was in some ways warranted given ‘GFA

support’ was not even a ‘shared value’ in the 1998 election 
(transfers from UUP voters tended to go to the anti-GFA DUP and

representativeness of symbols developed in the post-GFA era, 
from 2002 Alliance preferred ‘common’ flags being used more (e.g. 
the EU flag), but without this, supported flying the Union flag on 
designated days. Arguably it is more ‘unifying’ (or representative) 
to fly the Union Jack and tricolour together, but Alliance saw this as 
not representing the current constitutional status, believing that it 
‘would reduce them to symbols of single political/national identities 
rather than symbols of sovereignty’ (see Party News Archives, 
2013) albeit more nationalist-leaners may see this as a fairer 
solution and unionists would want the flag flown all-year round. 
Alliance’s approach to flags serves to de-couple it from unionism in 
a similar way to how the earlier re-designation put it ‘back in the 
unionist box’ (although it received criticism from both sides). 
Exemplarily, in 2012 Alliance was attacked after Belfast City 
Council voted to support its flag position and ‘it exposed an 
emerging fault-line in NI between the liberal cosmopolitan middle 
classes in Alliance and elements of loyalism over a wider range of 
issues’ (Melaugh, 2013 in Morrow, 2023, p. 53). Subsequently, not 
long after Alliance realised that other parties were not willing to deal 
with the flag issue as part of the 2014 Haass agreement, Ford 
explained Alliance refused to support the document that avoided 
this issue as Alliance felt it needed to be addressed. This of course 
pushed it into the unionist camp, given unionists did not endorse 
the document and nationalist parties did (Irish News, 2014). 
 
Of course, achieving a ‘shared future’ pushed Alliance’s 
focus on breaking down the ‘division’ in NI even bargaining for this 
issue to be engaged with when sectarian agendas clashed. For 
example, Alliance used the SF and DUP’s preference for the party 
to take the Justice ministry to bargain for greater efforts to push its 
own shared future vision. It demanded that the programme for 

 
50
Cohesion, Sharing and Integration (CSI) be dealt with before it 
would take the ministry and the party ultimately walked out of the 
Cohesion, Sharing and Integration Working Group, partly because 
the inclusion of a clear flags policy in the Shared Future strategy 
was refused by unionist parties (Belfast News Letter, 2012, j). 
Moreover, Alliance expected, in exchange for exploring shared 
services as favoured by Sinn Féin, which it considered a 
constructive move, that SF should consider Alliance’s own 
proposal for tackling costs of division in NI (see Northern Ireland 
Assembly, 2009, p). In this way, Alliance sought to extract 
concessions from each traditional party although arguably it could 
be said to be more representative to demand both communities 
halve44 their position45. 
 
Stage 3 of evolution: Part of a ‘pan-nationalist front’ with the 
other pro-remain parties? 
 
Solution first, but not the nationalist solution 
 
Post-2016, NI leaving the EU dominated Alliance’s agenda. 
Brexit raised considerations regarding Alliance’s place on the 
moderate nationalism-unionism spectrum. Despite their different 
constitutional aspirations, Alliance and the nationalist SDLP shared 
similar anti-Brexit positions, albeit the SDLP message was always 
‘nationalist-coded’. Lexically, both questioned the consent of NI 
being dragged out of the EU, but the SDLP leader referred to ‘the 
people’ as the people from the ‘North of Ireland’ as opposed to 
using the legal and neutral46 name ‘Northern Ireland’ (see Northern

deemed Brexit or the DUP and the UK’s approach to it and the

(e.g. when the UK unilaterally walked away from the Protocol 
agreement). However, with Brexit’s unfolding, Alliance was less 
‘adamant’ that it was now the ultimate end of the Union than the 
SDLP was (although the SDLP was not triumphalist in this belief). 
For example, the SDLP leader declared that ‘My firm view now is 
that the United Kingdom is coming to an end’ (House of Commons, 
2020, a). As opposed to a ‘Union doomsday narrative’ which 
aligned with nationalist aspirations, Alliance held a ‘solution-based 
narrative’ i.e. that finding a workable solution to the Protocol could 
actually help the Union’s longevity (see House of Commons, 2022, 
a). Of course, what Alliance defined as a ‘solution’ was not very 
nationalist-coded. Even the SDLP supported a pragmatic 
approach47 to the Protocol, but Alliance never saw unification as a 
‘favourable solution’ to the Brexit issue. For example, the leader 
Naomi Long criticised an evaluation that unity would address ‘no-
deal Brexit’ economic problems: ‘If you remove the border 
tomorrow and Ireland is united, we would still be impacted hugely 
by Brexit as the UK and Irish economies are so interlinked’ (Belfast 
News Letter, 2019, e). Similarly, Alliance would continuously try to 
‘neutral-code’ Brexit-related issues, that is, promoting that dealing 
with Brexit did not have to be about dealing with the ‘domestic’ 
constitutional issue. Specifically, Alliance supported ‘decoupling’ of 
issues such as the challenges of Brexit, or promoting the special 
status issue, from the constitutional issue and the wider aspiration 
of a united Ireland (for example, see Northern Ireland Assembly, 
2016, c). Overall, while Brexit certainly added fluidity to Alliance’s 
approach to constitutionality the SDLP and Alliance’s solution to 
Brexit was not to dramatically overlap in the sense of generating

52
an Alliance move to align with the SDLP on support for a united 
Ireland as the solution despite their broader shared anti-Brexit 
position. Again, Alliance sought to navigate a distinct and more 
neutral and ‘non-aligned’ approach to dealing with Brexit fallout.   
 
Not completely ‘anti-DUP’? 
 
Alliance’s firm and consistent pro-remain position puts it in 
a contrasting place to unionism48. Alliance always put the blame for 
Brexit, particularly a hard Brexit - and hence the need for the 
Protocol - back on the choices made by the DUP (or the UK 
government)49. As Alliance’s Stewart Dickson Member of the 
Legislative Assembly (MLA) remarked, ‘It is not our [Alliance] 
protocol; it is the DUP's protocol… It is the responsibility of a party 
that chose extreme Brexit, and that is where we are’ (Northern 
Ireland Assembly, 2021, b).  However, it was not that Alliance 
advocated that the DUP’s views around the Protocol (and the 
Protocol Bill) should be ignored, but rather Alliance did not want it 
to dominate in mapping what happens to the majority of NI (such 
as in terms of said Bill). As Alliance’s Stephen Farry noted, ‘…we 
have to address the  views of the DUP, alongside the views of 
others…but it is not consistent with democracy to allow that view 
to dictate what happens to the overwhelming majority of people 
in Northern Ireland’ (House of Commons, 2022, c).  Although, of 
course, Alliance’s evaluation of what the majority wanted aligned 
also with what it wanted as a party, that is, the majority do not want 
the Protocol scrapped, but want the problems associated with it 
fixed so it can deliver for NI (see House of Commons, 2021, f). 
 
48 Although the UUP and DUP’s position on Brexit was not as close as that of the SDLP

the Protocol, but unlike the DUP did not support collapsing the Assembly in response to 
it, and the subsequent withdrawal of the First Minister (FM) (see Northern Ireland 
Assembly, 2022, h).  
49 It is also reasonable to suggest that Alliance was more strained in its criticism of the 
EU’s approach to the Brexit negotiations, over the UK government (see House of

53
Nevertheless, neither was it that Alliance ‘never’ admitted when it 
had common ground with the DUP in certain areas around Brexit, 
as for example in terms of their agreement on ensuring the need 
for unfettered access from NI into Great Britain (GB) (see House of 
Commons, 2020, d). Ultimately though, even if there are instances 
of Alliance expressing that a DUP voice should be included on 
Brexit-related issues, or that they agreed with the DUP on some 
specific details, out of all the NI parties, Alliance’s Brexit position 
contrasted most with the unionist DUP. In this way, Brexit provides 
the context for a striking contrast between Alliance and the main 
party of political unionism during this period. 
 
Cleavage within (and made up of) cleavages 
 
Alliance was pro-remain like the SDLP (and SF and the 
GPNI) without viewing a UI as the favourable alternative and was 
critical of the DUP’s approach to Brexit and the Protocol, while still 
recognising the need for its perspective (and agreeing with it in 
parts). However, Alliance emphasised another overlapping, but 
more specific cleavage between (and made up of) Leave-Remain 
and Unionism-Nationalism – i.e. between those who Alliance saw 
as the ‘fantasists’ who put forward ‘unicorn solutions’ to Brexit (e.g. 
Borders 2.0) and ‘pragmatists’ who saw that the issues of the 
Protocol and similar concerns could only be dealt with through 
negotiated, legal and practical solutions. Therefore, related to the 
‘decoupling’ of Brexit-related issues and constitutionality, from a 
political standpoint Alliance needed to play down ‘the constitutional’ 
to allow ‘the pragmatic’ - the side it was on - to survive. The reality 
is though that in NI it is impossible to fully separate identity politics 
from economic or other issues as the Protocol does impact on 
unionist identity as did police reform and as do Irish language 
signs. However, Alliance was not ignorant of, or towards, those 
(mainly everyday unionist people, rather than unionist politicians) 
who potentially sat closer to the ‘fantasist’ side in terms of not 

 
54
wanting an Irish sea border for emotional/identity reasons – albeit 
Alliance, as ‘pragmatists’ still accepted this sea border was a 
necessary evil. For example, Alliance’s John Blair MLA stated ‘Any 
border drawn across the island or down the Irish Sea brings 
emotional and political implications. However, in pragmatic 
terms…there is more movement on the island than across the Irish 
Sea...’ (Northern Ireland Assembly, 2020, g). Alliance has 
continued to take the ‘mature approach’ that while ‘pragmatically’ 
something is needed in NI (e.g. institutions, frameworks etc) it 
recognises the emotional and political relevance of some practical 
governance aspects for identity communities. Of course, Alliance 
arguably bordered on ‘fantasist’ or at least uncompromising when 
it called for the ‘rigorous implementation’ of the Protocol. However, 
it ultimately shifted to a more flexible position in May 2022, likely in 
recognition that the majority did not want the Protocol scrapped but 
wanted changes to how it was implemented. Although Alliance 
recognised the challenges associated with the Protocol, it also 
came to realise how it could bring opportunities and a competitive 
advantage for NI.  
 
An equivalent to the ‘Forums’ today 
 
Brexit prompted more civic discussion events on 
constitutionality, including those organised by Ireland’s Future (IF). 
Mimicking its non-attendance at the New Ireland Forum (1984) due 
to its maximalist demand for unity, Alliance did not attend a 2022 
IF conference, which it called a ‘rally to endorse a united Ireland’ 
(Irish News, 2022, k). However, as Alliance’s attendance at the 
Forum for Peace also revealed, the party partakes in ‘Irish-
organised events’ but assesses them on an individual basis (it later 
accepted invitations to other IF events). Also, similarly to how 
Alliance would not support any boycotting by either side of the 
earlier Forums, in NI currently it expects unionists and nationalists 
to engage in civic discussions at equal rates. For instance, while 

 
55
leader Naomi Long would see it as a good idea for unionists to 
engage in New Ireland conversations, she maintains ‘It’s equally 
important for nationalism to engage in the wider conversation about 
devolution...’ (Irish News, 2022, j). Alliance also would assume a 
‘weathervane’ role like it did with the GFA in similar events. For 
example, Stephen Farry said Alliance would take on a ‘critical 
voice’ if needed when participating in Ulster centenary events 
(Belfast Telegraph, 2020, Q). In principle Alliance could label ‘all’ IF 
events as advocating a path to a UI that Alliance would strongly 
oppose; one where NI as a community need not be reconciled in 
advance. Specifically, IF’s document ‘Proposals for the period 
between 2024 and 2030’ argues that there should be no 
preconditions, such as reconciliation before a referendum is held 
and, reconciliation will only follow after reunification (Ireland’s 
Future, 2024, p. 6). This clashes strongly with Alliance’s position 
which seeks a united NI before a united Ireland.  Nevertheless, 
Alliance will not stay completely away from IF’s conversations, 
especially given the public support for them from parts of the 
community. Even more than the issue of Brexit, legacy is 
considered the biggest bugbear in NI. As Stephen Farry noted, 
‘Dealing with the legacy of the past in Northern Ireland is an even 
more thorny and difficult issue than Brexit, to put it in some context.’ 
(House of Commons, 2020, e). In a February 2020 LucidTalk poll 
(TheDetail.tv, 2020) substantial proportions of Alliance (35%) and 
GPNI (32%) voters believe that legacy issues such as unsolved 
conflict/troubles related deaths, outstanding court cases, and 
inquests, should be "left in the past"  Comparatively, fewer believe 
legacy issues should be resolved before a border poll is called 
(26% Alliance and 13% GPNI). However, Greens would like to see 
these legacy issues dealt with under a new structure in a new 
Ireland. Alliance recognises the legacy issues that particularly 
without effective prior engagement would likely poison a 
referendum and dealing with these issues for Alliance is likely a 
legitimate justification to postpone a poll. This desire to postpone a 

 
56
referendum, potentially to deal with conflict legacies and build a 
more united NI or for other reasons, is probably best understood 
as the core view within the party.  
 
U-turn not a unionist-turn  
 
Alliance saw a border poll referendum as a distraction from 
what should be the core goal of restoring power-sharing in 2017 
(Belfast Telegraph, 2017, M). This illustrates again Alliance’s 
central commitment to prioritising devolution over any referendum 
issue. However, it revived the ‘distraction’ itself in 2022 when it 
publicly asked the SoS to clarify the conditions for calling a 
referendum (Irish News, 2022, L). Alliance likely saw the return of 
more stable power-sharing in 2020 as providing a less hostile 
context to explore the Constitutional Issue (CI). Even more 
‘distractingly’, leader Naomi Long in 2022 suggested Alliance 
would ‘undoubtedly’ take a Constitutional Position (CP) in the 
future – a more ‘non-neutral’ position – at least if taking the broad 
view that being neutral means setting aside any discussion of the 
party taking a CP. However, by 2025 Long had again U-turned, 
saying it might ‘make sense’ for it not to take a position, and the 
membership may decide to treat a referendum as a conscience 
issue (Belfast News Letter, 2025, o). Although it was not as drastic 
as in 1997 when Alliance moderated its pro-union position, 2022 
showcased Alliance stepping beyond a position of not engaging 
with referendum calls or saying it is up to the NI people, but then 
later ‘reverted’ back to a more explicitly ‘neutral’ position in 2025. 
Although this may reflect genuine uncertainty in the party on its 
position and a lack of sufficient internal discussion on what 
language Long and the party should use, it still illustrates that 
Alliance’s approach to the CQ is open to development and change. 
These dynamics within the party are explored in depth in the later 
chapters.  
 

 
57
While the post-Brexit context showed some flux in its 
approach, Alliance ultimately softened the assessment that 
discussing a referendum is a ‘hostile act’. In 2013 Alliance’s 
Stewert Dickson MLA criticised SF’s calls for a referendum as 
contradictory to efforts for reconciliation: ‘He will find it hard to 
reach out across the divide when he continues to use the 
inflammatory language of a border poll.’ (Party News Archive, 
2013, I). Broadly, Alliance is striking a better balance between 
being ‘very’ closed off or open to engaging with a referendum by 
not raising fears around a referendum (e.g. partaking in 
conversations on it), but also not wanting to ‘over-engage’ with the 
prospect currently (e.g. bringing back the ambiguity on whether it 
will take a CP in the future). Alliance often uses the narrative that 
people are not woken up by border or Protocol issues, but rather 
real issues. For example, Long said, ‘Whilst people may have 
aspirations, either to remain in the UK or for a united Ireland, at the 
moment those are not the things that are waking them up in the 
middle of the night’ (Press Association, 2022). Although it should 
be questioned to what extent this is distinct to Alliance voters or 
those it seeks to represent, given most SF voters also choose 
issues like the cost of living as the current priorities. At centre 
though, this issue is ultimately not Alliance’s priority as a party and 
the party’s position and rhetoric would not suggest the UK 
government should deal with the CQ as a priority, even if it could.  
 
Ultimately looking across its history as a party, Alliance is far 
more complex than a small ‘u’ unionist party if it ever was one. It 
has consistently been willing to take distinct stances from unionist 
parties from its earliest days and reinforced a clearly distinct 
identity. Through the pre-GFA talks period and the agreement 
negotiations itself, it sought to understand and challenge the 
perspectives of the traditional green and orange parties in a 
context-specific and issue-dependent way while emphasising one-
community, pragmatism, and putting the broader public interest 

 
58
first. From the post-agreement period to Brexit, Alliance 
increasingly emphasised its liberal credentials. As the questions of 
symbols and representation became increasingly fraught, Alliance 
sought to chart a balanced and neutral middle ground as a 
pragmatic step, all the while not relinquishing a preference for more 
encompassing and unifying symbols. Brexit and the associated 
fallout presented the most significant changepoint for Alliance 
since the GFA. Despite its strong Remain stance, Alliance sought 
to build its own pragmatic approach to address the core issues for 
NI without compromising its neutrality on the CQ. In sum, Alliance 
has evolved from an initial grounding as the most moderate of the 
pro-union parties to represent for much of its existence and more 
than ever a liberal, centrist, non-aligned and constitutionally neutral 
party and the most successful party of the centre-ground in NI. 
 
What was/is the Green Party of Northern Ireland? 
 
A. ‘A bit’ Irish and ‘a bit’ British – Transboundary Origins 
 
While SF is cross-jurisdictional, the GPNI uniquely 
recognises all jurisdictions that it works in50. Historically, the GPNI’s 
origins appear more ‘British’ given its predecessor, the NI Ecology 
Party was a branch of the British Ecology Party which used the 
label51 in NI first in the 1981 local elections (Ark, 2003, a). Yet, this 
suggestion downplays how, as the GPNI grew, it looked to 
incorporate ideas from both British and Irish GPs in its strategic 
development.  For example, the Green Light (1990, a) listed that 
step 1 of 7 for a new GPNI working group was to collect copies of 
strategy or policy from other GPs in the ROI, UK and Euro Greens 
to help guide the groups’ own paper on the particular interest area.

operates). Speaking on targets, former GPNI MLA Brian Wilson

C. Leftist, as well as environmentalist: Was the party open to 
an alliance? 
 
Although the GPNI is a ‘niche’ party it is not a single-issue 
pressure group, even if it is primarily associated with 
environmentalism. The GPNI does not even assume that all its 
supporters are diehard eco-warriors. Back in 2014, Agnew 
answered that those core environmentalists who always vote GPNI 
make up 2% across NI, but John Barry’s re-election in North Down 
was a result of groundwork (Belfast Telegraph, 2014). 
Fundamentally, the GPNI sees environmental and social justice as 
intrinsically linked in that a whole social transformation is required 
to address environmental crises, and vice versa tackling social 
issues requires starting with eco-concerns. This means that in a 
way even if ‘environmentalism’ is their ‘single-issue’, due to these 
intrinsic 
ties 
between 
the 
environment 
and 
the 
social, 
‘environmentalism’ is then made up of linked ‘sub (social) issues’. 
Environmentalism is not then a ‘single-issue’ in reality. For the 
GPNI, the only true ‘single-issue’ parties are the outdated ethnic 
parties.  
 
GPNI’s Dr John Barry stated previously ‘The unionist and 
nationalist parties are real single-issue parties, and it is time for a 
new generation of parties to rise and take their place’ (i.e. a new 
progressive centre) (Irish News, 2003, b). Of course, some view 
green and ‘red-er’ socialist perspectives as ‘incompatible’; that is, 
only by replacing the capitalist framework with a socialist one can 
environmental measures work, and they cannot succeed by just 
creating legislation in the current capitalist structure (Socialist 
Standard, 1990). However, even if tension exists between the 
ideologies, the GPNI saw left-wing/socialist parties as closer allies. 
Early on, the GPNI considered downplaying its niche uniqueness 
to form a left-wing alliance for the purposes of survival. After the 
resignation of Sara Parkin, considered a major asset to the GP in 

 
64
GB, Peter Doran, the GPNI representative on the UK regional 
council was pessimistic for the GPs in Britain and NI who failed to 
attract active support. The suggested next moves were either the 
prospect of continued decline, or radical reform like a party 
formation that brought together Red and Green (Green Light, 1992, 
k). Even early on, this was not a one-sided allyship. Leftist parties 
also saw electoral benefit in joining with green forces. For instance, 
in the 1994 European elections, the GPNI, some Labour groups 
and the Democratic Left supported the Peace Coalition (i.e. June 
Campion's candidacy) (Ark, 2002). Notably, it is unclear whether 
the GPNI would have accepted their active base, becoming ‘active’ 
for leftist party allies. Specifically, an early membership form (1991) 
stated ‘You can join the Green Party if you accept and wish to 
further it's [sic] aims and do not belong to any other UK political 
party’ (although this was a rule for many UK parties). Of course, if 
the GPNI actually became part of a ‘left alliance’ this may impact 
the perceived constitutional neutrality of the party (if like the PBP it 
is pro-UI, rather than the smaller socialist parties which are 
constitutionally-neutral’ albeit electorally irrelevant). However, 
while debates might exist on whether GPNI’s ideology can align 
with socialism, or whether these electoral coalitions risked the party 
losing its niche brand, it is difficult to argue that the GPNI did, or 
does, prioritise constitutional change if it undermines the leftist 
mission (to whatever degree this is held internally). Illustratively, 
former leader Steven Agnew viewed SF’s call to cut corporation tax 
(undermining public services) to equalise it with the ROI as 
evidence that its priority is to get closer to unity, not to protect the 
poorest and most vulnerable in NI society as it claims to do 
(Northern Ireland Assembly, 2014, b). The Greens instead have 
always prioritised these groups and goals ahead of constitutional 
issues. 
 
 

 
65
D. Transboundary in origins and structure, but more ‘Ireland-
leaning’? 
 
The GPNI saw significant changes to its electoral fortunes, 
and structure in the 2000s. In 2007 Brian Wilson won the party’s 
first seat in North Down, and the party made big wins in the 2009 
European election with 15,764 votes up from just 4,810 in the first 
stage in 2004 (CAIN, 2004; 2009). By 2011, reflecting its 
membership growth, and new confidence (alongside probably 
wanting to be taken more seriously as a party) the GPNI elected its 
first Northern Ireland leader (spokesperson) to specifically lead its 
operations in Northern Ireland (Belfast Telegraph, 2011, c).  
 
Additionally, the GPNI’s transboundary origins extended 
deeper into its structural configuration. The GPNI’s 2005 vote to 
become part of an all-island organisational framework with the 
GPROI suggests it was ‘Ireland-leaning’.57 Policy-wise, all-island 
or 
cross-border 
environmental/sustainable 
development 
approaches are interpreted as more ideologically attuned to 
nationalism by unionism (at least politically) (see Barry, 2009, p. 
47)58. However, this downplays that the party became ‘all-island’ to 
personify the GFA’s cooperative principles not to symbolise 
constitutional ‘unification’. At the time, GPNI’s Dr John Barry said, 
‘The motion passed yesterday is based upon an evolutionary logic 
of greater co-operation and allows the Green Party to be unique in 
not just supporting the Good Friday agreement but actually living it 
though its new organisational structure.’ (Irish Times, 2005).  Of 
course, arguably, the GPROI becoming a region of an all-island(s) 
 
57 Actually, reinforcing how the GPNI is not always perceived or interpreted as more 
‘Irish-leaning’, in 2011 following a debate during the 2010 AGM on how to best promote 
the language, the then leader Steven Agnew was accused of being unsupportive of Irish 
language rights which the leader strongly contested (see Irish News, 2011, c; d). 
58 This has real, practical consequences for the shape of climate policy in NI. In 2021, 
former leader Claire Bailey introduced a Private Member’s Climate Change Bill which 
noticeably contrasted the unionist-supported DAERA discussion paper on the bill 
which omitted cross-border or all-island dimensions, focusing more on technical 
concerns (Chang and Puchot, 2021, pp. 2-3). 

 
66
framework with the UK Greens, including the GPNI, is the ‘most’ 
representative of GFA relationships (North-South; East-West). 
However, being ‘all-island’ is not ‘all-Ireland’ especially as the GPNI 
wanted, through the new organisation structures, to also 
strengthen links with the GPs in Scotland, England, and Wales, 
which GPNI members could now become members of (Irish Times, 
2005). By the time Clare Bailey became the new party leader in 
2018, the party’s all-island status was a lesser talking point (e.g. it 
re-voted in 2011 to remain part of the all-island framework). Not 
only representing the cooperative principles of the GFA in its 
structure, the GPNI would continue to represent its progressive, 
liberal values though the identity of its candidates. Specifically, in 
the 2016 Assembly elections, Ellen Murray was the first openly 
Transgender person to run for any party across the island.  
 
The GPROI decision to enter into the 2020 government 
coalition with Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael resulted in some 
commentators suggesting the GPNI ensured its own interests were 
reflected in the coalition deal (Irish Times, 2020). This was seen by 
some as a potential step ‘too far’ in terms of the GPNI ignoring 
regional boundaries and getting involved in ROI politics. In 
contrast, Arlow (2025) finds that the GPROI manifesto in 2020 
provided no discussion of reunification, suggesting these parties 
were potentially more reluctant to engage in NI issues than the 
much smaller GPNI (Arlow, 2025 p. 858). However, the Greens 
have often explicitly and unapologetically emphasised that issues 
transcend boundaries and require island-wide solutions for 
example, when making the case that ‘the Irish Sea border has 
always existed for women in Northern Ireland’ who are forced to 
travel for reproductive healthcare (Northern Ireland Assembly, 
2021, K). Even while this may look like an ‘Ireland-leaning’ ethos, 
it is fundamentally instead driven by the Greens’ emphasis on 
issues and their impact rather than a constitutional outlook. Also, 
declaring the GPNI as more ‘Ireland-leaning’ undersells how the 

 
67
party can take positions that may be interpreted (incorrectly) as 
‘British-leaning’ but are ultimately rooted clearly in issue and policy 
preferences. Illustratively, the DUP’s Jim Wells mocked the GPNI 
for seeking to align with Westminster’s legislation banning 
foxhunting and distancing from the position of the GPNI despite its 
all-island structure by saying that this meant it had ‘recognised 
partition’ (Northern Ireland Assembly, 2010, b). This shows its 
ability to draw on influences from both its British and Irish sister 
parties. Even within the GPNI’s written outputs, the party 
‘transcended ideological barriers’ moving between ‘wordings’ (or 
even included Gaelic Irish alongside English) often associated with 
constitutional connotations. Within manifestos, the GPNI moves in 
and out of saying ‘Good Friday Agreement’ and ‘Agreement’ or 
‘Belfast’ or ‘British/Irish agreement’ or ‘British-Irish Agreement’ 
(even when the other content is pretty much the same between 
manifesto years), sometimes adding in slashes or no slashes.   
 
  
‘Transboundary-ness’ is inherently linked to the limited 
weight that the GPNI places on sectarian identities. If anything, it 
appears the GPNI would prefer to move beyond Ireland-UK 
boundary issues and to better acknowledge and reflect the 
diversity within NI.  For example, former leader Clare Bailey MLA 
questioned why initiatives around flying flags in South Belfast were 
debated as if it is only a unionist-nationalist issue, when other 
communities like the Chinese, LGBT and Polish population have 
their own flag-related concerns (Northern Ireland Assembly, 2016, 
U). Unlike flag issues which remain a very ‘real’ and defining point 
of contention in NI, the GPNI even advocated for symbolic changes 
to the structure of NI’s constitution, including within a draft paper of 
the GFA review. GP members in NI and ROI argued for the British 
government to repeal the 1701 Act of Settlement which enshrines 
institutionalised sectarianism against Catholics (not allowing 
members of the monarchy to marry Catholics or be a Catholic). 
Simultaneously, the GPNI sought to reiterate its anti-classist main 

 
68
identity that rejects the monarchy, saying it is not endorsing 
monarchies by proposing this (Press Association, 2004). The GPNI 
also seeks to push beyond the strictures imposed by the identity 
underpinnings of NI’s governing institutions. Agnew viewed how 
the Justice Minister is appointed differently to other ministers props 
up a system of ‘sectarian attitudes of keeping the other out’ 
(Northern Ireland Assembly, 2016, V). For the GPNI, non-
sectarianism and normalisation has to allow any party to take on 
any role in government. This contrasts with Alliance who navigate 
this differently and holds the Justice Minister role as the ‘acceptable 
middle’ even while it too believes in non-sectarianism and 
normalisation. Potentially this speaks to more of a pragmatic 
approach to these questions of normalisation from Alliance 
compared to the Greens, but this also means Alliance strategically 
benefits from getting such high-profile positions, which may also 
partly explain why the GPNI as another non-ethnic party criticises 
this approach.  
 
E. A party of ‘pro-Remain’ – Firm(er) commitment? 
 
As a party of peace and non-violence, the GPNI admired the 
EU’s contributions to building peaceful relations between states but 
was against any attempts to form a ‘militarised and federal EU 
superstate’ (NI Assembly Election Manifesto, 2003, p. 20). Also as 
a party of direct democracy, it previously suggested that the 
European Parliament should be granted the right to initiate 
legislation as it is the only EU institution directly elected by the 
people (Green Party European Manifesto, 2009, p.12)59.  However, 
as a party of ‘issues’ it took ownership of and defended against the 
undermining of environmental protection after Brexit. Remarking 
on how provisions of the proposed Environment Bill posed an eco-
 
59 Even during the peace processes, the GPNI (and GPROI) called for the EP to appoint 
an independent commission on NI to help facilitate the build towards peace (Irish 
Times, 1994, b). 

 
69
threat to NI, Bailey (and former MLA Rachel Woods in another 
contribution) asked ‘Are we willing to accept a future outside the 
EU with lower environmental protections? As Greens, we will not.’ 
(Northern Ireland Assembly, 2020, T). While the GPNI holds firm to 
its issue stances, this opens it up to accusations of alignment to 
the traditional blocs, even by their centre-ground counterpart, 
Alliance.  
 
Alliance’s Dr Stephen Farry referred to the proposed anti-Brexit 
coalition between GPNI and the nationalist parties in the 2017 
General Election as ‘in essence a nationalist reaction to a unionist 
pact’ (Irish News, 2017, W). But this overlooks that the GPNI 
reached across the spectrum to reject Brexit. Specifically, Agnew 
also met with Ulster Unionists in attempts to create an anti-Brexit 
electoral pact (Irish News, 2017, W).  Moreover, GPNI also was 
‘firmer’ than Alliance in rejecting Brexit, whereby Alliance appeared 
quicker to (begrudgingly) accept the outcome of Brexit. In this way, 
Alliance is a more ‘traditional’ party in this context (i.e. the decision 
is made to move on) but the GPNI (unlike in the ROI) see 
themselves as ‘outsiders’ in the NI system and embrace the 
position of standing out on the issue even into the longer-term. In 
this sense, ‘holding firm’ against Brexit also led Bailey to opt out of 
contesting Belfast constituencies in the 2019 Westminster General 
Elections to prop up the nationalist parties to maximise the pro-
remain vote. Unlike 2017, this was a ‘firmer’ stance against Brexit 
as it did not previously stand aside, but Alliance called these pacts 
‘patronising, both presuming you can dictate who your supporters 
vote for and they cannot decide for themselves if they wish to vote 
tactically’ (Belfast Telegraph, 2019). However, Bailey notes her 
endorsement of the SDLP in 2019 in South Belfast, did not equate 
to her encouraging Green supporters to transfer to the SDLP in the 
2022 Assembly elections (Daily Mirror, 2022). Therefore, it was not 
a matter of promoting Green Party supporters to propel 
nationalism’s electoral fortunes. It was again about taking what was 

 
70
seen as the strongest and most effective stance in line with the 
party’s position. Also, Alliance was not always so ‘anti-pact’ if it 
meant propping up the GFA, a core strategic mission of the party’s 
history. Alliance in 2001 withdrew from the Westminster election 
contest in North Down to prop up the pro-Agreement Unionist vote, 
encouraging Alliance supporters to support Lady Hermon.  
 
The GPNI more broadly rejects the framing of Brexit explicitly 
through an identity affiliation lens. Former leader Agnew disputes, 
like Alliance, the statistic on 85% of unionism [having voted 
"Leave"].  Agnew noted, ‘I query that and I query continually 
breaking down this society into unionism versus nationalism — 
"green and orange", as it is often put, although there are shades of 
green.’ (Northern Ireland Assembly, 2016, x). Beyond only rejecting 
the statistic itself, both GPNI and Alliance clearly agree that the 
underlying idea of constantly framing and breaking down the issues 
and attitudes by ethno-national camp is reductive and unhelpful 
when views are actually more complex that than and vary among 
individuals from these identity groups including on issues like Brexit 
rather than being fixed or given based on an identity affiliation. 
Importantly, despite being Remain, the GPNI is a more issue-
based, eco-socialist radical party than Alliance which is more 
economically-centrist and liberal, meaning the GPNI focus in terms 
of Brexit (and other major issues such as Covid) tended to more 
regularly stretch beyond business. Illustratively, the GPNI’s Rachel 
Woods stated, ‘It is not just businesses suffering as a result of 
COVID-19, and it is not just businesses that will need to prepare 
for new arrangements arising out of Brexit.’ (Northern Ireland 
Assembly, 2020, f)  
 
F. Issues-Party – ‘The Future’ defined by ‘issues’ 
 
When remarking on the party’s constitutional position, 
former leader Steven Agnew generally reverted back to how it was 

 
71
up to the people in NI to decide on the constitutional question (not 
the party). However, the party moved away from using the Principle 
of Consent to ‘block’ reflection on the CQ. Rather, by ‘framing’ the 
future through climate60 issues, it stood away from debating the CQ 
from a binary position, but showed it was not ignoring it. Although 
on board with proper planning ahead of a referendum, when asked 
as to whether the GP would take a position on a future referendum, 
former leader Clare Bailey said they have a ‘wider vision for the 
future of these islands’ focused on dealing with the climate crisis 
(Daily Mirror, 2022). Here, as is revisited in the empirical chapters, 
the GPNI’s vision for the future is directed by its core ‘issue’ of 
climate change, in whatever constitutional status. In sum, the 
Greens are able to talk and think about the constitutional future as 
a subset of how they are able to talk and think about the future 
more broadly defined by salient issues, the most significant of 
which is climate change, and now the constitutional issue has 
become one of these salient issues (as discussed later in the 
empirical chapters). Although, it was not a ‘quid pro quo’ situation 
given the GPNI expected those of a binary CP to take positions on 
and generate progress on ‘green issues’ but did not pressure itself 
to engage with the CQ directly. For example, Bailey declared ‘I 
want those [who] promote the notion of a New Ireland to set out 
their position on mitigating climate change in this new 
dispensation, as well as [etc]…I’d also ask the same questions of 
those who avow the protection of the union, particularly in a post-
Brexit Britain’ (Irish News, 2019). Here the GPNI is presenting a 
counter to Agarin et al. (2025)’s observation that the public’s 
concern for the Lough Neagh crisis has become ‘ethnicised’ when 
included in the aligned parties’ political programmes to serve their 
 
60 The GPNI often express a sense that they are not afforded credit for leading on 
climate issues from the traditional aligned parties. However, potentially, the GPNI does 
not credit those Assembly representatives who have recognised the party’s (specifically 
former GPNI MLA Brian Wilson) pioneering and radical contributions to green politics 
in NI like the former SDLP MLA Alban Maginness (see Northern Ireland Assembly, 
2010, a). 

 
72
strategic needs, rather than nature (p. 649). Like Alliance, the GPNI 
appear to have gone through a period of arguing it will take a 
position if planned for, but as is discussed in the empirical chapters, 
they do not appear to have ‘backtracked’ in the way Naomi Long 
did in 2025. Bailey states ‘We have seen through Brexit, when you 
throw a referendum out — without a plan — what it leads to is 
disaster, so if we have a plan for a border poll then we will take a 
position on it’ (Irish Independent, 2022). 
 
Again, separating the relevance of constitutionalism for 
climate, the GPNI recognises that borders ‘matter little in the face 
of climate breakdown’ (BBC News, 2019). However, it was not 
ignorant to the ‘reality’ of how the success of constitutional 
settlements can be ‘dependent’ on green issues. For example, 
Agnew thought that those higher ups in the SNP came to recognise 
that had the Scottish referendum passed, Scotland prospering as 
an independent nation would require capitalising on renewable 
energy sources (Northern Ireland Assembly, 2012).  However, 
while the GPNI focuses on making ‘the future’ better for climate 
progress, regardless of the constitutional status of NI (potentially 
even if that means changing the constitutional status), the GPNI 
recognises that the legacy of the past still defines this segregated 
society, where even gangs still coerce communities and changing 
the constitutional status of NI does not automatically address these 
legacy issues. As former GPNI MLA Rachel Woods noted ‘We 
know that this has been a political process rather than a peace 
process.’ (Northern Ireland Assembly, 2021). The GPNI continues 
to remain aware of cultural sensitivities, even if these do not guide 
their decision-making directly. For example, the former GP ROI 
leader, Eamon Ryan, credited Clare Bailey with pushing for a name 
change to the ‘shared island’ unit from the ‘united Ireland’ unit in 
the Department of the Taoiseach (Slugger O’Toole, 2020). 
However, as an ‘owner’ of green issues, in contemporary NI, it 
continues to fight to move ‘blame away’ from climate action and 

 
73
targets, or climate’s perceived enemy (i.e. the farming community), 
and towards the real ‘troublemakers’ like policies which do not help 
NI to meet EU directive targets for ammonia or the leadership of 
the Assembly failing to set NI up to continue to compete in the 
green economy, or the uncertainty of Brexit (see e.g. Northern 
Ireland Assembly, 2020, L).  
 
Section 2: Methodology 
 
Design, ontology and epistemology 
 
Rather than examining culture (ethnography) or building a 
substantive theory from the ground-up (grounded theory), this 
research seeks to discover and understand a phenomenon, a 
process, or the perspectives and worldviews of the people involved 
(Merriam, 1998, p. 11). Therefore, an inductive research strategy 
is employed which involves searching for patterns in the data and 
formulating an explanation from those patterns (Bernard, 2011). 
The patterns form the foundation of this intrinsic case study which 
is chosen because of its ‘uniqueness’, rather than because it 
represents other cases (Crowe et al., 2011, p. 5). As a case, the 
‘contemporary political centre-ground in Northern Ireland’ holds a 
structural core because it exists as an observable entity with 
people who represent it, rather than strictly as an abstract political 
position between nationalism and unionism.   
 
Given the interest in party activist perceptions, this research 
employed an interpretivist paradigm, which stresses the 
importance of individual views, subjectivity and interpretation.  
Those from a positivist tradition typically take realism as an 
ontology which assumes reality is governed by a set of universal 
laws and is independent of the perspectives of individuals. 
However, this thesis does not see the world as something stable 

 
74
and directly observable, rather it is something we actively 
construct. Following from this interpretivist outlook, the project is 
built on a premise that there is no singular, fixed, objective reality 
that can be identified and observed. Instead, reality can be 
understood as a combination of multiple realities that are 
dependent on individual people. From this relativist ontological 
outlook, our views, attitudes, and beliefs are important in the 
construction of our world and reality (Kriukow, 2022).  
 
From this ontological position, the epistemological approach 
follows as regards to how knowledge is acquired and how to study 
the reality around us.  Again, positivism often takes ‘objectivism’ as 
the epistemological approach where individuals’ attitudes and 
perspectives inhibit our capacity to observe the reality directly. 
Positivists believe that the world around us is consistent and 
structured. Positivists seek to employ the scientific method and 
most commonly utilise quantitative methods. They seek to 
understand and measure social and political phenomena in a 
systematised way. However, this project follows from the 
perspective that the world, rather than being observable and 
knowable in an objective fashion, is instead constructed and 
understood through our values, belief systems and  interpretations. 
Therefore, to better understand the centrist party activists, this 
means listening to their self-constructed views and thoughts in 
order to explore that reality (Kriukow, 2022; Grix, 2002). Therefore, 
this dissertation relies on qualitative methods which allow for the 
exploration of these processes – primarily semi-structured 
interviews (SSIs). 
 
Unit of Analysis and Unit of Observation 
 
This dissertation focuses on the analysis of the 
constitutionally neutral parties of the centre-ground. These parties, 
Alliance and the GPNI, constitute the unit of analysis of this study 

 
75
but to interrogate these parties, there are a variety of options in 
terms of the unit of observation. There are a number of distinct 
options for how to assess these parties and their associated 
identities, ideologies, and constitutional outlooks internally. There 
are four major options from existing literature. First, there is the 
potential use of manifesto and parliamentary speeches data to 
examine party-level policy positions (e.g. Dinas and Gemenis, 
2010), but this does not capture the divergence of views, personal 
belief systems, and emotions within the party at the people-level. 
Secondly, there is the option of the use of surveys to capture the 
attitudes of voters from the centre-ground (e.g. Peterburg and 
Oshri, 2024). However, this is cost-intensive and logistically 
challenging but also theoretically, this tends to overlook the party 
as an independent actor and the role of the supply-side internal 
party organisation, variety, and debate in shaping both how the 
party itself approaches questions of identity, issue orientation and 
the constitutional question and the potential role of the party itself 
as directing and orienting its voter base on the demand-side. Third, 
there is the option of examining the attitudes of those within the 
party membership through the administration of a membership 
survey. In this case, however there is already path-breaking work 
from Tonge et al (2024) on the Alliance membership which richly 
explores the attitudes and preferences of Alliance members on a 
broad range of issues. Finally, there is the option, selected in this 
thesis, to examine in depth and systematically the perspectives of 
party activists who more than voters shape the direction of the party 
and ultimately constitute the party on a day-to-day, organisational 
basis. Within this thesis ‘party activist’ is defined as an individual 
who has a ‘formal association’ to Alliance or the GPNI. Said ‘formal 
association’ could mean they are an active member, councillor, 
MLA or MP. Being a voter of either party is not enough for the 
individual to meet the inclusion criteria. This thesis provides the first 
such extensive qualitative examination of the identities, ideologies, 
and constitutional attitudes of Alliance and GPNI activists as the 

 
76
units of observation and the individuals who, at the ‘people-level’, 
constitute the parties of the centre-ground in Northern Ireland.  
 
Method  
 
A. Semi-structured interviews 
Following from the chosen ontology and epistemology, SSIs 
allowed for exploration of spontaneous issues introduced by the 
activist, while pursuing a number of less structured questions 
(Ryan et al., 2009, p. 310). As opposed to completely unstructured 
interviews, the semi-structured nature of the interviews ensured 
that certain relevant themes were consistently asked about. 
Compared to focus groups, respondents in individual interviews 
offer more detail into their feelings, thoughts and worldviews and 
are more likely to raise socially sensitive discussion topics (Guest 
et al., 2017, p. 693). Given party activists were to be asked about 
themes which could reveal answers not on par with the ‘party line’, 
a group setting was avoided to allow for richer discussion on issues 
of identity and constitutionality. The decision was also taken to 
make all interviews anonymous and confidential as the identities of 
interviewees could become clear from the content of the 
discussions. Also, with a recognition of the sensitive and personal 
nature of identity and constitutionalism for NI persons, the activists 
could receive the main questions in advance, and suggestions for 
alterations were welcomed. For example, one preferred language 
of border poll over ‘united Ireland referendum’ and that ultimately 
led to the ‘re-construction’ of the interview guide. Sharing the 
questions prior to the interview is not without risk of predetermined 
answers and participant bias (Haukås and Tishakov, 2024), but it 
also helps with recall and preparing for answers with specificity 
(Robinson et al., 2021). The interview guide focused on a number 
of major themes consistently although there were adaptations and 
consolidation of topics and individual questions over time. The first 

 
77
of the primary themes typically were questions focused on party 
appeal and membership, or what personally attracted these 
activists to the parties or the characteristics of the party that made 
it unique in their eyes. Second, the activists were asked about their 
personal opinion on their party’s constitutional position. The 
interview would then generally pivot to the factors that would 
influence their own preference in the context of a border poll and 
their perspectives on the factors that would influence other party 
activists. The interview would discuss the shape of conversations 
and preparations within the party regarding a future border poll. 
Following this, activists often would be asked about positive and 
negative impacts of a potential United Ireland or status quo result 
moving from a focus on the general to the personal over the course 
of interviews. Interviewees were typically asked about strategies to 
accommodate those who identify as Irish in Northern Ireland and 
British in a United Ireland. The activists were offered an opportunity 
to share their ethno-national background in the interview and 
discuss the impact of it on their vote choice in a border poll. The 
topics of Brexit, the Protocol and their potential influence on 
activists’ constitutional thinking were also raised during the SSIs. 
Before the broad concluding question, activists were often asked 
about the issues of the potential timing of a border poll or readiness 
for a poll. An example of a utilised interview guide is in Appendix B. 
‘Closed’ questions which tend to close enquiry down, rather than 
open it up were avoided (Timonen et al., 2018, p. 6). This reflected 
how the aim of the data collection was not to quantify the 
constitutional preferences and identity make-up of the interviewed 
activists (e.g. how many GPNI activist were pro-UI), but glean 
reflections on issues of party participation, centrism, identity, 
constitutional preferences and lived experiences in NI since Brexit. 
Of course, these themes are not mutually exclusive and so, the 
inclusion of overlapping questions in the guide allowed the 
researcher to revert back to earlier threads to gain more 
information (Charmaz, 2006, p. 32). This also contributes richness 

 
78
to 
the 
understanding 
of 
internal 
dynamics, 
interpretive 
understandings, and diverse perspectives on major identity and 
constitutionality themes in these parties of the centre-ground as an 
extension on previous work.  
 
The SSIs were administered face-to-face because the 
impersonal character of telephone interviews can prevent natural 
encounters and rapport (Shuy, 2003), which is necessary when 
looking for private information such as socio-political attitudes 
towards Irish unity (Frey et al., 1990). However, when active data 
collection began, decisions were made to change from conducting 
in-person to online interviews given the escalation in the Covid-19 
pandemic. The completed set of interviews then includes a 
combination of online and in-person interviews (34 online, 10 
offline). Despite initial apprehension, allowing interviewees to talk 
from the comfort of a familiar space (e.g. some were in a home 
office) allowed for friendly and slower pace to draw out more 
detailed insights. The shape of the online interviews mirrors 
findings from Deakin and Wakefield (2014) whose comparison of 
in-person and Skype interviews revealed ‘that Skype aided rapport 
building and afforded greater flexibility, and cost savings’ (see Oliffe 
et al., 2021, p. 2).  
 
After the interviews were conducted, and transcribed, the 
researcher immersed themselves in the data to identify not only the 
views being put forward, but instances of emotion strain or 
excitement (e.g. whether they appeared uneasy about their party 
taking a CP, or excited about the prospect of constitutional 
changed). As a pragmatic constructivist researcher they tried to 
‘make sense out of the data by ‘consolidating, reducing, and 
interpreting’ what people have said in order to make ‘meaning’ 
(Merriam, 1998).  To improve integrity, the researcher practiced 
ongoing self-reflection and self-scrutiny to ensure that their 

 
79
interpretations of what interviews found was rooted in the data 
(Polit and Beck, 2014)  
 
B. Sampling and recruitment 
 
In terms of sample size, the aim of qualitative research is to 
generate enough data to allow for patterns, concepts, categories, 
dimensions or properties of the phenomena to emerge (Glaser and 
Strauss, 1967). The sample size was increased until no new 
themes or codes or insights emerge as is commonly referred to as 
‘data or theoretical saturation’ in Grounded Theory (Saunders et 
al., 2018, p. 1898). Crouch and McKenzie (2006) suggest that less 
than twenty participants in a qualitative study helps to build 
interview-interviewee relationship. However, this research kept to 
this for one party under examination, the GPNI, but more data was 
needed from Alliance to reflect the proportional party size in 
Northern Ireland. A total of 44 interviews were conducted (17 GPNI, 
27 Alliance). A non-random purposive sampling strategy – ‘the 
deliberate choice of a participant due to the qualities the participant 
possesses’ (Etikan et al., 2016, p. 2) – was applied to locate 
Alliance and GPNI activists. Specifically, the websites of the 
Alliance Party and the GPNI were accessed and the details of all 
party representatives including councillors, MLAs, MPs, leadership 
and party offices were collected. The researcher then created a 
contact list of all of the emails for these potential recruits for the 
study. Alliance Youth and Youth Greens as well as public blogs of 
party activists and select social media accounts were also utilised 
to expand the potential recruitment pool. Certain civil society 
associations were also contacted to inquire about any potential 
avenues to access interviewees although of course, there were 
limitations here due to the non-party affiliation of these bodies.   
 
 Potential participants were emailed in 2022 to ask would 
they be interested in partaking in an interview, and then those who 

 
80
responded later got an email to confirm would they still like to 
partake. At this point, the researcher typically outlined the potential 
options to conduct the interview online or offline, asked 
respondents whether they would like to receive a list of the main 
interview themes as well as their availability and schedule for the 
interview and any other queries they had. Interviewees were 
informed later about the confidentiality and anonymity details and 
provided with the relevant documentation. The project also 
employed ‘snowball sampling’ (Goldstein, 2002). Interviewees 
were contacted by email for suggestions on potential additional 
interviewees who may be willing to participate. This contact was 
made once a relationship and rapport had been established with 
the original interviewee. The in-person interviews were primarily 
conducted in libraries, hotel lobbies, constituency offices, and 
university premises.  
 
All of the interviews for this thesis were conducted between 
July 2022 and March 2024. The Stormont Assembly was collapsed 
for the period between May 2022 until the Executive was restored 
in February 2024. This means the suspension of the Assembly 
overlapped with most of the period during which the fieldwork was 
conducted for this thesis. It is possible that this may have 
influenced the perspectives that interviewees expressed, and this 
context is important to consider. However, the interviews were not 
primarily focused on attitudes towards Stormont itself and the 
impact on inferences regarding the key themes of this thesis should 
therefore be limited. The return of Stormont was addressed when 
appropriate. Given many interviews were conducted via Zoom, the 
location, identities (communal, gender etc) were very diverse – 
albeit those conducted in-person mainly (not exclusively) were 
from Lisburn and Belfast. Here, the value of online interviewing is 
again realised. The recruitment produced a large sample of forty-
four interviewees across Alliance and the GPNI. Based on publicly 
available information, there was substantial variation by age from 

 
81
those contacted via youth branches of both parties to those who 
were very long-serving in the two parties. There were interviewees  
from all age cohorts from 18-24 through to 60+. Although gender 
was not assumed, public records clearly indicate that there were 
men, women and those who identified as transgender among the 
interviewee pool. There were a greater number of male 
participants, but a significant minority of women resulting in a 
diverse gender spread to the sample. Similarly, employment status 
varied from those at university through to those who indicated they 
were near to retirement, but most were of working age. In terms of 
class background, very few interviewees in Alliance referred to their 
class. Of this small number who did, they typically shared they were 
middle-class. Proportionally more in the GPNI shared their class 
background, including those who were middle-class or strongly 
working-class. A number of activists shared their professional 
occupations including those who work in academia, former 
soldiers, researchers, business owners and party employees. 
Interviewees were from a variety of locations within Northern 
Ireland from both urban and rural areas and from west and east of 
the Bann even if predominantly drawn from larger population 
centres. There were also interviewees who came from the Republic 
of Ireland, other parts of the United Kingdom and North America 
although these activists were now living in NI. Activists came from 
all communal backgrounds including nationalist, unionist and non-
NI identity communities, and they varied in their seniority including 
grassroots activists, councillors and MLAs within the parties. The 
sample included those who were recent recruits to the party as well 
as those with decades of service. As reiterated later in the empirical 
discussions, while those who were more willing to share their 
specific preference on the constitutional question (beyond 
undecided) tended to be from a grassroots level within the party, 
the length of time within the party did not appear to be a major 
determinant of their views. Overall, while this qualitative sample 
does not allow for statistical generalisation, the diversity and scope 

 
82
of the sample allow for the research to make valid inferences about 
the activist group in both parties. 
 
C. Secondary Sources 
 
Unlike the theoretical framework defined by Creswell 
(2003), which involves the presentation of a specific theory, the 
thesis theoretical framework follows from Merriam’s description. It 
is ‘the structure, the scaffolding, the frame’ of this study and is 
derived from the ‘concepts, terms, definitions, models and theories 
of a particular literature base and disciplinary orientation’ (Merriam, 
2001). Given the limited (but growing) literature on the political 
centre-ground in NI, the previous conceptualisation from Chapter 
1 provides this ‘base’ before the proceeding focus on Alliance and 
the GPNI. 
 
Alongside, SSIs the researcher also collected and sieved 
through analysed media and political debate discourses, the 
archival research from Linen Hall’s online political archive ‘Divided 
Society’, and the Lucid Talk polling data. Although the intention was 
to identify findings that do or do not triangulate interview 
conclusions, the data mainly serves to inform the case selection. 
Relevant media and debate sources were identified using key word 
searches related to the project’s core concepts, focus and context 
(e.g. by party, party leader or united Ireland, Brexit) via LexisNexis 
and TheyWorkForYou. A major collection of all relevant publicly 
collected post-Brexit LucidTalk polling data segregated by party or 
‘Other’ identity was constructed and is employed at various points 
through the case selection discussion and empirical analyses to 
add context. It should be noted that for the GPNI in particular as a 
small party, there are small samples and cell sizes for these 
analyses and therefore, these results should be interpreted with 
caution. However, this data is primarily a resource for 
understanding voters’ attitudes while the core added value and 

 
83
emphasis of this project is in its exploration of the attitudes, 
perspective and interpretations of ‘activists’ as the embodiment of 
these parties themselves. The researcher continued to revisit the 
short-hand reflective research journal that was kept during the 
examining of media/ debates in NVivo. Similarly using key word 
searches related to the thesis themes (e.g. “united Ireland”, “Irish 
unity”), the party manifestos of Alliance and the GPNI were 
reviewed to identify relevant sections that would expand the depth 
on the two parties. By condensing large data amounts into more 
manageable amounts of understandable information, qualitative 
data analysis tries to arrive at lessons, conclusions or inferences 
(DeCarlo, 2018). Given the sheer quantity of data that this study 
aims to gather and analyse, computer-assisted qualitative data 
analysis software enhanced the speed and efficiency of data 
analyses for the additional document and archival materials (Séror, 
2005) but  this was not employed for interviews as it was more 
practical and in keeping with the reflective nature of the analysis to 
use more manual practices. This additional documentary, polling, 
media and archival data did however provide additional critical 
information sources to inform whether the perspectives of my 
interview participants align with the wider political party and help 
triangulate between diverse forms of data in identifying and 
deriving the key patterns and inferences. 
 
Researcher Position 
 
Given the researcher themselves is not ‘separate’ from the 
process within a ‘subjectivist epistemology’, there is a recognition 
that they are influencing the research context and it is influencing 
them. Similar to McEvoy’s own reflection on interviewing in a 
divided society, the researcher was pushed to ‘think about how to 
manage my identity as a young Catholic female’ when researching 
in NI. Similarly again, activists sometimes assumed the 
researcher’s own identity along the traditional divide. As McEvoy 

 
84
also notes ‘I was, therefore, alerted to the possibility that my identity 
had an impact and had to analyse carefully the responses: what 
the interviewees may have said, or may not have said’ (2006, p. 
186). While the researcher does not identify as Catholic or 
nationalist, activists often contextualised their answers in relation 
to the researcher being from the Republic of Ireland (ROI) in a 
Dublin university. For example, one activist who was from the ROI 
assumed that they had shared similar experiences and 
perspectives as to how the Protestant community was perceived in 
the South. 
 
 The issue of the researcher’s own position on the CQ did not 
get raised frequently and the interviewer did not ask directly about 
the interviewee’s constitutional preference. Generally, the 
interviewer and interviewee welcomed hearing about the other’s 
position if they were openly willing to offer it61. Despite activists 
being so-called ‘elites’ (councillors, MLAs, members), the 
interviewer never felt compromised and was even complimented 
on their approach and professionalism. Unlike McEvoy’s 
experience, the researcher did not face any patronising 
commentary (e.g. being called ‘love’ or ‘lass’ as McEvoy e.g. p. 
185) and instead felt treated very respectfully throughout the 
interviewing process. The only interference was the age of the 
researcher, given some activists would frame their answers around 
‘your generation’ (e.g. they do not want to see a return to violence 
with a border poll for those younger people like my generation). 
Similarly to McEvoy, the researcher employed probing as a means 
to ‘challenge stereotypes and get beyond the party line’ (p. 188). 
While never intrusively engaging with personal, constitutional, or 
other identities, oftentimes the conversation became more collegial 
and offered a comfortable space to share their thinking.  
 
61 It was unusual for the interviewer to be asked directly by an interviewee. If they 
were, they explained they did not have a firm, fixed preference.  

 
85
 
Of course, ethical considerations reinforce the need for 
reflective practices and a reflexive approach to consent, and 
human consideration must be revisited throughout the study to 
ensure ethical interviewing (Sin, 2005). Therefore, any data shared 
that might have been overly confidential so as to identify the activist 
was not included in the final study (e.g. certain constituency 
names). The researcher is also a professional conflict mediator 
who has been trained in interpersonal communication skills, active 
listening skills and strategies to encourage parties to speak their 
minds. This training was useful when gathering subjective 
perspectives on Brexit and a united Ireland in a sensitive and 
respectful manner. In light of these considerations, the project 
received formal ethical approval from Dublin City University on 20th 
May 202262. 
 
Conclusion 
 
  
Like Alliance, the GPNI has undergone periods of evolution 
and progress towards articulation of a core philosophy and ethos. 
Unlike Alliance however, the GPNI’s core identifying markers have 
followed from its status as an issue-based party which generates 
the expectation internally that it engages with and positions itself 
on key policy concerns up to and including future constitutional 
debates. For the Greens this is considered compatible with its non-
aligned status and constitutional neutrality as while it engages with 
the traditional blocs staying true to its consensus-building 
principles and strong commitment to mediation, this is through the 
lens of advancing its progressive agenda on key issues as its main 
priority. In this way, the GPNI comprises a critical but distinct 
component of the centre-ground in NI to its larger compatriot, 
Alliance.  
 
62 See Appendix A for ethics documentation including Informed Consent Form. 

 
86
 
Taken together, these two parties, Alliance and the GPNI 
constitute the centre-ground of contemporary NI politics at a time 
of uncertainty and major constitutional debate following from Brexit 
and the striking developments of the last decade. This project 
proceeds from here to examine these parties, their conceptual 
markers and internal dynamics and debates from the ground up by 
exploring the attitudes and understandings of activists that 
fundamentally embody and actively construct these parties and 
their particular place in the modern NI political environment they 
represent. 
 
 
 

 
87
Chapter 3: Conceptual markers of Alliance activists: 
‘Less-aligned’ rather than non-aligned and the role 
of Alliance values 
 
Introduction 
 
This chapter examines the conceptual markers of 
membership of Alliance as the largest and most prominent party of 
the centre-ground. In particular, the chapter explores the realities 
of ‘non-alignment’ which when viewed through the prism of 
activists’ experiences and perspectives is better reconceived as a 
spectrum of alignment which waxes and wanes rather than a fixed 
position. The first sections consider how activists came to be non-
aligned and the role of background, ideology, openness to other 
groups and perspectives, the rejection of blocs and labels and then 
explores the status of many activists as ‘less aligned’ rather than 
non-aligned. In this sense, the chapter demonstrates that for 
centre-ground activists’ non-alignment in the truest sense is 
extremely challenging or essentially impossible in a context like NI. 
People are still influenced by their backgrounds but not in 
straightforward ways. It is better to understand this as an ongoing 
process of 'reduction of alignment' navigated by activists in Alliance 
in various ways. Due to socialisation and also for logistical reasons 
existing identities cannot be totally escaped but their impact can be 
lessened and there are also periods and dynamics through which 
activists become partially ‘re-aligned’ as these influences tend to 
reassert themselves. For Alliance activists there are however a true 
set of ‘Alliance values’ they seek to embrace such as openness, 
and tolerance. There is a residual influence of the identity 
backgrounds activists come from as they have reduced (if not
