eliminated) their alignment to these identities. Despite these 
residual effects though, activists still seek to embody these Alliance 
values.  
 

 
88
Conceptual marker: Non-alignment  
 
Alliance’s ‘civic-ness’ is built on its ideological vision for a 
liberal, united NI, rather than on having representation of both 
communities in its make-up or support. Given this, the Alliance 
activists reinforce the party’s ‘civic-ness’ in representation given 
many come from either (or neither) community. However, the 
diversity in their identities - at least nationally as many hold mixed 
affiliations to British, Irish and Northern Irish - makes it difficult to 
‘group’ activists. It is easier to say what many are ‘not’ in identity 
terms – Alliance activists are not (really) unionist (in identity which 
is different to background) or strongly British (albeit they may partly 
identify as British). Of course, not having a coherent identity (aside 
from not being unionist or strongly British) could be interpreted as 
an identity. However, this thesis interprets identity ‘positively’ by 
what the activists define themselves as (unionist/Protestant/British 
or nationalist/Catholic/Irish) rather than not. Ultimately, what neatly 
binds Alliance activists is their support for the party’s ideological 
vision, as opposed to most fitting into one distinct identity (again, 
not background) bloc. Also, compared to ethno-nationality, religion 
was not as discussed in the interviews potentially because as many 
activists alluded to, religion was not a major thing in their household 
growing up, and so many are not really used to speaking about it 
in detail. In general, the activists used the interview space to talk 
more around their or others’ community and national identities.  
 
Conceptual marker: Non-alignment – Being in Alliance means 
being mixed? 
 
Although Alliance activists do not generally fit into one 
distinct identity bloc, there was still an innate feeling that being 
‘mixed’ makes people particularly suited to being in the non-
nationalist Alliance. Actually, certain activists (9; 24) unprompted 
told the interviewer that they were still a sort of hybrid in their 

 
89
‘identification’ or wanted to build the community society they did 
not have growing up, specifically ‘despite’ not coming from mixed 
marriages or a cross-community household or area (similar to 
Stojanovic description of ‘neithers’ who do not necessarily come 
from mixed families mentioned in the conceptualisation chapter). 
Activist (9) outlined ‘…I'm an atheist now…so I'm just about the 
worst protestant that you can find…I was speaking to [someone] 
recently who was shocked that I was a protestant because my 
name is [traditional Irish name] …Although I don't come from a 
mixed marriage, I am sort of a hybrid there... lived in [UK] for four 
years when I went to uni…’. These activists likely recognised the 
ingrained assumption that outsiders may have of Alliance as 
particularly attractive for those from mixed marriages.  
 
Even in terms of ‘identity’, often activists who came from 
mixed marriages also shared how they felt stronger affiliation to 
one identity over another; generally Irish over British, even if they 
might go by Northern Irish now in their lives (6; 22). These activists 
may not then truly display category fluidity which ‘involves free 
movement between two categories with the same range, and, 
where it is significant, involves the ability to take on the whole 
identity contents and repertoires associated with each category 
and to move between them at will’ (Todd et al, 2006, p. 330). These 
activists may not pass back and forth to their British identity with 
such ease compared to their Irish identity. For example, despite 
being mixed, one activist (6) says if they are travelling, they will 
certainly use their Irish passport and they feel very strongly in their 
Irish identity. This activist does not appear as attached to unionism 
or their Britishness, but they also hold attachment – but not 
necessarily equally – to all identities listed in the interview guide 
including British, Irish, Northern Irish. Therefore, again, it does not 
appear that most Alliance activists ‘coherently’ come from mixed 
backgrounds/marriages or may not even hold equal identification 
with their mixed background, if they are from one.  

 
90
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned – Openness transcends in 
relationships 
 
Coming from a mixed marriage is not a prerequisite to 
support Alliance, but those in Alliance are open to entering into 
relationships including marriages with people from different 
backgrounds. They also sometimes frame their opinions on a UI or 
their own identity ‘with reference’ to the identity/background of their 
partner. Although the popular focus is on how being socialised in 
mixed parentage influences identity make-up, Alliance activists 
show being in a relationship with an ‘Alliance person’ could soften 
the position of the spouse/partner, sometimes enough to move 
them to support Alliance – the ‘openness is infectious’. For 
example, one Alliance activist (10) says ‘…now I'll say that my 
[spouse] is an Alliance voter as well and I'm a party member…but 
I think, for me, my upbringing and my background have influenced 
me to be more centre-ground and more progressive because that's 
the way my parents are’. While here, the relationship is illustrative 
of the process through which an understanding and application of 
Alliance values comes to alter the perspective of the parties. 
However, in turn, there are other relationships which more directly 
‘embody’ the ethos of Alliance in which partners from distinct 
backgrounds 
recognise 
and 
respect 
their 
own 
personal 
backgrounds without an expectation of them giving up their pre-
existing identity. For example, one activist (26) appears to have 
entered into a mixed marriage, but has not changed their own 
identity at all, and sees that ethos as reflected in Alliance – for them 
their ‘Irishness’ is a personal choice - ‘…come from a large 
nationalist family…My wife comes from a loyalist background…and 
we made a conscious decision when we married, we were not 
going to change religion, because to me, like the ethos of the 
Alliance, mutual respect…our children were brought up to 
decide…’.  
 

 
91
Conceptual marker: ‘Less-aligned’ - Alliance activists and a 
great resistance to ‘pick a side’ 
 
Even if they do not come from mixed backgrounds, many 
Alliance activists are what is called ‘less-aligned’ i.e. they do not 
appear to comply with either the Protestant or Catholic hegemony 
or support the associated causes, but they are not fully ‘non-
aligned’ without any relationship to an identity background. 
Considering the patterns across all activists, Kulle’s (2003) 
definition is most useful to apply to Alliance in that generally 
Alliance activists are not 'non-aligned' which ‘seems a conceptual 
impossibility since nobody is really non-aligned anywhere’ but 
‘less-aligned’ which allows the space for recognition that activists 
do have ‘some form of alignment, felt or ascribed’ (p. 96). Given 
activists ‘actively’ chose a non-binary party - despite often coming 
from an aligned background - they might be better able to resist 
pressures to ‘pick a side’. Again, if most activists are ‘less-aligned’ 
this could be considered a ‘coherent identity’ but this would be 
negatively defined by what it is not (i.e. aligned), which goes 
against this thesis’ definition of identity. Notably, sometimes it is 
difficult to determine whether the activists’ ‘resisted alignment’, that 
is, some brought up the scenario of being asked in Northern Ireland 
to pick your identity on a survey or form but the activists themselves 
do not reveal what identity box they would ‘tick’ in these scenarios 
(but they also do not say they would abstain from filling out the 
survey/form altogether). However, this ‘resistance’ to re-align could 
characterise those activists who explain how even though their 
family or parents have raised them with an Alliance-type ethos or 
hold similar political values to them, the activists can resist slipping 
back into binary identities or cultural biases to a ‘greater degree’. 
Somewhat contrary to Kulle (2003), despite these ‘less-aligned’ 
activists being overdetermined because they are positioned 
between conflicting discourses, they may not always conform in 
situations (e.g., when picking who to vote for, ticking a specific 

 
92
identity box) to their traditional identity just to avoid sanctions if they 
fail to align (e.g., risking the upset of their family). For example, 
activist (1) despite being ‘brought up with this kind of very Alliance 
upbringing’ (this is not that they were from a mixed background just 
their family has had a lot of experience of both communities), the 
activist also sees in their parents a need to align with one 
community, and the activist has felt pressures from them at times 
to align with their traditional background (e.g. pressuring them into 
selecting Catholic in the census even though they identify as 
‘Other’). Additionally, one activist (11) who goes by Northern Irish 
can see within their own family this bias in them even if they share 
a lot of the same political thinking as the activist – ‘…And to call 
yourself Northern Irish...means you're moving past those divisions 
that kind of…I don't want to say plague, but almost haunt the older 
generations, like I can see it within my own family sometimes, it's 
a thing of like, even if they are progressive, even if they do feel like 
they have a lot of the same political ideas as me…they will still 
always have that like bias in their heads about being British or Irish, 
and about the other community…’. 
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Re-alignment, even if just 
when narrativising as an Alliance activist 
 
Positioning is ‘the ways that speakers/signers/writers orient 
themselves toward a community and reflect their degree of 
involvement in it’ (Zengilowski et al., 2023, p. 2). Use of ‘we’ implies 
positioning, belonging to, a sense of groupness. Now, sometimes 
activist’s ‘re-alignment’ with the background they distance from 
could be ‘unintentional’. For instance, within interviews using the 
‘we’ pronoun, activists sometimes ‘re-group’ themselves with their 
former traditional communities showing a subliminal sense of 
belonging. For instance, one activist (7) even catches their choice 
of words - referring to Protestants as a separate group to 
themselves but pauses at one point to reflect on whether they 

 
93
should be using the plural pronoun – ‘the Protestants because they 
believe, they, we believe…’. However, on the flipside, sometimes 
activists – unintentionally – ‘distance too much from’ the traditional 
communities in NI through their use of language (e.g. unionists are 
a completely other group to themselves). Specifically, Alliance (and 
GPNI) activists often refer to ‘the’ unionists or ‘the’ nationalists, 
othering these two groups from Alliance or themselves and making 
it that ‘unionists’ or ‘nationalists’ are akin to a homogenous group 
(e.g. not making the distinction between political unionism, or hard 
versus soft unionists, etc). However, this could have been for 
brevity purposes (e.g. they could not just list each form of unionism) 
rather than an indication that they see unionists as all the same. 
Also, when given the space to reflect, one activist (13) clarified that 
they know that unionism exists on a spectrum, or there are different 
strengths of association to nationalist background. However, the 
activists illustrate the potential, at least when expressing a view on 
identities they consider to be ‘extremes’ – activists can realign and 
distance completely with their own, or the broader communities of 
Northern Ireland. This can follow from an increased understanding 
of the ‘other community.’ For example, activist (36) coming from a 
Protestant Unionist Loyalist (PUL) background originally has 
shifted towards support for a UI through an increased awareness 
of nationalist history and experiences over time and a realisation 
that they did not understand nationalist ‘hurt’. It is notable though 
that this activist still articulates that they do not fully understand 
nationalism even now and still sees themselves as ‘middle of the 
road’ despite moving towards a firmer position in support of a UI. 
However, most activists live in the ‘in-between’ or, indeed the ‘less-
aligned. They generally have distanced from strict adherence to 
either their unionist or nationalist background, but may still identify 
as British and Irish or Northern Irish, but this is to varying degrees 
across the group.  
 

 
94
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Transitioning to ‘less-
aligned’ in Alliance 
 
Of course, the ‘transition’ to less-aligned has not been the 
same for all activists. Another potential form of identity change is 
not necessarily a change in identity, but a change in 
‘comfortableness’ with a sense of self as being non-aligned. For 
example, one activist (10) guesses that maybe when they were 
younger they did not feel so confident in their identity as ‘not’ being 
very strongly unionist (not a complete change to nationalist as 
never was or would be) – ‘… but I think as I've matured and…Being 
a more active Alliance member, I do see that...that is the mature 
position, that we need to be much more practical’. For this activist 
it appears they were always ‘less-aligned’ but became comfortable 
with this overtime. For another activist (20) it is less clear whether 
they started out as not ‘less-aligned’ and became comfortably so 
gradually. Specifically, it is less clear whether their feeling of being 
uncomfortable with being seen as Northern Irish prevented them 
from getting an Irish passport or their specific job role (and Brexit) 
was the driver behind why they did not initially, but they do explain 
that they ‘were of a time when to be…Northern Irish was an 
embarrassment in England, but now I no longer have a difficulty in 
having both passports’. At least, there may be an element of feeling 
more comfortable with being ‘less-aligned’ than previously.  
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Who cares! - Lacking 
emotional attachment to country or identity in Alliance 
 
Although Alliance activists are often ‘less-aligned’ they do 
not necessarily view holding dual passports as a uniquely Alliance 
‘thing’. This is also reflected broadly in the increase in NI people 
applying for their Irish passports since Brexit. One activist (24) 
explains they have friends who are to some degree even ‘anti-Irish’ 
that have both passports and use them for practical reasons. 

 
95
However, often the same activists who admit they use either 
passport to skip long custom queues also admit that they don’t 
have a very strong emotional feeling either way – ‘…there is not a 
big emotional attachment either way to UK, Ireland’ (e.g. 9). This 
lack of emotional attachment and apparent lack of care for personal 
identity is unlikely from the ‘anti-Irish’ friends of the activist. Notably, 
it sometimes was unclear whether individual activists identified as 
‘neither’ British and Irish or ‘both’ British and Irish’ as they would 
switch up their self-identification as the interview progressed. 
However, this in itself shows a lack of ‘care’ about their identity 
labels: they put such little weight on their self-defined labels, that 
they are happy to define themselves as ‘all of the above, and none’ 
even in the same interview (British, Irish, Northern Irish, both, none 
etc). It is a stretch to argue that that even Alliance activists do not 
care ‘at all’ about identity issues given Alliance does not operate in 
complete binaries. There is no expectation that one should be 
100% in favour of the Union Flag or Tricolour being the national 
flag nor is there an expectation that activists should be 100% 
against all national symbols. 
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Where are the unionists in 
Alliance? 
 
The activists reveal the reality of how Alliance allows 
openness and cross-culture and community approaches and this 
variety attracts activists. It is potentially the case that this pull is 
greater for those from a unionist background. However, there is 
nothing specific about the nature of Alliance as a supposed home 
for ‘very soft unionists’ that attracts these activists in particular. 
Instead, they explicitly are drawn to Alliance for the cross-
communal and openness values it espouses. Even with the degree 
of ‘distancing’ amongst Alliance activists from their traditional 
background, Alliance remains a home for those ‘from a unionist 
background’, but critically, nobody is using ‘unionist’ as their label 

 
96
(which again shows the difference between background and 
identity). Even one activist (7) who fitted closely to the unionist bloc, 
still did not fit into the ‘typical’ unionist bracket given they ‘don't 
understand the unionists drive for the union above all else’. In this 
way, it is best to understand reduced alignment for those from a 
unionist background in Alliance as a rejection of what they perceive 
as the obsession over identities and the potency attached by others 
to these identities rather than a rejection of the identities per se. 
For some activists (1, 11) they identify that they are able to escape 
their cultural biases to a ‘greater degree’ than some of those in their 
family, but they are still not immune to bias or the potential to be 
influenced in terms of vote choice. Given the extent of socialisation 
into these ties in NI, complete rejection of one’s identity is highly 
unlikely but this type of reduced alignment and embrace of a 
distinct set of values instead is a much more sustainable and 
acceptable dynamic for many activists.  
 
 Of course, if activists were ‘typical’ unionists then a unionist 
party would likely have been a better fit for them than Alliance, but 
this is not the affiliation or set of preferences they hold. Of course, 
it is not that many activists called themselves a ‘nationalist’ either. 
Ultimately rather than a ‘soft unionism’ they explicitly admire 
Alliance because of its cross-culture, ideals and faiths. Externally, 
as the previous chapter explains, Alliance as a ‘party’ battles 
images that it is a small ‘u’ unionist party externally. However 
internally, the evidence from activists challenges this image by 
providing a view from the ‘people-level’ where backgrounds in 
unionism over nationalism do not stand out and the core role is 
played by commitment and attraction to Alliance values.  
 
 
 
 

 
97
Declining Britishness – A new trend amongst Alliance 
activists? 
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Did Brexit get rid of the 
‘British’ Alliance activists? 
 
Although there is a general ‘less alignment’ among Alliance 
activists, in terms of national identity, they appear ‘less’ aligned to 
their British identity in particular (i.e. there were not many ‘British-
only’ identifiers). Even as interviews progressed, some of those 
from another part of the UK illustrated they were not ‘strictly British’; 
that is, they were more English than British and would like an Irish 
passport even if they cannot get one (e.g. activist 7; again here 
assuming an Irish passport is an indication about identity which is 
not always the case) and/or they were English but they see 
themselves as Irish and Northern Irish in a way too since living in 
NI (activist 40). Despite Brexit unsettling the question of Northern 
Ireland’s place in the UK, it does not appear to exclusively explain 
this movement away from Britishness among Alliance. There is a 
wider perception and perhaps expectation that Brexit specifically 
changed the connotations of Britishness that drove Alliance 
members away from affiliating to this identity, but in the interview 
evidence here this is not the primary pattern that emerges. Brexit 
may provide partial context but changes in affiliation away from 
Britishness do not follow from Brexit as a ‘sudden shock’ 
specifically. Several activists appear to have distanced from their 
NI-coded Britishness because they don’t like how those in NI 
present Britishness, or its association to Westminster and ‘the 
English’, or some are just ‘more Irish’ than ‘less British’ (e.g. 
activists 24; 36; 40). Of course, there may be an ‘underlying Brexit 
current’ to these reasons – that is, they may not want to be 
associated with versions of English nationalism, because of how 
the UK government handled Brexit, although this connection is not 
often explicitly made by Alliance activists in the same way that it is 

 
98
by GPNI activists. However, beyond this sample, it cannot be 
overlooked 
that 
Alliance 
has 
more 
individuals 
from 
a 
Catholic/nationalist background than in the past, and the English 
imperialist interpretations of the Brexit agenda has been off-putting 
for some Alliance persons.  
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Nobody in Alliance wants 
to be seen as British? 
 
For most activists, the reasons given for distancing from 
‘British’ may not be so ‘new’ (i.e. driven by Brexit), but rather 
reflective of perceived national realities. Some activists question 
why they would go by British as this is not a label that Scottish or 
some English people always or often go by (e.g. activist 1) or 
conversely, certain activists said being British is for the ‘mainland’ 
(e.g. activist 26). Also, using situational fluidity theory to explain 
how LQBTQ+ people decide which label to use, Holmes and 
Ghaziani (2025) find certain LGBTQ+ persons select certain labels 
strategically to buffer against policing and other social conflict (e.g. 
respondents who identify with established terms, like gay, will use 
queer instead to hide the stigma they perceive as attached to those 
more traditional terms). This avoidance of ‘stigma’ might explain 
social identification as Irish by activists whereby activists might go 
by Irish to avoid being associated with the British and English 
labels in line with a situational constructivist logic to identity 
utilisation. Therefore, activists seem to, at least, recognise the 
negative associations of Britishness and Tonge et al (2024) 
reinforce how these associations exist in Alliance itself stating 
‘Alliance appears far less British than was once the case, and 
sometimes British identity can even provoke negativity’ (p. 265)  
although the source of the ‘negativity’ is up for debate based on 
this sample. For instance, activists (9; 15) say depending on where 
they are, they would say they are British or Irish ‘…and most likely 
Irish and a lot of that is usually due to connotations of how people 

 
99
view British people outside of the UK’ (activist 9). It appears to be 
the case that Alliance and the centre-ground generally may have 
embraced the principles of the GFA agreement and the capacity to 
select into British or Irish or both identities situationally more than 
others in NI.  
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Source of declining 
Britishness – Just don’t want to be seen as a unionist? 
 
For Alliance activists, there is a sense that the meaning of 
Britishness can be differentially interpreted and reinterpreted to 
align more closely with the signifiers and values they seek to 
affiliate to. This is distinct from unionist identity which is considered 
by activists to be more fixed and as such likely to generate clearer 
negative reactions and dis-affiliation. This may stem from the 
understanding that important features of British identity have 
themselves changed but that unionist identity has been slow to 
reflect this. Modern approaches to an understanding of the role of 
the monarchy in British society, the impact of secularity on British 
Protestantism and the reality of different racial and faith-based 
communities, have marginalised the importance of monarchism 
and the Protestant religion on the mainland but these persist at the 
core of unionist identities (at least from the perspective of Alliance 
activists who consider themselves more liberal and open in their 
values) in NI (Southern, 2007, p. 74). While the ‘…British identity 
can even provoke negativity’ (Tonge et al., 2024, p. 265) it appears 
certain activists were more explicit in separating Britishness and 
unionism either in meaning or political self, or a Northern Irish 
version of British often resulting in their less ‘negative’ view of what 
Britishness is. For example, it may be that they rather associate 
themselves, or similarly to these patterns among Alliance activists, 
,as one GPNI activist (14) does, also associate their political sense 
of Britishness to England over unionism. In this case they rather 
pick England over NI’s version of Britishness despite coming from 

 
100
a unionist background. This GPNI activist’s (14) British identity is 
‘more attached to politics in England versus the politics of the 
unionists in Northern Ireland’.  
 
However, a lack of comfort with how Britishness is displayed 
in Northern Ireland is not necessarily enough to push others away 
from their personal ‘Britishness.’ For example, one activist (24) who 
identifies as Northern Irish says if they had to pick British or Irish, 
they would probably go with British but also thinks ‘the British in 
Northern Ireland are more British than the British’, that is, ‘there are 
more flags in the Shankill Road then there are in England probably 
during the 12th.’ For this activist, there is a sense that British-
leaning, unionist-coded individuals are ‘overcompensating’. 
Ultimately though, the activist would say they are Northern Irish as 
for them British identity is more associated with conservative 
values and Irishness is associated with violence. 
 
Clearly not all Alliance activists have dropped their 
‘Britishness’, but there is a ‘lessening alignment’ especially if the 
activist makes a direct link between being unionist and British in NI. 
Although, it might be the case that a negative association with 
unionism can also impact on ‘Irishness’ – albeit this link was less 
discussed among activists. For example, one Alliance activist (13) 
who does not now feel tied to a British or Irish identity said 
throughout their young adulthood they swung between how they 
would identify when they were at university with the Irish identity, 
even though they come from a unionist background. Although, it 
was not apparent whether this activist’s understanding of unionism 
is different now compared to how it was then as they explained 
their identification as Irish was more a rejection of what they had 
seen as a unionism that did not represent them, such as at the 
time, some sections of unionism were saying homophobic things. 
While Todd et al.’s (2006) key argument is that identities move not 
only over time but in context, someone's class or gender identity 

 
101
may come to the fore over their loyalist identity (and so we should 
never assume absolute binaries, either in analysis or in designing 
institutions), this activist reveals how identity can change in terms 
of its meaning. If the activist’s (13) understanding of unionism has 
changed, so might their understanding of their Irishness, but this 
was left open in the interview. Although again, it is difficult to 
compare whether it impacted their Britishness as being British was 
never part of their family experience despite being unionist, which 
shows how even coming from a unionist ‘background’ and being or 
feeling British do not always go hand in hand for many activists. 
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Sense of belonging for 
Alliance activists 
 
It was already clarified that an activist’s background and 
identity often do not align (e.g. they come from a unionist 
background, but no longer identify as such). However, if the feeling 
of belonging is linked to self-identification, another potential reason 
that Alliance activists appear ‘less British’ is because more have 
grown more comfortable crossing the border. Again, there might be 
‘underlying’ Brexit reasons for any ‘new-found’ comfortableness. 
For example, they can see Ireland is evolving, while the UK having 
left the EU is becoming less progressive (this would be a 
perception as talked about in the next chapter). For example, as 
one activist (21) asks ‘At the end of the day, what actually is it to be 
Irish? Like, as Ireland as an island becomes more diverse, it is no 
longer just, "Oh, you're a Catholic who farms or a Catholic who 
works in Dublin’. Irishness in the minds of activists is an 
increasingly fluid and interpretable concept with potential 
consequences for constitutional thinking. In terms of preferences 
potentially following from a sense of Irishness, how an Alliance 
activist might define Irish means even those not born in ROI/NI can 
define Irish in a way that allows them to identify with Irishness 
without tying this to a preference for a UI. For one activist (17) who 

 
102
was born in another part of the UK, but with Irish parents, they 
would see themselves as Irish because of how they define Irish 
which includes the diaspora. 
 
Alliance activists clearly retain identity affiliations but also 
recognise broadly how the meaning of identities are changing. 
Depending on the nature and scope of this change, this generates 
a greater or lesser pull or push towards these affiliations based on 
how these align (or not) with their core Alliance values. However 
for most activists in their perception of the ROI (or ‘the South’) is 
wrapped up in a nostalgia from their travels there, or they seemed 
to derive a more relaxed vibe from life and the Southern people 
(e.g. activists 11; 2; 1). This attraction to the South and Irish identity 
is not therefore necessarily ‘new-found’. For example, in one 
activist’s (1) assessment, Southern life was where their family 
holidayed, so it has always got this ‘sunny kind of glow’ to it 
whenever they go down. This pull to the South is then rooted for 
these activists less in a sense of recent change, but in a sense of 
nostalgia or warm personal feelings. On the other hand, this 
suggestion that they feel ‘less British’ because they are more 
comfortable in the South is not wholly convincing especially as it is 
not entirely consistent. Specifically, one activist (9) who feels ‘…like 
I'm in a foreign country when I'm in Dublin, and that just sort of is 
innate to me..’ actually, feels more Irish than British in their dual 
identity. This contrasts with another activist (24) who would be 
more British than Irish if they had to pick, but when they go to 
Dublin or down South, to them it is a different country, it is just they 
have always been brought up that way with a British community 
background. In this sense, these feelings are less about identity 
than they are about personal sense of belonging. There is a 
continuous ‘disconnect’ in which that feeling of belonging is not 
associated with strength of national identification but this does not 
always match with regional affinities. These two activists feel better 
in Britain over Ireland, but do not feel a need to be in Britain. They 

 
103
would not necessarily vote for the Union in a referendum and one 
of them is ‘maybe 51% of the way towards voting for a UI’ (but could 
‘easily’ swing back). Both of these activists (24; 9) feel like the ROI 
is foreign to them, but one is more British than Irish, and the other 
more Irish than British, and one is undecided on the CQ, while the 
other is currently more swayed by a UI. In this sense, there is not 
a straightforward and linear association demonstrated between 
national identity, regional affiliations and constitutional voting 
preferences, again demonstrative of the fluidity of these feelings 
within the centre-ground. 
 
The declining Britishness within Alliance could also stem 
more from use of the Northern Irish label, rather than either British 
or Irish. Even for those who were Northern Irish first, very rarely did 
any activist express their Northern Irish identity as a subcategory 
beneath a British superordinate identity (like those in Unionist 
parties tend to in McNicholl et al, 2019). Of course, this might reflect 
the general declining sense of Britishness. Interestingly, one 
activist (1) who now chooses to (partially) go by Northern Irish does 
so as they no longer define Northern Irish through a British lens – 
‘So, I see Northern Irish becoming more inclusive that middle-
ground other…before, it would have been very much, in my head, 
associated with band marching, the 12th…’.  
 
Being Irish in Alliance – sovereignty, geography or even 
situation? 
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Alliance activists are not 
less British, but more Irish? 
 
Similar to the previous explanation that the declining 
Britishness within Alliance could also stem from increased 
identification with the Northern Irish label, potentially it could be that 
Alliance is attracting more Irish-only, or Northern Irish-Irish or those 

 
104
whose Irishness is stronger as part of dual identities. Rather than 
becoming ‘less British’ Alliance could be becoming ‘more Irish.’ It 
is not that they want to avoid negative associations of Britishness 
but instead they may go by Irish more than British, given their family 
were mainly from this background or they were brought up this way. 
Also, for those who are neither totally Irish nor British, some still 
are more ‘not British’ than ‘not Irish’ such as activist (4) who said 
they do not feel themselves to be ‘100% Irish’ but they most 
‘certainly’ do not feel British. There appears to be more explicit 
attachment to ‘Irishness’ amongst the Alliance activists, even if 
they do not really see themselves as either. However, being ‘more 
Irish’ does not equate to being more ‘nationalist’ – an important 
distinction, as one activist (1) notes they are not ‘Irish enough’ to 
be Irish nationalist. These testimonies indicate that there is 
persistence and utilisation of binaries for the ‘non-aligned’ or ‘less-
aligned’ in the sense that binaries can be a means of determining 
what you are not and creating a sense of distance from particular 
identities even if fluidity is retained in determining the positive 
sense of identity in terms of what you are.  
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Alliance activists are still 
Irish in the UK or in a united Ireland 
 
Identity is a personal construct for many Alliance activists. 
Speaking on British identity, two activists (38; 26) see it as a 
personal choice; that is, you can identify whatever way you choose. 
They declare some variation of, if you want to be British be British 
or if people want to identify with any particular identity, they can 
choose to do so (activists 26; 38). In this way, for certain activists 
the individual experience of identity and its alignment with their 
sense of self is key. This is distinct from the use of identities as 
broader social labels which can have more negative social 
consequences than the individual-level utility of a clarity of self-
understanding and self-conceptualisation can provide. Given this 

 
105
breadth of pernicious effects, some have worried that centring 
social identities inevitably entrenches and amplifies oppression 
(Brown 1995, cited in Ritchie, 2021). Others contend we would be 
better off eliminating social labels altogether (e.g. Dembroff and 
Wodak 2018, 2021). Therefore, relaying a core difference between 
being in Sinn Féin or the SDLP and being in Alliance, several Irish-
only (or Irish-Northern Irish) activists are not pushing for a united 
Ireland to reinforce their sense of being Irish. Notably, activist (15) 
supposes a united Ireland might give them a little bit more of a 
feeling of being whole in being Irish in Ireland, but ultimately it took 
the activist a long time in the interview to offer this reflection, and 
for the most part they were very firm in their belief that they are 
very happy to be Irish in NI ‘without’ a UI. Awarding themselves the 
freedom to construct their identity also means activists can 
‘distance’ from how they were brought up, even though the 
previous activist came from a Protestant background and they 
know it was a strange move to decide they would go by Irish at the 
time they chose to.  
 
Ultimately, the majority of activists asked think Irish 
identifiers and nationalists are already well accommodated in NI 
currently, which could explain why some are happy enough to be 
Irish without a united Ireland. Paul Bew (1998) argued that the GFA 
was a victory for unionism, as it offered Irish identifying people 
enough inside the UK to not want a UI in any urgent way. This may 
also apply to Alliance activists who are undecided as it reduces this 
sense of urgency. There is also a key role for local experiences in 
this process in which Irishness serves as an everyday reality for 
people and conditions their existence, but this does not operate as 
a strong national identity or as ‘Irishness’ in the sense of 
constitutional preference. One activist (21) recognises others might 
feel differently, but they feel welcomed in their own sense of 
Irishness, but this will mean different things to the sense of 
Irishness held by others (this could be conditioned by the fact they 

 
106
are from a nationalist area). They observe things that connect 
people across this island in which people who might not identify as 
Irish but still are in some part connected due to Irish history and 
genealogy. They went on to explain that they do not feel there is 
anything that they could not do now in NI that they would be able 
to do in a UI. Another activist (1) feels similarly accommodated 
saying ‘apart…a couple of policies, I think people are included in, 
in day-to-day life, whether they're Irish or Northern Irish anyway. 
And I suppose I can say that because I see predominantly a 
nationalist, republican area…the small minority of unionism here. 
So, it's kind of, it's built in their culture here.’  
 
There are also influences of structural and institutional 
conditions. Another activist thinks this is because the GFA awarded 
Irish people the right to be Irish in NI, the relevance of the border 
was diminished, and the ‘whiff of cordite’ potentially associated with 
this ‘part’ of their identity was reduced. It may be that these 
conditions particularly facilitate Irish identifiers as this was the 
identity with the more challenging connotations during the 
Troubles. Activists brought up on a variety of occasions how British 
identifiers in NI are no longer feeling accommodated, which may 
be due to a perception that these British identifiers now feel they 
are on the defensive as this dynamic of identity connotations has 
been reversed in the post-GFA era. Again, at the structural level, 
another activist (5) suggests that gradual historical changes, like 
actions to promote equality for Catholics has allowed Irish people 
to become better accommodated in NI. 
 
In terms of accommodating Irish identifiers, what came 
through surprisingly given Alliance as a party was vocally 
supportive of the Irish Language Act (‘ILA’) being established as 
set out in the New Decade, New Approach (‘NDNA’) deal in 2020, 
was the ILA itself did not seem to be or at least was not evaluated 
as a major source of accommodation. Specifically, it reflects a 

 
107
feeling from some Alliance activists (e.g. 4; 5) that the ILA is not 
such a revolutionary piece of legislation that is going to change the 
landscape of Irish learning as it is sometimes portrayed. The 
legislation may be seen as a relatively minimal change and 
essentially a basic expectation and change opposed only by 
hardline unionists. This is potentially also a product of increased 
confidence among Irish identifiers in itself reflected in the broader 
patterns discussed above. 
 
Conceptual 
marker: 
Less-aligned 
- 
Alliance 
activists’ 
Irishness is not based on symbolism or sovereignty 
 
Although Alliance activists tend to lack emotional 
attachments to either identity, for those who primarily identify as 
Irish, their identity is still not built on emotional symbols of Irishness. 
For example, they do not really care for the tricolour specifically 
(38; 26). Even if they feel some pride in being ‘Irish’, they do not 
need to reinforce their Irishness by ‘flag-waving’. For example, one 
Irish Alliance activist (5) seems to advocate for minimising all 
symbolic displays of patriotism, including in a UI, even if they admit 
their own feelings of patriotism in the interview. Of interest here are 
the inclusive and exclusive roles symbols can play in the formation 
and maintenance of group identity. As Armstrong notes, symbols 
can act as ‘traffic lights’ signalling boundaries to in-group and out-
group members (1982: p.7), but this is not the core of identity as 
interviewees emphasise it. Often Alliance activists promote almost 
a ‘civic’ version of Irish identity which is not defined by sovereignty 
(or national symbols), but ‘geography’. That is, they are born in 
Ireland, so they call themselves Irish albeit there is variation here 
in the emphasis they place on the island of Ireland versus Northern 
Ireland as a region within that.  
 
Whether activists define ‘geography’ by Northern Ireland or 
Ireland could have greater repercussions should a UI happen and 

 
108
it may make less sense to identify as Northern Irish if the entity no 
longer continues. However, given activists are open to constructing 
their identity independent of constitutional status, they may be 
relatively open to transitioning their identity as such change would 
require. One Northern Irish activist (11) suggests this is a possibility 
as they can see themselves being happy enough to call themself 
Irish under a UI. This activist expresses that Northern Irish and Irish 
culture (flags, symbols) in general tend to be quite similar which 
means it would not be a big ‘culture shock’ for them personally for 
things like flags to be changed - ‘I can see myself…like if it did 
happen being…we're part of Ireland…yeah, I'm happy enough to 
call myself Irish. But like I don't really see myself attached too much 
to either sides symbols or flags or cultures, if you know what I 
mean. Like Northern Irish and Irish culture in general tends to be 
quite similar, and it's not like it would be a massive culture shock 
for me personally…for that to be a change. I don't think flags play, 
or symbols play a big part in my life’. However, those activists (of 
which there are very few) who do see Northern Ireland and Irish 
culture as more distinct or care more about the symbolic elements 
may not be as open to ‘giving up’ their Northern Irish label. Many 
activists acknowledge a certain degree of overlap between Irish 
and Northern Irish cultures both for straightforward components 
such as ancestry (e.g. 40; 15), but they also recognise that 
Northern Irish people have had a different life and special bond 
than a person from Dublin and London. Given many activists 
recognise a difference between Irish and Northern Irish identities, 
even culturally there is a striking and somewhat counterintuitive 
pattern in which activists express certain offence when people from 
the ROI do not see their Irishness as the same as Northern 
Ireland’s Irishness (e.g. activist 21).  
 
Resonating with national symbols where this does occur 
does not itself secure an activist’s reverence to nationality. For 
example, an Alliance activist (4) who felt the Union flag 

 
109
‘represented something’ for them, did not feel close to their British 
identity and tended to frame this as a somewhat reluctant 
attachment to express. However, the symbols did not resonate to 
a sufficient extent for the activist (4) to determine their 
constitutional preference given they have no issue at all if someone 
said that the Union Flag is going under a UI, as long as what is 
replacing it is something they have ‘bought into’. This speaks to an 
openness to a change in symbols (which many activists would be 
fine with, even those who are Irish), but a rejection of the idea of NI 
just being ‘consumed’ into the Republic as it already is under a UI, 
where NI becomes just another part of the ROI and its history, 
culture and uniqueness is ‘replaced’ with what already exists in the 
ROI. Such a rejection would reflect the preference of many Alliance 
activists more broadly even those who may identify as (partially) 
Irish (e.g. activist 14).  
 
Conceptual 
marker: 
Less-aligned 
- 
Alliance 
activists’ 
Irishness is not based on symbolism or sovereignty, but is 
‘situational’  
 
Again, drawing on situational fluidity theory to explain how 
LQBTQ+ people decide which label to use, Holmes and Ghaziani 
(2025) illustrated people refrained from using labels that they 
anticipated were unfamiliar or potentially confusing (e.g. calling 
themselves gay rather than queer) – their decision operated as a 
so-called ‘cultural anchor’. This may similarly explain why some 
Alliance activists would go by ‘Northern Irish’ when in Northern 
Ireland, but ‘Irish’ when away as it is easier than trying to explain 
to outsiders the complexities around the Northern Irish and Irish 
identities. For example, one activist (21) who primarily identifies as 
Northern Irish says if they were on a foreign holiday they would say 
‘I’m Irish’ as opposed to getting into the ‘political hotbeds’ of 
Northern Irish identity. As another example, if someone asked them 
what their nationality is, one Northern Irish activist (2) says when 

 
110
on holidays they would identify as Irish because people don't 
understand the localisms. The activist (2) says ‘…if someone 
asked me what my nationality is…that's the thing when you're on 
holidays, I would identify as Irish because people don't understand 
the quirks that we have locally, but I would just identify as being 
Northern Irish.’ 
 
Although identity is a self-construct for many activists, these 
particular activists showcase how outsiders and scenarios can 
somewhat influence this self-construction (at least temporarily 
when abroad). Although some are happy to employ their Irish 
passport for practical reasons to skip airport queues, this still 
seems like more of a personally beneficial choice rather than a 
fundamental change to identity affiliation. Many recognise a 
difference between being Irish in the ROI and in NI (or British in NI 
and GB), even if they are both views as valid and equal forms of 
being Irish. However, by going by Irish when abroad for ease of 
communication, it appears Alliance activists can feed into a 
perception that being Irish in NI means the same as being Irish in 
ROI, given the likelihood is these outsiders would associate being 
Irish with the Republic. For instance, one activist (21) told a story 
about how they spoke to a group from the ROI before and got this 
sense from them that they were not seen as the same kind of Irish, 
and it is the same in London, or GB, in that they feel distinct from 
those others around them. In this way, activists relate how the 
experience of being Irish or British in Northern Ireland is not 
automatically the same as Irish and British in the ROI or UK 
respectively and as such, any sense of Irishness is always likely to 
be partial and situational for those from NI. This remains a concern 
for such individuals in thinking about how they will fit into a UI 
personally but of course also points to the limitations of the status 
quo.  
 
 

 
111
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - More permanent – not 
based on situation and switch back, not based purely on 
geography 
 
Excluding those activists who are only Irish now in Northern 
Ireland, some Alliance activists will be open to a ‘new national 
identity’ under a united Ireland which ‘transcends the boundaries’ 
of being Irish, British and Northern Irish. This might particularly be 
the case for Alliance activists because this grouping tends to be 
open to the potential for meanings of identity to change as the 
socio-political context itself changes. This idea of a ‘new national 
identity’ under a UI was prompted by a particular activist (24) who 
envisions potentially aligning themselves with a new identity that is 
not quite Irish, not British, but also not Northern Irish under a UI. 
The activist expresses that being Northern Irish in a New Ireland 
would not really make sense, but nor do they think they would feel 
comfortable saying they are Irish but they could get on board with 
a ‘New Irish’ identity because they do not associate themselves 
with the ROI nor do they associate themselves with being British in 
full either (although British would be the identity they would feel 
closer to).  
 
It should be noted that, Alliance activists are not naive to how 
Irishness under a UI could become contentious, as there would be 
the potential that division is created between the ‘original’ Irish and 
those coming from NI (or maybe even this grouping that may be 
known by activist 24’s term ‘New Irish’). For example, activists 
expressed the idea that were was a potential danger that there 
would be a ‘real Irish’ (i.e. those form the current ROI) and then 
‘Northern Irish’ (from the current NI) and the latter would not be 
discriminated against as such but would be considered different 
and treated with a degree of weariness, distrust, suspicion (e.g. 

 
112
activist 18)63. For the centre-ground, the question of whether an 
equitable ‘permanent’ Irishness in the context of a future UI or 
alternative NI arrangement could be constructed in a way that 
embraces those from the current ROI and NI respectively remains 
open, and there are varied ideas about the extent to which this is 
achievable and which constitutional arrangements would be 
necessary or sufficient to facilitate it. Notably, many Alliance (and 
GPNI) activists to varying degrees identify as Northern Irish 
illustrating that this identity is not strongly associated with any 
particular constitutional preference. 
 
Conceptual marker: Less-aligned - Being Irish not based on 
being Irish 
 
With the rise in Irish passport applications in NI, and 
although Brexit is not clearly the reason for the declining 
Britishness of Alliance based on the declared views of the activists, 
potentially some in Alliance are becoming more Irish-focused. This 
is not because they necessarily identify as Irish culturally, but 
because post-Brexit that is now more strongly linked to their 
European identity, and their policy preferences on EU membership 
with Europeanness. In addition, for those who constitute a party 
based on lesser alignment/non-alignment in a divided society, an 
alternative encompassing identity such as Europeanness as a 
guide could be useful to provide a clearer cohesive tie and 
Irishness in a post-Brexit era may provide a pathway to this 
European identity. European identity is also now linked to 
economic issues, given the post-Brexit impacts on the UK 
economy, and liberal values have increasingly become associated 
with support for Europe compared to Britain where liberal values

elements is the extent to which Alliance activists’ sense of 
European-ness is overwhelming enough to push them to identify 
more with their Irishness, as the ROI is more ‘in’ the EU than the 
UK – do they connect in their heads being European and Irish, even 
within the context of Brexit? This could mean that if European 
identity is strongly drawn upon by Alliance activists and those they 
represent in the context of a border poll that would likely render the 
referendum a referendum on membership of the EU and generate 
strong Alliance support for a UI. However, the pattern that emerges 
here is that European identity does exist, but it is typically not 
particularly salient and is instead more situationally relevant or a 
‘nested identity’. The nested identities model (Brandtken, 2022; 
Beswick, 2020, pp. 26-27) suggests that different identities are 

 
115
layered where one belongs to a smaller, more local community 
which is in turn nested within a larger identity, and this ties here to 
constructivist conceptions of identity where individuals holding 
multiple identities mobilise distinct identities to greater or lesser 
degrees in different social contexts. European identity even with 
the heightened salience of Brexit does not appear to be the central 
driver and generator of cohesion we may think albeit it does have 
a role to play for Alliance activists. In this way European-ness is 
nested within larger identities, and it seems unlikely that this 
European identity will be sufficiently salient and ‘activated’ to shape 
voting patterns in a referendum given the other identities likely to 
exert greater effects in this context. 
Conceptual 
Marker 
– 
Constitutional 
Neutrality 
and 
Constitutional preference at the ‘people-level’ 
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - Figuring out 
what is ‘undecided’ 
 
This chapter has already discussed how national identity, 
communal identity, background and feeling of belonging are not 
always aligned as traditionally assumed. This thesis now moves 
beyond identity alignment specifically to consider how the centre-
ground exemplified by those who constitute it understand and 
conceive of constitutional neutrality as a key conceptual marker of 
Alliance as a party of the centre-ground.  
 
First when thinking about constitutional neutrality, a 
distinction must be made between those who are ‘firmly’ undecided 
and those who are ‘less steadily’ undecided. Some are ‘less 
steadily undecided’ given they had very specific conditions that 
shape their attitudes in which they seek information and context in 
order to ‘firm up’ a preference. These include the timing of when 
the referendum is called, the potential for a hybrid model other than 
rule from Dublin on offer, and the desire for the decision to be made 

 
116
in a context back first to the context pre-Brexit. In the latter case, 
that would mean they would not vote for a UI or would be 
encouraged against voting for it tomorrow (4; 20). On timing, 
activist (4) would not vote for a UI in five years but thinks NI might 
be ready in 10-15 years but only five more years makes a 
significant difference. Here, factors ‘external to the result itself’ like 
the timing or type of UI (which is not specified in the GFA) are 
determinants. Some activists are more fluid in their preferences. 
Activist (9) who comes from a Protestant (albeit not strongly 
unionist) background, may be 51% of the way towards voting for a 
UI, but that could ‘easily swing back’ (so they are torn in the 
middle). Even at one point in the interview, this activist who is 
‘currently’ more pro-UI refers to themselves as part of a group of 
‘those of us who would be wanting to keep the status quo’ which 
showcases just how swiftly some activists’ constitutional 
preference (CP) can float between pro-UI and pro-Union when 
expressing their perspectives on the possibility of constitutional 
change. It appears that these ‘less steadily undecided’ do not have 
the same long-term attachment to their constitutional preference 
compared to the activists who would firmly be considered ‘decided’ 
(talked about in the next section).  
 
A key question that recurs here is whether those who are 
undecided favour the status quo or does this only come into play 
when making an active voting decision between the status quo and 
a UI. Some activists can complicate this further, appearing to be 
happy with a UI result, but also wanting a complete consideration 
of how NI works in the UK. For example, activist (7) is not pro-union 
straightforwardly but would like a version of direct rule in NI or a 
model comparable to NI being treated like Alaska. In this sense the 
goal is to get rid of Stormont rather than to ‘choose’ a UI. 
Fundamentally as with the Greens (albeit expressed differently), 
there is a key role for the options on offer in determining Alliance 
activists’ positions and preferences rather than ‘neutrality’ in an 

 
117
unconditional fashion. Activists seek additional context on the 
nature of a potential UI, the nature of a vote for the Union (which 
does not assume the current status quo) and the timing and 
process of any poll or transition. This is a more complex and 
conditional form of neutrality and so constitutes a challenge for the 
party to resolve given the variety of positions among its activists. 
This key marker of ‘neutrality’ is further complicated as it is highly 
conditional on these options being revealed.  
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - Figuring out 
who is undecided in Alliance 
 
The 2014 media storm and backlash towards the late Anna 
Lo MLA of Alliance publicly sharing her personal pro-unity 
preferences showcases that it might be fine to ‘hold’ a 
constitutional preference in Alliance, but publicly expressing said 
preference is something different. This might explain why activists 
who shared a strict preference were typically at a more grassroots 
level within the party as it might be easier for these less prominent 
activists to share their personal preference without the fear of 
implicating how the party is seen. However, this is not to say those 
who said they were undecided in the interview were being 
untruthful, or those who did not share a preference at all in the 
interview were undecided. The role of activists in shaping external 
perceptions of the party is seen very clearly in how they interact 
with the CQ. Potentially Alliance does have people with 
constitutional preferences that make it ‘less civic’ because the 
existence of these people suggests the party is not ignoring the 
constitutional question (as might be expected from a non-sectarian 
party) - ‘it is bit perhaps unfair for people to say that Alliance tries 
to ignore the constitutional issue as I am sure many supporters, 
members would be explicit in their views, it is just it is not the priority 
issue for them’ (activist 6). Some suggest that by attending panel 
discussions like Ireland’s Future (or even engaging with this thesis 

 
118
project), it can be seen as engaging in the discussion (e.g. activist 
22 emphasises it is because the party believes in dialogue) and 
hence is not deserving of assumptions that it ignores the CI.  Select 
activists explain that given Alliance is not so concerned about what 
constitutional status NI has and believe this means there is little 
reason to ask Alliance activists about it even, suggesting the 
interviewer should instead direct these questions to parties from 
the traditional blocs or ideological poles (e.g. activist 7). In many 
ways, this appears to reflect a concern with internal stability and 
external self-image. Although activists believe the discussion 
around the issue in the party would be civil (mentioned later), for a 
party that defines itself as neutral, it could damage the party’s 
external self-image if many in it were publicly seen to be sharing 
their constitutional preferences with each other. Interviewing the 
traditional bloc parties on these issues would present little 
challenge to those parties’ activists as their positions on this issue 
is the basis for their own internal cohesion. Instead for Alliance, 
even though there are clearly preferences within the party, there is 
a barrier for some in Alliance to express their opinions on the 
constitutional question or national issues, given they do not define 
themselves along the binary, but often in the middle and 
expressing these views can then challenge their own cohesion 
which is built on instead remaining neutral.  
 
While activists imply that there are those in Alliance’s ranks 
that are pro-UI, pro-Union and undecided, there is a question of 
how they come to this assumption given some also say they do not 
know how others in the party would vote (e.g. activist 13) or do not 
really focus on the constitutional question in the party and thus 
imply it does not come up as a topic (at least formally). Several 
activists return in this context to the party line that the party is not 
really talking about or focused on the CI or talking about taking a 
CP as it is dealing with other more pressing issues like the cost-of-
living crisis (e.g. activist 22). Assuming this is genuine, it is striking 

 
119
that there is more willingness to engage this issue (it appears) in 
the GPNI who are very issue-oriented. It again seems that 
neutrality and not compromising this internally is a particularly key 
value for Alliance. 
 
Of course, activists do often suggest that the party casually 
talks about the constitutional issue. For example, activist (13) said 
given it is not something that they talk about with others in Alliance 
to a significant degree, they could not point to people in the party 
and say what their constitutional preference is. Very few activists 
were very clear in quantifying precise positions of their colleagues, 
for example activist (24) said of anyone they have talked to, and 
they know quite a few in the party, only two would be open about 
what their position is, or maybe others are scared to say, or they 
just don’t know. Few activists express a preference openly 
including most grassroots activists but of the small number who do 
express a clear view, these were only at that grassroots level. This 
adherence to a form of strict neutrality appears to constitute, in its 
extreme form, a strategy of ‘don’t ask, don’t tell’. It is possible that 
if a high-level activist did share their preference, potentially lower-
level activists would feel a greater permission to express views 
themselves but currently the party is quite protective of its external 
image of neutrality. There is also a concern outsiders could come 
to confuse personal for party preference, as one activist (36) 
alludes to. Illustratively, they do not think Alliance should ignore the 
CP and should allow their members and MLAs a personal vote, 
and individual members and politicians should be able to express 
their preference, but they recognise ‘…that gives rise to difficulties 
if you've got very prominent Alliance people coming out one way or 
the other…’. Interestingly, there is little evidence from the 
interviews that activists believe there would be any (or large 
numbers) of non-voters in a referendum in Alliance and this again 
suggests many have or would come to a position, but can't express 
it or avoid having discussions to develop it. 

 
120
Alliance activists talked about how Alliance has dealt with 
big issues before and ultimately as above activists trust their party 
members to make a rational decision at the time of the party 
deciding to pick a position, but Alliance appears slower to embrace 
the debate and decision-making process on this issue than the 
Greens. Alliance in its behaviour over time (e.g. its initial reluctance 
to support the Hume-Adams talks where the GPNI insisted there 
was no time to lose) is defined by the need to slowly consider and 
come to a position given neutrality is a core value. This contrasts 
with the Greens coming to a position more quickly and decisively 
as, while they are also ‘neutral’, engaging with and positioning on 
issues is ultimately core to their self-image and self-understanding. 
Within Alliance, many activists reinforce that the party already has 
experience of discussing, debating and dealing with difficult issues 
civilly. For example, one activist (23) explains Alliance have had 
other issues where there has been a difference of views, but have 
held a respectful debate and discussion and ‘[we] have been able 
to land in a position and people then get in behind it; at the end of 
the day, [we’re] democrats as well’. Another activist (22) does not 
label the conversation in the party around taking a CP as a difficult 
conversation, as the party has had many difficult conversations 
throughout the peace processes, and while constitutional change 
is a huge issue, they would not necessarily say it would be difficult 
because the party has a broad spectrum of people who all get on 
and it would be a very civil conversation and evidence-led. As in 
Todd and McEvoy (2023) where some of the women’s group 
participants spoke of the risk of people getting upset or angry in 
discussions and the need for a supportive environment to help 
manage these feelings, Alliance feels it is well-placed to create this 
type of environment internally based on the previous discussion. 
Again, the activists believe the discussion in Alliance would be civil, 
but most think extensively discussing it now internally would 
distract the party from dealing with more pressing issues (e.g. the 
cost-of-living crisis) impacting the NI people. 

 
121
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - Being an 
Alliance ‘brand’ of decided 
 
Those with a firmer decided position are the exceptions 
within Alliance even if some have specific preferences about what 
should be involved. In particular, most do not want a border poll 
called now, they would prefer if their party remained neutral on the 
constitutional question currently, and they are not out cheerleading 
for their constitutional preference. Even though they were more 
firmly ‘decided’ they also still wanted to know the answers to 
practical or policy questions such as what healthcare will be like 
under a UI. There are still clear distinctions from those in aligned 
parties too. Unlike a typical SDLP or UUP activist, these activists 
are not entirely supportive of their party taking a collective party 
position, at least currently. Specifically, those pro-UI activists within 
Alliance are not calling for a referendum now. For example one 
activist (5) is strongly pro-UI but they still said they ‘cringe’ at 
certain calls for an immediate referendum. Some decided activists 
seem to have a little ‘shame’ about the sense of cheerleading for a 
UI outcome, for example, the same activist (36) said they are 
invested in change that is probably ‘stronger’ than simply that they 
‘want it’ but showed a desire to not be seen as succumbing to the 
jubilant aspect of national identity, given their non-nationalist 
background. This is potentially reflective of Alliance scepticism or 
as the Greens sometimes frame it a ‘snobbishness’ towards 
traditional identities.  
 
There are also those who frame the referendum as divisive 
as it constitutes ‘change’ where the status quo is not framed as 
such. This potentially has roots in a certain ‘soft unionist’ thinking 
classically associated with some in Alliance although this is 
sometimes distinct from their personal level of comfort with 
alternative outcomes. For example, a pro-union activist (40) saw a 
referendum as not a ‘positive thing’, albeit they may not be overly 

 
122
concerned about a UI result as they consider themselves an 
internationalist and do not hold one particular identity. 
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - De-coupling 
the political and the constitutional 
 
Most of the time what attracts the decided activists to 
Alliance is not very different to those who are undecided, as their 
pull to Alliance is based on admiration for the party’s qualities. They 
are attracted by its non-sectarianism and/or liberalism and/or 
cross-community dimensions (which is certainly the case for 
activists 40 and 5), or in some cases this can even be more tactical 
as in the case of activist (36) who reveals they only recently joined 
Alliance to contribute to its winning the previously solid unionist 
seat in their constituency. Activists often highlight what could be 
called the ‘party appeal-constitutional party position’ dynamic; that 
is, there is an apprehension about the party taking a constitutional 
position because the appeal of the party itself is precisely that it 
does not take a position and vice versa so the party not having a 
constitutional position is what makes the party appealing.  
 
Alliance in not engaging with the constitutional issue at 
large, may give activists ‘true freedom’ to shape their constitutional 
thinking without party influence. It appears that some decided 
activists ‘completely decouple’ their thinking around the CQ from 
their political thinking (i.e., supporting Alliance) or initially going into 
Alliance they already felt one way about the CQ and being in 
Alliance has not moved their position. For example, one Alliance 
activist who takes a pro-UI position (5) and another Alliance activist 
(40) who takes a pro-union position explained how being in Alliance 
does not majorly influence their thinking around a border poll. 
Explicitly, the activist (5) explains if a border poll were to be called 
within the next five years, the things that would influence them 
personally as an Alliance supporter if they were considering the 

 
123
issue without being an Alliance supporter would probably be the 
same. The other activist (40) recognises that Alliance supporters 
like any other political party supporter come with their own 
motivations that makes them support that party, so, they ‘are going 
to be unable to disentangle the fact that…’, for example, that they 
voted to Remain and/or are an internationalist, born in England. 
However, if Alliance decided to take a position it would change how 
close the activists feel to the party, rather than their constitutional 
thinking as it was formed prior to joining the party.  
 
There is an important subset of Alliance activists and the 
wider centre-ground they represent who do not have traditional 
aligned backgrounds for the specific reason that they were born, or 
have lived extensively, outside of NI which has particular 
consequences for their constitutional views. For example, one 
activist (4) has lived in many different countries so they feel 
comfortable pretty much anywhere, and as such the identity issue 
would not be important to them in a referendum. Another activist 
(27) also said they have lived abroad, in GB and lived and worked 
in other countries, so their traditional background will have no effect 
on them in a referendum. In turn, even though they might have lived 
in NI for a long time, some ‘non-Northern-Ireland-born’ activists 
situated themselves as somewhat separate from those from NI, 
with these activists coming from ‘beyond the binary’. For those with 
a ‘stake’ in NI’s future, even if you originally are not from there, 
does not always provide a sense of ‘entitlement’ to determine 
whether a UI happens or not. For example, while the previous non-
NI activist (40) has got a ‘stake’ in NI now and so they would hope 
to have a say in a referendum, this is not the same feeling held by 
another non-NI activist (12). This activist (12) expresses that 
despite how their child is born here and there is a ‘stake’ in their 
future, the activist does not think they personally have as much of 
a right to determine NI’s future as someone who has been brought 
up in NI and would have more affiliation. It appears that having a 

 
124
dedication to a party in NI (i.e. becoming an activist) and having a 
stake in the future on NI (or your child does) in itself does not mean 
activists always award themselves self-entitlement to determine 
the constitutional outcome. 
 
Constitutional Neutrality - Leaving it as a conscience vote – 
terms and conditions apply 
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - Activist’s 
uncertainty - Leaving is a conscience matter, at least currently 
 
Most activists were interviewed prior to leader Naomi Long 
MLA switching from stating that the party will ‘undoubtedly’ take a 
CP in the future to stressing that Alliance members may decide it 
is best not to pick a side. Given most Alliance activists hoped, or 
predicted, it would be left as a conscience vote, the Leader’s new 
perspective is catching up with the activists’ already existing 
preference. Although Alliance activists very rarely indicated what 
way they thought the party would go if it had to pick (especially 
compared to GPNI activists), Alliance has created a sense of 
uncertainty about which way it would move, if it had to, even among 
its own activists albeit there are rare exceptions where activists 
have a stronger view on what the party may do.  
 
Activists appear to believe that Alliance or its supporters 
would decide on the party’s CP, if it had to pick, not on emotional 
or tribal aspects, but on rational facts and on what is best for NI. It 
will not be a ‘willy-nilly’ decision - one activist (22) notes that the 
party is clear that it will consider all sides, the benefits or not of a 
UI, the downsides and upsides of the Union, and they say the time 
will come when that conversation will be had, but they do not think 
it will be any time soon. By taking a position based on pragmatic, 
evidence-based assessments (e.g., economic benefits) rather than 
emotional nationalism or unionism, their belief is that Alliance could 

 
125
lead the debate in a more moderate direction. That is, the activists 
have trust in the party to make the right choice.  
 
Alliance seeks to strategically position itself as making a 
clear-eyed rational decision as it is the ' issue owner' of neutrality 
and therefore it makes the case it is the 'owner' of decisions 
grounded in rationality. The reality is messier in that it is likely there 
are a variety of positions within the party and there is not true 'non-
alignment' but 'less alignment' for many activists. In the context of 
the scrutiny of a CP debate, those influences, backgrounds and 
positions could also have influence and internally could be 
conflictual with external consequences for undermining the 
Alliance image of 'rational neutrality'.   
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - Difference 
between activists’ trust in Alliance to make the right choice 
and wanting the party to 
 
Even with said trust, some activists did express 
apprehension around the party taking a CP and this was mainly 
(but not only) ‘loss-based’. Activists were mindful that taking a CP 
risks the party losing support, or losing its core ethos, or losing the 
trust afforded to it as not being distracted by the CQ, or really fears 
for the party’s loss of credibility and goodwill that has been built up 
by the party not taking a stance, even though the decision will be 
made democratically within the party. For one activist (38) who 
indicates that the party decision will not be based on feelings, also 
indicates that if the party took a binary position, that undercuts the 
reason they initially picked to support it as Alliance would ‘lose’ its 
non-sectarian party identity. For another, activist (6) that trust is 
there, but their apprehension is less ‘loss-based’. They would trust 
the party to make a nuanced choice but are more worried in the 
context of a referendum about the ‘wider response’ for example 
they would not like to see a repeat of the 2012 flag protests and 

 
126
the polarisation of politics led by other parties instead. There are 
clearly a number of different strands within Alliance. There are 
some activists who fear alienating voters attracted by an absence 
of identity affiliations and who see that as their own 'identity' and 
then there are those worried about internal divisions due to the 
reality that there are different positions and backgrounds in the 
party. In this case there is severe caution about engaging in these 
discussions even internally. Then there are those concerned about 
engaging on the CQ as distracting from daily issues.  
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - Do activists 
see any gains from taking a CP? 
 
As mentioned, taking a pragmatic decision means Alliance 
could lead the debate in a more moderate direction, but activists 
themselves seem to see far fewer ‘gains’ from taking a CP. Alliance 
activists potentially may see staying neutral as not a loss per se, 
but not entirely a gain, because it would be easier in a sense to 
come out on one side, as it would be less challenging when 
formulating policy. Illustrating this, one activist (10) said that in the 
past, ‘Alliance would have been criticised, ‘You're sitting on the 
fence’ and that is the more difficult place to be, like you are not just 
wedded to it blindly, you have to try to think about the policy 
implications...’  
 
Even with ‘conditions’ applied, very few activists really 
considered there to be ‘gains’ from the party taking a CP. 
Potentially it would attract more Alliance activists, or it would finally 
bring an end to the criticism that Alliance is ‘sitting on the fence’. 
Indirectly, one activist (40) recognised the party staying neutral 
would itself be a ‘loss’ in terms of its base, as it would put Alliance 
in a slightly weaker position with voters in nationalist-leaning areas 
because they would want Alliance to pick a position, but ‘directly’ 
the activist’s own preference was for the party to remain neutral. 

 
127
Ultimately, given those interviewed activists who are 
‘decided’ on how they would vote in a referendum, in general also 
would like their party to leave it as a conscience matter, it appears 
Alliance is making the right choice to prioritise the preferences of 
those who actually make up their activist base. This is still likely the 
right choice even at the expense of losing potential new activists 
who would be drawn in by more formal engagement with the CQ, 
and potential new activists who are ‘decided’ would likely still want 
the party to stay neutral anyway. Ultimately, this is a zero-sum 
game as Alliance would lose as many potential activists as they 
would gain by taking a CP.  
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - Having a 
‘condition’ to take a ‘position’ 
 
There is a spectrum of activists who range from more 
apprehensive to more relaxed about the party potentially taking a 
CP. Even at the end of the spectrum that was more ‘apprehensive’, 
some Alliance activists may not be completely closed off to the idea 
of the party taking a position, but may have strict conditions that 
they see would need to be met before the party can do so. By 
having ‘conditions’ these types of activists showcase they may not 
feel ‘comfortable’ being in a party that arbitrarily decides on matters 
which ultimately could redefine the party’s core ethos, that is, they 
take the constitutional question seriously and it is not something to 
be knee-jerk about. For example, even for the activist who is fearful 
for the party’s credibility (40), they believe the party should or could 
decide only when the facts are presented to it. One activist (4) does 
not have a problem with the idea of Alliance taking a position, and 
says the party are going to have to at some stage, but this activist 
does not think that Alliance or anyone is in any kind of a position to 
take a stand one way or another ‘until we know exactly what it 
means’. Given it was commonly mentioned by activists that they 
want to know what a UI ‘looks like’, the activist likely means they 

 
128
do not want the party deciding until the shape of a UI is very clear, 
such as in terms of what way will the economy or healthcare be 
organised. However, there is a question as to whether requiring 
conditions that are unrealistic or extending the timeframe out over
