a very long period of time or indefinitely is ultimately a means of 
retaining effective neutrality. In essence, this may be a way of 
protecting Alliance’s self-image as ‘rationally neutral’ by invoking in 
the name of ‘full information’ such a set of requirements in terms of 
conditions and certainties on options and the process involved that 
it means neutrality extended into the future as no position can be 
taken in any relevant time frame. 
 
A few more ‘relaxed’ activists think politicians making big 
decisions and having a say on big matters, like the party taking a 
CP, is just part and parcel of being in politics. In this sense, it is just 
a mundane decision that would have to be made like any other in 
a political party. These activists conveyed the clearest sense of 
comfort with the capacity of the party to engage with the issue and 
take a position. For example, if the question was in front of Alliance, 
one activist (3) thinks it is about taking part in the democratic 
process through the party and the party will need to decide how to 
navigate through that. They say ultimately that is why they joined a 
party in order to have a say on significant matters and that would 
be one of the big matters that comes up in front of Alliance. 
However, this activist seems to assume that the position that the 
membership can vote for is ‘neutral’, as they say that Alliance 
people/members will take different views on it, ‘but everyone 
understands that the party would have to take a position, and that 
position could be no position’. Another activist (23) says the 
prospect of making a decision is just ‘part of politics’ where 
decisions are what ‘we have to make most days’. They do not think 
that it would be like abortion, where it was a matter of conscience, 
and Alliance would have to take a position on it but the position 
itself would be dependent on many factors, like the economics, 

 
129
health service, etc. This activist was unusual in not considering the 
CQ to be an issue where a conscience vote was most appropriate. 
There is notably a difference between an activist not being 
particularly concerned about their party taking a CP and activists 
not caring as to what the choice actually is. One activist (27) was 
slightly flippant about the prospect because they explain how 
ultimately it is an anonymous choice and secret when each Alliance 
member actually votes so it doesn’t really matter as you can still 
vote whatever way you want in the booth. This activist does not 
believe the party will take a position in the future or there will be a 
whip on it. There is an interesting distinction here between those 
who are concerned (or not) about the ballot itself (which this activist 
clearly is not) or about the debate internally leading up to the ballot 
which seems to be the basis for much of the concern expressed by 
others given the potential divisiveness this may generate. 
 
While the ballot itself is secret and the party members will 
have freedom to make their decision as to which direction the party 
should take, this does not mean the party itself cannot generate 
influence, even subliminally, over its own members’ thinking. For 
example, activist (24) noted how they cannot remember a time 
when a UK minister or representative was brought to a party 
conference as a speaker, while the Tánaiste was the keynote 
speaker at its 2024 party conference. In this sense, it is possible 
that there can be a subliminal message and possible influence over 
members, when they see a standing ovation for an Irish 
representative and hear criticism for the British government. 
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - Beyond the 
loss-gain: Some opening up among Alliance activists 
 
Beyond activists recognising the losses and (less so) any 
gains, activists still do not want their party to ‘ignore’ the 
constitutional issue and believe Alliance can play an important role 

 
130
in the wider debate, despite the challenges and potential risks of 
taking a firmer position within that debate.  
 
Alliance activists expressed differing views, with some 
believing that the party should take part in discussions before a 
referendum is called on the basis that good quality information and 
debate can held avoid the experience of the Brexit referendum. 
Some went further and thought that Alliance taking part might help 
some unionists take part as a form of role model  for participation 
in these discussions. It appears that when it comes to Alliance 
encouraging unionism to partake, some believe the onus is on 
unionist parties, and others just think it is up to Alliance to set an 
example by attending to show it is alright to attend these types of 
constitutional conversations (e.g. activists 23; 4). For example, 
activist (23) knows that Alliance has taken part in some of those all-
Ireland discussions, and they think that is healthy for people to see 
that it is not something to be frightened of, and to share those 
conversations and to encourage people to come forward. They do 
not think it does any harm to have those conversations before a 
referendum as this enables Alliance to call for information on what 
a UI would involve in terms of healthcare, taxes, etc., as a core 
Alliance condition for a referendum.  
  
While apprehensive about their party taking a position, even 
some of those at the ‘nervier’ end of the spectrum can envision 
Alliance not just ignoring the referendum or the CQ, but being a 
party that ‘has a list of questions that needed to be answered’ for 
the people or gets answers from other parties on their constitutional 
positions (e.g. activist 17; 40). This ties back to the self-image of 
Alliance as the ‘rational neutral’ party that focuses on the 
acquisition of evidence for effective decision-making discussed 
above, albeit in this case its role is in seeking out this information 
from other sources for public use rather than for internal decision-
making. For example, one activist (40) does not think Alliance 

 
131
could say nothing at all, but equally they do not see Alliance (or 
themselves) wanting to campaign on a particular outcome, but it 
could take on a role like it did leading up to elections, in that 
Alliance would be saying to the aligned parties what would they do 
about that, what would you do about assets, healthcare, etc., under 
your preferred CP. Although there is a question of how ‘truly 
impartial’ this role is, as it may involve accepting information that 
itself is not impartial, or in the past, as Alliance has given out 
information, rather than just collecting it, this raises additional 
questions about impartiality. For example, during the GFA process 
Alliance opened played a role in providing information for the public 
to combat all the half-truths being spread by other parties about the 
agreement (as discussed in the case selection in chapter 2). This 
may be a role that Alliance would seek to take on once again with 
likely inevitable contestation over the impartiality of this information 
from others that disagreed with it. 
 
Basically, harking back to the accommodationist bridge-
building role that Alliance played during the GFA, other activists 
don’t think or see that Alliance would take a position and would like 
the party working as an honest broker in a conversation on the 
referendum. For example, one activist (10) would see the party 
helping people to wade through all the emotion and the passion 
and try to make a mature informed decision on what is best for 
them. A bridge-building role for the party still might be risky 
compared to a data collection role, as the party could potentially 
direct, and bias, the flow of information. It also would mean Alliance 
would ‘revert back’ to the accommodationist civic party category 
that it had moved away from (see conceptualisation chapter). 
  
The idea of the party giving the ‘facts’ during the period of 
an actual referendum is something that many activists are also 
open to, even those who are fairly apprehensive about the party 
taking a CP. One activist (2) explicitly recognises a contradiction 

 
132
between wanting Alliance to stay neutral and also to give the facts. 
The activist outlines that it is important to have a campaign which 
provides the hard evidence for both sides, ‘but if you’re doing that, 
then I am unsure are you taking a position on it’. In this sense, there 
is a potential tension activists note between Alliance providing 
information externally to shape a debate, but seeking not to shape 
any potential internal debate.  
 
There was a greater hesitancy among activists towards the 
party developing a policy document on a referendum. However, 
they may be more open to the party creating an ‘internal’ – not 
publishable – policy document. For example, one activist (1), is not 
against the party creating a policy for itself on the views inside the 
party, but caution remains about how a policy document with wider 
circulation may be perceived, rightly or wrongly, as affiliated with a 
particular position.  
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - See you on the 
other side – Alliance role post-referendum 
 
 
Although many envision Alliance playing a role before a 
referendum or during a referendum campaign, others’ vision of 
Alliance is cast much further into the unknown in the event of a UI. 
There were a few ‘accommodationist architects’ who have a bigger 
vision for Alliance in ensuring accommodation and fair 
representation for both communities when building a new state or 
UI. This is in itself is like Alliance playing an ‘honest broker’ role, 
but ‘after’ the referendum. Most of these ‘accommodationist 
architects’ were well-established in the party and saw the party 
playing an active, state-crafting role which maybe makes it more 
convincing that this is a role the party could actually play as these 
higher-level politicians could have more direct insight on how this 
would work and the commitment to it the party would make. For 
example, one activist (13) thinks Alliance in its bridging position in 

 
133
the middle would play an important role in trying to create a new 
state that to the greatest extent possible can bring in both sides in 
a relatively amicable way. Another activist (9) thinks Alliance has 
an important role under a UI to play as a party in ensuring that 
unionism is not left behind and that it is accommodated with a 
‘strong voice politically’, even perhaps ‘over-accommodated’ in 
some 
cases64. 
These 
‘accommodationist 
architects’ 
also 
demonstrate the interconnectedness of different aspects of the 
party in terms of its constitutional vision (i.e., the party values 
accommodation and equal treatment of all communities). Many 
activists will be influenced in a referendum by whether identities 
are properly accommodated under whichever constitutional 
outcome (discussed more in the next chapter) and how activists’ 
vision for the party itself is to make sure this accommodation 
happens.  
 
Conceptual marker – Constitutional Neutrality - Still the big 
question – when should the debate begin? 
 
Timelines are the trickiest to determine with Alliance in 
terms of when the debate should begin on the CI, and there are a 
variety of positions on this. There is a clear sense that Alliance 
activists believe Alliance should be involved in conversations but to 
a significant degree, this involvement is contingent on a 
referendum being close to being set in motion as well as a diverse 
range of other factors being in place. Activists believe the party 
should engage in events such as Ireland’s Future in the short-term. 
The timeline question instead primarily seems to arise as to when 
conversations are taken to mean something more substantive. This 
type of bigger conversation appears to mean a stage when the 
‘long campaign’ has begun, and Alliance makes the assessment 
 
64 Many activists in both parties believe that no matter how much you do, there 
are some who will not accept it (e.g. Alliance activist 7). 

 
134
that the party should dive into this process. For example, activist 
(40) lists a number of potential elements required: that nationalists 
have to reach out to unionists and include them and what they 
want, signs that there was a shift in the polls and broader 
conversations beginning to move towards that, then Alliance would 
start to engage in that conversation. This renders it relatively vague 
as to what precisely is needed for Alliance to engage despite the 
widespread belief that Alliance should ultimately be involved.  
 
Other activists are less enthusiastic about the party 
encouraging unionists’ participation now because this type of role 
is perceived by them as potentially ‘selling’ the idea of a UI or 
‘leading the way forward in the debate’ which is not the mission of 
Alliance or its activists. For example, some emphasise the 
responsibility of nationalists (e.g. activist 28) to make the case for 
a positive vision for a New Ireland to people. But as activist (28) 
says ‘now that’s not our vision, our vision is to make Northern 
Ireland as good as it can be regardless of where it sits’. Similarly, 
one activist (2) recognises that if SF is leading the charge in terms 
of the conversation/preparations the unionists will shut down, but 
also notes if it is being led by Alliance, then it ‘looks like we're 
driving the whole argument’, which is not something they would be 
particularly content with. Therefore, they think it is something that 
should be led by the Secretary of State (SoS) and also a relevant 
Minister from the ROI government rather than Alliance. 
 
However, sometimes it is difficult to determine what exactly 
Alliance activists mean by a party taking the ‘lead’ in terms of the 
referendum debate. Although the previously mentioned activist 
(28) does not put the onus on Alliance to sell a ‘UI’ vision, they also 
see Alliance taking a ‘leadership role’. They think Alliance should 
start pushing at the point where it looks like a referendum is going 
to happen, ‘so we need to be talking about this and we need to 
understand this’ and that becomes the justification for Alliance to 

 
135
actually start to play more of a ‘lead role in that process’. But what 
does the activist mean by ‘lead role’, in terms of referendum 
conversations and getting people informed and talking about a 
referendum? Does it mean the party takes on a more neutral role, 
like gathering facts/evidence to give to the public, or does it even 
mean organising its own events around the CQ? It appears that 
this could be Alliance engaging in discussions on a referendum and 
informing people and presenting distinct perspectives, but not 
necessarily leading a campaign for any specific position. In its 
preferred role as the  'rational neutral' party, it seeks to create the 
opportunity to hear different perspectives to have that debate. 
 
Conclusion  
 
This chapter has mapped the identity profile of Alliance 
Party activists across two conceptual markers, non-alignment and 
constitutional neutrality, drawing on a substantial body of interview 
material. Several key findings emerge. First, Alliance activists are 
best characterised as ‘less-aligned’ rather than non-aligned: they 
have distanced themselves, to varying degrees, from the 
communal identities of their background, while retaining residual 
attachments that surface in discourse, particularly in moments of 
unreflective self-expression. The transition to less-alignment is an 
ongoing process and it is shaped by both personal biography and 
structural context, including the experience of party activism itself. 
Second, the Alliance cohort exhibits a notable and multi-causal 
decline in British identification that cannot be straightforwardly 
attributed to Brexit, though Brexit may be a contributing factor. It 
also reflects longstanding discomfort with the specifically Ulster 
unionist inflection of Britishness, an increasing proportion of 
activists from Catholic and nationalist backgrounds, and a more 
general tendency to question the coherence of British identity as a 
meaningful category. A minority retains a Britishness redefined in 

 
136
civic, non-unionist terms, and the decline of Britishness has not 
produced a corresponding growth in Irish nationalism. Third, Irish 
identification among Alliance activists is widespread, but 
distinctive, civic, geographic, situational, and chosen rather than 
politically sovereign. Most Irish-identifying activists are comfortable 
being Irish within the current Northern Irish constitutional 
framework, and do not understand a UI as a necessary condition 
of their Irishness. This suggests a decoupling of Irish identity from 
Irish nationalism.  
 
On the CQ, Alliance activists span a wide range of positions 
from firm pro-unity to firm pro-union, with a substantial and 
heterogeneous undecided middle. The expression of constitutional 
preference is socially constrained within the party context, and 
most decided activists hold their preferences in a characteristically 
Alliance way, linked to assessment of evidence and decoupled 
from their political allegiance to the party or a specific 
programmatic point of view. Alliance activists see a potential key 
role for the party in the provision of information to the public 
although this raises questions about the extent to which the party 
can take on the role of conveying ‘the facts’ while not undermining 
its own neutrality. Activists also see Alliance as serving as 
architects of accommodation, serving first to encourage unionist 
participation in referendum debates and as a key guarantor of 
protections for unionists and accommodations of unionism in any 
potential UI. The party’s institutional neutrality on the constitutional 
question is, for now, broadly supported by its activist base, not least 
because that neutrality is itself part of what makes Alliance 
politically distinctive and potentially understood as the best current 
strategy given the internal and external risks that both engaging in 
the debate and seeking to identify a position may present. 
 
 
 

 
137
Chapter 4: Identity versus pragmatism: 
Understanding the constitutional deliberations of 
the practical Alliance activists 
 
Introduction 
 
Given the emphasis that Alliance activists place on the 
party’s self-image as a ‘rational neutral’ party that considers an 
issue based on empirical evidence, this chapter seeks to more 
systematically explore the perspectives and interpretations of 
activists of deliberations on the constitutional question to discern 
the extent to which identity, emotion and affect are displaced in 
favour of a focus on ‘the evidence.’ In reality, the chapter 
demonstrates there is a significant role for a wider range of factors 
than this ‘rational neutral’ frame would typically acknowledge.  
 
Factor 1: Identity as a factor? 
 
Non-emotional and non-ideological? 
 
Given Alliance’s pragmatism, preference for evidence-
based decision-making and realism, it seems (undecided) activists 
are missing the ‘human part’ of the constitutional question and 
could be considered ‘immune’ to the influence of emotion, affect 
and identity as compared to those active within more traditionally 
aligned parties. There is, of course, a substantial literature 
illustrating the role of rationalist decision-making in attitude 
development and political behaviour such as the Rochester School 
of vote choice (see Amadae and Bueno de Mesquita, 1999). 
However, over-emphasising the rational can overlook the role of 
identity (e.g. Horowitz, 2000) and the emotional and affective 
(Kecmanovic, 2005) especially when political questions tied to 
nationalism and national identity arise and the realities of the 
discourses and perspectives of activists shows that despite this 

 
138
broader self-image of the party internally there is a wider role for 
identity than these types of rational models imply. As well as an 
‘immunity’ to the ‘irrational’, this conception of activists also implies 
a superiority that is not demonstrated by Alliance activists 
themselves. Activists are at pains not to suggest that voting based 
on practical policy aspects is inherently better to voting based on 
emotive-ideological aspects (e.g. activist 22).  Similarly, emotion is 
not something that activists will entirely distance from. Alliance 
activists will not feel unemotional about a border poll even if they 
may not feel particularly emotionally attached to either national 
identity. Exemplifying this, one activist (10) said ‘for me personally, 
I don't think that...the emotions and the passions would get in the 
way. But I'm saying that because I don't think I feel emotional about 
being British or Irish…’65. 
 
Certain Alliance activists do at times though suggest that 
Alliance are rational and nationalists and unionists are 'irrational'. 
Activist (18), for example, suggests you do not want a citizen 
assembly where it is all Alliance people who turn up as the Alliance 
people are already won over to looking at the world in a different, 
potentially rationalist way, and that it needs to be open enough that 
you have the ‘raging republicans and looney loyalists’ taking part 
too. This is indicative of something of a partial disregard at least for 
those deemed to relay ‘too much’ on strong identity affiliations. It is 
not however that all aligned individuals are seen as equally and 
immovably ‘irrational.’ For those who are aligned, but of a more 
moderate persuasion, economics and healthcare are seen as two 
things by activists that could make the ‘ideological’ nationalists 
‘rationalists’. It is mostly those with more extreme alignments that 
are seen as more resistant to movement based on material or 
policy dimensions. 
 
65 The activist did say ‘but I might feel emotional about things like the welfare state 
and whether I can get iPlayer. [Laughter]…’. 

 
139
As discussed in earlier chapters, the reality of non-alignment 
is in fact reduced rather than eliminated affiliations. There is not an 
out-and-out denial from most activists of this, and some indeed 
acknowledge that the notion that they would vote based purely on 
rational terms, and without any influence of their background would 
potentially be untruthful on reflection. One activist (15) also 
recognises their perception of themselves as predominately 
rational could be built on them being untruthful. While they feel they 
are primarily a person who approaches life in a rational way, this 
does not mean they can say that they always truly do this and at 
times, this is closer to what they tell themselves than the reality of 
how they think and behave. It is also the case that what is framed 
as ‘rational’, classically for example materialist arguments about 
differential economic outcomes from a UI or staying in the Union, 
can itself be shaped by or invoked for identity-based/ideological or 
‘irrational’ dimensions. Activists are not unaware of how economic 
discussions and models can be manoeuvred in a particular way to 
support a certain argument around a preferred constitutional 
outcome. For example, one activist (14) thinks the economy is one 
of those arguments now for some other people where they will use 
it if it helps their argument, and it is not actually a top priority. What 
is intended to be an economic argument is ultimately in these 
cases a sovereignty argument. That said, the largest proportion of 
activists were clear in conceding a role for their background and 
socialisation in shaping their vote even while the self-image of the 
party as ‘rational neutral’ is significant. 
 
Of course, some activists were adamant that their 
background won’t impact their constitutional thinking, but 
potentially these activists are those who come from more ‘extreme’ 
versions 
of 
their 
community 
background 
(i.e. 
strict 
unionists/nationalists) and would be more likely to want to distance 
themselves completely from these backgrounds. For example, one 
activist (18) thinks that they will vote for what logically makes 

 
140
sense, but they appear to have come from a strict DUP/Orange 
Order background. Potentially, the utter disgust they reveal in their 
interview for this type of politics and associated values pushes 
them towards a position they identify specifically as driven by 
rational logic. Moreover, some openly reflect on their assumptions 
that it won’t have an impact, or they will make a rational choice. 
Even one activist (3) who does not think their traditional community 
will impact their vote choice also recognises it is easy to say that, 
and they can understand how you could subconsciously take 
things from your background. Some activists answered on whether 
their background would impact their vote choice with reference to 
their family unit (e.g. parents, relatives) and that their family was 
their ‘background’. For most, there is the perception that families 
will not ‘directly’ influence their vote choice in a referendum (i.e. my 
parents support a UI, so I do). The word ‘directly’ is important 
because those such as activist (3) will be ‘indirectly’ influenced by 
their family, but not in the sense that they will be influenced by how 
their parents vote, or that their familial background will push them 
to align with one constitutional preference over another. Rather, 
they will be influenced by how their current family (their family 
crosses both sides of the main NI traditional communities) would 
be embraced, and the future for them would be at the forefront of 
their thoughts, rather than their background and how they grew up.  
 
Of course, the primordialist perspective may suggest that, in 
the same way that even if a person no longer identifies with their 
innate identity (e.g. they converted to a different religion in 
adulthood), but, for example, in times of war will ‘revert back’ to this 
innate identity (McKay, 1982), then some might argue that if a 
referendum is called, these activists might ‘revert back’ to their 
traditional ethno-nationality. Essentially, the constitutional threat 
posed by unification and the referendum would function similarly to 
a conflict which also presents a potential 'existential threat' or 
primal threat to the survival of the ethnic group or threat to the 

 
141
nation. The referendum and potential defeat of the unionist position 
and unification would similarly be a major threat to the nation and 
would motivate those who would have potentially otherwise de-
emphasised their national identity. However, as in the previous 
chapter, these centre-ground activists also are almost innately 
‘resistant’ to aligning themselves by orthodox identities, which 
helps explain why they chose to join a non-binary party in the first 
place. Therefore this, (combined with how primordialism itself is a 
weak theory of identity e.g., Fearon and Laitin, 2000), would lean 
towards an expectation that these activists would not ‘revert back’ 
to their traditional identity when choosing how to vote in a united 
Ireland referendum.  
 
Apathy? Intensity of feelings around a UI or status quo outcome 
 
 
The lack of intensity of feeling connected to constitutional 
outcomes may broadly reflect the lack of emotional feeling of many 
activists about the constitutional question in which they don’t 
imagine a UI is going to suddenly fix or solve the problems currently 
in NI and instead all it does is change who ‘controls the purse 
strings’ (i.e. it shifts from Westminster in the UK to the Dáil in 
Dublin). 
 
 
Alternatively, this lack of intense feeling may result from an 
expectation of remaining in the UK, and that activists have a clear 
idea of what the ‘status quo’ looks like, which is to say, it is much 
of the same. However, for such reflective thinkers, Alliance activists 
can often (not always) take it for granted that the status quo will 
just be more of the same, such as when remarking on how it is 
more of an unknown what a UI looks like. For example, one 
Alliance activist (9) says ‘And obviously… it's very easy to know 
what we're voting for if we vote for a continuation of the status quo, 
okay? Like, that's fairly clear, so that doesn't need to be ironed out. 
What we don't know is if we vote for change, what we're getting’. 

 
142
Sometimes it was implied that the status quo is going to be more 
of the same, as when directly asked how the status quo result will 
impact them, some activists respond that they would get a sense 
of ‘ease’ from knowing things won’t really change that much. Given 
how often it comes up that Alliance activists assume that a status 
quo is more of the same, potentially what is needed to better inform 
this undecided grouping is not just the publication of a plan around 
what a UI looks like, but also what a status quo result looks like to 
‘prove’ nothing will change. Additionally, a status quo vote is 
generally considered a neutral or positive outcome. For example, 
one activist (22) sees a status quo result as more than just ‘the 
same’ and asks what would voting to remain in the UK mean, would 
that involve greater devolution or other changes. This could be 
perceived as pro-union bias, but this is seen instead as an 
opportunity for a better version than the ‘current union’ as in reality 
there is a hope for more on the other side of a result. 
 
 
The easy-going attitude to the potential outcomes of a 
referendum might also somewhat reflect how a significant few see 
they can or would just acclimatise swiftly into their new life under a 
UI, or that they are the type of person who when they go to a place 
they buy into that community (e.g. activist 40). For example, one 
activist (20) (who would not stay in NI if there was a UI) feels very 
comfortable in the Republic as a visitor and feels it is almost like 
coming home, and if they moved to somewhere well away from the 
border under a UI, they would be very comfortable and would 
immediately get into the ‘groove’ of life there. Not only do some 
activists think they would assimilate into a UI quickly, one activist 
(7) thinks NI people in general would quickly become accustomed 
to their new existence. They believe NI people would have to get 
used to a new tax/health system, etc., under a UI, but generally 
people get used to things very quickly. 
 

 
143
 
This attitude might also somewhat reflect how so many 
Alliance activists envision that in a UI at the ‘day-to-day’ level life 
would not change a whole lot at least not in the shorter-term, or 
unless there are major macro problems. Therefore, they are not so 
‘scared’ about the unknown of a UI, because they sense that daily 
life will look a lot like it does now. Activist (28) for example thinks 
there's going to be a very long transition period, and ‘we're not 
going to see any significant change to our day-to-day lives 
overnight’ even if in the longer-term things would change. However, 
it is important to note, that some activists (4; 9) see the ‘day-to-day’ 
impact as dependent on certain things like the Protocol’s 
implementation, or the extent to which security becomes an issue. 
 
Ranking - much different than moderates? 
 
For the (reflective) rationalist activist cohort they will likely 
prioritise policy issues in a referendum. However, potentially, the 
‘ranking’ that each activist gives to each policy issue (e.g., 
healthcare, economy, Brexit, etc.) could change by the time a 
referendum actually rolls around. Alliance activists often mention 
how unionists are quite a pragmatic lot who would care about 
‘normal things’ in a referendum (at least independent of political 
party unionism) and how nationalists who are happy enough in the 
status quo in practical terms, such as with their job status, might 
not necessarily make the jump to a UI (e.g. activist 4). Therefore, if 
those who are ‘aligned’ can make ‘practical or pragmatic’ 
deliberations in a referendum, there is a question of what makes 
the deliberations of those who are active within the non-aligned 
Alliance so different from moderate unionism or nationalism. Even 
one Alliance activist (36), who sees Alliance influenced by the 
same factors as the moderates in a referendum does not know if 
there are truly factors that ‘uniquely’ would influence Alliance 
supporters, given Alliance sit in the middle. As they outlined, ‘…the 
factors that would encourage both moderate elements of 

 
144
nationalism and unionism, whatever those issues would be, 
Alliance are going to be comfortable with…’. However, where 
Alliance activists may differ is their ‘ranking’ of factors. That is, the 
ideological/constitutional aspect will rank lower in terms of priorities 
for them in a referendum and the more practical policy elements 
will rank higher than for unionists/nationalists. Similarly, in the 
Tonge et al., 2024 review of policy preferences (in terms of vote 
choice rather than a referendum) ‘where Alliance members differed 
is in the downgrading of constitutional issues. They ranked third in 
the electorate’s priorities (below only Brexit and the National Health 
Service (NHS)) in 2019, but for Alliance members they lay far lower’ 
(pp. 218-219). 
 
Overarching question – information is key no matter where ‘issue’ 
is on the priority list 
 
Although the ‘ranking’ that Alliance activists give to each 
policy issue in their ‘priority list’ will be dependent on the individual 
activist, the most commonly recurring factor likely to influence their 
decision is that (most) Alliance activists will be influenced by the 
answer to the ‘better off’ question (i.e. will I be better off; will my 
family be better off; will NI be better off in a UI or remaining in the 
UK). Several mention they want to see or be told the benefits of a 
UI or see a ‘detailed plan’ of what a UI looks like before they can 
decide which constitutional outcome is ‘better’ as discussed 
previously. One Alliance activist (11) notes a referendum is 
something they have thought about in terms of the need for a well 
thought out plan about how the country would be integrated, and 
the prospect of a UI needs to provide something that is better than 
the status quo and if it does, this needs to be clear and specific 
such as providing better wages or a pathway to a better economy. 
If those making the argument and campaigning for a United Ireland 
can provide a detailed plan that would show that, it would be a big 
factor in which way the activist would personally vote.  

 
145
Currently, Alliance activists (and GPNI) are still looking for 
each side to ‘present’ their visions of each constitutional outcome. 
As one Alliance activist (36) says ‘..nobody is actually coming up 
and saying, "This is what a [New Ireland] looks like”’. This is similar 
to Todd et al.’s focus group finding on undecided people in North 
and South where focus group participants ‘wanted information 
about economic impacts and about proposals for public service 
delivery on healthcare, benefits, housing and transport, but they 
also wanted to discuss those issues as part of a process to develop 
a vision of what a united Ireland would look like before referendums 
are called’ (p. 145).  
 
This desire for ‘information’ might explain why several 
activists answer that they don’t really know how a UI would impact 
the lives of those in NI or what a UI means to them, precisely as it 
has not been laid out to them. It does though also reflect how this 
is not talked about within the party internally at a formal level. This 
pattern may be more specific to a non-aligned party like 
Alliance. Again, there is though a question as to how far are the 
activists going to get the information they require given they are 
clearly not willing to go so far as to be on board with their party 
leading the conversation at this point. It may be that there are 
unreasonable expectations about the amount of information 
needed for most voters as they will use heuristics to inform their 
decision, but for Alliance activists or in particular those activists 
who come closest to the 'rational neutral' paradigm discussed 
above, they will want as much information as possible. This means 
the emphasis activists place on the need for detailed discussion 
and explanation of the options and evidence for what the outcome 
will look like is quite particular to groups within the party as 
compared to the wider population or even activists from other more 
identity-aligned parties. 
 
 

 
146
Factor 2:  Back to Alliance’s early justification - Better 
economically and socially  
 
Alliance have traditionally justified their pro-union stance 
based on how being in the UK was best for NI from an economic 
and social perspective. This section explores the extent to which 
activists still hold this view and the role it plays in shaping their 
attitudes towards the CQ and a potential referendum today. 
 
Economic – UK still has NI’s best interests? 
 
Even though there were still some questions around 
whether the ROI could afford NI, despite new research questioning 
the size of the subvention66, a select few activists were already 
‘sold’ on the economic benefits of a UI. For some this is based on 
‘what you get’ in the future under a UI (i.e. better economic 
benefits). For example, one Alliance activist (9) thinks the 
‘economic argument is largely won to be honest…if you look at 
other reunification projects worldwide, like Germany, the economic 
benefits to the poorer region for lack of a better word, are usually 
quite great…’. However, it should be noted that while this individual 
activist draws a direct comparison between a UI and German 
reunification, this is not something Alliance at large promotes. 
Former Deputy leader Stephen Farry did not see it as a like-for-like 
comparison, as for instance, there was widespread support across 
both parts of Germany for reunification unlike what will happen in 
the context of Ireland (Houses of the Oireachtas, 2021). Others 
may also base this assertion on a comparison between how the 
ROI’s economy is performing better than NI’s economy and so a 
UI will be better off economically because the ROI already is. For 
example, one activist, (4) says ‘a lot of the questions’ around 
whether slightly wavering Alliance voters who might be of a slightly 
 
66 Doyle, J. (2021). ‘Why the 'Subvention' does not Matter: Northern Ireland and the 
All-Ireland Economy.’ Irish Studies in International Affairs, 32(2), pp. 314-334. 

 
147
unionist persuasion would be hit economically by a UI ‘will have 
been answered by the fact that your [interviewer is from the ROI] 
economy is in pretty good shape and has been by comparison to 
ours’.  
 
The international survey-based vote choice literature 
concludes that voters generally are sociotropic, so, caring more 
about national than personal (pocketbook) economic conditions, 
backward-looking, and myopic (Kiewiet and Lewis-Beck, 2011). 
The Alliance activists here typically focus on these broader 
perceptions of the performance of the national-level economy 
rather than the personal pocketbook as conditioning their 
expectations and which they project onto the wider debate and 
decision to be made on the position of the party and swing voters. 
More broadly, not everyone was as convinced as the previous 
activists, as some think the comparative economic benefit depends 
on what level of the economy you are looking at, or how far into the 
future you are talking about. For example, one activist (15) 
suggests that the ROI’s economy is not as good as it seems, that 
is, on the surface it always looks great, but the reality is somewhat 
different. Another activist (6) thinks it is potentially difficult to 
answer whether NI people would economically prosper in a UI, as 
while it might be a negative in the short-term, ‘you would also have 
to look at the long-term’. 
 
 
There is a potential differential relevance of economic 
issues dependent on age. At an individual-level, it may be expected 
that the economic issue is not going to be as high up on the priority 
list for some demographics even among Alliance activists. 
Although one activist (11) guesses their younger age probably 
prevents them from understanding the economic benefits of a UI, 
it did not appear that activists of a more mature age were especially 
informed around the economic benefits of a UI relative to those 
who were younger. An interesting perspective offered by activist 

 
148
(3) was their understanding that while the economy would be the 
key factor for most age groups, for younger people, the activist’s 
sense was that the economy would not be as important as a 
motivation for a growing number of younger people as compared 
to issues such as civil rights and the protection of minorities.  
 
Both an economic and social issue – the NHS not viewed through 
‘rose-tinted glasses’ 
 
In post-Brexit politics in Ireland, both north and south, there is 
a renewed interest in the opportunities and barriers to an all-island 
healthcare system. For instance, in a plethora of debates and 
presentations on constitutional futures, healthcare has emerged as 
a key issue. Access to the UK National Health Service (NHS) could 
be a key factor preventing voters in NI from supporting a UI. In a 
2019 Northern Ireland Life and Times Survey, respondents were 
asked whether the two different healthcare systems would 
influence their vote in a referendum on a UI. Overall, 52% said that 
it would discourage them from voting for a UI (Heenan, 2021). How 
then do activists in Alliance consider and approach this issue?  
 
What came through in the interviews is the majority of Alliance 
activists who did not view the NHS through rose-tinted glasses. 
Similar to the patterns observed in Todd et al’s (2023) focus group 
research on those in the South and North who are undecided on 
how they would vote in a referendum, several Alliance activists 
would move their position on the NHS within their interview, even 
in the middle of a single contribution. They might start off talking 
about their concerns around having to pay to visit a GP under a UI 
as happens in the ROI, to then recognising that the NHS is 
ultimately becoming more privatised or the HSE more socialised, 
or asking the interviewer (who was from the ROI) whether you can 
actually get treatment in the South at least, even if you have to pay 
for it.  

 
149
However, while ‘healthcare’ is deemed a ‘pragmatic/practical’ 
factor shaping attitudes in this project, this is not to suggest that 
activists were unaware of how emotionally-laden of an issue the 
‘NHS’ is for other people besides themselves. Some recognised 
that there is an ‘emotional attachment’ to the NHS as an institution 
which they do not necessarily see as a bad thing (activist 22), or 
that it will be an emotional reaction from people if the NHS is not 
guaranteed under a UI and the NHS is abolished (in particular as 
the NHS is embedded in what it means to be British) (activist 4). 
There is evidence here of how the materialist issue of healthcare 
provision can again be emotional, affective and ‘irrational’. Again, 
these activists reinforce the image of activists as ‘reflective 
rationalists’ (i.e. moving their own position on the NHS), but it would 
appear they at least see themselves, as more ‘robotic’ when it 
comes to the NHS as they do not (to their own minds) have this 
unadulterated ‘emotional bond’ to it that others do.  
 
If age does play into which factors would influence the Alliance 
activists, potentially the relevance of healthcare as a factor could 
be age-dependent. Certain activists speculate that younger 
generations may be less committed to the idea of the NHS as a 
provider of care than older generations are, although there is little 
evidence that this pattern is replicated among activists themselves 
in their own preferences. For example, one activist (21) suggests 
there will be some younger voters who are less concerned (albeit 
this does not mean necessarily they will not care at all) about the 
health service argument in a referendum as they do not rely on it 
so much - ‘…for example, you'll have 18-year-olds who don't really 
care about the health argument… because…they're not using the 
health service…and why should they really care about health… 
when they can have this new constitutional change?’ Another 
younger activist (22) is more discerning on age, healthcare and the 
centre-ground. They note if you look at who thinks about the NHS 
more, it is probably older people, those who have disabilities, 

 
150
people who rely on services more, and if you also look at the make-
up of the centre-ground it tends to be younger, but obviously there 
are people with disabilities in the centre-ground, so one cannot 
make broad generalisations.  
 
Factor 3: Not many unionists or British-only in Alliance – but 
still care for unionist accommodation in a united Ireland? 
 
Fabricated fears? 
 
While not going as far as wanting the party to be 
‘accommodationist architects’ where the party ensures all identities 
feel safe and accommodated in any UI model, the place of 
unionism in a UI is a very big priority for many activists in 
considering the CQ as is the extent to which they have been 
‘brought along’ in the conversations at the time of a referendum. 
Although several activists who come from a unionist background 
have distanced from it, just by having family who are unionists it 
feeds into their own considerations around a referendum or UI. 
Several Alliance activists also recognised that the unionist fear 
around a UI stems from a fear that they will be treated badly in a 
UI in the same way unionists treated the nationalist community 
when they held power in the past although several also think that 
British people/unionists already fear their identity is under threat in 
the current context in NI. 
 
 It seems the presumed apprehension of unionists is 
grounded mainly in perceptions about what will be taken away from 
unionists, rather than forced upon them in a UI, for example, not 
many think unionists fear they will have to learn Irish under a UI. 
There is an underlying current here that while activists recognise 
the fears or apprehension of unionists about a UI or referendum, 
some seem to think that ‘in reality’ some of these fears would not 
actually come about. Specifically several reflect on, again 

 
151
sometimes in a single contribution where concerns are initially 
highlighted, that in reality the unionist communities’ fears around 
their place in a UI (or the threat to their identity in a UI) is overstated 
given some activists were not convinced, for example, that unionist 
politicians are going to be excluded from government, or that their 
religious freedom is going to be undermined. For instance, one 
activist (38) declared ‘…it's not as if…the Dáil is going to kick out 
these unionist politicians as then that's exactly what unionism did 
for nationalism for years’. Another activist (7) says certain issues, 
including the extent of religious freedom under a UI are important, 
but are now quite minor points as they are fairly well-settled, as 
there is no prospect of losing religious freedom in a UI. Ultimately, 
a UI is not viewed as much of a threat, as it might have been in the 
past for Alliance activists. This is in fact a common theme across 
both parties of the centre-ground. Activists from both parties 
consider unionist accommodation in a UI to be important and want 
it to be considered in developing their constitutional perspective. 
There is though a concern about the retention of signifiers of 
identity in a UI as for example being required to indicate British 
identity on state paperwork and applications even with the goal of 
accommodative representation can lead to the perpetuation of the 
identity binary even in a UI/New Ireland.  
 
How to accommodate unionists? – cultural celebration? 
 
How far can unionist concerns about cultural difference and 
political identification in a UI be addressed by institutional or 
constitutional reform? For a UI to be minimally acceptable, 
unionists’ everyday cultural choices, practices and preferences 
would have to be respected. They would have to be able to freely 
pursue their British-oriented interests and British-centred cultural 
practices. 
 

 
152
As mentioned, several activists think that potential ways to 
accommodate unionist or British identities are things that would be 
likely to be facilitated, for example one activist (6) imagines that the 
marches on the 12th July would be able to continue under a UI. 
What became clear is many activist suggestions of ‘how to 
accommodate’ are rarely innovative. That is, the focus is on 
unionists continuing to be and to identify, do, celebrate and get 
what already is in place in NI, although maybe these could be 
codified under a UI. One of the biggest things that activists think 
could accommodate unionists is to allow them to continue to 
celebrate their culture in a UI. Alliance activists’ suggestion may 
actually not be too far off, given one Alliance activist (11) who is 
from a unionist background themselves, sees cultural celebration 
as a key means of accommodation, as they know how these 
cultural and symbolic elements matter to those in the community 
they come from. They say ‘I think a big thing will be ensuring that 
their traditions aren't taken away from them. Because I know 
coming from the community that things like the 12th of July and 
being able to fly the British flag is a big thing for them. Being able 
to like celebrate things like the monarchy is something that they 
hold like quite dearly’. Given this, while some activists think that 
most unionists can be accommodated through an approach that 
respects dimensions of their culture, others suggest political 
unionism or hard-line unionism would be more entrenched, require 
more than symbolic gestures and instead need active unionist 
representation. For example, one activist (9) outlines ‘…in terms of 
bringing political unionism along, you know, it's not just about that 
symbolism [of Stormont as an institution], it's also about, you know, 
jobs and…making sure that they…are given that funding and 
financial clout to continue…to have a say and act as 
spokespeople…for the unionist people’. For those on the harder-
line end of the unionist spectrum, one element another activist (13) 
mentions 
is 
ensuring 
they 
have 
‘meaningful 
political 
representation’. Options pitched in research on this issue include 

 
153
suggestions of guaranteed seats in the Irish Cabinet or over-
representation in the Seanad. There is still though some scepticism 
about affording disproportionate power to unionists in a UI. One 
activist (14) shares that in Westminster NI have 18 seats out of 650 
which is very little power, so in a new Ireland NI would have 
considerable political power. This is to the advantage of NI, but 
power is still not going to be overly weighted towards NI and an 
advantage of this is this also guarantees unionists cannot set the 
tone of everything in that context. 
 
Despite this, oftentimes non-aligned Alliance activists were 
not totally comfortable sharing what they believe could 
accommodate unionists or British people under a UI, because they 
do not come from that background or have distanced from it. 
However, potentially the activists would have been more 
comfortable answering on what they thought would not be an 
acceptable or legitimate means of accommodation. They can see 
there are legitimate and illegitimate ‘forms of celebration’, for 
example, they would not support paramilitary flags or activities in 
any setting. One activist (9) said there are places where ‘we need 
to draw the line’ in terms of ensuring that unionism’s symbols are 
celebrated and included, that is, the ‘same rules apply that we 
would apply currently’, such as Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) flags 
and Soldier F banners are not appropriate in any context. 
 
For some, accommodation and consideration of unionist 
perspectives while valuable is only an interim stage and can 
distract from more inclusive progress that moves beyond 
community representation in general in the longer-term. There was 
a desire among some activists to get NI to a point beyond there 
being ‘cross-community’ interactions and conversations in which 
there is a transition away from having people or their conversations 
defined by what community they come from at all. Speaking on 
their involvement in a community project with persons from 

 
154
different backgrounds, one Alliance activist (7) was deliberately 
trying to avoid the term ‘cross-community’ when explaining that 
accommodating identities in NI (or a potential UI) may involve 
including people in general, not explicitly attempting to include 
people from both communities. Also, another activist (4) of course 
coming from a cross-community party, says people on the ground 
are very able to work together, although they are not encouraged 
to do so by politicians. That is, NI ‘should be a community that has 
a conversation, not cross-community conversations’. 
 
Cultural celebrations are still not the biggest concern? 
 
Many Alliance activists suggest a way to accommodate 
unionism (at least less hardline or political forms) under a UI is to 
allow for them to continue their forms of cultural expression. 
However, it appears that what the vision for flags or symbols under 
a UI are, is still considered of secondary importance for several 
Alliance activists. The more practical questions are the ones that 
need to be answered and not avoided for Alliance activists, as one 
Alliance activist (17) said, those who talk about flags and national 
anthems, are really avoiding answering the more practical 
questions, such as what salary will public servants be paid. In this 
view, for these types of activists this is why Alliance needs to be 
involved in the current constitutional conversations to ensure that 
the focus is more on practical over symbolic issues. However on 
the flipside, for the cohorts within Alliance that emphasise the need 
to accommodate unionists, then Alliance must also ensure that the 
maintenance of culture and symbols is part of these conversations. 
Although there would be sympathy from Alliance activists for those 
unionist or British identifiers who do not see themselves as 
represented by the tricolour under a UI, a few also do not think 
others will worry too much about symbols under a UI. This 
somewhat clashes with the activists who think allowing unionists to 
continue their cultural expression is important for their 

 
155
accommodation. One Alliance activist (17) would be open for 
anything in terms of a flag under a UI, like a tricolour with an NI flag 
in the corner, ‘it would not worry me much, and I don't think it would 
worry most people much, to be honest’. 
 
Also, despite downplaying their own attachment to symbols 
in the same way that Alliance activists think there are ‘illegitimate 
forms of cultural expression’ (e.g. paramilitary flags), Alliance 
activists do display some respect for symbols, but not commonly 
based on nationalism. They support symbols as representations of 
distinct identities and cultures, but they are opposed to their use in 
certain ways such as when they are stuck on lampposts to mark 
territory. Also, maybe it would be expected that Alliance activists 
would be happy to associate themselves with the European flag, 
for example at one point Alliance as a party was on board with the 
Assembly putting its focus on developing shared symbols, 
including a flag for NI and supported the greater use of the 
European Flag (in terms of public use). However, flying the 
European flag was not really brought up by this sample, although 
one activist (14) still agrees that ‘those kind of issues like what flag 
we wave, maybe matter less to Alliance because we have chosen 
a party that is purposely not a flag-waving party’, but also says 
‘Although you could argue in 2016, we were waving the EU flag’. 
However, this likely was more of a ‘metaphorical flag’ to represent 
Alliance’s pro-remain position for the EU, rather than a real 
‘European flag’. 
 
Keeping the tricolour?  
 
While it is the centre-ground that needs to be persuaded to 
vote one way or another in a referendum, there is also a recognition 
by activists that the unionists have to be ‘persuaded’ not to 
necessarily vote for a UI, but convinced by SF and ROI that a UI 
would be a warm and welcoming place for them. As one activist 

 
156
(22) notes the aim would not be to get people from the pro-British 
community to be voting for a UI, it is to make them feel at least 
comfortable and safe, at home in a UI. However, there was not 
much consensus from activists around whether two flags can or 
should co-exist in a UI, even on public buildings – although it was 
rarer that activists just say you only need the tricolour under a UI. 
 
 In 2003, Alliance proposed that a new flag should be 
adopted to represent all communities in NI. However, two activists 
saw how previous attempts to combine symbols were a somewhat 
messy process. This partly explains why one of these would not 
want to get rid of the tricolour under a UI, but both also recognise 
how the tricolour has in a way (historically) represented peace 
between unionists and nationalists. One of the activists (18) thinks 
it would be a nonsense to get rid of the Irish flag, the Irish flag was 
meant to represent the orange, green and middle, although they 
could see the regional flags being used again. However, this 
activist does not think there needs to be a new flag and told a story 
of how they were involved in a Belfast city council event to create 
a flag and the resulting tie-dye flag was not well accepted. Another 
Alliance activist (21) also understood how the tricolour was meant 
to represent peace between the two sides. They also considered 
the messiness of the crest for the police service which combines 
British and Irish symbols, but this activist instead thinks that maybe 
the easiest way to is by allowing British and Irish symbols to sit 
alongside each other and coexist in a UI. This same activist thinks 
there is people who would never accept governance under the 
tricolour, so there does need to be a change within how the state 
would present itself. There was ultimately little consensus from 
activists regarding wither two flags can or should co-exist in a UI, 
although it was rare that activists would say that only the tricolour 
is needed under a UI.  
 

 
157
There was also a recognition of the hesitancy or potential 
hesitancy from the ROI towards changing things under a UI. 
Alliance activists can see a lot of these things being too much 
compromise for the ROI, or express scepticism about the 
openness of people in the ROI to symbolic changes, such as the 
idea of changing the national anthem or flag (e.g. 14; 4). However, 
there was also a worry from Alliance (and GPNI) activists about 
what happens if the ROI public does not want a UI. Several wonder 
what would happen after a result in a referendum where NI votes 
for UI, but the ROI does not – a scenario, one activist (20) 
describes as NI having “cheated on your partner” in Scotland, 
Wales and in England. While this is a legal possibility, it is thought 
highly unlikely based on existing polling. As discussed in Todd 
(2021), in a ‘Two Traditions Paradigm’ the existing institutions 
would continue in a UI with continued funding, either proportional 
to use or with parity between the traditions or an agreed mix. 
Instead in a ‘New Ireland Paradigm’, the aims of diversification, 
choice and mutual enrichment of traditions would govern 
organisation throughout the island. However, the broader idea of a 
UI as an opportunity for the construction of a holistic reimagined 
almost utopian ‘New Ireland' is an idea much more commonly 
referenced by the Greens even though there are elements of the 
discussion here of a new flag and traditionally from Alliance that 
touches on this paradigm. In Alliance, for those favouring a ‘New 
Ireland’ there is limited consistency in terms of how much of this 
society and its symbols should be entirely crafted as ‘new’ from the 
ground up versus adaptations from what is currently in place in NI 
and the ROI. Generally Alliance though seem to be much more 
focused on the 'efficiency' arguments for a UI and related material 
issues than 'reimagining a New Ireland' like the radical Greens (as 
discussed in later chapters).  
 

 
158
Factor 4: Brexit – not such a game changer? 
 
For many, Brexit is considered the key inflection point and 
defining issue that has shaped the salience of and engagement 
with the CQ. For voters, in an October 2017 LucidTalk poll the most 
dramatic score comparison was that for Alliance/Greens/Others 
the likelihood of voting for a UI comparing the impact of Brexit 
leading to NI being better-off versus Brexit leading to NI being 
worse-off was a 10% greater likelihood of voting in the first case for 
a UI compared to a likelihood of voting for a UI of 57% if Brexit led 
to NI being worse off (LucidTalk, 2017). This was seen as a big 
danger signal for the pro-union campaign (i.e. NI in UK) i.e. if Brexit 
goes badly for NI (i.e. in this group of voters’ opinion) then this 
could aid the pro-UI campaign. The broader expectation for centre-
ground parties is that Brexit acted as a shock that shifted opinions 
on and engagement with the issue. Counter to other work on the 
influence of Brexit on thinking on the CQ, activists interviewed from 
Alliance did not strongly emphasise the role of Brexit as explored 
below.  
 
Sticky issue 
 
While Alliance activists’ issue rankings will be responsive to 
changes in the socio-political or economic context, a select few 
activists illustrate that potentially some factors (specifically Brexit) 
may be ‘stickier’ than others – that is, some factors will be more 
difficult to make better or fix, and so are more likely to get stuck at 
the current rank that the activists assign it to. While some activists 
do speculate that the UK could be back in the EU by the time of a 
referendum (e.g. activist 21), others see Brexit as an issue likely to 
have to be considered as part of the referendum debate for some 
time. For example, two activists (9; 6) showcase that while social 
issues have or could be dealt with, Brexit is – in comparison – not 
something that is solved or even solvable. Specifically, the activist 

 
159
(9) thinks the Brexit issue has ‘not lessened’, but in terms of those 
social issues, that is ‘a little bit more off the agenda now’ due to the 
Westminster legislation brought into NI that decriminalises same-
sex marriage and abortion. Also, activist (6) thinks the threats to, 
or actions against social progress and rights from the particularly 
hard-right Conservative government that was in power when 
interviewed could be protected against and reversed, if maybe a 
Labour or Labour-Lib Dem coalition came in in England. However, 
again they see the Brexit issue as ‘stickier’ stating that ‘...but a lot 
of things like Brexit you simply cannot reverse and it has set things 
in motion for decades that will probably have negative 
consequences’.  
 
Sticky issues, but not the decider 
 
Even if Brexit is a stickier issue for activists than social 
issues, this does not mean that Brexit currently sits (or is stuck) 
high up on the priority rankings of Alliance activists. Many Alliance 
activists recognised that rejoining the EU would be a perk of a UI, 
or it makes the idea of a UI more appealing, but many also suggest 
that Brexit’s impact on NI should not be overhyped, particularly 
given NI remains partly in the EU and NI people still can hold Irish 
passports which award them rights similar to an EU citizen. For 
example, activist (2) says Brexit does make a UI more appealing 
but this is not the determining factor in generating support for a UI 
as a number of benefits are already in place as NI people uniquely 
can choose to designate as Irish and can have an Irish passport, 
which allows them all those conditions like to travel around Europe 
and to skip the lines at the airport. While these material benefits 
may still be protected outside the EU, there are less concrete but 
still meaningful feelings of loss that inform activists’ thinking. Even 
though some recognise that NI still has access to the EU, it still 
induces the activists’ feeling of being detached from a progressive 
entity like the EU. For example, one activist (9) knows NI has ‘not 

 
160
lost’ access to the single market, but recognises ‘the loss’ of feeling 
part of a multilateral setup which those like themselves who have 
a global and outward-looking view on life would crave. Immediately 
after the Brexit vote, some activists were more actively considering 
a UI. In the initial days subsequent to the vote they were tempted 
to campaign to go back in the EU, or they reflected more about how 
if NI just became part of UI, it would be back in the EU. Activist (1) 
shared in the initial days after Brexit, they considered ‘what if we 
just became a united Ireland, we would be back in the 
EU…because ultimately there is a lot of flaws over at the EU, but 
there has been good things that have come from the EU…’. 
However, that was a ‘gut-reaction’, and since then they have not 
really considered cheerleading for constitutional change in the 
same way they might have wanted to immediately after the Brexit 
vote. Mainly some see the Brexit question as an opportunity to vent 
their frustrations at the British government. As one Alliance activist 
(23) says, probably Brexit has made them think about [UI] again 
just in terms of the losses, probably more in ‘their distaste and 
disgust for how this part of the world has been treated by the UK 
Government, as opposed to ‘I am definitely now going to go 
towards a united Ireland’. As well as affecting attitudes to the UK, 
there have also been effects on how some activists think about 
Irishness in a post-Brexit context, even if this is not the sole 
influence. For example, activist (10) explains that Brexit has been 
a part of what has made them think directly about being part of 
Ireland, but so has other aspects such as how their job brought 
them to the ROI and they had family that previously lived in Dublin, 
etc. In this way, Brexit is a secondary influence rather than a 
changepoint. However, in terms of attitude change, Brexit appears 
to have moved Alliance activists towards further engagement with 
the issue, but without them cheerleading for a particular result.  
 
There are alternative avenues through which Brexit can be 
interpreted which can weigh on constitutional preferences too. For 

 
161
some, Brexit is an economic issue, but it can also be seen as a 
cultural issue for others or speak more broadly to a wider sense of 
progressiveness or regression. One Alliance activist (22) considers 
Brexit an economic factor, unless you are a young person, for 
example, where you have experience of Erasmus and it is probably 
more of a cultural thing. Others make a connection between 
progressiveness of the two states and Brexit as illustrative of a 
sense of regression while the ROI has been liberalising, ‘I suppose 
socially, I'd say the Republic has been sort of…more 
progressive…than the direction of travel in the UK, if you know 
what I mean, with Brexit…’ (activist 28). 
 
Stickier, but still 
 
Even if Alliance activists were to more broadly recognise 
that social issues are less sticky (i.e. easier to solve than issues 
such as Brexit) this is not to suggest that activists are currently 
convinced that social issues are ‘fixed’ within either the NI or ROI 
context. Not everyone was strongly convinced of this, despite the 
introduction of the Westminster legislation to make access to 
abortion available in Northern Ireland, or despite their own 
recognition that the ROI has become progressive since its 
distancing from the Catholic Church or since the Repeal the 8th and 
the same-sex marriage referendums. Some recognise that ‘in 
reality’ despite the Westminster legislation, abortion rights and 
services are not being supported in NI. For example, one Alliance 
activist (23) claims that despite abortion being legislated for people 
cannot access reproductive healthcare and other civil liberties in 
NI. Additionally, the ROI’s reputation of being a more progressive 
state is not without some – albeit very little – scepticism from a 
select few activists.  A small few (e.g. 20; 14) still see the ROI as 
conservative-coded, even if they also mentioned more generally 
that the South has taken progressive steps or is generally more 
modern than NI. For example, one Alliance activist (20) says rural 

 
162
Ireland is ‘probably as Catholic and socially non-liberal as it ever 
was’, but the ROI is in parts a European state in a way that 
‘Northern Ireland is a vestige of something from the 1960s’. 
Overall, this is suggestive that there are internal differences of 
opinion on whether old understandings of what the ROI is like and 
concerns about that still apply or not and this may also be important 
and not necessarily 'changed by Brexit.’ 
 
Protocol – party line, and a line to a UI? 
 
Activists had expressive perspectives on Brexit, but when 
asked about the impact of the Protocol on their thinking around a 
UI, they often talked more broadly on the Protocol, that is, how it is 
not new that NI is treated differently to GB, or not new that it is 
difficult to trade into NI (e.g. 18; 7); or how some see the Protocol’s 
varying impacts on businesses. As an explicit example, one 
younger activist (3) says the part they would ‘focus on’ would be 
the decision to leave the EU and the ‘future direction’, rather than 
the Protocol which is just something that has happened as a 
necessity out of the decision to leave the EU. Moreover, potentially 
the way some see the Protocol could be indicative of their UI 
preferences. On one side those who are undecided suppose the 
more issues that the Protocol creates or if politics gets bogged 
down over Protocol negotiations or a hard border is introduced, the 
more appealing it becomes to be one Ireland. However, on the 
other side, a pro-UI activist (36) says a working Protocol would also 
make a UI more straightforward ‘And of course, this is where 
unionists are so worried because a successful implementation 
makes the transition to a united Ireland easier…’ which is more 
about the demonstrative logistical effects from an efficiency point 
of view rather than about the attractiveness of the option. 
 
While there was some discussion as to how the Protocol has 
given advantages to those in NI, activists often in the same answer 

 
163
would talk about how NI ‘could have’ the status of somewhere like 
Monaco, Switzerland or Singapore if a different direction was taken 
in terms of Brexit. For example – ‘To me Northern Ireland could 
have been, could still be, uh, a, like a Singapore. We, we, we could 
be this wonderful, successful, almost a, a countrywide Freeport, we 
have the chance for the best of both worlds. We really do’ (activist 
7). While some describe the protocol as the best of both worlds for 
NI, this is not the perspective of these activists, and the reality of 
the protocol falls well short of these ideals. This also suggests that 
there is still potentially ‘more to gain’ from a UI beyond the realities 
of the protocol so the protocol does not ‘deactivate’ the case for a 
UI as discussed by some above. 
 
The Protocol also functions as something of a boundary 
maker as the Protocol operated as the breaking point for the 
emergence of polarisation as attested to by certain activists. In this 
way, as the Protocol served to reinforce and reactivate traditional 
boundary lines, a referendum and central focus on the CQ could 
well serve as a very heightened version of what was observed with 
the Protocol. Activist (4) says ‘if the economy was shown that it 
would be stronger in an all-Ireland, then possibly, they would be a 
bit more open to engagement because their constituents would be 
telling them that they should be getting involved. But the other side 
of that… and the very, the very obvious and immediate outworking 
of the protocol is that the unionist, uh, electorate are saying to their 
representatives, "You are absolutely right to, to take the stand 
you're taking against the Protocol”.’ Activist (7) similarly argues the 
Protocol is an example of polarisation that becomes potent ‘only 
when it is whipped up by our political class’. There is a clear 
concern that these dynamics and mechanics around the Protocol 
may foreshadow similar developments in the run-up to a 
referendum and harden and polarise identity boundaries. 
 

 
164
Factor 5: The logistics: What Alliance activists want in terms 
of a border poll – when, how and who? 
 
Alliance does not favour extensive speculation on when a 
referendum may occur, and instead Alliance’s Stephen Farry has 
outlined that it is a ‘condition-led’ rather than ‘date-led’ process as 
set out in the GFA (Houses of the Oireachtas, 2021). Alliance 
contends that NI people are more interested in the ‘what’, that is 
what a potential UI would look like, rather than the ‘how’, that is, 
the mechanics around having a border poll (Houses of the 
Oireachtas, 2021, b). However, despite the focus on the actual 
substance of what a UI would look like, Alliance actors do still have 
views on how the process should operate. As Farry outlined, ‘I 
understand the need for a citizens’ assembly as part of that 
process, although we are not at that stage just yet…I would 
suggest…that the best people to do that are in universities, 
colleges and civil society organisations for now’ (Houses of the 
Oireachtas, 2021, c). This contrasts with the GPNI who, as 
discussed in later chapters, emphasise the primacy of citizens’ 
assemblies and advocate moving up the timeframe to prioritise 
having such an assembly sooner rather than later. Although 
Alliance does recognise there are only two options in a referendum, 
Farry at the Joint Committee on the Implementation of the Good 
Friday Agreement (JIGFA) has shown a willingness to talk about 
other models within a single Irish state or some form of shared 
sovereignty from a theoretical/academic perspective, with 
recognition that these models may get more consensus. In light of 
this and given that Alliance emphasise the specific conditions and 
processes that are critical to their support for a border poll, this 
section examines activists’ perspectives on the particular logistical 
details they would like to see to encourage engagement with it. This 
includes the options on the table as well as the mechanics of the 
process (Houses of the Oireachtas, 2021, d). 
 

 
165
Putting a frame around their border poll thinking – take your time? 
 
Todd et al.’s (2024) focus group research on those who are 
undecided on their vote choice in NI and ROI found ‘that most [NI] 
participants who raised the issue of timing argued that referendums 
should not be held in the ‘short term’, but they went on to propose 
a relatively short timeframe’ (e.g. 4 or 5 years, or 2 to 5, or 5 to 10) 
(pp. 140-141). Most Alliance activists not only did not envision a 
referendum for ‘at least’ a decade, but a referendum in five years 
seemed like far too soon for many67. Additionally, many were not 
opposed to a referendum ‘in principle’ (that is, they do not fear one 
because it risks a UI) with many seeing it as an inevitability (even 
if 10-15 years away), but that is not the same as the activists 
thinking that NI is in the best position for a referendum to be held. 
When it comes to NI being ‘ready’ for a referendum, the vast 
majority do not think it is ready now, or it is not quite ready, or it is 
not ready, but getting closer, or it could be ready, but they don’t 
know when that is. For example, Alliance activist (38) thinks it 
would be ready in ‘another 10, 15 years’, or activist (18) says it will 
be, but not now and they don't think it will be in five years, they 
think it could be ‘10 or 15 years away’. Ultimately very few saw NI 
as ready for a referendum now. One Alliance activist (2) recognised 
that maybe NI is being ‘prepared’ for a referendum now, but 
ultimately, this is not the same as them saying that NI is currently 
prepared for it. Activist (2) asks ‘are we being prepared now’, 
saying the question is asked all the time, coming up more and 
more, and it is discussed extensively in the media and publicly. 
Also, there was the recognition that the discussion around a 
referendum is ‘already taking place’ – as one Alliance activist (4) 
says ‘quite frankly it is already taking place in the nationalist 
community anyway, so we need to be in there and part of that’ – 
 
67 Very few activists from the GPNI or Alliance expressed a view that a BP could or 
should happen within five years. A rare exception was GPNI activist (14) who did 
think it was likely there would be a BP within 5 years.  

 
166
but again, this is not the same as an activist saying that NI as a 
whole is ready to engage with the idea of calling a referendum and 
even the activist does not think Alliance should just yet be outlining 
a constitutional position. However, other activists create a sense 
that debating the timeframe does not matter, as a referendum is 
essentially an inevitability at this point (although it would be 
doubtful that they want Sinn Féin pushing this message and 
therefore making a border poll an imminent and central issue). For 
example, one Alliance activist (11) does not think the country will 
ever be ready for a referendum, but it is going to happen either 
way, it might be five or 25 years, but they think in their lifetime it will 
happen.  Whether activists considered a UI as an inevitability or 
not, some expressed that they do not see the point in fighting 
against the inevitability of having to live with either referendum 
result, including living in a UI, if that was the result (and partake in 
conversations around it).  For example, one Alliance activist (26) 
says people will have to, whether they like it or not, learn to live 
with what referendum decision is made. These discussions are not 
confined to Alliance as the GPNI similarly believe the starting gun 
has been fired on the debate, and that the likelihood of a 
referendum 
in 
the 
short-to-medium-term 
has 
significantly 
increased while most Green activists would similarly define NI as 
not being ‘ready’ for a referendum now given the debate is only 
beginning. The GPNI, like Alliance, believe preparations and 
conversations must occur in order for NI to be ‘ready’ for a 
referendum. 
 
 Ultimately, Alliance activists emphasise ‘taking our time’ 
when it comes to the lead-up to any referendum (and also a 
transitionary period if the vote was for a UI) to allow for space for 
the necessary conversations and preparations to take place. For 
example, one Alliance activist (1) does think a referendum will 
happen, but they don’t know whether it will or should as soon as 
some of the nationalist politicians are pushing for, i.e. five to 15 

 
167
years as they worry that would be ‘rushing it’  because you need to
