‘work through’ some of the issues. However, in the same vein, 
some might ask when is the ‘cut-off point’ for Alliance activists, that 
is, when will they feel that NI is sufficiently prepared enough to take 
that vote – not all believe this can be delayed indefinitely (e.g. 
activist 13). 
 
Trigger for a referendum – what you cannot use and a legitimate 
outcome 
 
Alliance activists have strong opinions on what you ‘cannot 
use’ to trigger a referendum. Some like activist (2) said you can’t 
just look at the census figures and say a referendum is needed now 
as there are more Catholics ‘because equally I have friends who 
are Catholics who are happy with the status quo’. Other activists 
also said who is elected to the Assembly cannot be used as a 
trigger to call for a referendum because parties who designate as 
Other do not take a CP (e.g. activist 14). Also, while there is an 
acceptance from activists that it is up to the Secretary of State 
(‘SoS’) to call the referendum there is sympathy with those who 
think this is an unfair process. For example, one activist (1) thinks 
it is ‘hard to swallow’ for people with an Irish identity that this is the 
SoS’s call. However, there is also a ‘democratic line’ that even if 
the majority want a UI, and the rest don’t, several note the majority 
should win the day. As one activist (9) notes, ‘that’s just the nature 
of democracy’. However, while this is democratically legitimate, it 
constitutes a bare majority. It seems to clash with Alliance’s ethos 
to be satisfied with the bare majority supporting a UI in this way as 
Alliance strongly emphasises the need to maximise cross-
community support wherever possible. It similarly appears to clash 
with this ethos to define the threshold of being ‘ready’ for a 
referendum as simply that there are more nationalists than 
unionists in NI, which is how a surprisingly significant number of 
activists describe ‘readiness’. Although even the activist (9) who 

 
168
said that a UI can be won on 50% plus one vote still appears to tie 
a legitimate outcome to having a worked-out plan for a UI as well 
as achieving this simple majority threshold. They said, ‘we need to 
know what sort of health service we are going to work within, how 
Stormont is going to function…so all of that sort of stuff needs to 
be worked out before we go to a border poll and then we go for 50 
plus 1, it is a legitimate outcome’. Another activist (4) is more 
explicit in critiquing the 50% plus one even if they see it as 
democratically legitimate. However, they again want clarity and 
preparation beforehand to allow for a legitimate outcome, and they 
think more broadly people need to be brought along (again this a 
somewhat vague Alliance term): ’We need to have brought 
everybody along with us to a position, not that we should say yes 
to a UI but, we’re agreeing on what Northern Ireland should be like 
in the future and once we have that, then we can have the border 
poll as then the answer will actually be legitimate whether its 
remaining in status quo or united Ireland’. While accepting a bare 
majority voting mechanism, activists seek to reconcile this with the 
Alliance ethos by also building a clear framework for a UI in 
combination with this. 
 
There seems to be a common assumption among activists 
that nationalists themselves are being told by nationalist parties, or 
they commonly believe that if a referendum is called then 
automatically, they will get a UI because they are being told 
repeatedly that they would get their prize (activists 7; 15). Activists 
are though sceptical of this and worry about this as the basis for a 
strong push to trigger a referendum now as in reality, this level of 
support is not in place as not all of those from a CNR background 
alone, never mind the centre-ground, support a UI. As activist 7 
says ‘the nationalist community, because they are being told, 
repeatedly told that if we had a border poll, which is theirs by 
right…they would get their…United Ireland…I don't think it's true 
yet…I do think it would result in a staying within the UK for the next 

 
169
period, because I don't think that all Catholics want to leave the 
United Kingdom’. 
 
Need everyone at the table 
 
Several activists think even unionists see a referendum is 
on the horizon, ‘…even for …unionists there’s an understanding 
that since Brexit that there is a border poll on the way at some 
point…and there’s more people preparing for that…’ (activist 3). 
However, while certain activists think unionists see a referendum 
as on its way, they also recognise how unionists are still excluded 
from the constitutional conversations happening, or emphasise 
their inclusion in future referendum talks is paramount. However, 
arguably, certain Alliance activists are (unintentionally) awarding 
unbalanced power to unionists to sway the direction of the 
constitutional debate by only seeing conversations around a 
referendum as having value if unionists or their representatives are 
engaged with. As activist (2) outlines, ‘So I think they need to 
involve, you know, you need to have everyone in the room. There’s 
no point a nationalist party going off, having these conversations, 
deciding what the rules are. It needs to be done in consultation with 
all of the key parties’. Also, activists’ understanding of why 
unionists are not partaking in the current constitutional 
conversations (e.g. Ireland’s Future) are not consistent. Some 
seem to put more blame on the unionists/leaders themselves for 
not participating, while others explain that the constitutional 
conversations are not welcoming environments, as they are 
sometimes framed by a narrative that a UI is the only outcome that 
could come from a referendum68. For one activist (24) this does not 
take away the responsibility of the pro-UI side to accommodate 
unionism. They would not expect unionists to partake in these 
 
68 As mentioned in the case selection of the methodology chapter, this was a reason 
that Alliance refused an invitation to the New Ireland Forum in 1984. 

 
170
constitutional conversations, for those who want a New Ireland, it 
is their argument to make ‘…It is for them to make the sacrifices 
that they think are suitable and reach out, like to say “Even though 
we know you are not taking part in our discussions, we know this 
is the point of most concern”’.  
 
However, there is a difference between wanting unionists to 
partake in the conversation, and expecting them or forcing them to. 
Very few activists even acknowledge that unionists are ‘slowly 
beginning’ to engage in the constitutional conversations, that is, it 
seems a long way off for many – aside from one activist (28) who 
is a rarity in suggesting that the unionists are starting to engage:  
‘the groundwork of that has started, like you see people that are 
Ulster unionists maybe going to the Feile or they would be get 
involved in panel discussions around this’. There may be 
alternative avenues outside of the traditional nationalist parties and 
classic arguments that could facilitate engagement with the CQ 
and a referendum by unionists. For example, Alliance member (6) 
thinks that Ireland’s Future / United UK (civic groups) are generally 
good at presenting a case for the UK or a UI, but in a way that is 
not party political or reliant on the old flag-waving arguments:  ‘Like, 
there's a lot of talk about, for example, the fact that a united Ireland, 
maybe we get back into the EU, so here's all the economic benefits. 
Whereas, the UK ones generally say, "Well, the UK is the fifth or 
sixth-largest economy. It's a member of NATO, the UN Security 
Council, a lot of these are really able to put aside the old debate”’. 
In addition, potentially, some activists might think reframing the 
conversation to not only focus on a UI and Union option, but also 
to focus on rejoining the EU, rather than rejoining the ROI (via a 
UI) may be effective in enticing more diverse communities to 
engage with the issue. However, one activist (20) recognised that 
theme would not be considered so neutral by loyalism. They 
explain that Alliance did not want to partake in the ‘Ireland’s Future’ 
conference on the basis that there is a preconceived outcome, but 

 
171
recognises if you were to say, let’s have a conference about how 
NI could come back into Europe, that would please those in 
Alliance, but ultimately ‘scare’ committed loyalists.  
 
Some Alliance activists were asked how they believe the 
conversations around a referendum can be made a comfortable 
space for unionism but there was little in the way of a systematic 
reply. It is clear that they want this but don’t know how to actually 
do it – apart from avoiding conversations like Ireland’s Future that 
assumes a UI is the only potential outcome. Stephen Farry has 
separately focused on the ‘facilitators’ and as above, there is a 
focus here on civil actors – ‘the more it can be established that 
discussions are being facilitated by independent or impartial 
facilitators, particularly in civic society and academia, the more 
chance there is in the short run to get civic unionist actors at least 
to engage’ (Houses of the Oireachtas, 2021, e). Most say it is 
possible and preferable to seek to engage unionist civil society 
activists to take part in discussions and in research if it is not a 
campaigning group, but neutral or academic.  
 
Who has Responsibility? Governments, the UI campaign, or 
Alliance?  
 
There is significant debate as to where responsibility lies in 
determining who should develop the proposal for a referendum, the 
options on the table, timeline, and proposed transition process 
afterwards if there is a pro-UI outcome. This could be understood 
as a ‘process model’ where the Irish state is afforded substantial 
responsibility in the preparation, implementation, and potential 
transition from a referendum. This would mean the Irish 
government would have responsibility more broadly in leading the 
conversation and process. However, there are also alternatives 
which variously emphasise Irish and British government 
engagement before a potential referendum with a stronger role for 

 
172
the British government as the SoS is responsible under the GFA 
for calling a referendum, or shifting responsibility to the wider pro-
UI campaign to specify a process, set out the terms of any options 
and outline a transition model. There are also proposals for civil 
society and academic institutions to play a major role in the 
development of options and specification of potential processes to 
hold and transition from a referendum. In light of this, Alliance 
activists were asked to consider how they assess who is afforded 
responsibility and any potential consequences for Alliance’s role in 
the process.  
 
For Alliance activists when it comes to the responsibility around 
preparing for a referendum, the weight seems to go towards the 
Irish government or the pro-UI side (or both). However, Alliance 
activists were not arguing that the British government has no role 
in preparation, but broadly some potentially think the Irish and 
British government could have different roles which could in turn 
be differently weighted, for instance, the Irish government could 
have more of a ‘framing role’ for what a UI would look like while GB 
would have greater responsibility for handling the financial side. 
One activist (23) notes it is important to ensure that the British 
government is there to support the people who have made that 
decision that this is going to be an all-Ireland decision and that they 
really need to be behind that and ensuring that there is nothing that 
they are doing that would be potentially aiding that small cohort of 
people who would not want that for ideological, rather than 
pragmatic reasons. This is also a common theme among GPNI 
activists. For example, Green activist (23) also noted that ‘the 
British government would be less happy to have that conversation 
about a border poll than the Irish government hopefully would be’.  
 
However, others are clear that – even though the Irish 
government might be more open to a referendum – the British 
government still has an important role in facilitating the change if 

 
173
the result was a UI and as such responsibility cannot solely fall on 
the 
ROI 
government. 
In 
particular, 
there 
should 
be 
intergovernmental engagement in this process. British and Irish 
government engagement would though be particularly difficult if the 
British government is particularly unionist-leaning or the Irish 
government is ‘very’ nationalist. There is then an assumption and 
necessity that the two governments engage in good faith not 
dissimilar to the need for such good faith in the collaboration on the 
Protocol. This likely requires a considered, slower and thoughtful 
process to be effective and not to generate destabilising effects. 
This need to ‘tip-toe’ puts off another activist from the idea of both 
governments (and even Alliance) publicly talking about and 
prepping for a UI. Activist (28) thinks discussions are probably 
going on behind closed doors about how this assumed UI might 
look, but for anything to happen in the public sphere, it is too soon: 
‘sort of the British government are found to be in discussions 
around this, you know, they're, "Oh, you're looking to get rid of 
us?”.’ They also think the Irish government need to be careful too:  
‘if they push too hard too soon they're in the same position as us 
[Alliance], they're going to be accused by the unionists of, "This is 
what you want. This is what you've been after all along”.’  
 
However, as two activists illustrate, the approach of the 
governments to a referendum speaks to how certain party activists 
understand the appropriateness of Alliance starting to develop its 
own policy on a referendum (although as mentioned in the previous 
chapter, most would not be on board with the party at least 
publicising a policy). Alliance activist (14) suggests that the idea of 
the party developing a general policy around a referendum would 
be meaningful only once the state has afforded a referendum to 
Ireland because otherwise none of the policy discussions could 
actually be brought about in reality: ‘this question is more…for 
the…Irish government… you know, rather than Alliance. I 
think…the Irish government really has to be the ones that are, like, 

 
174
organising this to a certain degree because…Alliance could have 
policies on this. But unless….it’s actually going to be the state 
affording it in Ireland…It would be essentially just like a think tank’. 
Alternatively, it may be appropriate for Alliance to develop a policy 
once the governments have decided on the broader post-
referendum settlement. For example, one activist (13) thinks when 
it is not even known what the financial settlement with the UK and 
system of governmental/political structures would look like, they 
are unsure how you can begin to frame meaningful policy. This 
could be understood potentially as two stages to the process with 
differential responsibility in each stage. The Irish government is 
expected to play the lead role in Stage 1 in the run-up to a potential 
referendum with a more equal share of responsibility in Stage 2 
following a potential referendum with a UI outcome where the two 
governments must then work to manage the transition politically, 
socially and economically. However, this point about the need for 
a sense of the settlement afterwards means that while the Irish 
government is afforded primary responsibility to play the lead in 
Stage 1 this does not mean everyone agrees that the British 
government is 'off the hook' until Stage 2 even if it is 'less 
responsible' in Stage 1 than the Irish government.  
 
Some think that not only do the Irish and British 
governments need to be open and ready for a UI if that was the 
result, but believe the Irish parties need to be ready for a UI too 
where all the different ROI parties need to be in agreement around 
what a UI looks like, or ready to start the work should that be the 
result. This is of course particularly relevant to Stage 1 where the 
Irish state has to play the lead role, and Alliance activists see the 
challenges in this. For example, activist (9) thinks it probably needs 
to be an agreement from FF/FG/SF on this before a referendum, 
so that regardless of what happens in terms of national elections 
in the ROI ‘we have a pretty good idea of what the policy space is 
going to look like’. Another activist (21) questions if the different 

 
175
pro-UI political parties even in the ROI (e.g. SF, FF, FG, etc.) 
cannot even agree on a single vision of a UI, how is everyone 
across the divide going to agree. The activist says if the pro-UI 
parties with their own views/recommendations on a UI across the 
island are not even ready to sit down and agree on one single 
vision and be ready for that then they ‘don't know how they're going 
to sit everyone down right across the political divide’. This ties back 
to the wider pattern in which Alliance activists see many conditions 
as needed for a referendum process that they are comfortable with 
and some of these conditions are not just in NI, but in ROI politics 
too especially given the significant responsibility that activists 
afford to the Irish government in leading this process as above. The 
Shared Island unit is a potential example of this, but much of the 
work as above may be better afforded to civic society in the ROI 
given the preference for and evidence of the greater effectiveness 
of civic-led processes discussed previously. 
 
Factor 6: Stability and reconciliation – fitting these within 
activists’ constitutional perspectives 
 
Institutional stability 
 
A non-functioning Stormont, or one resistant to reform, is 
often perceived as something that would make a UI more 
appealing. However, ultimately, the Alliance activist who was 
interviewed after Stormont returned after collapsing did not think it 
impacted their vote, but it proved a referendum’s inevitability to 
them. This activist (24) did not think it changed their view of 
whether they would vote or not vote for a UI, but it has changed 
their view that at some point it is inevitable that there will be a 
referendum and perhaps a UI at some point and if anything, it has 
made them more aware of how strategic some of the parties like 
SF are. A reformed Stormont might be considered one that allows 
for stability to prevent a scenario where there is not enough trust 

 
176
between parties to keep to their word in terms of a post-referendum 
result. Activist (6) thinks a stable and consistent government and 
political system is key so that whenever the result comes in there 
is the respect from politicians to implement the result, as ‘you 
wouldn't want [an] American scenario where one side refuses to 
accept and it all falls apart’. However, it appears that activists do 
not have much faith in other parties to be able to tackle the 
complexities of a UI. Some in particular express this as ‘NI can’t 
even do X (e.g. agree on education, get government working on 
something resolvable) so how could we NI or NI and ROI, ever do 
Y (e.g. agree on education for the whole-island, have a mature 
conversation on bigger issues). One activist (18) says ‘so if we 
cannot come to a decision about an 11-plus, how in the hell on the 
whole island are we ever going to come to a decision about what 
our education system looks like, and that is just one aspect’. 
Similarly, it does feel to one activist (13) that in NI as it is difficult to 
get the government up and running now over issues that to them 
seem easily resolvable, the idea that there can be a move beyond 
to deal with bigger questions feels a long way off. Activists (40; 28) 
also contend that not only would a functioning executive 
demonstrate that NI can work but allowing SF and nationalists to 
take the First Minister role and pass legislation like the Irish 
Language Act would allow Irish identifiers to feel more effectively 
accommodated in NI potentially reducing support for the need for 
a UI69. There is then a sense that institutional (in)stability is both 
potentially driving support for a referendum/UI, but also could be 
illustrative of the problems of seeking to engage with debate on the 
CI in the context of a referendum. In turn, one activist (21) explains 
that in NI, there is division between and within parties on all sides 
of the divide, so it is difficult to see how the nationalists, unionists, 
or Alliance themselves could be ready for a referendum and 
‘coalesce around one single idea’ externally or indeed internally. 
 
69The Executive has since been restored with SF’s Michelle O’Neill as First Minister. 

 
177
This may mean that beyond the stability of governmental 
institutions in NI, the parties as institutions themselves may 
struggle to hold together if they face a shock like having to prepare 
for and deal with referendum given, they are already divided. It is 
particularly striking that this activist at least sees this as a potential 
issue within Alliance. One potential reason for this is that the 
discussions of a referendum are currently happening in the 
abstract and the responses of activists are themselves often to 
hypothetical scenarios. There are in essence a variety of 
competing abstract visions of what a referendum/UI would involve. 
If instead the party was involved in a set of meetings on for example 
the 11+ or GP services, or  LGBT+ rights and was presented with 
a formal proposal from the Irish government as to how these would 
be dealt with, then they would have something specific to say yes 
or no to, or to propose an alternative to and this may itself mean 
that the party’s decision-making processes can be followed in 
responding which may itself be the key to maintaining cohesion.  
 
Societal stability 
 
 
As mentioned, Alliance would rather focus on making NI as 
good as it can be regardless of the constitutional status. For 
Alliance, they ask how NI can focus on moving forward towards 
constitutional change before it itself as a society is reconciled. It 
appears for certain activists that a reconciled NI is one which is 
more appealing for the ROI or UK. For instance, one Alliance 
activist (20) says until NI can sort out its issues internally as a 
segregated society, put an end to the legacies of the past, and 
create an integrated society between all communities, then NI is an 
‘unappetising’ partner for anybody else. A reconciled NI is also for 
some activists an NI ready to talk about a referendum. For 
example, one activist (12) implies that NI as a place still defined by 
deprivation and social isolation cannot have ‘a peaceful or sensible 
discussion about a border poll’. However, it also appears that a 

 
178
referendum ‘followed by’ a status quo result - not necessarily the 
status quo constitutional status on its own - can in a way provide 
Alliance activists with what they want in terms of a more stabilised 
society. This is because some see that for a window at least, the 
constitutional issue does not dominate or distract NI. For example, 
one activist (14) thinks if it was a big victory for the union, like 40/60, 
it would shut down the conversation and there is potential there for 
more stability for a condensed period. Another activist (13) similarly 
revealed that a clear status quo verdict in a referendum would allow 
for these major questions to be put to bed in such a manner as to 
allow for a focus on making NI work. Of course, in reality, it is not 
necessarily the case that a referendum with a 60/40 or similar 
margin would actually generate long-term ‘closure’. However, 
many activists would not see this condensed period of ‘stability’ as 
long-lasting and some also could see a scenario after a status quo 
result like the Scottish independence referendum where it will 
create continuous cycles of referendums, which itself is 
destabilising (e.g. activist 13). On balance, this instability may not 
persist necessarily to quite the same degree. There is likely a key 
role here for how close the result ultimately is of any (initial) 
referendum in shaping the scope and schedule for future 
referendums subsequently. For example, Alliance activist (14) says 
if there is a vote 45/55 or closer (in favour of the status quo), 
subsequent polls would be every seven years, which may play a 
role in making a UI a reality and actually be more beneficial in terms 
of planning for this in the longer-term.  
 
 
For a small number of activists, there is a view that at some 
point in the future, it will become natural that people would want a 
UI or naturally obvious when people would want a UI without even 
the need for a referendum. For example, Alliance activist (4) says 
‘In fact, we should get to the stage where a border poll actually is 
not necessary, that it's just obvious that's what everybody wants or 
doesn't want’. In this scenario, the ideal situation is NI gets to a 

 
179
point where it does not even need a referendum because it will be 
obvious after people are brought together in a more integrated NI 
whether a UI is the right option or not, and so in this scenario where 
all questions are answered than there should be very little violence 
after a referendum. Similarly, activist (27) feels that if there is an 
evolution towards ‘more common sense…all living properly side by 
side’, a focus on jobs, housing and education then a referendum 
can happen without any major issues as it will follow from a natural 
consensus. While this is not a common view and is necessarily 
somewhat idealistic, it may explain why some in Alliance set many 
conditions for a referendum as they believe 'ideally' a UI would just 
emerge as a 'natural view' rather than it being a competitive clash 
of positions through an intense and potentially divisive debate and 
referendum process. In turn, this may partially be a means of 
explaining the understanding of neutrality for some in Alliance as 
there is, in this view, no need to take a position and compromise 
neutrality for a referendum when a preferable ‘natural’ transition to 
a UI could take place later. An alternative way to interpret similar 
comments from activists is that Alliance believe the referendum 
debate distracts from work on societal reconciliation and stability 
and functioning institutions which if all in place would produce 
'natural' transition to UI later. Specifically, if there is school 
integration and all-island cooperation then the conditions emerge 
for this type of more ‘straightforward’ transition. For example, an 
Alliance activist (5) who is pro-UI and Irish even thinks bigger 
conditions like all-island development and cross-border integration 
needs to occur before it is a good move for Alliance to take a CP 
(which by this logic would be a pro-UI position) and would occur in 
the context of a wider ‘natural’ transition rather than a majoritarian 
referendum. 
 
Political versus people 
 
Todd et al’s (2022) study on ‘moderates’ found how they 

 
180
tended to be distant from ‘politicians’: ‘politicians as a group were 
almost universally referred to using “they” and sentiment toward 
politicians was generally quite negative’ (p. 892). However – apart 
from one activist (7) who interrupts their thought process to 
remember that they are actually part of the political classes – 
‘…and therefore our political class, of which I'm one I shouldn't 
forget’ despite being ‘politicians’ themselves, they generally speak 
about politicians (or political leaders) as a separate group from 
themselves. Several activists in particular separate politicians and 
‘the people’ of Northern Ireland by maturity, as most of the time 
they see Northern Irish society as more mature than the politicians 
they vote for. Another activist (22), suggests most of the progress 
in Northern Ireland (e.g., it is more openly LGBTQ+-friendly than 
before and it is more of a metropolitan society) has been in spite of 
the politicians and the government because Northern Ireland is a 
very resilient, resourceful, and adaptable population. However, this 
is not to say that Alliance activists do not see constitutional issues 
as still a major driver for voters and ‘the people’, but many instead 
see these issues as becoming less salient in NI. Although it does 
appear that certain activists see the Protocol and also the collapse 
of Stormont as something that is making ‘the people’, or at least 
unionists, less reconciled to current conditions. The Protocol is not 
really impacting the activists’ own views of their identity but they 
still see how it is a source of tension. Even though they think that 
the people of NI are quite resilient and get on, the previous activist 
(22) thinks that people currently are very polarised because of the 
Protocol and as Stormont was collapsed70, and to then engage in 
what will ultimately be a polarising referendum is a bad idea. 
Another Alliance activist, activist (4) thinks unionists ultimately are 
generally a pragmatic lot, but with the Protocol the unionist 
electorate are saying to their representatives, ‘you are right to take 
your stand against the Protocol’, so it just shows that ‘we have a

long way to go to bring them into the conversation’ around a 
referendum. 
 
Structural stability 
 
In line with the findings of Todd et al (2022, p.892) on 
moderates, this thesis finds that on average, there is a greater 
degree of criticism currently levelled at the DUP than SF by Alliance 
activists. However, this is not to suggest that Alliance activists are 
not critical of SF particularly in the context of their rhetoric around 
a referendum and potential UI, but SF and nationalism is currently 
seen as more progressive and in line with Alliance positions than 
conservative Unionism. At a more personal-level, some say that 
they, or others, don’t identify with ‘either’ side because one is 
associated with IRA violence and the other with stubbornness or 
conservativeness. For example, one activist (1) said, ‘Because at 
this moment in time, especially for people I'm seeing, it's like, ‘Oh 
God, don't say…I'm a unionist because, you know…that 
associates me with…Ian Paisley and the DUP. And don't say I'm a 
nationalist because…that's the IRA and Sinn Féin’. Another 
Alliance activist (24) said if someone asked them are they British 
or Irish, they would say Northern Irish because they do not define 
themselves with either of the others, for them, one side is 
conservatively Christian and the other side has violence associated 
with it. However, in both these examples (1; 24) the 
‘Irish/nationalist’ side is described as associated more with 
paramilitaries and violence, even if the activists see both sides as 
having ‘bad’ connotations. However, when it comes to a 
referendum, activists’ collective assessment is that extreme 
Loyalism would be more likely to cause havoc than the nationalist-
side (CNR) or if the result did not go their way, although many 
viewed civil unrest as likely to happen ‘regardless’ of the vote 
outcome. This evaluation is partly based on how some think those 
from more extreme wings of Loyalism would be more likely to take 

 
182
up arms. Activist (23) guesses, those who aspired to have a UI 
would be disheartened if there is a status quo result, but they do 
not know that they would be taking to arms, unlike potentially those 
from a PUL background. Given this, it should be noted that even if 
Alliance activists are not as ‘balanced’ in their evaluations of the 
unionist-side versus the nationalist-side when it comes to civil 
unrest, there is also a perception that loyalist paramilitarism is not 
‘organised enough’ potentially to cause major security breaches or 
chaos. That is, they may think that the loyalist-side would be more 
likely to cause unrest, but in reality, they won’t be able to do so to 
any great extent. For example, one Alliance activist (4) says ‘quite 
frankly loyalists are not particularly well-organised…they don't 
have the same idealism as the Provisional IRA…they are simply 
reactionary’. Another activist (9) thinks the security situation, which 
would primarily be reactionary violence from loyalist paramilitary 
groups, is a major concern, but they don’t think these groups would 
be able to ‘organise in a significant way that would cause upset to 
the security services but they’d cause a lot of harm and damage as 
well’. The overall evaluation that any major challenges to stability, 
if they do arise, would primarily come from Loyalism is also based 
on how some mention that nationalists would largely go down a 
constitutional avenue rather than a dissident republican route 
should the result be the status quo, and/or dissident mobilisation 
would not get support (e.g. activists 15; 9). 
 
Factor 7: Wooing or winning over Alliance? 
 
Who is ‘wooing’ the centre-ground?  
 
O'Malley (2023) identified that ‘Professor Duncan Morrow, 
former Alliance Party chair, cautions that the increase in support 
for a border poll among some Alliance voters signified a comfort 
level with an Ireland led by moderate leaders such as Leo Varadkar 

 
183
and Simon Coveney, but an Ireland led by Sinn Féin would be 
another matter’ (p. 8). However, while the activists in this sample 
might be more comfortable with these ‘moderate leaders’ under a 
UI, it is not that they would necessarily be satisfied with these 
centre-right parties in power under a unified model. For example, 
one Alliance activist (15) would be put off from a UI led by a SF 
government and is reticent towards SF both because of their 
history and their position on the Troubles, but also, they practically 
find SF difficult to work with. However, this activist (15) and another 
activist (20) who also seemed very apprehensive regarding a SF-
led UI, do not want to create a perception that by being reticent 
towards SF, that they are pro-FF and pro-FG. The activist (20) 
notes it is not that they are an FF ‘fan’ in the sense that ‘Micheál 
Martin is a nice person, but that's just the perspective of this side 
of the border’. The other activist (15) is no big fan of FF and FG 
either and sees them as somewhat conservative in many ways, 
although they are not as bad as the UK Conservative Party. 
Interestingly this activist self-defines as more left, but appears to 
prefer the centre-right parties to SF, if they had to pick. 
 
 
While a UI led by a SF government could be a ‘deterrent’ for 
Alliance activists to support a UI, there may be a slight perception 
that, at least currently, SF are doing a better job at ‘attracting the 
vote’ of those undecided in Alliance (and the undecided more 
generally). For example, one Alliance activist, (36) said that ‘Sinn 
Féin in particular are wooing that middle ground and the unionist 
side are attacking me as [part of] the pan-nationalist front’. 
Nonetheless the activist (24) knows since Stormont has been back 
both SF and the DUP leader are acting more strategically as they 
know the last place to get votes is from the centre and the actions 
of both parties can push and pull them through their tone and 
actions on distinct issues. However, the activist also seemed 
particularly convinced that SF is taking on characteristics of 
Alliance and SF is seeking to align with Alliance positions not the 

 
184
other way around, and unionists are only beginning to respond. 
However, it is possible that what could ‘turn off’ Alliance from Sinn 
Féin is its use of language and tone, as for example John Blair 
MLA’s criticism in the media of SF for the ‘tiocfaidh ár lá’ speech71: 
‘for anyone in our society who identifies as British and who is told 
by Sinn Féin they will be welcome in a united Ireland, this speech 
will be seen as nothing but offensive and hyperbolic rhetoric’ (Irish 
News, 2019, b). Alliance see the need for Irish nationalism to tone 
down the discussion of the IRA and the inevitability of a UI (e.g. 
activist 36) or the aggressive pushing of a UI (e.g. activist 15). It 
will be key to SF’s strategic engagement with the centre-ground as 
to whether they can adopt a discourse that does not engender 
opposition or critical reaction like this while still mobilising its base 
with rhetoric activating identity.  
 
 
Although potentially since these interviews, contemporary 
political unionism is doing a better job at representing a form of 
unionism that would be attractive to Alliance activists. According to 
a February 2025 LucidTalk poll (Belfast Telegraph, 2025), the DUP 
Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly had a 47% approval 
rating with Alliance Party voters, making her the most popular DUP 
minister among Alliance supporters at that time [although in March 
2025 Alliance deputy leader Eoin Tennyson blamed the DUP for 
the slow pace of delivery from the Executive]. One Alliance activist 
(6) suggests the civic groups on the ‘unionist side’ rather than the 
unionist parties are putting effort into ‘wooing’ them. The activist 
senses many pro-union civic groups probably are not as connected 
to unionist parties as they are keener to reach out and say ‘we want 
to persuade you to stay in the UK’, whereas maybe unionist 
politicians feel they do not see the need to debate as, “we are 
safe”’’ as these parties instead feel that the result will be remain in 
 
71 This was in response to the use of the phrase by Sinn Féin's Martina Anderson in the 
context of potential border checks at a hunger strike memorial rally in 2019. 

 
185
the UK and this lack of engagement from the parties is also 
potentially cited by others (e.g. activist 36). Potentially Alliance 
questions whether the DUP realise their mistakes and harm 
induced for themselves following from Brexit, which could lead to 
strategic learning ahead of a referendum and alterations to strategy 
if this self-reflection had occurred or if these patterns are more 
ingrained, the self-harm of the Brexit approach for the DUP may be 
re-enacted. 
 
 
The extent to which some Alliance activists are being 
‘wooed’ by the pro-union perspective is conditioned by how they 
interpret the meaning of Britishness as connected to support for 
the union in a referendum. The activist (23) says probably most 
people tend to go with the status quo (i.e. would support it in a 
referendum) as it is what they know, it is not necessarily a 
‘preference or a love for king and country and flag...’. One Alliance 
activist (14) believes there may be some role of symbols of 
Britishness in underpinning their attachment to the union but is 
likely only to exert a partial role. They say that the very fact they 
are used to seeing the Union Jack in the unionist area that they 
currently live in means they, at least, will be more aware of any 
changes to symbols under a UI than someone who grew up in a 
nationalist area, even if said symbols do not mean too much to 
them anyway, as they ‘don't particularly care for flying of either flag 
on public property’. This means while there may be some 
attachment to these visible illustrations of British identity this is not 
necessarily a determinant of how they will approach a choice 
between the union and UI. Also, even if an activist feels more 
comfortable with one symbol over another, this does not mean they 
are not open to change should the constitutional settlement 
change. One strategy to enhance the capacity to ‘sell’ the union 
argument is to position advocates of this position as ‘pro-union’ 
rather than as unionist given the potential political connotations 
(e.g. activist 22). Even if the pro-union side, or unionist NI 

 
186
politicians are not particularly ‘off-putting’, if the activists have a 
negative view of the ‘union’ defined by British politicians that also 
might influence whether they are being ‘wooed’ to the union over a 
UI. More generally, while many activists did not like ROI politicians, 
there seems to be a particular distrust for, or lack of belief in, UK 
politicians. For example, one activist (7) seems to suggest they can 
believe in the Irish electoral system and government, but less so 
the Westminster system and avoids Westminster politicians in 
general. Another activist (36) said they ‘have had their fill of English 
politicians’.  
 
Wooing is not winning! 
 
Again, it is important to reiterate it is not necessarily that 
nationalists and the pro-UI side have ‘won’ Alliance activists over 
and there is no clear overall majority, but there is some partial 
evidence for movement in this direction as recent survey research 
found Alliance members are more pro-united Ireland compared to 
previous survey research (Tonge et al., 2024, p. 167). There is not 
even a consensus around which option (i.e., remaining in the UK 
union or a UI), is more ‘sellable’. For example, some think a UI or 
New Ireland is easier to sell as this is a new option, while others 
think it is at least easier to sell the status quo because it is less of 
an unknown, as previously discussed. Specifically, one activist (24) 
said the status quo is always more difficult to defend as being able 
to discuss a new alternative is always more straightforward as 
nobody actually knows what it is. Alternatively, though, one activist 
(6) says ‘when you're defending the status quo, it would probably 
be easier because you know what it's going to be like’. It appears 
most Alliance activists would follow the line of making NI work first 
which could in turn imply support for the status quo at least in the 
medium-term and ties back to the pattern of Alliance emphasising 
both the need for the right conditions for a referendum/UI, but also 
on making NI work as the priority. For activist (15) for example, 

 
187
there are a range of policy issues in the short-to-medium term that 
can be addressed in NI under the current arrangement as well as 
wider governance issues that would have a more significant impact 
on people’s lives than making a constitutional change to a UI and 
these issues in NI in the near-term should then be the priority. 
Again, a key element here is how a ‘United Ireland’ or ‘New Ireland’ 
is defined and interpreted as the understanding and framing of 
these options generates differential responses. For example, 
activist 23 was extremely on board with the idea of a New Ireland. 
The interpretations of these options and the how they are 
understood is likely to influence what is more sellable to Alliance 
and the centre-ground.  
 
Conclusion 
 
This chapter has explored key factors through which 
Alliance Party activists expect to deliberate when confronted with 
a referendum on a UI. The evidence does not support a simple or 
uniform picture, but several significant conclusions emerge. First, 
while Alliance activists genuinely see themselves as pragmatic, 
evidence-based deliberators, this self-image requires qualification. 
They are candid about how background and socialisation impacts 
their constitutional thinking, and their neutrality reflects a specific 
configuration of values rather than indifference. Second, economic 
performance and healthcare arrangements are widely seen as 
central to deliberation, but activists lack the credible, detailed 
information needed to reach confident assessments. Many feel this 
informational deficit extends to the wider public debate, and see 
Alliance's perceived neutrality as placing it in a key role in relaying 
such information. 
 
Third, accommodating the unionist community is a genuine 
and non-negotiable priority for most activists, even those 

 
188
personally distanced from unionist identity. This reflects both party 
values and personal backgrounds, though some underlying 
assumptions about unionist concerns may warrant more critical 
examination. Fourth, Brexit is a significant yet not decisive factor, 
whose weight will depend on the political context at the time of any 
poll. The evidence substantially qualifies the view that Brexit has 
been or will be a straightforward driver of constitutional 
reconsideration among the centre-ground.  
 
Fifth, activists hold demanding views about the process, 
timing, and conditions for a legitimate border poll, rooted in 
commitments to inclusion of unionism. In more extreme forms, 
however, these conditions risk indefinitely deferring serious 
engagement with the question. Sixth, institutional and societal 
stability are seen as prerequisites for a referendum, with activists 
emphasising the need for solid foundations in Northern Ireland's 
political culture before any transition is attempted. Finally, Alliance 
activists constitute a heterogeneous and genuinely persuadable 
constituency, one not easily directed by party leadership and 
therefore a challenge for any actor hoping to move them decisively 
in either direction. Winning them over will require not tribal appeals, 
but patient, credible, and detailed articulation of what each 
constitutional outcome would mean for everyday life in NI. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
189
Chapter 5: GPNI activists’ conceptual markers: Just 
a Bunch of Civic Environmentalists? 
 
Introduction 
 
This chapter examines how the non-ethnic, constitutionally 
neutral orientation, but fundamental focus on issues and taking 
clear issue positions together manifest among the activists of the 
GPNI. While constitutional neutrality and non-ethnic alignment are 
conceptual markers shared between both parties of the centre-
ground, for the GPNI there is also a key role for the party’s strong 
issue orientations. As an issue-based party, the working-class 
focus of the party intersects with this issue orientation. In particular, 
it explores how GPNI activists navigate internal class cleavages, 
distinct ideological commitments, issue ownership and party brand 
identity, constitutional issue engagement, and the relative position 
of the Greens versus Alliance as the proverbial ‘middleman’ in the 
changing constitutional climate.  
 
Manifestation 1: The intersection of class and ethno-
nationalism in the GPNI 
 
A. Conceptual Markers – Working-class Focus and Non-
alignment 
 
Working-class Brand and the De-alignment from Sect 
 
The issue-based GPNI faces specific electoral challenges in 
NI where ethno-nationalism is prioritised over class issues. 
Working classes in NI tend to not act on their ‘critical understanding 
of the interests and grievances that they share’ given the focus on 
the well-established ‘imagined communities’ (Coulter, 1999, p. 93). 
However, there are certain class dimensions to wider NI politics in 
which more middle-class and working-class voters vote for the 

 
190
SDLP and UUP and SF and DUP respectively. In this sense, there 
is a version of classic class consciousness present in NI, which 
largely operates within the national identity blocs whereas the 
GPNI places a more independent emphasis on class issues. 
However, this reflection assumes that the GPNI is an ‘outlet’ for 
working-class politics, but not all activists were at least initially 
convinced by the party’s working-class credentials. For example, 
one GPNI activist (11) was turned off from joining the party when 
they were younger because those they met who were the same 
age were middle-class. It was only when they went to university 
and met with party reps who really cared about working class 
concerns that they were able to see the interconnection between 
class and environmental issues more clearly and they think the GP 
itself does a lot of good grassroots work in working class areas. 
Therefore, while this thesis ‘places’ the GPNI into a conception of 
an issue-based working class-oriented party, active membership 
may be needed for activists themselves to fully appreciate how the 
party genuinely reflects this orientation.  
 
Broadly, party members contribute to building the party 
‘brand’, playing a ‘symbolic role in the chain of representation’, 
often showing how the party is not just a party of elites, but adds to 
the party’s perceived authenticity by being a visual symbol of its 
support in communities (Scarrow and Gezgor, 2010, p. 827). 
Applying this logic, the GPNI activists are ‘advertisements’ for the 
working-class nature of the party and so felt the need to reiterate 
the authenticity of the working-class ‘brand’. Implicitly, some 
activists raised their ‘middle-class’ background or how they 
represent a ‘non-working-class’ area in NI, but to emphasise that 
their class or elected area does not ‘truly’ represent the core GPNI 
working-class image. Sayer (2002) explains how people shy from 
talking about their social class, as it is itself a moral signifier and 
subject that can cause embarrassment, particularly among 
working-classes who can feel a social shame engaging with the 

 
191
topic. However, these activists appeared more ‘embarrassed’ by 
their ‘middle-class-ness’ that is ‘off brand’. For example, one GPNI 
activist (2) is ‘slightly different’ from a lot of their Green colleagues 
in that they run a business and have respect for market forces, they 
are also a landlord but believe in regulation, albeit ultimately, they 
care for people and have concerns about the Tory government. 
Interestingly, in contrast to certain Green activists admitting they 
are middle-class, Alliance activists would sometimes admit they are 
more socialist which again does not fit with the Alliance ‘brand’. 
One such activist (1), noted they were a little more socialist than 
some of the Alliance policies, while stating that Alliance is centre-
left, not left and socialist. For both Greens and Alliance then, there 
are activists whose class and/or ideological background does not 
neatly match with the party brand, but these activists still feel a 
need to represent the groups and beliefs the party stands for.  
 
Reality of (non-) alignment  
 
Theoretically, strong primordialists (e.g. Geertz, 1963) 
would see ethnic identity as from the ‘givens’ of existence and 
stable, while class is a more ‘constructed’ and permeable identity. 
However, for GPNI activists, ethno-nationality is treated as the 
more ‘constructed’ option: you can pick and choose your ethno-
national identity, but not your class. In reality, this was not such a 
clear-cut process as assumed given the instances of ‘re-
attachment’ to ethno-nationalism. Certain GPNI activists ‘re-
attached’ themselves to their unionist background such as when 
(partly) sympathising with unionists’ fears of a UI, or frustrations 
with the NI Protocol in identity terms. As one GPNI activist (1) 
relays ‘Coming from my background…I feel like I can criticise the 
unionists a bit more than somebody from the outside can. I get very 
annoyed at their rhetoric sometimes, but I genuinely do appreciate 
the very genuine fears they have about the place of unionists being 
subsumed within a united Ireland.’ This GPNI activist not being in 

 
192
a ‘unionist’ party and not seeing themselves as ‘unionist’ may elicit 
less defensiveness against their criticism from ‘true’ unionists then 
another GPNI activist not from that background. As Hornsey and 
Imani (2004) explain outgroup criticism may be seen as motivated 
differently, and so, less tolerated than that by ingroup members, 
whose criticism might be perceived to be about bettering the in-
group (p. 366). GPNI activists (sometimes unintentionally) can 
simultaneously criticise the background they come from and no 
longer identify with that background but also sympathise with it or 
recognise how it still biases them, even if they try not to let it. For 
example, one activist (6) discussed the ridiculousness of some of 
the stuff the unionists get annoyed at such as dual language 
signage, but they feel especially for older generations of British 
people who fear a UI and while being pro-UI themselves. They also 
have concerns about ROI historical commemorations as they are 
from this original unionist background. In this sense, the push-pull 
of identity that Green activists experience explains their 
membership and engagement in the party; the non-sectarian, de-
aligned nature of the party allows for the experience of ‘flux’ in one’s 
own identity that membership of parties beyond the centre-ground 
does not. 
 
Additionally, some GPNI activists ‘re-attach’ to their 
traditional background as a blocker to comment on identity or 
constitutional issues. Even if some GPNI activists do not identify 
strongly with their community anymore, they still feel that coming 
from a traditional bloc (e.g. unionism) means they do not want to 
speak for anyone from the community that they do not come from 
(e.g. nationalism). Or, at least, being from one community, even if 
they no longer identify with it, means they desire to be able to draw 
on the opposite bloc’s perspective to offer better insights on said 
community. For example, activist (3) from a unionist background 
felt uncomfortable commenting on accommodating the Irish identity 
in NI without having a nationalist individual to draw on for 

 
193
perspective. Similarly, there was an awareness of how coming 
from a particular bloc (i.e. unionism) means it is easier for them to 
feel more comfortable than other GPNI supporters in the current 
constitutional status quo. Here, non-alignment is not the full reality 
as activists – subtly – acknowledge how they still view the world, at 
least partially, through their ethno-national identity despite the 
class lens and non-aligned position that the party emphasises.  
 
Admitting Identity  
 
As a non-sectarian party in a divided society and institutional 
configuration that encourages traditional affiliations, the GPNI 
faces a distinct challenge wherein the non-aligned nature of the 
party can constitute a basis for embarrassment about ‘conceding’ 
identity background influences. Unlike the traditional parties, 
activists are hesitant about what they consider ‘admitting’ their 
identity. For example, activist (16) articulates that there is some 
‘shame or embarrassment about admitting people’s motivations’. 
Another activist (10) sought to make sense of this by outlining how 
NI citizens and activists themselves can experience one or even 
both identities: ‘I would say I, at times, have felt British and, at 
times, have felt Irish…and I think that's true for a lot of people in 
Northern Ireland, and I know that a lot of people, if they're strongly 
unionist or strongly republican, maybe won't admit that, but I think 
even for them that's true because we do have such strong 
influences of both’. This may be best understood as being able to 
cohere with one’s ‘true’ self in the Greens in which any identity 
background or indeed any combination of backgrounds or views 
can be facilitated and engaged. This is the reality of a more flexible 
and lesser alignment: distinct identities are below the surface, but 
individuals may come to articulate the version they feel most 
comfortable with and consider the complexities of the identity 
perspectives of others without ‘reducing’ people or communities to 
one perspective or set of interests. 

 
194
Primarily class over sect? 
 
As the above showcases, several GPNI activists admit their 
class background, and distance at times from their ethno-
nationality, but some also make a case whereby class is pre-
eminent for opponents, particularly the centre-ground’s Alliance. 
GPNI activists see Alliance as class-coded in that they are 
considered by the Greens to be a middle-class party perceived to 
represent middle-class interests. Alliance is not just ‘unionist’ for 
the Greens but ‘middle-class unionist’ and for some they are 
alternative middle-class unionist representatives (e.g. activists 7; 
2; 11). 
   
Although Rønn (2025) does not directly explore the relationship 
between sect-class at the micro-level, certain dynamics are 
applicable to GPNI activists. Rønn (2025) recognises instances 
where class grievances or identities compete or outweigh sect’s 
significance (e.g. social movements that transcend sectarian 
divides). Here, class is treated as at least equally relevant in how 
activists think of what they represent and what their challengers 
represent including in the non-aligned space. For example, a GPNI 
activist (11) who is pro-UI (in the long-run) is also extremely 
connected to their working-class identity and had to navigate 
wanting a UI; while feeling like they were losing things that are 
important to them and others from working-class communities, like 
UK funded charities. For them, there were clear instances where 
the class lens has to be considered, as the wider party would 
espouse too. In another specific example, the same activist (11) 
was able to get their Level 3 NVQ in First Aid through the cadet 
force as an opportunity made available to someone from a working-
class background, but they do not know what the cadet force is like 
in the ROI and as such whether such opportunities would be 
available even in their preferred UI. Certain activists showcased 
how their own middle-class background does not direct their 

 
195
political or constitutional focus, but class itself does. For instance, 
one GPNI activist (4) does not expect much of an impact of a united 
Ireland on them personally as they are middle-class but part of 
them would be more interested in effects on working-class 
Protestants. 
 
Furthermore, there are additional influences on position beyond 
class and ethno-national identity. In some cases, there may be a 
‘split the difference’ type of de-alignment where it is it difficult to 
analyse the ‘source’ of their preferences i.e. ethno-nationality or 
Green principles. Specifically, one GPNI activist (8) favourably 
assesses having regional governance under a UI, partly due to 
their re-attachment to their traditional background, but also it simply 
aligns with green thinking. The activist who came from a Protestant 
background, but very much no longer sees themselves as such, 
says ‘…even as someone who… doesn't really associate myself 
with unionism… I suppose we still want to have that sense of 
identity and as someone who's really passionate about grassroots 
democracy, I think that is really important because the people in 
the local area know what is needed…’ 
 
However, as a caveat, posited class interests can sometimes 
also be ‘used’ to justify a constitutional position (e.g., working-class 
interests will be argued to benefit the constitutional position that is 
already preferred by the activist). Although not the dynamic 
described by Rønn (2025) of class-identities as subordinate to sect 
whereby communities defined by class are grouped by sect and 
pushed into the sectarian politics framework (p. 7) here would be 
another form of subordination whereby class is used as 
justification. 
 
 

 
196
Manifestation 2: Interactions between the overlapping 
elements of the GPNI’s ‘issue-based’ orientation 
 
B. Conceptual Marker - Issue-based: Join for the leftism, but 
stay for the environment, or vice versa? 
 
It would be a mistake to determine that GPNI activists 
always support, and continue to support, the GPNI primarily 
because of their leftist ideology. Firstly, this would not directly 
explain why they chose to support the GPNI over another 
leftist/socialist party in the first place, specifically People Before 
Profit (i.e., another non-ethnic, integrationist party). For example, 
some activists’ (5; 6) admit that their own political leanings would 
also encompass a lot of PBP’s political foundations or ideologically 
the activists sway between both GPNI and PBP, but ultimately the 
GPNI wins the day for them because ‘I don't think their [PBP]’s 
green platform is as well-formed and as well-integrated…as the 
Green Party (activist, 5) and ‘just as a party and as a community of 
people and as a praxis…I feel like the Greens have more potential’ 
(activist, 6). Petitpas and Sciarini (2022) show how left-wing voters’ 
decisions between two very similar leftist parties in Switzerland 
(Greens and Social Democrats) is based not only on issue position, 
but also on how they keep or change their assessment on the most 
competent party on a given issue (‘issue competence’). These 
GPNI activists potentially made (and importantly, maintain) an 
assessment that despite the ideological similarities between PBP 
and GPNI, the GPNI is more ‘competent’ in terms of dealing with 
the green issue pragmatically and in mobilising towards policy 
change and implementation, and so this helps to swing their 
choice. 
 
Looking back from a post-Brexit vantage point, certain GPNI 
activists supported the leftist dimension of PBP’s Brexit campaign, 
but their association with the Leave side was unappreciated due 

 
197
primarily to its anti-immigration rhetoric. For example, one GPNI 
activist (1) liked the Lexit campaign and again thought PBP was 
quite strong on environmental issues too, but they could not 
understand how PBP could then stand with parties such as the 
Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) with racism on the rise caused by 
Brexit’s implications for negative attitudes towards immigrants. 
Unsurprisingly, few GPNI activists presented reasons to switch 
support to PBP. Activists mentioned PBP’s support for a United 
Ireland and PBP’s willingness to take a clear position on this. While 
activists admire many of PBP’s positions and some share this 
support for a UI, they also see potential issues with the GPNI 
adopting a similar approach on non-leftist and more identity-based 
constitutional issues. Activist  (10) for example admires many of 
PBP’s policy positions but sees their support for a United Ireland 
as potentially undermining the extent to which PBP can grow 
support among working-class Loyalists. This is seen as an 
exemplar of the potential risks of the GPNI taking similar positions 
on constitutional issues and inhibiting their opportunities for growth 
across the communities in similar ways. However, PBP are 
typically less willing to compromise on left issues, so if the GPNI 
becomes too pragmatic and downplays its niche positioning to be 
electorally competitive (like the GP in ROI arguably did to enter the 
2020 coalition), some with stronger socialist views may prefer PBP. 
Reflecting Bergman and Flatt (2020) by moving away from its 
‘owned’ issues like environmentalism or leftism, the niche GPNI 
could ultimately hurt its vote share through moderating on issues 
and prioritising electoral performance.  
 
Secondly, to determine that GPNI activists ‘continue’ to 
support the GPNI primarily because of their leftist ideology treats 
party attraction or support as stable. Existing studies recognise 
how party members’ ideological preferences can weaken over 
time, which could contribute to the likelihood they will leave the 
party (Wagner, 2017, p. 347). However, for some activists it is not 

 
198
a matter of their ideological preferences weakening, but the 
‘intensity’ of it moves between issues; they become more 
committed to issues they were less focused on when they initially 
joined. They might have joined for primarily leftist or environmental 
reasons, but since being in the party they have come to learn and 
develop a niche concern for both left and eco issues together. 
Therefore, the reasons that they ‘stay’ in the party might not be the 
same reasons that drew them to it initially. For instance, one GPNI 
activist (1) explains they initially were drawn to join the GPNI for 
recycling/animal welfare reasons (and those issues are still 
important to them), but ‘after I joined’ they came to realise that the 
party was more than this type of party and is more politically 
rounded across the board with fully fleshed out policies on a very 
wide variety of social issues. Another activist (6) was drawn to the 
party due to its leftist orientation whereby the activist ‘also had an 
interest in environmental issues, but honestly that was 
secondary…And I learned more about that, the longer I was in the 
Greens, and that became more of a passion for me and now I can 
see that the two are so intricately connected.’  
 
Collignon et al (2023) find left-wing GP members in England 
who mainly joined to campaign on social justice over eco-issues 
were much more vulnerable to exiting the party when the 
mainstream party shifts position (such as leaving to join Labour 
after Corbyn’s election as leader, p. 849). This could have major 
implications for the GPNI in the current post-Brexit context where 
unification is more likely. Specifically, activists like (6) who ‘initially’ 
joined for more leftist reasons could be at least ‘more vulnerable’ 
than those who joined due to environmentalism to leaving the GPNI 
in a UI, which will offer more left-leaning parties than currently 
competing in NI (e.g. Social democrats, Labour, PBP), particularly 
given the activist (6) recognises there are more left party options in 
the ROI. One alternative of course could be that we will see a 
diversification of issue emphases in the Green Party’s programme 

 
199
in a united Ireland that will allow them to better compete with the 
wider range of socialist parties that will be available in a UI as 
occurred when the GP in England and Wales lost its anti-austerity, 
far left niche to Labour (Dennison, 2020) 
 
Identity versus ideology 
 
The GPNI is seen by activists as home to the ‘rebels’ in NI 
as they have a post-ethnic outlook. Activists reinforce this as some 
see their own identity configurations as ‘confounding’ (activist 13) 
or ‘contrarian’ (activist 12). The latter is from an extended working-
class Catholic background, and although they are genuinely 
agnostic their perceived community background would say they 
are probably going to be a soft nationalist. However, they consider 
themselves a ‘contrarian’ in that they are an Anglophile after living 
in England for seven years and while there might be those 
pressures of family on them to vote for reunification almost as a 
reflex, they care more about who (i.e. pro-UI or pro-UK side) is 
selling it best to them. However, there is an element of pragmatism 
too in their thinking, as the activist (12) identifies as Irish, they are 
born on the island of Ireland, but they are a pragmatist and are a 
UK citizen and they feel some within republicanism would say they 
are not a UK citizen and refuse to recognise partition and, that is 
not a practical reality in their view.  
 
The GPNI also has to manage another, much smaller 
cohort, those activists socialised outside NI who are drawn to the 
GPNI solely by ideology and feel very confounded by the import of 
these ethno-national identities. A GPNI activist (13) considers 
traditional allegiances ‘confounding’ in this part of the world given 
they come from a family of English Catholics, which does make 
them feel they are from ‘beyond the binary’ and quite disconnected 
from either tradition sometimes. Another non-NI-born GPNI activist 
(4) feels a ‘place apart’ in how they still view politics through the left 

 
200
and right lens (rather than unionist-nationalist), despite being in NI 
for years. Although potentially, this is not ‘unique’ to those from a 
non-NI background, but activists who support non-aligned parties 
like the GPNI or Alliance, already are won over to viewing politics 
through a more ‘normal’ political lens. However, these GPNI 
activists socialised outside NI could be ‘more’ against the party 
engaging with identity or constitutional issues as it is not been a 
part of their own experience to the same degree (of course some 
were from UK or ROI and as such partially socialised by these 
identities, but not NI specifically) and engagement with these 
issues would instead be pushed on them by their party support. 
Alternatively, they could be ‘less’ deterred from engaging on these 
issues and taking a CP because they did not experience the 
negative implications of being in a divided society. These activists 
epitomise how the GPNI is a natural home for activists with these 
complicated and in some cases very different identity affiliations 
and more pragmatic perspectives, but in reality, they must operate 
alongside those who have a firmer CP and those who have 
distanced themselves from, but retain, an identity affiliation as 
above. 
 
Issue ownership – choosing between the ‘centre-ground’ options 
 
Issue ownership – and more specifically what issue the GP 
‘owns’ – is particularly relevant when understanding activists 
support of the GPNI over Alliance, if they are drawn to the 
‘conceptual marker’ shared by these parties – their constitutional 
neutrality. 
Of 
course, 
some 
(including 
Alliance 
activists 
themselves) suggest Alliance is on par with the GPNI in terms of 
tackling environmental concerns (e.g. Alliance has its own Green 
New Deal) which would not then explain why they would switch 
from Alliance to GPNI if they care mainly about the environment 
side of things. However, it appears that activists value their party 
as the ‘truest’ to its issue-based agenda (i.e. the GPNI ‘owns’ the 

 
201
ecosocialist, environmental issue). For example, one activist (7) 
says ‘I would say we're the only party that has an ecosocialist 
ideological perspective… we're the only party that has the 
environment and climate at its heart’ or another activist (3) would 
like to think the GPNI is most ‘authentic’ in terms of the environment 
(and social issues). However, it may be the case that 
environmentalism rather than a sudden affiliation to leftism could 
explain the switch from Alliance to GPNI, despite them both being 
‘constitutionally-neutral centrist parties. Even one GPNI activist 
(17) was previously fairly high up in Alliance, came to feel Alliance 
were not doing enough in terms of environmentalism, which was 
their key issue, so they later moved to the GPNI.  
 
While the GPNI activists know they ‘own’ environmentalism, 
they also recognise that for those who care about leftist issues 
there is a challenge from Alliance. GPNI activists recognise and 
commend the success and contribution of Alliance on a number of 
shared priorities. Certain activists appear deflated that although 
they are aware of Alliance lacking ‘leftism’, those outside the GPNI 
‘bubble’ might not know the truth (or even care) about Alliance not 
really being so left. For example, one GPNI activist (10) does not 
think that people in NI necessarily are aware that Alliance is not a 
left-wing party (or that being left matters to many). Some GPNI 
activists viewed Alliance as representing a ‘surface-level leftism’; 
that is, when you look at the details particularly economically, they 
are not in reality a left party. For example, one GPNI activist (3) 
states ‘…sometimes, because of some of the stuff that they talk 
about, whether it's social or environmental things, it could maybe 
give the impression that they're a wee bit more left-leaning than 
they really are. But when you drill down…’ Again, reflecting this 
‘surface-level leftism’ another activist (6) shares Alliance ‘speak the 
language of some of those parties probably coming from a, like, 
social democratic approach…But…when push comes to shove, 
they're not driven by an anti-capitalist ideology at their heart’. 

 
202
However, this is potentially strategic by GPNI activists who 
separate themselves from the wider set of left of centre voters, 
whereby they are and seek to represent themselves as more 
‘engaged or hyper-aware’ leftists who can recognise that Alliance 
is not sufficiently left.  
 
Issue ownership – Meaning neutral by ‘default’ 
 
While Alliance positions itself as not truly aligned, there is a 
perception among Green activists that this is a non-alignment or 
neutrality that is a product of Alliance being defined by its ‘reaction’ 
to the traditional blocs. In this way, for GPNI activists Alliance is a 
product of traditional NI ethno-national politics and positions itself 
as the middleman between the ethnic parties tactically and 
ideologically and as such, Alliance still operates within and not 
independent of this ‘ethnic spectrum’. For some GPNI activists 
then, their party might be seen as the ‘true’ neutral party because 
it exists beyond the divide and is focused on NI’s future. However, 
even if GPNI activists do see Alliance as ‘less deserving’ of its 
position in or as the ‘neutral’ centre-ground, several still recognise 
the growth of Alliance as a positive thing as it shows the middle is 
growing, even though it has ended up costing the GPNI electoral 
support. GPNI activist (2) says ‘The middle ground of the north is 
still finding its feet. Certainly, as a part of the Green Party, I had 
hoped that we would capture that more…I think the last assembly 
elections showed that the Alliance were capturing it more…I have 
no issue with that, my personal view is, the stronger the middle 
ground is, the more the extremes are pushed aside and 
minimalised and their influence diluted.’ 
 
Several activists across both parties would agree that a 
strength of their own party is it is not focused on identity or 
sectarianism. However, some in Alliance called out the GPNI for 
ignoring these types of issues completely, while Alliance 

 
203
recognises they need to be dealt with even if the party disagrees 
with them. For example, Alliance activists (3; 15) think that quite 
often the Greens tend to shy away from sectarian politics, as they 
say it has nothing to do with them and that they are focused on 
other/green issues but while Alliance activists commend Green 
action on these issues, for the Alliance activists, these identity 
issues still need to be dealt with. However, on the flipside, some 
GPNI activists actually assess Alliance as ‘shying away’ from the 
constitutional question, with their perception heavily informed by 
Alliance’s decision to not attend a particular ‘Ireland’s Future’ 
conference. At the same time, the GPNI also thinks Alliance is 
directly connected to the constitutional issue, as some activists see 
that Alliance’s existence is still dependent on the binary divide. For 
example, one activist, (10), suggests Alliance have a ‘strange 
symbiotic relationship to the constitutional issue’ whereby they 
would say that the GP are more truly embedded in a commitment 
to social justice and therefore the CI is pushed down its priority list, 
but for Alliance the constitutional issue is important as it is 
fundamental to their identity that they are the ‘Not unionist Or 
nationalist’ party. Although the GPNI sees the aligned parties as 
‘outdated’ some in the GPNI view Alliance as also still stuck in the 
‘past’ in this way. For example, whilst for years one GPNI activist 
(2) was an Alliance member, and they saw Alliance as ‘still caught 
up in the conflict of the past and they just wanted to get to the point 
whereby Northern Ireland is beyond that’. Alliance, for their part, do 
not deny this and in many ways take ownership of this status and 
role.  
 
Overall, regardless of how GPNI or Alliance interprets the 
extent to, which they themselves, or each other, are engaging with 
the constitutional issue, it appears that the GPNI’s own neutrality 
is more ‘moveable’ compared to Alliance. For Alliance, being 
neutral is a defining identity of the party. However, being an ‘issue-
based’ party, i.e., a party that takes positions on salient issues of 

 
204
the day, is core to the identity of the GPNI. In this way, the GPNI is 
‘neutral by default’ until it makes the evaluation that it should take 
a position on an issue. Therefore, it can ‘move away’ from being 
neutral on the CI, if the CI becomes an issue of greater salience, 
which it now assesses to be the case in the post-Brexit era. For 
Alliance, being neutral is more fundamental to the party’s self-
identity. 
 
Issue-based - Any Green Party will do?  
 
Albeit on environmental (not party) activism, Botetzagias 
and van Schuur (2012, p. 517) illustrate how past activism in 
environmental movements predicts green party members’ activism 
in current movements as they have been familiarised with the 
ideology and the goals of the movement. Similarly, as a baseline, 
there was an expectation that GPNI activists would join any green 
party if they had prior exposure to, interest in and had participated 
in one in another region. Being a GPNI activist potentially meant 
supporting ‘a’ GP regardless of what country you are in, given 
select activists (activist 15, 8) switched their involvement/support 
from the GP in England and Wales to the GPNI when they returned 
to NI. However, it was unclear whether these activists switched to 
the GPNI only because they wanted to support ‘a’ GP or because 
they wanted to keep supporting a more eco-socialist party 
‘regardless’ of whether it was a green party or not. For instance, 
illustrating this confusion, one GPNI activist (8) implies it was an 
organic switch to the GPNI for them based on the identity of the 
party: ‘I was part of the Green Party in England and Wales as well, 
so I was going to then, transfer over that way.’ But also their initial 
motivation appears ‘issue-based’: ‘I guess I didn't know anything 
about People Before Profit when I moved back here, like I said, I 
was part of the Green Party in England and Wales, mostly because 
of the environmental side of things and social justice, those are the 

 
205
two key things for me and so I was always just going to get involved 
in [the GPNI]’.   
 
There is an association and partial issue ownership of 
leftism and environmentalism together for GPNI activists, so 
potentially it is not enough for it to be ‘a’ GP as it must have these 
issue positions given it is that combination that the activists are 
attracted by. Reflecting this, the GPNI activists were critical of the 
GPROI. GPNI activists often did not see the GPROI as really that 
‘left’ and/or generally it was recognised that the GPROI’s decision 
to enter into the 2020 coalition was not wholly supported by the 
GPNI. For example, one GPNI activist (6) struggled to picture 
themselves in the GPROI, due to the GPROI’s lacking left 
credentials and the unrepresentative nature of their politics: And 
I've sometimes gone, "if I lived in the south, I'm not sure I would be 
in the Greens.” I think the left-wing part of me would win out and I'd 
have to join a different party…And it's not to do with the activists 
on the ground... it's just the leadership… But also…in the north… 
[I] think we overwhelmingly voted against some of the stuff that has 
subsequently happened72, [whereas in the South] …this is what 
people want in the Greens, so then I feel a bit like...it doesn't 
represent me and my politics.’ Again, these insights are particularly 
relevant to the post-Brexit era where a UI is more likely. Referring 
back to Collignon et al (2022), if the GPNI is no longer a distinct 
entity under a UI and the GPROI remains the only ‘GP option’ if 
these activists who want to support an eco-socialist party and not 
just ‘a’ GP then the weak ‘left credentials’ of the GPROI could mean 
these current activists would be more vulnerable to moving their 
support to a left party that is operating in the ROI. However, if they 
support any party that is ‘a’ GP they might be more likely to support 
 
72 This appears to be a reference to the socio-economic policies of the GPROI in 
government. 

 
206
