the GPROI under a UI, especially if their support is primarily based 
on environmentalism.  
 
Even beyond whether the GPROI issue ‘salience’ on leftism 
is too weak for GPNI activists, the context itself is just too different. 
Again being ‘a’ GP is not enough. As one GPNI activist (1) details 
‘And this is not a criticism to the Green Party in the south…But I 
think even whenever we've had things that they want to, like, 
maybe release statements or something up here and we've had to 
be like, "You can't say that, while that might not sound offensive to 
you, we know how this is going to be taken."…And these are just 
things that have never crossed their mind before…Not 
everyone…but it has arisen’. However, the context itself may not 
be enough to push GPNI activists to assess another GP as ‘too 
different’ given some recognise an ‘ideological closeness’ between 
the GPs in Scotland and NI, especially as they are both more left-
leaning. Here, the Scottish Greens satisfy the GPNI’s desire for 
dual-issue ownership. While aware of the party’s good network with 
GPs across Europe (and the Greens in England and Wales like the 
ROI are less left wing), one GPNI activist (16) notes ‘…but there is 
certainly, like, a strong fraternal relationship between the Greens in 
Northern Ireland and in Scotland...I think most of us would see 
them as quite left-wing.’ Given a number were or said they would 
have been Labour supporters when in England, it reinforces that 
activists would not be hopping their support between regional GPs, 
as leftism is the key draw. Fundamentally, it is clear that issue 
ownership over a leftist agenda is key to the distinctive appeal of 
the GPNI as evidenced by the attraction the party presents to those 
including from Labour and especially more socialist Labour 
backgrounds in the UK. While other party options may be available, 
this distinct issue ownership profile and ideology is a key distinct 
draw marking the party apart.  
 
 

 
207
Manifestation 3: Time to move away from constitutional 
neutrality? 
 
C. Conceptual Marker – Constitutional neutrality 
 
1. Sense-making of the ‘new’ engagement with the constitutional 
issue 
 
Currently, the GPNI espouses a neutral position on the 
constitutional question but in recent times, the party has begun to 
engage further with the issue, how to frame it, what the necessary 
conditions and most effective designs are for a potential 
referendum, and what potential position to take. This change of 
approach may have been noticed by voters. Although the majority 
of voters in a Lord Ashcroft KCMG PC poll (2021) revealed that 
they thought the Greens took a neutral position (51%), this is only 
a slight majority, and a relevant amount (37%) think they take a 
nationalist/Republican position.  
 
Compared to Alliance, GPNI activists were generally more 
open to engaging with the constitutional question. There is a 
question of why activists, especially at lower levels (i.e. non- MLAs 
or councillors) appear open to their party actively engaging with the 
CI. The broad conclusion here is that the party is now considering 
whether to move towards engaging on the CQ and referendum as 
it is an issues-based party. This is likely to produce challenges for 
the Green Party as engagement along these lines clashes (or is 
perceived to clash) with the constitutional neutrality that marks the 
party out but the party activists feel it may be worth engaging in this 
way irrespective of the challenges it presents as functioning as an 
issues-based party that responds to salient issues and policy 
questions is the core party identity. However, this decision to move 
to engage with the issue and take this calculated risk is a relatively 
recent phenomenon raising questions about why the decision has 

 
208
been taken to move on this now. There are a variety of potential 
reasons that emerged and were explored with activists and are 
now considered in turn. 
 
Reason 1: Easier to communicate about ‘the future’? 
 
One potential reason could be down to how the GPNI as a 
party is more of a comfortable space to engage with the CI without 
the baggage of sectarianism. For example, strikingly, one GPNI 
activist (13) noted in an unprompted fashion, that they know that 
constitutional conversations are something that the GP in NI is 
planning on having in the near future, and continued that this is one 
of the differences between Greens and Alliance, that it is fine to 
have these conversations and ‘it is not inherently sectarian to do 
so’. Another activist (12) recognises how the GPNI can talk about 
this issue without some of the ideological or aspirational phrasing 
used by traditional identities in particular Republicanism: ‘So, I 
think that's an important distinction about how we can present a 
uniquely Green alternative on these issues or these conversations.’ 
‘Communicating like a Green’ is a way of talking about the future 
in a way that can consider constitutional issues without leaning on 
traditional identities as part of this wider canvas of what ‘the future’ 
looks like. Todd and McEvoy (2024) observe that language is a big 
barrier to participation in constitutional conversations, as terms like 
‘Irish unity’ are triggering of traditional ideo-identities that many 
have distanced from, or are disheartened about (p. 177). 
Participants in their study recommend that more engagement with 
these conversations likely requires moving away from binary, 
ideological discourses towards more normal issue agendas. 
However, GPNI activists recognise their party is in a way already 
doing this more broadly – it can have wider discussions of ‘the 
future’ because their approach to communicating is about planning 
and building a future and so that involves dimensions like climate 
but also constitutional issues and institutions if this fits into their 

 
209
discussion on non-ethnic themes like climate change. Also, the 
activists themselves are not ‘fearful’ of language associated with 
constitutional issues. For example, they were more likely than 
Alliance to both use the phrasing and support ‘Joint Authority’ while 
Alliance tended to just talk about British and Irish governments 
working closer together. This is quite striking in itself. For example, 
Alliance activist (23) refers to the idea of NI as a sub-region 
governed with ‘input from the southern government…and maybe a 
bit less from Westminster, a kind of…dual responsibility’, but there 
is a noted reluctance to use the comparable (and familiar) term of 
joint authority. 
 
Reason 2: Issue party means applying an issue lens? 
 
Another logic linked to the above for why GPNI activists 
appear more open to engaging with the CI is while the GPNI 
conceptually is post-ethnic, activists do not see this post-ethnic 
approach as being a substantive way of breaking away from those 
blocs. The party is instead seeking not to apply the identity lens 
and applying an ‘issue’ lens. Fundamentally, the party is driven by 
its issue-based party status in which the party at its core engages 
with and takes positions on major salient issues. It tackles these 
issues head on. This includes the CI which has now become more 
salient since Brexit and given discussion of a potential border poll.  
In this way, the GPNI does not shy away from identity issues and/or 
the constitutional question (as it would accuse others of doing) but 
instead seeks to consider these through this distinct issue-based 
prism. Specifically, select GPNI activists imply the GPNI is not as 
snobbish about sectarian issues as other parties. GPNI activist (10) 
explains: ‘So, I think the Alliance sits somewhere oddly in that sort 
of triumvirate as, "Look at us, we’re not sectarian." And it gets 
people’s backs up. And, I mean, I'm very careful…I appreciate why 
people have the constitutional issue as their biggest issue.’ Other 
activists call out as elitist Alliance arguments that it will consider the 

 
210
CQ and a potential UI based on rational evaluation rather than 
ideology. Of course, from an Alliance perspective this thesis finds 
that Alliance activists do not deny their party is built from the two 
blocs but instead offers a way out of these camps but there is 
evidence here of a clear alternate prism attached to each party 
when thinking about how and to what extent to engage with these 
constitutional questions. 
 
There is also an openness to the GPNI taking a CP because 
activists believe outsiders will perceive it differently. Activist (16) 
illustrates the particularly ‘strong’ position of influence the ‘centre-
ground’ generally would have if its politicians came down in support 
of a side. They contend it would potentially make the UI concept 
more palatable to a wider audience and would change what the 
entire campaign looked like rather than it just being seen as a SF 
campaign otherwise. The core lesson follows, all these activists 
would see any position/policy from the GPNI – whether it was pro-
UI or not – as being moulded differently, and ‘perceived’ differently 
than nationalist positions or campaigns as this would be a different 
type of campaign and different framing of the question focused on 
distinct issues and built around the Green lens of a new vision for 
the future. Of course, this may not be the case in reality, but it 
shows how activists could ultimately push their party to move on 
this as a party with an issue focus and a desire to remake a more 
radical departure for the future, whatever the risks and potential 
contentiousness of further engagement or position-taking. 
 
Reason 3: Issue party means image is secondary? 
 
Another reason GPNI activists may care less about the risks 
of engaging with the CQ is if it believes otherwise critical issues 
would be neglected by a party that prides itself on engaging with 
the key issues of the day. The GPNI does not fear damaging its 
‘neutral party’ image if it means tackling salient issues. Activists 

 
211
mentioned their party’s courage in dealing with more divisive 
issues, or pioneering efforts in policies such as on the 
decriminalisation of drugs. GPNI activists view their party as an 
‘issues party’ defined by taking positions on bigger questions and 
are expected to do so whether that is climate, drug 
decriminalisation or the CQ. Activists recognise their party cannot 
avoid the discussion, and that is part of being an issue-based party 
even if sometimes that means taking positions that will be 
unpopular generally or in one community versus the other. One 
GPNI activist (7) talks about weathering the storm when it comes 
to encouraging unionists partaking in the debate, and the same grin 
it and bear it attitude could contribute to the openness. This activist 
(7) explains, ‘the Greens are often seen as the kind of eco wing of 
the Shinners…so there's a danger that we are seen as promoting 
inclusion of unionists in this debate, that we could be accused of 
that…well, there's nothing we can do about people's perceptions. 
Let's just take it on the chin and be open and honest with people 
about, this is a train that's now leaving, it's not that getting on board 
and the next stop is Dublin, it's that you've got to make your case 
[for maintaining the Union]’. Of course, Alliance also has to take the 
accusations of being on the fence if it stays neutral (e.g. activist 6). 
The GPNI's party identity as seen internally is that the party has to 
take positions whereas the Alliance party identity is that it must be 
neutral on the CQ and identity issues such as a referendum. 
 
Reason 4: Activity dependent? 
 
Another explanation for why GPNI activists appear more 
open to engaging with the CI could be down to what kind of ‘activity’ 
this is interpreted as. For certain GPNI activists, policy 
development on a border poll was viewed more as a positive move 
towards thinking about the ‘right way’ to hold a referendum or the 
future direction of NI. Alliance activists appeared more hesitant 
towards developing policy along these lines because they did not 

 
212
see it in this way as being about how to carry out a referendum 
rather than the party recommending how to actually vote in one 
(e.g. activist 10). For example, GPNI activist (5) also seems on 
board with the party starting to develop a vision about how to have 
these conversations even if they are hesitant about the party taking 
a CP: ‘I think you could probably hear my hesitancy as well around, 
should it have a constitutional position or not? We're in a particular 
moment, I think, right now where these conversations are 
important. So I think the Green Party Northern Ireland should 
absolutely start taking positions on making conversations happen 
or making that space or starting’. Again, the GPNI as an issues 
party is not ‘afraid’ to take a position, especially when developing 
the right approach to productively considering the issue and 
creating the context for a meaningful and respectful debate itself 
necessitates substantive engagement. 
 
Reason 5: Going the direction they want anyway? 
 
Given most of those who predicted the party would come 
out as UI if it had to pick between the options also personally 
supported unification, an argument could be made they know they 
can talk about the CI without a strict fear that the party would move 
away from their own personally preferred position. This does not 
mean however they want the party to lose its cross-community 
appeal. For example, the prospect of the party taking a CP does 
not make one activist (6) nervous personally as they feel it would 
probably be the position they agree with (i.e. pro-UI), but they feel 
if the Greens were to take a CP, that would be the end of any hope 
of being a cross-community party (at the ‘party-level’), and so that 
makes them nervous. This illustrates the difference between party 
risks and personal preference. Again though, this is not however 
seen as a ‘red line’ that should inhibit engaging with the issue. 
 
 

 
213
Reason 6: Top-down? 
 
The issue with the previous reasons (1-5) is it is doubtful that 
activists only recently have come to realise that their party is not 
comfortable engaging with constitutional issues. One argument 
that could be made is that it is a ‘top-down’ decision, that is, 
leadership or prominent GPNI reps want to move the party towards 
active engagement, and this has trickled down to the wider 
membership. However, this argument ultimately assumes that 
lower-level activists take their cue from higher up levels, which may 
or may not be the case especially as the GPNI takes a grassroots 
approach with respect to the influence of membership over party 
policy and positions. Overall, while GPNI activists do refer to what 
leadership say and may partially take their cues from them, they 
also have their own strong principles, positions, and perspectives. 
Also, one of the GPNI activists (1) who was interviewed earlier on 
in this project before the announcement at the AGM where the 
leadership declared the party would be moving towards an active 
role, got the sense that GP members are seeing the CI as an issue 
that needs to be addressed in the party more than it was previously, 
particularly since Brexit and the dealings around the Protocol. This 
suggests that at both leadership and lower activist levels there is a 
growing consensus across the board that this issues-based party 
must now engage the issue. 
 
2. Sense-making of the GPNI’s ‘ability’ to engage more with 
constitutionalism 
 
While the previous section cared more about why/if there is an 
openness to engaging with the CQ, GPNI activists also view their 
party as ‘able to engage’ with this issue – specifically in engaging 
with discussions with unionism on the CQ or participating in 
constitutional conversations itself like Ireland’s Future. 
 

 
214
Party specific infrastructure to (not) allow for the engagement  
 
Todd and McEvoy (2024) explain that there are particular 
situational impediments to engagement where there are limits to 
resources, access to information, education and avenues to and 
capacity for communication (p. 176). Given the GPNI’s small size 
without MLA representation in the Assembly, GPNI activists might 
consider a situational obstacle for the party to be is its lack of major 
infrastructure. As one GPNI activist (3) said, ‘And I think especially 
in a party that's got very little resources and…it's all volunteer-led, 
we don't have any staff…it's quite difficult to even do the things that 
we need to do just operationally… and that the constitutional 
question, it'd be great to have time to discuss it, but we probably 
don't’. Here, the barrier is not an avoidance of engagement with the 
constitutional issue in the sense that is too sensitive a topic for a 
‘non-aligned’ party, but the obstacle is infrastructure; there is not 
the time nor resources to engage. 
 
Taking the honest broker role from Alliance? 
 
Within Todd and McEvoy (2024) many participants focused 
on two resources needed for participation: time and skills. Having 
the ability to be able to talk about the CQ is implied to have been 
developed over time, but really it is something built into the GPNI 
based on how it is perceived (or thinks it is perceived) in terms of 
not being a threat to unionism. For example, the activist (10) 
shares, ‘this is partly because we are small and partly because 
people don’t really get us’ that the GP have a way in to unionism 
because the GP have not been in direct opposition to unionist 
parties. In addition, the activist outlined how the GP have worked 
directly with loyalist communities and loyalist groups on smaller 
community and charity projects. 
 

 
215
Beyond whether GPNI activists perceive that their party is more 
non-threatening to unionism or an honest broker, another activist 
(11) explains by virtue of its lobbying group status, on the ground, 
there is definitely much that the GP can do so it ‘should use itself 
as a pressure group’ for those in government and unionist parties 
to partake in a pre-border poll framework that is developed and the 
opinions that come from that.  
 
 In addition to its experience as a lobby group and the 
relationship to unionism, another activist (15) suggests that GPNI’s 
willingness to work with both communities potentially is bred into 
the broader consensual culture of the green movement. They 
explain how the non-hierarchal structure and pattern of consensual 
agreement within the party could provide it the means to bring the 
unionist community into the conversation around the constitutional 
question. 
 
While there might be a recognition that in reality externally, the 
GPNI may not be seen in the same light as it frames itself internally, 
most activists did see the party, at least, as more ‘not unionist’ than 
Alliance, and thought unionists would think the same. For example, 
the activist above says, unlike Alliance which has more unionist 
baggage and their heartlands are in traditional unionist areas, the 
Greens get support from a less clearly defined unionist identity 
cohort and is genuinely seen as being more neutral than Alliance 
and perhaps would be seen as more honest brokers. This is 
important in engaging nationalists but also critical given more 
fraught relations at times between unionists and Alliance 
specifically. This could limit Alliance’s ability to play the classic 
honest broker role when it comes to bringing in and engaging 
unionists around constitutional debates and pre-border poll 
frameworks. 
 

 
216
For Alliance there is a fear of being seen as ‘soft unionist’ if 
seen to be running away from this debate whereas the Greens are 
willing to engage with all sides, as they engage with any side 
regardless because it is about the need to engage on ‘the major 
issues’ for a party defined by this as a core ethos. There is a sense 
that activists could potentially be okay with the idea the GPNI would 
be willing to go as far as representing unionism in constitutional 
discussions, but this is not something that would work for Alliance. 
For example, one GPNI activist (12) keeps saying to their unionist 
friends, if you do not engage with this conversation, then there is 
nobody ‘fighting your corner except us’, so as the discourse 
evolves, unionism could cut its nose off to spite its face by not 
participating. One Alliance activist (9) however, says they do not 
think Alliance would be comfortable sitting in representing unionism 
on a panel but they do see how it could – ‘There's no reason why 
we couldn't facilitate that sort of discussion, but I think the nature 
of our party, the ethos of our party would facilitate a less-
confrontational…conversation’. 
 
Overall, the argument above still stands regarding the Greens 
relationship to unionism and the opportunity this provides for them 
to use this relationship to better shape the broader constitutional 
debate, but of course it is not the ‘ideal’ actor necessarily to play 
this role as articulated by activists. For example, while comparing 
the GP may be better positioned to have conversations with people 
such as those in the loyalist community than Alliance and a section 
of unionists that Alliance have alienated, activist (3) also feels it is 
probably going to be the same sort of civic organisations that were 
responsible for starting talks running up to the GFA that are likely 
to be the only people who are likely to make headway in terms of 
trying to convince people to get involved in discussions. This likely 
means a role but only a partial one for the GPNI in facilitating this 
engagement. 
 

 
217
3. Not the ‘normal’ neutral 
 
The debate on how the party should address the constitutional 
question does seem to be developing within the party. There is 
however uncertainty about how to do this, without being seen to 
de-prioritise eco-socialist issues, either in terms of party image or 
just practically as they are a small party with very limited resources. 
Of course, for some outsiders the big issue will be not which 
position should they take, but ‘if’ they take a position, as the GPNI 
is likely in 10 years to have voters from a unionist background. 
However, several GPNI activists suggested ways the party could 
take a position that were imaginative in nature, and very unique to 
the GPNI, but ultimately were not pro-UI or pro-Union. For 
example, one activist (15) who is unsure about their feelings 
around the GPNI taking a CP explains their view around the party 
expressing a two-futures idea where the party needs to articulate 
an idea of what the GP would be like and what it would like a single 
Irish jurisdiction to look like, and, they think the GP can express 
that without necessarily saying that it advocates for unification. 
Here, the GPNI activist continues to navigate the CI in a way that 
engages with the issue from the lens of ‘the future’. However, some 
of those who suggest these more ‘imaginative positions’ likely 
would take issue with saying their position is basically neutral by 
another name because it almost minimises the legitimacy of such 
a multi-faceted position which is not just the party keeping its mouth 
shut on being UI or pro-Union, which ‘neutral’ could be defined as. 
For example, ultimately activist (15) thinks that the ‘two-futures’ 
idea ‘distinguishes’ the GPNI from the Alliance view, which is 
‘either to avoid the question or to say that they will remain explicitly 
neutral or to be... very softly pro-status quo which Alliance often fall 
into’. However, this thesis still would define these imaginative 
positions as neutral but recognises them as different from the 
formulaic or typical conception of neutrality. Another activist (14) 
explicitly comments on how they would not describe their ‘creative 

 
218
idea’ for a potential constitutional position as ‘neutral’ per say, it is 
just ‘something different’ and more about actively ‘positively 
creating 
new 
ways 
of 
thinking 
about 
democracy 
and 
borders…creating new and fresh thinking…as distinct from solving 
a nineteenth century problem’. Here the activist is trying to square 
this with a wider Green vision and party brand that is not neutral in 
the classic sense, but still non-ethnic and above all focused on ‘the 
future’. 
 
The GPNI and its activists also pride themselves on being 
‘rebels’ or radical in NI and from this there is a sense of ‘guilt’ that 
being neutral on the CQ is not something that is seen as fair from 
the perspective of others. For example, one GPNI activist (6) 
knows the party staying neutral may not be ‘good enough’ for some 
because it is more important to them and they maybe lived with the 
constitutional status impact such as the conflict and the associated 
violence. For another GPNI activist (3) ‘I suppose I really kind of 
hope we're never going to be in the position that we need to take a 
defined position on it and…I think to some people, that might seem 
a bit lacking in conviction or being bold enough…’. This is best 
understood again through the lens of the Greens as an issues-
based party. The party and its activists seek to apply the lens of 
being focused on the future in a holistic sense which generates a 
sense of responsibility to take a position on these issues given how 
much of an impact on what the future will look like they will have.  
 
Even though they are open about the party starting to 
engage more with the CI, or see other Greens wanting to, certain 
activists (12; 1) do not want to present the party, or themselves, as 
suddenly prioritising the CQ. Instead, they recognise the need for 
the party to engage with the CI is becoming increasingly apparent, 
or they accept that the party will have to decide on a CQ at some 
point as it is a party operating in a context where this is a critical 
and increasingly salient issue. Activist (12) thinks it is still right that 

 
219
now is not the time for the GP to deal with the CQ, but they do 
believe this window is getting shorter. There is a clear sense here 
that the issue is pushing its way to the forefront and while the party 
is starting to realise this, the activists are still trying to get back to 
their focus on wider issues as a caveat to their movement towards 
engaging the CQ. The other activist (1) shares that they still believe 
there are much bigger things in NI that affect ordinary people such 
as climate change (again referring back to the core issue priority), 
but they also appreciate that as a local party in this context the GP 
has to deal with the local issues that are important to people, and 
there will come a time that the party does have to decide. Perhaps 
the GPNI can take a position, but in a ‘neutral way’ that is still 
aligned to green thinking, that is it does not have to ‘give up’ its 
nicheness to take a position. Others like activists 7 and 5, despite 
believing the party should remain neutral, currently still think it 
would be slightly easier for the GP to take a position than it would 
be for Alliance: I think it  would be slightly easier for the Green Party 
to take a position than it would be for Alliance, actually… the Green 
Party could make…an easier argument in a certain sense or one 
that allied more clearly with their values as a party’ (activist 5).  
 
Returning to the principles and ideology of the party, it still 
appears that taking a position that ‘aligns’ to green principles 
means taking a ‘nationalist, or united Ireland’ position. There is a 
question whether these activists or others, would think it would be 
straightforward to use and, if so, how any of the founding principles 
(e.g. ecological wisdom, social justice, nonviolence and, in 
particular, subsidiarity) to rationalise the party coming out in 
support of remaining in the Union. Even broadly it appears that the 
UI argument is easier to make and for this to ‘resonate’ based on 
green principles. One activist’s (12) assessment is that it is an 
easier sell from those on the centre-left or progressive politics who 
could probably sell it to GP members better, a different vision of a 
new state, rather than what the UK is, and particularly through the 

 
220
last years of Tory governments and austerity. A useful example is 
the Scottish Greens who came out as pro-independence and 
interviewees were asked about this.  
 
Many of the same arguments around grassroots democracy 
and getting away from Britain are seen as rationalising a UI tied to 
subsidiarity and were articulated as such, yet most activists wanted 
their party to remain neutral currently. However, a certain activist, 
who saw how it was beneficial for the Scottish GP, was one of the 
few who wanted the GPNI to take a position. GPNI activist (13) said 
it is not as easy to justify a UI as an independent Scotland: ‘I have 
deep misgivings about the British state…Scotland is clearly voting 
to the left of the rest of the UK and is distinct culturally, if nothing 
else…’. There is likely cross-pollination of observing another GP 
taking a stance and affiliated with a CP in Scotland which leads 
some GPNI activists to believe this is necessary for the GPNI to 
do. However, the activists illustrate that maybe it is not so 
‘straightforward’ to compare the GPNI and Scottish GP taking a CP 
because NI and Scotland are two different contexts, or 
alternatively, unification and independence are not directly 
comparable forms of constitutional change. Green support for a UI 
therefore could be understood as a similar path to Green support 
for an independent Scotland as access to a more progressive and 
liberalising society and so in line with Green priorities and issue 
interests. However, an occasional activist was more sceptical 
about the ROI as representing the progressive alternative avenue 
that a more progressive potential independent Scotland does 
within the UK (activist 5). 
 
Conclusion 
 
This chapter has traced three key manifestations of the 
GPNI's 
conceptual 
markers 
(non-alignment/civicness, 

 
221
constitutional neutrality and for the GPNI, issue orientation); 
working-class focus, issue-based identity, and constitutional 
neutrality as they appear in the accounts of party activists. In each 
case, the picture that emerges is more complex and more 
contested than the markers themselves might suggest. Working-
class focus is sustained through party branding even where 
individual activists' own class backgrounds are ambiguous or 
middle-class. It generates genuine material trade-offs for activists 
from working-class communities, and it intersects with ethno-
national identity in ways that vary considerably across the activist 
base. Issue-based party identity and the commitment to eco-
socialism as the organising principle of political action is deeply 
held. Activists join and stay for reasons not only tied to leftism and 
the intensity of their commitment shifts across issues over time, 
and the party's claim to 'own' the eco-socialist issue structures its 
competition with both PBP and Alliance in politically significant 
ways. Constitutional neutrality, finally, is not a static posture, but a 
dynamic and internally contested orientation. In a time of an altered 
political context, activists are increasingly aware that the party's 
neutrality is under pressure and many are open to or actively 
supportive of a more engaged role for the GPNI in constitutional 
deliberations, though the form and content of that engagement 
remain subjects of debate. There is diversity to the drivers of this 
engagement ranging from the party’s wider ethos, the role of Brexit, 
the party’s scope to reach out to unionists, and differential top-
down and bottom-up processes. 
 
Taken together, these three manifestations illuminate the 
GPNI as a party whose conceptual identity is not simply imposed 
from above through leadership, but is actively negotiated, 
sustained, and complicated by the activists who constitute its 
membership and day-to-day engine. The working-class ethos, the 
eco-socialist commitment, and the principle of constitutional 

 
222
neutrality each are performed in different ways and with different 
degrees of self-awareness by the GPNI's activist base. 
 
 
 

 
223
Chapter 6: Constitutional mind-set of the 
constitutionally neutral activists 
 
Introduction 
 
This chapter explores the factors and prisms through which 
activists as the core of a party with a position of constitutional 
neutrality navigate the constitutional question. It engages with core 
Green Party commitments on issues such as the environment and 
eco-socialism and how these influence support for a referendum or 
CP, the utopian versus rationalist assessments of a potential UI and 
what it offers, the design of an effective process for debate and 
transition, but also the interaction of residual identities and 
preferences rooted in affiliations as well as commitments to the 
Green agenda and issues.  
 
Factor 1: The environment under each constitutional set-up: 
Do you need a UI to achieve all-island policy and climate 
transformation? 
 
Unsurprisingly, the environmental impact will influence the 
constitutional decisions of many GPNI activists. However, even for 
several pro-UI activists, this does not mean they enthusiastically 
recognise that the ROI or its governmental approach to the 
environment is clearly better. For example, one activist who is pro-
UI in the longer-term (11) says compared to the British 
government, Ireland is ‘slightly, just slightly slightly better’ in terms 
of fracking licenses and pesticides due to being in the EU, and 
other internal reasons. As mentioned in the earlier chapter, the 
conceptualisation of a UI is envisioned as a future that is more than 
simply changing the constitutional status to flip what is currently in 
place. A UI is attractive in the main only if it generates a more 
holistic set of changes in what is the ‘New Ireland’ than just joining 
the current ROI.  

 
224
 
There are three potential avenues for environmental progress 
on an island-wide basis There are certain distinct logics through 
which it may be more ‘convincing’ that a full-blown united Ireland is 
necessary to achieve what an activist hopes to achieve in terms of 
the environment but that is not the only option. In the first 
‘implementation argument’ a GPNI activist thinks that NI’s 
environment would be better in a UI as they think an all-island 
approach would be a more efficient means of addressing eco-
issues.  However, given the scope for all-island cooperation without 
a constitutional change it is difficult to understand under this logic 
why they think a UI is necessary. For some Greens and in particular 
nationalist-inclined Greens, a UI is favoured as a means of diluting 
unionist or Westminster control, and this is what will allow for better 
eco-action. In this way, all-island decisions become achievable 
which in practice they are not currently, given the attitude of 
unionism and the British Government. As indicated in the 
assessment of the First Environment Minister of the devolved 
assembly currently mutually beneficial all-island engagement on 
the environment is not free of ideological resistance from those of 
a broadly unionist perspective who are wary of any ‘all island’ or 
‘cross-border’ environmental/ sustainable development agenda 
(Barry, 2009). A UI would clearly overcome these roadblocks for 
many Greens. 
 
If instead they think that NI’s environment would be better 
because in a UI NI would be back under EU legislation, than it 
makes more sense why they see a UI as an environmentally 
beneficial outcome. This is the second potential avenue. 
Otherwise, if the activist views a UI as better for the 
climate/environment from a stand-point of ‘nation-building’ this is 
the ‘radical argument’ and provides a very clear reason why it is 
possible to understand why a UI would receive Green support for 
environmentalist reasons. Academic Seán Fearon recognises the 

 
225
‘implementation and radical argument’ in justifying the positives of 
a UI. Commenting on this idea in terms of electricity trading across 
the island, Fearon (2021) explained ‘A unitary all-Ireland state can 
and should make implementing climate policy, and the 
infrastructural commitments underpinning it, more effective and 
responsive.’ But, again, this appears in theory to be possible 
without a UI specifically if alternative cooperative mechanisms 
were in place on the island. However, Fearon ultimately goes 
further to develop a justification closer to the radical position 
explaining that ‘Unity is in essence a process of nation-
building…More specifically, this new dispensation can create 
political space to make the required structural changes and secure 
a safe climate future.’ 
 
Given this, some activists (5; 8) themselves are convinced that 
partition in certain ways works against achieving an all-island 
environmental policy, as there are barriers created by the 
bureaucracy of having a border, or even more specifically the 
uncertainty created by the border about which side of the border 
has responsibility for dealing with the environment. Activist (5) said 
‘...in theory, you could…but of course, the red tape, the political 
symbolism...all of the things that go along with that when you have 
a border and you have the divisive nature of that border, I think, 
make it very difficult.’ For this reason, an implementation argument 
for a UI follows, as an all-island approach to the environment short 
of unification would not ultimately have meaningful success. 
However, in turn, a United Ireland without nation-building and 
transformational change more broadly is considered by some to 
have limited benefits or even detrimental consequences. 
‘Degrowth’ or ‘Post growth’ perspectives argue that living 
standards are not solely determined by economic growth, but that 
instead redistribution and a circular approach to production can 
achieve the same goals but an ‘implementation argument’ 

 
226
deemphasises these strategies as compared to more radical 
reimagination approaches (Fearon and Barry, 2022). 
 
Fearon and Barry (2022) outline how an economic transition 
underpinning Irish reunification that intensifies and geographically 
extends the neoliberal growth models would see a New Ireland 
accelerate, rather than reverse, patterns of unsustainability we 
currently observe in both jurisdictions. Further to this, Fearon and 
Barry are critical of those arguing that a New Ireland would need a 
smaller public service than the two separate administrations 
currently operating and see this as a potential neoliberal scaling 
back of the state, which if replicated across the board in the 
approach to a UI would leave the new state no better off and 
potentially worse off than the two states it has replaced on issues 
of sustainability and distributive justice. 
 
For many there are limits to the synergistic and implementation 
argument here and instead the idea of a broader 'reimagined 
future' is at the core of it. While a GPNI activist might say they are 
primarily motivated by, for example, the ‘environment factor’ in a 
referendum, to that activist they see the ‘environment factor’ as not 
just ‘will a UI be better for the environment’ but a much broader 
factor linked to ‘social issues’ like economic transformation. For 
example, one GPNI activist (16) – who is pro-UI anyway - reiterates 
this is not a cop-out, but for them, the issues (environmentalism 
and socialism), are so interlinked they cannot differentiate them so 
a whole economic transformation and revolution is necessary to 
address climate change and vice versa. In seeking to make 
progress on all of these things, this is understood as being easier 
to achieve in a UI as the idea of starting a new state and having 
constitutional change creates the opportunity for more substantive 
and radical changes of various forms deemed necessary. These 
arguments are perhaps most common among those already 
committed to the idea of a UI and could be read as retrospective 

 
227
justification of that position, although there is a clear link to the core 
issue agendas of the Greens.  
 
Being a Green supporter does influence what issues voters 
care about as these are policy-oriented voters of a niche party 
(Siers, 2025) but also how they weigh and interpret issues even 
where other voters care about them nominally to some degree. 
While it was difficult to figure out which factors would ‘uniquely’ 
influence Alliance activists in a referendum over the more 
moderate elements of unionism or nationalism, select GPNI 
activists are able to see how ‘shared factors’ (i.e. factors that will 
come into the deliberations of everyone) will influence GP 
supporters in a ‘uniquely green way’. Therefore, this is a different 
interpretive framework for Green supporters. Being Green in this 
sense provides a lens around constitutionality that others do not 
have access to. For example, one activist (6) demonstrates that 
maybe being green offers you a ‘lens’ to recognise the immediate 
impacts of environmental and energy regression and even though 
they think those external to the party would be partially influenced 
in a referendum by some perception of the ROI doing better in 
terms of energy, ultimately it would take longer for outsiders to 
understand the impact of this and it would need to be explained in 
economic terms. In this way, GPNI activists have a sense that 
GPNI members and voters have a much stronger engagement with 
the environment and longer-term consequences than they believe 
many other voters have. This can also connect to the advantages 
of ROI EU membership in terms of renewables and lower energy 
prices, and this is seen as potentially an influence over people in 
NI’s support for a UI in a referendum, but this will likely be much 
more readily apparent and important for GPNI voters and 
members. For example, even though the previously mentioned 
activist (6) thinks people will be influenced by Brexit in a 
referendum again they think ‘being green’ impacts what aspect of 
Brexit will be influential. They shared that ‘everybody will be 

 
228
influenced by Brexit in different ways, but probably for different 
reasons than a Green party person would be’. This is because 
others will not be looking at environmental policies coming from the 
EU, they will instead be thinking more about issues such as their 
kids’ ability to go to university in the EU. While in the end very few 
non-GPNI members or voters are likely to have the environment as 
their number one issue in a poll, while a plan is being developed 
GP activists can argue then as it will be very close even if just 1% 
of people are swayed by a strong green agenda, it could make the 
difference and therefore a plan for a New Ireland should appeal to 
this 1%. 
 
How does a UI and the ROI stack up as an economic 
alternative? For some, the ROI does not offer a particularly distinct 
alternative given its export-oriented growth model and comparable 
neoliberal capitalist ethos. These anti-capitalist attitudes are again 
demonstrative of the pre-eminence of ideological commitments in 
the Greens which can sometimes ‘override’ their ethno-national 
preferences/identity. As GPNI activist (1) outlines ‘... I don't identify 
as British because I hate all the kind of, like, colonial imperial 
history to do with it…But also...if there was a referendum tomorrow, 
I don't think I would vote to be part of a united Ireland as Ireland is 
now, because to me, it's a bit of a parasitic capitalist hell.’  In reality, 
given so many activists see Dublin and Belfast, London and Dublin, 
NI and the ROI, etc., as very much the same (as many Alliance 
activists do also) the common evaluation of the ROI as ‘capitalist’ 
is still not necessarily the biggest turn off because they do not think 
NI is much less ‘capitalist’ in comparison to ROI, or Belfast is much 
less ‘capitalist’ to Dublin. Ultimately for leftist Greens, these states 
are all capitalist. This assessment is backed up by one activist (4) 
who ‘backtracked’ on their initial assumption in the interview that 
the ROI is more ‘big-business-focused’ given NI has also been 
attracting big tech companies into the region. Notably, while the 

 
229
ROI is attacked as being neo-liberalist capitalist, there was no 
major discussion about the UK in this regard.  
 
Factor 2: Dealing with the ‘shock’ of leaving the EU: How 
Brexit impacts GPNI’s activists’ constitutional thinking at 
different ends 
 
In Northern Ireland, political elites have drawn on Brexit as an 
opportunity: to achieve a united Ireland in the case of Nationalist 
leaders, or to strengthen the union for Unionist elites (Evershed 
and Murphy, 2021; Gormley-Heenan and Aughey, 2017). By 
sculpting Brexit in this way, leaders have prioritised their own 
groups’ political agenda over intergroup harmony. However, the 
‘vision for opportunity’ is not the same for GPNI activists. In their 
case, there is instead the core idea of different versions of these 
visions of opportunities like the reimagined eco-socialist future in a 
UI discussed above. Brexit generated this shock in thinking about 
how NI fits within the UK and ignorance of England towards NI. 
Realistically it was a shock for wider society in NI among the 
Remain voting population that were confronted with this ignorance 
and served either to harden pro-UI attitudes among Green 
nationalists or lead to questions for pro-Union or neutral Green 
activists. By threatening the GFA and raising the spectre of a return 
to a border on the island, Brexit has triggered a ‘constitutional 
moment’ generating a shift in thinking about island-wide relations 
and accelerated reunification debates (Todd, 2017). Stephen Farry 
recognised that technically the structures of the GFA were not 
challenged by Brexit in itself, but it potentially hurt the spirit of the 
agreement, impacting people’s scope to hold many diverse 
identities, and causing people to revert back to their single 
identities (Northern Ireland Assembly, 2017, a). 
 
GPNI’s own Euroscepticism as regards the EU neoliberalist 
agenda explains why at least compared to Alliance more GPNI 

 
230
activists exist at the ‘extreme’ ends in terms of Brexit’s impact on 
their constitutional mindset. Certain GPNI activists expressed that, 
to some degree, their personal Euroscepticism or cynicism about 
the EU was perhaps not reflective of the wider GP population. For 
example, one activist (3) knows there are many Green Party 
people who would potentially be less cynical about the EU than 
them, but they still feel the institution is somewhat ‘unreformable’. 
In fact, several activists expressed this sense that their 
Euroscepticism does not reflect strands within the GP more 
broadly. Returning to the EU is not something they are thirsting for 
albeit on balance, apart from one activist (7) who is radically 
Eurosceptic to the point they would not vote remain if they had their 
time all over again, Brexit is still viewed as a ‘bad thing’ to have 
happened. This is likely the difference between hard (i.e., 
fundamental anti-EU project) and soft (i.e., conditional opposition) 
(Taggart and Szczerbiak, 2002). As there is a greater 
Euroscepticism but ultimate pro-Remain preference among 
several GPNI activists, this means there are some who are 
indifferent about a United Ireland within the EU. As discussed later, 
at the other extreme, some other activists’ constitutional 
deliberations are instead strongly shaped by returning to the EU 
via reunification. 
 
Brexit increased feelings of Europeanness among those in 
remaining states ‘because the constructed identity of a united 
Europe strengthens in such a crucial situation of endogenous 
crisis...’ (Breitmoser, 2021, p. 74). Within this context, it makes 
sense why one very soft unionist activist (4) credits EU 
membership as the driving force behind why they now support a 
UI. However, endogenous shocks assume a ‘sudden’ effect on 
identity but, in reality, the impact appears to come from how Brexit 
showed to activists that the English do not care about NI, but they 
also reveal that they already knew this before Brexit even came 
about. In this way, this process shows that Brexit just ‘reinforced’ 

 
231
their pre-existing perception rather than formulating it and, 
potentially other longer-standing factors (e.g. they (4) considered 
themselves part Irish) could also have contributed to this change. 
More broadly, with respect to the idea of Brexit ‘reinforcing’ pre-
existing perceptions rather than generating new views, some 
activists like 16 and 17 outline how their resentment for how NI was 
treated by the UK in terms of Brexit was tied to a form of grievance 
that had already largely solidified prior to Brexit, such as when they 
went to university in England. However, the frustrations and 
resentment they had from university seems to overlap with the 
inferiority that Brexit conferred, similar to how the young people in 
Todd and McEvoy (2023) ‘who had gone to college in the other 
jurisdiction noted the ways they were misunderstood or stigmatised 
in that jurisdiction’ (p. 8). Activist (16) similarly outlined ‘…sort of 
the lack of knowledge…really cemented that…you do feel like a 
second-class citizen, to some extent…as a UK citizen, but not part 
of mainland Britain’. 
 
Sometimes it is indeed hard to see how Brexit has impacted the 
activists’ view of their ‘Britishness’ as some seem to talk about their 
view of the EU as having already changed before Brexit. GPNI 
activist (1) said they got a view of the EU after working and living 
around Europe after leaving school, but also after Brexit they 
‘realised’ that they do not resonate with this form of Britishness as 
their identity, having seen Brexit fought on issues like immigration. 
Another activist (10) explains ‘on balance, I feel more Irish than 
British and particularly now...the version of being British that I 
would have felt isn't the Britain I recognise anymore’. There is a 
shock to their self-understanding of their own Britishness but also 
to what Britishness meant generally as Brexit offered a very 
specific view of it that Green activists and supporters were 
especially uncomfortable with. Rather than Brexit generating this 
from whole cloth though, this likely had some deeper roots. 
Changes in attitudes to Britishness and the EU were already in 

 
232
motion for some but Brexit constituted the strongest of exogenous 
shocks on top of this that ultimately leads to confrontation with 
identity and attitudes.  
 
This shock to their understanding of Britishness now enables a 
potential vision of how the Britishness of Green supporters 
(different from the vision of Britishness Brexit brought into focus) 
could actually be accommodated with adjustments in a UI that 
facilitated 
that 
'progressive 
Britishness' 
and 
a 
form 
of 
Europeanness that ‘Brexit Britishness’ has dispensed with. Brexit 
led to a realisation that Britishness does not have to be a 
connection to the UK in the traditional way as that is no longer a 
Britishness that Green supporters feel affiliated to. One GPNI 
activist (7) thinks reunification would have to lead in some way to 
a rethinking and reimagining of Ireland and Irishness and it would 
require a reimagining of Britishness in Ireland, and by ‘rethinking’ 
flags, anthems and symbols under a UI. Another activist, (15), who 
liked the idea of the GPNI articulating a ‘two-futures’ idea’ also can 
see a future in NI where Irishness is embraced the same way as in 
the South. The activist explains ‘you can imagine a future in 
Northern Ireland where Irishness is more central or treated equally 
to Irishness from Cork or Irishness from Kerry’.  
 
As mentioned previously in a distinct fashion, Brexit has 
impacted at the ‘extremes.’ For some, it completely changed views. 
For example, it made some activists pro-UI, or another activist (5), 
who is not from NI or Europe, went from feeling not much at all 
about a united Ireland or thinking about constitutionality – as that 
was not even remotely part of their upbringing to feeling something. 
Brexit ‘shifted the balance a little bit’ in terms of making them see 
the positives of returning to the EU and for them this shift ‘from 
nothing to something’ about a UI is significant. However, the most 
radical of the activist cohort would be closer to a pro-Lexit position. 
One very Lexit activist would vote leave in a Brexit referendum if 

 
233
they had their time all over again and they also see a positive in 
Brexit in terms of a UI. This GPNI activist (7) shares Brexit and how 
its consequences have fast-forwarded the reunification debate, 
which in some respects ‘you could say it is good, as now we are 
dealing with an issue that we were kicking down the road for maybe 
a decade or so’.  
 
Although, as among Alliance, many GPNI activists also 
were ‘in the middle’ whereby Brexit made them think more 
generally about the state of the Union or showed them just how 
badly NI is treated by the UK government, but it has not 
dramatically altered constitutional thinking. This is still evidence of 
a 'shock', though one which is unlikely to be a radical 
transformation of views, but forces supporters and activists to 
begin that reckoning as it has for many in NI. This is, however, 
especially true for the Greens given their focus on wider values and 
issues which now require redress and imagination about what the 
future may involve.  
 
Factor 3: Who should run the UI? The GPNI don’t just want 
Irish Tories 
 
For GPNI activists when considering the CQ and a potential 
UI, there are three distinct dimensions for the potential 
transformation in governance to be considered. Each of these 
dimensions must be assessed in terms of the scope to make 
substantive improvements (or avoid something worse) for 
someone who is a GPNI activist. 
 
A. Tier 1: FF/FG/Tories in the Union 
 
The first dimension Green activists must consider is the nature 
of the government that the ROI would have if and when unification 
were to occur and the implications for GPNI issue preferences. In 

 
234
this respect, the changing face of ROI politics is critical to consider. 
Combining survey data since 1973 and all Irish election studies 
between 2002 and 2020, Müller and Regan (2021) show that the 
average Irish voter now leans to the centre-left. This move of ROI 
politics to the left could in principle be a pull factor for Green 
activists for whom the ROI may increasingly look like the 
progressive constitutional option. GPNI activists are particularly 
concerned with who would be ‘governing’ this unified Ireland. The 
conservative nature of ROI politics turns off several GPNI activists 
as in reality not everyone is convinced currently that the ROI or its 
government is moving more to the left at least compared to the UK. 
This suggests that the patterns Müller and Regan identify have not 
convinced GPNI supporters/activists yet and this is likely 
connected to the growth model in the South, housing problems, 
and the issues with public services in particular the health service. 
For example, one activist (3) notes that if there truly is a left 
government in the Republic which ends up doing good for the 
planet and people, it might sway people to a UI in the GP that may 
have been on the fence or would have not originally supported a 
UI. They say if it ends up with ‘Irish Tories rather than British 
Tories… does that really…benefit anybody? I’m not banking on a 
left-leaning utopian government coming in the Republic anytime 
soon, sadly…’  
 
There is a question here as to whether GPNI activists who are 
pro-UI due to a desire to ‘decolonise’ NI (these activists are 
discussed more later) would reject a UI even if they still assessed 
the ROI as conservative by the time a referendum is called. Activist 
(6) would be willing to ‘trade-off’ having a practically Tory ROI 
government for a bigger voice for NI in politics and they justify their 
support based on NI getting a stronger voice, rather than outright 
decolonisation in the first instance ‘… know that the government in 
the south right now are very neoliberal and practically Tories 
themselves but I just feel like in the longer term... It's better to have 

 
235
a say on this island than be screaming into the void of UK politics 
or British politics…’.   
 
In turn, there is the question of who would govern Britain if 
rejecting a referendum and remaining in the UK. Would this be the 
Tories again? Labour? Reform? The challenge for those within the 
Greens who favour retaining the union is to frame this as the more 
leftist and/or progressive choice. This will clearly be partially 
dependent on the governing parties and coalition in the UK, but 
also on how those with unionist-coded backgrounds engage with 
and seek to frame the choice for the wider party to make.  
 
An activist (15) can see the potential of someone’s leftism 
to ‘override’ their unionist ideology in their evaluations and result in 
the somewhat counterintuitive outcome of a unionist-coded 
individual believing an SF government73 would be attractive. Also, 
in a way one activist (12) sees how it can work in the reverse, in 
which the more left-leaning the politics of the UK goes the more 
likely it is to pull unionists who are on the left back: ‘And I think that 
people...in the unionist camp are missing a trick of appealing to 
people on the left or centre-left by talking about the UK’s radical 
history…the suffragettes, the Chartists, the trade union movement, 
abolition of slavery...things that I like about the UK in politics, 
there's nobody selling that version of the UK to me.’ 
 
There is of course scope for the conditions to change by the 
time a referendum is called. For example, support for a UI by Green 
activists is likely conditional on the identity of the British governing 
parties. Years of Tory government for ideological reasons is 
especially distasteful to the Greens and is likely to generate 
rejectionist impulses towards the constitutional status quo. 
 
73 SF in the ROI is very clearly identified as left-wing and distinct from NI SF as 
below. 

 
236
However, the Tories may not be in power and/or Brexit 
consequences and the relationship to the EU may be addressed. 
If these issues are addressed, this likely changes the calculus. 
Activist (12) for example said when answering on the impact of 
Brexit on their constitutional thinking, ‘a little, but not hugely, I don't 
know, part of me thinks that the UK will return to the European 
Union within the next fifteen years… [What] made me question the 
constitutional question a bit more, is these successive Tory 
governments over the last number of years…So, I think that's an 
unanalysed element, people just go with Brexit, but I think there's 
really something in these Tory governments' austerity, populism…I 
think that's maybe caused people to question it in addition to 
potential loss of EU citizenship’. 
 
B. Tier 2: Sinn Féin, but ROI Sinn Féin not NI 
 
The second dimension to consider in terms of governance 
transformation in the run-up to a referendum and the nature of the 
potential alternatives on offer to the Greens that they must consider 
in choosing whether to support constitutional change is the scope 
for major change in electoral politics in the South, Of course, as 
above this could mean a general move to the left and/or a UI itself 
leading to a renewal of what the New Ireland will look like to fit an 
eco-socialist Green agenda. If instead there is not that major 
radical change, then who will govern a UI is likely to be quite similar 
to the current ROI. This could however be a change from FF/FG 
and if a potential left government was likely to be elected (even 
without encompassing radical institutional change) likely led by SF 
and potentially involving the Social Democrats, PBP or the GPROI 
themselves, then this may be more attractive to Green activists in 
a way that traditional ROI politics would not be. There are however 
specific issues with this as a change of direction that could entice 
GPNI support especially given the key role likely to be played in 
any such left government in the South by SF. 

 
237
 
There is a lack of knowledge between North and South in 
terms of things like public services and the broader political 
environment. Todd et al., (2023) outlined how ‘In each of the four 
focus groups, low levels of awareness about life and policy on the 
‘other’ side of the border, and how public services such as health 
and education were currently provided, were openly acknowledged 
by the vast majority of those taking part’ (p. 130). In this project, a 
similar pattern emerged in terms of familiarity with SF in the South. 
There was a mixed perception of SF that seemed to be reflective 
overall in a desire to know more about how politics works in the 
ROI. One activist (5) frames this as a lack of knowledge, saying 
‘…again, this is where…I don't feel like I know enough about the 
day-to-day, like, politics of it. So, like, is Sinn Féin in the south like 
Sinn Féin in the north?’ Activist (15) felt it was not necessarily a 
bad thing that SF was doing well because that success may show 
that voters in the Republic would be on a similar wavelength to the 
kind of people in the GPNI given SF’s appeal in the South primarily 
connected to its centre-left politics. Also, Green activists identify 
different types of supporters of SF in NI to ROI. Activist (15) 
explains that SF would want some of the same centre-left things 
as the Greens do, like dealing with the housing crisis, and their 
success is rooted in leftism, not because it has been shouting 
about a UI or defending the IRA constantly as would be the case 
(from the activist’s perspective) in NI. One example of more 
effective tone-conscious communication instead from SF which if 
repeated systematically may court the centre-ground also came up 
among GPNI activists when, at the time of some interviews, Queen 
Elizabeth died, and some activists brought up the public message 
from the SF leader. For some GPNI activists (4; 10), the type of 
message and language used by SF in this case showcased what 
would ‘win over’ those who might feel like they will be excluded in 
a UI, that they will not be alienated or make some strands of 
unionism feel genuinely understood and engaged with. At the same 

 
238
time, SF even in the ROI are not seen as having the same type of 
left-wing politics so the GP could still differentiate itself or the leftist 
credentials of SF may still be questioned by some. In the case of 
activist (3) they questioned the leftist credentials of SF ‘…I suppose 
that's taking into account that, if Sinn Féin really are a left party, 
which is up for debate because they certainly aren't up here 
[laughter]…’. GPNI activists do have particular admiration for Sinn 
Féin’s efforts to build a socialised healthcare model in the ROI. For 
example, while private payment for healthcare and the influence of 
the Roman Catholic Church are a UI turn-off, one activist (6) also 
recognises there is much work going on in the south with parties 
like SF leading on attempts to improve healthcare provision. 
 
SF for others is seen as part of the picture of a ‘reimagined 
future’ provided for by a potential UI. Some activists seek a UI as a 
form of socialist utopia, but both this cohort and even among those 
who also hold more pragmatic views and are more focused on 
weighing up the evidence, what an SF UI government would mean 
in terms of the scope for major change is a key consideration. Even 
if SF are considered left, they are not considered the same type of 
left as the GPNI, in the same way the Greens taking a UI position 
would not be the same thing as the nationalist parties being pro-
UI. For example, activist (15) views SF in the ROI as left, but see 
their leftism as different to GPNI left-libertarianism, and connects it 
to potential authoritarian tendencies within SF.   
 
C. Tier 3: GP in government, but a version of the GP which is 
more like GPNI versus GPROI 
 
The consideration of whether to support a UI for the GPNI is 
also dependent on an additional internal dimension, in terms of 
what the future is likely to be for the party itself if a UI were to come 
to pass both strategically and then as an issues-based party in a 
New Ireland.  

 
239
First, there are practical considerations in terms of voting and 
strategy. Activists consider whether a UI could offer a better chance 
for representation due to PR-STV and prospects for government. 
This means the practical considerations of electoral system 
currently and in a possible UI are being considered as this will 
affect the prospects for the party and its influence on issues in 
parliament and in government. There is also the perspective that a 
change in constitutional status would enable the Greens to have a 
say as NI does not get that with Westminster and the Greens and 
other micro parties could have more of a say in a UI. For example, 
when answering could a UI offer anything to NI that it does not 
already have, one activist (9) shares ‘A Green Party in government 
would be something. So there's a different electoral system, which 
probably could be for the benefit of Green Party and smaller 
minority parties to get a foothold…’  
 
Next, there are strategic considerations for the GPNI activists 
in terms of potential competition with the current GPROI especially 
as the GPNI is much smaller. This raises a number of questions. 
How do they look at the current Greens in the South? Would they 
have sway over GPNI in the event of a UI? What does the Green 
record in ROI say to GPNI supporters about what the future might 
hold? It may be that a Green party in government is more likely to 
be offered by a UI given the ROI has shown how the Greens can 
go into coalition, but it may be more preferable again that a Green 
party under a UI can become a challenger to SF from the left and 
generate a politics with a left-oriented centre of gravity. Of course 
this would still require the Greens to significantly grow. 
 
Alliance activists have a greater dilemma than the GPNI 
activists about the survival of their party after a UI result. Even if 
the GPNI is forced to merge with the GPROI, at least there will still 
be a place for green politics, while Alliance risks losing relevancy. 
However, this pessimistic angle was not the majority view from 

 
240
activists. Although some activists question the relevancy or fit of 
Alliance in a UI – one Alliance activist, (4), recognises the 
possibility that Alliance becomes ‘niche’, and possibly even 
‘irrelevant’ in a UI - on balance though, more Alliance activists still 
envisage an existence for Alliance beyond a unity vote (this 
matches the findings from the focus group research from Tonge et 
al., 2024, p. 184). For example, one activist (18) thinks Alliance 
would also have great opportunities to expand under a UI even 
though it would become a minority party.  However, even though 
some recognise that Alliance would still be needed given its 
mission to unite all communities would not suddenly be achieved 
under a UI (e.g. activist 20), the party could still change with this 
new constitutional arrangement. As one activist (24) explains, there 
will still need to be a cross-community uniting party in a UI, but that 
does not necessarily need to be Alliance, it could be ‘Alliance 
reincarnated’ with members from unionism and nationalism 
integrated into a new party. Some might have to reconsider 
whether they would be in Alliance, or maybe those who Alliance 
appeals to might change in a UI context, which would in turn affect 
the ‘type of activist’ within Alliance.  
 
The other idea is not that the success of any post-UI Green 
Party is the influential factor, but the success of the current Green 
Party in ROI. The GPROI itself could influence the voting decisions 
of those in the GPNI, particularly how its success in government 
would be illustrative of the potential success of green politics. 
Exemplifying this, when commenting on what they speculate could 
sway those undecided GP voters towards voting for a UI, one GPNI 
activist (2) says ‘Essentially, has the Green Party in Ireland had any 
success? Has it influenced policy?...Because that will be critical 
evidence that being a Green Party member can influence the 
future.’ A major question for activists to consider is to what extent 
the GPNI assesses that the GPNI will no longer exist as a separate 
entity to the GPROI under any UI model. Some activists suggested 

 
241
explicitly and others implicitly that there would be an amalgamation 
of the two parties. For example, activist (9) seemed to suggest it is 
obvious the GPNI would not exist while others seemed to consider 
the potential for two parties to persist in a UI. Given this, potentially 
the idea of the GPNI ‘officially’ joining up with the GPROI under a 
UI jurisdiction might not be a completely uncomfortable prospect 
for GPNI activists given even at this stage most activists were 
indifferent to, or unconcerned by, the party’s all-island status (it was 
not even clear to select activists whether the official label was ‘all-
island’ or ‘all-Ireland’). Even the most ‘British-identifying’ activist (9) 
concedes (after stating that being an all-Ireland party turns off 
some voters) that it makes sense that the party is all-Ireland, as 
opposed to all-UK, for environmental purposes as they share the 
same eco-landmass. Activists present the ‘all-island status’ as 
something that does not really bother them, or it is at least not an 
issue in general apart from specific times such as the 2020 ROI 
coalition-building period and when the motion for this status was 
first passed. Alternatively, they view the status as not really an 
issue because as much as the GPNI have links with the GPROI, it 
has great relationships with the GPs in the UK too. While the GPNI 
supporters may not be ‘ideologically resistant’ to the all-island 
status, they are resistant towards being considered the same as 
the GPROI. Bolleyer (2010) accounts for the evolution of the 
GPROI away from its more radical and bottom-up, grassroots-led 
roots towards a more elite-led, moderate organisation. The GPNI 
has a greater persistence of radicalism and member-led policy 
positioning, which likely underpins this distinct self-image and 
distance from the GPROI observed among the GPNI activists.  
 
Ultimately for many Greens especially those who see a UI as 
the radical socialist destination, the identity of the governance of 
the New Ireland is less important than the creation of this New 
Ireland itself. As an issues-based niche party the focus is on the 
issues. For this reason, there will always be an attitude alongside 

 
242
'who would govern a UI' and/or 'what would be the institutional 
advantages for Greens in a UI' that is focused instead on the party 
making progress on issues as this is the core mission for a party 
not defined by its constitutional position and ethno-national identity.  
 
Factor 4: Not everyone is ‘undecided’ – being not so neutral in 
a constitutionally neutral party  
  
The GPNI as a constitutionally neutral party has activists 
and members who are not neutral and not driven by evaluations of 
wider policy positions and the Green interpretative framework. This 
section provides an investigation of the extent to which core 
identities do actually still shape their views instead in a post-conflict 
divided society where such identities are difficult to escape.  
  
‘Nationalist-coded greens’  
  
Firstly, there are ‘nationalist-coded greens’ (e.g. activist 7) 
who do not deny that their nationalist upbringing could influence 
them, but they are not ideologically nationalist. Instead they may 
hold a ‘superordinate, cosmopolitan’ identity, but they do think the 
evidence is weighted towards reunification being the better 
outcome in a referendum. This cosmopolitan identity acts as a 
barrier against becoming pulled too much towards the ideology of 
nationalism, that is, ‘a cosmopolitan identity is seen as an 
expression of selfhood that transcends cultural identity and 
collective belonging’ (Skovgaard-Smith and Poulfelt, 2018, p. 130). 
Clearly their reasoning is inflected, often self-consciously, by the 
conditions of their upbringing and socialisation. The cosmopolitan 
identity functions as a kind of ideological insulation and barrier 
against the pull of ethno-nationalism, but it does not and cannot 
wholly neutralise formative influences of background. This is 
important to acknowledge in a post-conflict divided society and not 
unexpected, but still critical for this internal debate in the party.   

 
243
It would be difficult to categorically argue that ‘nationalist-
coded greens’ motivations for a UI result are ‘purely’ evidence-
based. GPNI activist (7) notes ‘I mean, only a fool would deny that 
one's upbringing and even subconscious socialisation and so on 
will have no bearing. I mean, even though I'd self-describe myself 
as a Marxist and an internationalist rather than a nationalist… I 
would have to admit that…you're brought up in an anti-British 
context’74. However, it appears that the activist has been ‘more’ 
convinced by a united Ireland for a long time but previously they 
were convinced more from an ideological angle (republicanism) 
now they state they are convinced by the evidence albeit the 
activist (7) considered the NI statelet as never sustainable anyway. 
However, the biggest indicator of the extent to which identity or 
evidence is the driver of views will be if there is a change in 
preference to match the evidence, such as if new evidence for 
more effective environmental protection goes towards the UK. 
Gesiarz et al. (2019) find  people are influenced to stop gathering 
data earlier when they have reached a desired conclusion. 
However, this activist (7) does not appear to have a ‘cut-off point’ 
for gathering data as being in the Union is seen as at least not 
preventing (even if not quite advancing) constructive eco-
cooperation and this can be acknowledged where the evidence 
appears to counter their own position: ‘You know, for example, we 
already have hydrogen buses that are made in Ballymena being 
used in Dublin. Now, but there, that's an example against what I've 
just said because there we have partition does not stop positive 
moves in the decarbonising renewable energy direction’.  
 
Additionally, activist (7) also does not think all ‘prejudices’ are 
unjustified, as sometimes a prejudice that has some evidence 
behind it is actually a warranted and reasonable belief and they 
think there is also a legitimacy behind forms of instinctive 
 
74 The activist (7) is not necessarily talking directly about their own family unit here. 

 
244
nationalism even if they are critical of this position themselves. In 
this sense it is of course reasonable to expect that one’s cultural 
background and wider ideological view has an influence, which is 
separate and for some may be stronger than policy positions on 
the environment. Even for a constitutionally neutral party’s activists 
this cannot be unexpected in a society where identities have been 
such strong socialising forces. Are GPNI activists actually 
convinced by the ‘evidence’ that a united Ireland is the better 
choice for the environment, or are those pro-UI activists who 
already want a UI using the eco-evidence to reinforce their pre-
existing bias? GPNI activist (1) still thinks that your identity is not 
trumping your environmental concerns as you specifically joined a 
party that works against that, but on reflection says ‘Like, 
sometimes it's even hard to recognise in yourself if you're, almost 
not like stretching the facts to fit your case…Like, "Oh, I think being 
part of a united Ireland would be better for the environment, 
because I really want to join a united Ireland”… Or like the, the 
other way’. It is clear that there is an element of both dynamics at 
work and in different proportions for different individuals but it is 
very challenging to ultimately assess in each case which influence 
predominates.  
  
‘Green-coded Nationalists’  
  
Secondly, there are ‘Green-coded nationalists’ who are eco-
socialists that support the GPNI’s primary focus on issues, but hold 
a deeper connection to the nationalist aspect of their identity. For 
example, while one GPNI activist (16) recognises the strength of 
the environmental argument and policy logic around a UI, 
ultimately their pro-UI stance comes from their identity and long-
standing aspiration as a nationalist. Activist (16) calls themselves 
a soft nationalist. Although cosmopolitan identity might act as a 
barrier, cosmopolitan identities have often been tied into and 
organised along traditionally dominant ethno-divisions, meaning 

 
245
for example that republican and state-centred feminists, or green 
and orange socialists have existed in Northern Ireland history (see 
Todd, 2016, p. 10). These ‘green-coded nationalists’ are not ‘Sinn 
Féin supporters’ in a GPNI body as even if ideologically nationalist 
or more pro-UI, they decided to express their politics through a 
party which is not focused on unification. However, while activist 
(16)’s drive towards the GPNI somewhat comes from their 
‘socialist’ identity, they admitted they initially joined the GPNI 
because they got a job with the party, and so would they have 
joined a nationalist party if they had worked for it? It seems they 
would still have supported the Greens as they have had a long-
term affinity with the GPNI, and they would have always been a 
supporter and their first vote was for the former GPNI leader, Clare 
Bailey.    
  
Activist (16) explains their sense of Irishness and nationalism 
and support for a pro-UI is not built on symbols like flags and they 
would be happy for all of those to be brand new but they 
acknowledge there will always be people on the island who will 
need these traditional symbols from one or both communities. 
Activist (15) who is not explicitly pro-UI but is an Irish nationalist, 
also does not put much weight on symbolic representations of their 
identity, a theme also in Alliance. The activist (15) would like to a 
see a state where the cultural identities of all the peoples of Ireland 
are represented in some way in the state. They explain that might 
well be through symbols or tokenistic displays but that is probably 
fine because much of cultural identity comes down to symbols and 
does not necessarily go much further than that. In this sense, 
independent of the degree or explicitness of support among very 
strong Irish identifiers, there is still a rejection of the idea of a 
‘United Ireland for the Irish.’  
  
The above are exemplars of those for whom the GPNI's issue-
based identity is genuinely and deeply held, but who 

 
246
simultaneously maintain a substantive, rather than incidental, 
connection to Irish nationalist identity and a long-standing 
aspiration towards unification. They acknowledge and engage this 
more directly. The challenge here for the Greens as a 
constitutionally neutral party is whether such individuals could,
