given alternative evidence, support an alternative to a UI (e.g. 
status quo in referendum) or if identity affiliations and aspirations 
make this too challenging despite their commitment to Green 
issues. This will be an important internal challenge for the party to 
navigate as it engages more with this debate and a potential 
referendum.  
 
Overtime - Gradual change via interactions  
  
Although exogenous shocks like Brexit are often assumed 
to generate attitudinal change that can happen ‘in a moment’ this 
perspective does not easily explain how other activists’ movement 
to a pro-UI position operated as ‘gradual change’, that is how the 
narrative moved as they moved through life and encountered 
experiences which prompted periods of re-evaluation. As one 
activist (10) explained, ‘prior to Brexit, I would say that I would 
always have been more pro-unity than anti-unity anyway, all right’. 
These processes of change over time are relatively common if 
sometimes overlooked in accounts of political attitudinal change as 
Lindgren and Wåhlin (2001, p. 359) explain: ‘The identity 
construction of the individual can be perceived as a process of self-
reflexion that arises as a person moves through time and space, 
and 
through 
different 
organisational 
and 
institutional 
environments.’ Of course, it is important to recognise here that this 
may not be full-blown identity change and it is difficult to determine 
whether this is a preferential change or a fundamental change in 
identity. It should be therefore understood that identity change 
need not be so drastic, for example entirely from British to 
Irish.  For one former Protestant GPNI activist (10) having lived in 

 
247
two communities and being an academic ‘opened their eyes’ to 
seeing a united Ireland as a more positive option. They grew up in 
the unionist community and then moved to the nationalist 
community, which ‘gives you a totally different perspective on 
everything’ and being an academic ‘gives another layer of nuance 
in there because you have studied and been exposed to different 
theories and had an opportunity to develop more nuanced 
thinking’. They aptly conclude ‘So, all of that, I think, breaks down 
any of that, traditional background.’ This is an illustrative case of 
the dynamics through which the flexibility and movement of 
identities and preferences are difficult to box in as the activist is 
pro-union not Protestant or Catholic, identifies as neither, but more 
Irish on balance. This is evidence of the multiplicity and of identities 
that form the membership of this type of party and the reality of 
what the ‘centre-ground’ allows.  
 
Of course, the impact of living in both communities likely 
depends on how superficial the interactions were to change 
potential stereotypical views held, but it appears that cross-group 
friendships associated with greater perspective taking and reduced 
intergroup anxiety and prejudice play a key role here (see 
Hewstone et al., 2006). For example, GPNI activist (3) grew up in 
a house where religion and politics were not talked about, but for 
them the key change was their attendance at a Catholic secondary 
despite being from a middle-class soft unionist background. This 
was an experience they were positive about as they learned about 
a ‘different side’ of NI they would not have experienced if they had 
gone to a different secondary school in their area, which has a very 
unionist-leaning demographic. They are now more pro-UI albeit 
they are very against calling a referendum imminently. In other 
cases, it is difficult to pinpoint when attitudinal change occurs. For 
example, activist (17) came from a soft unionist background and 
practising Presbyterian family but came over time to lean towards 

 
248
a pro-UI position even if it is unclear precisely when this happened 
and this appears to be a multi-stage, evolving process.  
  
Overtime – Pragmatism and experiences of academia   
  
Activist (10) also said that while part of the reason they are 
from a unionist background but would be much more likely to vote 
for a UI is how they have lived in both communities, part of it is also 
due to ‘pragmatism’. Activist (4) also thinks a UI is a ‘pragmatic 
choice’ because they think being back in the EU makes sense, but 
it is less clear whether activist (10)’s pragmatic reasoning for a UI 
is due to their academic experience and evaluation of a potential 
UI through this prism. There appeared to be a role for this academic 
perspective in how they expressed themselves on the issue. In this 
way, considering a UI the pragmatic choice is not an abstracted 
concept, and academia has instead allowed them to understand 
the feasibility of a UI, relative to the ideological ideals of 
it. However, this itself assumes that academia is the space for 
pragmatic thinking. Activist (10), and another activist (7) (a 
nationalist-coded green previously discussed) tended to imply that 
being an academic means you are an ‘empiricist’ weighing up the 
evidence on which constitutional outcome is best (from a non-
ideological perspective), but both these activists themselves 
already appear swayed towards a UI being the better option. 
Therefore, it remains difficult to conclude that being an academic 
is engendering a more rational evaluation of the evidence or 
whether these activists already held these views. It may be that 
those who tend to be activists, and perhaps Green activists in 
particular, go into academia already convinced that a UI is the best 
option from an ideological perspective. At the same time it is 
interesting to note that activist (10) in particular came from a PUL 
background, but still opened themselves up to alterative 
perspectives that may not have been available to them in earlier 
years of socialisation. This is suggestive that, at least from a 

 
249
socialisation point of view, academia may have a distinct influence 
even if the notion of academics simply weighing the empirical 
evidence up to decide upon their support for the available options 
is less well-supported.  
  
Definitional (or still gradual?)  
  
Of course, the previous discussions of ‘gradual change’ 
dynamics assume that there was indeed a ‘movement’ towards a 
pro-UI position from a pro-union position, but it might be the case 
that a pro-UI Protestant was ‘always’ pro-UI and this is not 
necessarily the same as a route to 'conversion'. For instance, one 
GPNI activist (6) explains that they have always felt there are many 
ways to be a Protestant in NI and they were brought up as a ‘lefty 
Prod’ as their family was active in socialist/communist circles. 
Potentially it was not a ‘gradual change’ as it was for the previous 
activist (10) that made them pro-UI, but being pro-UI is to them a 
representation of their own ‘lefty Prod’ upbringing. Notably, this 
activist was the only interviewee to mention Marxist or Communist 
interactions. It has been their belief that in order to facilitate a united 
Ireland, the community must be united towards this common goal 
and they are strong believers in the power of socialism as a means 
to unite the opposing communities who will then be more amenable 
towards republican aspirations. As they explain, ‘there are different 
ways to be a prod in this place and that's…the version that I was 
exposed to, coupled with the fact that…our family holidays, through 
my whole childhood and teenage years were just traveling around 
Ireland…’. However, again, an element on learning ‘…I was just 
learning 
about 
the 
history 
of 
British 
colonialism 
and 
imperialism’. There is then potential evidence that certain activists 
consider support for a UI as a natural companion to leftist beliefs 
in a ‘’definitional’ sense. However, there is also a role for additional 
gradual dynamics as the activist refers to socialisation over time 

 
250
too in their experiences of travelling in Ireland and learning about 
Irish and British colonial history incrementally.   
  
Decolonisation – ‘sub-source’  
  
If it can be said that a left ideology aligns with principles of unity, 
it adds complexity to the understanding of another ‘sub-source’ of 
certain former PUL activists’ greater pro-UI preference, specifically 
decolonisation frameworks. For Green social movements, 
sustainable development is strongly tied to post-colonisation and 
decolonisation frameworks of understanding (Doran 1994; Barry 
2004 in Barry and Doran, 2016. p. 329). It appears that the same 
activists (10; 6) (who also experienced a gradual shift in views) 
revealed what may be assumed to be more ‘republican’ reasons 
for why they want unification around decolonisation and settlement 
as the interviews progressed. However, of course, these 
decolonisation-based arguments for unification could be rooted in 
the Green decolonisation and post-colonisation narratives outlined 
above. Another activist (11) who is from the Shankill Road with a 
Protestant background, but is pro-UI in the long-run explains ‘…for 
me, there isn't too much you could do on this side of things, in terms 
of adding to what already is in Northern Ireland to make me want 
to stay in the union, because despite the fact that I could potentially 
use [?] the NHS, I'm still for a united Ireland because, for me 
anyway, I like the idea of un-colonising the country, almost’. They 
share this revelation after listing their pros and cons for and against 
a UI albeit the timing of the border poll is critical to this activist. In 
turn, activist (10) thinks they would feel more settled in a UI and 
out of ‘this contested state’ and activist (6) would just like it to be 
‘done and settled’ through a UI, so an ‘awful limbo’ will not be 
passed on to the next generation.  
 
 
 

 
251
Unionist-coded greens / Green-coded unionists   
 
Unionist-coded Greens are the clear inverse of the 
nationalist-coded Greens above. To understand the preferences 
for all of these cohorts of activists, the key is the differential 
weighting they afford to evidence and the impact that constitutional 
options play in support for policy and issue preferences versus the 
role of identity. For unionist-coded Greens as for nationalist-coded 
Greens it is the evidence that takes precedence whereas for 
Green-coded unionists and nationalists it is identity that is 
fundamentally more salient. Unionist-coded greens are a relatively 
small cohort and of course, this may potentially inhibit the 
maintenance of the party’s neutrality. As discussed previously, this 
may potentially explain the tendency of the Greens to be seen as 
one activist described as the ‘eco wing of the Shinners’. 
 
A former pro-union activist (8) from a unionist background is 
evidence-based in their analysis of a UI. They see themselves as 
a rebellious person and they reflected on whether their rebellious 
nature could push them away from their traditional upbringing as a 
unionist. However, what separates this activist (8) from those more 
pro-UI (former) PUL activists above is they would not necessarily 
be inclined to vote for a UI, and instead they would need enough 
information to know what they are voting for and what is going to 
happen. In this way, they are somewhat akin to the ‘nationalist-
coded greens’, in that if they were to support a UI, it still would be 
based more on ‘evidence’ rather than just a desire to ‘rebel.’ To 
support a UI though, there would have to be a shift in the evidence 
base to alter their views.   
  
One activist (9) interviewed was clearly a Green-coded 
unionist. As expected in the GPNI, it appears their ‘cosmopolitan 
identity’ superseded their ethno-nationality when deciding which 
party to support, specifically activist (9) has been invited to join 

 
252
unionist parties in the past and it was not for them because of their 
‘socialist outlook’. However, when it comes to voting in a border 
poll, their ‘tribal’ identity will be salient, as their vote ultimately 
comes down to their Britishness more than their Green Party 
membership and this will therefore likely be a pro-union vote, albeit 
factors like Brexit and the environment could sway them and there 
is a degree of hesitancy to this view. 
 
Interestingly, given the common argument that a more 
federal governing system would be more attractive to unionists in 
the event of a United Ireland, there was an expectation that this 
Green-coded unionist activist would want a ‘federal United Ireland’. 
However, this activist (9) was not actually on board with this long-
term. Ultimately, what is observed from activists reflects most 
research to date on the general NI population (i.e., an initial 
assumption that Stormont would continue under a UI, followed 
quickly by reasons why it might not or should not or cannot) 
creating uncertainty around the activists’ overall perspectives. 
Other activists including former Protestant activists such as (11) 
don’t want Stormont to become a permanent fixture in a UI. 
 
Factor 5: Non-violence – Legitimacy of the party taking a 
stance, and the non-legitimacy of violence 
 
Interview 
discussions 
also 
explored 
the 
depth 
of 
commitment to the value of nonviolence in the Greens as this 
pertains to potential violence that may emerge in the context of a 
referendum. Perhaps surprisingly in a 2021 poll, a very large 
proportion  of GPNI (95%) and Alliance (86%) voters agree the 
dispute over NI's status remains unresolved and there is still a 
potential for violence in the future, In particular, this section 
considers attitudes a) as to whether it is legitimate for the GPNI to 
believe violence is a reason not to have a referendum but also b) 
discussing legitimacy of violence itself according to GPNI activists. 

 
253
There are in essence three distinct strands of thought that emerged 
among GPNI activists on these issues: 
 
1. The risk of violence is of such significance and scale; there 
is a need to be careful about considering having a 
referendum at all;  
2. A certain degree of violence may occur and while that 
violence is illegitimate, it will be a representation of 
marginalisation and therefore there is a need to design the 
best possible process to minimise it;  
3. There is inevitability to violence occurring, but it will just 
have to be dealt with effectively.  
 
Non-violence being an explicit goal of GPNI ultimately probably 
persuaded one activist (14) to join the party and if a referendum is 
called in the next five years ‘…the factors I’ll be looking at are not 
so much the “oh who's putting up a good case for a united Ireland 
or who's putting up a good case for a Union”, it's who's putting up 
a good case for a non-violent transition…and whether that's to a 
transition towards, some form of united Ireland or it’s a transition 
towards a reinvented Northern Ireland, it needs to be about, how 
do we do this without inflaming the tensions and setting the scene 
for more violence...’. Opposition to violence follows as a deep-
seated principle and as such deters some from support for a 
referendum. Notably, activist (10) felt, while supportive of a UI in 
the general sense, that in the current environment having a 
referendum is ‘like throwing an incendiary device in. And I just do 
not see that it would be, in any way, healthy…’. Of course, this is a 
contentious debate. The opposing perspective is exemplified by a 
leading Belfast academic who has said the threat of violence must 
not be an argument against any future referendum on a united 
Ireland being decided by a simple majority vote, even if it is 50 per 
cent plus one (Irish Times, 2019). However, for the GPNI this is a 
more essential and meaningful consideration as it is at the core of 

 
254
the party as non-violence is one of the four principles that all Green 
Parties operate by. In this sense, the concern regarding violence 
following from a referendum that the Greens may choose to 
support constitutes a key challenge to alignment of potential policy 
and principle. 
 
The issues around the Protocol were considered a ‘taster’ 
of how the UI debate will or how a UI result would be responded 
to. Sometimes, unintentionally talking about the reaction to the 
Protocol, or how the debate was carried out around it, also pushed 
some GPNI activists to revisit their understanding of ‘democracy’. 
For example, one activist (7) viewed the Protocol as an indication 
of how a debate around a UI will have to deal with all sorts of 
interpretations, misinterpretations, what counts as evidence, and 
at its core the essence of democracy, that is, non-violent 
disagreement, with violence as an illegitimate response. Another 
activist (11) notes how the Protocol was responded to by political 
unionism illustrated to them what an unhealthy way to cope with 
not getting your way looks like and, while this is democratic in a 
sense, it is not seen as aiding democracy in Northern Ireland 
generally and in the case of a UI similar dynamics would 
occur. This activist feels though that delaying a referendum is 
preferable as the conditions within the community currently risk 
serious unrest if there was to be a UI in the short-term. GPNI 
activist (1) similarly said ‘...if the whole situation wasn't managed 
correctly…And I hate saying this because almost by saying it, 
you're almost giving, like, a legitimacy to it. But I really do fear that 
it would descend into, like, violent conflict again…And maybe that 
is just because of the way we grew up, that you always think it's 
around the corner… but…and the genuine anger…that people feel 
it's not a huge leap to see how it could go back to there… And like, 
again like, I don't want to exaggerate it because maybe it won't’. 
 

 
255
For some it may be that the risk of violence leads to 
opposition to a border poll due to the commitment to nonviolence 
in which the response to the Protocol functions as a taster. 
However, for others this Protocol violence and the threat or 
possibility of violence around a referendum would, in certain cases, 
be understood as the product of resentment and a sense of 
marginalisation that needs to be proactively addressed. As 
Schwartzmantel (2010) outlines, the mobilisation of violence is ‘an 
expression of anger, directed against institutions, symbols, and 
processes which proclaim…inclusion yet do not live up to the 
aspiration to provide…adequate recognition of particular identities 
of…sections of the citizen body. It may not be only those who are 
marginalised who resort to violence… this is a powerful cause of 
the resort to violence and… presents a challenge to liberal 
democracy…’ (p. 228). Some in the GPNI see majoritarianism as 
the cause of potential marginalisation and thus of violence. For 
example, one GPNI activist (7) suggests the GPNI could adopt a 
position to advocate to change the current threshold needed to 
pass a referendum such as saying it should be a two-thirds majority 
as opposed to 50% +1 although ultimately the activist did not agree 
with this higher threshold. This would in reality involve changing the 
terms of the GFA and would require a particular ‘generosity of spirit’ 
as the same activist put it. However, ultimately the activist also said 
concerns around violence cannot prevent unification if the majority 
want it. The risk of longer-term violence is seen as a reason to 
ensure to effectively design the process of debate, organisation of 
a referendum and potential transition but if this process is 
unmanageable based on evidence, then for some this may be a 
reason not to hold a referendum. A more poorly designed process 
would likely generate greater marginalisation and resentment and 
render potential violence more legitimate. If instead, a fair, 
transparent and equitable process is designed, and violence was 
still to follow then in this case the legitimacy of the process further 
underlines the illegitimacy of a violent response as the most 

 
256
reasonable measures possible have been enacted to seek to 
address potential marginalisation from the outcome. This is tied 
closely to Green support for citizens’ assemblies as part of this 
process. 
 
A third view emerged that violence cannot, irrespective of 
scale be enough to block a referendum/UI as not only is any 
violence illegitimate, but some degree of unrest is also inevitable 
and as such can only be deterred and controlled. In some cases, 
this view was expressed based on the belief that potential violence 
will in reality be relatively marginal while in other cases, it appears 
activists operated on the basis that the threat of violence is always 
to some degree around the corner for NI and as such cannot 
determine strategy or policy. For GPNI activist (4), they would still 
vote for a UI anyway, as they assessed that even violence during 
the Troubles was localised, but also expressed a sense that NI is 
used to the threat of civil unrest. As GPNI activist (11) similarly 
explains, ‘And that slightly, only slightly, puts me off because I do 
think that a united Ireland is something inevitable. And so, whether 
the community I'm part of, there is civil unrest or not, I think it's 
going to happen…I try not to let it affect my opinion too much 
because, in my opinion, it is inevitable, but it's just how much…’. 
This further underlines the need to develop a process that is as 
inclusive as possible and minimises the risk of civil rest or even 
violence.  
 
Factor 6: Hyper-support for citizen assemblies? 
 
Activists express support for civic-led approaches, but there 
is a question here as to whether this is a preference for citizens’ 
assemblies specifically or ‘participative’ democratic mechanisms 
more generally. The GPNI believe the starting gun has been fired 
on the debate, and that the likelihood of a referendum in the short-

 
257
to-medium-term has significantly increased while most Green 
activists would define NI as not being ‘ready’ for a referendum now 
given the debate is only beginning. The GPNI, like Alliance, believe 
preparations and conversations must occur in order for NI to be 
‘ready’ for a referendum. There are a variety of potential options 
available here. First, there is a broadly participative approach 
which would mean not a formal CA right now, but a much more 
grassroots debate, alongside sector specific debates in trade 
unions, farmers, health workers etc.  The hope here is that this may 
see a consensus on some issues (at least among UI advocates) 
narrowing down the areas where a CA might help.  
 
While the activists might be open to a greater range of 
alternatives, maybe the ‘hyper-support’ for CAs or even civic 
forums in the GPNI could actually limit activists understanding of 
alternative models/mechanisms for constitutional dialogue (or 
potentially even more political party-led forums). Even one GPNI 
activist (5) openly admits that all they really know about is CAs in 
terms of preparing for a referendum, ‘So the conversations and the 
preparations…need to…ready the ground for what kind of futures 
we're looking at both north and south…What they are is a bit 
trickier…I suppose I don't really know anything other than…things 
like citizens assemblies, but it would be really interesting to know 
what other countries have done in this regard, like when Germany 
reunified…’.  
 
Activists also feel a more civic style of preparation for a 
referendum are the types of discussion that their party could really 
play a role in or lead, which inclines them towards it. It is the type 
of engagement that GPNI can actually get involved with or lead, 
compared to other parties. For example, one activist (5), thinks it 
would be interesting to see how it would go if the Greens ran some 
kind of civic forum, imagining a future UI or a vision for the future. 
Also, another activist (16) notes as the conversation across the 

 
258
island progresses, the GP has a role in ensuring that civic 
engagement and a direct democracy model is central to how those 
policies and the plan for a UI are drawn up. To take on such leading 
roles in a referendum, even if it could be seen as not explicitly 
neutral on the constitutional question, would be a position the 
Greens could thrive in because they know they will be able to justify 
the need for civic-led mechanisms based on green principles of 
grassroots democracy. In this way, they can decouple the 
constitutional connotations around taking on such roles because 
there is a need for the ‘people’s voice’ in building a referendum or 
UI. Of course, another simpler reason that the GPNI activists are 
particularly pro-citizens’ assemblies is due to the fact that the ROI 
ran lots of CAs that GPROI attended. This was also a component 
of the ethos the Scottish Greens sought to develop around their 
approach to independence. 
 
Tie to vision for the future in New Ireland with assembly / 
opportunity to develop civic ethos 
 
Building on this previous point, the Scottish Greens 
campaigned 
for 
independence 
in 
their 
manifesto: 
‘With 
independence, Scotland can develop a new written constitution for 
Scotland through a citizens’ constitutional convention. Scotland 
can become an independent republic based on participatory, local 
democracy, where politicians are always elected through 
proportional representation’ (Scottish Greens, 2014, p. 12). There 
is complementarity to how the GPNI activists consider citizen 
assemblies a tool to ‘discuss’ a referendum or a UI, but also in how 
their civic ethos is mirrored in how they envision building a New 
Ireland. Activists are not just promoting an inclusive process in 
constitution-making or following the GP principle of grassroots 
democracy, but by actively encouraging overall increased citizen 
participation, they actually showcase their desire to build a truly 
democratic New Ireland. For example, one activist (15) would like 

 
259
to see mechanisms for civic input being used to shape any new 
constitution, and these mechanisms themselves being included 
within any constitution: ‘It has to be a much more deliberative 
process in that, that involves people…the Irish state already has 
mechanisms for citizens' assemblies, and the Good Friday 
Agreement was supposed to have…Civic Forum…there are those 
ideas around ordinary people having for a, it has been a part of 
both parts of Ireland. So, I think that it would be great to have them 
in the constitution but also use them as a way of having a 
constitutional conversation that...we really build a kind of a new 
jurisdiction that people can agree on.’  
 
Notably, those in Alliance seem comparatively less focused 
currently on the use of CAs in contrast to the GPNI and sometimes 
can be quite critical. Alliance activist (2) for example outlines the 
view that politicians are citizens too, and so CAs would just be what 
is already in the Assembly as this is the primary venue for 
representation. Even though they are critical, the activist is still 
though supportive of co-design and more generally, Alliance 
activists still also don’t think the conversations and preparations 
around a referendum should be dominated or only dominated by 
the political parties. They also recognise the potential for civil 
society and/or businesspeople-led conversations to become their 
own echo chambers and/or the need to try to pull in ordinary people 
and diverse voices into these types of discussions. Ultimately 
though, the GPNI is the party of the centre-ground that embraces 
these deliberative mechanisms most directly and this is rooted in 
the party’s values and broader ethos both in terms of how to 
structure debate but also potentially the new society they foresee 
as potentially emerging from this debate. 
 
 

 
260
Factor 7: Building a New Ireland – a ‘Utopia’? 
 
Some GPNI activists, as above, will support a UI as a New 
Ireland and a means of building a vision of a new future and the 
opportunity for that. Others will not, and will, as above, base their 
decision on the evidence, which is dependent on the alternative in 
the UK and/or dependent on who governs a new ROI-style Ireland 
and what that looks like (see Factors 1 and 3 above). For those 
supporting a more radical position, there is a question as to 
whether GPNI activists’ ideas border on ‘unrealistic utopian 
thinking’ about what a UI would involve, that, if accurate, would 
reflect some Alliance activists’ view of the Greens as lacking logical 
thinking.  
 
Rather than treating this thinking as simply naïve, it is worth 
exploring what it means to be ‘utopian’ in one’s thinking in this 
context. Levitas argued that imagining an alternative society 
involves an idealised representation of the present. Accordingly, 
utopias can be conceptualised as visions for better societies that 
emphasise equality, progress, and social justice. More specifically, 
an active utopia fires up our social imagination of an open future 
and generates hope in the possibility of a reimagined social world 
(Webb, 2013). From this, it is worth exploring what 'Designing a 
New Ireland' constitutes, how this should happen, and what the 
New Ireland should prioritise and involve as this is a paradigm that 
both Greens and others apply to the notion of a UI.  As Todd (2021) 
discusses, ‘On a New Ireland Paradigm, the task would be to 
create a new constitution that would affirm a set of constitutional 
values by reference to which the specific institutions and cultural 
provisions on the island would be assessed over time. On the New 
Ireland Paradigm, identities are in a process of evolution and 
change, and thus a new political symbolism is appropriate to a 
united Ireland.’ From this perspective GPNI activist (1) would posit 
the potential ‘New Ireland’ as ‘…if the united Ireland can be this 

 
261
kind of like chance to almost create a kind of – I know this sounds 
really utopian, but, like a new socialist society, then amazing…’. 
However, many of the ideas that GPNI activists have about building 
a new constitution, have already occurred in the ROI without a UI 
even happening, so this is clearly not too ‘unrealistic.’ For example, 
activist (12), explains what would appeal to them and GP members 
is a new constitution which is progressive, socially liberal and 
embeds certain rights like the rights of nature. Many of these have 
already been enacted (e.g., the abortion and marriage equality 
referendums), or are in progress, so this should not necessarily be 
considered utopian thinking, as this is already part of contemporary 
ideas of a better ROI. There is some partial overlap here with 
thinking from Alliance activists. Alliance activist (15) also think 
thinks ‘a UI could create a chance to really revisit and redo 
everything and try and make it better’. However, there is an 
illustrative contrast here with the GPNI in that the same Alliance 
activist also emphasises that this perspective would be ‘the idealist 
in them the politician in them would see it as being a dog’s dinner’. 
In this way, there is evidence of the differential attitude to ‘utopian 
thinking’ in the two parties of the centre-ground. 
 
For other activists though, visions of a UI are potentially 
unrealistic, vague, and can colour a rational debate. For example, 
GPNI activist (13) said regarding their preference for devolved 
assemblies in a ‘united Ireland…this is, it's my sort of pie-in-the-
sky, [laughter] thinking that on a provincial basis…’  and more 
broadly is slightly sceptical of the catch-all nature of discussion of 
what a UI would involve ‘…If those were concrete ideas, I would 
have more faith in "New Ireland" as a label.’ For this type of activist, 
the debate returns to the considerations of the current ROI, the 
current UK, the direction of travel in and likely governments of each 
state. Often both GPNI and Alliance activists also make a 
comparison between the UI referendum and Brexit referendum. 
They do not want ‘a Brexit 2.0’ whereby the campaign was full of 

 
262
lies and people did not know what Brexit actually meant (e.g. GPNI 
activist 7).  
 
Moreover, in constructing a new society, certain activists 
would not like the idea of manufacturing national symbols, 
including under a UI. For example, one activist (9) thinks all these 
symbols, flags and other languages can exist in their own right in 
any region and another activist (13) - who likes the idea of a civic 
constitutional conversation - also sees how artificially building 
symbolic elements can result in a messy mix of traditions. 
Specifically, in terms of flags and anthems the activist’s (13) 
preference would be against trying to fit something new and to just 
allow these things to develop naturally, rather than synthetically try 
and create what would end up being a pretty uncomfortable 
mishmash of different traditions. While there is an understanding 
of the need to build new institutions and the need for a new 
constitution and constitutional civic conversations, as a post-ethnic 
party there is certain scepticism expressed by activists about the 
need to reconstruct the symbols of nationalism.  
 
On building a New Ireland again there is a battle between 
certain ways of accommodating the unionists in a hypothetical UI, 
and again the GPNI’s working-class identity or anti-conservative or 
leftist priorities. For example, one GPNI activist (10), states they do 
not feel attachment to what they view as ‘conservative’ unionist 
symbols despite coming from that background. That activist (10), 
who comes from a Protestant background, but is more likely to vote 
for a UI, also expresses their aggravations with symbols of the 
unionist/pro-union movement precisely because they associate 
these with very conservative values that they reject and the activist 
admits they need to remind themselves of the validity of such a 
position. The activist feels the same way about the monarchy and 
sees it as ‘where classism starts in the UK’ although on balance if 
keeping the monarchy would mean more unionists would keep the 

 
263
calm in a UI, than they would make the concession for the sake of 
peace. This is similar to views expressed by supporters of Scottish 
independence about avoiding potentially alienating support from 
those who feel a tie to the Royals. Notably, assessments of the 
ROI’s accommodation of identity groups are not straightforwardly 
explained by identity affiliations. Furthermore, one activist (5) 
without strong roots in an NI ethno-national community thinks the 
ROI may not be so experienced, compared to NI anyway, with 
addressing minority accommodation. Specifically, that activist says 
NI might be more used to than the ROI in talking about ‘how do you 
make minority populations feel welcome and share civic space’, so 
‘how to accommodate’ is probably the conversation that the ROI 
needs to start having in advance of any UI. Although even in NI 
currently they still believe the language act and flags policies only 
go so far in accommodating Irish-identifying people too. In contrast, 
activist (9), who, themselves is strongly British, feels in contrast 
that the ROI is very accommodating of different identities and 
groups. 
 
Conclusion 
 
This chapter has mapped the constitutional mindset of GPNI 
activists across seven interlocking factors. It is issue-filtered in that 
constitutional preferences are assessed as to how these contribute 
to wider issue priorities such as climate change as seen through 
frameworks 
differentially 
emphasising 
effective 
policy 
implementation versus more radical frameworks. There are 
impacts of Brexit dependent on attitudes towards Europe which 
vary from pro-Remain to left-coded euroscepticism. It is also varied 
as the activist base contains nationalist-coded greens, green-
coded nationalists, several activists who have gradually moved 
from unionist backgrounds towards pro-UI positions through 
experience and decolonisation reasoning, and at least one green-

 
264
coded unionist producing a diversity that the party's formal 
constitutional neutrality papers over without resolving which will be 
a challenge into the future. There is a focus on procedure with 
activists united in their preferences about how any constitutional 
change should be deliberated and decided through citizens' 
assemblies, inclusive civic processes, and non-violent democratic 
engagement. There is also to some extent a focus on vision and 
opportunity as there is a significant mode of thinking about a New 
Ireland that is aspirational and ‘utopian’ while the more analytically 
rigorous among them acknowledge the practical requirements of 
accommodation. 
 
 
 
 

 
265
Conclusions 
 
Summary and Contributions 
 
This thesis has examined, from the ground up, the identity and 
constitutional mind-set of activists in NI’s two main parties of the 
political centre-ground: the Alliance Party and the Green Party of 
Northern Ireland (GPNI). Drawing on forty-four semi-structured 
interviews conducted across the post-Brexit period, supplemented 
by archival and media analysis, it has pursued an intrinsic case 
study of what it means, internally and practically, to occupy the 
centre-ground in a post-conflict divided society. 
 
The conceptual framework developed in Chapter 1 argued that 
the most analytically defensible definition of the centre-ground 
combines two markers: civicness and non-alignment to ethnic 
interests, and constitutional neutrality on the binary question of 
Northern Ireland's constitutional status. This definition identifies 
Alliance and the GPNI as the contemporary centre-ground's core 
instances while preserving meaningful distinctions between them 
and the aligned moderate parties with which they are sometimes 
conflated (see conceptualisation chapter). The empirical design 
then explores these parties as an intrinsic case study to provide an 
examination of the activist base that constitute these parties as the 
centre-ground in NI. This core approach worked conceptually and 
methodologically. This research design allowed for the analysis of 
the centre-ground in a manner that was conceptually coherent by 
internally assessing parties from the ground-up and interrogating 
how the ‘people-level’ of parties personified by the activists who 
articulate and debate positions in party discussions and exert the 
key influence within the party over party policy positioning and 
organisational strategy. This provides a rich understanding of the 
diversity of internal perspectives within the parties and the 
reflections on identity, ideology and constitutional thinking of those 

 
266
who make up the key collective actors, the centrist parties, 
representing the centre-ground in contemporary NI at a time when 
this is a critical growing cohort in NI politics and a ‘swing vote’ in a 
potential  constitutional referendum. There was a strong 
willingness of party activists to participate with a large sample of 
forty-four interviewees across Alliance and the GPNI with 
substantial variation by age and length of service, employment 
status from those of college age to those of retirement age, spatial 
variation across Northern Ireland with interviewees from urban and 
rural areas and West and East Ulster, diversity of identities 
including those from nationalist, unionist and non-NI backgrounds, 
and seniority within the parties including grassroots activists, 
councillors and MLAs. This provides substantive qualitative 
empirical richness adding depth and detail to the literature on 
Alliance and constituting the largest such study of the GPNI as a 
growing centre-ground force in Northern Ireland politics.  
 
The thesis also advances our understanding of national 
ideologies among the centre-ground by going beyond the catch-all 
term of the ‘neithers’ to explore the complex realities of de-
alignment, or as it is better understood, less(er) alignment. By 
engaging with those who are day-to-day activists and political 
practitioners 
within 
the 
centre-ground, 
there 
is 
a 
clear 
demonstration that in concrete terms the centre-ground blends 
those who have distanced from traditional identity blocs, but in 
some cases retain residual influences from their backgrounds and 
socialisation, those who prioritise forms of cross-community 
engagement, and those for whom distinct ideological, national, or 
especially issue orientation for the GPNI all condition a more multi-
faceted and intersectional identity even among those thought of as 
‘neither’ identity. The thesis, more broadly, demonstrates that a 
version of nested, multiple identities exists for many in the centre-
ground of NI politics rather than a ‘straightforward’ rejection of 
‘either’ identity that the ‘neithers’ label often seems to imply.  

 
267
There are also a number of key empirical contributions. The first 
of these concerns the identity of Alliance activists. Chapter 3 
demonstrated that non-alignment, foundational to Alliance's public 
self-presentation, is better understood as an ongoing aspiration 
than an achieved condition. Activists are more accurately 
characterised as 'less-aligned' (Kulle, 2003): they have distanced 
themselves from the communal backgrounds in which they were 
socialised yet retain residual attachments that surface in 
unreflective discourse, and in moments of re-alignment with the 
communities they nominally stand apart from. This provides an 
extension on existing literature on Alliance, in particular the work of 
Tonge et al (2024), which illustrates that there is no clear majority 
for a national identity group within Alliance and finds that while 
there is a plurality of members that identify as Northern Irish, there 
are also sizeable cohorts who identify primarily as Irish and to a 
slightly lesser degree British and Other (Tonge et al., 2024, Table 
9.1). The findings from this thesis confirm Tonge et al’s findings that 
Irish identity is still holding firm within Alliance, but there is a 
complexity, overlap and intersection of many of these identities for 
Alliance activists rather than these existing as separate categories 
even if Irish identity seems to be a stronger affiliation for those who 
combine Northern Irish and Irish identity. This is, interestingly, also 
the case for most of those born outside of NI in other parts of the 
UK who take on Irishness and Northern Irishness as connected, 
grounded identities based on their new home in NI and on the 
island of Ireland. 
 
Chapter 3 also documented a notable and multi-causal decline 
in British identification among activists which further confirms the 
findings of Tonge et al.’s (2024) survey of members. However, this 
dynamic is one that does not follow straightforwardly and only from 
Brexit, but reflects longstanding discomfort with the unionist 
inflection of Britishness in NI, a growing proportion of Catholic-
background members, and a broader scepticism about British 

 
268
identity as a straightforward category. Critically, this declining 
Britishness has not generated corresponding Irish nationalism; 
Irish identification, where present, is civic, geographic, and 
situational rather than constitutionally sovereign. It is worth noting 
that while it did not emerge from the interviews conducted for this 
project, it is possible that these patterns are also partially explained 
by a decline in Protestant participation in Alliance.  
 
The constitutional neutrality manifests as strong support for a 
conscience vote within the party on the CP. The findings from this 
thesis correspond with the patterns identified in Tonge et al (2024) 
in this respect. There are constraints on the degree of comfort in 
expressing a position for many activists and those who are decided 
in their preference express this in a manner that is not determined 
by party allegiance, but is expressed in line with a distinctly Alliance 
flavour of values and ethos. There are those who are more relaxed 
about Alliance taking a position and are less concerned about the 
consequences for the party. Most in Alliance see few key gains 
from the party taking a position and are conscious of potential 
pitfalls. 
 
Activists similarly consider there to be significant internal 
organisational challenges if the party were to seek to take a firm 
position as this would restrict the space and time available to 
engage with issues they consider to be of greater importance. It is 
difficult to assess the breakdown of preferences within the party 
given many present as floating voters and/or cannot assess 
straightforwardly the preferences of others in the party themselves 
as the constitutional question is not a major issue in the party 
currently. There is though greater willingness to engage with the 
issue externally in the public arena. 
 
There is also variation from activists on the roles they envision 
their party could take on should a border poll process become a 

 
269
stronger prospect. Activists fit within a spectrum as to how they 
understand the role that Alliance should play through this process. 
At one pole, some activists see a quite limited role for Alliance in 
which the party largely performs, for example, informational checks 
on the discourse of other parties while at the other end of the 
spectrum, Alliance performs a much more significant role akin to 
an ‘architect’ of accommodation of all communities in a UI.  
 
The next contribution concerns constitutional deliberation 
among Alliance activists. Chapter 4 demonstrated that the party's 
self-image as a repository of evidence-based, 'rational neutral' 
decision-making, while genuinely held, requires qualification. 
Activists acknowledge, with more candour than the rational-neutral 
framing suggests, the indirect influence of socialisation and 
background on their constitutional thinking. The chapter identified 
seven factors shaping reflective deliberation to different degrees 
and through varying mechanics: identity and socialisation; 
economic performance under each constitutional outcome; the 
future of healthcare arrangements; the accommodation of the 
unionist community in any prospective UI; Brexit as a significant, 
but contextually variable and less decisive factor than is often 
assumed; procedural and logistical conditions for a legitimate 
border poll; and societal and institutional stability as a prerequisite 
for constitutional transition. Most activists, including those with a 
personal constitutional position, support the party's institutional 
neutrality because that neutrality is itself part of Alliance's political 
appeal, and because most regard the conditions for a legitimate 
border poll as unmet. 
 
There is also a clear empirical contribution in the exploration of 
the GPNI's activist base, and this thesis constitutes the largest 
study to this point of this distinct centre-ground party within the NI 
political 
landscape. 
Chapter 
5 
examined 
three 
major 
manifestations of conceptual markers; party issue orientation, the 

 
270
relative influence of class and ethno-nationalism, and constitutional 
neutrality 
among 
activists, 
finding 
each 
more 
internally 
differentiated and more requiring of active maintenance than the 
markers themselves imply. Activists associate strongly with the 
party’s issue-based identity and the commitment to eco-socialism 
is well-embedded as the root of political mobilisation. There is a 
strong working-class emphasis, but this is negotiated alongside the 
distinct material backgrounds of a number of activists and 
intersects in notable ways with ethno-national backgrounds in a 
manner that varies extensively across the activist base. Most 
significantly, the chapter established that the GPNI's issue-based 
ethos generates a different logic of neutrality than Alliance's: for a 
party defined by engagement with major questions of the day, 
remaining silent on the CQ becomes increasingly difficult to sustain 
as that question rises in salience. GPNI activists are, in general, 
more open to their party actively engaging with constitutional 
deliberation than their Alliance counterparts. 
 
The thesis also maps GPNI activists' distinctive constitutional 
mind-set in Chapter 6. GPNI activists assess the constitutional 
question through an eco-socialist interpretive framework that 
reorganises 
conventional 
considerations: 
environmental 
sustainability and post-growth economics are first-order concerns, 
and constitutional options are evaluated substantially in terms of 
which outcome would better enable all-island environmental 
governance and social transformation. This produces genuine 
internal diversity between those emphasising an approach 
grounded in effective implementation versus more radical nation-
building visions. It is critical to activists in forming a preference to 
consider the potential governing parties of a UI, in particular the 
avoidance of a replacement of the UK Tories with ‘Irish Tories’ and 
concerns about the nature of a potential future SF government and 
its comparability to the currently constituted SF in NI and the ROI 
as well as questions about the Green parties’ own future. The 

 
271
thesis 
identified 
nationalist-coded 
Greens, 
Green-coded 
nationalists, activists who have gradually shifted from unionist 
backgrounds through biographical experience and decolonisation 
reasoning, and Green-coded unionists which the party's formal 
neutrality subordinates, but still this variety persists. This thesis 
also advances the work of Todd and McEvoy’s (2024) work on 
deliberation on constitutional questions by illustrating the centrality 
of deliberative processes to the GPNI’s approach to the 
constitutional issue in particular. For the GPNI, deliberation is at 
the heart of their collective values as a party and functions as a 
core party principle, but also serves as a central plank of their 
approach to how a United Ireland should be designed as well as 
how the structures and constitution of  a New Ireland should 
operate should it come into being by being embedded in the state’s 
operations from the outset and used as a means of reflection and 
reform as needed as the state takes shape. The GPNI's 
pronounced preference for citizens' assemblies and participative 
and particularly nonviolent, democratic mechanisms as vehicles for 
constitutional deliberation reflects both the party's principled 
commitment to grassroots democracy and a practical recognition 
that facilitated deliberation may be the most effective way to 
engage with the CQ without prematurely abandoning neutrality.  
 
More broadly, the thesis demonstrates how activists from both 
centre-ground parties engage in reflective consideration of their 
positions and approaches to ideological, identity and constitutional 
issues themselves during interviews. This evidences at the 
‘people-level’ the processes and operation of deliberation as it 
occurs on these major questions. This offers insights into how 
reflection and re-consideration can occur among the cohorts that 
actually decide on and shape collective party policy and 
engagement on issues extending further on the wider patterns of 
deliberation analysed in Todd and McEvoy (2024).   
 

 
272
Limitations and Avenues for Further Research 
 
Like all such projects, limitations bear acknowledgement. The 
purposive interview sample, while appropriate for inductive pattern-
finding, does not support statistical generalisation about all Alliance 
or GPNI members or voters. The fieldwork was conducted primarily 
during the Covid-19 pandemic and its aftermath, and some 
perspectives will have evolved; most notably in light of Alliance 
leader Naomi Long's 2025 retreat from an earlier signal that the 
party would 'undoubtedly' take a constitutional position in the 
future.  
 
These limitations point towards productive avenues for further 
research. A longitudinal study tracking the evolution of activist 
views as the constitutional debate develops would allow 
researchers to assess whether the conditionality culture 
documented here generates genuine engagement or indefinite 
deferral. Given the valuable insights provided by examining parties 
from the inside through engagement with party activists that 
‘constitute’ the party, there is significant scope to expand the 
analysis of party activists in Northern Ireland. By speaking to 
activists from the traditional aligned parties, SF and the SDLP on 
the nationalist side and the DUP, UUP and TUV on the unionist 
side, insights can be derived on how internally alignment and 
identity are understood and the extent of heterogeneity in activists’ 
perspectives on how the parties’ constitutional positions and 
strategy to communicate these are interpreted and understood as 
well as how activists feel these may need to better reinforced 
and/or reconciled with a changing political landscape in the coming 
years. As these activists shape party strategy and positioning 
internally, these activists can offer clear avenues to understand 
how the parties will approach constitutional debates and any 
potential referendum. It would also be productive to engage with 
activists from these aligned parties to better understand, in 

 
273
particular, how these parties will seek to reach out to win over non-
aligned voters from the centre-ground in any potential referendum 
on Northern Ireland’s constitutional status and the activists’ 
perceptions of the most effective means of communication and 
appealing to these voters.  
 
Comparative research across other divided societies such as 
Scotland, Catalonia, Belgium, and Bosnia would test which findings 
are specific to NI and which reflect more general dynamics of civic 
party activism in ethnically saturated political systems. Examining 
aligned parties in these contexts such as the Scottish National 
Party or Plaid Cymru through interviews with activists again 
potentially offers additional understanding of how these parties 
vary internally in their identities, articulation of their constitutional 
preferences, how they personally believe the question of 
constitutional status should be approached, and how this 
compares to how they believe the parties organisationally should 
approach it.  There is also the opportunity for further work on 
cohorts within Northern Ireland using alternative methods to further 
understand the nature of the centre-ground. A generational study 
focused on the GFA cohort within both parties would illuminate how 
the centre-ground is changing as biographical exposure to the 
conflict recedes. Qualitative research with ordinary voters and 
party sympathisers, rather than activists, would assess how far the 
patterns documented here extend into the broader centre-ground 
electorate. 
 
Concluding Reflections 
 
The picture that emerges from this thesis is neither the idealised 
post-ethnic politics the centre-ground is sometimes taken to 
represent nor the simple midpoint between unionism and 
nationalism to which its critics sometimes reduce it. It is something 

 
274
more interesting and more difficult. It is a space in which people 
with genuinely diverse backgrounds, identities, and constitutional 
preferences are attempting with internal contradiction, and against 
the grain of deep socialisation to practice a politics not defined by 
which side they are on. The clearest commonalities between the 
two parties are the multi-faceted and complex nature of de-
alignment and lesser alignment from identity backgrounds among 
the activist cores of the parties as well as the strong support for a 
conscience vote on any potential constitutional position either party 
may take. However, beyond this there is significant variation 
between the two parties.  
 
There is evidence of greater internal coherence within the GPNI 
on the constitutional question as they tend broadly as a party to 
clearly cohere around engaging on issues and as such this leads 
to widespread support within the party for constitutional 
engagement, even if this does not mean there is necessarily 
support for a clear constitutional position to be taken. At the same 
time, if there was to be such a position taken, there appears to be 
a prediction and/or preference for a United Ireland based on this 
sample. This is notable given there are a number of activists from 
Protestant-Unionist backgrounds within the party who are leaning 
towards a United Ireland position. There is similarly solidity and 
cohesion to the internal party support for deliberative processes in 
civic conversations in the run-up to and civic constitution-building 
in a potential United Ireland in which the party would play a role. 
For Alliance, there is a lesser surety on the question of how the 
party should approach constitutional engagement with a wide 
spectrum of perspectives and positions among activists on how 
much, what form, and the degree of comfort with constitutional 
engagement the party may engage in with any prospective border 
poll referendum. There is also widespread diversity in the opinions 
Alliance activists express on the constitutional question and it is 
difficult to identify any clear prediction or assessment of the 

 
275
constitutional position the party make take, not least because 
activists cannot clearly assess themselves the positions their party 
colleagues hold or may hold. There is also something of a structural 
‘neutrality by default’ within Alliance given the diversity of opinions 
on the issue and on constitutional engagement – this is a party 
defined by its neutrality (whether this is a product of a ‘reaction’ to 
the traditional blocs or not) and as such, there is a fundamental 
concern about both internal party unity and potential negative 
consequences externally for the party if it was to take such a 
position or perhaps even engage in a manner that many activists 
as arrayed along the spectrum of preferences discussed above 
were uncomfortable with. 
 
The following constitute the major takeaways of the project. 
First, the centre-ground is populated by the less-aligned rather than 
the non-aligned: people who have distanced themselves from 
ethno-national backgrounds without escaping them, and whose 
political identity is an ongoing negotiation with, rather than a 
transcendence of, inherited affiliations. Second, the two parties of 
the centre-ground practice constitutional neutrality differently. 
Alliance practice as a core identity marker generating institutional 
restraint and the GPNI as a position increasingly conditioned by an 
issue-based ethos that demands engagement. These different 
cultures will likely produce divergent trajectories as the 
constitutional debate intensifies. Third, the conditionality culture of 
the centre-ground is both principled and potentially self-limiting: it 
reflects genuine commitments to deliberation, inclusion, and 
evidence, but in its most demanding forms risks setting terms for 
engagement that are challenging to meet, potentially deferring 
participation in the constitutional conversation. Whether the centre-
ground can translate these values into effective political influence 
in the constitutional debate that NI increasingly appears likely to 
face is among the most consequential political questions of the 
coming 
decade. 
This 
thesis 
equips 
future 
researchers, 

 
276
practitioners, and citizens with a richer and more accurate 
understanding of the activists who will be at its heart.

Appendix A  –  Ethical Materials 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
304
Dublin City University – Research Project and Interview 
Procedures 
 
Introduction to the Research 
Research Title: “The centre-ground in Northern Ireland and the United 
Ireland debate”. 
 
This research is conducted within Dublin City University’s (DCU) School 
of Law and Government and the Institute for International Conflict 
Resolution and Reconstruction (IICRR). The IICRR awarded the Clinton 
PhD Scholarship in 2020 to Louisa Barry, who is completing this project 
as part of her PhD in Peace Studies. As of the 1st September 2022, this 
research is being funded by the Irish Research Council (IRC). 
 
Principal Investigator(s):  
Professor John Doyle is the Director of DCU’s Institute for International 
Conflict 
Resolution 
and 
Reconstruction 
(email 
address: 
john.doyle@dcu.ie). Professor John Doyle is the primary supervisor of 
the research project. 
 
Ms Louisa Barry is a PhD student with DCU’s Institute for International 
Conflict Resolution and Reconstruction and in the School of Law and 
Government (email address louisa.barry29@mail.dcu.ie) 
 
Other Investigators:  
The research project is being jointly co-supervised by Dr Erika Biagini 
who is an Assistant Professor in the School of Law and Government 
(email address 304rika.biagini@dcu.ie).  
 
Research Project  
This research aims to gain insight into how the Alliance Party of Northern 
Ireland and the Green Party Northern Ireland, and their supporters, are 
approaching issues related to the prospect of a border poll, constitutional 
change and the region’s future.  
 
Expectations of the Participant  
If a participant decides to participate in this research project, they will be 
expected to partake in at least one in-person or online interview, which 
the researcher will request to record (audio only). Participants’ audio will 
not be recorded without their permission. Interviews may last between 30 
minutes to 1.5 hours, depending on the time that the participant is able 
to make themselves available. 
 
Types of Questions  
Along with questions on their political party support, participants will be 
asked questions on themes of constitutional change, Irish unity, Northern 
Ireland’s future and EU membership. For instance, they might be asked 
to share their ideas on how Alliance and Green Party Northern Ireland 

 
305
supporters think about constitutional change or their positions on the 
future of the region as part of the centre-ground. These questions might 
explore the participant’s political opinions, religious or philosophical 
beliefs, or racial or ethnic origin.  
 
Important Note for Participants on Questions 
The decision lies with the participant on whether they would like to share 
a particular opinion or stance. Participants will also have the option to 
select whether they provide their information ‘on the record’ (i.e. they are 
named) or ‘off the record’ (i.e. they are not named) 
 
Protocol for Online Interviews 
If interviews are conducted online the researcher will use Zoom in a 
manner which is compliant with data protection requirements, and any 
other legal or regulatory requirements. The researcher will only use the 
DCU licenced version of Zoom and will implement the necessary 
procedures to make Zoom a safe environment for the researcher and the 
participants. Zoom will be set up to automatically store recordings in the 
Zoom cloud (which is a safe, password protected online storage method 
to which only the researcher has access). Additionally, files will not be 
transferred through the chat function on Zoom. 
The Use of the Data 
Participant data is being requested for the purposes of research for a 
PhD in Dublin City University (DCU). DCU’s Data Protection Officer is Mr. 
Martin Ward who can be emailed at data.protection@dcu.ie or called on 
01 7005118 / 01 7008257. A participant may wish to contact the Data 
Protection Officer if they believe their rights associated with data 
protection or GDPR legislation have been violated.  
A transcription service may be used to transcribe data. The transcription 
service will never have access to the names of those interviewed. Audio 
recordings will be deleted/ destroyed once transcription is completed in 
full. Participants should be aware that data will not be retained 
indefinitely. After the PhD is awarded, hard copy files of interviews will be 
destroyed. Additionally, data in electronic files will be held in a fully 
anonymized form until the researcher has exhausted publication.   
 
Confidentiality and Anonymity  
Participants can request for their data to be ‘on the record’ or ‘off the 
record’ (they are not named). In the case where ‘off the record’ is 
requested, personal data will be separated from direct identifiers so that 
a direct linkage to an identity is no longer possible.  
Participants should be aware that confidentiality of information provided 
cannot always be guaranteed by researchers. This is a genuine issue in 
all research fields conducted in small contexts/communities. In these 
contexts, there are additional (local) limits to confidentiality, that is, due 
to the small sample size participants’ identities may be recognized by 
others based on statements participants make or the titles held by 

 
306
elected representatives. Therefore, if there is any doubt about potential 
guess-work identifying people due to the small pool of participants, then 
participants should be reassured that the text of the PhD will not include 
any contextual data to allow this secondary identification. Confidentiality 
of information can only be protected within the limitations of the law – i.e., 
it is possible for data to be subject to subpoena, freedom of information 
claim or mandated reporting by some professions.  
 
Voluntary Involvement 
Participants have the right to change their mind at any stage and can 
withdraw from the research project at any point. If a participant requested 
to be ‘on the record’, they will be asked to consent to their data being 
used should they withdraw. If a participant requested for their data to be 
‘off the record’, their data will be disposed of should they withdraw. 
 
Rights Protections 
Participants have the right to lodge a complaint with the Irish Data 
Protection Commission. https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/contact/how-
contact-us). If a participant wishes to enact their right to access their 
personal data, please contact DCU’s Data Protection Officer, Mr. Martin 
Ward, who can be emailed at data.protection@dcu.ie or called on 01 
7005118 / 01 7008257 
 
Potential Risks  
There is a risk that the participant may experience emotional distress 
when speaking about political topics or face implications from political 
parties, groups or people who do not share their political positions. 
However, participants can withdraw from the project at any point or 
request to pause/ stop their individual interview. 
If a participant wishes to contact support services for any reason, such a 
service in Northern Ireland is listed below. 
• 
Lifeline is a free, confidential telephone helpline (Telephone number: 
08088088000/ Textphone: 1800108088088000) 
 
Potential (direct or indirect) Benefits  
By taking part, participants will contribute to a study on two political 
parties which are under-researched in academia. Participants will have 
the opportunity to share their voice and reflect upon their personal views. 
Participants’ insights will help inform the growing public debate on 
Northern Ireland’s constitutional future.   
 
Other Relevant Information 
Participants should be aware that given the number of elected officials 
from the parties under study are small, the confidentiality of participant 
identity will require some generalisation of description.  
Participants should be aware that their data potentially will be used at a 
later date for the purposes of publication. 

 
307
Participants will be emailed when the research project is completed and 
made available in the DCU DORAS open access depository.  
 
If participants have concerns about this study and wish to 
contact an independent person, please contact: 
 
The Secretary, Dublin City University Research Ethics Committee, c/o 
Research and Innovation Support, Dublin City University, Dublin 9.  Tel 
01-7008000, e-mail rec@dcu.ie 
 
 
 

 
308
Appendix B – Example of Interview Guide – GPNI75 
Main questions for your interview with Louisa 
 
1. With reference to your own reasons for supporting the Green 
Party Northern Ireland (henceforth, GPNI), what does the GPNI 
offer that is distinctive from the other parties in Northern 
Ireland? 
 
2. It is recognised that the 1998 Good Friday Agreement ensures 
the power lies with the people to determine Northern Ireland’s 
constitutional future. However, could you share your personal 
feelings around the prospect of the GPNI taking a constitutional 
position in the future? 
 
3. My research drew attention to the idea that it does not matter 
which position a political party or its representatives take on a 
border poll as at the end of the day the people will determine 
the vote outcome. Could you share your thoughts on this idea?  
 
4. If a border poll was called in the next 5 years, what ‘factors’ or 
‘issues’ do you think could be/ would be influential for you 
personally as a GPNI supporter, when deliberating which way 
to vote? 
 
5. If a border poll was called in the next 5 years, what ‘factors / 
issues’ do you speculate could sway ‘undecided’ GPNI voters 
towards voting one way or another?  
 
6. Are there any ‘factors / issues’ that would be particularly or 
uniquely influential for GPNI supporters in a border poll? 
 
7. We often hear about the different ‘conversations and 
preparations’ that should proceed the calling of a border poll. 
What should these ‘conversations and preparations’ look like 
and who has the real responsibility for preparing (not calling) for 
a potential border poll? 
 
8. If a border poll was called in the next 5 years and Northern 
Ireland votes to support the constitutional status quo, what may 
be the positive / negative impacts of this result for you? 
 
9. If unification happened, how do you think it would impact your 
life? 
 
 
75 This is essentially identical to an Alliance interview guide with adaptations. 

 
309
10. My research informed me about the diverse perspectives on 
how the Irish identity can be accommodated for in Northern 
Ireland. While some put their faith in tangible solutions like 
establishing an Irish Language Act or developing a legacy 
(flags, parades, the past) policy, others hope that Northern 
Ireland can work as a community to implement the values of the 
1998 Good Friday Agreement as a means to allow all identities 
to feel welcome. Excluding these examples, what else do you 
think can be done in Northern Ireland to help those citizens who 
identify stronger with Ireland over Britain feel more 
accommodated for within a Northern Ireland that remains in the 
UK? 
 
11. What do you think it means to be Irish / British / Northern Irish 
in Northern Ireland? 
 
12. If a united Ireland happened, what are your thoughts on 
introducing all new symbols (flags, anthems etc) and a new 
constitution, or should distinct symbols of ‘Britishness’ and 
‘Irishness’ co-exist? 
 
13. What do you think could be done to help those citizens who 
identify stronger with Britain over Ireland feel more 
accommodated for under a hypothetical united Ireland? 
 
14. Do you think that any aspect of your traditional identity or 
communal background could have an influence in how you vote 
in a border poll? 
 
15.  Has Northern Ireland losing its EU membership made you 
revisit or re-evaluate your thinking around a united Ireland, if so 
in what way? 
 
16.  Has, or could, the (successful / unsuccessful) implementation 
of the Northern Ireland Protocol make you revisit or re-evaluate 
your thinking around a united Ireland, if so in what way? 
 
17.  Although it is the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland’s 
decision when to call a border poll, do you think Northern 
Ireland as a community will ever be ready for a border poll? 
 
18.  Finally - do you think there are any important issues or points 
that relate to the shape of Northern Ireland’s constitutional 
future and the GPNI that I did not touch upon?

A Survey on Architectures and Energy Eﬃciency in Data
Center Networks
Ali Hammadi and LotﬁMhamdi
School of Electronic and Electrical Engineering, University of Leeds, UK
Abstract
Data Center Networks (DCNs) are attracting growing interest from both
academia and industry to keep pace with the exponential growth in cloud
computing and enterprise networks.
Modern DCNs are facing two main
challenges of scalability and cost-eﬀectiveness. The architecture of a DCN
directly impacts on its scalability, while its cost is largely driven by its power
consumption. In this paper, we conduct a detailed survey of the most recent
advances and research activities in DCNs, with a special focus on the archi-
tectural evolution of DCNs and their energy eﬃciency. The paper provides a
qualitative categorization of existing DCN architectures into switch-centric
and server-centric topologies as well as their design technologies. Energy eﬃ-
ciency in data centers is discussed in details with survey of existing techniques
in energy savings, green data centers and renewable energy approaches. Fi-
nally, we outline potential future research directions in DCNs.
Keywords:
Data center networks (DCNs), Architecture, energy eﬃciency,
virtualization, renewable energy for DCNs,
1. Introduction
Recent years are witnessing an unprecedented growth in data centers.
This is mainly driven by the plethora of services and applications housed
by modern data centers, such as web-search, scientiﬁc computations, social
networks, distributed ﬁles systems, etc. Data centers are at the heart of
almost every sector at the private, public and governmental levels. Today’s
data centers contain hundreds of thousands of servers, interconnected via
switches, routers and high-speed links. The design of modern data centers
