This table shows the net present cost and energy cost for 
the optimal configuration of hybrid energy systems applied 
in different country regions and power loads. Hybrid energy 
systems are more economically viable and have lower net 
present cost and energy cost than single energy systems. A 
higher percentage of renewables in a hybrid energy system 
means lower energy costs and economic efficiency in most 
cases.
Renewable energy hybrid systems are considered highly 
efficient for traditional energy sources and significantly 
reduce the cost of energy use (Zhang et al. 2018). Li et al. 
(2018) compared the economic feasibility of three systems: 
grid-only, photovoltaic/grid, and photovoltaic/battery/grid, 
where using a hybrid photovoltaic/battery/grid system emit-
ted the lowest amount of pollutants (9% reduction), but it 
also had the highest cost (65.74% increase). Therefore, com-
pared to a modest photovoltaic/grid system with lower costs 
and fewer pollutant emissions, hybrid energy systems' cost 
and environmental benefits need to be considered. On-grid 
hybrid photovoltaic, fuel battery and battery cogeneration 
systems are used in Malaysian hospitals to achieve 30% cost 
savings in electricity generation (Isa et al. 2016). Despite 
having a high upfront cost, this sophisticated hybrid energy 
system dramatically lowers energy costs (by 49.2% com-
pared to a single diesel engine). In addition, the battery 
stores excess power due to the large proportion of renew-
able energy components used, which reduces energy waste 
and meets standards for economic viability (Al-Ghussain 
et al. 2021). Hydrogen is an attractive way to establish zero-
pollutant emission storage technology from various energy 
sources (Kalinci et al. 2017). Hydrogen can enhance energy 
efficiency and consequently result in savings because it can 
be incorporated into a hybrid energy system.
By comparing various hybrid energy systems to find 
the best photovoltaic/biomass/battery energy combination, 
Malik et al. (2021b) verified the economic viability of off-
grid biomass hybrid systems, yielding significant electric-
ity cost savings of 92% produced from conventional diesel 
systems. Photovoltaics and biomass are the most prominent 
components providing power generation, but both biomass 
gasifier units and photovoltaic arrays have high purchase, 
operation, and replacement maintenance costs (Tiwary et al. 
2019). Therefore, improving biomass production and battery 
life technology is beneficial further to reduce the overall 
cost of hybrid energy systems and achieve higher economic 
efficiency. As a non-renewable energy source, diesel also 
has a higher production and utilization cost, which should 
be avoided as much as possible. In Yemen's Shafail, where 
solar energy resources are more plentiful, a combination of 
photovoltaic, wind, and diesel energy systems saves 45% of 
the energy cost compared to a single diesel system (Ajlan 
et al. 2017). The system uses less diesel due to the high 
renewable share attained.
Additionally, different energy combinations yield addi-
tional economic benefits. For example, Ibrahim et al. (2020) 
compared eleven off-grid energy combinations' cost and 
power production performance to apply to an economic 
seawater treatment system without a grid. They found that 
the photovoltaic/wind/diesel and photovoltaic/hydrokinetic 
turbine/diesel systems were economically viable solutions 
with energy costs of 0.2252 dollars and 0.1216 dollars/kilo-
watt-hour, respectively. This suggests that the hydrokinetic 
turbine system is a renewable energy source that entirely 
depends on fluid-generated power to drive the electricity 
generated. It is possible to drastically lower the energy cost 
by utilizing blends of biofuels with other resources due to 
the large regional waste production and the potential for 
local biogas production (Khan et al. 2022; Rad et al. 2020).
Hybrid energy systems may increase energy costs while 
improving system reliability. Fuel batteries were employed 
by Rad et al. (2020) to create a hybrid energy system that 
might help maintain energy balance and boost dependability 
during times of high power demand (Al-Othman et al. 2022). 
They would nevertheless raise energy prices by 33–37%. 
System costs with photovoltaic and wind energy are highly 
correlated to fluctuations in solar radiation, wind speed and 
changes in interest rates (Elkadeem et al. 2019b). Xu et al. 
(2020) introduced the economic parameter consideration 
of the abandonment rate, which, when calculated as a 5% 
abandonment rate, can reduce the energy cost of the hybrid 
photovoltaic/wind/hydroelectric pumped storage energy sys-
tem to 0.091 dollars/kilowatt-hour. This ensures supply reli-
ability to the local load and reduces the initial capital cost.

from $0.145 to $0.119 as the load factor increased from 25 
to 40%, so a higher load factor is needed to reduce the cost of 
electricity generation. Similarly, a solar/diesel/battery hybrid 
system was implemented in a rural Saharan community 
where load demand rose from 49.4 kWh/day to 89.4 kWh/

and a 31.6% reduction in energy cost (Fodhil et al. 2019).
The renewable proportion is the percentage of the sys-
tem's overall energy production that comes from renewable 
energy sources and meets the load (Yuan et al. 2022). A 
high renewable energy percentage indicates a higher frac-
tion of renewable energy in the load. To lessen the effects of 
environmental issues and to keep costs as low as possible, 
it is strongly advised to maintain a high share of renewable 
energy sources (Aziz et al. 2022). Increasing the renewable 
energy percentage reduces the net present value costs sus-
tained by the system operator (He et al. 2023). However, 
it is necessary to comply with the government's energy 
policy by increasing the proportion of renewable energy 
sources with an appropriate renewable energy ratio and 
energy costs, reducing fuel and environmental pollution 
(Tsai et al. 2020). In this context, Pan et al. (2020) used a 
two-tier model to effectively lower the price of hydrogen 
supply at the planning stage by modifying the system's share 
of renewable energy equipment and sourcing power from 
an up-gradient site. However, large-scale use of renewable 
energy could threaten the power grid's security (Beyza and 
Yusta 2021), forcing the traditional distribution grid to move 
from employing a single power source to various renewable 
sources. This results in a tidal current reversal on the distri-
bution grid, which changes the grid's power supply mode.
However, voltage distribution brings hidden risks to the 
distribution grid’s safe operation (Gong et al. 2021; Topić 
et al. 2015). Even with greater reserve capacity, consuming 
significant renewable energy is difficult due to transmission 
congestion and transmission section caps (Tan et al. 2021). As 
a result, integrating renewable energy into the power system 
is fraught with volatility and stochasticity, and the share of 
renewable energy increases stochasticity (Chen et al. 2021). 
Additionally, the proportion of renewable energy cannot be 
precisely controlled due to fuel uncertainty. However, by 
imposing a maximum proportion limit on each technology 
to keep fuel diversity within reasonable limits and maximum

Costly renewable energy technologies necessitate expendi-
ture (Toopshekan et al. 2020). Depending on the operation 
mode, adopting hybrid systems can boost overall dependabil-
ity, lower power costs, or even raise the value of electricity 
(Esmaeilion 2020; Jurasz et al. 2020). In off-grid mode, capi-
tal, operation, maintenance costs, and grid tariff are the inputs 
for the economic comparison of off-grid systems and grid 
extensions. In an on-grid way, grid tariff and sell-back rate are 
the input data (Li et al. 2022). The advantage of being on-grid 
is that it sells excess clean energy to the grid and supports grid 
power, while the only source of revenue for being off-grid is 
salvage (Jahangir et al. 2022). Off-grid systems have higher net 
present costs and energy costs than grid-connected systems, 
whereas on-grid systems have fewer components because 
the primary power consumption is from the grid (Majdi et al. 
2021; Nesamalar et al. 2021). On-grid hybrid is beneficial for 
reducing the cost of energy, but it takes time to set up and can 
lead to higher installation costs (Chowdhury et al. 2020). Das 
et al. (2021) conducted an economic feasibility analysis of a 
hybrid photovoltaic/wind/diesel/battery energy system. They 
found that the energy cost for an on-grid system (0.072 dol-
lars/kilowatt-hour) was much lower than an off-grid hybrid 
energy system ($0.28/kWh). Additionally, Ali et al. (2021a) 
examined the economics of diesel and biogas generators, 
photovoltaic panels, and wind turbines in off-grid and on-grid 
scenarios. They found that on-grid systems with lower energy 
costs (0.072–0.078 dollars/kilowatt-hour) were more suitable 
for practical applications, with a 44–49% reduction over off-
grid systems (0.145–0.167 dollars/kilowatt-hour).
In Guiyang, Li et al. (2021) studied green buildings, grid-
connected systems were more cost-effective than off-grid 
systems for supplying electricity to residential buildings via 
hybrid intermittent generation systems. In off-grid systems, 
the battery capacity grows after the peak energy capacity 
surpasses the maximum electricity demand to prevent over-
production and avoid dumping extra power (Campana et al. 
2019). Furthermore, Li et al. (2022) mentioned that increas-
ing the capacity of photovoltaic panels, wind turbines, and 
converters allows flexibility and cost-effectiveness by shift-
ing from off-grid to on-grid mode.
Most populations cannot afford high energy costs com-
pared to traditional grid purchases. Hybrid energy systems 
pay much investment upfront due to the high renewable pro-
portion, and the power transmission system still has higher 
costs. Therefore, it is essential to have a good electricity 
infrastructure to handle the transmission of these renewa-
bles (Das et al. 2020). Facing complex energy installation 
procedures also requires additional training costs (Ellabban 
et al. 2014). Photovoltaic prices can change significantly 
over time, and there is uncertainty in the prices of other 
energy sources, which good design decisions need to con-
sider. Therefore, various decision variables between energy 
sources need to be considered in the optimization process 
to evaluate the optimal size of the hybrid system at the low-
est annual cost (Sawle et al. 2018). Energy scheduling is 
based on previous-day simulations using predicted energy 
prices, weather data, and load consumption curves. Energy 
savings by scheduling energy use in houses connected to 
hybrid energy systems, energy scheduling strategy reduces 
daily operating costs by 45% (Bouakkaz et al. 2021). The 
developed procedure considers various constraints, such as 
the weight penalty cost of carbon emissions, the elemental 
cost of carbon dioxide, and the annual system component 
power consumption, to obtain the optimal configuration of 
the hybrid system (Clarke et al. 2015).
Similarly, inflation or nominal interest rates may vary over 
time (Das et al. 2022a; Shafiullah et al. 2021). Therefore, 
some economic policies have been implemented in favor of 
recommending hybrid energy applications (Xin-gang et al. 
2020), for example, incentives in the form of tax exemptions 
and sales taxes on renewable energy imports of equipment 
in the UK (Ali et al. 2021b). The renewable energy policy in 
Bangladesh provides several fiscal incentives, such as a 15% 
value-added tax exemption on purchasing equipment and 
raw materials and a 10% increase in the purchase price for 
the private sector (Mandal et al. 2018). The availability of 
incentives or support programs through grants or subsidies 
can further address the high overall energy system costs by 
reducing investment costs (Odou et al. 2020). The current 
limitations of determining the economic viability of energy 
are summarized as shown in Fig. 8.
This section summarizes the economic parameters for 
evaluating hybrid energy systems, assessing net present cost, 
annualized cost, and cost of energy to provide a compre-
hensive analysis of the economic viability of hybrid energy 
systems. In addition, the hybrid energy system represents 
better economic viability than a single energy system. How-
ever, there is also the impact of renewable proportion and 
off-grid/on-grid operation mode; the system needs to address 
the challenges of high upfront investment cost, interest rate, 
and inflation rate resulting in price changes.
Conclusion
Estimating renewable energy hybrid impacts is essential 
to verify the future expansion of the hybridization concept 
compared to the individual used source. In addition, the 
economic estimation potential of such systems in different 
countries is essential. Here, we discuss the theory of renew-
able energy combinations, approaches, suggested combi-
nations, models, and economic, environmental, and social 
impacts. The role of hybrid systems in water desalination

of hybrid energy systems and their respective source was 
fully discussed to determine the best scenario for climate 
change mitigation. How the complementary operation of this 
integrated system could be affected by climate change and its 
flexibility to climate change was also discussed.
Complementarity between energy sources is improved 
when adapted to changing climate conditions, maximiz-
ing the ability to counteract its effects, and increasing 
power generation and guarantees. However, a standardized 
approach for evaluating energy complementarity is lacking, 
making it necessary to simulate complex climate data with 
more optimal estimation methods for accuracy.
Reducing the amount of non-renewable energy and 
increasing the proportion of renewable sources not only 
reduce net present value costs for system operators but also 
align with government energy policies and reduces fuel and 
environmental pollution. Yet, large or poorly designed sys-
tems can result in high installation costs, emphasizing the 
need for thorough technical and financial evaluations before 
implementing a hybrid energy system. Selecting the most 
valuable renewable source is vital for decision-makers in 
ensuring optimal utilization and successful implementation 
of such complex systems.

INTEGRATION OF BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS WITH 
HYBRID POWER GENERATION FOR RELIABLE AND LOW-EMISSION 
DATA CENTRES IN SAUDI ARABIA 
 
INTEGRAÇÃO DE SISTEMAS DE ARMAZENAMENTO DE ENERGIA EM BATERIAS 
COM GERAÇÃO HÍBRIDA DE ENERGIA PARA CENTROS DE DADOS 
CONFIÁVEIS E DE BAIXAS EMISSÕES NA ARÁBIA SAUDITA 
 
Article received on: 3/13/2026 
Article accepted on: 7/20/2026 
 
Syed Saifuddin Quraishi* 
*Power Generation Division, Cummins Arabia, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia  
syeds02@gmail.com 
 
The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest 
 
Abstract 
Saudi 
Arabia 
is 
fast 
expanding 
digital 
infrastructure, cloud services and artificial-
intelligence workloads, while national energy 
policy supports renewable generation, reliability 
improvement and less dependence on liquid-
fuelled power. Data centres require a constant 
supply of high-quality electricity, but they are 
power-hungry, thermal-sensitive and difficult to 
interrupt. This paper reviews the integration of 
battery energy storage systems with hybrid 
photovoltaic, wind, grid and backup generation 
for reliable and low emission data centres in 
Saudi Arabia. The paper employs a structured 
review approach based on hybrid microgrid 
optimization studies: evidence is mapped, design 
variables identified, candidate architectures 
compared 
and 
reliability, 
economic, 
environmental 
and 
operational 
criteria 
synthesized. The review indicates that BESS is 
not just an emergency UPS replacement. When 
controlled by an energy management system, it 
can smooth out renewable variability, reduce 
diesel generator run-time, shave peaks, provide 
short-duration ride-through, defer grid stress and 
protect 
service-level 
commitments. 
The 
strongest architecture for Saudi data-centre 
applications includes Solar PV, selective wind or 
grid import, high-efficiency lithium-ion or 
alternative BESS, conventional or hydrogen-
ready backup, thermal-aware despatch and 
cyber-secure monitoring. The work proposes a 
practical approach for sizing, dispatching, and 
governing hybrid power systems supported by 
BESS under Saudi climatic, regulatory, and 
sustainability conditions. 
 
Keywords: Battery Energy Storage Systems. 
Hybrid Power Generation. Data Centres. Saudi 
 
Resumo 
A Arábia Saudita está expandindo rapidamente 
sua infraestrutura digital, serviços em nuvem e 
cargas de trabalho de inteligência artificial, 
enquanto a política energética nacional apoia a 
geração de energia renovável, a melhoria da 
confiabilidade e a redução da dependência da 
energia elétrica proveniente de combustíveis 
líquidos. 
Os 
data 
centers 
exigem 
um 
fornecimento constante de eletricidade de alta 
qualidade, mas consomem muita energia, são 
sensíveis 
à 
temperatura 
e

1 INTRODUCTION 
 
Data centres have become critical infrastructure for digital government, fintech, 
cloud hosting, industrial automation and artificial intelligence. Their value is not just in 
computing power, but also in availability, data integrity and operational continuity. The 
growth of data centres in Saudi Arabia is fuelled by Vision 2030 digital transformation, 
the localization of cloud services, smart-city initiatives, and demand from the energy, 
health, logistics and financial sectors. In the meantime, the Kingdom is investing in 
expanding renewable energy, modernising its grid and diversifying its industries with 
low-carbon solutions. The developments pose a strategic question: how can data centres 
get reliable power and reduce emissions in a hot climate where cooling loads and peak 
electricity demand are high? Hybrid power generation and battery energy storage systems 
provide a practical route to answer this question [1-4]. 
Alturki [1] provides a relevant techno-economic framework for evaluating hybrid 
microgrid configurations under Saudi operating conditions. demonstrates a relevant 
design logic for Saudi conditions. It assesses hybrid microgrid configurations in Yanbu, 
compares photovoltaic, wind, generator, battery and hydrogen components and ranks 
alternatives through techno-economic and environmental metrics like net present cost, 
levelized energy cost, renewable fraction and emissions [1]. Its structure is useful for the 
present review as there are similar design tensions in data centre energy systems. They 
must balance reliability, capital cost, fuel consumption, storage autonomy, renewable 
variability and operating control. But data centres usually have more demanding

availability, heat management, maintenance access, safety, emissions accounting and 
compliance must therefore be part of BESS integration. A generic global solution is 
insufficient; the architecture must be adapted to Saudi grid conditions, renewable-
resource profiles and digital-infrastructure regulation [10-13].

planning. It also gives practical implementation priorities for operators, investors and 
energy planners that have to balance the need for data centre growth against the 
development of sustainable power. The aim is to consolidate evidence from hybrid

3 DATA-CENTRE POWER DEMAND AND SAUDI ENERGY CONTEXT 
 
Data centres are extraordinary electrical loads, combining high power density, 
limited tolerance of interruption and strong coupling between information-technology 
equipment and cooling systems. A server hall not only consumes electrical power for 
computing, but also requires chillers, pumps, fans, power distribution units, transformers, 
fire systems, security systems and monitoring platforms. Enterprise workloads can lead 
to a relatively stable load profile, but the training of artificial-intelligence workloads, 
cloud bursting and edge-computing services can lead to sharper fluctuations. These 
dynamics are important because storage sizing based only on average demand may 
underestimate ramping, autonomy and reserve requirements [6,11,15]. Reliability is often 
approached with redundant grid feeds, diesel generators, UPS batteries and distribution

5 BESS FUNCTIONS WITHIN HYBRID DATA-CENTRE POWER SYSTEMS 
 
BESS can serve different purposes in a data-centre hybrid power system. The first 
is ride-through: batteries support the load during short disturbances, voltage dips or 
generator start-up intervals. The second is renewable smoothing: batteries soak up 
variable PV or wind output and release energy when generation dips. The third is peak 
shaving: batteries reduce grid import during high tariff or constraint periods. The fourth 
is reserve management: batteries keep a minimum state of charge for emergency 
operation. The fifth is grid support. Batteries may provide frequency response, voltage 
support or demand-response capability, where regulation and interconnection rules allow. 
These functions are overlapping and the control logic must prioritise them instead of 
dispatching the battery to a single purpose [2,3,9]. The core principle for data centres is 
that the benefit of revenue or emissions reductions must never be undercut by the need to 
hold an emergency reserve to ensure service continuity. A BESS fully discharged for peak 
shaving may not be available during a grid outage. Thus, the energy management 
system should define protected state-of-charge bands. For example, one band may be 
dedicated to UPS ride-through, another to generator transition, another to renewable 
smoothing, and another to economic despatch. Battery cycling should also be limited by 
cell temperature, C-rate and degradation cost. These guardrails turn the battery from a 
simple storage device into a reliability-managed asset [2,19]. 
The design decisions depend on the battery chemistry. The efficiency, modularity 
and rapid response of lithium-ion systems has made them the dominant choice in many 
stationary applications today. From a safety and cycle life perspective, lithium iron 
phosphate cells are attractive, whereas nickel-manganese-cobalt systems may have higher 
energy density but require careful thermal and fire risk management. Flow batteries and 
sodium-based systems may be better suited for long-duration applications where space is

7 SIZING AND DISPATCH CONSIDERATIONS 
 
BESS sizing for data centres should be based on critical load, not total site 
nameplate. Critical load includes IT systems, network equipment and essential cooling 
for safe operation. Non-critical auxiliary loads may be curtailed or delayed in emergency 
operation. The minimum BESS energy capacity should be sufficient to meet transfer and 
ride-through needs, and additional capacity can be used for renewable smoothing, peak

Despatch should be built on forecast windows. Day-ahead forecasting estimates solar 
output, cooling demand, grid constrains and expected IT workload. Despatch is updated 
hourly based on weather, cloud cover, wind speed, and actual load. Then real-time control 
fixes deviations. This staged approach is aligned with the literature on renewable energy 
management where deviations from the planned schedules are minimised by forecasting 
and rolling optimisation [4,7]. The forecast must include thermal behaviour for data 
centres as high ambient temperature increases the cooling demand when PV output may 
also be high but battery-room cooling becomes more expensive. 
A useful despatch objective aims to minimise weighted cost, emissions and 
reliability risk. Cost terms include grid energy, fuel, battery degradation, maintenance and 
demand charges. Terms for emissions include the carbon intensity of the grid, the 
emissions from the fuel used by the generator and the impacts of the battery’s lifecycle. 
Reliability terms penalise low reserve, high battery temperature, generator unavailability 
and violation of autonomy requirements. The energy management system should not just 
seek the cheapest kilowatt-hour; it should seek the lowest risk-adjusted cost of reliable 
low-emission service. This principle applies even more to cloud facilities that are 
subjected to strict service-level agreements [6,11,19]. Explicit attention to battery 
degradation is warranted. Deep cycling, high temperatures and high C-rate operation 
often reduce lifetime. If degradation in the despatch algorithm is neglected, the apparent 
savings obtained from peak shaving may be offset by early replacement. Degradation-
aware scheduling uses the battery usage as a costed resource. It may select shallow cycles 
for daily smoothing, reserve deeper cycles for emergencies, and reduce operation during 
thermal stress. This is especially true in Saudi Arabia, where ambient conditions can 
increase the cooling energy for battery enclosures and thermal design becomes part of the 
financial optimisation [19,20].

8 RELIABILITY AND EMISSION ASSESSMENT 
 
Reliability assessment should take into account adequacy and operational 
resiliency. Adequacy is the ability to meet load over time with available generation and 
storage. Operational resilience asks at what speed the system detects, isolates and 
recovers from disturbance. Power-system reliability studies can be used to obtain indices 
such as loss of load expectation, loss of energy expectation, outage duration, autonomy 
hours and generator start success. Metrics specific to the data centre should include 
service level exposure, UPS transfer success, cooling ride through and time to stable 
recovery. Previous Saudi microgrid research demonstrates that configuration comparison 
can identify suitable compromises between economic and environmental performance [1] 
how the comparison of configurations can identify the best compromise between 
economic and environmental results [1,10]. 
An emissions assessment should include both direct and indirect effects. Direct 
emissions are from generators and fuel systems. Indirect emissions include grid 
electricity, battery manufacture and replacement, maintenance logistics and sometimes 
cooling-water treatment. Renewable energy and efficient storage despatch replace high-
carbon grid or generator operation for lower emissions in hybrid systems. The benefit 
however depends on the battery roundtrip efficiency, the cycling strategy and the carbon 
intensity of the charging energy. Charging batteries from fossil generation only to 
discharge later may reduce peaks but may not reduce emissions . Hence, carbon-aware

9 TECHNO-ECONOMIC DISCUSSION 
 
BESS delivers economic value to data centres through avoided outages, reduced 
generator run time, deferred infrastructure, lower peak demand, renewable utilisation and 
possible grid services. Downtime can affect customers, legal obligations and reputation. 
The value of avoiding an outage may be more than energy savings. Still, capital allocation 
should be demonstrated with clear metrics. Net present cost, levelized energy cost, 
replacement cost, operating cost and degradation cost should be evaluated at the same 
time. The reference microgrid paper uses HOMER style configuration ranking. This is 
appropriate because hybrid systems consist of interacting cost variables rather than one 
independent technology [1]. Saudi Arabia, with its abundant land and high cooling 
demand during the day, could benefit from PV-plus-BESS. The Wind-plus-BESS system 
is site-specific and may be more relevant in proximity to suitable corridors or coastal 
industrial zones. Grid-plus-BESS might be the simplest initial step for urban data centres, 
particularly when renewable procurement is possible but on-site generation is scarce. 
Generator-plus-BESS reduces fuel consumption by enabling the generators to run more 
efficiently or to be off during short disturbances. Hydrogen-ready options could become 
strategic as green-hydrogen supply chains mature, but short-term decisions should 
consider availability, storage safety and cost [1,18,21]. 
Regulatory and customer value should also be included in a financial evaluation. 
Sustainability, resilience and data residency are increasingly demanded by cloud 
customers as evidence. Operators that can demonstrate lower-emission power, audited

10 SAFETY, CYBERSECURITY AND GOVERNANCE 
 
The safety requirements of the BESS integration need to be designed from the 
beginning. Battery rooms or containers need adequate space, ventilation, thermal 
monitoring, fire detection, suppression planning, emergency isolation and maintenance 
procedures. Operators should train personnel to recognise thermal runaway warning 
signs, state-of-charge limits and emergency response. Safety is no different than 
reliability, an unreliably managed battery system can be an operational hazard. Site design 
should also incorporate access for replacement, spare modules and end of life recycling. 
Cybersecurity is as critical in hybrid power systems as they rely on sensors, controllers, 
inverters, metres and energy-management software. A compromised controller could 
tamper with battery despatch, falsify state of charge, or interfere with generator 
coordination. For data centres this risk is significant, because the power system directly 
underpins digital services. Zero-trust access, network segmentation, secure firmware 
updates, logging, incident response and backup control modes will be put in place. 
Further, national cybersecurity and cloud regulations emphasise the need for secure-by-
design energy infrastructure [12,13,24]. Governance should specify who is allowed to 
change despatch settings, reserve thresholds, generator rules and maintenance schedules. 
4. It also needs to set out how energy performance is reported to management and 
customers. A governance model may include monthly reliability reviews, quarterly 
battery health analysis, annual emissions verification and incident post-mortems 
following major disturbances. Energy systems in data-centres are too critical to be treated 
as mere facilities equipment; they should be treated as part of enterprise risk management 
and digital-service assurance [11,15,24].

11 RESEARCH GAPS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS 
 
There are several research gaps. First, open literature provides limited Saudi-
specific data-centre load profiles. More empirical studies are needed on the interaction of 
IT utilisation, cooling demand, seasonal temperature and renewable output. Second, more 
research is needed on degradation-aware despatch under hot-climate conditions. Tests on 
batteries in the laboratory do not always simulate field operation in desert climates. Third, 
practical comparisons among lithium-ion, flow, sodium-ion and hybrid battery-hydrogen 
systems are needed for different data-centre size and autonomy requirements [3,18,19]. 
Fourth, future work should combine water use and cooling technology with power-system 
optimisation. A carbon-reducing facility that increases demand for scarce water may not 
be truly sustainable. Fifth, the operation of the grid-interactive data centre should be 
investigated under the Saudi regulatory conditions. BESS may participate in demand 
response or ancillary services, but must do so in a manner consistent with service 
continuity and interconnection rules. Sixth, the energy-management layer should be 
studied as an important attack surface for cybersecurity research. These gaps demonstrate 
that BESS-supported data centres require more than equipment purchase; they require a 
new planning discipline [11,12,15]. 
Digital twins can be used in future research to validate despatch policies before 
deployment. A digital twin could bring together weather forecasts, PV output, battery 
health, generator performance, grid signals and IT workload predictions. Then it could 
simulate scenarios such as outages, heat waves, dust events, fuel interruptions and sudden 
increases in AI workload. This would allow operators to test policies in live service 
without risk. Hence, the most promising research direction is an integrated reliability-
carbon-cost digital twin for Saudi data centres supported by real operational data and 
validated by pilot projects [7,10,22].

12 CONCLUSION 
 
This review has explored the integration of hybrid power generation with battery 
energy storage systems for reliable and low emission data centres in Saudi Arabia. From 
the analysis it is seen that BESS can support much more than emergency ride-through. It 
is coordinated with solar PV, wind, grid import and backup generation, and can smooth 
renewable output, reduce generator run-time, shave peaks, preserve service continuity 
and improve emissions performance. The most powerful Saudi architecture is a controlled 
hybrid system where BESS, renewable generation, backup assets, cooling systems and 
data-centre operations are managed through an integrated energy-management platform. 
The review also reveals that technology choice must be driven by reliability and lifecycle 
governance. Performance is limited by battery capacity, power rating, state-of-charge

Interpretable 
Gradient 
Boosted 
Credit 
Scoring 
Under 
Macroeconomic Stress Testing in Banks and Model Explanations 
Marcus Foster, Claire Marchand, Benoit Masson 
Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry and Health Sciences, University of Melbourne, Melbourne, 
Australia 
Abstract: 
The transition from traditional statistical methods to advanced machine learning algorithms in 
bank credit scoring has significantly improved predictive accuracy, yet it has introduced 
substantial challenges regarding model interpretability and regulatory compliance. This paper 
presents a comprehensive academic investigation into the application of interpretable gradient-
boosted decision trees for credit scoring, specifically focusing on their performance and 
explainability under severe macroeconomic stress scenarios. As global banking regulatory 
frameworks increasingly mandate stringent stress testing procedures alongside transparent risk 
modeling, the necessity for models that can seamlessly integrate microeconomic borrower 
characteristics with macroeconomic indicators has become paramount. Through an extensive 
methodological framework, this research demonstrates how gradient boosting algorithms can 
effectively capture the complex, non-linear interactions between individual financial behaviors 
and systemic economic shocks. Furthermore, the study operationalizes advanced explainable 
artificial intelligence techniques, rooted in cooperative game theory, to demystify the internal 
decision-making processes of the gradient-boosted architecture. By analyzing variations in 
predictive behavior across baseline, adverse, and severely adverse economic climates, the 
research illustrates how the fundamental drivers of default risk dynamically shift during 
economic downturns. The findings reveal that while gradient boosting models maintain superior 
discriminative power under stress, the relative importance of systemic variables such as 
unemployment and interest rates escalates disproportionately, fundamentally altering the risk 
profile of retail loan portfolios. The insights generated from this research provide critical 
guidance for financial institutions seeking to deploy high-performance machine learning models 
that satisfy both internal risk management imperatives and external regulatory scrutiny. 
Keywords: Credit Scoring, Gradient Boosting, Macroeconomic Stress Testing, Explainable 
Artificial Intelligence, Financial Risk Management 
 
 

 p g . 2 7 7 
1. Introduction 
1.1 The Evolution of Credit Scoring in Banking 
The discipline of credit scoring has undergone a profound transformation over the past several 
decades, evolving from purely subjective human judgment to highly sophisticated, data-driven 
algorithmic decision systems [1]. Historically, financial institutions relied predominantly on 
linear statistical methodologies, primarily logistic regression and linear discriminant analysis, to 
evaluate the probability of default among retail and corporate borrowers [2]. These traditional 
techniques, while computationally efficient and inherently transparent, were constrained by their 
inability to capture complex, non-linear relationships and intricate interaction effects among 
diverse predictive variables [3]. As the volume, velocity, and variety of financial data expanded 
exponentially, the limitations of these parametric models became increasingly apparent, 
prompting a paradigm shift toward machine learning paradigms within the financial risk sector 
[4]. Among the myriad of available machine learning techniques, gradient boosting algorithms 
have emerged as arguably the most effective approaches for processing the heterogeneous tabular 
data typical of credit portfolios [5]. By sequentially constructing an ensemble of weak learners, 
typically decision trees, gradient boosting models systematically minimize prediction errors, 
thereby achieving unparalleled discriminatory power in distinguishing between reliable and 
high-risk borrowers [6]. However, the widespread adoption of these powerful algorithms in 
production environments has been significantly hindered by their inherent complexity, leading 
to their categorization as black-box models. This opacity directly contradicts the fundamental 
principles of prudent risk management and consumer protection, which demand that credit 
decisions be transparent, justifiable, and free from hidden biases [7]. 
1.2 The Imperative for Interpretability 
In the highly regulated ecosystem of global banking, predictive accuracy alone is an insufficient 
criterion for the deployment of a credit scoring model. Regulatory bodies worldwide have 
established stringent guidelines mandating that financial institutions must possess a deep, 
comprehensive understanding of how their internal risk models arrive at specific conclusions 
[8]. The imperative for interpretability serves multiple critical functions. Primarily, it ensures 
compliance with fair lending laws by allowing auditors and compliance officers to verify that 
the model does not inadvertently discriminate against protected demographic groups through 
proxy variables [9]. Furthermore, interpretability is essential for the issuance of adverse action 
notices; when a consumer is denied credit, the institution is legally obligated to provide specific, 
understandable reasons for the rejection, a task that is notoriously difficult when utilizing 
complex ensemble methods [10]. Beyond regulatory compliance, model explainability is a 
crucial component of internal model risk management. Financial institutions must be able to 
validate that their models are learning genuine, robust financial relationships rather than merely 
memorizing spurious correlations present in the historical training data [11]. The emergence of 
explainable artificial intelligence has provided a suite of analytical tools designed to bridge the 
gap between model complexity and human comprehension. Techniques grounded in cooperative 
game theory offer mathematically rigorous frameworks for decomposing the output of complex 
algorithms into individual feature contributions [12]. By attributing precise importance values to 
each input variable for every individual prediction, these methods allow risk managers to 
thoroughly interrogate the model's logic, ensuring that its decision boundaries align with 
established economic intuition and domain expertise [13]. 
1.3 Macroeconomic Stress Testing 
While assessing idiosyncratic borrower risk is the foundation of credit scoring, the systemic risk 
posed by broad macroeconomic fluctuations represents a separate, equally critical dimension of 
financial stability. The global financial crisis underscored the catastrophic consequences of 

 p g . 2 7 8 
evaluating credit risk in a static economic vacuum, revealing that models trained during periods 
of economic expansion often fail spectacularly when subjected to sudden economic contractions 
[14]. Consequently, modern regulatory frameworks necessitate comprehensive stress testing 
exercises, requiring banks to quantify the potential deterioration of their capital adequacy under 
hypothetical scenarios of severe economic distress [15]. Traditional approaches to stress testing 
often involved simplistic, aggregated shifts in default probabilities, failing to account for the 
granular, non-linear ways in which macroeconomic variables interact with specific borrower 
characteristics [16]. For instance, a sudden spike in the national unemployment rate does not 
affect all borrowers equally; individuals with high debt-to-income ratios or those employed in 
highly cyclical industries exhibit far greater sensitivity to systemic shocks than those with 
substantial liquid reserves and secure employment [17]. Integrating macroeconomic indicators 
directly into machine learning-based credit models allows for a much more nuanced and precise 
estimation of portfolio risk under stress. Gradient-boosted models, with their capacity to map 
complex interaction surfaces, are particularly well-suited to identifying the specific thresholds 
at which combinations of microeconomic vulnerabilities and macroeconomic deterioration 
trigger a cascading increase in default probability [18]. This research seeks to rigorously explore 
this intersection, analyzing how interpretable gradient-boosted models process and react to 
severe macroeconomic shocks. 
2. Literature Review and Background 
2.1 Machine Learning in Credit Risk Assessment 
The academic and practitioner literature surrounding credit risk assessment is vast and rapidly 
expanding, reflecting the ongoing transition toward advanced computational techniques. Early 
comparative studies in the domain consistently demonstrated the superiority of artificial neural 
networks and support vector machines over traditional logistic regression in terms of raw 
predictive accuracy [19]. However, the specific structural characteristics of credit datasets, which 
predominantly consist of categorical variables, missing values, and highly skewed continuous 
distributions, eventually revealed the limitations of distance-based and purely continuous 
mathematical architectures [20]. Subsequent research increasingly highlighted tree-based 
ensemble methods as the optimal solution for tabular credit scoring data. Random forests 
provided the initial breakthrough, utilizing bagging techniques and random feature selection to 
reduce model variance and prevent overfitting [21]. The evolution from parallel bagging to 
sequential boosting marked the next significant leap in predictive capability. Gradient boosting 
frameworks introduced sophisticated regularization parameters, advanced missing value 
handling, and highly optimized hardware utilization strategies, allowing for the rapid training of 
deep ensembles that effectively captured the most minute non-linear patterns within financial 
datasets [22]. Numerous empirical studies have since codified gradient boosting as the 
benchmark standard for credit risk modeling, consistently outperforming both traditional models 
and other advanced machine learning approaches across diverse geographical and temporal 
datasets [23]. Despite these established performance advantages, the literature also emphasizes 
a critical caveat: the marginal gains in predictive accuracy provided by highly complex 
ensembles are frequently offset by the exponential increase in model opacity, necessitating 
parallel advancements in interpretability methodologies [24]. 
2.2 Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Finance 
The burgeoning subfield of explainable artificial intelligence has generated substantial literature 
aimed at resolving the intrinsic tension between model performance and transparency. Early 
attempts at interpretability largely relied on model-agnostic surrogate approaches, wherein a 
simple, transparent model such as a linear regression or a single shallow decision tree was trained 
to approximate the predictions of the complex underlying algorithm [25]. While computationally 

 p g . 2 7 9 
inexpensive and intuitively appealing, these surrogate models often suffered from low fidelity, 
failing to accurately capture the precise non-linear decision boundaries that made the complex 
model desirable in the first place. Another popular approach involved localized explanations, 
which perturb input data points to observe the resulting changes in predictions, thereby 
approximating the local decision space around a specific instance [26]. However, the most 
significant advancement in financial explainability emerged from the application of cooperative 
game theory. By conceptualizing the prediction process as a cooperative game where individual 
features act as players collaborating to generate a final payout, researchers could utilize 
theoretical frameworks to distribute the prediction output fairly among the input variables [27]. 
This approach satisfies critical mathematical properties, including local accuracy, missingness, 
and consistency, providing a theoretically sound foundation for model interpretation. Within the 
context of banking, the adoption of these game-theoretic frameworks has revolutionized model 
validation. Risk managers can now generate global feature importance rankings that are 
mathematically robust, while simultaneously providing individualized explanations for every 
single loan application [28]. The literature underscores that the integration of such rigorous 
explainability frameworks is not merely an academic exercise, but a mandatory prerequisite for 
the responsible deployment of machine learning in regulated financial environments. 
2.3 Integration of Macroeconomic Variables 
The synthesis of microeconomic borrower data and macroeconomic indicators within predictive 
models represents a complex challenge that has garnered significant attention in contemporary 
financial literature. Traditional credit scoring systems were typically compartmentalized; 
baseline default probabilities were calculated using individual borrower attributes, and 
macroeconomic stress was applied post-hoc through aggregate portfolio-level scalars [29]. This 
bifurcated approach fundamentally ignores the intricate interaction effects between a borrower's 
specific financial situation and the broader economic environment. Recent advancements have 
advocated for a unified modeling approach, wherein macroeconomic variables such as gross 
domestic product growth, inflation rates, central bank interest rates, and localized unemployment 
figures are appended directly to the individual borrower records during the model training phase 
[30]. By exposing the machine learning algorithm to multiple macroeconomic cycles during 
training, the model learns not only the static risk profile of a borrower but also their dynamic 
sensitivity to economic fluctuations. The literature demonstrates that gradient boosting 
algorithms are exceptionally adept at discovering these cross-level interactions. For example, the 
models can automatically learn that a borrower with a variable-rate mortgage and limited savings 
is exponentially more likely to default during a period of simultaneous interest rate hikes and 
rising unemployment, whereas a fixed-rate borrower with identical savings may remain 
relatively stable [31]. The ability to capture these highly specific, non-linear sensitivities is 
precisely what makes advanced machine learning models invaluable for modern, granular stress 
testing exercises. However, the literature also warns of the challenges associated with this 
approach, particularly the scarcity of long-term training data encompassing multiple severe 
economic downturns, which can lead to model instability if not carefully managed through robust 
regularization and validation techniques [32]. 
3. Methodology and Analytical Framework 
3.1 Data Acquisition and Preprocessing 
The empirical foundation of this research relies on a comprehensive, synthesized dataset 
constructed to mirror the complexities and nuances of a large-scale European retail mortgage 
portfolio. To ensure the findings are robust and applicable to real-world banking environments, 
the dataset encompasses over one million individual loan records spanning a fifteen-year 
temporal window, thereby incorporating multiple distinct phases of the economic cycle. The 

 p g . 2 8 0 
feature space is broadly categorized into two primary domains: individual borrower 
characteristics and macroeconomic indicators. Borrower-specific variables include origination 
metrics such as the loan-to-value ratio, the debt-to-income ratio, primary applicant income, 
employment status, credit bureau scores, and the precise geographical location of the 
collateralized property. Behavioral variables, updated on a monthly basis, track the payment 
history, current delinquency status, and outstanding principal balance. The preliminary phase of 
the empirical analysis necessitated a rigorous and comprehensive data sanitization protocol, 
designed to address inherent inconsistencies typical of large-scale retail banking repositories. 
Missing values in continuous variables were addressed using advanced multivariate imputation 
strategies that preserve the underlying conditional distributions, while categorical missingness 
was treated as a distinct informational category, recognizing that the absence of information in 
credit applications often carries significant predictive value. Outlier detection mechanisms were 
implemented to cap extreme values at the ninety-ninth percentile, preventing the gradient 
boosting algorithm from heavily weighting anomalous data points. Continuous variables were 
subsequently standardized to stabilize the learning process, and categorical variables underwent 
specialized target encoding to transform high-cardinality geographic and occupational data into 
continuous numerical formats without drastically expanding the dimensionality of the feature 
space.

3.2 Gradient Boosting Model Architecture 
The core predictive engine utilized in this study is based on a highly optimized gradient boosting 
framework designed specifically for efficiency and scalability when processing large tabular 
datasets. The architecture constructs an ensemble of decision trees sequentially, with each 
subsequent tree meticulously designed to correct the residual errors generated by the combined 
predictions of all preceding trees. Unlike traditional random forests that build deep, independent 
trees, this architecture relies on shallow, weak learners constructed in a highly controlled manner. 
The learning process is governed by a specified loss function; given the binary classification 
nature of the credit default problem, the model minimizes the binary cross-entropy loss over the 
training data. To prevent the model from rapidly overfitting the training set and memorizing 
idiosyncratic noise, a robust suite of regularization techniques is employed. These include 
restrictions on the maximum depth of individual trees, constraints on the minimum number of 
observations required in terminal leaves, and a learning rate parameter that scales the 
contribution of each newly added tree. Furthermore, stochastic elements are introduced into the 
training process through the random subsampling of both the training instances and the available 
feature space prior to the construction of each individual tree. The hyperparameter tuning process 
was conducted utilizing a rigorous grid search methodology integrated with a time-series cross-

 p g . 2 8 1 
validation strategy. This temporal validation is critical in financial modeling; rather than 
randomly splitting the data, the model is trained on historical data and validated strictly on future 
unseen data, thereby preventing temporal data leakage and ensuring that the model's performance 
metrics accurately reflect its expected predictive power in a live production environment. 
3.3 Macroeconomic Stress Scenario Design 
To adequately evaluate the resilience of the loan portfolio and the behavioral dynamics of the 
predictive model under extreme conditions, this study operationalizes a comprehensive 
macroeconomic stress testing framework. The framework is built upon three distinct 
macroeconomic scenarios designed to simulate varying degrees of economic stability and 
deterioration. These scenarios are applied to the most recent cross-section of the loan portfolio 
to forecast default probabilities over a prospective twelve-month horizon. The Baseline scenario 
represents the consensus economic forecast, characterized by moderate, stable gross domestic 
product growth, steady unemployment rates aligned with the natural rate, and inflation figures 
maintained closely within central bank target ranges. The Adverse scenario introduces a 
significant but historically common cyclical downturn, simulating a mild recession with 
contracting economic output, moderate increases in unemployment, and corresponding 
adjustments in central bank interest rates. The Severely Adverse scenario is engineered to 
replicate a catastrophic, systemic financial crisis akin to the events of the global financial crisis. 
This scenario postulates a precipitous contraction in gross domestic product, a dramatic, 
sustained surge in the national unemployment rate to double-digit levels, severe depreciation in 
residential property indices negatively impacting collateral values, and high volatility in short-
term interest rates. By feeding these distinct macroeconomic trajectories into the trained gradient 
boosting model alongside the static borrower characteristics, the research can meticulously 
quantify the portfolio's sensitivity to macroeconomic degradation.

3.4 Interpretability Framework 
The transformation of the gradient boosting architecture from an opaque black box into a fully 
transparent and interpretable system is achieved through the integration of an advanced 
attribution methodology based on cooperative game theory. This framework assigns a specific 
numerical value to each input feature, representing that feature's precise marginal contribution 
to the final prediction for a given borrower. The calculation process involves assessing the 
model's prediction across all possible combinations and permutations of the input features to 
determine the isolated impact of each variable. Because evaluating every possible coalition of 
features is computationally intractable for complex models with numerous variables, the 
framework utilizes highly sophisticated approximation algorithms optimized specifically for 

 p g . 2 8 2 
tree-based ensembles. These algorithms traverse the internal structure of the decision trees to 
compute the exact attribution values efficiently. The resulting values possess properties of 
additivity, meaning that the sum of the feature contributions, combined with the model's baseline 
expected value, perfectly equals the final predicted probability of default. This mathematical 
consistency is absolutely essential for regulatory approval. In the context of stress testing, this 
interpretability framework is deployed iteratively across the baseline, adverse, and severely 
adverse scenarios. By comparing the feature attribution values for the exact same borrower under 
different macroeconomic conditions, the research can isolate exactly how the model alters its 
internal logic when confronted with systemic economic shocks. This methodology provides 
unprecedented visibility into the complex interaction effects learned by the algorithm, 
illuminating the specific mechanisms through which macroeconomic stress propagates down to 
the individual borrower level. 
 
Figure 1: Comprehensive Schematic of the Interpretable Macroeconomic Stress Testing Architecture 
4. Results and Discussion 
4.1 Model Performance Evaluation 
The initial phase of the results analysis focuses on evaluating the fundamental discriminative 
capability of the gradient-boosted model across the various simulated economic environments. 
Model performance was rigorously quantified using several standardized metrics, primarily the 
Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve, which measures the model's ability to 
correctly rank order borrowers from highest to lowest risk regardless of the specific classification 
threshold. Additionally, precision, recall, and the F1-score were computed to provide a 
comprehensive view of the model's accuracy, particularly concerning the identification of the 
minority default class. Under the Baseline scenario, the gradient boosting architecture 
demonstrated exceptional predictive prowess, achieving an Area Under the Curve significantly 
higher than industry standards for traditional logistic regression models applied to similar 
portfolios. This superior performance confirms the model's ability to leverage complex non-
linear patterns within the historical data. When subjected to the Adverse and Severely Adverse 
scenarios, the model maintained its robust rank-ordering capability, although a slight, expected 
degradation in overall performance metrics was observed. This degradation is a well-
documented phenomenon in stress testing, occurring because severe macroeconomic shocks 
introduce systemic noise and unprecedented conditions that slightly dilute the predictive signal 
of microeconomic behavioral variables. However, the gradient-boosted model exhibited 

 p g . 2 8 3 
remarkable resilience compared to benchmark models, proving that its intricate decision 
boundaries, which incorporate macroeconomic interactions, allow it to adapt its risk assessments 
effectively even when the underlying economic paradigm shifts drastically.

4.2 Impact of Stress Scenarios on Default Probabilities 
The application of the macroeconomic stress scenarios resulted in substantial and non-linear 
upward shifts in the predicted probabilities of default across the loan portfolio. In the Baseline 
scenario, the distribution of default probabilities was heavily skewed toward the lower end of 
the spectrum, reflecting a fundamentally healthy portfolio under normal economic conditions. 
However, the transition to the Severely Adverse scenario triggered a profound transformation in 
this distribution. The aggregate expected default rate for the portfolio increased exponentially, 
simulating severe capital depletion for the institution. Crucially, the model demonstrated that the 
impact of the severe macroeconomic shock was not distributed uniformly across the portfolio. 
Borrowers with specific vulnerability profiles, such as high pre-existing debt-to-income ratios 
and employment in cyclically sensitive industries, experienced catastrophic increases in their 
individual default probabilities. Conversely, highly affluent borrowers with substantial equity 
buffers and stable employment exhibited a much lower elasticity of default relative to the 
macroeconomic deterioration. The gradient-boosted model successfully captured these complex 
interaction effects, applying localized penalties to vulnerable segments while maintaining 
relatively stable risk assessments for insulated borrowers. This granular, non-homogeneous 
expansion of risk highlights the immense value of integrating macroeconomic variables directly 
into machine learning models, as it prevents the dangerous underestimation of risk 
concentrations that often occurs when using simplistic, aggregate stress multipliers. 
4.3 Feature Importance Dynamics Under Stress 
The most profound insights of this study emerge from the application of the game-theoretic 
interpretability framework, which reveals how the internal logic of the gradient-boosted model 
dynamically adapts to different economic environments. By analyzing the global feature 
importance rankings across the scenarios, a distinct paradigm shift in the drivers of default risk 
becomes evident. Under the Baseline scenario, the model primarily relies on idiosyncratic 
borrower behaviors to assess risk. Variables such as recent payment history, credit bureau scores, 
and current credit utilization rates dominate the importance hierarchy, indicating that in a stable 
economy, an individual's past financial behavior is the most reliable predictor of future 
performance. However, as the economic environment transitions to the Severely Adverse 
scenario, a radical restructuring of feature importance occurs. Macroeconomic indicators, which 
played a secondary or tertiary role in the Baseline scenario, surge to the forefront of the model's 
decision-making process. The national unemployment rate and the residential property index 
become the dominant drivers of predicted default, effectively overriding the historical behavioral 
variables. The interpretability framework mathematically demonstrates that in a severe crisis, 
systemic economic forces exert such overwhelming pressure on consumer finances that an 

 p g . 2 8 4 
individual's previously stellar credit history loses much of its protective predictive value. The 
model intelligently learns that a widespread collapse in housing equity and massive job losses 
will force even historically responsible borrowers into default.

5. Conclusion 
This comprehensive academic investigation has systematically demonstrated the viability, 
efficacy, and profound analytical advantages of deploying interpretable gradient-boosted 
decision trees for credit scoring within the context of rigorous macroeconomic stress testing. The 
empirical analysis confirms that gradient boosting architectures possess the necessary 
computational sophistication to accurately model the complex, non-linear interactions between 
highly granular microeconomic borrower characteristics and broad, systemic macroeconomic 
indicators. While the machine learning model delivered superior predictive accuracy and rank-
ordering capabilities under baseline economic conditions, its true value was realized during the 
simulation of severe economic shocks. By utilizing advanced explainable artificial intelligence 
techniques grounded in cooperative game theory, this research successfully illuminated the 
previously opaque internal mechanics of the ensemble model. The findings conclusively show 
that the fundamental drivers of retail credit risk are highly dynamic and highly sensitive to the 
prevailing economic climate. The observable shift in feature attribution—from idiosyncratic 
behavioral metrics during periods of stability to systemic macroeconomic indicators during 
periods of crisis—proves that the model accurately captures the economic realities of 
catastrophic market downturns. The ability to precisely quantify these shifts at the individual 
borrower level provides a monumental advancement over traditional, aggregated stress testing 
methodologies. 
6. Managerial and Regulatory Implications 
The insights generated by this research carry significant implications for both financial 
institution management and global banking regulatory authorities. For risk managers, the 
demonstrated framework offers a powerful tool for dynamic portfolio management and highly 
targeted capital allocation. By understanding exactly which combinations of borrower attributes 
and macroeconomic shocks trigger cascading defaults, institutions can proactively adjust 
underwriting standards, design targeted intervention programs for vulnerable borrower 
segments, and optimize their capital reserves with a level of precision previously unattainable. 
From a regulatory perspective, this study provides compelling evidence that the adoption of 
advanced machine learning techniques does not necessitate a compromise on model transparency 
or explainability. The successful application of mathematically robust feature attribution 
methods satisfies the stringent requirements for model interpretability, ensuring that financial 
institutions can leverage the predictive power of artificial intelligence while remaining fully 
compliant with fair lending laws and internal model governance standards. As the global 

 p g . 2 8 5 
economy continues to navigate periods of unprecedented volatility, the integration of 
interpretable machine learning architectures with comprehensive macroeconomic stress testing 
will undoubtedly become a foundational pillar of resilient and responsible financial risk 
management. Future research should seek to expand upon this framework by integrating 
alternative, high-frequency data sources and exploring the intersection of macroeconomic stress 
with emerging systemic risks, such as climate-related financial vulnerabilities.

GD202.full_text:
Green AI: A systematic review and meta-analysis of its definitions, lifecycle
models, hardware and measurement attempts
Marcel Rojahna,∗and Marcus Gruma
aUniversity of Potsdam, Junior Chair of Business Information Systems, esp. AI-based Application Systems
Karl-Marx-Str. 67, Potsdam 14482, Germany
Abstract
Background: Across the Artificial Intelligence (AI) lifecycle - from hardware to development, de-
ployment, and reuse - burdens span energy, carbon, water, and embodied impacts. Cloud-provider tools
improve transparency but remains heterogeneous and often omit water and value-chain effects, limiting
comparability and reproducibility. Addressing these multi-dimensional burdens requires a lifecycle ap-
proach linking phase-explicit mapping with system levers (hardware, placement, energy mix, cooling,
scheduling) and calibrated measurement across facility, system, device, and workload levels.
Objectives: This article (i) establishes a unified, operational definition of Green AI distinct from
Sustainable AI; (ii) formalizes a five-phase lifecycle mapped to Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) stages,
making energy, carbon, water, and embodied impacts first-class; (iii) specifies governance via Plan-Do-
Check-Act (PDCA) cycles with decision gateways; (iv) systematizes hardware and system-level strate-
gies across the edge-cloud continuum to reduce embodied burdens; and (v) defines a calibrated mea-
surement framework combining estimator models with direct metering to enable reproducible, provider-
agnostic comparisons.
Methods: This review synthesizes 103 studies through a meta-analytical framework operationalizing
164 terms across the Green AI lifecycle. Using taxonomy-guided annotation, each source was situated
along three analytical axes: lifecycle phase (e.g., design, training, end-of-life), impact vector (energy,
water, material intensity), and system layer (hardware-software boundary). Concepts were mapped to
standardized LCA stages and consolidated into a task-level process model. Mechanisms from High-
Performance Computing (HPC) management were examined for their transferability to AI. Finally, mea-
surement approaches were contrasting estimator-based tools with direct metering to evaluate calibration,
reporting completeness.
Results: This article delivers four main contributions: (1) a unified, operational definition of Green
AI extending beyond training efficiency to energy, carbon, water, and embodied material footprints with
standardized and transparent reporting; (2) a comprehensive five-phase lifecycle mapped to LCA stages
and structured by PDCA with decision gateways; (3) hardware and system-level strategies across the
edge-cloud continuum, informed by rigorously transferable HPC techniques; and (4) a hybrid measure-
ment architecture combining estimators with direct metering for reliable calibration and standardized
reporting. Remaining gaps include inconsistent metrics, limited attention to water and Scope 3 impacts,
provider-specific dashboards that hinder comparability, and a lack of reproducible, calibrated measure-
ments across hardware tiers.
Conclusions: Combining definition, lifecycle processes, hardware strategies, and calibrated mea-
surement, this article offers actionable, evidence-based guidance for researchers, practitioners, and pol-
icymakers.
The framework improves green model/infrastructure choices, context-aware scheduling,
transparent reporting, and resilient long-term circularity.
∗Corresponding author. ORCID: 0000-0002-2231-5690
Email addresses: marcel.rojahn@uni-potsdam.de (Marcel Rojahn ), marcus.grum@uni-potsdam.de
(Marcus Grum)
Preprint – November 2025
arXiv:2511.07090v4  [cs.AI]  13 Nov 2025

Preprint – November 2025 – Rojahn and Grum – Green AI: A systematic review and meta-analysis of its
definitions, lifecycle models, hardware and measurement attempts
1. Introduction
Artificial Intelligence (AI) accelerators, such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and domain-
specific Tensor/Neural Processing Units (TPUs/NPUs), have become the default compute substrate for
training transformer-based and large-scale multimodal models [1, 80]. Realizing these capabilities has
entailed an impressive scale-up in model size and training, from millions to billions of parameters in
publicly reported models, together with operations such as matrix multiplications and attention mech-
anisms [14, 89]. As a result, training deep neural networks and large language models requires sev-
eral orders larger energy demand than conventional machine-learning approaches, with the factor driven
by model size and training duration [68, 78]. Beyond operational energy and carbon emissions, re-
cent syntheses emphasize additional environmental burdens - including water consumption and embod-
ied impacts across the hardware supply chain - that remain underrepresented in model-centric accounts
[12, 40, 50, 91]. This escalation makes Green AI a first-class design maxim for modern AI systems.
At the same time, cloud providers expose emissions tooling (e.g., dashboards for location- and
market-based accounting), signaling a shift toward operational transparency. Methodologies, however,
differ across providers, often lack water and Scope 3 (value-chain) coverage, and impede cross-system
comparability [8, 34, 63]. At the application level, end-to-end AI systems - combining perception, lan-
guage, and decision components - can increase energy demand at deployment when subjected to large
request volumes, long context windows, strict latency service-level objectives, and heterogeneous edge-
cloud placement constraints [56].
Despite notable progress, the field lacks an AI-specific lifecycle-wide and calibrated standard that
unifies energy, carbon, and water measurement and reporting, integrates embodied impacts, and enables
reproducible comparison across hardware tiers and deployment contexts. Existing efforts frequently
optimize isolated segments - data centers, algorithms, or runtime kernels - without a consistent linkage
across the AI lifecycle [56, 75].
On the other side, accurate assessment of Green AI requires coordinated, multi-level measurement:
facility-level metrics (e.g., Power Usage Effectiveness, PUE; and Water Usage Effectiveness, WUE),
system consumption, hardware telemetry (e.g., Running Average Power Limit, RAPL; and Performance
Monitoring Counters, PMCs), workload profiling (step/batch), and lifecycle-complete coverage (e.g.,
hardware, development, and end-of-life) [30, 56]. Indirect estimators must be calibrated against direct
measurements to ensure valid reporting.
Contributions. This article advances the literature through four key contributions: (1) a unified
definition of Green AI concise, comprehensive, delineated from Sustainable AI; (2) a Green AI lifecycle
that maps five phases and subphases to Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) stages, exposing often-overlooked
Scope 3 and water-related impacts alongside energy and carbon; (3) a hardware- and software-aware
realization and governance framework that formalizes Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) loops with decision
gateways based on Phase Completion Criteria (PCC) and Performance-Environmental Thresholds (PET),
transferring HPC techniques into AI pipelines; (4) a measurement architecture that combines indirect
estimation (e.g., emissions models) with direct power metering to calibrate discrepancies and standardize
reporting across energy, carbon, and water.
On this basis, the following research questions are addressed:
• RQ1: How should Green AI be defined and delimited relative to adjacent concepts, and which
principles govern its lifecycle-wide application?
• RQ2: Which phases and subphases constitute the Green AI lifecycle, and how do they map to Life
Cycle Assessment (LCA) stages?
• RQ3: Which hardware components and system architectures enable improved performance per
watt and reduced embodied impacts across the lifecycle?
• RQ4: How can environmental impacts (e.g. energy, carbon, water) be measured and reported
consistently across the lifecycle, including calibration of indirect estimators with direct measure-
ments?
Page 2 of 71

Preprint – November 2025 – Rojahn and Grum – Green AI: A systematic review and meta-analysis of its
definitions, lifecycle models, hardware and measurement attempts
• RQ5: Which open challenges and research priorities (benchmarks, reporting schemas, uncertainty
handling, circularity, governance) are needed to advance lifecycle integration of Green AI?
Section 2 surveys the core Green AI literature and adjacent economic and social perspectives. Sec-
tion 3 details the methodology, including taxonomy-driven coding and trend analysis. Section 4 reports
findings addressing RQ1-RQ4. Section 5 synthesizes major challenges and outlines the research agenda
(RQ5). Section 6 synthesizes implications for model and infrastructure selection, carbon- and context-
aware scheduling, lifecycle governance, and PDCA-based decision gateways; it also delineates limita-
tions and threats to validity, including systematic literature review (SLR) coverage bias, uncertainty from
estimator-meter discrepancies, provider-specific dashboards that hinder comparability, and incomplete
treatment of water and Scope 3 impacts. Section 7 consolidates the contributions into concrete guid-
ance and a prioritized agenda covering standardized benchmarks and reporting, calibrated measurement
procedures, uncertainty disclosure, and circularity at end-of-life.
2. Foundations and prior research in Green AI
Green artificial intelligence (AI) is concerned with maintaining task performance while minimizing
environmental impacts across the full lifecycle, including operational energy use and carbon emissions,
cooling-related water use, and material (embodied) footprints in hardware supply chains [40, 50, 75].
Early evidence on the training-related footprint of large models [2019] motivated subsequent studies
along complementary levers: algorithmic efficiency, hardware and placement choices, compiler/runtime
optimizations, and data and storage management - each targeting energy and carbon reduction under ex-
plicit quality and latency constraints. Within the algorithmic family, pruning and quantization, together
with related compression methods (e.g., knowledge distillation, low-rank adaptation, and sparsity), re-
duce compute and energy demand while controlling accuracy loss [100].
Operationalizing Green AI. Operationalization spans multiple system layers. On the hardware side,
energy-efficient accelerators and context-aware placement across the edge-cloud continuum enable im-
proved performance per watt under regional energy mixes and cooling technologies, including cooling-
water intensity [12, 24]. At the runtime level, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, power capping,
queue-level energy budgeting, and locality-aware scheduling translate established high-performance
computing (HPC) practices into modern AI pipelines. On the data and storage side, de-duplication,
tiered storage, retention policies, and automated data-quality gates curb unnecessary data movement and
redundant compute [16, 17]. Frameworks from green software engineering (e.g., GAISSA; [59]) artic-
ulate concrete development and inference practices that can be transferred to AI-centric systems, while
noting the additional hardware- and model-induced impacts specific to AI deployments.
Holistic perspectives and lifecycle alignment. Green-ability models propose quality attributes and
metrics - such as energy consumption, resource usage, and system longevity - that support architecture-
level Green AI assessments [16, 17]. Complementary studies argue for end-to-end integration of energy-
aware practices across lifecycle stages [41] and for aligning AI processes with standardized LCA con-
cepts, ensuring that upstream (raw-material extraction, component manufacturing, transport) and down-
stream (inference, maintenance, reuse) effects are captured alongside model-centric impact metrics.
Sustainability dimensions and access. Sustainable AI entails environmental, economic, and so-
cial dimensions [88]. Incorporating efficiency and footprint metrics into research evaluation can realign
incentives toward lower-impact solutions. Lower resource requirements can broaden participation by
reducing entry costs for under-resourced institutions and enabling more equitable access to experimen-
tation [24, 75].
Positioning. Prior studies deliver important building blocks but remains fragmented: some strands
target algorithms or hardware in isolation, others focus on software practices or socio-economic aspects.
What is still missing is an integrated, lifecycle-explicit synthesis that (i) clearly distinguishes Green AI
from broader Sustainable AI, (ii) maps AI phases and subphases to standardized LCA stages, (iii) formal-
izes governance via Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) loops with decision gateways based on phase comple-
tion criteria (PCC) and Performance-Environmental Thresholds (PET), and (iv) couples estimator-based
Page 3 of 71

Preprint – November 2025 – Rojahn and Grum – Green AI: A systematic review and meta-analysis of its
definitions, lifecycle models, hardware and measurement attempts
reporting with calibrated direct measurements to consistently cover energy, carbon, and water. The re-
mainder of this article addresses these gaps.
3. Methodological approach to this research
This systematic literature review (SLR) follows established guidance for evidence synthesis in in-
formation systems and software engineering and reports according to the Preferred Reporting Items for
Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) [46, 65, 82, 86]. All raw export files are avail-
able in the replication package. Figure 1 outlines the eight-step process adapted from Thomé et al. 2016;
the following sections detail database coverage and search strings (Phase 1), eligibility criteria (Phase 2),
screening and de-duplication procedures with inter-rater agreement reporting (Phase 3), and extraction,
appraisal, and synthesis methods (Phase 4). To strengthen validity, the protocol was pre-specified, with
dual coding and inter-rater agreement.
