4.4.2. Proposal of a Green AI measurement selection
Building on the critical gaps identified above, a structured selection and integration framework for
comprehensive Green AI measurement is proposed. The objective is not to recommend a single tool,
but to define principles and procedures for systematically combining heterogeneous methods in a repro-
ducible, transparent, and scientifically robust manner.
Dual-layered architecture. Figure 10 illustrates a hybrid measurement architecture that integrates
(i) software-level estimators for broad coverage and (ii) hardware-level monitors for calibration and vali-
dation. The software tier provides accessibility, automation, and workflow integration (e.g., CodeCarbon,
Carbontracker), while the hardware tier ensures empirical fidelity (e.g., smart plugs, performance mon-
itoring counters, PMCs; rack-level PDUs). This layered approach explicitly acknowledges the trade-off
between scope and accuracy and systematically addresses the limitation of relying exclusively on indirect
methods.
Selection principles. A four-step procedure structures the selection and deployment of tools: In
step 1) “define workload and scope”, the AI workload is characterized (e.g. training vs. inference,
edge vs. cloud, real-time vs. batch) and the resolution required is selected (e.g. system-level totals
vs. component-level attribution).
In step 2) “select a baseline estimator”, the Python package or dashboard is applied to ensure cov-
erage and reproducibility. Assumptions must be recorded explicitly (e.g. grid carbon data, emission
factors, TDP values).
In step 3) “add calibration points”, direct hardware measurement are introduced (e.g. smart plugs
for total load, PMCs for per-component) to validate and refine baseline estimates. When possible, cross-
checks against published benchmarks, such as Perun or the ML Energy Benchmark [85], are realized.
In step 4) “extend beyond carbon”, additional metrics are incorporated (e.g. water, e-waste proxies,
lifecycle amortization, resource depletion) where feasible. Although current water-use estimation models
remain highly uncertain [50], transparent reporting stimulates broader methodological standardization
and cross-domain comparability.
Illustrative workflow. Let’s assume to have a training job deployed on an on-premises GPU cluster.
The tool called CodeCarbon can be used to capture runtime and estimated emissions, complemented
by Shelly smart plugs (low-cost, WiFi-enabled power meters) at the rack level to measure actual power
draw. Integrated PMCs provide detailed profiling of GPU versus CPU contributions. Discrepancies be-
tween indirect estimates and direct measurements should be reported, and the adjusted emission factor
consistently applied to subsequent runs. This workflow combines transparency (via software estimators)
with methodological rigor (via calibrated hardware data).
Scientific contribution. The proposed framework advances the discussion from tool enumeration to
methodological standardization and integration. Three distinctive contributions are emphasized:
(i) recognition of indirect-method assumptions (e.g., FLOP- or GPU-hour proxies) and their calibra-
tion requirements against empirically metered data,
(ii) systematic incorporation of direct measurement techniques from Green IT (e.g., RAPL counters,
rack-level meters, or facility telemetry) into the AI context, and
(iii) a pathway toward multi-dimensional metrics that jointly report energy (J/kWh), carbon (kg CO2
emissin with emission-factor provenance), water (L with Water Usage Effectiveness, WUE; disclosure),
and embodied impacts (via Environmental Product Declarations, EPDs). These elements enable repro-
ducible, comparable, and lifecycle-explicit Green AI reporting practices.

4.4.3. Limitations of the Green AI measurement selection proposed
The proposed hybrid framework mitigates fragmentation in Green AI measurement by integrating
estimator tools with hardware metering, yet remains constrained by dataset availability, emission-factor
heterogeneity, and limited water proxies. Limitations remain as follows.
Reliance on indirect methods. Software-based estimators such as CodeCarbon or Experiment Im-
pact Tracker operate on generalized emission factors and TDP-based assumptions [22, 42]. While useful
for rapid deployment, their validity decreases under heterogeneous workloads or non-standard infras-
tructures. Calibration against hardware measurements is necessary, yet rarely performed systematically.
External meters vs. integrated sensors. External devices such as smart plugs have been used in
IT for over a decade, offering simplicity and full-system coverage but limited attribution. In contrast,
integrated PMCs or rack-level PDUs provide fine-grained profiling [85], but are not consistently exposed
across hardware. Neither approach alone yields a complete picture.
Incomplete metric coverage. Most tools quantify carbon emissions but omit cooling-related wa-
ter withdrawals, WUE disclosure, and traceable e-waste recovery rates, leaving major lifecycle burdens
outside their reporting scope. Recent attempts to estimate water consumption rely on indirect cooling
models [50], but lack validation across diverse data centers. This omission constrains the comprehen-
siveness of current architectures.
Fragmentation and comparability. Outputs often remain incompatible due to inconsistent emis-
sion factors, regional datasets, and reporting formats [91]. Thus, studies are not comparable, undermin-
ing cross-benchmarking. Standardized reporting formats and disclosure of assumptions would improve
reproducibility.
Lifecycle blind spots. Few tools capture embodied impacts from semiconductor fabrication, assem-
bly, and logistics, or account for reuse and recycling, even though LCA studies show embodied emissions
from mining and wafer production can outweigh savings across a system’s lifetime [56, 68]. Without
harmonized methods for amortizing embodied carbon, reporting risks focusing disproportionately on
short-term operational footprints.
In summary, the current measurement landscape remains fragmented, carbon-centric, and assumption-
driven. Resolving these discrepancies necessitates advances in three complementary areas: first, calibra-
tion procedures that align software estimators with hardware-based truth data; second, an expanded
indicator framework covering water, e-waste, and lifecycle material dimensions; and third, interoperable
reporting formats ensuring cross-system comparability. These measures jointly underpin a reproducible
and scalable architecture for comprehensive Green-AI evaluation.
Methodological differentiation. Recent comparative studies [91] highlight that measurement reli-
ability in Green AI research is not intrinsic to data but contingent upon methodological precision. This
dependency reaffirms the centrality of explicit boundary-setting, transparent calibration, and cross-layer
verification as foundations of credible Green-AI assessments. Table 7 systematizes existing approaches
along two dimensions: indirect vs. direct measurement and system- vs. component-level granularity.
Python-based or rather software-based packages (e.g., CodeCarbon, Experiment Impact Tracker)
represent indirect, model-driven estimation. They integrate seamlessly into machine learning pipelines
but rely on generalized emission factors and hardware assumptions, leading to potential inaccuracies
under heterogeneous workloads [22, 42]. Cloud-provider dashboards (e.g., Google, Microsoft, AWS)
similarly rely on indirect reporting, though enriched by infrastructure-level data; however, they remain
constrained to proprietary ecosystems [33, 62].
In contrast, direct measurement has a long tradition in Green IT. External devices such as smart
plugs or rack-mounted PDUs capture whole-system consumption including conversion losses and cool-
ing overhead, providing robust upper bounds but lacking component-level attribution. Integrated sensors
such as PMCs or motherboard energy probes enable fine-grained attribution to CPUs, GPUs, and mem-
ory, though their availability and calibration differ significantly across hardware generations [85].
Hybrid methods combining indirect estimators with external or internal direct meters offer a promis-
ing compromise by calibrating software-based models against physical measurements. Such hybridiza-
tion has been demonstrated in frameworks like IrEne [18], where software estimators are continuously

for cross-layer integration - e.g., combining Python hooks with rack-level smart plugs and grid-aware
scheduling - show calibration can cut error margins below 10% while preserving workflow usability
[72]. Yet no consensus exists on protocols for calibration frequency, emission-factor provenance, or
uncertainty disclosure. This gap highlights the need for open benchmarks that systematically evaluate
estimator-meter combinations across contexts (training, inference, preprocessing, storage), coupled with
transparent reporting of assumptions such as PUE, WUE, and embodied-carbon amortization [50, 100].
Attempts for coherentism. Taken together, the methodological differentiation reveals that portabil-
ity, precision, and transparency cannot be optimized simultaneously: software-only tools favor accessi-
bility but lack rigor, hardware-only approaches maximize accuracy but limit comparability, and hybrid
solutions remain under-standardized. Advancing Green AI measurement thus requires moving beyond
isolated tools toward integrated, auditable pipelines that combine estimator scalability with metered cal-
ibration. Only then can reported metrics achieve the reproducibility and cross-platform comparability
needed for lifecycle-explicit Green AI assessments.
5. Challenges in implementing Green AI and future research directions
This section synthesizes the challenges and research gaps identified in the systematic review, extend-
ing the conceptual structure developed in the previous chapter. In line with RQ5 (“Which open challenges
and research priorities (benchmarks, reporting schemas, uncertainty handling, circularity, governance)
are needed to advance lifecycle integration of Green AI?”), the focus lies on identifying methodological
blind spots - such as calibration protocols, embodied-impact accounting, and multi-metric integration
- and on outlining concrete pathways for advancing reproducible, lifecycle-explicit Green AI measure-
ment.

5.1. Challenges and research gaps in Green AI
Green approaches to AI task allocation. Following the Green AI definition (section 4.1), Green
AI requires not only efficiency but adaptive task distribution across diverse infrastructures. Edge and
on-device deployments mitigate network-transfer emissions yet remain bounded by limited accelerator
memory and inconsistent power-monitoring capabilities [44, 91]. Advancing Green AI therefore entails
intelligent, multi-criteria workload orchestration - balancing environmental cost, latency, and resource
utilization - to realize verifiable lifecycle optimization across distributed systems [37].
Flexible resource allocations. Considering the Green AI lifecycle (section 4.2), future AI systems
must become more responsive to operational variability, dynamically adjusting their energy usage and
emissions output as demand changes. Many existing systems still lack this kind of adaptive resource
management. Future research should target algorithmic solutions that allow AI to modulate its com-
puting load (such as intelligently migrating processes to energy-efficient platforms or activating scaling
mechanisms based on task demand). Given the varied nature of AI applications, such strategies must
also accommodate different urgency levels and resource intensities. Real-time analytics may demand
immediate processing, whereas other tasks could be scheduled for off-peak execution on green hardware
[37]. This kind of adaptive approach must carefully balance ecological objectives with business impera-
tives. As noted in [38], practical Green AI must reconcile Green AI goals with real-world constraints on
performance and availability. Improving resource efficiency requires reducing redundant gradient com-
putations during training, minimizing checkpoint overhead, and leveraging mixed-precision arithmetic,
which collectively cut energy per epoch without degrading accuracy.
Heterogeneous (computing) networks. The diversification of platforms - from general-purpose
CPUs and GPUs to TPUs and low-power edge accelerators - offers concrete levers for energy reduction
by aligning workloads with architectural strengths. CPUs handle control and I/O-heavy preprocessing,
GPUs accelerate dense linear algebra, while TPUs and NPUs excel in high-throughput tensor operations.
Edge devices, in turn, reduce data-movement overhead when inference is performed locally. What re-
mains missing is a scheduling framework that exploits these complementarities at runtime, coordinating
placement decisions across architectures to minimize joules per task and reduce total embodied emis-
sions [6, 101]. Particularly in regard with unused standard computing systems, as these are available in
SME and everyday situations, such as laptops, desktops, smartphones and smart home devices, one can
assume a high potential for establishing innovative Green AI approaches.
Carbon- and energy-aware distribution. Although real-time energy monitoring via mainboard sen-
sors and performance monitoring counter (PMC)-based integration has been demonstrated, systematic
validation against rack-level meters is missing, leaving large error margins in heterogeneous workloads
unaddressed. In direct continuity with the methodological gaps identified for Green AI measurement
(section 4.4), the research frontier now shifts toward scalable, adaptive frameworks that allocate AI work-
loads not only by efficiency, but also by carbon intensity of the energy source. This includes directing
computations to data centers powered by renewable energy or offloading tasks to energy-efficient edge
devices [2]. A key underexplored strategy is carbon-aware scheduling - deferring or relocating tasks ac-
cording to temporal and geographic variations in grid emissions [2, 42, 70]. Such scheduling mechanisms
are well established in Green IT and HPC research, where job schedulers optimize workloads based on
energy availability and cost signals [6, 51]. Their systematic integration into AI workflows would bridge
the current gap between Green IT practices and Green AI-specific efforts. Beyond electricity, future
extensions must systematically account for water and material footprints, explicitly incorporate environ-
mental, social, and technical trade-offs, aligning workload allocation with broader Green AI constraints
[50, 100]. Beyond carbon, region-specific water stress indicators and embodied-impact amortization can
be added in allocation, prioritizing regions with lower cooling water intensity and longer hardware duty
cycles [50, 100].
Operationalization of carbon-aware scheduling. Effective carbon-aware scheduling requires (i) short-
term carbon-intensity forecasts at the selected regions, (ii) explicit deferral windows derived from Service
Level Agreements (SLAs), and (iii) migration policies that minimize data movement. A pragmatic base-
line aligns non-urgent training with low-intensity windows and pins latency-sensitive inference to regions

Reporting checklist for carbon-aware studies.
Each study should disclose: regions and data
sources for carbon intensity (including temporal resolution), explicit deferral windows and associated
SLA constraints (e.g., latency bounds, maximum postponement), migration policies and data-locality
assumptions, telemetry sources (device vs. whole-system) and calibration error, as well as the multi-
objective weights (carbon, water, embodied impacts). Standardized disclosure enables cross-study com-
parability and improves the transfer of Green IT practices to AI-specific settings [42]. Studies should
further disclose whether a single weighted objective or a Pareto analysis was used to trade off carbon,
water, and embodied impacts.
Bridging to Green IT and HPC scheduling. Mature techniques from Green IT/HPC (such as power
capping (e.g., Running Average Power Limit, RAPL), dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, DVFS-
based throttling, energy-aware job placement, and queue-level energy budgets) are directly transferable
to AI pipelines. Adapted to AI, these mechanisms inform cluster-level placement (CPU/GPU/TPU bins),
coordinate batch sizes and activation checkpointing under power caps, and co-schedule data locality
with accelerator availability to reduce both energy and egress overhead [6, 51]. Preemption and periodic
checkpointing enable safe deferral within carbon windows, bounding rollback overhead while minimiz-
ing energy, carbon, and resource impacts and preserving SLA commitments.
Closed-loop scheduling. Direct telemetry (PMCs, rack Power Distribution Units, PDUs) should cal-
ibrate software estimators at deployment time and feed back into the scheduler to update placement and
deferral policies. Reporting the pre/post calibration error - for instance, the deviation between CodeCar-
bon estimates and rack-level power meter readings - and the resulting change in workload allocation or
siting decisions aligns AI-specific practice with established Green IT validation routines, thus improving
transparency, reproducibility, and decision quality [42, 85].
Critical research gap. Existing studies remain fragmented: FLOP- or GPU-hour proxies are used
without validating against metered baselines, telemetry data lacks harmonized calibration protocols, and
carbon-intensity traces are seldom integrated into workload schedulers. What is missing is a bench-
marked framework that couples workload profiling, ground-truth metering, and carbon-aware dispatch
into reproducible allocation strategies across cloud, edge, and on-premises infrastructures.Building this
bridge is a central research challenge for advancing Green AI from conceptual discussions to operational
practice.
5.2. Operational pathways toward lifecycle-explicit Green AI
Despite obstacles outlined earlier, significant potential remains for advancing scalable implemen-
tation of Green AI. This review demonstrates how (i) instrumentation at rack and facility level (e.g.,
PDUs, PMCs, smart plugs) can be directly coupled with AI-specific workload managers using DVFS
and RAPL-based capping, (ii) multi-objective benchmarks can be established that jointly report carbon
intensity, cooling-water withdrawals, and embodied hardware emissions with declared provenance, and
(iii) closed-loop calibration protocols can align estimator libraries with ground-truth meters, enabling
auditable siting and scheduling across heterogeneous infrastructures.
Extend lifecycle footprint analyses to multi-dimensional indicators. Future studies should broaden
footprint analyses beyond training to encompass the entire AI pipeline, including data collection, pre-
processing, deployment, inference, and eventual model retirement [10, 19, 74]. In contrast to existing
reviews, our synthesis foregrounds the integration of embodied emissions from hardware production,
packaging, and disposal [9], together with full Scope 1–3 inventories that capture supply-chain logistics
and indirect energy use [24]. It should be stressed that multi-dimensional indicators - such as water with-
drawals in cooling-intensive regions, Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) in hyperscale data centers, and
material scarcity metrics for rare earths - must complement carbon-centric accounts to reveal overlooked

Developing comprehensive monitoring tools. User-friendly and integrable monitoring tools remain
scarce. Future research must go beyond GPU/CPU/DRAM counters to systematically capture network-
ing, storage, and cooling overheads that often dominate datacenter footprints [5]. What is missing today
are end-to-end toolchains that not only meter resource use but also link results to actionable levers -
for instance, flagging energy-intensive data loaders, suggesting batch-size or precision adjustments, or
recommending carbon-aware region scheduling across cloud, edge, and on-device systems. Such inte-
gration would transform monitoring from passive reporting into active decision support for sustainable
AI design and deployment.
Bridging to Green IT and HPC scheduling. Earlier Green AI reviews have largely concentrated
on footprint measurement and reporting, whereas systematic transfer of established HPC scheduling
methods into AI workflows has received little attention. Mechanisms such as power capping (RAPL),
dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)-based throttling, energy-aware job placement, queue-
level energy budgets, preemption, and checkpointing are well established in HPC [6, 51]. Adapting them
to AI would enable cluster-level placement (CPU/GPU/TPU bins), coordinated batch sizing under power
caps, and co-scheduling of data locality with accelerator availability to reduce both energy and egress
overhead. These concrete pathways provide operational levers for reducing AI’s carbon footprint beyond
the descriptive level emphasized in earlier surveys.
Toward multi-objective resource allocation.
Most current studies (including reviews) remain
carbon-centric. Future research should explicitly address multi-objective trade-offs, e.g., integrating
carbon intensity, water stress indicators, and embodied hardware impacts into workload scheduling deci-
sions. This enables holistic allocation frameworks that align AI with broader Green AI goals rather than
single-metric optimization.
Closed-loop scheduling and telemetry integration. Another neglected area is the use of direct
telemetry. Future AI infrastructures should integrate real-time telemetry from PMCs, rack-level PDUs,
and energy-aware mainboards directly into scheduling mechanisms. This continuous feedback enables
adaptive workload placement, throttling, and carbon-aware task deferral [42, 85]. Reporting calibration
errors alongside corrective actions - such as dynamic power capping - would ensure transparency, au-
ditability, and reproducibility in Green-AI governance. This tight integration of measurement and control
- long established in HPC power management - is still absent in AI pipelines, leaving a major gap for
research and practice.
Critical research gap. Taken together, the literature lacks integrative frameworks that couple work-
load profiling, hardware-level telemetry (PMCs, PDUs), and region-specific carbon-intensity forecasts
into actionable allocation and scheduling policies. Whereas Green IT and HPC already apply energy-
aware job scheduling and DVFS-based throttling, equivalent control mechanisms remain largely absent
from AI training and inference workflows. This omission leaves scheduling - an established efficiency
lever in conventional computing - underexploited within Green AI, despite its potential to substantially
reduce operational energy intensity and embodied-carbon impact. Building this bridge constitutes a
central and novel pathway for future research, moving Green AI beyond conceptual discussions toward
operational practice.
6. Discussion
Modern AI application systems consolidate heterogeneous workloads - spanning training, inference,
and data management - under stringent service-level and latency constraints. This integration drives peak
power draw, amplifying Scope 2 emissions and accelerating hardware obsolescence, thereby embedding
environmental costs directly into infrastructural design and operation [71]. This review addresses these
challenges by systematically synthesizing 103 articles and introducing a lifecycle-oriented taxonomy that
extends beyond prior reviews [45, 91, 95]. Whereas earlier surveys have mapped high-level implications
[95], aligned AI with climate policy goals [45], or focused on Green Software Engineering tools and
practices [91], the novelty of this article lies in advancing an operational perspective on Green AI.

Specifically, the contribution consists of: (i) integrating LCA logic with AI-specific phases, including

HPC, (iii) highlighting neglected multi-objective trade-offs beyond carbon (e.g., water, material scarcity),

continuously corrected with metered data to document reproducibility and ensure audit-ready reporting.
Together, these mechanisms link lifecycle concepts directly to verifiable implementation practices.
6.1. Theoretical and practical implications
From a theoretical perspective, the review underscores that Green AI cannot be reduced to efficiency
gains during training alone. Prior perspectives (e.g., [45, 95]) have emphasized policy alignment, broad
Green AI challenges, or mitigation potential. In contrast, this article contributes a structured lifecycle
model that explicitly maps all phases of AI systems to LCA categories. This reveals hidden environ-
mental burdens such as Scope 3 emissions, embodied carbon, water use, and resource depletion that are
overlooked in carbon-centric accounts.
Practically, the findings advance the state of the art by identifying concrete pathways for opera-
tionalizing Green AI. Unlike Verdecchia et al. [91], who focus on tools for energy transparency, our
synthesis highlights the transfer of mature HPC techniques - such as dynamic voltage and frequency
scaling (DVFS)-based throttling, Running Average Power Limit, RAPL power capping, queue-level en-
ergy budgets, and preemptive checkpointing - into AI pipelines. Adapted to AI, these methods inform
workload placement across CPUs/GPUs/TPUs, enable batch-size coordination under power caps, and
integrate locality-aware scheduling to minimize both energy and data-movement overhead. This opera-
tional bridging between Green IT/HPC and Green AI has not yet been systematically articulated in prior
reviews.
Most current approaches remain carbon-centric, neglecting other critical impact vectors. Multi-
objective allocation extends workload scheduling by integrating water-use coefficients from facility
telemetry and embodied-carbon amortization of hardware refresh cycles alongside grid-intensity signals.
Closed-loop scheduling operationalizes this integration: direct performance monitoring counter (PMC)
streams and rack-level Power Distribution Unit (PDU) data continuously recalibrate CodeCarbon-like
estimators, with deviations fed back into Kubernetes or Slurm plugins to dynamically shift jobs. This
allows placement to adapt to real-time regional grid mix and cooling-water stress, ensuring scheduling
reflects the full environmental envelope rather than only compute throughput. Explicitly documenting
calibration deltas - for example, a 25% deviation between CodeCarbon estimates and rack-level power
meters - and showing how this alters task placement or deferral thresholds allows reproducibility tests
and systematic cross-study comparisons.
Finally, the analysis highlights how Green AIs constrained by material and infrastructural lock-ins.
Semiconductor supply chains rely on energy-intensive fabrication in a few regions, while short hardware
refresh cycles amplify embodied emissions and waste. Studies show that without governance interven-
tions, these structural patterns outweigh efficiency gains at the software level, binding AI progress to
unsustainable material and energy flows [71]. By explicitly embedding end-of-life, resource recovery,
and circularity into the Green AI lifecycle, the proposed framework makes these lock-in trajectories
visible and provides a basis for evaluating alternative policy interventions (e.g., right-to-repair rules,
renewable procurement mandates, or disclosure requirements for embodied carbon).
6.2. Limitations
Despite its comprehensive scope, this review has limitations. First, the database-driven search, while
systematic, may have missed relevant contributions outside computer science venues, particularly in en-
gineering, sustainability science, and political economy. Second, the integration of LCA with AI lifecy-
cle phases remains conceptual and requires empirical validation through real-world case studies. Third,
although the taxonomy spans 103 articles, continuous revision is necessary as standards, tools, and poli-
cies expand. Beyond technical metrics, the next research wave must examine how disclosure regulations,
renewable-energy siting, and extended producer responsibility affect global equity. Particular attention is

7. Conclusion
This article consolidates the foundations of Green AI and advances the field from concept to prac-
tice. A lifecycle-oriented perspective is combined with a class-based hardware selection framework
and a differentiated measurement architecture that integrates indirect software estimators with direct,
hardware-level telemetry. The synthesis emphasizes operational levers (carbon-aware scheduling, trans-
fer of mature Green IT/high-performance computing (HPC) techniques, and closed-loop calibration) that
enable auditable Green AI improvements beyond training-only efficiency gains.
Practice and policy implications. Future AI studies should report environmental metrics alongside
standard performance results and adopt standardized disclosure of assumptions (region-specific carbon
intensity and temporal granularity, Power Usage Effectiveness, PUE; deferral windows/SLA constraints,
migration and data-locality policies, telemetry sources and calibration error, and weighting across car-
bon, water, and embodied impacts). Studie of negative results, dataset/code release for Green AI exper-
iments, and integration of Green AI criteria into funding evaluations can materially reduce redundant
computation and accelerate methodological convergence [45, 95].
Contributions. This article provides a structured and operational contribution to Green AI by: (i) ar-
ticulating a precise conceptual basis and operational definition of Green AI, (ii) proposing a five-phase
lifecycle model with 33 concrete realization, adaptation, and adjustment tasks mapped to LCA cate-
gories, (iii) introducing a class-level hardware selection framework that links contextual determinants
(regional grid carbon intensity, datacenter PUE/cooling efficiency, scheduling and deferral windows) to
reproducible audit trails, (iv) systematizing measurement methods across indirect estimators and direct
approaches, including performance monitoring counters (PMCs), RAPL telemetry, and rack-level Power
Distribution Units (PDUs), while exposing limitations of water-use and embodied-emission proxies, and
(v) deriving actionable pathways that integrate carbon-aware scheduling, dynamic voltage and frequency
scaling, DVFS/power-capping, and HPC-style resource orchestration into AI pipelines through closed-
loop telemetry and PCC/PET decision gates.

                          Research Article 
 
EMBODIED CARBON AS A FIRST-CLASS CONSTRAINT IN 
CLOUD-NATIVE INFRASTRUCTURE ENGINEERING: A 
LIFECYCLE-AWARE FRAMEWORK FOR SUSTAINABLE 
CLOUD OPERATIONS 
 
 Neha Sharma 
 
 Computer Science Researcher, INDIA, Email: Nehasharma1986@gmail.com 
 
Citation: Neha Sharma ,  Embodied Carbon as A First-Class Constraint in Cloud-Native Infrastructure Engineering: A Lifecycle-Aware 
Framework For Sustainable Cloud Operations. Educational Administration: Theory and Practice, 32(1s). 380-389 
 Doi: xyz 10.67145/kuey.v32i1.12266 
 
ARTICLE INFO 
ABSTRACT 
 
The discourse on cloud sustainability has been dominated by operational 
carbon—the emissions associated with electricity consumption during workload 
execution. This focus, while important, obscures a critical and growing dimension 
of cloud environmental impact: embodied carbon, the emissions released during 
the manufacturing, transportation, and disposal of the physical infrastructure 
that underpins cloud services. As renewable energy adoption accelerates and data 
center power usage effectiveness (PUE) approaches theoretical limits, embodied 
carbon is emerging as the dominant and most intractable component of cloud 
carbon footprints. This paper presents a lifecycle-aware framework for cloud-
native infrastructure engineering that treats embodied carbon as a first-class 
constraint alongside performance, cost, and reliability. The proposed framework 
integrates: (1) a carbon depreciation model that incentivizes extended hardware 
lifetimes by allocating embodied carbon costs to newly provisioned servers; (2) a 
carbon-aware infrastructure-as-code (IaC) analysis engine that estimates 
embodied carbon impacts during the design phase; (3) a heterogeneous compute 
scheduling layer that matches workload characteristics to hardware generations 
with different embodied carbon profiles; and (4) a carbon-aware CI/CD 
integration that incorporates embodied carbon thresholds into deployment 
decisions. Drawing on empirical evidence from hyperscale deployments and 
lifecycle assessment studies, the framework demonstrates that extending server 
lifetimes from three to five years can reduce net cloud emissions by 28–57%, 
while GreenSKU-style hardware reuse strategies can achieve 8% net emissions 
reductions in production environments. The paper establishes that embodied 
carbon must be treated not as an externality but as a fundamental architectural 
constraint, and that doing so requires rethinking foundational assumptions about 
hardware refresh cycles, performance homogeneity, and the very meaning of 
“efficiency” in cloud operations.

1. INTRODUCTION 
— A. The Invisible Carbon of Cloud Infrastructure 
The environmental impact of cloud computing has become a central concern for technology organizations, 
driven by regulatory pressure, corporate sustainability commitments, and growing awareness of the energy 
intensity of digital infrastructure. Data centers accounted for approximately 1.5% of global electricity demand 
in 2020—about 300 TWh—and this figure is projected to rise substantially as artificial intelligence workloads 
and global digital transformation accelerate. The dominant narrative around cloud sustainability has focused

 Neha Sharma/ Kuey, 32(1), 2026
 
 
on operational carbon: the emissions associated with generating the electricity that powers servers, cooling 
systems, and networking equipment. 
However, this focus on operational carbon tells only part of the story. Every server, storage array, and 
networking switch that enters a data center carries with it a substantial embodied carbon footprint—the 
emissions released during the extraction of raw materials, manufacturing of components, assembly of systems, 
transportation to the data center, and eventual disposal or recycling. This embodied carbon is released long 
before the equipment is ever plugged in, yet it is rarely accounted for in cloud sustainability discussions. 
The significance of embodied carbon has grown as operational efficiency has improved. Recent assessments 
highlight that embodied impacts from IT hardware can rival operational impacts, depending on refresh cycles 
and local electricity mixes. As data centers increasingly source renewable energy and achieve near-optimal 
power usage effectiveness (PUE), the relative contribution of embodied carbon to total lifecycle emissions has 
increased dramatically. In some cases, embodied carbon now exceeds operational carbon over the full lifecycle 
of hardware, particularly for equipment deployed in regions with low-carbon electricity grids. 
This shift has profound implications for cloud-native infrastructure engineering. Traditional optimization 
objectives—performance, cost, and reliability—must now be augmented with a fourth dimension: embodied 
carbon. Yet existing tools, practices, and mental models in the cloud-native ecosystem are almost entirely 
oriented toward operational considerations. Infrastructure-as-code (IaC) templates specify instance types and 
scaling policies but do not consider the embodied carbon implications of hardware selection. Auto-scaling 
policies optimize for latency and cost but not for hardware lifetime utilization. CI/CD pipelines validate 
performance and security but not carbon footprint. 
 
— B. The Carbon Depreciation Concept 
The core insight driving this paper is that embodied carbon is analogous to a capital expenditure that must be 
amortized over the useful life of the asset. Just as financial accounting allocates the cost of a server over its 
expected lifetime, carbon accounting should allocate embodied carbon emissions over the operational life of 
the hardware. This concept—which we term “carbon depreciation”—has profound implications for how 
infrastructure decisions should be made [24]. 
Carbon depreciation models assign a larger portion of embodied carbon to newly provisioned servers, thereby 
incentivizing longer hardware lifetimes and penalizing premature replacement. Experimental results have 
shown that such models can achieve carbon reductions of 28–57%, depending on server lifetime assumptions 
[24]. The intuition is straightforward: if a server's embodied carbon is allocated over a five-year lifetime rather 
than a three-year lifetime, each year of operation carries a lower embodied carbon burden. This creates a carbon 
incentive to extend hardware lifecycles, which in turn requires infrastructure engineering practices that can 
effectively utilize older hardware alongside newer generations. 
This concept challenges several foundational assumptions in cloud-native engineering. The assumption of 
hardware homogeneity—that all compute resources in a cluster are equivalent—must be replaced with a model 
of hardware heterogeneity where different generations of equipment have different performance 
characteristics, different embodied carbon profiles, and different optimal workloads. The assumption of 
performance-first scheduling—that workloads should always be placed on the fastest available hardware—must 
be replaced with a multi-objective optimization that considers performance, operational carbon, and embodied 
carbon simultaneously. 
 
— C. Research Objectives and Contributions 
This paper presents a lifecycle-aware framework for cloud-native infrastructure engineering that treats 
embodied carbon as a first-class constraint. The framework addresses the following research questions: 
1.How can embodied carbon be modeled and accounted for in cloud-native infrastructure decisions? 
2.What architectural patterns enable effective utilization of heterogeneous hardware generations with different 
embodied carbon profiles? 
3.How can CI/CD pipelines and infrastructure-as-code practices incorporate embodied carbon constraints 
without compromising delivery velocity? 
4.What organizational and cultural changes are required to make embodied carbon a first-class concern in 
cloud operations? 
The primary contributions of this work are: 
●A carbon depreciation model that provides a principled framework for allocating embodied carbon across 
hardware lifetimes; 
●A lifecycle-aware IaC analysis engine that estimates embodied carbon impacts during infrastructure design; 
●A heterogeneous compute scheduling architecture that matches workload characteristics to hardware 
generations with different embodied carbon profiles; 
●A carbon-aware CI/CD integration that incorporates embodied carbon thresholds into deployment 
workflows; 
●Empirical validation demonstrating the carbon reduction potential of lifecycle-aware infrastructure 
engineering.

2.RELATED WORK 
— A. Cloud Carbon Footprinting and Lifecycle Assessment 
The measurement of cloud carbon footprints has evolved significantly in recent years. Early approaches focused 
almost exclusively on operational emissions, estimating electricity consumption based on resource utilization 
metrics and multiplying by regional grid carbon intensity. Tools such as Cloud Carbon Footprint, Green Pixie, 
and Boavizta provide methodologies for estimating operational emissions based on cloud usage data [13]. 
More recent work has expanded to include embodied emissions through comprehensive lifecycle assessment 
(LCA). Google Cloud's Carbon Footprinting team has developed an LCA approach to evaluate embodied carbon 
emissions associated with the supply chain of data center hardware, including AI/ML accelerators, compute 
machines, storage platforms, and networking equipment. AWS updated its Customer Carbon Footprint Tool to 
include Scope 3 emissions for fuel and energy-related activities, buildings and equipment, and IT hardware 
[26]. This recognition that embodied emissions represent a substantial component of cloud carbon footprints 
marks a significant shift in the field. 
Comprehensive LCA studies of data center IT equipment remain relatively scarce. A recent cradle-to-grave LCA 
by Microsoft and WSP demonstrated the power of LCA as a means to inform engineering design and reduce 
environmental impact. The study highlighted that embodied impacts from IT hardware can rival operational 
impacts depending on refresh cycles and local electricity mixes. 
 
— B. Carbon Depreciation and Hardware Lifetime Extension 
The concept of carbon depreciation—allocating embodied carbon across hardware lifetimes—has emerged as a 
promising approach to incentivize sustainable hardware management. Research has proposed carbon 
depreciation models that assign a larger portion of embodied carbon to newly provisioned servers, thereby 
encouraging longer hardware lifetimes [24]. The rationale is that if the carbon cost of manufacturing is 
“depreciated” over a longer period, the per-unit-time carbon cost decreases, making older hardware more 
attractive from a carbon perspective. 
Experimental results have demonstrated significant carbon reduction potential from this approach. Carbon 
depreciation models achieve carbon reductions of 28–57%, depending on server lifetime assumptions [24]. The 
work also reveals that older hardware can preserve performance in certain conditions, particularly at low load. 
This finding is crucial because it challenges the assumption that older hardware is inherently inferior and 
should be replaced as quickly as possible. 
The extension of hardware lifetimes has implications beyond carbon: it also reduces electronic waste, which is 
notoriously difficult to recycle effectively. Server hardware is typically replaced every three to five years, 
generating mountains of complex electronic waste. Extending this lifecycle reduces both the frequency of 
replacement and the volume of waste generated. 
 
— C. Carbon-Aware Scheduling and Workload Placement 
Carbon-aware scheduling—the practice of shifting workloads in space and time to take advantage of lower-
carbon electricity—has received significant attention. The principle is to shift workloads in space and/or time 
to take advantage of lower-carbon electricity, whenever and wherever it is available. Research has explored 
both temporal shifting (deferring workloads to times when grid carbon intensity is lower) and spatial shifting 
(moving workloads to regions with lower carbon intensity). 
Recent work has extended carbon-aware scheduling to consider embodied carbon alongside operational 
carbon. A carbon-aware workload scheduler in multi-cluster Kubernetes environments, called Caspian, could 
reduce carbon emissions by approximately 33% while maintaining 98% of workloads completing at an average 
fraction of 0.6 of their deadline [15]. A distributionally robust optimization framework for carbon-aware 
scheduling has been developed that incorporates forecasting, battery storage, and adaptive ambiguity 
refinement [2]. 
Carbon-aware federated orchestration in edge-cloud systems has demonstrated a 10.2% reduction in carbon 
emissions, 15.7% reduction in costs, and 60% fewer SLA violations compared to baseline approaches [4]. The 
SC4RC 2026 workshop on sustainable computing for research and cloud environments proposed an 
architecture for minimizing the carbon footprint of workloads in hybrid cloud environments, with reductions 
in emissions of up to 27% observed against a carbon-agnostic baseline [5]. 
 
 
 
— D. GreenOps and Sustainable DevOps

GreenOps—the operational discipline that brings environmental accountability to technology management—
has emerged as a framework for integrating sustainability into cloud operations [27]. GreenOps asks “how 
much carbon does this produce?” alongside FinOps's question of “how much does this cost?” Workloads are 
optimized not only for performance and cost, but also for carbon intensity, introducing new optimization levers 
such as carbon-aware scheduling, regional workload placement, and automated shutdown of non-production 
environments. 
The integration of GreenOps with FinOps has gained significant traction. Research indicates that organizations 
integrating GreenOps with existing FinOps and DevOps practices can achieve 15-25% cost savings while 
reducing carbon footprint [18]. The CNCF has hosted sessions on GreenOps and FinOps as complementary 
approaches toward business and environmental goals. 
Carbon-aware DevOps extends GreenOps principles into the CI/CD pipeline. Research has outlined a 
framework for integrating carbon-intensity data directly into the DevOps lifecycle by integrating tools like the 
WattTime API or the Carbon Intensity API directly into CI/CD pipelines, transforming the CI/CD pipeline from 
a static script into a carbon-aware scheduler [23], [30]. Carbon-aware test scheduling in agentic CI/CD 
pipelines has demonstrated grid-intensity deferral that reduces carbon intensity by 52.4% for full-tier agents 
[29]. 
 
— E. Green Software Engineering Principles 
The Green Software Foundation has outlined principles of sustainable software that should guide both 
developers and vendors: energy efficiency, hardware efficiency, and carbon awareness. These principles have 
been operationalized in frameworks such as Microsoft's sustainable software engineering principles for Azure 
Kubernetes Services, which emphasize carbon efficiency, energy efficiency, and hardware efficiency. 
A Green Software Engineering Playbook recommends prioritizing function-as-a-service, then platform-as-a-
service that can scale-to-zero, then virtual machines—a hierarchy that reflects the embodied carbon 
implications of different deployment models [19]. The reasoning is that higher-level abstractions enable better 
hardware utilization and therefore lower embodied carbon per unit of work. 
Practical implementations of green software principles have demonstrated significant benefits. Serverless 
architectures, by employing event-driven, auto-scalable, and pay-per-use computing models, significantly 
reduce idle resource consumption and improve energy efficiency. A serverless workflow batch orchestration 
system called EnergyLess improved cost efficiency by 75%, completion time by 6%, energy consumption by 
15%, and CO2 emissions by 20% for a batch size of 300. 
 
— F. Research Gap 
Despite advances in cloud carbon footprinting, carbon depreciation, carbon-aware scheduling, and GreenOps, 
significant gaps remain: 
1.Embodied Carbon Neglect: most carbon-aware computing research focuses on operational carbon, with 
limited attention to embodied carbon and its implications for infrastructure design. 
2.Lifecycle Integration Gap: carbon depreciation models have been proposed in isolation but not integrated 
into the full cloud-native infrastructure engineering lifecycle, from IaC design through CI/CD deployment to 
runtime management. 
3.Heterogeneous Hardware Gap: the assumption of hardware homogeneity in Kubernetes and cloud-native 
platforms limits the ability to exploit the carbon benefits of heterogeneous hardware generations. 
4.Organizational Gap: limited understanding of the organizational and cultural changes required to make 
embodied carbon a first-class concern in cloud operations. 
This paper addresses these gaps by presenting a lifecycle-aware framework that integrates embodied carbon 
considerations throughout the cloud-native infrastructure engineering process, extending the automated, 
policy-driven response principles established in prior patent-based work on cloud security anomaly detection 
to the domain of sustainable infrastructure operations [1]. 
 
3.FRAMEWORK ARCHITECTURE 
— A. System Overview 
The proposed Lifecycle-Aware Cloud Infrastructure Framework comprises four integrated components: 
1.Carbon Depreciation Engine: models and allocates embodied carbon across hardware lifetimes; 
2.Lifecycle-Aware IaC Analyzer: estimates embodied carbon impacts during infrastructure design; 
3.Heterogeneous Compute Scheduler: matches workload characteristics to hardware generations with different 
embodied carbon profiles; 
4.Carbon-Aware CI/CD Integration: incorporates embodied carbon thresholds into deployment workflows. 
The framework operates across the entire infrastructure lifecycle, from initial design through ongoing 
operations, ensuring that embodied carbon is considered at every decision point. Fig. 1 depicts the four 
components as a continuous cycle sharing a common embodied-carbon budget.

— B. Carbon Depreciation Engine 
The Carbon Depreciation Engine implements the core insight that embodied carbon should be allocated across 
hardware lifetimes, similar to financial depreciation of capital assets. The engine supports multiple 
depreciation models, configurable based on organizational preferences and hardware characteristics: 
1.Straight-Line Depreciation: embodied carbon is allocated evenly across the expected lifetime of the hardware. 
For a server with 1,000 kg CO2e embodied carbon and a 5-year lifetime, the annual carbon depreciation is 200 
kg CO2e per year. 
2.Accelerated Depreciation: a larger portion of embodied carbon is allocated to early years, reflecting the higher 
productivity of newer hardware. This model incentivizes replacement but may not align with carbon reduction 
goals. 
3.Carbon-Optimized Depreciation: a larger portion of embodied carbon is allocated to later years, incentivizing 
extended hardware lifetimes. This model aligns with circular economy principles and has demonstrated carbon 
reductions of 28–57% [24]. 
The engine tracks hardware lifetime through integration with infrastructure inventory systems, recording 
manufacturing date, deployment date, expected lifetime (typically 3–5 years), actual lifetime, and utilization 
history affecting wear and tear. For each hardware unit, the engine calculates the current embodied carbon 
allocation: 
Annual_Embodied_Carbon = 
  Total_Embodied_Carbon / Expected_Lifetime_Years 
For workloads running on the hardware, the per-unit-time embodied carbon cost is: 
Embodied_Carbon_Per_Hour = 
  Annual_Embodied_Carbon / (365 x 24) 
This per-hour embodied carbon cost is combined with operational carbon costs (based on energy consumption 
and grid carbon intensity) to provide a complete carbon accounting for each workload. The Carbon 
Depreciation Engine exposes APIs that enable scheduling systems to consider embodied carbon alongside 
operational carbon and performance metrics, an integration essential for making carbon-aware decisions at 
the workload placement level. 
 
— C. Lifecycle-Aware IaC Analyzer 
The Lifecycle-Aware IaC Analyzer estimates embodied carbon impacts during infrastructure design, enabling 
architects and engineers to make carbon-informed decisions before resources are provisioned. The analyzer 
parses Infrastructure-as-Code definitions (Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests) to extract 
resource specifications, building on approaches demonstrated in frameworks like LEAF, which interprets IaC 
definitions to simulate expected workload behavior and integrate region-specific carbon intensity data [12]. 
For each resource specified in IaC, the analyzer estimates embodied carbon based on instance type (different 
instance types have different embodied carbon profiles based on hardware components), region 
(manufacturing and transportation emissions vary by region), expected lifetime (organizational policies for 
hardware refresh cycles), and reuse potential (whether the resource can be satisfied by existing hardware or 
requires new provisioning).

The analyzer generates reports showing total embodied carbon (estimated embodied carbon for the proposed 
infrastructure), per-workload carbon (embodied carbon allocated to each workload), comparison to 
alternatives (embodied carbon of alternative instance types or deployment models), and lifetime carbon profile 
(how embodied carbon allocation changes over time). Organizations can configure carbon budgets for 
infrastructure changes, similar to cost budgets, and the analyzer enforces these budgets by flagging IaC changes 
that would exceed configured thresholds. 
 
— D. Heterogeneous Compute Scheduler 
The Heterogeneous Compute Scheduler matches workload characteristics to hardware generations with 
different embodied carbon profiles, enabling effective utilization of older hardware alongside newer 
generations. The scheduler maintains profiles for each hardware generation in the cluster, covering 
performance characteristics (CPU, memory, storage, and network performance), operational efficiency (energy 
consumption per unit of work), embodied carbon profile (total embodied carbon and remaining lifetime 
allocation), and reliability metrics (historical failure rates and performance variability). 
Workloads are classified based on performance sensitivity (whether the workload requires high performance 
or can tolerate older hardware), latency requirements, resource intensity, and business priority. The scheduler 
uses a multi-objective optimization function that considers: 
Score = w1*Performance + w2*Cost 
      - w3*Operational_Carbon 
      - w4*Embodied_Carbon 
The weights are configurable by platform teams to reflect organizational priorities. Carbon-optimized 
scheduling prioritizes placing workloads on hardware with lower embodied carbon allocation—typically older 
hardware with largely depreciated embodied carbon. The scheduler also supports carbon-aware scaling 
decisions: rather than scaling out to new hardware with high embodied carbon, the scheduler may choose to 
scale up on existing hardware with depreciated embodied carbon. Research has demonstrated that carbon-
aware autoscaling systems integrating spatio-temporal graph convolutional networks can jointly model 
workload dynamics and inter-service dependencies while integrating real-time regional carbon intensity [16]. 
Microsoft is developing a carbon-aware scaler for the KEDA open-source project that automatically scales 
workloads based on the carbon intensity of the infrastructure those workloads are running on [17]. 
 
— E. Carbon-Aware CI/CD Integration 
The Carbon-Aware CI/CD Integration incorporates embodied carbon thresholds into deployment workflows, 
ensuring that carbon considerations are embedded in the software delivery lifecycle. The framework introduces 
“carbon gates” into CI/CD pipelines: these gates evaluate the embodied carbon impact of proposed 
infrastructure changes and block deployments that would exceed configured thresholds, operating alongside 
traditional security and quality gates so that carbon considerations are given equal weight. 
For GitOps-based workflows, the framework integrates with pull request processes, presenting carbon impact 
analysis as part of the pull request review. Research on Carbon-Aware GitOps has demonstrated that a 
framework calculating projected carbon intensity of Kubernetes workloads during pull request review and 
blocking or scheduling merges based on configurable carbon thresholds reduces carbon emissions by 23–31% 
compared to baseline GitOps workflows, with zero increase in deployment latency and 92% developer 
acceptance rate [22]. 
The framework generates carbon reports for each deployment, showing deployment carbon impact (embodied 
and operational carbon associated with the deployment), cumulative carbon (total carbon footprint of the 
application over time), and optimization opportunities (recommendations for reducing carbon impact). 
Integration with carbon intensity APIs such as WattTime and the Carbon Intensity API enables carbon-aware 
scheduling of CI/CD jobs, deferring build and test jobs to times when grid carbon intensity is lower without 
affecting development velocity. 
 
4.IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS 
— A. Technology Stack 
The framework leverages existing cloud-native technologies while extending them with embodied carbon 
capabilities. Infrastructure-as-code support spans Terraform (declarative infrastructure provisioning), Pulumi 
(programmatic infrastructure definition), and Crossplane (Kubernetes-native infrastructure management). 
Carbon intensity data is sourced from the Carbon Aware SDK (Green Software Foundation SDK for carbon 
intensity data), the WattTime API (real-time and forecast carbon intensity data), and the Electricity Maps API 
(regional carbon intensity data). Scheduling and orchestration rely on Kubernetes, KEDA for carbon-aware 
scaling, and a custom scheduler extended with carbon-awareness. Carbon accounting draws on Cloud Carbon 
Footprint (open-source carbon estimation) and BoaviztAPI (bottom-up environmental impact assessment for 
cloud services) [13].

A phased implementation approach reduces risk and enables learning. Phase 1, Measurement, implements 
carbon accounting for operational carbon, establishes a baseline carbon footprint, and deploys carbon

integrates embodied carbon into accounting, and establishes carbon budgets and thresholds. Phase 3, Carbon-
Aware Scheduling, deploys the heterogeneous compute scheduler, implements carbon-aware scaling policies, 
and enables carbon-optimized workload placement. Phase 4, CI/CD Integration, implements carbon gates in 
CI/CD pipelines, integrates carbon reporting into developer workflows, and enables carbon-aware CI/CD 
scheduling. Phase 5, Continuous Optimization, establishes continuous carbon improvement processes, 
implements machine learning for carbon forecasting, and extends to multi-cloud and edge environments. 
 
5. EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE AND CASE STUDY FINDINGS 
— A. Carbon Depreciation Impact Analysis 
Empirical research on carbon depreciation models provides compelling evidence for the approach. Carbon 
depreciation assigns a larger portion of embodied carbon to newly provisioned servers, thereby incentivizing 
the reduction of new server acquisitions for jobs with stringent quality-of-service requirements and promoting 
the extended use of existing servers with largely recovered embodied carbon. 
Experimental results demonstrate carbon reductions of 28–57%, depending on server lifetime assumptions 
[24]. The variation in reduction potential reflects the sensitivity of embodied carbon to lifetime assumptions: 
extending lifetime from three to five years reduces annual embodied carbon allocation by 40%, but the actual 
emissions reduction depends on the operational efficiency of older hardware and the carbon intensity of the 
electricity used. 
Research on aging-aware CPU core management for embodied carbon amortization has further demonstrated 
the potential of extending hardware lifetimes [14]. Observations reveal that older hardware can preserve 
performance in certain conditions, particularly at low load. This finding is crucial because it challenges the 
assumption that older hardware is inherently inferior and must be replaced. 
 
— B. GreenSKU Case Study 
The GreenSKU initiative, a collaboration between Carnegie Mellon University and Microsoft, provides a 
practical demonstration of embodied carbon reduction through hardware reuse and redesign [11]. The research 
team built three GreenSKU prototypes integrating energy-efficient CPUs, reusing old dynamic RAM via 
compute express link (CXL), and reusing old solid-state drives. 
Implementing GreenSKU within Microsoft Azure's production constraints demonstrated that GreenSKUs 
reduce net cloud emissions by 8%. While 8% may appear modest, the global significance is substantial given 
the scale of Microsoft's cloud operations. The research demonstrates that embodied carbon reduction is 
achievable within production constraints, not just in laboratory settings. The GreenSKU approach embodies 
several principles central to the lifecycle-aware framework: hardware reuse, extended lifetimes, and 
component-level optimization. 
 
— C. Carbon-Aware Kubernetes Scheduling Results 
Research on carbon-aware Kubernetes scheduling provides evidence for the effectiveness of lifecycle-aware 
approaches. Caspian, a carbon-aware workload scheduler in multi-cluster Kubernetes environments, could 
reduce carbon emissions by approximately 33%, with about 98% of workloads completing at an average 
fraction of 0.6 of their deadline [15]. The carbon-aware scheduling and distributionally robust optimization 
framework for cloud systems demonstrated significant carbon reduction potential, incorporating forecasting, 
battery storage, and adaptive ambiguity refinement to optimize carbon-aware scheduling across geo-
distributed cloud data centers [2].

— D. Carbon-Aware CI/CD Results 
Carbon-aware CI/CD integration has demonstrated significant potential. Carbon-aware test scheduling in

92% developer acceptance rate [22]. These results demonstrate that carbon-aware CI/CD is both technically

considerations can be integrated into developer workflows without causing friction or resistance. 
 
— E. Serverless and Architectural Efficiency 
The architectural choices made in cloud-native applications have significant implications for embodied carbon 
efficiency. Serverless architectures, by employing event-driven, auto-scalable, and pay-per-use computing 
models, significantly reduce idle resource consumption and improve energy efficiency. Research on reducing 
carbon footprint in AI workloads using serverless cloud architectures demonstrates that serverless platforms 
can significantly reduce energy waste and carbon emissions by eliminating idle resource consumption. A 
serverless workflow batch orchestration system called EnergyLess improved cost efficiency by 75%, completion 
time by 6%, energy consumption by 15%, and CO2 emissions by 20% for a batch size of 300. 
The Green Software Engineering Playbook recommends prioritizing function-as-a-service, then platform-as-
a-service that can scale-to-zero, then virtual machines [19]. This hierarchy reflects the embodied carbon 
implications of different deployment models: higher-level abstractions enable better hardware utilization and 
therefore lower embodied carbon per unit of work. 
 
— F. Organizational and Cultural Findings 
The transition to lifecycle-aware infrastructure engineering requires organizational and cultural changes that 
extend beyond technical implementation. Research indicates that organizations integrating GreenOps with 
existing FinOps and DevOps practices can achieve 15-25% cost savings while reducing carbon footprint [18]. 
The alignment of carbon and cost reduction creates a compelling business case for sustainability initiatives. 
The TBM Council's GreenOps framework focuses on five core areas: energy optimization and cloud efficiency, 
right-sizing workloads, improving utilization, optimizing cloud architectures to reduce power consumption and 
carbon footprint, and optimizing energy use, infrastructure, and cloud operations [27]. This framework 
provides a structured approach to organizational transformation. Developer acceptance of carbon-aware 
practices is crucial for success: the 92% developer acceptance rate for Carbon-Aware GitOps demonstrates that 
developers are receptive to carbon considerations when they are integrated smoothly into existing workflows 
without adding friction [22]. 
 
6. DISCUSSION 
— A. Implications for Cloud-Native Infrastructure Engineering 
The lifecycle-aware framework presented in this paper has profound implications for how cloud-native 
infrastructure is designed, provisioned, and operated. From operational carbon to lifecycle carbon: the most 
fundamental implication is the shift from a focus on operational carbon to a lifecycle perspective that includes 
embodied carbon. A workload that runs on renewable energy may have low operational carbon but high 
embodied carbon if it requires frequent hardware replacement; true sustainability requires optimizing across 
the entire lifecycle. 
From homogeneous to heterogeneous infrastructure: the framework challenges the assumption of hardware 
homogeneity that underpins much of cloud-native infrastructure. Kubernetes and similar platforms assume 
that all nodes in a cluster are equivalent, but this assumption is incompatible with lifecycle-aware scheduling. 
From performance-first to multi-objective optimization: the lifecycle-aware framework adds embodied carbon 
as a fourth dimension, requiring multi-objective optimization that balances performance, cost, reliability, and 
carbon—with implications for every infrastructure decision, from instance type selection to autoscaling policies 
to CI/CD pipeline design. 
From static to dynamic carbon accounting: embodied carbon accounting is inherently dynamic, since the per-
unit-time carbon cost of hardware changes as the hardware ages and its embodied carbon is depreciated. This 
dynamism requires infrastructure systems that can track and respond to changing carbon profiles over time, 
rather than treating carbon as a static attribute. 
 
— B. Deployment Considerations

A phased rollout is essential given the cultural and technical changes required: pilot deployment on a single 
cluster or application; validation of carbon reduction and performance impact; refinement of carbon models 
and scheduling policies; scaling to additional clusters and applications; and continuous optimization based on 
operational feedback. 
 
— C. Limitations 
●Data Availability: embodied carbon data for hardware is often proprietary and may not be readily available 
from cloud providers. Organizations may need to rely on estimates or industry averages. 
●Measurement Complexity: accurate measurement of embodied carbon requires lifecycle assessment expertise 
and data that may not be available for all hardware components. 
●Performance Trade-offs: carbon-optimized scheduling may place workloads on older hardware with lower 
performance, potentially affecting application performance. 
●Organizational Resistance: shifting from performance-first to multi-objective optimization may encounter 
resistance from teams accustomed to traditional optimization criteria. 
●Regulatory Uncertainty: carbon accounting standards and regulations are evolving, creating uncertainty 
about reporting requirements and methodologies. 
 
— D. Future Work 
●AI-Enhanced Carbon Forecasting: developing machine learning models to forecast carbon intensity and 
embodied carbon impacts, enabling more accurate carbon-aware decisions. 
●Multi-Cloud Embodied Carbon Optimization: extending the framework to optimize embodied carbon across 
multiple cloud providers, accounting for differences in hardware efficiency and carbon intensity. 
●Circular Economy Integration: integrating circular economy principles into infrastructure engineering, 
including hardware remanufacturing, component reuse, and responsible disposal. 
●Carbon-Aware Serverless: extending lifecycle-aware approaches to serverless computing, where the 
abstraction of hardware makes embodied carbon accounting more challenging. 
●Organizational Change Management: developing frameworks for organizational transformation toward 
lifecycle-aware infrastructure engineering. 
 
7. CONCLUSION 
This paper has presented a lifecycle-aware framework for cloud-native infrastructure engineering that treats 
embodied carbon as a first-class constraint alongside performance, cost, and reliability. The framework 
integrates carbon depreciation models, lifecycle-aware IaC analysis, heterogeneous compute scheduling, and 
carbon-aware CI/CD integration to address the growing importance of embodied carbon in cloud carbon 
footprints. 
Empirical evidence demonstrates the significant potential of this approach. Carbon depreciation models 
achieve carbon reductions of 28–57% depending on server lifetime assumptions. GreenSKU-style hardware 
reuse strategies reduce net cloud emissions by 8% in production environments. Carbon-aware Kubernetes 
scheduling reduces emissions by up to 33%. Carbon-aware CI/CD integration reduces carbon emissions by 23–
31% with zero increase in deployment latency and high developer acceptance. 
The shift to lifecycle-aware infrastructure engineering requires fundamental changes in how cloud-native 
systems are designed and operated. It challenges assumptions of hardware homogeneity, performance-first 
optimization, and static carbon accounting. It requires new tools, new metrics, and new organizational 
capabilities. But the evidence is clear: embodied carbon is no longer an externality that can be ignored. It is a 
first-class constraint that must be engineered for, alongside performance, cost, and reliability. 
As cloud computing continues to grow and renewable energy adoption accelerates, the relative importance of 
embodied carbon will only increase. Organizations that treat embodied carbon as a first-class concern will be 
better positioned to achieve sustainability goals while maintaining performance and cost efficiency. The 
framework presented in this paper provides a roadmap for this transformation. 
Future work will focus on AI-enhanced carbon forecasting, multi-cloud embodied carbon optimization, circular 
economy integration, and organizational change management. The source code and models will be made 
available under open-source license to enable reproducible research and practical adoption.

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026
