963 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
Sustainable Cloud Computing Through Hardware Lifecycle Optimization 
 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu 
Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani, India 
 
Received: 28.01.2026 
Revised: 02.02.2026 
 
Abstract 
The fast growth of the cloud computing infrastructure has increased the concern of the environment in 
terms of energy consumption, carbon emissions, and electronic waste production in the global data 
centres' operations. A strategic model to reduce these intersecting issues is to use hardware lifecycle 
optimization to increase the useful life of the server equipment by intelligently placing workloads, 
predicting failures, and actively reusing the equipment through reuse programs. Instead of conforming to 
aggressive refresh cycles that focus on the performance gain at the expense of abandoning functionality- 
based infrastructure, lifecycle-sensitive strategies align the workload needs with the hardware capabilities 
of heterogeneous populations of equipment of different ages and performance attributes. Container 
orchestration systems and advanced resource management systems make it practical to implement 
workload-aware deployment to place less important applications on optimized legacy infrastructure, and 
leave current-generation equipment to use cases with high performance requirements. Sustainability 
deliverables that can be put into place with the use of full lifecycle management include lower carbon 
emissions that would be caused by manufacturing avoidance, lower volumes of electronic waste, and 
better resource conservation, which will result in significant changes to the environment. Economic 
incentives such as lower procurement costs, better utilization of assets, and increased resilience in the 
supply chain co-locate the financial incentives with the environmental ones and make hardware lifecycle 
optimization both an ecological necessity and a commercially viable operational approach taken by cloud 
providers dedicated to responsible management of infrastructure. This work focuses on architectural and 
operational mechanisms rather than empirical quantification, aiming to establish a systems-level 
framework for lifecycle-driven sustainability in cloud infrastructure. 
 
Keywords: Hardware Lifecycle Optimization, Sustainable Cloud Computing, Electronic Waste 
Reduction, Workload-Aware Deployment, Data Centre Energy Efficiency. 
1. Introduction 
The unparalleled proliferation of cloud computing infrastructure has resulted in serious environmental 
issues that require a strategic intervention by the technology providers, policymakers, and enterprise 
stakeholders in the entire global digital ecosystem. The energy consumption of data centres and data 
transmission networks has become a significant source of electricity in the global market, and the size of 
its demand is increasing along with the further digitalization of the economy, the growth of the use of 
artificial intelligence solutions, and the development of cloud services across all industries [1]. The 
International Energy Agency (IEA) notes that even though energy efficiency in data centres has become 
significantly more efficient due to technological advancement and optimization of operations, the total 
electricity consumption of data centres has been on the increase, with the digital services demand 
surpassing the efficiency in data centres [1]. This continuing incremental trend highlights the 

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026 
10.48047/jocaaa.2026.35.01.77 
964 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
insufficiency of efficiency gains in dealing with the environmental ramifications of cloud infrastructure 
proliferation. 
Simultaneously with the growing energy requirements, the short hardware lifecycle cycles defining 
hyperscale cloud computing add to the electronic waste problem on the planet, which has emerged as one 
of the fastest-growing waste streams globally by the Global E-waste Monitor [2]. Premature retirement of 
functional server equipment leads to loss of the embedded resources,such as precious metals, important 
raw materials, and the energy that was consumed during the manufacturing processes [2]. Hardware 
lifecycle optimization models can be used to tackle these interrelated issues by extending the useful life of 
infrastructure by intelligently placing workloads, using systematic reuse programs, and implementing 
predictive maintenance plans. The article discusses the environmental forces that demand sustainable 
cloud practices, assesses lifecycle-conscious approaches towards hardware utility extension, and evaluates 
the multidimensional results that could be obtained through an extensive application of such solutions in 
the context of cloud computing. 
 
2. Environmental Impact of Hyperscale Cloud Infrastructure 
The ecological footprint of hyperscale cloud services involves a variety of facets. These extend far 
beyond the amount of pure power that often occupies the sustainability debate in the technological 
industry. Data centres are important nodes of world energy systems. They require electricity continuously 
to run computers and to ensure relevant thermal conditions. Additionally, they power ancillary systems 
such as lighting, security, and administrative systems. According to the comprehensive analysis by the 
International Energy Agency, data centres and data transmission networks already represent a significant 
portion of global electricity demand [3]. This demand will grow as digital transformation gains 
momentum in economies and societies worldwide. Patterns of electricity usage by data centres are 
characterized by specific properties. These include high capacity factors resulting from 24x7 operation. 
Concentrated loads may also overstretch local grid infrastructure in areas with major facility clusters. 
The sources of electricity used in data centres have a major impact on carbon footprint. Facilities powered 
by renewable electricity achieve largely reduced carbon lifecycles compared to those relying on fossil fuel 
production. According to the International Energy Agency, renewable electricity deployment has been 
rising at a higher rate in recent years [3]. However, most data centre facilities remain connected to grids 
with high carbon content. This means electricity consumption is directly translated into greenhouse gas 
emissions. Such emissions contribute to climate change. Geographic differences in grid carbon intensity 
introduce environmental impact variations between facilities in different regions. This occurs even when 
facilities have identical equipment setups and operating procedures. These variations are especially 
significant for location choices and power acquisition strategies affecting sustainability outcomes. 
The electronic waste trade around the world poses intricate environmental and social issues. This trade 
has arisen due to technology infrastructure activities. Many studies have investigated these transboundary 
waste streams. Research on e-waste trade networks has shown complex patterns in material transfer 
between nations [4]. Developing countries frequently receive large amounts of surplus equipment from 
the industrialized world. This occurs despite international accords aimed at controlling such flows. The 
dynamics of global e-waste trade reveal concerning patterns. Informal recycling activities in recipient 
nations often lack sufficient environmental regulations. Safety measures to prevent pollution and 
occupational health risks are inadequate [4]. These risks disproportionately affect vulnerable groups. 
Cloud infrastructure operators have an obligation to ensure their equipment scrap processing does not 

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026 
10.48047/jocaaa.2026.35.01.77 
965 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
contribute to these deleterious trade flows. This requires attentively choosing recycling vendors. It also 
means verifying adequate handling throughout the entire disposition chain. 
Cooling systems represent a major aspect of data centre environmental impact. They consume substantial 
electricity and necessitate water resources in many facility designs. This is particularly true for designs 
using evaporative cooling technologies. Dense computing hardware has demanding thermal 
characteristics. These require uninterrupted cooling processes. Cooling can account for significant 
portions of overall facility power consumption [3]. This remains true despite persistently increasing 
cooling efficiency. Novel strategies such as liquid cooling and free-air economization have been 
introduced. Data centre cooling has received growing attention due to water consumption concerns. This 
is especially relevant in water-stressed areas. Cloud facilities in these regions compete with agricultural, 
industrial, and municipal users for scarce water resources. The total water impact of global data centre 
operations constitutes a significant freshwater withdrawal. Sustainable operators must tackle this through 
efficiency enhancement and alternative cooling methods. 
 
Fig 1: Environmental Impact of Hyperscale Cloud Infrastructure [3, 4] 
 
The inherent environmental expenditures of server hardware are substantial. These include energy, water, 
chemicals, and materials used in manufacturing processes. These processes transform raw materials into 
advanced computing hardware. Semiconductor fabrication is particularly resource-consuming. It requires 
ultrapure inputs and produces different waste streams. This occurs despite being only one part of the 
entire server manufacturing system. The embodied environmental investment in every server unit 
represents a sunk cost. This cost is essentially forfeited by pre-empting equipment retirement. Hardware 
lifespan extension is becoming an even more critical sustainability measure [4]. The relative weight of 
embodied contribution to operational impacts increases with grid decarbonization. Traditional hardware 
refresh models focus on promoting hardware performance. They do not properly consider the 
environmental impacts of accelerated hardware replenishment. This lifecycle approach to hardware 
refresh directly challenges such traditional models. 

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026 
10.48047/jocaaa.2026.35.01.77 
966 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
3. Extending Hardware Life Through Lifecycle-Aware Strategies 
The concept of lifecycle-conscious hardware utilization represents a radical shift from traditional 
approaches. Old cloud infrastructure management frameworks focused on fleet homogeneity and 
aggressive hardware refurbishment schedules. These were chiefly influenced by performance factors. 
Studies on data centre energy efficiency indicate that historical growth trends, albeit significant, have 
been moderated by optimization strategies [6]. The International Energy Agency's critical review of data 
centre energy models highlights that efficiency gains have somewhat countered mounting workload 
volumes. The result of this efficiency curve is a platform for expanding hardware useful life. Operational 
upgrades can improve effectiveness without necessitating equipment replacement. This consequently 
decreases procurement amounts needed to meet increasing service demands. Importantly, it preserves the 
resources embodied in operational infrastructure. 
In evaluating data centre electricity consumption patterns, various factors impact energy use [6]. These 
include improvement of equipment efficiency, innovations in facility design, and workload management 
practices. Together, these factors determine how well infrastructure converts electricity consumption to 
useful computing output. The IEA review emphasizes that understanding consumption models enables 
better decision-making. By recognizing such dynamics, cloud service providers can identify optimal 
intervention timing. They can make targeted investments to increase hardware usefulness. This involves 
enhancing current system performance as opposed to wholesale replacement. Optimization of operations, 
firmware updates, and configuration improvements can enhance deployed equipment performance. These 
measures can ensure competitive capability over longer durations than planned refresh cycles. This is 
achieved without the environmental impact associated with manufacturing new hardware. 
Research on data centre energy optimization has established foundational strategies for improving 
efficiency in shared infrastructure settings. Ahmed's study on optimization strategies for data centre 
energy efficiency identifies multiple approaches for reducing power consumption [5]. These include 
virtualization techniques, workload consolidation, and intelligent resource allocation. Cloud service 
providers can implement these strategies to make informed decisions about energy costs of workload 
placement choices. This visibility into power consumption supports optimization strategies. These 
strategies consider energy efficiency metrics such as Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), Carbon Usage 
Effectiveness (CUE), and watts-per-compute-unit ratios, as well as traditional performance metrics such 
as throughput, latency, transactions per second, and resource utilization rates. Such approaches may 
extend hardware life further. Existing equipment can be optimized to run efficiently rather than being 
replaced. Inefficiencies that could be addressed through better management no longer necessitate 
equipment replacement. 
Optimization strategies developed for modern data centres provide complex approaches for matching 
workloads to appropriate hardware. These strategies consider energy efficiency features alongside 
performance demands. Research demonstrates that power usage can be optimized through various 
techniques including dynamic voltage scaling, server consolidation, and thermal management [5]. This 
enables cloud service providers to reduce energy demand across various workload-to-hardware 
assignments. They can choose configurations that minimize power usage without violating performance 
constraints. These features allow lifecycle extension. Cloud service providers can extract maximum value 
from available hardware through better utilization. Performance improvements need not rely solely on 
equipment upgrades. 
Maintenance and replacement techniques can be applied at the component level. This enables systems to 
achieve longer lifespans by accounting for individual component degradation. Server systems comprise 

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026 
10.48047/jocaaa.2026.35.01.77 
967 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
various components. These include processors, memory modules, storage devices, and power supplies. 
Each component exhibits different failure modes and deterioration characteristics over time. Failed or 
worn components can be selectively replaced [6]. This maintains functionality of remaining hardware that 
still satisfies operational needs. Overall system lifespan increases while material usage remains minimal. 
This maintenance method contrasts with wholesale system replacement. Traditional replacement methods 
dispose of large amounts of functional hardware alongside truly outdated or failed components. 
Firmware and software optimizations are perhaps the most appealing lifecycle extension techniques. They 
expand hardware capabilities without requiring physical modifications. No additional materials are 
consumed. These optimizations align with broader data centre efficiency strategies identified in current 
research [5]. Updates can increase security posture and improve power consumption characteristics. 
Instruction execution efficiency also improves. Similarly, operating system improvements, hypervisor 
updates, and workload runtime optimizations benefit cloud service providers. Administrators can retrieve 
better performance from current equipment through software changes alone. These improvement 
mechanisms can meaningfully extend hardware life through continuous development. Deployed hardware 
evolves beyond its initial deployment state through ongoing enhancements. 
 
Fig 2: Extending Hardware Life Through Lifecycle-Aware Strategies [5, 6] 
 
Secondary markets for server equipment offer economic means of broadening equipment usefulness. 
They provide ways to match equipment with subsequent uses beyond initial deployment settings. 
Organizations with stringent performance demands may find their equipment no longer meets their needs. 
However, this equipment can retain significant value for users with different requirement profiles. 
Certification and warranty provisions for refurbished equipment help address buyer reliability concerns 
[6]. They also motivate equipment maintenance that preserves resale value. Such market mechanisms 
keep functional hardware in productive use. Equipment avoids entering waste streams prematurely. 
Financial gains from remarketing equipment partially offset original procurement costs. 

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026 
10.48047/jocaaa.2026.35.01.77 
968 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
4. Workload-Aware Deployment and Resource Matching 
Workload-sensitive workload deployment strategies put into practice lifecycle optimization concepts and 
principles by systematically aligning the needs of the applications with the capabilities of the 
infrastructure of heterogeneous populations of hardware, consisting of different ages and performance 
properties. The studies conducted by Google in managing large-scale clusters have shown that complex 
resource management systems can enhance efficiency by a large margin, by placing workloads across the 
available infrastructure, in comparison to the use of simple allocation methods [7]. The cluster 
management problems explored in this study can also be applied to the lifecycle optimization scenarios in 
which heterogeneous hardware generations can have different capability profiles that need to be aligned 
to the different workload demands in order to realize the best total fleet value. 
The resource management systems that have been produced in large-scale computing environments can 
be used to offer an architectural pattern that can be used in the operation of lifecycle-conscious 
infrastructure. Studies that consider cluster management at scale indicate that the workload placement 
choice has a strong effect on resource utilization efficiency, whereby the ineffective workload placement 
choice leads to stranded capacity despite aggregate demand exceeding the available resources [7]. Such 
results encourage the investment in advanced scheduling to one that is able to take into account several 
placement aspects such as hardware generation, component age, energy efficiency nature, and workload 
performance needs. Optimal placement when there is heterogeneity in the hardware is far more complex, 
and a combination of an algorithmic method is needed that is capable of searching large solution spaces to 
determine placements that meet the multidimensional constraints. 
Container orchestration platforms have become the key to the realization of workload-aware deployment 
strategies in modern cloud environments. As part of the information regarding sustainable software 
engineering in Azure Kubernetes Service, it is stated that the distribution of containerized workloads can 
be effectively spread across the infrastructure available and meet the needs of resource limitations and 
optimization goals [8]. Container orchestration offers the abstraction of application deployment to core 
hardware dependencies, which means that complex place policy can be used to locate workloads to the 
relevant infrastructure, based on current conditions and needs. The flexibility enables lifecycle 
optimization as it enables older hardware to support the relevant workload without the need to modify 
applications and/or change deployment. 
The principles of sustainable software engineering that are formulated in the context of cloud-native 
applications introduce models that are to be used when assessing the environmental impact in addition to 
the traditional performance and cost measures during application development and deployment cycles. 
According to the documentation by Microsoft, application design that is conscious of sustainability views 
resource efficiency, proper scaling, and the use of infrastructure as its major concerns and not as 
supplementary ones [8]. Applications designed in these principles possess properties that are friendly to 
lifecycle-optimized deployments, such as resource-efficient usage, graceful performance under limited 
conditions, and infrastructure heterogeneity tolerance. These design styles allow applications that can be 
run on older hardware when they are suitable without compromising the quality of service. 
Performance sensitivity characterization is the ability to make fine workloads to hardware correspondence 
that extends beyond capability correspondence to application tolerance of performance variations. 
Different applications have different sensitivities to infrastructure-related attributes such as processing 
speed, memory latency, storage throughput, and network bandwidth. High-performance sensitive 
applications need high-quality infrastructure to sustain an acceptable level of service, whereas the less 
sensitive ones can be put into old hardware that provides satisfactory but not optimal performance [7]. 

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026 
10.48047/jocaaa.2026.35.01.77 
969 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
Illustrated systematization of workload performance sensitivity establishes the information base of smart 
placement of workloads that allocate high-performance hardware to the truly demanding use cases and 
place the tolerant workloads on the right legacy infrastructure. 
Quality of service frameworks formulate a mechanism of varying workload treatment according to the 
proclaimed requirements and the service level promises made. Workloads that run under lax quality of 
service commitments can afford to run on older hardware with smoothly degraded performance 
properties, whereas those that have strict guarantees have preferred access to high-quality infrastructure 
[8]. These models allow cloud providers to provide specific levels of service using specific hardware 
generations and develop pricing mechanisms that persuade customers to optimally describe what they 
need instead of falling back on the high-end. The distribution of demand among hardware generations 
guarantees the fact that the older equipment can still be used in productive applications, and it will 
become an income-generating investment that will not be deemed unprofitable to keep going. 
 
Fig 3: Workload-Aware Deployment and Resource Matching [7, 8] 
 
The economic impact of workload-sensitive deployment is not solely about direct hardware savings and 
can also include the energy-saving benefits that can be achieved by means of optimal positioning. Studies 
have shown that the nature of workloads greatly determines the pattern of energy consumption, with a 
particular workload consuming more or less energy on a given hardware setup compared to others [7]. 
Placement algorithms that exploit energy efficiency and performance requirements can minimize the total 
infrastructure energy usage through allocating workloads to hardware on which they can run optimally. 
These energy savings augment the environmental advantages of lifecycle extension by decreasing the 
operational impact, as well as the reduction in the impact of embodied impact through the service life of 
hardware. 
 
5. Sustainability, Economic, and Societal Outcomes 

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026 
10.48047/jocaaa.2026.35.01.77 
970 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
The performance indicators achievable through comprehensive hardware lifecycle optimization are 
substantial. These include carbon emission reductions, decreased electronic waste, and resource 
optimization. Together, these factors create significant environmental impact when implemented at the 
grand scale of global cloud infrastructure. Environmental reporting demonstrates organizational 
commitment to mitigating the environmental footprint of cloud operations [9]. This is achieved through 
multiple approaches such as purchasing renewable energy, improving operational efficiency, and 
addressing hardware lifecycle management. Environmental transparency through complete sustainability 
reporting enables stakeholders to assess provider performance. It also establishes accountability systems 
ensuring continuous improvement in environmental outcomes. 
Carbon reduction policies recorded in major provider environmental reports address two emission 
categories. These include operational emissions related to electricity use and embodied emissions 
embedded within infrastructure hardware and facilities. Google's environmental programs exemplify this 
comprehensive approach [9]. The company ensures that electricity consumption is matched with 
equivalent carbon-free energy sources. This effectively neutralizes the climate impact of operational 
energy consumption. Extended hardware lifespans provide additional embodied carbon coverage. 
Responsible material sourcing and proper end-of-life management compensate for high carbon emissions 
in manufacturing. These emissions would otherwise be wasted through premature equipment disposal. 
Such comprehensive models considering both operational and embodied effects demonstrate advanced 
understanding of digital infrastructure's complete carbon footprint. 
Circular economy principles offer conceptual frameworks for redesigning cloud infrastructure. These 
frameworks envision circulating material flows rather than linear sequences from production to disposal. 
The focus on maintaining materials in productive states for extended periods aligns directly with lifecycle 
optimization goals [9]. Maximum value should be extracted from hardware before end-of-life processing. 
Implementing circular approaches requires specific organizational capabilities. These include equipment 
refurbishment programs and component recovery systems. Partnerships with certified recyclers capable of 
extracting full material value from retired equipment are essential. These functions transform end-of-life 
processing from waste generation to value recovery. Embedded resources are reabsorbed into productive 
processes. 
Electronic waste management by cloud service providers has substantial environmental and social 
consequences. This results from the concentrated volumes of equipment flowing through retirement 
processes. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) highlights that effective electronics 
recycling prevents dangerous substances from entering the environment [10]. These substances include 
lead, mercury, and flame retardants. Proper recycling also enables reuse of valuable materials in new 
products. Cloud service providers handling high volumes of server equipment can develop exemplary 
recycling programs. These programs maximize material recovery while ensuring proper treatment of 
hazardous elements. Such initiatives establish industry standards that influence broader e-waste 
management practices. 
Donation programs provide additional avenues for extending hardware utility beyond commercial 
deployment. Working equipment can be transferred to educational institutions, nonprofits, and other 
recipients. These organizations may derive continued value from systems no longer meeting commercial 
requirements. According to the EPA, donating used electronics to schools and other institutions extends 
product lifecycle [10]. It also provides technology access to underserved communities. Cloud service 
providers can design equipment retirement programs that identify donation opportunities before directing 

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026 
10.48047/jocaaa.2026.35.01.77 
971 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
equipment to recycling. This approach maximizes overall utility from hardware investments. It also 
supports technology access goals aligned with broader corporate social responsibility commitments. 
Lifecycle optimization delivers significant economic benefits. These include direct cost savings from 
decreased procurement needs, improved asset utilization, and extended depreciation periods. Financial 
returns on infrastructure investments improve substantially. Large capital investments in hyperscale 
infrastructure create significant pressure to maximize long-term asset productivity [9]. This contrasts with 
short-term approaches emphasizing high replacement frequency and accelerated capital consumption. 
Lifecycle optimization investments that extend average equipment service life generate measurable 
returns. These returns manifest as avoided procurement costs and enhanced capital efficiency. Benefits 
compound across large equipment populations. These financial advantages provide strong business 
justifications for sustainability investments. Such justifications exist independent of environmental 
motivations. 
 
Fig 4: Sustainability, Economic, and Societal Outcomes [9, 10] 
 
Social consequences of sustainable cloud infrastructure management extend beyond environmental 
benefits. These include supply chain responsibility, labor policies, and community impacts throughout 
cloud operations' geographic footprint. Purchasing power concentration within large cloud service 
providers creates both opportunities and obligations [10]. These enable influence over upstream 
manufacturing processes through procurement specifications and supplier negotiations. Equipment 
disposition practices similarly affect downstream recycling operations and processing communities. 
Holistic lifecycle responsibility requires attention to these extended impacts alongside direct operational 
considerations. Cloud service providers serve as custodians of global technology value chains. Their 
influence extends well beyond immediate business territories. 
 
6. Future Directions and Industry Integration 
The sustainable cloud computing in the future will be more focused on the lifecycle optimization with the 
core infrastructure planning, procurement, and product design processes, instead of looking at 

Journal of Computational Analysis and Applications 
VOL. 35, NO. 1, 2026 
10.48047/jocaaa.2026.35.01.77 
972 
Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu et al 963-974 
 
 
sustainability as a specific project that may be dealt with as a different program. Existing best practices 
have shown that being responsible to the environment and being commercially viable can support each 
other instead of contradicting them, and that such precedents would probably affect the practice industry- 
wide, as values of responsibility grow more intense among customers, investors, and regulators. 
Implementing the lifecycle considerations in the strategic implementation of cloud operations would 
entail organizational modifications that cover procurement specification, operational processes, retirement 
processes, and measurement systems, collectively instill sustainability into the regular decision-making 
processes. 
New regulatory demands in various jurisdictions are an indicator that governments are paying attention to 
data centre environmental performance, which will probably force practices that are already voluntary in 
the industry to become best practices. Compliance requirements based on regulatory frameworks on data 
centre energy efficiency, carbon disclosure, and electronic waste management are directly supported by 
the lifecycle optimization capabilities. Companies that actively establish good sustainability capacities put 
themselves at a better position to abide with the changing demands and to evade possible discontinuities 
caused by regulatory shifts that trap the unprepared operators, who are forced to make changes to the 
normative practices. 
The technologies of artificial intelligence and machine learning can promise significant benefits of 
optimizing the lifecycle by improving the characterization of workloads, predictive maintenance, and the 
optimal allocation of resources. The research groundwork that has been developed so far on the 
management of clusters at scale is a place of departure in creating more advanced optimization systems 
that are able to take lifecycle considerations and the more conventional scheduling criteria. Automated 
systems that could make optimization choices in real time can react to the changing environment more 
quickly than process-driven approaches and may reach the same efficiency level that cannot be attained in 
manually-managed systems, and also keep up with the changing workload due to the capacity to adapt to 
changing workload patterns and infrastructure states. 
When the industry works together on the sustainability standards and standards of best practice, the 
lifecycle optimization approaches are more readily adopted, as the individual organizations have to put in 
fewer efforts to develop their effective programs. Core initiatives with regard to equipment certification 
standards, component interoperability requirements, and end-of-life processing specifications provide a 
common infrastructure that reduces barriers to entry and provides quality standards that could help assure 
the market of refurbished equipment and recycled materials. These forms of collaboration are especially 
useful in dealing with issues that cut across organizational borders, such as the development of secondary 
markets and investment in recycling infrastructure, involving the coordination of many stakeholders 
across technology value chains. 
The sustainability metrics of hardware lifecycle management can be measured and reported to make 
accountability and continuous improvement possible, and give transparency to stakeholders regarding 
organizational performance in terms of the environment. Standardized measurement procedures and 
reporting models can be used to achieve meaningful benchmarking and minimize compliance burden due 
to harmonized requirements that allow meaningful comparison across organizations and across time. The 
changing environment of the sustainability reporting demands poses incentives to the creation of effective 
measurement solutions capable of meeting various stakeholder informational demands, as well as 
assisting with the management and optimization processes on the internal level.

Conclusion 
Prior studies estimate that embodied emissions account for a substantial fraction of a server’s 
lifetime carbon footprint. Optimization of the lifecycle of hardware is a revolutionary business 
model of cloud computing that meets the eco-friendliness of cloud computing infrastructure and 
portrays an attractive financial rationale of cloud computing providers and business operators. The 
environmental case is based on conserving the embedded resources in the manufacturing of 
servers, minimizing the production of electronic waste, and minimizing the constant consumption 
of resources that is experienced in the traditional hardware replacement cycles. With the help of 
workload-sensitive deployment strategies, proactive maintenance programs, and organized 
equipment reuse programs, cloud operators can make meaningful extensions to the lifecycle of 
hardware, and this without reducing customer service quality in a wide range of applications. The 
economic case fits well into sustainability goals due to less capital expenditure on the acquisition 
of new equipment, better use of the current assets in the population of heterogeneous 
infrastructure, and greater capacity to endure disruption in the supply chain. In the future, the 
regulatory trend, investor demand, and customer needs will positively reward companies that show 
environmental leadership in terms of demonstrated hardware life cycle and reduced waste. Cloud 
platforms as accountable custodians of global infrastructure can play a competitive differentiation 
role and make a valuable contribution to climate change and resource constraint issues that impact 
all areas of the digital economy.

metadata.name: Embodied Carbon and Life Cycle Assessment of Data Centre Structures: A Review of Sustainable Construction Materials (United Kingdom Focus)

GD205.full_text:
ISSN 2522-9400             European Modern Studies Journal                     Vol 9 No 6 
available at www.journal-ems.com 
DOI: 10.59573/emsj.9(6).2025.15 
 
213 
European Modern Studies Journal, 2025, 9(6) 
Embodied Carbon and Life Cycle Assessment of Data Centre 
Structures: A Review of Sustainable Construction Materials (United 
Kingdom Focus) 
 
Paul Eloke  
School of Computing, Engineering & Digital Technologies,  
Teesside University, Middlesbrough, United Kingdom 
 
Abstract. The rising popularity of cloud computing and artificial intelligence is fuelling 
the fast expansion of data centres in the United Kingdom (UK), which is causing serious 
environmental problems due to the embodied carbon emissions caused by building them. 
Although grid decarbonization is reducing operating emissions, a significant portion of the 
sector's carbon footprint is now attributable to the embodied carbon emissions that are included 
in materials like steel and concrete. This study compiles the recent research on sustainable 
material options and design optimization tactics in the construction of data centres in the UK, 
with an emphasis on embodied carbon and life-cycle assessment (LCA) methods. It highlights 
the emission reduction potentials of recycled and hybrid steel systems, cross-laminated timber 
(CLT) structures, and low-carbon concrete variations (e.g., GGBS, LC³, and geopolymers), by 
evaluating these materials. In order to reach the UK Green Building Council's goal of a 50% 
reduction in embodied carbon by 2030, the research delves into circular economy strategies 
such as modular building, material reuse, and retrofitting. According to the results, precise 
LCA benchmarking is made more difficult by a lack of data openness, uneven approaches, and 
insufficient regulatory enforcement. To improve sustainability performance, accountability, 
and comparability in the UK data centre industry, the research suggests extended open-access 
databases, BIM-integrated life cycle assessment tools, and harmonised embodied carbon 
reporting systems. 
 
Keywords: Embodied Carbon, Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), Data Centres, Sustainable 
Materials, Circular Construction, Net Zero 
 
Introduction 
One pillar of the UK's digital economy is the country's rapidly expanding data centres, 
which, in the face of mounting climate imperatives, create serious environmental difficulties. 
The need for a solid data infrastructure has skyrocketed due to the growing dependence of both 
private companies and public agencies on cloud computing, AI, and big data analytics. 
Forecasts indicate that the UK data centre industry will increase from its 2025 valuation of 
around $15.23B at a CAGR (compound annual growth rate) of 13.31% to a 2030 valuation of 
$48.45B (Mordor Intelligence, 2025). The rise is most noticeable in London, where the number 
of megawatts (MW) expected to be taken up will reach 183 in 2025, up 58% from 2024 and 
double the amount in 2021, mostly due to the actions of hyperscale operators (CBRE, 2025). 
According to Cushman & Wakefield (2025), operational capacity in the EMEA area increased 
by 21% to 10.3 GW from mid-2024 to mid-2025, while the national capacity was at 1.6 GW 
in 2024. The material intensity of the industry is highlighted by this development (Arup, 
2025a). Building a single hyperscale plant might necessitate thousands of tonnes of steel, 
concrete, and cooling infrastructure, which in turn increases the strain on resource extraction 
and the supply chain.  
Data centres have extraordinary material and energy requirements beyond their size. In 
terms of global power consumption and CO₂ emissions, they make up more than 1%. UK-

 
 
 
 
                                                  European Modern Studies Journal                           journal-ems.com 
 
214 
European Modern Studies Journal, 2025, 9(6) 
specific forecasts suggest that AI-driven workloads might double energy usage by 2030 
(Carbon Brief, 2025; Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, 2025). Data centres in the 
UK used more than 10 billion litres of water per year for cooling, and they accounted for an 
estimated 2-3% of the country's electricity consumption in 2024, the same amount as several 
power stations' worth of production (Hall, 2025). The industry's use of carbon-intensive 
materials, such as virgin steel and Portland cement, increases emissions in the upstream phase 
of a facility's lifetime, which may account for as much as 20% of that total (UK Green Building 
Council, 2023). 
While digital services do allow efficiency benefits elsewhere, the physical infrastructure 
of these services runs the danger of undercutting larger sustainability goals, and this 
contradiction is brought to light by these dynamics, which put a pressure on grids. At the heart 
of this conflict is the fact that data centres' greenhouse gas (GHG) profiles differ in two key 
areas: embodied carbon and operational carbon. These two areas require separate approaches. 
Carbon emissions from energy usage during a building's lifetime, or operational emissions, 
have long dominated discussions about this topic. Conventional structures, which rely on 
electricity and cooling from fossil fuels, produce between 70 and 90% of all emissions (Roux 
et al., 2016). This is particularly noticeable in data centres: according to the European Data 
Centre Association (2023), a medium-sized UK facility may produce 50,000 to 100,000 metric 
tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO₂e) per year just from power usage, supposing a grid 
carbon intensity of 150 gCO₂/kWh. There is hope, nevertheless, that operating emissions from 
nuclear power plants might fall 80-90% and the UK's system could decarbonise to near-zero 
intensity by 2035 thanks to renewable energy (Climate Change Committee, 2025).  
Embodied carbon, on the other hand, is a rising percentage of lifecycle impacts and is 
"locked in" upfront. It includes emissions from material extraction, production, transportation, 
building, and decommissioning. Evidence from statistics supports this change. Worldwide, 
11% of emissions from energy-related sources are embedded carbon from building materials; 
when operations are included, the total amount of embodied carbon from buildings is 39% 
(World Economic Forum, 2024). Embodied emissions account for 20% of total sector 
greenhouse gas emissions in the UK built environment; however, with low-energy designs that 
reduce operating loads, this number rises to 50% or even more (UK Green Building Council, 
2023). Lifecycle assessments (LCAs) show that high-density steel frames and concrete 
foundations account for 30–50% of the total embodied energy in contemporary data centres 
(Birch et al., 2023). The embedded emissions for each 100 MW plant in Europe, according to 
research conducted in 2025, were anticipated to be 1-2 million tCO₂e. This is the same as 10-
20 years of operational output on the current grid (Ramboll, 2025). Airedale (2025) argues that 
embodied emissions are irreversible once materials are deployed, unlike operational carbon, 
which may be offset through efficiency and renewable. Therefore, it is vital to reduce emissions 
upfront if we are to take near-term climate action.  
The UK has set a legally enforceable goal of achieving net zero greenhouse gas emissions 
by 2050 under the Climate Change Act 2008 (as amended), which is in line with this objective 
and the country's ambitious climate framework. A 78% decrease in emissions from the built 
environment is required by 2035, according to the Seventh Carbon Budget (Climate Change 
Committee, 2025), which places a focus on whole-life carbon assessments that incorporate both 
the embodied and operational phases. In addition, the Infrastructure and Projects Authority 
(2022) notes that the Government Construction Playbook requires quantifiable carbon 
reduction pledges in procurement, such as embodied carbon standards for frameworks and 
materials. In line with the Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard, which limits embodied 
emissions for new non-domestic structures to 550 kgCO₂e/m² (Ministry of Housing, 
Communities and Local Government, 2024), it supports MMC and low-carbon alternatives like 
as recycled aggregates. These rules and sector-specific guidelines for data centres come 

 
 
 
 
                                                  European Modern Studies Journal                           journal-ems.com 
 
215 
European Modern Studies Journal, 2025, 9(6) 
together, for example, the UK Green Building Council's Whole Life Carbon Roadmap, which 
mandates a 50% reduction in embodied carbon by 2030 via material substitution and circular 
design (UK Green Building Council, 2023). Still, there are gaps in strong data and 
accountability, which are critical to making success.  
Despite these pledges, the industry is still struggling with a major issue: data centres in 
particular suffer from a lack of trustworthy embodied carbon data and standardised reporting 
standards. Embodied evaluations are not as consistent as operational measures, which are 
enhanced by standardised instruments such as the Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) index. 
Scope 3 embodied impacts make up to 90% of a project's upstream footprint, but they are 
largely ignored in the current UK construction reporting that is governed by the Streamlined 
Energy and Carbon Reporting (SECR) framework (Parliamentary Office of Science and 
Technology, 2022). Because of problems with proprietary Environmental Product Declarations 
(EPDs), uneven life cycle assessment (LCA) approaches, and disjointed supply chains, just 
25% of developers consistently estimate embodied carbon, according to a 2023 UKGBC study 
(UK Green Building Council, 2023). This lack of transparency is particularly noticeable in data 
centres, where large-scale construction projects frequently include several suppliers from 
different countries. Unfortunately, there is currently no mandated standard for reporting 
emissions from steel or concrete, which causes voluntary disclosures to be under-estimated by 
20-30% (World Economic Forum, 2022; Ofwat, 2024). Therefore, there is a lack of standards 
for reductions to be enforced by politicians and investors, which causes a delay in aligning with 
net zero trajectories and a perpetuation of reliance on high-carbon materials (AECOM, 2025).  
To fill these gaps, this study synthesises knowledge on life cycle assessment (LCA) and 
embodied carbon in sustainable building materials used in UK data centre constructions. Using 
quantitative life cycle assessment (LCA) comparisons, it seeks to develop approaches to half 
embodied emissions by 2030 while preserving structural robustness by evaluating low-carbon 
alternatives such cross-laminated lumber, geopolymer concrete, and recycled steel. Its goal is 
to help achieve the goals of the Seventh Carbon Budget and to guide procurement according to 
the Construction Playbook by filling up data gaps. Here is the breakdown of the review: 
Methods for embodied carbon measurement in data centres are detailed in Section 2, which 
also provides critiques of tools such as the ICE Database and the EN 15978 standards. Using 
case studies from the United Kingdom, Section 3 compares conventional and sustainable 
approaches in material-specific LCAs. Cost premiums and regulatory hurdles are some of the 
obstacles to adoption that are discussed in Section 4. Section 5 concludes with policy 
suggestions and a proposed unified reporting mechanism. Using this perspective, the analysis 
sheds light on the unrealised possibilities of eco-friendly materials and lays out a realistic plan 
to reduce carbon emissions from one of the UK's rapidly expanding infrastructures. 
 
The Role of Embodied Carbon in Data Centre Construction 
As operating emissions decrease due to grid decarbonisation, embodied carbon becomes 
an increasingly important factor in the environmental impact of data centre development. The 
transition to renewable energy sources increases the relative importance of upfront emissions 
in the United Kingdom, where data centre capacity is expected to grow by over 20% in the next 
five years to meet the demands of artificial intelligence and cloud computing (Institution of 
Engineering and Technology, 2025). According to GRESB (2025a), data centres were 
responsible for 1-3.5% of the world's greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in 2023. However, by 
2030, hyperscale facilities are expected to increase this number to 8%. A thorough lifecycle 
assessment (LCA) shows that operational and embodied carbon are clearly separated, which 
highlights the importance of focused mitigation during the building phase. According to Roux 
et al. (2016), operational carbon is the most common kind of emissions in energy-intensive 
buildings, making about 70-90% of the total. This carbon is obtained from the power consumed 

 
 
 
 
                                                  European Modern Studies Journal                           journal-ems.com 
 
216 
European Modern Studies Journal, 2025, 9(6) 
by servers, cooling systems, and auxiliary systems. This amounts to 2% to 3% of the UK's total 
electrical consumption in 2024, and it might double by 2030, when artificial intelligence 
workloads use an estimated 35% to 50% of data centre power (Carbon Brief, 2025). According 
to the European Data Centre Association (2023), a 100 MW facility may release 100,000-
150,000 tCO₂e per year just from running the facility's operations, based on a grid intensity of 
150 gCO₂e/kWh. Nevertheless, operational percentages might decrease to 20-30% of lifespan 
totals as the UK moves towards near-zero carbon energy by 2035, supplemented by offshore 
wind and nuclear power (Climate Change Committee, 2025).  
In contrast, in clean-energy scenarios, 50-80% of whole-life emissions are embodied 
carbon, which includes materials' extraction, production, transportation, building, 
maintenance, and end-of-life (EOL) (Opna, 2025). Due to the frequent hardware upgrades that 
occur every three to five years, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) systems can 
account for as much as 88% of the total lifespan carbon for data centres, making the problem 
even worse (Opna, 2025; Arup, 2025a). According to Schneider Electric (2023), scope 3 
emissions from supplier chains contribute significantly to this, making about 38-69% of overall 
footprints. The carbon footprint from server racks alone is comparable to that of the building's 
MEP carbon. It is estimated that a hyperscale UK facility may permanently lock in 1-2 million 
tCO₂e per 100 MW, which is comparable to 10–20 years of operating production at present 
(Ramboll, 2025). There is a serious risk that the sector's expansion may lead to emissions that 
are in conflict with the UK's Seventh Carbon Budget, which mandates a reduction of 78% in 
emissions from the built environment by 2035 (Climate Change Committee, 2025), due to this 
inversion where embodied emissions surpass operational emissions.  
Materials with high carbon content that are designed for load bearing, fire resistance, and 
quick deployment are commonly used in UK data centre constructions. In order to withstand 
heavy server loads and seismic activity, the majority of structural components, including slabs, 
walls, columns, and foundations, are made of concrete. This material can be either precast or 
cast-in-situ (GBC Engineers, 2025). Though they cut down on on-site time by 30–50%, precast 
concrete panels and hollow-core slabs emit 0.8–1.2 tCO₂e/m³ due to their cement content 
(Stantec, 2025). Reinforcing concrete and forming frames or trusses, steel is highly regarded 
for its ductility and its ability to span elevated floors and plenums (GBC Engineers, 2025), 
accounting for 5-15% of the total weight. Recycled steel reduces emissions from 1.8-2.5 
tCO₂e/t by 50-70% compared to virgin steel (UK Green Building Council, 2023). In order to 
minimise thermal bridging and achieve airtightness, the building envelope consists of concrete, 
insulation (such as mineral wool or foam), and steel cladding on the walls, roofs, and facades. 
This helps to keep cooling needs down, as seen by U-values below 0.15 W/m²K (Stantec, 
2025). According to Opna (2025), a typical 10,000 m² facility may have 20,000–30,000 m³ of 
concrete, 2,000–4,000 tonnes of steel, and 10-15% embodied carbon from envelope materials. 
The remaining 40–60% would come from MEP cabling and chillers. These materials put 
longevity ahead of sustainability, although being overly precise, such calling for very deep 
foundations, can increase material consumption by 20-30% (Stantec, 2025).  
There are potential for low-carbon shifts since there is a considerable variation in 
emissions compared to different types of building. Despite their lighter profiles and adaptability 
to modular expansions, steel-framed buildings are susceptible to supply chain volatility and 
produce 233-480 kgCO₂e/m² in embodied carbon (Steel Construction Institute, 2023). Systems 
mostly composed of concrete, such as precast panels or flat slabs, have fire ratings that are 
better but vary from 300 to 500 kgCO₂e/m³, driven by the clinker content of the cement (GBC 
Engineers, 2025). As shown in Microsoft's US tests, which reduced emissions 35-65% 
compared to baselines (Stantec, 2025), hybrid techniques combining steel-concrete composites 
with timber components reach 200-350 kgCO₂e/m². According to the Steel Construction 
Institute (2023), warehouses similar to edge data centres in the UK can benefit from glulam-

 
 
 
 
                                                  European Modern Studies Journal                           journal-ems.com 
 
217 
European Modern Studies Journal, 2025, 9(6) 
timber frames on concrete bases, which can reduce the cost of steel gateways by 20-40%. 
According to EN 15978 LCAs (not including MEP), they are summarised in Table 1 for non-
residential archetypes that may be used in data centres. 
 
 
Lifespan, structural redundancy, and material choice are important design levers that 
significantly impact embodied carbon. The norm for data centres in the UK is a 50-year design 
life, which means upfront emissions are amortised, but the materials used must be robust. 
Modular retrofits may prolong this life to 60 years, which decreases GWP by 17% per year (de 
Paula Filho et al., 2023). Oversized beams and foundations add more carbon to material 
demands, which are already 15-25% higher due to structural redundancy, although value 
engineering, such as reduced deflection standards, has saved 12-30% of steel on UK projects 
(Stantec, 2025). The most significant effect is achieved through the choice of materials; for 
example, using recycled steel reduces GWP by 42% and, depending on end-of-life strategies 
such as incineration rather than landfilling to prevent methane spikes, geopolymer concrete or 
cross-laminated timber (CLT) hybrids reduce it by 50-65% compared to Portland cement 
baselines (de Paula Filho et al., 2023; Opna, 2025). According to example studies conducted 
in Luxembourg that were similar to those in the UK, steel-concrete composites achieved <300 
kgCO₂e/m² objectives through efficient grids and recycling, outperforming concrete frames by 
32% (LETI, 2023). Implementing strategies like DfMA to achieve 20% material efficiency in 
data centres is in line with the low-carbon requirements outlined in the Construction Playbook, 
which supports the development of net-zero routes (Infrastructure and Projects Authority, 
2022). 
 
Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) Methodologies and Standards 
Over the course of a data centre’s full existence, from the extraction of raw materials to 
their eventual disposal, life-cycle assessment (LCA) offers a methodical framework for 
analysing the environmental implications. The concepts of life cycle assessment (LCA) are

These figures exclude operational phases, highlighting upfront potentials: a shift to hybrids could 
halve emissions in new builds (UK Green Building Council, 2023). 

 
 
 
 
                                                  European Modern Studies Journal                           journal-ems.com 
 
218 
European Modern Studies Journal, 2025, 9(6) 
based on international standards and guarantee that impacts such as embodied carbon, resource 
depletion, and toxicity may be accurately and consistently measured (International 
Organisation for Standardisation, 2006a; 2006b). Defining objectives and scope, conducting a 
life-cycle inventory (LCI) analysis, conducting a life-cycle impact assessment (LCIA), and 
finally, interpreting the results are the four iterative steps highlighted in ISO 14040. To 
eliminate any room for confusion when allocating resources, these standards specify functional 
units (e.g., kgCO₂e/m² floor area for structures) and system boundaries, and ISO 14044 details 
the necessary criteria for the quality of inventory data and impact categories, including GWP 
through IPCC methodologies (International Organisation for Standardisation, 2006b). 
According to the British Standards Institution (2011), EN 15978 modifies these for use in 
building construction by incorporating product and assembly modular assessments. These 
assessments cover the product stage to construction (A1-C4) and the usage to end-of-life (B1-
D) phases. These allow for the identification of hotspots in data centres, such as the 
manufacture of high-emission steel, which in turn guides the selection of sustainable materials.  
To help achieve net-zero goals in the UK, LCA is in line with sector-specific 
recommendations. According to the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) Whole 
Life Carbon Assessment (WLCA) standard, 2nd edition (2024), reporting for non-domestic 
buildings, including data centres, must comply with EN 15978. This standard specifies 
thresholds for embodied carbon, such as <625 kgCO₂e/m³ (RICS, 2024). The focus is on future 
grid decarbonisation scenario modelling. Aiming for embodied carbon reductions of 50% 
through material passports and circularity, the London Energy Transformation Initiative 
(LETI) Climate Emergency Design Guide (2023) offers practical processes for early-stage 
LCA integration (London Energy Transformation Initiative, 2023). In addition, the 
Construction Playbook's procurement standards are harmonised with the 2030 objectives 
established by the UK Green Building Council's (UKGBC) Net Zero Whole Life Carbon 
Roadmap (updated 2025), which is 50% lower than 2019 baselines, among other things. This 
is achieved through phased evaluations. Hyperscale operators' ESG reporting and these 
standards' intersection encourage EPD-verified inputs for data centres.  
Processes that are considered inside an LCA system are defined by its limits, which 
affects how thorough and accurate it is. According to Circular Ecology (2025), 70-80% of the 
embodied effects in UK projects fall under the Cradle-to-gate (A1-A3) framework, which 
encompasses extraction, production, and transit to site. This framework is appropriate for 
material suppliers. On-site emissions, such as gasoline use, are captured by cradle-to-site, 
which extends to A4-A5 (building). Because data centres typically last 30–50 years and reuse 
accounts for 20–40% of their impacts, a cradle-to-grave approach covering the whole lifetime 
(A–D) is necessary (Ecochain, 2025a). This approach includes B6 (operational energy) and 
C/D (demolition/recycling). For modular parts like server racks, gate-to-gate's emphasis on 
separate operations is ideal. According to the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (2024), 
although WLCA compliance is best achieved via a cradle-to-grave approach, partial boundaries 
run the danger of underestimating the project by 15-25%.  
For effective LCA, practitioners in the UK use digital technologies in data centre 
projects. When it comes to quick iterations, 80% of RICS-assessed schemes utilise OneClick 
LCA, which offers cloud-based processes with 250,000+ validated datasets, BIM interface, and 
automatic GWP calculations complying with EN 15978 (One Click LCA, 2025a). Hyperscalers 
love eTool's scenario-based modelling for embodied/operational trade-offs because of its 
popular Australian-UK calibration (eTool, 2025). Even though it's primarily designed for usage 
in North America, Athena Impact Estimator may accommodate modifications in the United 
Kingdom by way of bespoke steel and concrete inventory (Athena Sustainable Materials 
Institute, 2025). Sixty percent of UK-based LCAs rely on free, country-specific embodied 
variables provided by the University of Bath's Inventory of Carbon and Energy (ICE) Database 

 
 
 
 
                                                  European Modern Studies Journal                           journal-ems.com 
 
219 
European Modern Studies Journal, 2025, 9(6) 
(e.g., 0.41 tCO₂e/t for recycled steel) (University of Bath, 2025). By using these technologies, 
the entire certification process may be streamlined, cutting evaluation time in half.  
Data openness and comparability continue to be difficulties, even though there have been 
advancements. Only 30% of UK vendors provide EPDs, which means that data is fragmented 
and leads to the usage of proxies, which increases uncertainty by 20% to 50% (UK Green 
Building Council, 2025). According to a review published in 2025 by Anyanya et al. (2025) in 
the Frontiers journal, GBRS, similar to BREEAM, differed 15-30% from WLCA due to 
methodological differences, such as allocation criteria or biogenic carbon credits. Global 
supply networks obfuscate Scope 3 granularity, and transparency difficulties, such as 
proprietary algorithms in solutions like OneClick, make the problem worse (Olanrewaju et al., 
2024). To tackle them, there has to be harmonised ontologies for AI-driven interoperability 
(One Click LCA, 2025b) and EPDs are obligatory under the Construction Products Regulation 
(2025). 
Figure 1: LCA Process Diagram Adapted for Structural Design Workflow 
 
This iterative diagram, adapted from ISO 14040, integrates structural workflows: e.g., 
BIM inputs at LCI for real-time optimisation in data centre design (Lamperti Tornaghi et al., 
2018). 
 
Sustainable Structural Materials and Carbon Reduction Strategies 
Data centres in the United Kingdom are expected to see a doubling of capacity by 2030, 
and the building phase accounts for 30-50% of lifetime emissions (Ramboll, 2025). As a result, 
the use of sustainable structural materials is crucial for reducing embodied carbon. Strategies 
are focused on material substitution, design efficiency, and novel technologies to attain 
standards of less than 300 kgCO₂e/m², in line with the UKGBC's goal of a 50% reduction by 
2030 (UK Green Building Council, 2025). Using life cycle assessments (LCAs), this part 
investigates prospective low-carbon substitutes for common building materials including 
concrete, steel, and wood, as well as new binders and optimisation methods.  
Alternatives to Portland cement clinker, which is responsible for 80-90% of the emissions 
from calcination in concrete, are used in low-carbon concrete mixes through the use of 
supplemental cementitious materials (SCMs) (Stantec, 2025). A steel by-product called ground 
granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS) may replace 50-70% of cement, reducing embodied 
carbon from 350-450 kgCO₂e/m³ to 150-250 kgCO₂e/m³ (IStructE, 2023). According to Arup 
(2025a), GGBS concretes have been used in the foundations of UK data centres, which has 
resulted in a 45% reduction in impacts while keeping compressive strengths over 40 MPa. Fly 

 
 
 
 
                                                  European Modern Studies Journal                           journal-ems.com

phase out due to coal reduction demands storage or imports (May and Abbaspour, 2024). The 
combination of calcined clay and limestone in limestone calcined clay cement (LC³) results in 
50% clinker reduction, 120-200 kgCO₂e/m³, and improved durability for seismic-resilient slabs 
(Al-Obaidy et al., 2022). By geopolymerizing industrial wastes such as slag or fly ash with 
alkaline activators, alkali-activated materials (AAMs) are able to completely remove clinker, 
resulting in 50-150 kgCO₂e/m³ a savings of up to 80%. However, there are challenges with 
scalability when it comes to procuring the activators (Almonayea et al., 2024). According to 
research on fly ash geopolymers, AAM pilots have reduced foundation emissions at hyperscale 
plants by 56% (Setiawan et al., 2023).  
To reduce its 1.8-2.5 tCO₂e/t impact during basic oxygen furnace (BOF) manufacturing, 
steel is undergoing advancements in recycling and lightweight designs (Steel Construction 
Institute, 2023). Mills in the United Kingdom, such as Liberty Steel, have achieved 0.5 tCO₂e/t 
with renewable energy, a 70% reduction in emissions compared to non-recycled steel produced 
using electric arc furnace (EAF) techniques that use 90-100% waste (UK Green Building 
Council, 2023). Modular expansions supported by EAF steel frames reduce material utilisation 
by 15-20% in data centres (GBC Engineers, 2025). For gateways, lightweight truss designs that 
use optimised profiles or hollow sections can further reduce quantities by 20-30%; for example, 
parametric models have been shown to produce 300-400 kgCO₂e/m² (Cundall, 2025). The use 
of steel in conjunction with concrete or timber in a hybrid frame improves efficiency; for 
example, a study by de Paula Filho et al. (2023) found that steel-concrete composites decreased 
beam depths by 25%, reduced embodied carbon to 250-350 kgCO₂e/m², and strengthened fire 
resistance.  
Hybrid technologies that use lumber and biogenic carbon sequestration have made cross-
laminated timber (CLT) a potential replacement for traditional wood in data centre modular 
construction. When forestry credits are taken into consideration, the upfront emissions of CLT 
panels made of laminated softwood—which store 0.5-1 tCO₂e/m³ net—are negative (Stantec, 
2025). As demonstrated in speedy assembly trial projects at UK edge facilities, CLT hybrids 
with concrete bases may reach CO₂e/m³ levels between 150 and 250 kg, which is 40 to 60% 
lower than steel counterparts (Arup, 2025a). According to the UK Green Building Council 
(2025), modular CLT pods allow for off-site prefabrication, which results in a 50% reduction 
in on-site emissions and makes disassembly easier for circularity. The use of charring layers or 
intumescent coatings can help reduce the impact of fire regulations and moisture sensitivity; 
insurers are also starting to approve buildings with up to eight stories (Steel Construction 
Institute, 2023). Deeper decarbonisation is promised by emerging technology. Infused with 
CO₂ as it cures, carbon capture concretes mineralise it into stable carbonates; CCUS varieties 
made by Heidelberg Materials sequester 10–20 kgCO₂e/m³, for a total of 100–200 kgCO₂e/m³ 
(Gensler, 2024). Geopolymer binders, which originate from AAMs, use metakaolin or rice 
husk ash to reduce carbon emissions by 70 to 90% in test projects (Hu et al., 2025). Although 
supply chain improvements are necessary for scalability, these allow for zero-clinker slabs in 
data centres (Meta, 2024).  
Integrating real-time simulation for carbon-minimal designs, structural optimisation is 
achieved through the use of digital twins and parametric life cycle assessment. Using AI-driven 
iterations, digital twins optimise grids to cut steel by 15-25% throughout facility lifespan 
modelling (Petri et al., 2025). By balancing spans and loads, parametric methods like as 
Cundall's scripts assess thousands of variations, resulting in a 20-30% reduction in embodied 
carbon (Cundall, 2025). These lead to savings of 10–40% in UK projects, which is in line with 
RICS WLCA (Springer, 2024).

Circular Construction and Reuse Opportunities 
The United Kingdom's data centres have a staggering 1-2 million tCO₂e per 100 MW 
facility, making them a prime candidate for embodied carbon reduction initiatives guided by 
circular building concepts. In accordance with the circular economy directives of the Seventh 
Carbon Budget, the industry may achieve upfront emission reduction of 30-50% by focussing 
on reuse, modularity, and retrofits (Climate Change Committee, 2025). Prefabrication and steel 
recycling are two methods that reduce waste and provide flexibility for AI-driven growth; 
recycling may redirect as much as 97% of emissions from virgin steel (Arup, 2025a). One 
example of a circular economy practice is the recycling of structural steel pieces via reusing

Stockmatcher. Practical examples prove feasibility: By using big hollow sections with >70%

Place, on the other hand, achieved embodied savings despite greater upfront costs thanks to its 
design-for-deconstruction (DfD) strategy, which allowed for demountable steel-concrete floors 
(Arup, 2025b). According to Arup (2025b), these technologies are suitable for data centres' 
load-bearing requirements, and the repurposing of steel from the 1960s at Euston Tower is an 
example of industrial reusing.  
Due to the ability to assemble and disassemble modules off-site, modular design and 
prefabrication greatly enhance reuse. According to Camp Hill's lifecycle study, which was cited 
by the World Economic Forum in 2025 and One Click LCA in the same year, factory-built 
modules minimise embodied carbon by 35-54% and site waste by 90%. Scalable pods with 
reversible connections, as per ISO 20887, provide 80% material recovery at end-of-life in data 
centres (Arup, 2025b). The KLON-03 facility at Kao Data's Harlow site is a prime example of 
this; it uses prefabricated low-carbon shells to deploy 17.6 MW quickly, and it uses hybrid 
cooling and 100% renewable power to achieve BREEAM excellence while reducing emissions 
from transportation (Kao Data, 2025). Especially in London Docklands, where existing 
warehouses are being renovated to accommodate the growing need for connection, the concept 
of circularity is being increasingly integrated into industrial structures. Reusing envelopes from 
converted 1980s office complexes reduces embodied carbon by 40% compared to demolition 
(Hyphen, 2025), for example, Hyphen's 6,000 m² data hall. Digital Realty's Cloud House and 
YRM's Telehouse West are two examples of iconic buildings in the Docklands that recycle 
steel and repurpose riverfront structures for river-dock cooling, thereby increasing the useful 
life of the assets involved (Digital Realty, 2024). Retrofitting the former Mercure Hotel in 
London, Elstree, Ark Data Centres has implemented modular steel structures, recycled 
materials to reduce waste, and liquid cooling to reach Tier III efficiency (Ark Data Centres, 
2025).  
The decision to rebuild a building or extend its life depends on lifecycle evaluations. A 
facility that is 30 years old can have its embodied emissions reduced by 20 to 40 percent by 
targeted retrofits, however high-refresh MEP systems require modular updates (J Dunton 
Associates, 2025; Arup, 2025a). According to Seagate's study, which shows a 30% net savings 
(Seagate Technology, 2025), extending low-carbon grids is more common than replacing 
outdated sites, which leads to over-specification. Hyperscalers in the United Kingdom can 
achieve their 2030 goals with the help of hybrids like Ark's phased Elstree expansions, which 
support a reuse marketplace while balancing resilience and decarbonisation. 
 
Comparative Case Studies 
The tactics of the United Kingdom, the European Union, and the United States in relation 
to data centre projects with publicly available embodied carbon data show that regional rules 
and market maturity are driving both different and convergent approaches. Through the 
implementation of whole-life carbon assessments (WLCA) during design and supplier 
collaborations for low-carbon alternatives such as recycled aggregates, Equinix's LD14 facility 
in London was able to reduce the embodied carbon of structural steel, concrete, and rebar by 
30% when compared to national benchmarks in the UK. Certified UK hyperscalers adhere to 
the requirements of BREEAM New Construction V7, which include publicly available data 
entry for exceptional credits and embodied carbon benchmarking. Using HYBRIT fossil-free 
steel, which is made by hydrogen reduction, the Västerås data centre in Sweden, which is part 
of the EU, was able to reduce emissions for steel by 90% (equivalent to one tenth of traditional

BF-BOF processes) and save 5,900 tCO₂e in total. Incorporating recycled steel and low-carbon 
concrete, the FRA3 facility in Frankfurt further demonstrates EU trends by reducing embodied 
effects without sacrificing hyperscale resilience, in accordance with the Level(s) framework. 
Hybrid cross-laminated timber (CLT) with steel and concrete was tested at Microsoft's Virginia 
data centres across the Atlantic. Embodied carbon was reduced by 35% compared to steel 
baselines and by 65% compared to precast concrete, thanks to the use of prefabrication to 
compensate for the material intensity.  
These results are greatly affected by the tactics employed in design and materials. A 
'avoid-reduce-innovate' triangle was made possible in Equinix LD14 by early WLCA hotspot 
identification; for example, repurposing buildings prevented new materials by 15-20% and 
geopolymer concrete cut cement emissions by 50%. By reducing the volume of trusses, AWS 
Västerås was able to cut in half the amount of carbon embodied in steel, which is usually 20-
30%, through value engineering. Microsoft's CLT hybrids improved adaptability for future 
retrofits and optimised spans using parametric modelling, replacing 40% of high-carbon 
concrete slabs. These interventions highlight the long-term effects of short-term choices, such 
as using 50% clinker in EU concretes, which result in savings after 30–50 years. According to 
Arup’s Net Zero Data Centre Design Guide (updated 2025), hybrids can save costs by 20–40%.  
Successful methods tend to follow certain patterns: (1) Recycled/EAF steel (with a 70% 
lower GWP) and biogenic wood are material-led substitutions that decrease emissions by 30-
65%. (2) Parametric LCA digital tools allow for iterative optimisation, as shown by Microsoft's 
15% steel savings. (3) Circularity through prefabrication and DfD protocols increases reuse 
rates to 60-80%, according to the EU's Built4People. Scope 3 disclosures are required for 
BREEAM certification, and projects with this certification routinely report embodied footprint 
reductions of 25–40%. All of these examples together are in favour of standardising reporting 
in order to reduce scale, with the goal of reaching <300 kgCO₂e/m² by 2030 in the midst of 
grid decarbonisation. 
 
Challenges, Data Gaps, and Policy Implications 
Multiple obstacles, such as methodological discrepancies, a lack of data, and disclosure 
hesitancy, make it difficult to achieve net zero in the UK while pursuing low-embodied carbon 
data centre architectures. These obstacles pose a threat of 1-2 million tCO₂e per hyperscale 
facility as the industry grows and is projected to use 8-10% of UK power by 2030. This would 
undermine the Seventh Carbon Budget's goal of reducing the built environment by 78% by 
2035, as stated by the Climate Change Committee in 2025. To tackle these, we need to evolve 
policies and integrate workflows so that we can use the latent mitigation potential of embodied 
carbon.  
The lack of baseline data and inconsistent approaches constitute a fundamental obstacle. 
Steel and concrete embodied carbon estimates differ by 20-50% due to differences in system 
boundaries (e.g., cradle-to-grave vs. cradle-to-gate) and allocation rules (e.g., cut-off versus 
economic) (Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, 2024). Despite EN 15978's harmonised 
framework, these issues persist. Because there are no industry-specific standards, MEP systems 
in data centres increase Scope 3 impacts: Because cooling infrastructure inventory data is not 
consistent, a 2025 LSBU assessment of UK facilities discovered that LCA findings differed by 
30% (Whitehead, 2025). Analysis of new constructions by AECOM revealed that 
methodological deficiencies lead to a 15-25% overestimate of material hotspots, demonstrating 
the difficulty structural engineers have in prioritising changes without strong standards 
(AECOM, 2025). This lack of transparency makes it harder to compare different options, which 
slows down research towards low-carbon hybrids.   
The fact that private data centre operators, mainly hyperscalers like Microsoft and AWS, 
who own 70% of the capacity in the UK, are not very forthcoming only adds insult to injury.
